World.title: Trump says Iran war ‘highly unlikely’ to resume
World.content:
File image of US President Donald Trump. Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP.

US President Donald Trump cast doubt on renewed fighting with Iran, telling CNN it was “highly unlikely,” ahead of a meeting with mediator Qatar’s prime minister on Monday.

Trump has threatened to resume strikes in recent weeks, with US media reports suggesting that hostilities could restart after last Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The president told CNN in an interview on Sunday that renewed fighting was “highly unlikely,” but warned that his decision “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement.”

“I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them,” he said.

Trump is scheduled to meet Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who is also the country’s foreign minister, at the White House on Monday.

The meeting will be Trump’s first with a foreign leader since a massive midterm loss that saw his Republican Party lose control of Congress.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi suggested on Sunday that peace talks had been paused while the political fallout of the vote was being assessed.

“For the past few days, there has been no more travel (by mediators), and the reason for this is the shock that the election results in the United States have caused to everyone,” Araghchi told state television.

“We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward,” he added.

– ‘They had enough’ –

Trump has acknowledged that the highly unpopular war with Iran — which began with US-Israeli strikes in late February — was at least partially responsible for the Republicans’ defeat.

Araghchi said Monday that the US president “clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel.”

“Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars,” Araghchi said on X. “They had enough. So has our region.”

In Sunday’s CNN interview, Trump once again suggested that the economic pressure Iran is under will force its leaders into accepting the United States’ terms.

“They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301 percent inflation,” Trump claimed. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.”

Iran’s official figures put inflation at nearly 90 percent year-on-year in September.

Iranian state television said the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz was attacked overnight Sunday, hours after the official IRNA news agency reported two explosions there.

Various regional powers, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been trying for months without success to bring a definitive halt to the war.

Outright fighting has largely subsided, but Iran continues in its efforts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global energy supplies, while the US Navy maintains its own counterblockade of Iranian ports.

World.title: Gospel singer Toluwanisings for burial today
World.content:
The burial of gospel singer Olayemi Bolaji, popularly known as Toluwanisings, is scheduled to hold on Monday in Ibadan, Oyo State, weeks after his death.

The funeral arrangements, released on the late singer’s official Instagram page on Monday, indicate that the lying-in-state will hold between 9am and 10am, while the burial service is scheduled for 10am to 11am.

The ceremony will take place at Banjola Event and Conference Centre, No. 20, Hope Road, Alakia, Ibadan.

The funeral announcement, which bears the inscription, “Forever in our Hearts, always in our Lives,” did not disclose the location of his interment.

The singer’s family had announced his death in the early hours of October 14, 2026.

World.title: Who is Alice Huang, Chinese exec accused of spying on Nvidia CEO?
World.content:
This screengrab from video footage by CTI obtained via AFPTV on November 9, 2026 shows Alice Huang (2nd R in pink), a Chinese executive linked to the data centre company called Megaspeed, attending a dinner hosted by Nvidia’s chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang (2nd L in black back facing camera) at a restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025, during Computex, the island’s top tech expo. Chip giant Nvidia’s board announced on November 8, 2026 it opened a probe into Huang after he acknowledged an affair with a woman US officials say was working for Chinese intelligence. The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen Huang — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said. (Photo by various sources / AFP) / – Taiwan OUT / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE – MANDATORY CREDIT “AFP PHOTO / CTI via AFPTV- NO MARKETING NO ADVERTISING CAMPAIGNS – DISTRIBUTED AS A SERVICE TO CLIENTS

Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports.

Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International.

Here is what we know about her and the company:

– Who is Alice Huang? –

Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to the New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot.

Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born head of the world’s most valuable company.

The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry.

The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications.

An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile, or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited.

– How are the pair connected? –

Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Sunday he was “deeply sorry” for being “unfaithful to my wife”.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang.

The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees.

At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press livestreams show.

Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back.

They later leave the restaurant in the same car.

– What is Megaspeed? –

US officials concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal.

At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI.

Megaspeed’s website says it is “a core business partner of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region”.

On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 “associated members”.

When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed’s website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line.

The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore government’s website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road.

– Has Megaspeed helped China evade US restrictions on chips? –

Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI.

The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China.

The company has also reportedly been under investigation by Singapore authorities, who the Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025.

AFP has contacted Singapore’s police and the home affairs ministry for comment.

Last year Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg’s reporting “contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers”.

World.title: Gunmen kill security operative, three others in Plateau attack
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa, Jos

Gunmen have killed three residents and a security operative during an attack on Bel village in Sho community, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State, while several other persons sustained injuries.

The attack reportedly occurred at about 9 p.m. on Sunday when the gunmen stormed the community and opened fire on residents.

A resident of the community, Mr Bulus Bot, who confirmed the incident, said the attackers invaded the village at night and shot indiscriminately at innocent citizens.

“The gunmen stormed the community at about 9 p.m. and opened fire on innocent citizens, leaving some people dead and others injured,” he said.

Bot described the incident as a disturbing attack on the community, noting that residents were caught up in the violence when the gunmen opened fire.

He said some persons sustained injuries during the attack, adding to the concern among residents over the safety of people in the area.

The Publicity Secretary of Berom Youth Moulders Association, Rwang Tengwong, also confirmed the killings and identified three of the victims as Emmanuel Pam Dachung, 15; Joseph Gyang, 28; and Emmanuel Yohanna, 32.

He alleged that a soldier was also among those killed in the attack, bringing the reported death toll to four.

Tengwong condemned the attack, describing the killing of innocent residents as unacceptable, and called on security operatives to track down those responsible.

He urged security agencies to ensure that the perpetrators were identified and brought to justice, stressing the need for decisive action to prevent further attacks on communities in the area.

Efforts to get a reaction from security operatives on the attack were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: 2027: Tinubu Can Go to Sleep, Aiyedatiwa”ll Deliver Ondo in a Landslide, Says Ajulo
World.content:
*Ondo Attorney-General says Aiyedatiwa’s 18 Pro-Max electoral record, expanding APC membership, grassroots mobilisation put Ondo firmly on President’s political map

Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Ondo State, Dr Kayode Ajulo, SAN, has declared that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu can rest assured of Ondo State’s support in the 2027 presidential election, expressing confidence that Governor Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa will deliver the state for the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Ajulo, who is currently in Cambridge, United Kingdom, disclosed that he was cutting short his study to return to Akure ahead of the APC mega presidential rally scheduled for Wednesday, April 11, in furtherance of the party’s preparations for the 2027 general election.

Speaking with confidence about the political atmosphere in Ondo State, Ajulo said the President had every reason to count on Governor Aiyedatiwa, whose electoral record and growing political influence, he argued, had significantly strengthened the APC’s position across the state.

“President Tinubu should go to sleep on Ondo State.

“Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa has the political structure, grassroots reach and leadership capacity to deliver the state for him in 2027.

“We are not merely making promises; we are standing on an established electoral record.

“After what we witnessed in the 2024 governorship election, which I call the 18 Pro-Max victory, there is little doubt about the depth of the APC’s political reach in Ondo State.

“The Governor won across all 18 local government areas and 3,933 polling units.

“That is a remarkable electoral statement.

“Beyond the election, the political landscape has continued to evolve, with opposition leaders and members joining the APC, reflecting the growing attraction of the party under Governor Aiyedatiwa’s leadership,” he enthused.

Ajulo, who chairs the Legal Committee of the Ondo State APC Presidential Campaign Council, particularly referenced the governor’s recent meeting with over 1,000 Senior Special Assistants and Special Assistants, during which he charged them to return to their respective wards and mobilise support for President Tinubu and the APC.

According to him, the meeting was more than a routine political gathering; it demonstrated the governor’s determination to translate political structures into grassroots engagement and sustained mobilisation ahead of the election.

“As Chairman of the Legal Committee of the Ondo State Presidential Campaign Council, I can assure you that we are organised, prepared and committed to the task ahead.

“Interestingly, as things stand, President Tinubu’s candidacy is the only one whose candidacy has not been subjected to the kind of litigation challenging the nominations of some other Presidential Candidates; in fact, other candidates are on shaky grounds.

“We will work assiduously with the Governor, strategically, legally, financially, physically, with other party leaders to ensure that Ondo State remains a strong pillar of support for the President in 2027,” he said.

Ajulo also attributed the APC’s growing political confidence to what he described as the complementary development efforts of the Tinubu administration under its Renewed Hope Agenda and Governor Aiyedatiwa’s OUR EASE Agenda.

He maintained that the combination of federal policies and the Governor’s development initiatives was creating a basis for sustained public engagement with the party, while urging the APC to consolidate its achievements through effective governance and continued engagement with the people.

“The Renewed Hope Agenda of President Tinubu and Governor Aiyedatiwa’s OUR EASE Agenda are complementary development visions.

“What matters ultimately is the impact of governance on the lives of ordinary Nigerians and the people of Ondo State.

“Governor Aiyedatiwa understands that electoral victories are sustained not merely by political calculations but by leadership, accessibility, performance and the confidence of the people.”

The Attorney-General also commended Governor Aiyedatiwa for his handling of the affairs of the Ondo State APC, particularly his efforts to manage disagreements arising from the last party primary and maintain cohesion among party stakeholders.

He described the governor’s approach as an important demonstration of political maturity, inclusive leadership and an understanding that party unity remains essential to the APC’s preparations for 2027.

Ajulo said the forthcoming presidential election would provide another opportunity for the APC to demonstrate its political organisation and consolidate its presence in Ondo State.

World.title: State Police: When Numbers Add Up But Records Don’t
World.content:
As 30 State Houses of Assembly back the constitutional amendment, a puzzling information gap over Abia and Kano states, and fears of political abuse ahead of 2027, demand urgent safeguards. Sunday Aborisade reports.

Nigeria’s search for a more effective policing architecture has entered a critical constitutional phase. The National Assembly reports that 30 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly have approved the proposed amendment establishing State Police.

That figure exceeds the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of 24 states.

Yet the way the approvals have been tallied has exposed an apparent communication gap between the federal legislature and some state assemblies, raising questions about how a reform of this magnitude is being managed.

The controversy began when Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, told plenary last week that 30 state legislatures had approved the amendment.

From his record, the six outstanding states were Benue, Oyo, Cross River, Niger, Abia and Kano.

He explained that the National Assembly had discharged its duty by passing the proposal and transmitting it to all 36 state legislatures.

Abia quickly disputed the claim. In a statement the same day. The Chief Press Secretary to Governor Alex Otti, Ukoha Njoku Ukoha, described reports that the state had yet to approve the bill as inaccurate and misleading.

He insisted that the Abia State House of Assembly had passed it as part of a reform meant to strengthen community-based policing and improve the security of lives and property.

The government also reaffirmed its readiness to work with the Federal Government and other states towards implementation.

Kano presented a different wrinkle. During the same proceedings, Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Jibrin Barau, told colleagues that the Kano Assembly had submitted its response, which was being conveyed to the National Assembly.

He acknowledged a delay but maintained that the legislature had done the needful. Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio welcomed the news.

The developments pose uncomfortable questions: Why did the Senate list Abia as silent when its government says the bill was passed? Why did the Deputy Senate President have to offer fresh information on Kano from the floor?

Is the problem delayed transmission of documents, poor communication between the two tiers of legislature, or weak verification mechanisms in the National Assembly? And does the confusion matter at all, given that the threshold has already been crossed?

It does, because there is a vital distinction between a state assembly passing a resolution and the National Assembly formally receiving it.

Abia’s statement establishes the state’s position, but the Senate’s list suggests the communication was not reflected in official records when Bamidele spoke.

Barau’s intervention similarly indicates that Kano’s response had been delayed or not fully processed.

A constitutional amendment of this weight should not be managed through fragmented information, informal assurances or last-minute interventions at plenary.

Clerk to the National Assembly and the clerks of the affected state legislatures should establish a reliable verification mechanism so that official records accurately reflect the decisions of all 36 states.

The credibility of the process rests not only on securing approvals but on demonstrating transparency and institutional efficiency.

Bamidele disclosed that state legislatures have until November 15, 2026, to communicate their decisions. The Clerk to the National Assembly formally conveyed the request to all 36 Houses on October 15, giving them 30 days.

He warned that any assembly that failed to respond by the deadline would be deemed to have withheld approval, or face whatever constitutional implications might follow.

Akpabio had urged him to give the outstanding states a definite timeframe so that the National Assembly could establish whether they supported or rejected the alteration.

Section 9 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, prescribes the procedure for alterations, including approval by at least two-thirds of the State Houses of Assembly. The requirement is affirmative approval by the prescribed number.

With 30 reportedly on board, the threshold of 24 has been exceeded by six, so the remaining states cannot individually frustrate the amendment, although their decisions remain politically significant.

The National Assembly should therefore be guided by the Constitution rather than administrative assumptions about silence, and should concentrate on completing the process transparently instead of creating needless uncertainty around approvals already obtained.

Growing support for State Police reflects a recognition that the centralised policing arrangement has struggled to meet the country’s complex security challenges.

The Nigeria Police Force operates largely as a centrally controlled institution, with commands deployed across states and local government areas.

Although the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, exercises operational authority through that structure, governors, who are constitutionally the chief security officers of their states, have repeatedly complained of limited control over police deployments.

The contradiction between their responsibilities and their powers has long fuelled the debate.

State Police could address some of these limitations. Its most immediate advantages would be better intelligence gathering and faster responses to threats.

The dangers facing communities in Borno, Katsina and Zamfara differ considerably from those confronting rural communities in the South-east, South-west and South-south.

Decentralisation could let states craft strategies suited to their geography, culture and criminal realities.

Officers recruited locally would better understand the terrain, community relationships, criminal networks and local security dynamics.

Formations in rural areas could build ties with traditional rulers, farmers, transport operators and residents who hold useful information, strengthening early-warning systems and encouraging prevention over reaction.

Delays in requesting federal deployments during emergencies could shrink, with adequately equipped states responding faster to kidnappings, communal clashes and armed robbery.

The reform could also create jobs for young Nigerians, spur investment in surveillance, forensics and specialised investigation, and foster healthy competition among states.

Better security, in turn, could attract investment, revive agriculture, strengthen commerce and restore public confidence.

These benefits, however, are not automatic. They depend on recruitment, training, funding, intelligence coordination, operational independence and accountability.

Despite the legislative momentum, opposition parties, civil society organisations and rights activists remain wary.

Their concern is less with decentralisation itself than with whether Nigeria’s political and institutional environment is mature enough to stop state-controlled police from becoming instruments of oppression.

With the 2027 general election approaching, opposition parties fear governors could use the formations to intimidate rivals, disrupt campaigns, harass supporters and shape the electoral environment.

In states with intense competition and powerful incumbents, partisan policing cannot be dismissed. A governor who controls recruitment, funding and operations could influence investigations involving political associates or opponents.

There are also fears that officers could be used to restrict freedom of assembly, block lawful gatherings or intimidate activists and journalists, a worry sharpened by Nigeria’s history of political violence, misuse of security agencies and selective enforcement of the law.

The central question is whether state police personnel will serve the Constitution and the people, or become extensions of the political machinery of whoever occupies Government House.

Rights groups point to the risk of abuses, including arbitrary arrests, unlawful detention and extrajudicial killings, in the absence of robust accountability.

Finance is another worry. Several states already struggle with salaries, pensions and other statutory obligations, yet State Police would demand heavy spending on recruitment, pay, training, vehicles, communications, forensic laboratories, intelligence systems, weapons management and welfare.

Underfunded states might field poorly equipped forces unable to confront sophisticated criminal networks, and gaps between rich and poor states could produce an uneven national security landscape.

Without clear jurisdictional boundaries and intelligence-sharing arrangements, rivalries between federal and state formations could emerge, which criminals operating across state lines would readily exploit.

Perhaps the most pressing challenge is timing. With another general election looming, State Police could significantly alter the political and security environment.

In states where governors seek re-election or back preferred candidates, the temptation to deploy officers for partisan ends could be considerable, while opposition parties will expect equal protection for all political actors.

The credibility of the reform will therefore depend on whether the amendment and subsequent legislation contain sufficient safeguards for political pluralism and electoral competition.

State police officers must not become the personal security apparatus of governors or ruling parties. They must remain accountable to the law, operate within defined constitutional limits and exercise professional independence.

The Independent National Electoral Commission must retain its authority over election administration, while security agencies protect voters, candidates, officials and materials impartially.

State Police must never hand incumbent governors additional political advantage.

Passing the amendment is only the beginning. A comprehensive legal framework must settle recruitment, command structures, funding, operational jurisdiction and accountability.

Five requirements stand out. First, recruitment must rest on merit, competence and transparent standards, not political loyalty, ethnic considerations or personal ties to state officials.

Second, state police must operate under clear human rights obligations, with effective disciplinary procedures and independent oversight, and complaints of unlawful arrests, torture, killings and abuse of authority must be promptly investigated and sanctioned.

Third, the appointment and removal of state police commissioners should not be left entirely to governors. A process involving independent oversight and legislative scrutiny would better shield the force from interference.

Fourth, the National Assembly must set minimum national standards for training, conduct, weapons management, intelligence coordination and inter-state cooperation, and define the relationship between federal and state formations, especially in cases of terrorism, organised crime and kidnapping networks that cross state lines.

The Federal Government must keep an effective coordination mechanism for national security threats without undermining state police institutions.

Fifth, funding must be sustainable. States must show they can maintain professional police services without diverting resources from education, healthcare, infrastructure and other essential needs.

Civil society, security experts and human rights groups must also take part meaningfully in designing the implementation framework.

The rising support among state legislatures is an important development in the search for answers to Nigeria’s worsening insecurity. But the discrepancy between the National Assembly’s records and the positions communicated by Abia and Kano shows that even the administration of the reform needs closer attention.

The National Assembly should urgently reconcile its records with the affected legislatures, particularly Abia, whose government insists its assembly passed the bill, and Kano, whose approval was announced by the Deputy Senate President.

The November 15, 2026 deadline must not become an excuse for administrative confusion or needless controversy.

With 30 approvals reported, the priority is to verify the resolutions, complete the remaining constitutional steps and prepare a comprehensive implementation framework.

President Bola Tinubu’s eventual assent, should the process conclude successfully, will mark a constitutional milestone, but it will not automatically deliver better security.

The real test is whether Nigeria can build police institutions that are adequately funded, professionally trained, politically neutral and accountable to the people.

The fears voiced by opposition parties, civil society and rights activists must not be dismissed as mere resistance to reform; they raise legitimate questions about civil liberties and the survival of democratic competition.

Ultimately, Nigeria needs a policing system that brings security closer to the people without bringing the coercive powers of the state closer to the political interests of governors. Done right, State Police could strengthen national security, deepen community intelligence and restore public trust in law enforcement.

Done carelessly, the country could simply replace one centralised policing problem with 36 opportunities for political interference and human rights violations.

The National Assembly must therefore look beyond the impressive count of approvals and confront the harder question: how can Nigeria decentralise policing without decentralising impunity?

The answer will determine whether State Police becomes a genuine security reform or another constitutional experiment whose consequences Nigerians may live to regret.

World.title: One Suspect Killed, Another Arrested in Rescue Operation of 10 Kidnapped Victims, Gov Abiodun Commends DSS DG, IGP
World.content:
*Vows Ogun will not be safe haven for criminals

Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, has commended the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), Mr Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi, and the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Ridwan Disu, for their roles in the safe rescue of 10 passengers, including a youth corps member, abducted from a commercial vehicle around Orita Fufu, Awa-Ijebu, in Ijebu North-East Local Government Area of the state.

The rescue operation resulted in the killing of one suspected abductor and arrest of another.

Abiodun particularly applauded the DSS Director-General for providing critical intelligence and sophisticated security equipment that aided the tracking of the kidnappers and facilitated the rescue operation.

He also commended the Inspector-General of Police for his prompt directives and intervention, which galvanised the Ogun State Police Command and other security operatives into action, culminating in the release of the victims unharmed.

The governor, in a statement, declared that his administration would not allow kidnappers and other criminal elements to turn any part of the state into a safe haven, assuring residents that the government was intensifying efforts to ensure that criminals had no place in Ogun.

He warned that those who threatened the security of residents and commuters would be relentlessly pursued until they were brought to justice. He also urged residents to support security agencies by providing timely and credible information about suspicious persons, movements and activities in their communities.

The governor reiterated his administration’s commitment to strengthening collaboration with security agencies and providing the necessary support to protect lives and property across the state.

He called on residents to remain vigilant and cooperate with security operatives, stressing that collective action and prompt information-sharing were essential to preventing crime and maintaining peace in Ogun State.

World.title: Nigerian Defence Academy Helps Officers Discover Their True Selves, Says Ex-NSA
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

Former National Security Adviser (NSA), Major General Babagana Monguno (rtd), has said the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA) provides an environment for military officers to discover their true selves, understand their strengths and weaknesses and develop the leadership qualities required to serve the nation.

He said the institution is pivotal in shaping the character, discipline and professional outlook of officers, adding that the rigorous military training and academic exposure provided by the institution play a significant role in transforming cadets into disciplined, responsible and patriotic officers committed to national service.

He also noted that there has been a remarkable shift in thinking among contemporary military officers in Nigeria, saying: “We are becoming more and more alive to the realities of today and the demands of the contemporary security atmosphere, which imposes on us the need for self-preservation.”

Speaking at the official unveiling of a book titled ‘Rumbles in the New Academy,’ authored by Sub-Lieutenant Olufemi Akinwunmi, the erstwhile NSA said: “These are the sort of stories that we need to tell people because even we ourselves do not know ourselves at the point of moving into the Nigerian Defence Academy.

“As soon as you cross that gate and you are adopted into a new company or battalion, as is the case now, you drop your old self and you begin to discover your new self. And on the day of commissioning, all you are left with is a new person with a new set of values which you will carry on for the rest of your life.

“For us, the good thing here is that we forge friendships, relationships, very, very enduring, genuine friendships, fraternal relationships which do not expire. And this is one of the things that we have taken away from our training in the Nigerian Defence Academy. But more conspicuously is the change in attitude from boyhood to manhood. And now, of course, from girlhood to womanhood.”

The special guest of honour added: “In essence, there’s an evolution, there’s a seismic shift in the thinking of the contemporary military officer from what we used to know several decades ago. We are becoming more and more alive to the realities of today and the demands of the contemporary security atmosphere, which imposes on us the need for self-preservation.”

The chairman of the occasion and former Commandant of the NDA, Major General Chukwuemeka Onwuamaegbu (rtd), said the book is a must-read for all literate Nigerians.

Onwuamaegbu, who stressed the need to distribute the book to other military training institutions across the globe, said: “For those who did not experience it, and those who did but may have forgotten, I would strongly encourage you to pick up this book to remember what you went through. For those who never experienced it, the book offers an opportunity to understand what officers of the Army, Navy, Air Force and Police go through before earning the ranks they wear on their shoulders.”

A former Chief of the Naval Staff (CNS), Vice Admiral Awwal Zubairu Gambo (rtd), said the Nigerian Defence Academy is more than an institution for military training; it is an alma mater that shapes character, builds leadership, instils discipline and creates lasting bonds.

He said: “You may graduate from your alma mater, but your alma mater never graduates from you. The values, experiences and memories acquired here remain with us throughout our lives.”

He stated that what we fail to document today may be lost to generations yet unborn, adding: “As we celebrate this book, let us remember that ‘we inherit our institutions from the past, shape them through our contributions today and preserve them for generations yet unborn’.”

The author, Sub-Lieutenant Akinwunmi, said he wrote the book to preserve the institutional memory of the NDA.

World.title: Women in Mining Africa Advocates Stronger African Influence in Global Minerals Pricing
World.content:
Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

Women in Mining Africa (WiM-Africa) has called for stronger African participation in global minerals pricing, saying the continent must move beyond being a supplier of raw materials to developing the market intelligence, processing capacity and financial systems needed to influence the value of its mineral resources.

The Executive Director of WiM-Africa, Dr Comfort Asokoro-Ogaji, made the call while speaking at a roundtable on ‘Eastern Pricing 2.0: Integrating Futures, Physical Markets, Industry and Finance for the Next Stage of Global Metals Pricing,’ at the Shanghai Metals Expo 2026.

Asokoro-Ogaji said despite Africa’s possession of some of the world’s most strategic mineral resources, including copper, cobalt, lithium, manganese, platinum-group metals and gold, the continent continued to have limited influence over the systems through which their commercial value was determined.

She said the possession of mineral resources did not automatically translate into market influence, noting that producing countries could remain disadvantaged by inadequate access to market information, processing capacity, financial instruments and international commercial networks.

According to her, the expansion of Asian markets, particularly in metals trading, processing, financing and price discovery, presents an opportunity for African resource-producing countries to strengthen their participation in global minerals markets.

“Africa must not remain a passive supplier in an increasingly sophisticated global minerals economy,” she said.

She, however, cautioned that pricing power could not be achieved through declarations alone, stressing the need for African producers to improve product quality, reduce information gaps and strengthen their bargaining positions in international markets.

Using copper concentrate as an example, she explained that the actual value realised by producers depended not only on international benchmarks but also on mineral grades, moisture content, payable metal, treatment and refining charges, impurities, transportation costs and contractual terms.

She said inadequate laboratory testing, unreliable market information, limited financing and weak access to credible buyers could prevent African producers from securing the full commercial value of their resources.

To address these challenges, the WiM-Africa executive director identified five priorities, including stronger mineral market intelligence, investment in mineral testing and standardisation, expansion of beneficiation and processing, improved access to commodity markets and finance, and inclusive participation in the mining value chain.

She stressed that African producers needed access to credible and timely information on mineral production, grades, prices, buyers, processing capacity and trading conditions to negotiate more effectively.

On beneficiation, Asokoro-Ogaji called for a gradual transition from the export of largely unprocessed minerals to supplying products that meet higher industrial specifications.

She noted that regional collaboration would be necessary to achieve this, adding that not every mineral needed to be processed in every producing country.

The WiM-Africa chief also emphasised the importance of trade finance, working capital, secure payment systems, risk-management instruments and credible offtake agreements in strengthening African producers’ participation in international markets.

Addressing gender inclusion, she said women involved in mining, mineral trading, processing, cooperatives and mining-related services across Africa continued to face barriers to finance, equipment, technical expertise, market information and formal supply chains.

She argued that women must participate in value creation beyond mineral extraction, insisting that their inclusion in emerging pricing and trading systems was essential to building competitive and sustainable mineral markets.

“These are not merely questions of gender representation. They are questions of economic participation, competitiveness and market development,” she said.

Asokoro-Ogaji also highlighted WiM-Africa’s strategic partnership with Shanghai Metals Market, saying the organisation was seeking to create practical connections between African women-led enterprises and the technologies, market intelligence, industrial networks and commercial opportunities required to expand their businesses.

She called for deeper cooperation between African resource-producing countries and China’s industrial, financial and trading systems, urging partnerships that would extend beyond mineral purchases to include laboratory development, processing technology, professional training, responsible sourcing, investment readiness and direct relationships with buyers.

According to her, Chinese companies possess significant industrial expertise, processing capacity and access to major metals markets, while African countries offer mineral resources, emerging industrial markets and investment opportunities.

She maintained that Africa was not seeking to replace established international benchmarks with arbitrary national prices but to build the capacity to understand those benchmarks, negotiate better terms and retain a greater share of the economic value generated by its resources.

“The future of metals pricing should not be viewed solely as a contest between established Western benchmarks and emerging Eastern pricing centres. It should also be an opportunity to build more transparent, internationally connected and inclusive mineral markets,” she said.

She added that Africa needed to strengthen its institutions, processing industries, market intelligence and financial capabilities to translate its mineral wealth into industrial development and lasting economic opportunities.

“Africa has mineral power. It is time we built the market power to match it,” she said.

World.title: Cross River at the Crossroads: Why Continuity Under Gov Otu is Essential Against External Capture
World.content:
Joseph Abang Odok

Cross River State stands at a decisive political and economic juncture. For years it has carried the scars of the Bakassi Peninsula cession to Cameroon after the 2002 ICJ ruling and the subsequent loss of key oil wells, largely to Akwa Ibom following the 2012 Supreme Court decision. That loss stripped the state of littoral status and the associated 13 per cent derivation revenues, contributing to persistent fiscal pressure and higher poverty indicators relative to better-resourced neighbours. Successive administrations left heavy domestic debts, underutilised public assets and a trail of ambitious projects that often existed more on billboards than on the ground.

Governor Bassey Otu assumed office in May 2023 facing an inherited domestic debt exceeding N204 billion, demoralised public institutions, abandoned assets such as Tinapa and infrastructure deficits. His administration’s first term has prioritised recovery, fiscal stabilisation and consolidation rather than spectacle. Official figures show domestic debt reduced by more than N70 billion without fresh borrowing, bringing the stock to approximately N132.3 billion by March 2026. Internally generated revenue rose from N21.1 billion in 2022 to N46.3 billion in 2024 through improved mobilisation and discipline. Strategic assets have been reclaimed, including Tinapa from AMCON and nearly N1 billion from Etung Cocoa Estates. Efforts continue to restore oil-producing status and protect interests around Bakassi and the proposed Deep Seaport.

Infrastructure and human-capital investments have been tangible. Hundreds of kilometres of roads have been reconstructed or rehabilitated across the three senatorial districts. Education interventions include payment of WAEC fees for tens of thousands of students, construction and rehabilitation of classrooms, and the establishment of institutions such as the University of Education and Entrepreneurship in Akamkpa. Health upgrades cover primary healthcare centres, oxygen plants and recruitment of health workers. Tourism assets, including elements of Obudu Ranch and the Calabar Carnival, have seen revived activity and higher visitor numbers. Agriculture programmes have distributed seedlings, tractors and support to farmers, while digital fibre deployment and ICT training signal modernisation. Social investment payments targeting vulnerable residents have begun reaching tens of thousands.

These gains occurred under constrained circumstances. The state has operated without the oil derivation windfall enjoyed by neighbours and against a backdrop of national economic pressures. Independent commentary and stakeholder statements from former governors (with the notable exception of Benedict Ayade perceived to be fighting Gov Otu) have acknowledged the recovery focus. The Cross River State House of Assembly has formally endorsed Otu for a second term, citing legislative productivity and policy delivery. Northern senatorial stakeholders, youth groups and market women have similarly mobilised support, linking continuity to both state progress and alignment with federal priorities such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway.

There is overwhelming ignorance in CRS today with claims that CRS now has more money under Governor Otu. This is true only in naira value, not in dollar equivalence. Tinubu’s “more money to governors” claim is empty in real terms. Nominal FAAC allocations surged after subsidy removal and naira float. Pre-Tinubu (2022): N9–12tn ≈ $22–29bn (₦400-450/$). Under Tinubu: N21–35tn+ nominally, but only $14–23bn at N1,400-1,500/$. One comparison: six months pre-reform (~N6.36tn ≈ $13.8bn) vs post (~N13.5tn ≈ $9.2bn). States get thicker naira bundles that buy far fewer dollars for imports and projects. Devaluation and inflation erased the real increase. “Triple allocation” rhetoric ignores the currency collapse the same reforms caused. Rufai Oseni has consistently demonstrated these facts of no real value added to governors for those who follow him on Arise News

.

The political threat is real and illustrated by the Rivers experience. Nyesom Wike brings crisis wherever he becomes interested. Rivers and the PDP offer clear examples. As Rivers governor he expanded borrowing despite substantial resources, channeling leverage into party structures. In Rivers, periods of relative autonomy under Governor Siminalayi Fubara saw accelerated development that later stalled amid crises and a state of emergency. Within the PDP, his interventions repeatedly produced factional warfare, suspensions and institutional paralysis. Elevation to the FCT portfolio, with reported preferential access to funds outside standard Treasury Single Account constraints, enlarged the war chest for influence operations that now include judicial and political outreach. The Rainbow Coalition (a cross-party platform championed by Wike) aims to consolidate votes for President Bola Tinubu while positioning preferred candidates across parties for other offices. Analysts describe it as an instrument of continued political control rather than pure ideological alliance.

Cross River is too peaceful for Wike’s style of politics. Similar dynamics, combined with financial muscle from neighbouring interests, risk turning the state into an extension of external agendas. Buying influence among National Assembly members or local elite to block a second term bide of Governor Otu would expand that footprint and subordinate CRS priorities. Once a state is subordinated to external political machines whose primary loyalty lies elsewhere, local development priorities become secondary. Cross River, already poorer and fiscally scarred by the Bakassi cession and the 2012 oil-well losses to Akwa Ibom, cannot absorb a comparable interruption. Its poverty indicators remain elevated precisely because structural revenue losses were never fully offset; any halt in the current recovery trajectory would deepen deprivation rather than merely pause progress.

Governor Otu has navigated these pressures while fighting to reclaim assets and restore fiscal space amid competing claims from better-resourced neighbours like Rivers and Akwa Ibom. With their warchest they have allegedly used money to buy many appointments originally meant for CRS or removed already appointed people from CRS to swell their kitty. Reports of financial inducements directed at National Assembly members and local influencers form part of a broader pattern aimed at blocking continuity so that the Rainbow Coalition’s footprint can expand into Cross River. Under Otu the emphasis has been on internal recovery and measured federal engagement rather than subordination. A second term is framed by the governor himself as the shift from “clearing the bush and laying the foundation” to “building the house and filling it with prosperity”: industrial parks across the three districts, completion of the Obudu Cargo Airport and related logistics corridors, expanded youth and agricultural enterprise, digital civil service reforms, and conversion of recovered assets into productive ventures.

Critics will note that not every project is complete, that oil status restoration remains contested and not yet translating into derivation receipts, and that poverty reduction is a multi-year task. These are fair observations. Recovery from structural losses and inherited liabilities cannot be instantaneous. What distinguishes the current record is measurable debt reduction without new loans, revenue growth, asset reclamation, and a coherent second-term agenda grounded in those foundations rather than fresh announcements detached from delivery.

For Cross Riverians at home and in the diaspora, the choice is between consolidating hard-won stabilisation under a governor who has prioritised the state’s own balance sheet and institutions, or risking capture by larger political and financial machines whose primary loyalty lies elsewhere. The Rivers and PDP precedents show how quickly development momentum can be interrupted when local leadership is subordinated. Continuity under Otu offers the best prospect of defending Cross River’s residual sovereignty, completing the recovery phase, and converting it into shared prosperity. Stakeholders across the state have already signalled that preference. The 2027 election will determine whether that signal is heeded.

* Dr Odok, a Senior Lecturer, social change agent, lawyer and philosopher, writes from Abuja

World.title: Danjuma Endorses Tinubu in North Central Game Changer Ahead of 2027 Polls
World.content:
*Move will have impact in Taraba, Adamawa, Benue, Plateau, Kaduna, other

*Christians in identified places still angry over killings

Olawale Olaleye

Weekend’s endorsement of President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid by a former Minister of Defence, General Theophilus Yakubu Danjuma, has introduced a potentially consequential dimension to the battle for the Christian Middle Belt and parts of the North-East.

But with memories of unceasing killings, displacement and insecurity still fresh and ongoing in several communities, the question is whether the elder statesman’s considerable influence can translate into votes in 2027.



The decision by Danjuma, to openly endorse President Tinubu for a second term, has introduced a new variable into the unfolding political contest in northern Nigeria, particularly in the North-Central and parts of the North-East, where the retired general commands considerable respect and admiration.



According to sources, Danjuma’s position was hinged on the fact that since the north under former Nigerian leader, Muhammadu Buhari, served for two terms of eight years, it’s only fair that the south, currently represented by APC’s Bola Tinubu, should also serve out two terms of eight years. This he is said to believe will promote unity and national cohesion.

It is worth noting that for several years now, Danjuma has been a major financier of Christian causes in the North. In 2019, he helped to a large extent to sway Christian support to late President Muhammadu Buhari’s reelection.



So, he is a man of considerable means and stature amongst the Christian community in the North East and North Central.

However, coming barely ten weeks before the January 16, 2027 presidential election, the endorsement is significant not simply because of Danjuma’s stature as a former Chief of Army Staff, defence minister and influential member of Nigeria’s political establishment, but because of the constituencies in which his intervention could carry weight.



From Taraba, his home state, to Adamawa, Plateau, Benue and parts of Kaduna, Danjuma remains a recognised voice among sections of the Middle Belt’s political, traditional and Christian leadership.

His endorsement, therefore, presents Tinubu with an opportunity to broaden his political coalition in territories where the president’s Muslim-Muslim ticket encountered resistance in 2023 and where continuing insecurity has complicated relations between the federal government and affected communities.



Yet, the development has also thrown up an uncomfortable question: Can the endorsement of one of the region’s most influential figures sufficiently assuage the anger of communities still grappling with killings, displacement and the destruction of their livelihoods?

That question may ultimately determine whether Danjuma’s intervention becomes a genuine electoral game changer or remains an important, but limited, political endorsement.

How the Endorsement Unfolded

Danjuma’s position became clearer over the weekend when, at the 20th anniversary celebration of the Adamawa State Government House Chapel in Yola, he appealed for support for Tinubu’s re-election rather than that of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC).

Represented by a former Chief of Army Staff, General Ishaya Bamaiyi, Danjuma argued that the Tinubu administration had demonstrated a measure of inclusiveness through the appointment of Christians into important government positions, notwithstanding the controversy that attended APC’s Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket in 2023.



He also announced a donation of N250 million towards the expansion of the Government House Chapel and the provision of residential accommodation for its chaplain and deputy chaplain.

The declaration followed his participation in a high-powered delegation that met Tinubu at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, on Thursday, November 5.



The delegation included Plateau State Governor, Caleb Mutfwang; Taraba State Governor, Agbu Kefas; former Speaker of the House of Representatives, Yakubu Dogara; Minister of Defence, Christopher Musa; and APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda.

After the meeting, Dogara explained that the delegation had come to demonstrate solidarity with the president and discuss political cooperation, security and support mobilisation ahead of the election.

The sequence of events suggested that Danjuma’s public endorsement was more than a ceremonial expression of goodwill. It represented an unmistakable entry into the political conversation at a moment when the APC was attempting to consolidate its expanding northern coalition.

Why Danjuma’s Intervention Matters

Danjuma’s influence is not easily measured by the conventional instruments of electoral politics. He does not command a mass political party, nor is he known for the kind of routine electioneering associated with career politicians.

His strength derives principally from his standing in the military establishment, his longstanding relationships with northern political leaders, his philanthropic activities and the considerable respect he commands among sections of the Middle Belt.

He is also associated with a tradition of outspoken interventions on security, particularly the failure of government institutions to protect vulnerable communities.



This history makes his endorsement of Tinubu especially noteworthy. It gives the president a potentially credible intermediary in communities where the assurances of conventional politicians may carry less weight.

But such influence cannot also be confused with automatic electoral control. The Middle Belt is too politically diverse, and its grievances deeply rooted, for the endorsement of any individual to guarantee a wholesale transfer of votes.

The electoral figures from 2023 explain both the opportunity and the limitations.

What the 2023 Results Reveal

In 2023, the North-Central provided Tinubu with 1,670,091 votes, making the region his second-largest source of northern support after the North-West.

However, that aggregate strength concealed considerable resistance in some states with significant Christian populations.

In Plateau, Peter Obi of the Labour Party polled 466,272 votes, defeating Tinubu, who received 307,195 votes. Atiku secured 243,808. Obi’s advantage over Tinubu was 159,077 votes.



The outcome demonstrated that Plateau, despite the presence of an established APC organisation, was far from a secure presidential constituency for the ruling party.

In Benue, Tinubu managed a remarkably narrow victory, securing 310,468 votes against Obi’s 308,372, a difference of only 2,096 votes. Atiku finished with 130,081 votes.

The result was particularly instructive because Benue had already experienced serious security challenges and political disagreements over the protection of farming communities.



Nasarawa was another striking example. Obi won the state with 191,361 votes, ahead of Tinubu’s 172,922 and Atiku’s 147,093. The margin separating Obi and Tinubu was 18,439 votes.

Taken together, Plateau, Benue and Nasarawa demonstrated the existence of a substantial electoral constituency that was not persuaded by Tinubu’s candidacy in 2023, even though the APC maintained significant political structures across the region.

The North-Central contest is consequently not simply about winning new voters. It is also about understanding the concerns that influenced the choices of existing voters and whether those considerations have changed sufficiently since 2023.

Taraba: Danjuma’s Immediate Test

Taraba offers perhaps the most direct opportunity to assess the practical significance of Danjuma’s endorsement. Although geographically situated in the North-East, the state maintains deep political, ethnic and cultural connections with the Middle Belt.

In the 2023 presidential election, Atiku won Taraba with 189,017 votes. Obi came second with 146,315 votes, while Tinubu finished third with 135,165.

The distribution was revealing. Tinubu trailed Atiku by 53,852 votes, but the combined opposition vote was substantially larger than his tally.



Danjuma’s influence within sections of Taraba’s political establishment could help the APC consolidate support that was divided between the PDP and Labour Party in the previous election.

The political environment has also changed.

Governor Agbu Kefas, who was elected on the PDP platform in 2023, defected to the APC in December 2025. His presence in the ruling party gives Tinubu an incumbency advantage that was absent during the previous presidential contest.



A combination of Kefas’s administrative and political network and Danjuma’s influence could improve the president’s competitiveness.

Nevertheless, Taraba’s political divisions run deeper than party labels. Communities have different historical loyalties, and the former PDP electorate cannot automatically be assumed to have followed the governor into the APC.

Atiku retains a recognised political constituency, while Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), offers another option to voters, who supported him in 2023.

Taraba is therefore a genuine opportunity for Tinubu, but not yet a state that can safely be classified as an APC presidential stronghold.

Adamawa: Challenging Atiku on Home Ground

The significance of Danjuma’s declaration in Adamawa is equally compelling. Adamawa is Atiku’s home state and one of his most dependable electoral bases.

In 2023, Atiku obtained 417,611 votes, against Tinubu’s 182,881 and Obi’s 105,648. The former vice-president defeated Tinubu by 234,730 votes, one of the APC candidate’s most substantial deficits in northern Nigeria.

Danjuma’s decision to make an explicit appeal for Tinubu at a Christian gathering in Yola could introduce fresh debate within some of the state’s political and religious constituencies.



However, Adamawa cannot be reduced to its religious composition. Atiku has cultivated political relationships across the state for decades, while the influence of Governor Ahmadu Fintiri and competing local political structures add further complexity.

Even a considerable improvement in Tinubu’s performance among voters sympathetic to Danjuma would not necessarily erase Atiku’s 2023 advantage.

For Tinubu, a realistic political gain might be a reduction in the margin of defeat rather than an outright victory.

In a national election decided by relatively narrow margins, however, reducing a deficit can be almost as important as winning a state.

Plateau, Benue and Kaduna: The Security Burden

The more difficult challenge lies in communities where security concerns have become inseparable from political judgment.

In Plateau, particularly in areas affected by repeated attacks and communal violence, the issue is not merely whether the federal government has appointed prominent Christians to office.

For families that have lost relatives, farmland and homes, the more pressing questions concern physical protection, the prevention of further attacks, justice for victims and the ability of displaced people to return safely.



The June 2025 attack on Yelewata in Benue, where more than 100 people were reported killed, and other deadly attacks in Plateau have reinforced the seriousness of those concerns.

Amnesty International reported that violence had displaced more than 510,000 people across Benue by mid-2025, illustrating the extraordinary human consequences of the crisis.

The violence has multiple dimensions, including land disputes, competition over resources, criminality and failures of security enforcement. Nevertheless, the religious identities of many victims and some of the communities involved have made the issue particularly sensitive.



In Benue, Governor Hyacinth Alia’s APC membership offers Tinubu a political advantage, but the party’s narrow presidential victory in 2023 demonstrates how easily the electoral balance could shift.

In Plateau, Governor Caleb Mutfwang’s defection from the PDP to the APC in January 2026, alongside the influence of APC National Chairman, Yilwatda, has considerably strengthened the ruling party’s formal political position.



Yet Mutfwang’s membership of the APC does not automatically settle the preferences of the 466,272 voters who supported Obi in 2023.

Kaduna presents its own dimension. Atiku won Kaduna in 2023 with 554,360 votes, against Tinubu’s 399,293. Obi secured 294,494 votes, reflecting a substantial third-force presence in a politically divided state.

Southern Kaduna, where concerns about insecurity, communal relations and representation remain politically consequential, presents a particular test of the APC ability to rebuild trust.



Governor Uba Sani’s administration, his reconciliation efforts and Danjuma’s endorsement may however strengthen the ruling party’s political arguments. But voters’ assessments of safety and the government’s performance will remain important.

In Gombe, another North-East state with communities maintaining strong cultural connections to the Middle Belt, Atiku’s overwhelming 2023 victory presents a different challenge.

Atiku secured 319,123 votes, compared with Tinubu’s 146,977 and Obi’s 26,160. The president will require a significant political realignment to become competitive there.

The Muslim-Muslim Ticket and the Question of Representation

One of the more intriguing aspects of Danjuma’s endorsement is his argument that Tinubu’s appointments demonstrate greater inclusiveness than the controversy surrounding the 2023 ticket might have suggested.

The president and Vice-President Kashim Shettima were elected on a Muslim-Muslim ticket, a decision that generated considerable opposition among Christian organisations and political leaders.



Danjuma’s intervention introduces a distinction between the religious composition of an electoral ticket and the actual distribution of responsibility within government.

For the APC, that is an important argument. But it is also an argument that must withstand examination.

Political appointments may offer evidence of representation, but representation cannot substitute for security, effective governance or measurable improvements in living conditions.



Indeed, the principal danger for the ruling party would be to interpret the endorsement as evidence that the grievances of Christian communities have been resolved.

They have not necessarily been resolved, and the persistence of violence in some affected areas means that the government’s record will continue to face scrutiny.

What Changes in the 2027 Equation?

Three factors make the electoral situation considerably different from 2023.

First, the APC has attracted important governors and political leaders, who were previously aligned with the opposition. This has strengthened its organisational reach in states such as Plateau and Taraba.

Second, Danjuma’s endorsement brings an influential voice into the conversation at a time when the ruling party is seeking to address doubts about its acceptance in parts of the Christian Middle Belt.



Third, the opposition vote may be distributed differently in 2027.

Atiku is contesting on the ADC platform with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate, while Obi is running with former Kano State Governor Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso on the NDC ticket.

This arrangement means that the constituencies which supported Atiku, Obi and Kwankwaso in 2023 will again face competing appeals.

The consequences are far from straightforward. If Danjuma’s endorsement helps Tinubu attract a portion of former Obi supporters in Plateau, Benue or Nasarawa, it could reduce the opposition’s advantage.



Conversely, if the anger over insecurity remains intense, the same voters could retain their allegiance to Obi or consider another opposition candidate.

Atiku may also benefit where economic hardship and insecurity have created broader dissatisfaction with the incumbent administration.

There is no credible basis for assuming that all Christian voters will respond uniformly to Danjuma’s position, just as there is no guarantee that every voter who backed Obi in 2023 will do so again.

The Limits of Political Endorsement

Ultimately, Danjuma’s intervention is going to have a significant boost for Tinubu’s electoral fortune in the 2027.

Its potential is largely in helping the APC cross political and social boundaries that proved difficult in 2023.

Its limitation is that the concerns of affected communities are rooted in lived experience rather than merely in political endorsements.

For the president, the most persuasive evidence of progress will not come from the number of prominent personalities joining his campaign, but from whether citizens believe their communities are safer, their livelihoods more secure and their grievances adequately addressed.



Danjuma has made his political choice known. His considerable reputation could influence discussions among political elites and sections of the electorate in Taraba, Adamawa, Plateau, Benue, Kaduna and beyond.

But the election itself will establish how much of that influence translates into electoral support.

In that sense, Danjuma’s endorsement could change the political conversation across the Middle Belt. Whether it changes the voting figures will depend on the government’s performance, the opposition’s response and, above all, the judgment of voters, whose concerns cannot simply be wished away.

World.title: ADC Campaign: Tinubu Will Lose Election Despite Intimidation, Judicial Manipulation
World.content:
* Accuses govt of using security agencies against opposition, alleges growing attacks on parties, calls for international scrutiny

*Gana, Turaki-led PDP caution on reminisce of 1983, say country is boiling

Chuks Okocha in Abuja

African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has declared that President Bola Tinubu would lose the 2027 presidential election, insisting that intimidation, violence, and manipulation of democratic institutions cannot prevent his exit from office.

The council also accused the ruling APC of manipulating the judiciary and deploying security agencies against opposition parties in a desperate bid to retain power.

Director of Media and Publicity of ADC-PCC, Kola Ologbondiyan, made the assertions in Abuja, warning that the growing attacks on opposition members and supporters across the country pose a serious threat to Nigeria’s democracy.

Ologbondiyan cited the killing of several members of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Delta State, allegedly following an attack on the party’s campaign venue by suspected APC thugs.

He said the incident was part of a disturbing pattern of violence against opposition parties, particularly members of ADC, NDC, and Allied Peoples Movement (APM), in Kaduna, Kogi, Katsina, Kebbi and Sokoto states.

Describing the incidents as an assault on democratic freedoms, the ADC-PCC spokesman said, “This is not politics. This is state-sponsored terror against democracy.”

The council raised concerns over the preparedness and neutrality of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), alleging that the commission’s voter register database has been compromised and APC sympathisers have been deployed to sensitive positions within the electoral body.

It also alleged that security agencies were being used to harass, arrest, and intimidate opposition members across the country.

Ologbondiyan expressed particular concern over the alleged involvement of a serving director of a security agency in the APC Presidential Campaign Council as co-Director of National Security and Intelligence, describing the development as a violation of the law establishing the agency.

According to him, the alleged use of state institutions against political opponents reflect a government more interested in retaining power than submitting itself to a credible electoral contest.

“One thing is now very clear to all Nigerians: Tinubu is not preparing for an election. He is preparing for a coronation,” Ologbondiyan said.

ADC-PCC maintained that the alleged manipulation of judicial processes and electoral institutions would not guarantee Tinubu’s re-election, warning that Nigerians would resist any attempt to impose a president through what it described as compromised judicial decisions or electoral fraud.

It called on Nigerians to remain vigilant and prepare to defend their votes, democratic rights, and constitutional freedoms ahead of the 2027 general election.

The council also urged the international community, civil society organisations, religious leaders, and traditional institutions to pay closer attention to what it described as the deteriorating political and security environment in the country.

It warned that silence in the face of political violence could embolden those undermining democratic institutions.

ADC-PCC equally appealed to security agencies to remain politically neutral, stressing that their allegiance should be to the constitution and the Nigerian people, rather than any political party or individual.

“Those who allow themselves to be used as tools of oppression today will answer for their actions tomorrow,”Ologbondiyan warned.

The council insisted that the 2027 presidential election must be allowed to reflect the genuine will of Nigerians, declaring that no amount of intimidation, violence or institutional manipulation would stop the electorate from deciding the country’s political future.

Jerry Gana, Turaki-led PDP Caution on Reminisce of 1983, Say Country is Boiling

National Chairman of Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Taminu Turak,i and former Minister of Information, Professor Jerry Gana, alerted the country to the danger of tension within the political system, stating that political actors should be wary of the implications of the 1983 political episode.

Addressing a press conference on the increasing political tensions and violence, Turaki said, ”A little reminiscence of our political history will help us recall the imminent danger lurking on the road that the current ruling APC leadership is forcing the nation to travel.

He stated, ”In the First Republic, ‘Operation Wetie’ was the inevitable result of the asphyxiation of the opposition and the ruling party’s engineered crisis in the opposition political parties. The crisis continued unabated, and eventually that republic caved in.

“In the Second Republic, the governing party, refusing to learn from its predecessor and smarting from its hair’s-breadth survival through the judiciary in the 12 2/3 debacle, went all out to decimate the opposition.

”It deployed orthodox and unorthodox methods to attain what it christened a ‘moonslide victory’, using the power of coercion to enthrone leaders in opposition strongholds. The judiciary was complicit, giving judgements that did not reflect the reality at the polls. Eventually, that republic collapsed.”

Turaki said, ”We have taken the trouble of convoking this press conference, and of drawing on our history as a reference point, because we believe in the veracity of the postulation of the Spanish-American philosopher, George Santayana, that, ‘Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.’

“Today, the governing party, the All Progressives Congress, and the presidency, led by a pseudo-democrat, are speeding down the infamous lane that leads to democratic destruction: the lanes of constriction of the political space, violence against the opposition, the ‘buying’ and co-optation of opposition leaders, and the judicialisation of politics.”

According to the PDP chairman, ”History, both local and foreign, has shown that these lanes lead to only one destination: the death of democracy and the birth of full authoritarian rule, which subjugates the people and destroys the nation.

”The obvious question, then, is, is this what the Tinubu-led administration wants? In the entire political history of our country, never have Nigerians been more uncertain of the processes, institutions and general character of the forthcoming elections.

“This can be gleaned from Yiaga Africa’s third National Voting Intentions Survey (NVIS 3.0), released on 7 October 2026. While 84 per cent of Nigerians say they are likely or very likely to vote, 61 per cent say fear of violence could keep them away from the polls.”

Turaki explained, ”Only 34 per cent are confident that INEC will conduct credible elections, down from 45 per cent in the two previous rounds, while a staggering 63 per cent have little or no confidence that the judiciary will resolve electoral disputes fairly, rising to 81 per cent in the South-south.

”The results are damning in all critical respects.”

APC-PCC said such studies ought to cause the government to prioritise reducing tension and building confidence in voters, especially considering that less than 28 per cent of registered voters turned out at the last presidential election.

Ologbondiyan stated, ”Viewed through an objective lens, the president won with less than 40 per cent of the votes cast by that less than 28 per cent: about 8.8 million votes out of 93.4 million registered voters. That is a super minority, and a mandate resting on so thin a base carries a serious legitimacy deficit.

“If turnout was that low in 2023, without the anomalies we are witnessing today, we can only imagine how much worse the coming elections will fare.”

World.title: Starstruck Springboks meet Carlos Alcaraz (video)
World.content:
Springbok captain Siya Kolisi and several of his team-mates caught up with Spanish tennis superstar Carlos Alcaraz after his Paris Masters triumph. Image: Screenshot

Springbok captain Siya Kolisi and several of his team-mates caught up with Spanish tennis superstar Carlos Alcaraz after his Paris Masters triumph on Sunday.

Alcaraz beat American Ben Shelton 7-6 (7/5), 7-5 in the final.

The world No 3 was congratulated by the Springbok contingent backstage after claiming the title in the French capital.



Kolisi was joined by fellow Springboks Damian de Allende, Jesse Kriel, Malcolm Marx, Pieter-Steph du Toit and Jasper Wiese.

Different sports, same champion mentality 🏆🤝



Carlos Alcaraz meets the Springboks 🏉🎾#RolexParisMasters pic.twitter.com/f1B8GScQR8 — ROLEX PARIS MASTERS (@RolexPMasters) November 8, 2026

‘Delighted’

The players exchanged handshakes, hugs and congratulations with the six-time Grand Slam champion, who appeared delighted by the unexpected encounter.



During their conversation, Kolisi reminded Alcaraz that the Springboks had watched him play in Turin during a previous visit.

Alcaraz admitted that he was tired after a demanding week on court but said he was looking forward to taking a few days off before turning his attention to the ATP Finals in Turin.

The Springboks wished the Spanish star well and encouraged him to enjoy his break.



Kolisi shows off dance moves during tennis final

Kolisi also caught the attention of television cameras during the Paris Masters final.

The Springbok captain was spotted among the spectators and could not resist showing off a few dance moves in the stands.



It was a lighter moment for the Springbok skipper and his team-mates as they enjoyed some time away from their demanding schedule.

Siya Kolisi always brings the vibes 🕺



The Boks are already in Paris ahead of their Test against France on Friday night 🇫🇷🆚🇿🇦#SSRugby | #RolexParisMasters pic.twitter.com/743iNvLYLZ — SuperSport Rugby (@SSRugby) November 8, 2026

Springboks turn attention to France

The Springboks have travelled to France following their emphatic 66-7 victory over Italy in Turin on Saturday.



Rassie Erasmus’ charges will now face France at the Stade de France on Friday, 13 November, in their next Nations Championship encounter.

Kick-off is at 22:10 (SA time).

The clash is expected to provide a much sterner test for the world champions as they look to build on their impressive performance against Italy and maintain their winning momentum.
