In 2020, during Trump’s first term, Collins was the only GOP Senate incumbent or challenger who won in a state where the exit polls showed more voters disapproved than approved of Trump’s job performance.

The Voter Poll showed Collins on Tuesday again succeeded in attracting more voters who disapproved of Trump than almost any other Republican. But compared with 2020, more Maine voters this time disapproved of Trump (63 percent), and considerably more of those disapprovers supported Democrat Troy Jackson (80 percent) than backed her opponent in 2020 (71 percent). That tide of discontent with Trump’s performance carried Jackson to a comfortable 6-point win, even though 56 percent of voters said they did not believe the rough-hewn candidate had the right temperament for the job.

Collins was a tall tree in the political forest. Once it became clear that the current was strong enough to dislodge even her durable roots, it seemed clear that other Republicans with shallower attachments would be swept away as well.

The pattern extends

Supporters of Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton celebrate during an election-night watch party in Overland Park, Kansas, on Tuesday. Jim Vondruska/Getty Images

Moving west and south, Democrats won, almost always easily, the other races we identified as signaling a good night for the party, including ousting House Republicans in WI-3, IA-1 and IA-3, and winning the open seat Iowa governor race, as well as the governor and Senate contests in Ohio.

Most striking: Democrats across the Midwest ousted four House Republicans in strongly pro-Trump districts that we believed would fall only in a true tsunami: Ann Wagner and Victoria Spartz in the white-collar seats MO-2 and IN-5, and Michael Turner and Mike Carey in the more blue-collar seats of OH-10 and OH-15. Hamilton’s success in becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932 also pushed the night firmly into tsunami territory.

In the South, Democrats won all the races they needed to for a good night (such as the reelection victories by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Democratic Rep. Don Davis in NC-1 and Democratic House incumbents who beat gerrymanders in FL-14 and FL-25), as well as tougher contests such as Keisha Lance Bottoms’ history-making triumph in the Georgia governor race.

Sen. Jon Ossoff waves to the crowd after winning reelection, in Atlanta on Tuesday. Audra Melton for CNN

But, as in the Midwest, Southern Democrats also scored some truly historic wins. The headline so far was Annie Andrews’ Senate win in South Carolina (a state Trump won by nearly 18 points just two years ago). Democrats also notched tsunami-level wins in North Carolina House seats — including narrowly beating Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, in NC-9, a district Trump carried by almost 16 points. A win for Democrat Scott Colom in the Mississippi Senate race, which appears within reach as final ballots are tallied, would mark an even greater historic breakthrough for the party.

Texas was where all these trends converged most powerfully. Democrats posted solid wins by defending incumbents Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez, in TX-28 and TX-34, two heavily Hispanic South Texas districts that Republicans gerrymandered to weaken them. They won even tougher races in two other heavily Hispanic districts when sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia easily held the open seat of TX-35 and Pulido, a charismatic Tejano singer, routed Monica De La Cruz in TX-15-a district Trump had carried by almost 18 points. Democrats moved their gains into historic territory with Katy Stout’s victory in TX-23, a district that few considered within reach until recently.

Any win for James Talarico against Paxton in the Texas Senate race would have marked a very good night for Democrats, who had not captured a Senate seat there since 1988. But Talarico’s 12-point,1.2 million-vote advantage pushed the result deep into historic territory.

As impressive as Talarico’s victory was, even more remarkable was Gina Hinojosa’s win over three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott. While Talarico was well-funded, Hinojosa was overwhelmingly outspent. And while Paxton was a deeply flawed opponent, Abbott had been a dominant force in Texas politics for years. Yet Hinojosa crushed Abbott by about 700,000 votes to become the state’s first Latina governor — and record a victory that stands as the textbook definition of historic.

The common themes

People attend an election night watch party at the Grosse Pointe Democratic Club in Detroit on Tuesday. Nick Hagen for CNN

Democrats posted a similar record across the West. They won all the races we identified as the minimum for a good night (including flipping Republican-held House seats in CA-22, CO-8 and AZ-1). They won several tougher races (including flipping MT-1, AZ-6, and CO-5). And they barreled into historic territory by capturing the NV-2 House district (which Trump carried by 14 points), with a plausible remaining chance to flip CO-4, another double-digit Trump district. The Alaska governor and Senate contests, both of which would represent significant breakthroughs for Democrats, probably won’t be settled until mid-November; Democrats are favored strongly in the former and narrowly in the latter.

Our pre-election list of counties to watch fell out in a similar pattern. Democrats notched gains in each of the major groupings that we identified: urban centers, traditionally White suburbs, racially diverse suburbs, mostly working-class White counties we dubbed “blue-collar bellwethers,” Latino enclaves and rural redoubts. Measuring the swing in voting behavior compared with 2024 showed virtually every congressional district moving toward the Democrats. In states including North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Texas, virtually (or literally) every county moved toward the Democrats compared with 2024 in their Senate or governor races or both, according to the analysis of the Decision Desk HQ political website.

The Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for CNN and a consortium of news organizations underscored how the disenchantment with Trump drove those shifts. Beyond Trump’s 63 percent disapproval rating, a stunning 62 percent said he prioritized his personal interests over the country’s; 64 percent said he had the wrong priorities; 66 percent said his policies had hurt, not helped, the economy. Strong majorities of voters expressing each of those views backed Democrats.

The breadth of Trump’s decline hurt Republicans as much as the depth. During his first term, even as most voters nationally disapproved of his performance, Trump retained majority support in most Republican-leaning states — which helped the GOP oust several red-state Democratic senators in 2018.

But this year, a majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s performance in every state where Democrats flipped a Republican-held Senate seat; his disapproval ranged from 55 percent in South Carolina, to 57 percent in Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, 59 percent in Texas, 62 percent in North Carolina and 63 percent in Maine. At least 85 percent of the voters who disapproved of Trump supported the Democratic Senate candidate in each of those states except Maine. That left those GOP candidates in too deep a hole to escape. (In the national House poll, 86 percent of voters who disapproved of Trump voted Democratic, a number similar to the levels for Obama, Bush and Clinton, though slightly below the mark for Trump in 2018.)

And even in those previously Republican-leaning states, many of Trump’s specific initiatives faced majority opposition. Between 52 percent to 56 percent of voters in Florida, Georgia, Arizona and even Texas felt his immigration enforcement efforts had gone too far. (Two-thirds of Texas Hispanics felt that way.) Between 61 percent to 66 percent of voters in Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — the sort of blue-collar behemoths long considered most receptive to a protectionist trade agenda — said his tariffs had hurt the local economy. (Even majorities of non-college White voters in those states viewed the tariffs as harmful.) At least three-fifths of voters in Texas, South Carolina, Nevada and Georgia said Trump was wrong to attack Iran.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27. Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

All this discontent converged to produce last Tuesday’s historic repudiation of Trump and the GOP. When all races are called, Democrats could reach their biggest House majority since 2009 — or even since 1991. Democrats also could reach at least 55 Senate seats —something either party has done only three times since 2000.

It’s too early to say these breakthroughs have provided Democrats a lasting edge in the 50-50 stalemate that has defined the competition between the two parties for almost the entire 21st century. Predictions of realignment from each side after even big wins in recent years have all been frustrated.

But last week’s results represented an earthquake big enough to potentially reset the playing field. The Democratic wins will elevate to national leadership a diverse array of younger leaders that will bring new vitality into a party that many voters in recent years have seen as “doddering,” in the words of Democratic pollster Paul Maslin.

And while the big Democratic wins in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and potentially even Mississippi would undoubtedly be harder to replicate with the larger and more blue-collar electorate of a presidential year, they at least open new pathways for the party to an Electoral College majority beyond the handful of swing states that have dominated recent presidential campaigns.

If nothing else, the results shattered the hardening belief in both parties that Republicans had constructed impregnable fortifications across the 25 states that have voted for Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Those defenses haven’t crumbled, but they have cracked — and created the openings for new possibilities beyond the past quarter century’s unending trench warfare between two electoral coalitions that are utterly inimical in their vision for the country, but have been almost exactly equal in size.

World.title: Video: Giant whale sighting sparks debate in Hurghada
World.content:
The appearance of a massive whale near Umm Qamar Island, north of Hurghada, stirred debate among those working in marine-related sectors and marine life enthusiasts.

Divers and sailors have circulated videos and photographs documenting the creature’s appearance during a tourist excursion.

Speculation suggests it could be a fin whale, locally referred to as “al-Battan,” or perhaps a blue whale.

The General Administration of Red Sea Protected Areas said that there is no official, documented record of the incident.

With eyewitnesses insisting that a giant whale was indeed spotted in the area, while the relevant authorities remain cautious, citing a lack of verified information, questions have arisen as to whether one of the ocean’s largest creatures truly appeared in the Red Sea, and whether the circulating footage is sufficient to scientifically identify the species.

An incredible sighting

A boat captain in Hurghada and the person who filmed one of the circulating videos, Mahmoud Shazly revealed several details of the incident.

He explained that he was taking four German tourists on a snorkeling trip in the al-Erq area when, while sailing, a massive whale suddenly appeared in the water near Umm Qamar Island.

Shazly noted that the encounter took place around 2:00 PM, leaving tourists both astonished – they made sure to document the moment by capturing photos and videos.

Several individuals working in marine-related activities suggested that the whale could be a blue whale or a fin whale, based on its size and appearance in the video footage; however, a definitive identification would require an expert analysis of the images and videos.

Conversely, the General Administration of Red Sea Protected Areas has denied the existence of any official confirmation or documented information verifying the whale’s appearance, noting that no formal reports regarding the sighting of a blue or fin whale in the area have been received.

The administration explained that attempts to contact the person who filmed the video failed to establish the location or timing of the footage.

It emphasized the importance of exercising caution and accuracy, urging against drawing firm conclusions about the species of the marine creature before a scientific verification of the recorded footage conducted.

Second-largest animal on earth

The fin whale, known locally as “al-Battan,” is the second-largest animal on Earth, surpassed only by the blue whale.

It belongs to the baleen whale family, which uses specialized plates inside the mouth to filter water and extract food – these whales also periodically surface to breathe.

The waters of the Red Sea have previously been home to sightings of various whale species, particularly the humpback whale in the areas of Marsa Alam and Al-Qusair.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison over the deaths of 190 children
World.content:
A Kenyan cult leader has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, all but one of them children, in a campaign of abuse and forced fasting.

Paul Mackenzie, founder of the Good News International Church, was sentenced Friday alongside more than two dozen others at the Mombasa High Court.

Mackenzie preached that the world would end in August 2023 and that followers needed to fast in order to reach heaven. According to a Kenyan Senate report into the deaths, his teachings were based on “doomsday or end-times” beliefs. Children were scheduled to die first, followed by young people and women. Men were expected to stay alive long enough to bury the bodies before dying.

Mackenzie’s sentencing comprised of 100 years’ imprisonment for the murder of those who starved and 100 years for those who died by direct homicide.

In her sentencing remarks, Lady Justice Diana Kavedza said she did not impose the death penalty because it could strengthen the convicts’ belief that dying would reunite them with Jesus, rather than deter them. She also wanted to leave open the possibility that they could help locate the remains of missing children.

“In the respectful view of this court, such a sentence (the death penalty) would therefore fail to achieve deterrence,” she said.

Kavedza said 161 of the victims were children aged 9 or younger. Twenty-two were between 10 and 13 years old, and five were between 14 and 16. The ages of two others could not be established. She also said that several of the convicts’ children remained missing and were presumed dead.

The judge added that 183 of the 191 victims died from starvation, including 182 children and one adult. The remaining eight victims, all children, were suffocated, strangled or beaten to death.

Mackenzie had persuaded followers to abandon their homes and move to Shakahola Forest, in eastern Kenya, promising that fasting there would bring them closer to God and prepare them for heaven.

The court found that religious teachings were used to enforce the fast. Guards controlled followers’ movements and prevented them from leaving. Those who resisted were forced to comply, while children were restrained, denied food and punished when they tried to eat or escape.

Mackenzie was convicted of murder last month. In her ruling, Kavedza described how he used sermons and written materials to convince followers that the outside world was evil and that salvation could only be found in the forest. Messages extracted from his phone, including WhatsApp exchanges, showed that he had communicated with followers before they’d moved to Shakahola Forest.

Kavedza said most of those convicted hadn’t shown any remorse for their actions. Mackenzie smiled several times during Friday’s sentencing.

Survivors testified that deaths in the forest were celebrated as “weddings to Jesus,” with those who died regarded as “heroes of faith,” Kavedza said.

Postmortem findings cited by the judge showed that starvation was not the only cause of death. Some victims died from suffocation, neck compression or head injuries.

Authorities began exhuming bodies from Shakahola in April 2023 after reports that people had died while following Mackenzie’s teachings. They have recovered more than 400 bodies so far. The 191 murder convictions relate to the victims in the case decided last month, while further charges could follow.

Stephen Mwiti, whose six children died in Shakahola, told Reuters that his wife had taken his family there to fast. She was among those convicted in the case.

Questioning the decision to make children fast, Mwiti said: “Even if the adults had agreed to fast, what about the children?” He said no outcome in the case could undo the loss of his family.

Rodgers Shibutse, a Nairobi resident who identified his mother’s remains among those exhumed in February 2024, told CNN after the sentencing Friday: “I cannot say that I am 100% satisfied. It (the verdict) is not enough to pay for the life of my mum, but we have no other choice. At least, he (Mackenzie) cannot finish the 200 years in jail and will die eventually.”

This story has been updated with developments.

World.title: Liberia: Record Billions at the Top, Rising Hunger at the Bottom
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia – In central Monrovia, where vendors line the sidewalks with trays of biscuits, chocolate and soap, the national budget is not measured in billions. It is measured in how many customers stop, and how much they can spend.

By Rodney D Sieh

Patrick Mamligar, who sells snacks on those streets, told FrontPageAfrica earlier this year that the finance minister’s claims about an improving economy were simply not true.



His was one voice among many in that survey of traders and shoppers. Few of them could point to anything in their own lives that matched the government’s upbeat numbers.

The finance minister has heard the complaint before. Pressed on whether Liberians were feeling relief, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan asked whether the government was expected to hand out actual bread and butter before citizens accepted that their concerns were being addressed. The remark has followed him ever since.

The ledger and the street

On paper, Ngafuan’s second tour at the Finance Ministry has been a run of records. In September, the Liberia Revenue Authority crossed US$1 billion in domestic collections for the first time in the country’s history. On Friday, the government sent lawmakers a US$1.538 billion budget for 2027, the largest Liberia has ever proposed.

The minister points to growth of 5.1 percent last year, inflation brought under control and the absence of the budget shortfalls that dogged the previous government. In one interview, he summed up his case in a line: Liberia is “not where we want to be,” but no longer where it was.

He also argues that patience is part of the plan. Stabilizing prices, revenue and public finances, he has said, must come before any expansion that ordinary people can feel. Roads now, he insists, mean jobs and cheaper goods later.

His critics hear something else. Opposition leader Alexander Cummings has turned the debate into a slogan about eating today rather than waiting for tomorrow.

The opposition Citizens Movement for Change recently praised Ngafuan as eloquent, then questioned his credibility, citing audit gaps and unreconciled revenue records between the ministry, the LRA and the Central Bank. Last year, the General Auditing Commission flagged US$2.8 million in ministry payments without adequate supporting documents; Ngafuan called it a paperwork problem, not theft. Critics, including opposition figures, independent analysts and a former director of the ministry’s own budget department, now describe the lapses at the Finance Ministry as among the most serious failings of President Joseph Boakai’s Unity Party-led government. Some have openly called for the minister’s removal.

The sharpest challenge, however, has come not from his political rivals but from one of the government’s closest partners.

The World Bank’s paradox

On November 3, the World Bank launched the seventh edition of its Liberia Economic Update, titled Beyond Growth. Its central finding cuts straight through the government’s narrative: the economy grew, and so did extreme poverty.

By the Bank’s estimate, the share of Liberians in extreme poverty rose from 34.6 percent in 2024 to 36.1 percent in 2025 – in the same year the economy expanded 5.1 percent. Country Manager Georgia Wallen called it the paradox at the heart of the report.

The explanation lies in where the growth came from. Mining output jumped 17 percent. Agriculture, which feeds most Liberian households and makes up about a third of the economy, grew just 2.6 percent. In short, Liberia is growing fastest where few Liberians work.

The labour figures are starker.

About 78 percent of workers are in what the Bank calls vulnerable employment – street trading, small-plot farming or unpaid family work. Wage jobs make up just 20.9 percent of employment, a share that has barely moved in two decades. Reserves covered only about 1.6 months of imports at the end of 2025, leaving the country exposed if oil or food prices spike.

The Bank expects extreme poverty to ease to 33.2 percent this year, but only if farming recovers. It also anticipates a value-added tax (VAT) starting in early 2027 – a change that could push up prices at the very stalls where Liberians already feel squeezed.

None of this is Ngafuan’s doing alone. But as the minister who sets budget priorities, he owns the question the Bank is asking: why does so little of Liberia’s new money reach the farms, markets and households where most people make their living? Agriculture, the “A” in President Joseph Boakai’s ARREST Agenda, has received less than 1 percent of recent national budgets.

‘Lower inflation is not the same as lower prices’

One of the sharpest readings of the paradox comes from a man who once sat in Ngafuan’s chair. Amara Konneh, who succeeded him as finance minister under Sirleaf and now serves as a senator, told FrontPageAfrica that Liberia’s macroeconomic numbers may be improving, but too many Liberians are still not feeling it in their pockets.

Konneh points to the Central Bank of Liberia’s own August 2026 figures. Headline inflation was 4.6 percent, down from 5.6 percent a year earlier. But domestic food prices were rising at 11.1 percent, transport at 7.6 percent and imported fuel at 6.2 percent. “Lower inflation is not the same as lower prices,” he said. A bag of rice that became expensive does not get cheaper simply because prices are rising more slowly.

He noted that the World Bank attributes the rise in poverty largely to inflation and sluggish farm growth. With mining up 17 percent, agriculture up only 2.6 percent and manufacturing shrinking 2.8 percent, he argued, growth is happening in sectors where few Liberians earn a living. Some 86 percent of Liberian firms are microenterprises.

Konneh also questions why a stronger Liberian dollar has not brought prices down. He blames the cost of moving goods from the Freeport of Monrovia to rural markets – port charges, delays, storage and unofficial fees along trade routes. “Is the stronger Liberian dollar increasing the purchasing power of Liberians?” he asked. “If not, we still have work to do.”

His most pointed figure goes to the heart of how Ngafuan’s ministry spends. Citing the World Bank, Konneh said government capital spending fell from 8.5 percent of GDP in 2024 to 5.7 percent in 2025 – from about US$406 million to US$297 million – even as revenue climbed to record highs. “That should concern us,” he said.

Konneh proposes three fixes before Christmas: a single published schedule of port charges with clearance targets; regular Commerce Ministry price monitoring to make sure a stronger currency reaches shoppers; and temporary relief for small businesses hit by delays beyond their control. He framed his comments as constructive, acknowledging the government’s progress on stability. But, he said, stability “is a means to an end. It is not the end itself.”

The first time around

Ngafuan has been here before. He first entered Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s cabinet in 2006, at 35, as head of the Bureau of the Budget. He served as finance minister from August 2008 to February 2012, then moved to the Foreign Ministry until he resigned in 2015.

That first tenure is remembered for real achievements. Liberia reached the end of the World Bank and IMF debt relief process in 2010, wiping out close to US$5 billion in external debt. A new Public Financial Management Law passed in 2009, and civil servants began receiving salaries by direct deposit.

But it was also marked by the same tension that haunts him now. Growth in those years was strong, averaging about 7 percent a year between 2004 and 2014, according to the World Bank. Yet much of it came from mining, rubber and donor-funded reconstruction, and it did little to change daily life for most families. As late as 2016, more than half of all Liberians lived in poverty, and in rural areas the figure exceeded 70 percent.

Accountability questions surfaced then too. In 2010, a General Auditing Commission review of debt-relief-era spending asked Ngafuan and other former officials to account for more than US$1 million in expenditures made without vouchers during his time at the Budget Bureau. He rejected parts of the findings as riddled with errors.

The parallels are hard to miss: headline growth that bypasses the poor, audit queries that Ngafuan dismisses as paperwork, and a minister whose technical fluency wins praise from donors but not from the market. Last year he himself traced one of today’s documentation problems back to a 2011 contract he signed to modernize the ministry’s archives – a system, he admitted, that later broke down.

The case for the minister – and the test ahead

Ngafuan’s defenders say he inherited a broken budget, and that collecting more revenue is the first step to spending it well. They note that the 2027 plan raises health spending by 22 percent, sets new pay floors for teachers, adds about 4,350 public workers and, for the first time, commits to repaying nearly US$60 million the government owes the national pension fund.

Those are real promises. But Liberians have heard promises before, and the budget’s own numbers leave room for doubt. Part of this year’s billion-dollar milestone came from a one-off US$200 million signing bonus paid by steelmaker ArcelorMittal. Health still gets less than 9 percent of the budget, and agriculture barely features in the government’s summary at all.

The coming months will show whether Ngafuan’s economy can reach the street. Three markers matter most: whether extreme poverty falls toward the World Bank’s 33.2 percent projection; whether the planned VAT protects basic goods that poor families buy; and whether teachers, nurses and pensioners actually receive the money the budget promises them, on time.

Back on the sidewalks of central Monrovia, the verdict will not come from a report or a budget speech. It will come from whether more customers stop at the trays of biscuits and soap – and whether, at the end of the day, a vendor can carry home enough to feed a family.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Warns UP Against Rigging 2029 Elections As Mo Ali Fires Back Over War Remarks
World.content:
KINJOR, Grand Cape Mount County — The opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) has warned the ruling Unity Party (UP) against any attempt to manipulate the outcome of Liberia’s 2029 presidential and legislative elections, declaring that it will not accept what its leaders described as an attempt to steal the people’s mandate.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The warning dominated the party’s 2026 Martyrs’ Day celebrations held in Kinjor, Grand Cape Mount County, from November 4 to November 7, where senior CDC officials, former government officials, lawmakers, and partisans gathered to commemorate members and other Liberians who lost their lives during political struggles and confrontations with state security forces.



Mo Ali fires back

But the CDC’s warning has drawn a sharp reaction from senior Unity Party member Mo Ali, who accused the opposition of threatening another war and cautioned against what he described as the party’s reliance on conflict rhetoric.

Although the Unity Party has not issued an official response to the CDC’s statements, Ali took to his official Facebook page to challenge keynote speaker and former Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Paulita C. Wie over her remarks at the gathering.

“So CDC’s only tactic is to threaten war?” Ali wrote, questioning Wie’s reference to war and invoking Liberia’s civil war, which began on December 24, 1989.

He recalled that some Liberians who initially celebrated the arrival of rebel forces later became victims when those forces captured their communities.

“Some of the people who jubilated the coming of the rebels became some of the first victims when those same rebels captured their communities,” Ali stated.

He further accused the CDC of lacking the intellectual capacity to withstand the Unity Party politically, arguing that its leaders were relying on threats rather than constructive political engagement.

“Anyways, the only reason why the CDC is always threatening war is because they are bereft of any intellectual capacity to withstand the UP,” he wrote.

Ali also rejected the suggestion that Liberians would support another confrontation, declaring: “Liberians are tired of their war tactics and no one will follow that.”

He concluded with a direct challenge to the opposition: “If they want to fight, we will give them somewhere in the forest to go fight. Liberia is not for war mongers.”

Wie’s 2029 Warning

Ali’s comments followed Wie’s remarks at Saturday’s Martyrs’ Day program, where she warned that the CDC would not accept an appeal for peace if the 2029 elections were manipulated.

“Under Joseph Boakai as President, the government is corrupt, they are evil, they’re demonic, and they are a wicked government,” Wie declared, launching a blistering criticism of the Boakai-led administration.

Addressing former President George Manneh Weah, the CDC’s political leader and standard-bearer, Wie insisted that the party should not accept political compromises in the name of peace if its electoral victory were undermined.

“Former President Weah, we will not be accepting ‘for the sake of peace’ in 2029. If Unity Party wants war, we will give it to them. If they want peace, we will also give them peace. We will reciprocate whatever they give us,” she said.

Wie, who contested against Senator Abraham Darius Dillon in the 2019 Montserrado County senatorial by-election, previously served as Deputy Minister for Urban Affairs under the former Ministry of Internal Affairs, now the Ministry of Local Government. She has remained a vocal member of the CDC.

Her remarks reflected the increasingly confrontational tone adopted by several opposition figures as the country moves toward the next general elections.

Gray Joined the Fray

Former Montserrado County Representative Acarous M. Gray also reinforced the party’s position in a Facebook post on Sunday, November 8, declaring 2029 a victory year for the opposition and warning the Unity Party against entertaining thoughts of manipulating the electoral process.

“There’s one truth that UP has to hear very loud and clear: 2029 is a victory year for the opposition community,” Gray wrote.

He accused ruling party supporters of suggesting that they could steal the elections, warning that any such move could trigger serious political consequences.

“We don’t pray for chaos, but you will have a peaceful one if you get stupid. To even think about stealing the elections is for you to accept the total demise of your government and your existence,” he added.

Gray further predicted that the opposition would secure an overwhelming first-round victory, insisting that the Unity Party would have to relinquish power peacefully after the elections.

McGill’s Comments

The CDC’s electoral warning was accompanied by messages of party revival and renewed political mobilization from Margibi County Senator Nathaniel McGill, a former national chairman of the party.

McGill urged partisans to remain committed to the CDC’s political resurgence, assuring them that the party would survive and return to power.

“We need to deliver victory in 2029. I want you to go home and know that your party will remain supreme and your party will survive,” McGill told supporters.

He also announced plans to rebuild the party’s national headquarters, disclosing that Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe Taylor had pledged to contribute 50 percent of the cost, while he and the party’s standard-bearer and Executive Committee would provide the remaining 50 percent.

“On behalf of the standard-bearer and the EC, I will provide the balance 50 percent,” McGill said, expressing confidence in the party’s ability to regain political ground.

He also declared that Grand Cape Mount County would no longer remain politically aligned with the Unity Party.

Kowo Calls for Justice, Accountability

While the political warnings and subsequent exchanges dominated the public discussion surrounding the commemoration, CDC National Chairman Atty. Janga A. Kowo used his Martyrs’ Day message to emphasize the historical significance of the event, the need for accountability for unresolved political killings, and the importance of protecting democratic freedoms.

Addressing party leaders, militants, sympathizers, and residents of Grand Cape Mount County, Kowo conveyed solidarity from former President Weah, the National Executive Committee, and the wider leadership of the CDC.

He said the November 7 commemoration was not simply about remembering the deaths of party members but also about honoring their courage and sacrifices in the struggle for democracy, justice, freedom, and a better Liberia.

“Today, November 7, 2026, we gather in solemn remembrance of the courageous men and women who made the ultimate sacrifice in the struggle for democracy, justice, freedom, and a better Liberia,” Kowo stated.

The CDC chairman recalled the November 7, 2011, confrontation at the party’s national headquarters in Monrovia, when partisans assembled at the facility and were confronted by state security forces, resulting in deaths, injuries, and widespread suffering.

He described the incident as one of the darkest chapters in the history of the political institution, noting that the memories of those who died and the families affected remained deeply embedded in the party’s collective consciousness.

Kowo also extended the commemoration beyond the 2011 incident, remembering Comrade Tamba Momo, who was killed in Foya, Lofa County, in an incident the party attributed to supporters of the Unity Party.

He further remembered Comrade Joshua, whose killing in Monrovia brought grief and outrage to the CDC community, as well as residents of Kinjor who lost their lives during confrontations involving the Liberia National Police.

The chairman said the deaths of these individuals and other Liberians must not be forgotten, regardless of their political affiliations.

“The value of a Liberian life must never depend upon political affiliation. No family should be denied justice because of the political beliefs of a loved one,” he emphasized.

Kowo renewed the CDC’s call for credible, impartial, and transparent investigations into unresolved incidents of political violence and unlawful killings across the country.

He insisted that anyone found responsible for criminal acts must be held accountable through due process, irrespective of political affiliation, public office, or influence.

“Justice must never be selective,” he declared.

Kinjor Commemoration Carries Broader Significance

Explaining the decision to hold this year’s commemoration in Kinjor, Kowo said the gathering was intended to demonstrate that the memory of those who died in the struggle for justice and human dignity extended beyond Monrovia to every part of Liberia.

He expressed solidarity with Grand Cape Mount County residents and families still seeking answers over the deaths of their loved ones, stressing that the experiences of affected communities must be documented and preserved for future generations.

However, he cautioned that remembrance should also inspire a rejection of political violence, respect for the rule of law, and protection of the democratic rights of all Liberians.

“The greatest tribute we can pay to our fallen compatriots is to help build a Liberia where no citizen loses his or her life merely for exercising democratic rights,” Kowo said.

The 2026 commemoration was held under the theme, “They Carried the Struggle – We Carry Their Legacy.”

The annual Martyrs’ Day observance traces its origins to November 7, 2011, when a confrontation between CDC partisans and state security forces at the party’s national headquarters in Monrovia reportedly left people dead and others injured.

Over the years, the party has expanded the commemoration to remember other members and citizens who lost their lives during political activities and confrontations across the country, including incidents in Foya and Kinjor.

The four-day observance in Grand Cape Mount County culminated on Saturday with speeches and renewed calls for political mobilization, justice, and accountability.

World.title: Liberia: RIA Port Manager James Mulbah Tipped to Replace Siafa as Monrovia City Mayor; Shake-up comes amid mounting criticism of Siafa’s stewardship — and longstanding complaints that government has starved the city corporation of fund
World.content:
Monrovia — FrontPageAfrica has reliably learned that James K. Mulbah, General Manager of the Roberts International Airport (RIA), is set to replace John-Charuk Saah Siafa as Mayor of the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC).

By Rodney D Sieh

The expected change at City Hall comes after nearly three years of persistent public criticism of Mayor Siafa’s handling of the capital — over piling garbage, unpaid workers and contractors, and allegations of financial irregularities — even as the mayor and his supporters have argued that the national government has never given the MCC the money it needs to do its job.



From the Airport to City Hall

Mulbah was appointed General Manager of RIA by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai on February 28, 2024.

He officially joined the ruling Unity Party (UP) last December, declaring his confidence in the leadership and direction of President Boakai. Mulbah made the announcement during the Unity Party’s Homecoming Program, where he arrived at the party’s national headquarters accompanied by a large group of supporters.

“My joining Unity Party today is not a political game,” Mulbah told journalists at the time, adding that the UP was the first political party he had ever joined and that President Boakai’s stance against corruption was a major reason for his decision. Asked then whether he harbored ambitions for elected office, he said he could not predict the future and that his focus was on joining the party.

If nominated, Mulbah would require confirmation by the Liberian Senate, as Siafa did in 2024.

A Rocky Tenure

Siafa, nominated by President Boakai on January 27, 2024, and commissioned in March that year as Monrovia’s 28th mayor, succeeded Jefferson Tamba Koijee with promises to clean the city, restore transparency and depoliticize the MCC. He has been widely reported to be a close relative of the President.

But his tenure has been dogged by controversy. In June 2025, allegations of financial and procurement irregularities at the MCC surfaced in the press, including claims about the rapid elevation of staff to senior paid positions. Earlier that year, MCC contractors protested in front of City Hall on UN Drive over unpaid wages, and the mayor and the Civil Service Agency came under fire from civil society over the dismissal of civil servants that critics described as political retaliation.

Some of the sharpest attacks have come from within the ruling party itself. In September 2025, Queen Johnson, Deputy Director for Records at the National Port Authority and a staunch UP member, publicly called for Siafa’s dismissal, labeling him corrupt and incompetent. Days later, MCC employees planned a protest demanding his resignation over the city’s persistent sanitation problems. In March 2026, another UP loyalist publicly branded the mayor a criminal amid allegations tied to an audit of the MCC.

The mayor has had defenders. The Civil Society of Liberia (CSNL) dismissed the corruption claims as propaganda driven by suspended staff, including the comptroller, and credited Siafa with improving waste management. The MCC has also pushed back against FrontPageAfrica’s reporting on the deteriorating City Hall theater, insisting the mayor inherited the facility in ruins and has made progress rehabilitating municipal buildings.

Starved of Funds?

At the heart of Siafa’s defense has been a recurring complaint: that the national government has failed to fund the city.

Appearing before the Legislature for his first budget hearing in April 2024, Siafa blamed Monrovia’s filth on the government’s failure to allocate adequate funding to the city government. He told lawmakers the MCC needed US$11,023,583 to function effectively — with roughly US$2.8 million to be raised internally and about US$8.2 million expected from the national government.

Instead, the 2024 draft national budget allotted the MCC US$3,777,965.

Siafa also told lawmakers that the government’s direct support for cleaning Monrovia under the clean cities budget had been US$600,000 in fiscal year 2023, with a drastic US$400,000 reduction in 2024. He warned that government had paid only US$750,000 of a required US$1.5 million counterpart contribution to the World Bank-backed Cities Livability and Urban Services (CLUS) project, raising the risk that the project could be shut down.

In October 2024, the mayor said the MCC faced a severe manpower shortage, noting that 281 people responsible for cleaning the city had been classified as consultants rather than formal employees when he took office.

In August 2025, he argued that many of the MCC’s original mandates, such as zoning and land use, had been absorbed by national agencies like the Ministry of Public Works and the Liberia Land Authority, leaving the city with fragmented authority.

The 2026 national budget allocated US$4.5 million to the MCC — still well short of the mayor’s own estimate of what the city needs. In March 2026, Assistant Minister for Development Planning Wellington Barchu pledged to champion dedicated funding for solid waste management in the 2027 national budget.

Whoever takes over City Hall is likely to inherit the same dilemma: a capital that residents and critics say is drowning in waste, and a city government that says it has never been given the means to clean it.

World.title: Liberia: From Neglect to Rocognition – Visually Impaired Gets First High School in Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia – The Government of Liberia, through the Ministry of Education, has officially dedicated and turned over a newly constructed annex for the elevation of the Liberia School for the Blind and Inclusive Learning to a senior high level.

By Obediah Johnson

Located in Mango Town, Virginia Township, outside Monrovia, the school has been providing academic studies and psycho-social counseling to thousands of Liberians and other foreign nationals with visual impairment at the kindergarten, elementary, and junior high divisions for over 50 years.



The newly dedicated annex comprises three well-furnished classrooms with modernized armed chairs and chalkboards, an air-conditioned science laboratory, solar panels, running water, amongst others.

Funded by the government, through its Public Sector Investment Program (PSIP), the annex was dedicated as part of efforts to break the barriers surrounding the provision of quality and equitable education to Persons Living with Disabilities (PWDs) in the country.

Speaking at a program marking the turnover, Education Minister Jarso Jallah disclosed that the elevation of the school was intended to promote access to inclusive education in the country.

She said gone are the days when students and teachers in specialized schools in Liberia were abandoned or neglected.

“For too long disabilities have sometimes been treated as a specialized issue. But no longer are we going to do that. We want to say to our sisters and brothers who find themselves in disability institutions-as we plan for school, procure learning materials, and think about the administration of exams, we think of the inclusion of our young people who are in specialized institutions.”

She, however, encouraged persons living with disabilities in Liberia not to allow their current conditions or impairment to limit or restrict their vision and ambition in life.

“All our citizens should be given access to quality education. I want to take this time to thank our President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, a man of vision, and a man who understands what his people need; we are just his foot soldiers executing his mandate. So, we are here this morning in his name to say to the disabled community that he hears you, sees you, and he knows what you need, and he has come to deliver for you.”

She expressed gratitude for the increase in the number of students enrolled at the school from 60 to 115 this academic year.

She announced that the MOE is finalizing a procurement process for the renovation of the entire campus of the Liberia School for the Blind.

Minister Jallah used the occasion to acknowledge the sacrificial and indispensable roles being played by the administrative and support staff at the school.

She also recognized the tidiness of the only public school providing education to visually impaired students in the country.

She pledged that the government, through the ministry, would provide 25 scholarships to students completing their secondary education at the school.

She disclosed that a visually impaired Liberian student, William Yarsiah, is currently benefiting from the Chevening Scholarship and studying in London, United Kingdom.

“This is to tell you that you might have a challenge, but that challenge should not limit you.”

She said specialized teachers would also be trained to provide quality education to students with special needs across various schools in Liberia.

“We have come today not only to dedicate or turn over a building. Turning over a building is not yet complete equal access. We must empower the teachers to be able to deliver the quality instruction that you need. We are committed to continuing this venture with you to ensure that the students here will be talking about this experience for years to come.”

Minister Jallah assured that the government would continue to ensure that every Liberian has access to quality education, regardless of their status or condition.

She added that it would also continue to build an education system that expects children with disabilities to learn, achieve, and participate fully in the advancement of society.

She said the government encourages partnership from international donors and parents to fully equip the school with the needed educational materials and other technological equipment.

Minister Jallah expressed the hope that a similar gesture would also be extended to the School for the Deaf and Dumb in the same vicinity.

She further disclosed that the ministry has completed an assessment of all inclusive and specialized schools across Liberia.

She added that school supplies have also been distributed to these schools to enhance their operations, while they await specific and targeted interventions for their students.

She further endorsed a recommendation from the school’s Principal, Jackson Suah, to name the newly constructed annex “ Golden Jubilee,” in honor of the school’s over 50 years of existence.

For his part, Mr. Suah commended the government for its remarkable investment in the advancement of education for specialized learners in Liberia.

“We are not simply dedicating a building; we are celebrating a vision, strengthening commitment, reaffirming our collective dedication to advancing inclusive education in Liberia.”

He disclosed that the school is not merely a specialized institution for learners with visual impairment, but it is an inclusive education institution committed to providing equitable learning opportunities for students with and without disabilities.

He pointed out that the vision of the institution is to create an educational environment through diversity and respect for individuals, and to remove barriers to learning to ensure that students reach their full potential.

“We firmly believe that disabilities should never be a barrier to educational achievement or participation in society. Inclusive education is not an act of charity; it is a matter of justice, equality, human dignity and fundamental rights.”

He said the timely and commendable intervention made by the government would significantly strengthen the school’s capacity to deliver quality secondary education to learners.

Mr. Suah maintained that the annex would not only serve as classrooms for students, but it would also accommodate administrative staff.

He observed that the historic science lab, which is the first of its kind in the district, is a landmark achievement that will enhance practical scientific learning, promote innovation, encourage experimentation and expose students to hands-on scientific experience.

He added that it would also strengthen the teaching of science and help prepare students for higher education and future careers in science.

Mr. Suah said the new facility represents a concrete investment in inclusion and demonstrates that learners with visual impairment and other disabilities deserve access to quality secondary education, modern learning facilities, and an environment where their needs are recognized and their abilities are nurtured.

He noted that the annex is not just a structure of concrete and steel, but a building of hope, opportunity, empowerment, and educational progress.

“We are deeply grateful for this investment, which will positively impact generations of learners and strengthen the foundation of inclusive education in our country. In recognition of this historic achievement and the remarkable journey of our institution, we respectfully propose that the newly constructed school annex be named the Golden Jubilee Annex.”

World.title: Liberia: Bringing Regulation Closer – LTA Opens Consumer Service Center In Gbarnga
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County — The Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) has opened a regional consumer service center in Gbarnga, Bong County, in a move aimed at bringing telecommunications regulation closer to consumers, strengthening oversight of service providers and reducing the burden on rural operators who previously traveled to Monrovia to access regulatory services.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The facility will provide residents, community radio stations and local internet service providers with a regional platform to report poor network services, lodge complaints, resolve telecommunications-related concerns and process licensing and compliance requirements without making costly trips to the capital.



The opening forms part of the LTA’s decentralization agenda, which seeks to expand the regulator’s presence beyond Monrovia, improve consumer protection and strengthen monitoring of telecommunications services across the country.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, LTA Board Chairman Clarence Massaquoi described the center as the fulfillment of a commitment by the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to bring government services closer to the people.

He said the facility represents more than the establishment of another government office, describing it as a practical demonstration of decentralization and an effort to address the longstanding concentration of public services in Monrovia.

Massaquoi said local businesses, including community radio stations and internet service providers, would now be able to complete regulatory and compliance processes in Gbarnga rather than incur additional expenses traveling to Monrovia.

He added that the center would strengthen the Authority’s ability to independently investigate consumer complaints, assess reports of poor network performance and verify information provided by telecommunications operators.

According to him, the Board also intends to gradually transfer the management of the facility to qualified residents of Bong County as part of efforts to promote local participation in the regulatory process.

He said community members, students, market women, civil society organizations and youth groups would be engaged in public education initiatives to increase awareness of consumers’ rights and responsibilities in the telecommunications sector.

Massaquoi encouraged qualified residents of Bong County to apply for employment opportunities advertised by the Authority, emphasizing that local professionals should take advantage of opportunities created by the decentralization initiative.

He also disclosed that the Board hopes to acquire land in Gbarnga for the construction of a permanent regional office equipped with telecommunications monitoring facilities.

Such infrastructure, he said, would enable the Authority to monitor telecommunications installations across the county and independently assess the quality and performance of services provided by operators.

LTA Targets Poor Network Coverage, Service Gaps

LTA Commissioner Patrick Honnah described the opening as another milestone in the Authority’s decentralization efforts since its establishment in 2007.

He recalled that a similar consumer service center had previously been established in Grand Bassa County, with Bong County now becoming the next destination in the Authority’s efforts to expand regulatory services across Liberia.

Honnah said the Gbarnga facility would serve consumers, local internet service providers and community radio stations seeking assistance with complaints, licensing, compliance and other regulatory matters.

He explained that having regulatory personnel stationed in the region would eliminate the need for local operators to travel to Monrovia to process documents and address routine regulatory issues.

Beyond administrative services, the Commissioner said the center would strengthen the LTA’s monitoring of telecommunications operators, particularly in the areas of service quality, network coverage and consumer complaints.

He said the Authority’s engineering and compliance teams would use the regional presence to identify network dead zones, investigate service interruptions and engage mobile network operators in addressing persistent connectivity challenges.

Honnah also highlighted interventions undertaken through the Universal Access Fund (UAF) to extend telecommunications services to underserved communities.

He disclosed that the LTA had restored internet connectivity in Gbatala, Bong County, a community that previously lacked both internet and voice services.

He also cited the restoration of internet connectivity at a school in Division 33, Margibi County, saying the intervention had provided students with improved access to research materials and educational resources.

The Authority, he added, is working to upgrade 15 remote telecommunications towers from 2G to 4G technology to improve connectivity in underserved areas.

Honnah further disclosed that the LTA is encouraging Orange Liberia and Lonestar Cell MTN to share telecommunications infrastructure as a means of expanding coverage, reducing duplication and improving the efficiency of network investments.

He said similar interventions would be pursued in other underserved counties, including Nimba, Lofa and River Gee.

Senator Moye Wants Telecom Operators Held Accountable

Bong County Senator Prince K. Moye welcomed the establishment of the regional center, describing it as a practical step toward addressing the challenges created by Liberia’s highly centralized system of governance.

Drawing on his experience as a former representative, Moye said citizens have often been compelled to take local complaints to members of the national legislature, even when such concerns could have been resolved more efficiently at the county or regional level.

He argued that many telecommunications complaints brought to lawmakers could be addressed locally if relevant institutions had the necessary personnel, resources and authority to intervene.

The senator said the LTA’s expanding presence outside Monrovia should improve consumer protection and ensure that telecommunications companies are held accountable for the quality of services they provide.

However, he urged the Authority to ensure fair competition among mobile network operators and intensify efforts to extend coverage to communities that remain without reliable telecommunications services.

Moye specifically cited Winukwala, a major market town along the road to Grand Bassa County, which he said lacks GSM coverage despite its commercial importance.

He expressed hope that the establishment of the Gbarnga center would encourage telecommunications companies to prioritize communities that have remained underserved.

On behalf of the Bong County Legislative Caucus and local authorities, Moye thanked the LTA for selecting Gbarnga as the location for the new regional facility.

Lonestar Cell MTN Welcomes Initiative

A representative of Lonestar Cell MTN also welcomed the opening, describing the facility as an indication of renewed commitment to consumers in Gbarnga and Buchanan.

The representative said the center represents accountability, accessibility and empowerment for people who depend on telecommunications services for communication, education, business and innovation.

Reliable telecommunications services, the representative noted, are no longer a luxury but a necessity, making it important for consumers to have accessible institutions where their concerns can be heard and their rights protected.

The company also acknowledged the LTA’s efforts to place consumers at the center of telecommunications regulation, oversight and service delivery.

The opening of the Gbarnga Consumer Service Center marks another step in the LTA’s efforts to decentralize regulatory services and expand its presence across Liberia.

The Authority says it intends to establish similar facilities in other parts of the country as it works to strengthen regulatory oversight, improve service delivery, protect consumers and narrow the digital divide between urban and rural communities.

World.title: Liberia Tells African Tax Chiefs in Cairo That Home-Grown Revenue Is Replacing Aid Dependence
World.content:
Jallah said that when the current management team took charge in 2023, collections stood at roughly US$612 million. Donor funding was shrinking, and both the national domestic revenue mobilization strategy and the LRA’s own corporate plan had lapsed

Cairo, Egypt – Liberia used a continental stage this week to argue that it is steadily moving from reliance on foreign aid toward funding its own development. At the African Tax Administration Forum (ATAF) 2026 Annual Meetings and General Assembly in Cairo, Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) Commissioner General James Dorbor Jallah presented the country’s recent fiscal record and its plans for modernizing tax collection.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

He spoke during a session titled “Domestic Resource Mobilisation: Differentiated Pathways for a Diverse Continent,” where he shared how Liberia’s revenue authority has changed direction in the past few years.



From US$612 Million to Over a Billion

Jallah said that when the current management team took charge in 2023, collections stood at roughly US$612 million. Donor funding was shrinking, and both the national domestic revenue mobilization strategy and the LRA’s own corporate plan had lapsed.

Since then, he reported, collections climbed to US$699 million in 2024 and US$848 million in 2025. The current figure is about US$1.134 billion. Adding US$5 million brought forward from the prior fiscal year, he said, the total comes to approximately US$1.139 billion.

In his view, the numbers show that Liberia can increasingly pay for its own priorities, a notable shift for a country that has depended heavily on outside support for many years.

A Reform Agenda Built on Five Pillars

Jallah told delegates that the LRA’s transformation rests on five pillars: strategic leadership, technology and data, compliance and enforcement, customs and tax administration, and institutional integrity. Together, he said, they are meant to sharpen performance, raise collections, tighten enforcement and make the revenue system more answerable to the public.

On integrity, he revealed that 46 LRA employees were dismissed in 2025 for fraud and related misconduct. He described this as proof of the Authority’s refusal to tolerate corruption, and argued that a clean institution earns public trust, which in turn encourages taxpayers to comply willingly.

Putting the Numbers in Citizens’ Hands

Delegates also saw the LRA’s public revenue dashboard, an online tool through which citizens and other interested parties can view how much government is collecting. Visitors can track reported performance and download tables with monthly summaries, as well as figures broken down by revenue category and tax type.

According to Jallah, the platform currently refreshes in near-real time, and the Authority is working toward fully real-time updates. He said that giving people easy access to collection data helps them follow the revenue picture and understand how the country raises money at home.

The dashboard is one element of a wider transparency drive that also includes expanding electronic payment options and other online services.

Meet Fatu: The Virtual Taxpayer Assistant

The presentation also featured a live demonstration of the LRA’s virtual contact center, a project aimed at shortening the wait for answers to taxpayer questions and easing confusion about what people owe.

The virtual assistant, called Fatu, handled a mock query from a small business owner who wanted to know which taxes applied to them. The exercise showed how the service could put tax guidance within easier reach and give taxpayers another route to assistance.

Once fully built and running, the center is expected to support taxpayer education and allow individuals and companies to get advice without traveling to an LRA office.

More Than a Collections Story

Jallah stressed that raising more money is only part of the job. Lasting domestic resource mobilization, he said, also requires institutional reform, openness, accountability, engagement with taxpayers and dependable service.

He noted ongoing work to modernize tax administration and make compliance simpler for small enterprises, while keeping operations running smoothly as systems go digital. He concluded by restating the LRA’s goal of becoming a transparent, accountable and technology-driven institution able to underpin Liberia’s long-term growth.

Who Else Was on the Panel

The session gathered tax officials and academic experts to discuss how African states can boost domestic revenue under varying economic and institutional conditions.

Joining Jallah were Rasha Abdel Aal, Head of the Egyptian Tax Authority; Leonildo Joao Lourenco Manuel, President of the Board of Directors of Angola’s General Tax Authority; Yankuba Darboe, Commissioner General of the Gambia Revenue Authority; Rohit Ramnawaz, Director-General of the Mauritius Revenue Authority; and Richard Stern, Director of the Global Tax Program at Vienna University.

Participants explored the realities facing economies with large informal sectors, newly formalizing markets, rapid digital growth and abundant natural resources. They agreed that reform plans should reflect each country’s economic circumstances, development goals and institutional strength instead of following a single template for the whole continent.

World.title: Liberia Faces 323 Additional Maternal Deaths Annually as US$2.4 Million Health Funding Cuts Threaten Reproductive Care – Guttmacher
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia could experience an additional 323 maternal deaths annually, alongside more than 107,600 unintended pregnancies and 37,800 unsafe abortions, if reductions in United States and Swedish funding for family planning and sexual and reproductive health services continue, according to a new report by the Guttmacher Institute.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The report, titled “More Than Just the Numbers: How Funding Cuts Threaten Sexual and Reproductive Health in Liberia,” warns that the country has lost at least US$2.4 million in family planning and sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) support since 2025, leaving hundreds of thousands of women and couples at risk of losing access to contraception and other essential reproductive health services.



Released in November 2026, the assessment projects that approximately 327,700 women and couples in Liberia could lose access to contraception annually if the funding reductions persist.

The projected consequences include increased unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions and preventable maternal deaths, placing additional pressure on an already challenged healthcare system.

According to Guttmacher, the loss of external assistance follows the abrupt reduction of United States health support in early 2025 and Sweden’s subsequent decision to wind down its development assistance to Liberia.

The report indicates that US family planning disbursements to Liberia declined by 34 percent following the withdrawal of American assistance, with support for 2026 expected to fall close to zero.

Sweden, identified as Liberia’s second-largest development partner after the United States, announced in December 2025 that it would phase out its development assistance to the country.

That decision brought an end to its 2021–2025 cooperation strategy with Liberia, which involved approximately 1.85 billion Swedish kronor, equivalent to about US$197 million, across 39 projects, including programs supporting reproductive health, gender equality and youth empowerment.

Teenage Girls Face Growing Risks

The report identifies adolescent girls as among the populations most vulnerable to the funding reductions, warning that existing barriers to contraception could worsen as youth-friendly services, community outreach and free contraceptive distribution lose financial support.

Before the funding cuts, more than half of adolescent girls in Liberia who wanted to avoid pregnancy were not using modern contraception, according to 2024 estimates cited by Guttmacher.

Adolescent girls also accounted for 28 percent of unintended pregnancies nationwide during the same year.

If the US and Swedish funding reductions continue, the report estimates that Liberia could record approximately 22,400 additional unintended pregnancies among adolescent girls annually, representing a 62 percent increase over the 2024 baseline.

The institute further projects 9,300 additional unsafe abortions among adolescent girls each year.

Guttmacher warns that these outcomes could undermine girls’ education, employment prospects and their ability to contribute to the country’s long-term development.

It argues that the loss of reproductive health services does not only threaten the immediate health of young women but could also deepen social and economic inequalities.

Unsafe Abortions Could Increase Healthcare Costs

Beyond the human consequences, the report warns that reduced access to contraception could significantly increase the financial burden on Liberia’s healthcare system.

Before the funding reductions, an estimated 131,500 unintended pregnancies occurred annually among women aged 15–49 in Liberia, with approximately 54,500 ending in abortions.

Of those abortions, only about 15 percent were considered safe.

The report estimates that approximately 18,700 women required postabortion care annually, costing the health system nearly US$976,000. The overall cost of abortion-related care, including safe abortion services and treatment of complications, was approximately US$1.02 million.

However, if the funding cuts continue, the number of women requiring postabortion care could rise to approximately 34,000 annually, an 82 percent increase.

The annual cost of abortion-related care could consequently reach US$1.85 million, representing an additional US$833,500 in healthcare expenditure.

Guttmacher estimates that continued funding reductions could result in 37,800 additional unsafe abortions and 6,800 additional safe abortions annually, bringing the total number of abortions to approximately 99,100.

The report further explains that every 1,000 additional unsafe abortions could result in approximately 400 women requiring postabortion care, costing the health system about US$20,900.

It argues that preventing unintended pregnancies through improved access to contraception would be less costly than treating complications arising from unsafe abortions.

The institute estimates that ensuring all abortions are safe, rather than maintaining the current legal restrictions, could reduce annual abortion-related healthcare expenditure by approximately US$1.19 million compared with the projected cost under the current law following the funding cuts.

Public Health Bill Remains Stalled

The funding crisis is unfolding alongside uncertainty over Liberia’s domestic policy framework for sexual and reproductive health and rights.

The report notes that the Public Health Bill, passed by the House of Representatives in 2022, remains stalled in the Liberian Senate.

The proposed legislation seeks to modernize the country’s public health framework, expand access to safe abortion care up to 18 weeks of pregnancy and promote comprehensive sexuality education.

However, provisions relating to sexual and reproductive health and rights have faced pressure for removal, according to the report.

Guttmacher warns that weakening these provisions could further restrict access to essential reproductive healthcare at a time when external funding for such services is declining.

The institute maintains that the combination of reduced donor assistance and uncertainty surrounding domestic policy protections could reverse progress in improving reproductive health outcomes.

Guttmacher Calls for Urgent Government Intervention

Against this backdrop, Guttmacher is urging the Liberian government to take immediate steps to protect access to sexual and reproductive healthcare, particularly for women, adolescent girls and vulnerable communities.

Among its recommendations is the integration of sexual and reproductive health services across public health facilities, nongovernmental organizations and donor-supported programs.

The report also calls for greater investment in community health workers and ensuring that they are adequately equipped to provide reproductive healthcare in accordance with national guidelines.

Additionally, it emphasizes the need to prioritize and protect access to high-quality, age-appropriate health education.

The institute argues that investments in contraception and comprehensive sexuality education can help reduce unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, HIV infections and other sexually transmitted infections while lowering long-term healthcare costs.

It further links reproductive autonomy and access to sexual and reproductive healthcare to education, economic empowerment and women’s participation in decision-making.

According to the report, these factors are essential to Liberia’s broader economic development and its efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals.

A Broader Development Challenge

Guttmacher cautions that the consequences of the funding reductions extend beyond the health sector, potentially affecting national productivity, household welfare and Liberia’s long-term development objectives.

The projected increase in unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, adolescent pregnancies and demand for postabortion care could place additional pressure on government resources while limiting opportunities for women and girls.

The report concludes that protecting reproductive healthcare is not simply a matter of improving health outcomes but also an investment in human development and economic progress.

For Liberia, the challenge is particularly significant as the country confronts declining external assistance and the need to strengthen domestic financing for essential health services.

Without timely intervention, Guttmacher warns, the loss of contraceptive access and other reproductive health services could translate into thousands of additional health complications and hundreds of preventable maternal deaths every year.
