World.title: DStv Slashes Subscriptions From US$37 In Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia – Satellite television provider DStv has announced major subscription price cuts, simplified viewing packages, and an expanded entertainment offering in Liberia as its parent company, Canal+, repositions the brand as a more affordable, consumer-friendly platform across Africa.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

This followed CANAL+’s acquisition of MultiChoice last year, marking a new era for African entertainment and creating more opportunities to invest in content, innovation, and customer experiences across the continent.



Reflecting this ambition, MultiChoice Group, a CANAL+ Company, then introduced its most significant product update in years, bringing more of Africa’s greatest entertainment live to subscribers from 5 November.

The changes, officially introduced in Liberia on November 5, 2026, mark a significant shift in DStv’s pricing and service structure, thus promising subscribers more entertainment value for their money.

Among the most notable changes is the reduction of the Ultimate package, formerly Premium, from US 37 monthly, while the entry-level Starter package is now available for US$`7, a move expected to make satellite television more accessible to households and businesses that previously considered DStv too expensive.

Speaking during the launch of the DSTV promotional Radio takeover show THE LIVING ROOM, a customer interaction program on OK FM simulcast on Spoon FM, Prime fm, Hot fm and Cool fm over the weekend, the Digital Marketing Specialist at MultiChoice, Cynthia Awuor Joel, said the changes were driven by customer feedback and management’s decision to make DStv accessible to a wider audience.

Joel acknowledged that the company had received repeated concerns from subscribers who viewed DStv as an expensive service designed for a particular class of people, noting that the company had listened to those concerns and decided to restructure its packages, reduce selected subscription prices, and provide more entertainment options at different affordability levels.

“We have had people say DStv is for the rich. There’s that perception that DStv is for a specific calibre of people. But that’s not what represents our brand. We are here for entertainment, for African entertainment,” Joel explained.

She emphasized that the company’s new direction is centered on affordability, simplicity, and improved customer experience, adding that the restructuring is intended to allow more Liberian families to enjoy television entertainment within their budgets.

Under the new arrangement, DStv has streamlined its subscription structure into four major packages, including Starter, Select, Sports, and Ultimate, replacing the previous Access, Compact, Compact Plus, and Premium arrangements.

The Starter package, which replaces Access, costs US`$7 monthly and provides access to telenovelas, Africa Magic programming, children’s entertainment through Cartoon Network, and a Match of the Week offering for football enthusiasts.

The Select package costs US$`13 monthly and includes the Starter offering, with additional football coverage, including La Liga, more cartoons, movies, and other entertainment channels.

The Sports package, priced at US`$24 monthly, is designed for sports enthusiasts and provides access to DStv’s broader sports offering, including La Liga, UEFA Champions League, rugby, Formula One, and other major sporting competitions, while subscribers will also retain entertainment, children’s, and movie content available under the lower packages.

At the top of the new structure is the Ultimate package, now priced at US 61.77, offering the platform’s comprehensive entertainment experience, including more than 115 channels featuring international and African programming, movies, news, sports, and content from Arabic, French, Chinese, and Indian channels.

Meanwhile, as part of the launch campaign, MultiChoice has introduced a promotional offer allowing new customers to acquire a complete DStv starter kit for just US$14, as the package includes a decoder, satellite dish, and one month of Starter subscription at no additional subscription cost during the promotional period.

However, the company clarified that installation charges are excluded and may vary depending on the customer’s location and installation requirements, as the campaign is being promoted under the message that DStv is listening to customers and responding with more affordable entertainment options.

Joel then encouraged Liberians to take advantage of the offer by visiting the nearest DStv office or authorized dealership, noting that dealership information is also available through the company’s Facebook platforms.

She described the promotion as an invitation for more households to experience satellite television without the financial burden previously associated with purchasing the equipment.

Joel at the same time said that, beyond subscription prices, the transition also introduced a new visual identity for DStv, with the familiar blue branding giving way to a black-and-white appearance following Canal+’s acquisition of MultiChoice.

Addressing longstanding customer complaints, Joel said MultiChoice was also working to improve content delivery, particularly concerns about repeated movies and the delayed availability of newly released films on lower subscription packages.

She explained that the company intends to reduce the waiting period for new movies to reach subscribers on entry-level packages, ensuring that customers do not have to wait excessively long to enjoy fresh entertainment.

Joel also indicated that the Starter package would carry more channels than the previous Access offering, while the company continues reviewing customer feedback on local content, movies, and other programming concerns.

She acknowledged that improving the entertainment experience would be an ongoing process, emphasizing that the company remains open to suggestions from subscribers.

On channel adjustments following the migration, Joel explained that some customers might temporarily experience changes in their existing bouquets as the transition takes place in phases.

She advised subscribers who notice missing channels after 24 to 48 hours to contact DStv customer care for assistance, thus clarifying that Africa Magic Family has undergone a rebranding process, meaning some channels may appear under different names or logos.

She assured customers that its digital services, including the DStv application, online subscription payments, and streaming facilities, remain available, adding that subscribers can continue making payments through the DStv application and supported mobile money platforms, including MTN and Orange, while enjoying the digital services associated with their subscriptions.

Joel explained that the company was implementing the changes in phases rather than carrying out a complete overnight switch, urging customers to exercise patience during the migration.

She also clarified that customers who had already paid for their subscriptions before the transition would continue enjoying the services covered by their existing payments until their next payment or decision to upgrade.

Under the new arrangement, subscribers previously on Access will automatically move to Starter, with the option of upgrading to Select, Sports, or Ultimate according to their viewing preferences and financial capacity.

World.title: Nkana’s Kambole saves his best for last
World.content:
Nkana striker and Vice-captain Lazarus Kambole was left thrilled after netting his fourth goal of the season as Kalampa stunned NAPSA Stars 1-0 in the delayed Super League match at REIZ Arena in Lusaka on Sunday.

Kambole left it late to strike in the third minute of added time as Nkana secured a dramatic 1-0 win over NAPSA in Stream A.

The result lifted the Kitwe side to the top of the Stream A standings with 16 points from seven matches played.

“I am happy to have scored my fourth goal of the season. We are Kalampa,” Kambole said in a post-match comment.

Kambole was recently named Nkana FC Player of the Month for October.

Meanwhile, Nkana coach Elijah Tana is still preaching hard work despite his team enjoying fine form so far in the season.

Speaking after the match,Tana says he never lost hope his side would score, adding they could have scored two or three goals from counterattacks in the second half.

“We knew, we knew we would score. We knew. You saw Nkana, we had some counterattacks in the second half. We could have scored three or two,” Tana said.

In their next match, Nkana are scheduled to face FC MUZA in Mazabuka on Wednesday, 18 November, before travelling to Lusaka to take on Zanaco FC on Wednesday, 25 November.

World.title: “The Truth Will Emerge”: Lima MP Kaunda Thanks Supporters After Detention, Unveils Industrial Yard Plan
World.content:
Lima Constituency Member of Parliament Kelvin Kaunda has said justice will prevail in the assault case he faces, now that the matter is before the courts. He thanked the people of Lima and Zambians at large for standing with him while he was in detention. Mr Kaunda was recently arrested and charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm following an incident reported on 7 August during a campaign roadshow in Lusaka. Speaking for the first time since his release, the lawmaker said he had placed his faith in the judicial process to establish what really happened.

Mr Kaunda said the people of Lima had shown patriotism and remained strong throughout the period he was held. He said their support in a difficult time had meant a great deal to him. Turning to the charge itself, the lawmaker said he was confident the court process would clear the air.

“We want to thank the people of Lima and also the people of Zambia by and large for standing with us during the period of incarceration in which we have been alleged to have committed a crime. Now that the matter is before the court, the truth will eventually emerge as to whether or not we committed the reported crime,” Mr Kaunda said.

The lawmaker was quick to move from the courtroom to his constituency’s development agenda. He assured the people of Lima that the case would not distract him from delivering on the promises he made during the campaign, both in the constituency and beyond. Mr Kaunda said his commitments covered jobs, empowerment and infrastructure, and that all of them would be met before his term ends.

“In terms of development, we want to assure the people of Lima that we are equal to the task regarding our campaign promises. We promised jobs for young people. We promised empowerment for both men and women, as well as young people. We promised infrastructure development that will be delivered within our five-year tenure,” he said.

The centrepiece of his plan is the Lima Constituency Industrial Yard, which Mr Kaunda said would be launched in the next few days together with all leaders in the constituency. He described the yard as one of the most exciting initiatives on the table. It is designed to kick-start job creation, especially among young people and the less privileged. The lawmaker said the project was a response to the weight of expectation resting on the constituency’s unemployed youth.

Explaining why the industrial yard sits at the top of his agenda, Mr Kaunda said young people with ideas needed a place where those ideas could grow into livelihoods.

“There’s so much that is expected from our young people, in particular, who are without jobs. There is so much we expect collectively as a constituency when it comes to creating a platform for our young people who are involved in innovation and creativity to thrive. In terms of skills development, we are only as good as our people,” Mr Kaunda said.

The lawmaker said he remained committed to accelerating skills programmes that match what employers actually need. Rather than training young people for jobs that do not exist, he said his office was holding discussions with industry so that graduates of the programme would move straight into work. Mr Kaunda said the aim was to close the gap between training and employment that has left many young people with certificates but no jobs.

“Ours will be to provide demand-driven skills. We are talking to the industries so that once our young people are given the necessary skills, the industry out there will be quick to absorb them. We have quite an exciting package,” he said.

Mr Kaunda’s case will now be determined in court, where he will answer the charge arising from the August roadshow incident. In the meantime, the lawmaker has signalled that he intends to carry on with constituency business, starting with the launch of the industrial yard. For the people of Lima, the coming weeks will show whether he can keep both the legal battle and his development promises on track.

World.title: “Who Will Buy 10 Million Tonnes?” Mwelwa Tells Zambians To Stop Treating Leaders As Messiahs
World.content:
Political analyst Dr Lawrence Mwelwa has urged Zambians to stop treating political leaders as their messiahs. He warned that a nation which worships its leaders loses the power to hold them accountable. Dr Mwelwa said politics should never be a religion and patriotism should never be mistaken for blind loyalty. He said the country was being held back by political messianism and hero worship, in which supporters defend every statement simply because it comes from their preferred leader.

He set out the principle at the heart of his argument in three blunt sentences.

“Political leaders are not messiahs. Politics is not a religion. Patriotism is not blind loyalty to politicians,” Dr Mwelwa said.

The analyst said a country that worships its leaders cannot hold them accountable, and he warned that unquestioning loyalty comes at a cost to national progress. A citizenry that does not think for itself, he argued, can neither generate new ideas nor check those in power. He said the habit of defending leaders at all costs had turned too many supporters into cheerleaders rather than citizens. Dr Mwelwa put the danger in stark terms.

“A nation of robots cannot innovate. A nation of political zombies cannot hold power accountable,” he said.

Dr Mwelwa said citizens must ask hard questions whenever leaders make big promises. He pointed to two of the headline targets now driving national policy: 10 million tonnes of maize and three million tonnes of copper. Leaders, he said, should explain at what cost such production would be achieved and whether it could be sustained. He argued that ambitious numbers without a clear plan behind them should invite questions, not applause.

On maize, the analyst said the country’s present record raised an obvious problem that had not been answered. He said Zambia was already struggling to find markets for its current harvest, which made a fivefold increase difficult to explain.

“If we currently struggle to market two million tonnes of maize, who will purchase 10 million? Those are the questions leaders must answer, and citizens should ask,” Dr Mwelwa said.

Both targets sit at the centre of the Government’s economic plan. The Grow Zambia Agenda aims to raise annual maize production to 10 million metric tonnes while expanding soybean and wheat output, and to lift copper production to three million tonnes a year by 2031. President Hakainde Hichilema has described the copper target as an agenda for economic transformation, industrialisation, export growth and job creation. The Government is also pursuing a target of growing the national cattle herd from 5.2 million to 11 million by 2031, and of reaching 10,000 megawatts of installed electricity generation capacity within the same period.

The maize goal has also drawn concern from the agricultural sector. Agriculture Climate Action Foundation executive director Dr Oliver Kandela Bulaya has warned that proposed increases in corporate income tax in the 2027 National Budget could undermine the very ambitions the Government has set for farming. The proposal would raise the rate for farming and agro-processing businesses from 10 to 15 percent, and for fertiliser manufacturers from 15 to 20 percent. Dr Bulaya said higher input costs could weaken the drive to reach 10 million tonnes of maize and expand soybean and wheat production.

Dr Mwelwa said the kind of questioning he was calling for should not be treated as hostility towards the Government or any leader. He said asking difficult questions was not rebellion but a sign of responsible citizenship. In his view, a healthy democracy needs citizens who weigh promises against evidence rather than accepting them on faith. Leaders who are confident in their plans, he argued, should have nothing to fear from being asked how those plans will work.

His position is set out at length in his book, The Thinking Patriot, which calls on Zambians to examine evidence, question promises and demand practical answers from those who lead them. Dr Mwelwa said leadership must welcome questions rather than worship. He summed up his philosophy in four words.

“Know, think, serve, lead,” he said.

World.title: LAZ Postpones Hearing Of Longwe’s Complaint Against Foreign Affairs Minister Haimbe
World.content:
The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has postponed the hearing of a complaint brought by United Party for National Development (UPND) member Charles Longwe against Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe. Mr Longwe said the matter was adjourned to a date to be advised, because both men were out of the country when it was due to be heard. He has since written to the LAZ asking for a new date so that he can appear in person with his witnesses. The postponement keeps alive an unusual case in which a ruling party member is pursuing a sitting Cabinet minister before the legal profession’s own regulatory body.

Mr Longwe said in a statement that the hearing could not proceed because of travel on both sides. He explained that each party was abroad on the scheduled date.

“The matter was adjourned to a date to be advised because Haimbe was away on official business in Moscow, Russia, while I was in Johannesburg, South Africa,” Mr Longwe said.

In a separate email to the LAZ, addressed to Veronica Nyanga, Mr Longwe formally requested an alternative date for the hearing. He said he was still outside the jurisdiction and that his circumstances were not suitable for him to proceed virtually. He also asked for more time to prepare himself and his witnesses properly. Mr Longwe said matters raised in Mr Haimbe’s response to the complaint had only been brought to his attention that same day.

Mr Longwe said Mr Haimbe had retained lawyers to contest the complaint, a step he said he welcomed. He expressed confidence that the LAZ, as a statutory body, was well equipped to adjudicate the matter and give guidance to all parties. Rather than treating the minister’s legal defence as an obstacle, Mr Longwe presented it as a sign that the process would be argued on its merits. He said he was ready to have the issues tested before the association.

The UPND member insisted that his action was not personal. He said the complaint was made in the national interest, with the sole purpose of safeguarding institutions and upholding the integrity of the court. Mr Longwe urged citizens to be law-abiding and to reject hypocrisy and prejudice. He said every individual should operate under the rule of law regardless of status, wealth, political party, religion, region or whether they serve in the current administration.

The LAZ matter is not Mr Longwe’s only action involving the minister. He has also lodged a complaint with Inspector General of Police Graphael Musamba against Mr Haimbe and UPND Secretary General Batuke Imenda, alleging the fabrication and presentation of documents before the Constitutional Court. Mr Longwe’s complaint concerns two purported meetings of the UPND National Management Committee, which he says were cited in a sworn affidavit filed at the Constitutional Court Registry under cause number 2026/CCZ/009. He alleges that the affidavit was filed by a legal team headed by Mr Haimbe on behalf of Mr Imenda, the first respondent in that matter.

In that complaint to the police, Mr Longwe questioned whether some of the people recorded as attending the meetings could have been present. He said Mr Haimbe was in Nairobi at the 2025 COMESA Summit at the time, while Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane was in Brussels attending the 2025 Global Gateway Forum. Mr Longwe asked the police to investigate and take action if any breach of the law was established. He copied his complaint to the Drug Enforcement Commission and the Police Public Complaints Commission.

Mr Haimbe and his lawyers had not commented on Mr Longwe’s latest statement at the time of publication. The allegations have not been tested before any tribunal, and the LAZ hearing will be the first forum in which the minister’s response is formally weighed. A new date for the hearing is yet to be set.

World.title: “Be Positive For Once”: Hichilema Hits Back At Social Media Negativity, Names New Mines
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has told Zambians to drop the negativity on social media and embrace the opportunities his Government has created. He said citizens who look abroad for a better life often underestimate how tough things are out there. The Head of State said he felt fortunate and lucky to be Zambian, because God had endowed the country with immense natural resources for citizens to tap into and lead productive lives. He was speaking when he hosted a meet-and-greet at State House in Lusaka in honour of the Junior Chipolopolo, the national Under-15 men’s team crowned 2026 FIFA Under-15 Tier B World Cup champions.

President Hichilema said he had noted with sadness social media posts that portrayed the country in a negative light, even though the Government had opened up immense opportunities for citizens to thrive. Drawing on his own years abroad, he challenged the idea that life is easier elsewhere.

“I see on social media a lot of negativity among our citizens, but when you turn the leaf, there is an opportunity. Just be positive for once. Some think it is easier to live in Europe or elsewhere, but it is tough out there because the population is huge and talented,” President Hichilema said.

The President then told a personal story about the friends he left behind when he chose to come home. He said they had dismissed the idea of returning to Zambia, but the tables had since turned in his favour.

“I studied and worked there, and when I told my friends, ‘Let us go back to Zambia,’ they said they could not go back to poverty. Over time, those of us who returned home became far better off, and when I go there, ndine nimabagulila tuma lunch (I am the one who buys them lunch),” he said.

Mr Hichilema challenged citizens to embrace a culture of hard and smart work and to be good ambassadors for their country. He said he would keep showcasing Zambia’s vast economic opportunities as the nation’s chief investment officer. The Head of State said his flagship Grow Zambia Agenda was designed to expand the economy and create opportunities for young people through free education, the school feeding programme, business opportunities and job creation. He added that the agenda was also strengthening social safety nets, including the increased Social Cash Transfer for the elderly.

The President used the gathering to set out where he believes the next wave of wealth will come from. He described North-Western Province as the country’s new Copperbelt, with new mines coming up in Mumbwa in Central Province, Isoka in Muchinga Province and Sinda in Eastern Province. He said the high-resolution aerial geological survey undertaken by his administration would make more tenements available for exploration and development. Mining, he said, was no longer confined to one region.

“The mines is not just the Copperbelt. We have an expansion of mining sector in North-Western Province, Central Province and Eastern Province,” President Hichilema said.

He linked the new mines directly to what the country can afford to spend on its young people. The President said a growing mining sector would widen the national revenue envelope, allowing more investment in youth and the arts.

“We believe we will open a new mine in Sinda, Eastern Province, very soon. A new mine in Isoka very soon, so you can see that the envelope can grow to a level where we can invest more in young people and the arts. When you see those targets, to us they mean a lot more than numbers. They mean economic growth, they mean more revenues and they mean more opportunities to support our children. You see how connected this Grow Zambia Agenda is?” he said.

The Head of State’s remarks build on a mining message his Government has been pressing in recent days. In a speech read on his behalf by Mines and Minerals Development Minister Brenda Tambatamba at the 2026 North-Western Mining and Investment Expo in Solwezi, Mr Hichilema said the mining sector had attracted about US$12 billion in investment commitments over the past five years. He said Zambia contributes about four percent of global copper supply and holds about six percent of the world’s known copper reserves. He described the target of producing three million tonnes of copper a year by 2031 as an agenda for economic transformation, industrialisation, export growth and job creation.

Ms Tambatamba told private sector players in Solwezi that the Government would leave no stone unturned in its drive towards the three-million-tonne target. She urged local suppliers of goods and services to mining companies to align themselves with the Grow Zambia Agenda and take advantage of the Local Content in Mining framework.

“You should start aligning yourselves to the Grow Zambia Agenda, the agenda to unlock the potential of this country,” Ms Tambatamba said.

World.title: Is Zambia Under A State Of Emergency? Changala Demands Answers On Political Detainees
World.content:
Civil rights activist Brebner Changala has demanded that the State tell the nation plainly whether Zambia is under a state of emergency. He said the continued detention of citizens who have not been taken to court has left many Zambians asking whether their constitutional rights are still guaranteed. Mr Changala also appealed to the Human Rights Commission (HRC) to be brave and press the State for answers on the status and whereabouts of all political detainees, particularly those facing sedition charges. He warned that official silence was only feeding speculation and wearing down public confidence in the national justice system.

Putting the question to Government in the plainest terms, Mr Changala said the nation deserved a straight answer.

“The State should clarify to the nation if at all Zambia is under a State of Emergency,” he said.

The activist wants the HRC to put three basic questions to the State: where the political detainees are being held, what their legal status is, and why they are being held at all. He pointed to the case of former Petauke Central Member of Parliament Emmanuel Jay Banda, whose lawyers have filed a writ of habeas corpus challenging his continued detention. Mr Changala said the case had raised serious questions about the rule of law in Zambia. Zambia Police confirmed on 16 October that Mr Banda, who had been on the run, was back in the country and would be formally charged.

Mr Changala explained the legal principle at the centre of his demand. He said habeas corpus exists to prevent the State from holding a person without justification. Under that remedy, the State has a duty to bring a detained person before a court and explain the legal basis for keeping him or her in custody. That duty, he argued, cannot be set aside however serious the allegations against a suspect may be.

On how far the State’s powers of detention go, Mr Changala was blunt.

“The Constitution does not allow indefinite detention,” he said.

He said that if the country was not under a state of emergency, then every detention should follow the law. In that case, all citizens should enjoy the freedoms guaranteed under the Constitution, including the right to liberty, freedom of movement and freedom from arbitrary detention. Mr Changala said Zambians needed to know which of the two situations they were living under. For him, the absence of an answer has become a matter of national concern in its own right.

He then posed the question he says ordinary citizens are now asking among themselves.

“Are we still a democracy governed by the Constitution, or are we operating under emergency powers that have not been declared?” Mr Changala asked.

The activist named the offices he believes owe the country an explanation. He urged the Office of the Attorney General, the Minister of Home Affairs and the Inspector General of Police to issue a clear public statement on the matter. Mr Changala also turned to the Judiciary, urging the courts to act swiftly on habeas corpus applications. Delayed justice in such matters, he said, amounted to a denial of freedom.

Mr Banda’s lawyer, Kambwa Aongola, who is handling the habeas corpus application, had promised to comment but had not done so by publication.

The question of how citizens hold power to account also drew comment from political analyst Dr Lawrence Mwelwa, who urged Zambians to stop treating political leaders as messiahs. Dr Mwelwa said the country was being held back by political messianism and hero worship, in which supporters defend every statement simply because it comes from their preferred leader. He warned that patriotism should not be mistaken for blind loyalty, and that a nation which worships its leaders loses the ability to hold them accountable.

Setting out his position in three short lines, Dr Mwelwa drew a firm boundary between citizenship and devotion.

“Political leaders are not messiahs. Politics is not a religion. Patriotism is not blind loyalty to politicians,” he said.

Dr Mwelwa said asking difficult questions was not rebellion but a sign of responsible citizenship. That is the same ground on which Mr Changala has now placed his demand: the State must say, on the record, whether the country is still living under the ordinary protections of the Constitution.

World.title: Beijing global media summit launches AI Newsroom standards
World.content:
Global media experts at the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing have launched a global initiative to establish Artificial Intelligence application standards in newsrooms.

The experts have since called for joint international governance and digital safety guardrails in the intelligent age.

The initiative, dubbed the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards, aims to ensure responsible and trustworthy use of AI in journalism while safeguarding the credibility of professional media.

The summit, which took place on Saturday, November 7, 2026 ran under the theme “Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action,” and was jointly organised by Xinhua News Agency and the People’s Government of Beijing Municipality.

It brought together nearly 500 media executives, politicians, think tank leaders, and delegates from the United Nations and other international bodies.

Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, Li Shulei, attended the summit alongside host officials to outline global media cooperation strategies.

Speaking during the opening ceremony, Secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, Yin Li, urged global news organisations to stand together in driving technological progress.

Mr Yin highlighted that the gathering coincides with the 95th Anniversary of Xinhua News Agency and noted that Chinese President Xi Jinping attaches great importance to the event.

“Media should bear social responsibility, foster peace, justice and democracy, and leverage new technology to advance human progress,” Mr Yin said.

He added that Beijing is ready to work with global media outlets to advance joint technological development and foster international exchanges.

And Xinhua News Agency President Fu Hua emphasised that AI enhances newsroom efficiency, diversifies storytelling, and streamlines workflows, but warned that technological adoption must come with strict verification.

“AI is able to enhance news productivity, diversify storytelling, and build intelligent media. However, AI calls for the erection of safety guardrails to ensure the credibility of professional media, “he added.

Mr Fu stressed that human editorial judgment and technology must work in tandem with AI to maintain public trust.

Addressing the assembly, United Nations Director General at the Office in Geneva, Tatiana Valovaya, highlighted the need to bridge the digital divide that ensures that developing nations benefit equally from AI advancements.

Ms Valovaya stated that while AI helps break language barriers and speeds up news production, it poses severe risks in data privacy violations and algorithmic bias.

“The risks are too consequential to leave to individual countries, hence the need for joint international cooperation on media governance,” Ms Valovaya said.

She called on media entities to shift from mere dialogue to joint implementation.

Media experts and delegates at the summit underscored the need for verification mechanisms capable of tracing content origins to counter fake news and digital misinformation.

Kenya Broadcasting Corporation (KBC) Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Agnes Nguna, also commended Xinhua News Agency for ensuring African media institutions are integrated into global technological advancements.

Ms Nguna praised China’s collaborative approach, stating that Xinhua News Agency has consistently treated African media organisations not as a case study, but as equal partners on the global stage.

Zambia took part in the summit and was represented by members of staff from led by Director Loyce Saili.

The department is positioning itself to be abreast with changing technological advancements in the media space for improved service delivery.

During his second term inaugural parliamentary speech, President Hakainde Hichilema encouraged the adoption of new technology in achieving the grow Zambia agenda.

World.title: President Hichilema leads remembrance day commemorations
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has led war veterans, service chiefs and Diplomats accredited to Zambia in commemorating Remembrance Day at the National Cenotaph in Lusaka.

President Hichilema laid wreaths in remembrance of Zambian, Commonwealth and foreign soldiers who died in various wars.

He was joined by Cabinet Ministers, Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa, senior Government officials, service chiefs, members of the diplomatic corps and several war veterans.

The solemn ceremony honoured men and women in uniform who paid the ultimate price in service to the nation and to peace.

Delivering the homily, Zambia Army Director General for Religious and Moral Services Branch, Brigadier General Reverend Shadreck Mwale, said those being remembered left behind families, children, dreams and unfinished stories so that others could enjoy peace.

He challenged those present to reflect on whether the fallen heroes would be proud if they returned and examined the nation today.

Brig. Gen. Mwale said the world is changing, with technology, security threats and society itself evolving, but certain values must never change, integrity, discipline, patriotism, compassion and responsibility.

He quoted John 15:13, greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

“Those we remember today did not give because they expected to gain, they gave because there was something greater to protect,” he said.

Brig. Gen. Mwale said service is not merely wearing a uniform, occupying an office or enjoying privileges, but accepting responsibility for the lives and welfare of others.

“Whether a soldier, police officer, public servant, teacher, parent or national leader, everyone has a responsibility to make somebody else’s life better,” he said.

“The true measure of service is not how much we have gained from our positions, but our contribution to humanity while in our positions,” he said.

The Zambia Army Director General for Religious and Moral Services Branch further urged Zambians to change their methods but never compromise their values, and to embrace technology, innovation and new ways of serving.

He added that technology can make people efficient and training can make them competent, but neither can automatically make them honest and compassionate.

“A uniform may command attention, authority may command obedience, but integrity earns trust and character earns respect,” Brig Gen Mwale said.

He warned against becoming so powerful that leaders forget the humanity of those they serve, and urged citizens to live a life worth remembering.

He said one day ranks will be handed over, offices occupied by others and uniforms worn by another generation, and the question will be what remains.

“Will people remember us for positions we occupied or for the lives we touched?” he asked.

Brig. Gen. Mwale encouraged those still serving not to allow disappointment to destroy their commitment, temptation to corrupt their character, or to forget why they began serving.

He said the next generation is watching, and that while Zambians remember yesterday’s heroes today, they must also ask what kind of heroes they are becoming today.

He concluded by praying that those who sacrificed their lives may never be forgotten, that their families may find comfort, and that those who serve today may be strengthened with courage, wisdom and integrity.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 9, 2026
World.content:
Seven Killed, More Than 100 Injured in Egypt Train Collision

At least seven people have been killed and more than 100 injured after two passenger trains collided in Egypt's Giza province, south of Cairo. Authorities said one train struck the rear of another while travelling along the line between Cairo and the southern city of Aswan, causing one train to derail and several carriages to overturn. More than 50 ambulances were dispatched to the scene. Emergency crews and cranes worked to clear the railway line. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi ordered an investigation and called for anyone found negligent to be held accountable. The cause of the collision has not yet been established. The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

ANC Suffers Worst-Ever Election Result in South Africa

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa's Electoral Commission has officially declared the 2026 Local Government Elections free and fair, with national voter turnout reaching 52%, an increase from 45.9% in the 2021 elections. The African National Congress emerged as the largest party with 30.76% of the vote. The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MK Party) came third overall with 9.76%. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%. However, the ANC recorded its worst-ever electoral performance, losing its outright majority in several major metropolitan areas amid growing voter dissatisfaction over municipal service delivery, unemployment, crime, and corruption. The DA retained control of Cape Town, while 127 of the country's 213 municipalities have hung councils, setting the stage for coalition negotiations. The IEC said that the elections were largely peaceful, with 90% of voters surveyed considering the process free and 91% describing it as fair.

34 Killed as Migrant Boat Sinks Off Senegal Coast

At least 34 people have been killed after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal near Kebemer, about 180 kilometres north of Dakar. The vessel was reportedly carrying people attempting to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the dangerous Atlantic migration route, which has claimed thousands of lives in recent years. Senegalese authorities initially reported that 21 bodies had been recovered and one person rescued, with search operations continuing as the death toll rose. The tragedy comes as authorities on El Hierro in Spain's Canary Islands have declared an emergency following a sharp increase in migrant arrivals. More than 3,300 people have arrived on the island in about 30 boats over the last month or so, sparking concerns about pressure on local facilities and emergency services.

Ruto Challenges Kenya's Opposition to Present Development Plans

Kenyan President William Ruto has challenged opposition leaders to present clear development plans, warning Kenyans against gambling with the country's future by electing politicians who lack concrete solutions to national challenges. Speaking during an interdenominational church service in Nyamira County, Ruto said political leaders should be judged by their policies and ability to address issues such as the high cost of living, unemployment, education, agriculture and infrastructure. He defended his administration's development record, citing investments in roads, healthcare, electricity and education, including the employment of 100,000 teachers. Ruto also announced that the government had allocated 1.2 billion Kenyan shillings to modernise tea factories in western Rift Valley, with further funding expected in the next budget. He additionally announced 11 billion shillings for 180 kilometres of tarmac roads in Nyamira, alongside plans for a new hospital and an international stadium.

UN Warns of Critical Aid Shortages as Sudan Displacement Crisis Deepens

United Nations agencies have appealed for urgent international assistance to support millions of people displaced by the ongoing war in Sudan, warning that humanitarian supplies are running dangerously low. The fighting that broke out in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has left millions in need of shelter, food and other critical assistance. The UN estimated that 15.4 million people urgently require shelter, but funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can currently assist only about one in 10 people in need. The International Organization for Migration said its emergency warehouses are now empty, while the UN refugee agency warned that women and children make up three-quarters of the country's internally displaced population. More than 5.2 million people have returned to their areas of origin. Many cannot access their homes or basic services because of destruction and looting. Sudan's 2026 humanitarian response plan, which requires 2.9 billion dollars, has received only 47% of its funding.

Close 

Somalia's HirShabelle Capital to Be Relocated to Hiiraan

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud said that the regional capital of HirShabelle will be allocated to the Hiiraan region in an effort to address growing political tensions and grievances among local communities, particularly the Hawadle clan. Speaking at the inauguration of HirShabelle's new leadership, the president said residents of Hiiraan had been granted the right to host the regional capital but would need to identify a suitable city where government officials could live and work. His announcement follows growing dissatisfaction among political groups in Beledweyne over political representation, the location of the regional capital and the leadership of the HirShabelle administration, which comprises Hiiraan and Middle Shabelle regions. Mohamud urged residents and opposition groups to remain calm and avoid retaliatory actions, saying their demands had been addressed. However, the relocation process still requires a formal decision by HirShabelle's leadership in line with the regional constitution. The newly appointed Vice President, Abdifitah Hassan Afrah, is also holding talks in Beledweyne to ease tensions and encourage dialogue.

World.title: South Africa: Three Killed in Grassy Park Shooting - South African News Briefs - November 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Three Killed in Grassy Park Shooting

Three men have been shot dead and another wounded in a suspected gang-related shooting in Grassy Park on the Cape Flats, reports SABC News. Police said that the victims, aged between 22 and 39, were sitting outside a premises in Glen Close when occupants of a white Toyota Tazz opened fire before fleeing. Police Spokesperson FC Van Wyk has said that no arrests have been made yet. He said detectives from the Anti-Gang Unit are probing the incident.

Cat Matlala Set to Testify at Madlanga Commission

The Madlanga Commission resumes its public hearings with alleged crime kingpin Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala expected to testify about his alleged links to senior police officials and individuals involved in criminal activity, reports EWN. The inquiry is also expected to hear from Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, KwaZulu-Natal Police Commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi and Crime Intelligence head Dumisani Khumalo. The commission is expected to submit its final report to President Cyril Ramaphosa by 25 January 2027.

Senzo Meyiwa Murder Trial Resumes in Pretoria

The Senzo Meyiwa murder trial is set to resume at the High Court in Pretoria, reports SABC News. This follows the conclusion of testimony by a second defence witness for accused number three, Mthobisi Mncube. Witness Thalente Ntombela disputed key state witness Constable Sizwe Zungu's account, accusing him of lying about being with the five accused on the day Meyiwa was murdered in 2014. Ntombela testified that accused number one, Muzi Sibiya, only moved to Gauteng in 2017 and had never been there before.

World.title: Africa: Rethinking the Frequency of UN Climate Summits After COP31
World.content:
guest column

As world leaders and critical stakeholders converge on Türkiye for the 31st UN climate summit, a difficult but necessary question hangs over the familiar ritual. The poser is: after more than three decades, is an annual COP still the best way to advance the global climate agenda?

The two-week conference opening on November 9 in Antalya will gather presidents, diplomats, scientists and activists to bring the climate emergency into sharp focus. Nearly 100 agenda items have been tabled for negotiations, ranging from climate finance and adaptation to loss and damage and energy transition.

I watched that familiar choreography up close at COP29 in Baku in 2024 – the endless pavilions, the late-night huddles over bracketed text, the stirring speeches about urgency followed by painstaking negotiations over wording. It was a powerful reminder of both the value and the limits of these gatherings.

But beyond the elegant speeches and communiques, we must ask whether the annual frequency of the summits has become a substitute for effectiveness. The case for moving from annual to biennial summits is not a call to retreat. Far from it. It is a plea for a more strategic, cost-effective and results-driven model of climate governance.



Success should be measured not by how often governments meet as output, but by how faithfully their pledges translate into cleaner air, safer communities and more resilient economies in places like Borno, Turkana, the Mekong Delta or the Amazon Basin as outcome. That conversation on the frequency of the summit deserves space at COP31, even if outside the formal negotiating rooms, for many reasons.

First is cost, and the burden is no longer just an African story. Hosting a COP is a massive logistical undertaking: security, accommodation, transport and conference infrastructure for 40,000 to 80,000 participants. The UK spent an estimated 300 million pounds to host COP26 in Glasgow. For any host, it is a fiscal stretch.

For African economies already juggling debt distress, food insecurity and energy poverty, the bill can be prohibitive. It also explains why, despite bearing some of the harshest consequences of the climate crisis, Africa has hosted the summit only five times in 30 years – COP7 in Marrakech in 2001, COP12 in Nairobi in 2006, COP17 in Durban in 2011, COP22 in Marrakech in 2016, and COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022.

The same hosting fatigue is felt elsewhere. Small Island Developing States, which face an existential threat from rising sea level, have never hosted a COP due to scale and cost. Latin America, home to the Amazon, has hosted only three times. When the venue rotates, the Global South often has to build a temporary city from scratch.

Then there is the carbon cost, which is becoming hard to ignore. A 2026 study in Communications Sustainability estimated that air travel by Party and Observer delegates from COP1 to COP29 generated about 710,282 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. More telling is the quantum trajectory: from 2,959 tonnes in Berlin in 1995 to 76,931 tonnes in Baku last year, an increase of roughly 2,500 percent!

Those figures do not capture the full footprint of the summits, but they reveal an uncomfortable paradox that delegates themselves whisper about in the corridors – thousands boarding long-haul flights to discuss how to reduce emissions. A biennial rhythm would halve the frequency of these mega-gatherings and create room for more virtual consultations, regional climate weeks from Africa to Asia-Pacific, and leaner forms of engagement.

There is also the question of implementation. Climate action needs time, and the most vulnerable need even more of it. The annual cycle leaves ministries in a near-permanent state of negotiation. Pledges made in November are barely converted into national budgets and sub-national projects before the next round of talks begins.

We see this at home. Recent floods in Nigeria displaced over a million people. Lake Chad has shrunk by more than 90 percent since the 1960s, deepening conflict between farmers and herders across sub-Sahara Africa. The Sahel is heating 1.5 times faster than the global average.

The pattern is global, and the costs are increasingly human. Global climate impacts now include catastrophic events such as the glacier collapse in Nepal that claimed over 1,000 lives with about 5,000 missing, and extreme heat in Europe linked to tens of thousands of excess deaths. In Pakistan, the 2022 floods caused over 30 billion dollars in damages before its recovery plan could be fully funded by the next COP.

In Brazil, deforestation rates in the Amazon fluctuate faster than annual finance pledges can track. In Vanuatu and Tuvalu, leaders travel each year to plead for survival, yet the Loss and Damage fund agreed at COP27 took another two years to become operational. These are not problems that can be solved between COPs.

A two-year interval would change the incentive. Delegates would return not with a fresh set of promises, but with evidence: how much of the long-promised climate finance actually reached adaptation in Africa, how many hectares of the Great Green Wall were planted, how many communities in Southeast Asia have embraced energy transition, and how many homes in Florida or the Philippines were retrofitted for resilience. That would shift COP from a stage for declarations to a platform for accountability.

Finally, there is credibility. When annual summits end with familiar hollow language and thin follow-through, public fatigue sets in. In Baku, participants listened to the chilling tales of young activists from Kenya and Indonesia who had travelled 48 hours by bus and plane to be there. Their frustration was palpable: "We come every year, but the floods still come every year too."

That fatigue is now visible across continents. Polls in Europe show declining trust that COP pledges will be met. In the US, cities like Phoenix and Miami are spending billions on heat and flood adaptation while federal negotiating positions shift with each election cycle. Communities losing homes in Maiduguri, harvests in Malawi or fishing grounds in Fiji are not waiting for another declaration; they are waiting for irrigation, crop insurance, early warning systems and resilient infrastructure.

Close 

Spacing the major conferences two years apart could restore a sense of occasion and scrutiny. Media coverage would be less routine, assessment by environmental rights advocacy groups would be more substantive, and the political cost of empty promises more palpable. The intervening year should not be a pause, but an accountability window.

This does not mean switching off climate diplomacy every other year. Technical negotiations must continue. The UNFCCC already has the architecture for annual synthesis reports, implementation reviews and regional climate weeks. What changes is not the continuity of work, but the frequency of the grand summit.

Yes, critics will worry that a biennial COP could sap momentum. That concern is valid, but urgency should compel better action, not simply more meetings. The UNFCCC has been indispensable in keeping climate on the global agenda. But no institution should be exempt from asking whether its operating model still fits the challenge it was built to address.

COP31 offers more than a negotiating deadline. It offers a moment to ask how we can make climate diplomacy work better for those who need it most. We all need it.

Aliu Akoshile, Editor-in-Chief of NatureNews Africa, writes via eic@naturenews.africa

World.title: Kenya: TikTok Removes 750,000 Videos in Kenya Over Content Violations
World.content:
Nairobi — TikTok removed more than 750,000 videos in Kenya for violating its community guidelines in the second quarter of 2026, highlighting the growing operational and regulatory demands facing digital platforms as online content consumption expands.

The short-video platform said it took down 750,185 videos between April and June, with 99.8 percent removed before users reported them, while 93.8 percent were taken down within 24 hours of publication.

The removals point to the increasing reliance on artificial intelligence and automated moderation systems to manage content at scale, as technology companies face mounting pressure to address misinformation, harmful material and online safety concerns.

TikTok also interrupted 80,640 LIVE sessions in Kenya during the period for violations of its community guidelines, while removing more than 46,000 accounts suspected to belong to children below the age of 13.



"About 99.8 percent of the videos removed in Kenya were taken down proactively before anyone reported them, and 93.8 percent were removed within 24 hours of being posted," the company said in its Q2 Community Guidelines Enforcement Report.

Globally, TikTok removed approximately 188.3 million videos out of more than 42.2 billion videos published during the quarter, representing about 0.4 percent of total uploads.

Automated systems accounted for 97.4 percent of global video removals, underscoring the platform's growing dependence on artificial intelligence to identify and enforce content violations.

However, the company reinstated approximately 6.3 million videos globally following successful appeals, raising questions about the accuracy of automated moderation and the balance between content safety and users' freedom of expression.

In Kenya, nearly 11,000 videos were removed under TikTok's policies on edited media and artificial intelligence-generated content as the platform stepped up efforts to address the risks associated with synthetic media.

The company has also introduced an in-app AI Literacy Hub in Kenya to educate users on identifying AI-generated content and using the technology responsibly.

The developments come as digital platforms face increasing scrutiny over child protection, misinformation and the economic and social consequences of harmful online content.

TikTok said it requires creators to label realistic AI-generated material and uses Content Credentials technology to help identify content created or significantly altered using artificial intelligence.

World.title: Kenya: Murkomen Vows to Isolate Paul Mackenzie in Prison Over Fears of Radicalising Inmates
World.content:
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children.

Nairobi — Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has vowed to ensure controversial preacher Paul Mackenzie remains in exclusive custody, citing fears that he could radicalise other inmates if allowed to interact freely with them.

Murkomen said the government would maintain strict custody arrangements for Mackenzie, who is facing charges linked to the Shakahola deaths, amid concerns over the potential influence of his teachings on other prisoners.

Speaking during a church service in Ikolomani Constituency, Kakamega on Sunday, Murkomen said the government would provide a secluded area for Mackenzie to serve his sentence, restricting his interaction with other prisoners.



"We will provide a secluded area to hold him to make sure that there will be no radicalisation again by the type of Mackenzies in this country," Murkomen said.

The CS's remarks followed intelligence reports indicating that Mackenzie had allegedly attempted to radicalise fellow inmates and police officers while in custody.

Murkomen said the arrangement was intended to prevent the preacher from using the prison environment to spread extremist religious teachings or influence vulnerable inmates.

The government is concerned that other prisoners could adopt Mackenzie's teachings and potentially establish similar movements after their release

The announcement comes days after the High Court in Mombasa sentenced Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for his role in the Shakahola massacre, which claimed the lives of 191 people, including 190 children and one adult.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache handed Mackenzie consecutive 100-year sentences for 183 counts of murder by starvation and eight counts involving direct homicide.

Twenty-eight co-accused were also convicted, receiving prison sentences ranging between 10 and 160 years.

The court found that Mackenzie orchestrated a system of religious indoctrination in which followers were instructed to starve themselves and their children in preparation for what he described as meeting Jesus.

The prosecution presented forensic evidence, medical reports and witness testimonies detailing how the fasting was enforced through intimidation, violence and confinement.

Murkomen commended the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP), the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and the Judiciary for their role in securing Mackenzie's conviction.

He said the government would take firm measures against religious extremism and radicalisation while safeguarding the constitutional right to freedom of worship.

Close 

"The Government will take firm measures to address religious extremism and radicalisation, without undermining the constitutional right to the freedom of worship," Murkomen said in remarks following the sentencing.

The Shakahola tragedy emerged in 2023 after investigators uncovered mass graves in Kilifi County, eventually recovering hundreds of bodies from the forest.

Mackenzie's sentencing marks a major development in the prosecution of the killings, although he continues to face separate proceedings relating to other alleged offences.

World.title: Senegal: Many Killed After Migrant Boat Sinks Off Senegal
World.content:
More than 1,300 people were reported dead or missing after embarking on the Central Mediterranean sea route to Europe last year, according to UN migration agency (IOM) data. The photo shows migrants and refugees being rescued in the Mediterranean after drifting in an overcrowded wooden boat.

The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

At least 34 people were killed after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal, according to the Senegalese Press Agency.

Thousands have died in recent years after embarking on boats from the Senegalese coast in order to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the perilous Atlantic route.

Initially, the Senegalese Ministry of the Interior stated that only one person had been rescued from the capsizing and that 21 bodies had been recovered.



The ministry added that the toll was "provisional" and that search operations were still ongoing.

The incident occurred near Kebemer, some 180 kilometers (around 112 miles) north of the capital, Dakar.

On Saturday, the ministry stressed the government's "determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries."

Senegalese authorities said they intercepted 142 migrants on a similar boat aimed at reaching Spanish territory on Friday. The boat included nationals of multiple West African countries.

El Hierro island declares emergency over migrant arrivals

Authorities on El Hierro Island in the Canary Islands declared an emergency on Saturday after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

El Hierro officials say that over 3,300 people have arrived on around 30 boats since the start of the month.

"We are very concerned... by this sharp increase in arrivals," Alpidio Armas, head of the El Hierro regional council, told Spanish television.

"This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions," he added.

Armas said that conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable."

El Hierro is home to about 11,400 residents.

Migrant arrivals reached a record high of 46,000 in 2024. Afterwards, arrivals have fallen sharply due to increased surveillance and cooperation with African countries.

World.title: South Africa: South Africa's ANC Hit by Worst-Ever Performance in Local Elections
World.content:
The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance, with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls.

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

ANC secretary general says outcome 'catastrophic'

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC's steady decline with voters

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

Close 

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

DA opposition holds large cities

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

World.title: Egypt: Egypt Train Crash Leaves Several Dead, Over 100 Injured
World.content:
A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying more than 100 passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.

At least seven people were killed in the train collision in Egypt on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.

The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.

Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.

The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.

El-Sissi says incident being investigated

In a social media post, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."

The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.

In recent years, Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines, but is still facing safety issues and repeated crashes while attempting to revamp its aging rail network.

World.title: JOHN MIZE: Democrat victory just means the fight for life has added importance
World.content:

Tuesday, Nov. 3, Americans cast their votes and turned congressional majorities against the pro-life cause.

It may be easy to despair, especially following two years of strong, pro-life leadership that accomplished a historic year of defunding many abortion providers from federal Medicaid dollars, but the pro-life movement has fought through hostile waters before — and won.

Here’s how we navigate the next two years.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Defending legacy pro-life provisions must be a first priority. We have known for months that the Hyde Amendment, protecting taxpayers from being forced to directly fund abortions, has been in the crosshairs for the next pro-abortion Congress.

But conscience protections for healthcare entities that choose not to provide abortions under the Weldon Amendment may also be on the line.

This pro-abortion majority wants to make Americans complicit in their extremism.

Both the Hyde and Weldon amendments have survived pro-abortion majorities before, including the 117th Congress. In 2021, the House Appropriations Committee advanced a Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education spending bill that omitted both Hyde and Weldon rider language.

Even though both chambers were led by pro-abortion majorities, pro-life organizations were able to rally, telling Congress that these protections are not up for negotiation.

This is the same message we must carry over the next two years.

Congress must also be reminded that preserving these riders is in its own best interest, attaining bipartisan public support.

According to the 2026 Knights of Columbus/Marist polling, 54% of Americans opposed taxpayer funding of abortion and 63% support conscience protections for healthcare providers.

'EXTREMIST' AND 'BARBARIC': MASSACHUSETTS DEMOCRATS BREAK RANKS OVER NEW ABORTION LAW

Pro-abortion members of Congress are also likely to urge the passage of the Women’s Health Protection Act. This bill is intended to codify the state of abortion extremism under Roe v. Wade, preventing any state or locality from restricting abortion before viability.

If this became law, it would also erase necessary safeguards for women like mandatory ultrasounds to confirm pregnancy or rule out ectopic pregnancies, eliminate waiting periods and allow unrestricted mail-order abortion.

Both the Hyde and Weldon amendments have survived pro-abortion majorities before, including the 117th Congress.

What pro-life groups have more accurately called the "Women’s Health Endangerment Act" has been fended off since it was first introduced in 2013. Under the 117th Congress, this bill passed the House of Representatives but did not reach the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome cloture in the Senate.

However, this new Congress is signaling less political restraint and may eliminate the filibuster to evade the necessary checks-and-balances of cloture. Pro-life groups must be unified in opposing this extreme tactic.

It is essential to remember that Congress is only one cog in the political machine, and we can still fight for life within the Trump administration and among the many states.

The pro-life movement has overcome many cycles of pro-abortion control since Roe and yet still was able to achieve the historic victory in Dobbs not too long after the 117th Congress.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Administrative agency action is still on the table. The Food and Drug Administration’s review of the abortion pill is still pending, and its latest update to the courts suggest final results will be available to the public by March 2027.

Restoring in-person dispensing requirements as a minimum repair to mifepristone’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy is still on the table. It’s even more essential now that the agency’s review is airtight and able to withstand partisan scrutiny.

The Trump administration still has the authority to finally rescind the Biden-era Office of Legal Counsel’s politicized Comstock opinion and fully enforcing the law through the Department of Justice.

Stopping the mail-order abortion scheme harming women across the country will be essential to combatting the losses of this week.

Still, we must not waver from our collective efforts in all 50 states. Losses in Texas showed us that we cannot become complacent in protecting life where we believe it to be the most secure.

World.title: PAUL TELLER: Foreign investors are milking US taxpayers. Congress should stop them
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

America has become too litigious. Even the slightest wrong seems to yield a lawsuit these days, lining the pockets of trial attorneys who profit from pitting Americans against Americans. But did you know that a new brand of lawsuit has emerged in recent years that has foreigners fueling the litigation and then taking the winnings at a lower — or even zero — tax rate?

That’s not fair and needs to stop.

Here’s how it works. A foreign sovereign wealth fund or other investment fund overseas eyes a potential or existing lawsuit in the United States and speculates that it could earn a significant financial return by contracting with one party, often the plaintiff’s side, to underwrite the large and growing costs of the lawsuit. When the plaintiff receives a financial reward from the court, the winnings tend to be taxed as ordinary income (i.e., at a higher rate).

WAVE OF OVERLOOKED 'LEFT-WING' LAWSUITS COULD COME WITH AN UNEXPECTED PRICE TAG FOR AMERICANS

But when the foreign underwriter that financed that same lawsuit collects its share of the winnings (decided in advance as a condition of funding the lawsuit), that money can be treated as a capital gain and therefore taxed at a lower rate than the plaintiff herself pays. And since foreign investors generally owe no U.S. tax on capital gains from American sources, the tax rate for the foreigner is often zero, even as the American plaintiff pays the ordinary income tax rate.

Again — not fair and needs to stop.

TREASURY FLAGS $8B IN SUSPICIOUS FOREIGN-DIRECTED TRANSFERS THROUGH US MONEY SERVICES FIRMS

Recently, in a Capitol Hill hearing, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply criticized this scheme of foreigners fueling American lawsuits and running away with a greater share of the winnings. Bessent is exactly right: Foreign financing of American lawsuits is indeed "a malignancy" on our judicial system, as he called it, that is draining money out of the U.S. economy, driving up prices across the board for American consumers and further encouraging litigiousness in American society.

As the secretary noted, these foreign financiers are asserting preferential tax treatment, avoiding U.S. taxes entirely and getting away with it. The result: American taxpayers are in fact subsidizing a practice that is driving up costs for American businesses and fostering higher prices for all Americans at the grocery store and at the pump.

SUPREME COURT CLIMATE CASE COULD BANKRUPT OIL COMPANIES, SEND GAS PRICES SOARING, EXPERTS WARN

Unbelievable!

What’s particularly offensive about this practice is that the impetus behind the capital gains tax rate being lower than the ordinary income tax rate on the same amount of money is the wholeheartedly American desire to reward risk-taking investment aimed at production and growth. But the foreign hedge funds and other international wealth funds that underwrite American lawsuits at the lower or zero tax rate are not investing in economic growth. Quite the opposite. They are seeking to profit from the restraint of growth, from lawsuits that siphon resources from the profit margins and bottom lines of American producers.

REPUBLICANS AREN’T STOPPING: GOP TO UNLEASH ANOTHER ‘BIG, BEAUTIFUL BILL’ WITH A NEW TARGET

Outrageous!

Congress should close this unAmerican, abusive loophole this year and put the billions of dollars in increased revenue toward pro-growth tax relief in America. In typical Beltway fashion, some politicos will assert that there’s not enough time to make this fix this year. That’s inaccurate. Right now, Congress is scheduled to be in session for at least five more weeks this calendar year, and there is room in the calendar to schedule additional days and (God forbid!) late nights in session. Yes, this might mean coming back to the office after scurrying around town to lavish holiday parties, but so be it. This issue is worth it.

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

Many in Congress, including House Republican leaders, have said that this year they want to pass another "reconciliation" bill (a special type of legislation not subject to the Senate filibuster, regarding revenues going in and out of the Treasury). That would be the ideal legislative vehicle in which to fix this foreign loophole and direct the resulting revenues back to the American taxpayer.

As the secretary noted, these foreign financiers are asserting preferential tax treatment, avoiding U.S. taxes entirely and getting away with it.

But if Congress can't get its act together soon, the White House should work with Bessent to see what actions the executive branch may legally take on its own to address this boon for foreign financiers.

Either way, this would be an easy win for American consumers and businesses, while defunding left-wing trial attorneys who continue to enrich themselves on the backs of excessive lawsuits.
