World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's FAA touts new AI-powered tool helping thousands of passengers avoid flight delays
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

EXCLUSIVE: The Trump administration's new AI-supported air traffic management tool has already helped reroute nearly 180 flights carrying approximately 24,000 passengers to avoid congestion, cutting flight times by more than 10 minutes on average, according to new Department of Transportation (DOT) data shared exclusively with Fox News Digital.

The Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART, has been operational for nearly six weeks, helping air traffic controllers identify more fuel-efficient routes and anticipate potential disruptions.

According to DOT, the technology has also saved nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight on average, offering an early glimpse of how the Trump administration hopes to reduce flight delays and cancellations.

TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE

"Under President Trump, we are making historic progress to revitalize air traffic control and improve the passenger experience for millions of Americans," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Duffy also said the technology would deliver broader benefits as the program expands.

"SMART will slash frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices."

One example came in October when a flight carrying 147 passengers from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Orlando International Airport avoided expected congestion after SMART recommended an alternative route.

SEVERE TURBULENCE DIVERTS NEW YORK CITY FLIGHT TO MIAMI, 8 INJURED

The flight had been scheduled to depart during a period when congestion was expected along its original path. SMART identified a route farther west, which air traffic controllers accepted, shortening the journey by 11 nautical miles and saving six minutes of flight time, according to DOT.

The technology combines 200 data streams, including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics, into a centralized platform.

Its AI-supported engine helps aviation specialists anticipate where congestion could develop and recommend more efficient routes before congestion builds.

The technology is also designed to improve how the FAA manages severe weather, a source of disruptions for U.S. air travelers.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

According to a DOT fact sheet, the agency's existing approach involves blocking off large rectangular sections of airspace affected by storms, even though weather systems are often irregularly shaped and safe corridors may remain available.

SMART is intended to provide a clearer picture of changing weather conditions, allowing aviation specialists to identify routes around storms and determine when restricted airspace can safely reopen.

Despite its AI-supported capabilities, SMART does not independently direct aircraft or replace human air traffic controllers.

A team of aviation specialists analyzes and validates SMART's data before sending scheduling recommendations to the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center. Those recommendations are then forwarded to local air traffic control facilities, where officials decide whether to accept them.

The initiative comes as the nation's busiest airports handle millions of flights annually.

According to DOT, approximately 6.5 million flights operate each year at the nation's 30 busiest airports. About 300,000 receive reroutes before departure, while 3.6 million experience airborne reroutes, vectoring or holding.

The FAA initially limited SMART's rollout to the National Capital Region in September before beginning validation efforts with air route traffic control centers in Miami, Jacksonville and Atlanta in October.

The agency plans to continue testing the system as it works toward expanding SMART to all 22 air traffic control centers nationwide.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While the early results involve a relatively small share of domestic U.S. flights, DOT says the technology is intended to help airlines operate more predictable schedules and ease pressure on air traffic controllers.

For travelers, the Trump administration's goal is fewer delays for passengers, shorter flights and less time lost to flight congestion.

World.title: Congress returns to brutal lame-duck stretch with shutdown deadline, leadership races: 'Closet is full of s—'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Lawmakers are back on Capitol Hill this week for the first time since the midterm elections, and Republicans have a slew of responsibilities in front of them before Democrats take over the reins of power in January.

"The lame duck is like that closet in your house where everybody's throwing a bunch of s--- into it," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. "And the closet is full of s--- now, and now we got to figure out how to get it all out of there."

Current federal funding levels run out on Dec. 11, and without another deal in place, Congress risks plunging the government into another shutdown. Some Democrats signaled to POLITICO that they could use President Donald Trump’s war in Iran as leverage in spending talks — which could very well lead to a fiscal cliff that could paralyze federal agencies.

But one House Republican, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told Fox News Digital they expect another short-term extension of current funding levels, called a continuing resolution (CR), through February or March of next year. The current CR was passed to cover the end of the last fiscal year ending Sept. 30 through next month.

TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

"No one wants a shutdown, I would think," that House Republican said. "Not even Dems."

HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS

Other legislative priorities Congress will have to reckon with in the next few weeks include the farm bill, which is passed every five years and sets food and agriculture policy for the country. Republicans are also aiming to pass a bill to revitalize the country’s transportation infrastructure and a bipartisan tax package before the end of the year.

Then there is also the looming debt ceiling deadline coming in January, which Trump will likely call on Republicans to deal with before Congress changes hands.

GOP lawmakers shared varying levels of optimism when asked about how productive they would be.

"It can be. It should be," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., said. "But my faith in some of my Senate colleagues is not real high, because I feel like they have a personal vendetta towards the president, and it's more about that than it is about passing legislation. We should do our business in Congress."

Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, said, "I think it's gonna be difficult to get a whole lot done. But we have done a lot of work leading up to the lame-duck session to prepare for passing a number of important bills, many of which are bipartisan."

But first, both House and Senate Republicans will need to face their losses in person — and consider how to rebuild.

WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL

"It’s going to feel like a funeral," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "It’s depressing even for those of us who won, because we lost so many good, quality members."

The first order of business this week will be choosing their new leaders for the next Congress.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running for the minority leader role unopposed for now.

And House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is vying for the minority leader role against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio.

MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS

But Moran and Stutzman both said Republicans would unify quickly after that drama is resolved.

"It should be immediate," Stutzman said. "If we're not paying attention to the American people, and we're focusing on leadership positions and personality fights, we're gonna continue to lose."

HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES DEFENSE PLAN TO SHIELD TRUMP FROM LOOMING DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATIONS

Moran said, "We understand now more than ever how important it is for us to come back together, coalesce and to regroup for the next election, and to prepare for the defense of democracy."

On Democrats’ side, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to glide into the speaker role after leading his party to a commanding victory.

Democrats’ leadership elections will take place the week after Republicans’ do.

And on the productivity front, Stutzman also called on the Senate to pass the election security-focused SAVE America Act, which Republicans are attempting to accomplish via the budget reconciliation process to sidestep the need for Democrat support. The House passed a blueprint for the bill in July.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has been working on the structure of that package for some time, but wasn’t so sure that if Republicans lost, it would be something the GOP had the political will to finish.

"It might turn to some people's attitudes in terms of support for it," Johnson said.

Then there’s permitting reform, which was on thin ice heading into Election Night until the White House and Senate Democrats struck a deal for a variety of wind projects to move forward. Whether Democrats support that now, and give Trump and the GOP a win on their way out, remains to be seen.

World.title: RILEY GAINES: Voters sent two midterm messages, and Democrats will only hear one
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

I’ll admit it. Tuesday night was disappointing.

I expected Republicans to lose more seats than they flipped. History suggested as much. But I certainly didn’t expect the results to be quite that bad.

Still, buried beneath the headlines celebrating Democratic victories was a rather inconvenient development for the political left. Americans may have voted to elect Democrats, but that doesn’t mean they’ve suddenly developed an appetite for the progressive social agenda again.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

In fact, on one of the most contentious cultural issues of the last several years, voters delivered a remarkably consistent message.

Keep men out of women’s sports.

In Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington, voters backed measures protecting female athletic competition on the basis of biological sex.

And these weren’t just Republican strongholds. Colorado and Washington are reliably blue states whose political leadership has spent years embracing progressive gender policies.

Yet the same electorate willing to put Democrats in positions of power also voted to reject a central pillar of the modern progressive agenda.

I don’t know how much clearer voters can make themselves.

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

For years, elected Democrats and their allies in the mainstream media have insisted that protecting women’s sports is an extreme position and that anyone who dares advocate for it is a hate-filled bigot. And believe me, that’s one of the nicer things I’ve been called.

I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too.

We’ve been told that acknowledging biological differences between men and women is transphobic. That girls who object to sharing locker rooms or competing against male athletes are the problem. That sports should prioritize inclusion and kindness, even when doing so comes at the expense of fairness and safety.

I’ve personally experienced what happens when you challenge that orthodoxy. I’ve also watched countless female athletes lose opportunities, endure public ridicule and face enormous pressure to remain silent simply for asking for something as basic as a fair shot.

I’ve watched politicians, university administrators and athletic organizations bend themselves into knots trying to explain why women should be expected to sacrifice their own opportunities in the name of inclusion.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

Voters made their position clear in 2024, when the Republican agenda prevailed nationally. Apparently, even after voting for Democrats in 2026, they still aren’t buying what the progressive left is selling on this issue.

Consider Colorado.

Opponents of the girls’ sports initiative reportedly raised roughly $4 million, with substantial backing from unions and progressive organizations, including Planned Parenthood. Proponents raised approximately $200,000, largely through grassroots efforts.

They prevailed despite being outspent nearly 20 to 1.

That’s a staggering disparity, and an even more telling result. At what point does the political left accept that this is a losing issue and give it a rest?

Women’s sports protections are not some fringe position held exclusively by Republicans. The issue cuts across party lines, and the people who have spent years insisting otherwise have a serious problem on their hands.

The cultural shift is evident well beyond the ballot box.

Look at the response WNBA player Sophie Cunningham has received.

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

After publicly expressing support for protecting women’s sports, Cunningham didn’t issue a groveling apology. She wasn’t shunned into professional exile. Quite the opposite.

Her public profile exploded. Her social media following and engagement skyrocketed. Her merchandise became some of the most sought-after in the league, and her Adidas shoes reportedly sold out almost immediately.

On Halloween, I saw countless young girls wearing her jersey and dressing up as Sophie Cunningham.

The notion that expressing a common-sense view about women’s sports is automatically a career-ending offense looks increasingly ridiculous.

For years, corporations, celebrities and athletes were conditioned to believe that stepping outside progressive orthodoxy would destroy their reputations.

That threat doesn’t carry quite the same weight anymore.

And I think that’s worth celebrating, particularly after an election that otherwise gave conservatives plenty of reasons to believe a serious reckoning is overdue.

But there’s another part of Tuesday’s results that Republicans would be foolish to ignore.

DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING

Affordability is a real problem. And I believe that was the bigger message voters sent on Tuesday by voting for Democrats.

Americans are tired of working harder just to afford less. They’re tired of watching their grocery bills climb, calculating how much they can spend at the gas pump and wondering whether homeownership will ever be a realistic possibility.

Image 1 of 2 next

Image 2 of 2 prev

Young people, in particular, are confronting an economy that often feels stacked against them. And when they express their frustration, they’re too often dismissed as lazy or entitled.

Sometimes that criticism is warranted. Most of the time, it isn’t.

I believe Americans have remarkably short memories about just how bad inflation became under the Biden administration. But telling a struggling family that things used to be worse isn’t going to make their next grocery bill any easier to pay.

People vote based on the lives they’re living, not just the economic statistics politicians would prefer they remember.

And when people feel financially desperate, promises of sweeping government intervention can sound awfully attractive.

That’s part of what makes socialism so dangerous. The promise of essentially free everything is appealing, particularly to generations that have never been adequately taught its historical consequences. Of course, nothing is actually free. The bill always comes due, whether through higher taxes, mounting debt or diminished economic opportunity.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

But dismissing every voter concerned about affordability as ignorant or entitled would be a serious mistake.

I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too.

But I don’t think the voters’ message of "affordability" in voting for Democrats is what Democrats will hear.

Elected Democrats will be tempted to interpret their victories as permission to expand DEI mandates, advance gender-transition policies for minors, allow boys access to the girls’ locker room, raise taxes, advocate for more lax immigration policies and continue placing ideological priorities ahead of the concerns of ordinary families.

Those are two very different mandates.

TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING

Winning an election doesn’t mean voters have endorsed every plank of your platform. And it certainly doesn’t mean they’ve abandoned their common sense.

Tuesday’s ballot initiatives should serve as a warning against making that assumption.

They should also give Republican lawmakers in politically competitive states some much-needed confidence.

Take Pennsylvania, where legislation protecting women’s sports has faced significant political resistance.

For too long, some Republicans have treated this issue as politically radioactive, apparently convinced that defending female athletes is too controversial to be worth the fight.

Well, voters in Colorado and Washington just offered a pretty compelling rebuttal.

If these protections can earn majority support in states that routinely elect Democrats, what exactly are Republicans in purple states so afraid of?

Of course, winning at the ballot box doesn’t mean the fight is over.

MATT CALKINS: AFTER YEARS OF THREATS AND INTIMIDATION, THE BULLIES IN THE WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE FINALLY LOST

Colorado’s newly elected Democratic governor, Phil Weiser, has already suggested that the state’s transgender-related ballot measures may need legislative adjustments.

And we’ve seen elsewhere, including Maine, how officials such as Secretary of State Shanna Bellows have resisted efforts to restrict male participation in girls’ sports.

I fully expect more legal challenges, political maneuvering and attempts to weaken these protections.

But those efforts only reinforce the larger point. When the public is given a direct say, the progressive establishment doesn’t always like the answer.

For a party that prides itself on defending democracy, it might consider respecting the democratic process even when the outcome is inconvenient.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

As for the next two years, Democrats will have an opportunity to show Americans what their governing priorities actually are.

And if recent history is any indication, I suspect they’ll provide plenty of reminders of why voters rejected their national agenda in 2024. For some reason, this is the hill they continually choose to die on.

Republicans, meanwhile, have work to do. They need to take affordability seriously, offer credible solutions and stop assuming that winning the cultural argument automatically translates into winning elections. It doesn’t.

Voters can agree with you on cultural issues and still vote against you when they feel their financial concerns aren’t being addressed. Tuesday’s midterm election results proved that these realities can coexist, and Republicans would be wise to recognize it.

Still, I refuse to confuse one disappointing election night with a wholesale cultural reversal.

I’ve spent years speaking with parents, students and female athletes across the country. I’ve seen firsthand how much the conversation has changed.

People who once whispered their concerns are increasingly willing to say them publicly. They’re less intimidated by the accusations, less willing to accept obvious contradictions and less interested in being lectured by institutions that have spent years squandering their trust.

That’s not something that disappears because one party has a good election night.

Political power changes hands. Cultural convictions are often much harder to reverse.

Democrats won important elections Tuesday. Republicans should take those losses seriously, learn from them and make the necessary adjustments.

But the voters also made something unmistakably clear once again. They haven’t suddenly decided that women and girls are undeserving of their own athletic categories, free from mediocre men.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

And if the progressive left believes Tuesday was a mandate to resurrect every unpopular cultural crusade Americans have spent years rejecting, they’re in for a rude awakening.

Democrats may have won the election. They haven’t won the culture.

World.title: Border Dem poised to wield ICE purse strings rejects socialist ‘defund’ push
World.content:

A longtime Democratic House member representing a southern border district said Immigration and Customs Enforcement is not going anywhere as "Abolish ICE" became a rallying cry for more than a dozen progressive Democrats elected or reelected in the midterms.

While the elections brought a new class of Democratic Socialists of America members to Congress, Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital that they make up just "one part of the spectrum" and that there are many "blue dogs" like himself who value strong border and immigration policies.

Cuellar also warned Democrats against returning to the Biden administration’s border policies.

DEM REP SETH MOULTON SAYS PARTY HAS NO IMMIGRATION PLAN, IS ONLY ‘OPPOSITION TO TRUMP’

"We just can't open up the border and just say anybody that wants to claim asylum can come to the borders. That policy under Biden administration — I hope that every Democrat running for national office doesn't do that anymore," Cuellar said.

Cuellar, who is currently the ranking member of the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, is poised to become chairman, giving him significant influence over how funding for ICE is allocated.

The congressman's district includes Laredo, where Border Patrol has a major presence. Cuellar has repeatedly broken with his party on immigration enforcement, including voting with Republicans in January to approve a DHS funding bill that included billions for ICE, though he later opposed a $70 billion Republican-backed enforcement package over concerns about oversight.

Cuellar has criticized ICE for pursuing immigrants without criminal records, even though federal law allows the agency to arrest people for civil immigration violations. He has also called for greater oversight of the agency.

"Anybody that thinks that what ICE is doing, going after nuns, going after pastors, going after dreamers, they think that's normal? I don't think Cuellar said, attributing the blue wave in Texas to Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.

The Abolish ICE movement became a flashpoint for the Trump administration amid sweeping immigration enforcement operations in major cities including Minneapolis, Los Angeles, Chicago and New Orleans. The operations have resulted in more than 1.3 million arrests and 1.2 million illegal immigrants being deported or leaving the country, according to the White House.

Democrats and immigrant rights activists have criticized ICE's tactics, which include targeting courthouses, churches and job sites, as well as conditions in detention centers. The agency has also faced fierce backlash over the fatal shootings of two American citizens by ICE agents in Minnesota just weeks apart in January 2026.

In the months that followed, Democratic governors in New York, California, Connecticut, Illinois, Maryland and Minnesota signed laws restricting local and state cooperation with federal immigration officials.

DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE

Meanwhile, ICE’s partnerships with Texas authorities have expanded through 287(g) agreements that allow local officers to assist with immigration enforcement, jail screening and administrative warrants. Texas law now requires most county sheriffs to seek these agreements.

Cuellar said local law enforcement should have a limited role:

"I think the local sheriff should report somebody that’s there illegally. I think that’s it. But anything beyond that, I think we need to have a discussion," Cuellar told Fox News Digital.

Like Cuellar, Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has been highly critical of ICE's tactics. At a rally in January, she criticized Gov. Greg Abbott for directing state agencies to make Texas land and facilities available for federal immigration detention.

During her time in the state House, Hinojosa voted against a 2017 bill requiring local law enforcement to cooperate with federal agencies.

But Hinojosa has never called for Texas to follow New York and other blue states' lead in ending all cooperation with ICE.

"She is from the border from Brownsville," Cuellar said. "I haven't heard her say that she supports the defunding ICE. I don't think she has said that. Does she probably believe in transparency and rail guards for ICE? Again, I don't want to speak for her, but I think she does."

Hinojosa has also sharply criticized Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, calling the operation a political "grandstand."

Operation Lone Star launched in March 2021 amid a sharp rise in border encounters that began in 2020 and accelerated after President Joe Biden took office. The operation deployed Texas DPS officers, National Guard troops and local law enforcement to combat illegal crossings, human smuggling and drug trafficking before expanding to include state arrests and prosecutions for illegal entry, construction of border barriers and migrant transportation.

In a recent CBS interview, former Border Patrol Chief Raul Ortiz said the Biden administration sent mixed messages to migrants and accused some officials of "embracing the chaos and crisis" at the southern border.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Cuellar agreed with Ortiz's assessment that the Biden administration didn't do its job securing the border.

"The Biden Administration had it wrong," Cuellar said.

Cuellar also criticized Abbott's deployment of Operation Lone Star, pointing to a January 2024 standoff in Eagle Pass, where Texas authorities seized control of Shelby Park and restricted Border Patrol’s access.

"You still got to work with border patrol, regardless if it's a Democrat or Republican at the White House itself," Cuellar said. "So I can understand why there was that criticism, but still the Governor should have done a better job working with us at the federal level. And I hope that this new governor — and I think she will — work with us."

Cuellar said there needs to be balance and nuance in how immigration policy is carried out and that he wants to work with Trump and Republicans over the next two years.

"There are Democrats who are willing to work with the administration, with President Trump, but it takes two to have a deal," Cuellar said.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital that deportations will continue.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Our mission is simple and non-negotiable: secure the border, protect American lives, and control everything and everyone coming into this country. We are focused on getting the job done and enthusiastically partner with any official dedicated to achieving that goal," CBP Assistant Commissioner Hilton Beckham said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to Hinojosa for comment.

World.title: The stoning of Stephen Miller, now running the Trump White House
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

When Donald Trump made the stunning announcement that Stephen Miller is his new chief of staff–preempting the New York Times by a few minutes–I literally said:

"Watch for a barrage of negative Miller stories in the next couple of days."

I was wrong.

It was the next couple of hours.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

MS NOW anchor Katy Tur said: "Donald Trump’s whole immigration agenda is Stephen Miller, and for Stephen Miller, it has always been absolutist: do whatever is necessary, as much as we can possibly do, be as cruel as possible as a warning sign for anybody who might want to come over."

WHITE HOUSE SHAKEUP CONTINUES WITH NEW DEPARTURE FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

"Stephen Miller, one of his most notorious staffers, will instead be taking over as chief of staff," CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins said from the White House driveway, adding: "He was one of two staffers, including Kristi Noem, who came out after Alex Pretti was killed in Minneapolis and called him a domestic terrorist."

Embed:

That New York Times story: "Miller, a deeply ideological Trump loyalist, has been the architect of some of the most polarizing domestic policies in Mr. Trump’s second term."

The conservative Federalist cited a past Miller comment on mass deportations: "At every turn illegal aliens have always been treated better than Americans."

And then there are the Democrats. Rep. Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight chairman, said: "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families… Stephen Miller should lawyer up."

Oh, and incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries called him "a dangerous xenophobe."

Of course, it’s a huge story, and should be covered as such. It’s about his record, and, putting aside the adjectives, it’s fair game. My purpose here is not to either defend or criticize Miller, who has been one of Trump’s most powerful aides since the first term.

Miller is, without question, one of the hardest of hardliners.

I cannot remember this kind of all-out artillery attack, seconds after a top White House appointment was announced. I don’t think anything else comes close.

And the sheer velocity and global reach of this negativity is being fueled in the digital battleground of social media.

That evening was just the first line of shock troops, who struck as soon as Trump announced that Miller would replace Susie Wiles, who has battled breast cancer, as his top aide. By the next morning, the cavalry had arrived.

The Wall Street Journal called Miller an "advocate of the no-holds-barred style of governing that delighted the president’s most die-hard MAGA supporters—and was repudiated by much of the rest of the country on Election Day."

Axios, describing Miller’s view of nearly unlimited presidential powers, said of Trump: "He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints."

The New York Post, headlining the old beer ad "It’s Miller Time," said that choosing the "pugnacious" official "removes almost all hope that the nation’s partisan warfare will ease after the elections." The president is "going to bring his pit bull along."

TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES

The Times, in its pair of stories, played some of the 41-year-old Miller’s greatest hits.

"Those include separation of migrant families at the border; the 2017 Muslim travel ban, directing the government to stifle critics of Mr. Trump; the ending of nearly all U.S. refugee programs; the widespread pressure campaign against American universities; extrajudicial boat strikes that have killed hundreds; and purges of officials deemed insufficiently loyal to Mr. Trump."

Miller also unleashed the military, "pitting masked, heavily armed immigration agents against residents of cities like Minneapolis and Chicago." Fact-check: True.

Maureen Dowd, not to be outdone, denounced the "gaudy, corrupt, vice-ridden, heartless rule, we have been living in Trumpsville. The demonic Trump conjured an American hell."

Miller hasn’t exactly stayed silent. He said Trump is "the most transformative political leader" in our history and has "single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it."

A day after the election, Miller led a call about pushing forward with mass deportations and, the Times reports, did not even mention the Democratic avalanche that was partially a protest against such policies.

The president says he loves watching the combative Miller on TV–a key credential for any Trump staffer.

Miller is certain to back Trump’s assaults on the mainstream media, ranging from denunciations and lawsuits to whether the press corps should be evicted from the White House.

Shortly before the election, Miller said on Elon Musk’s X that the Democrats have nominated candidates "who are all extremist, freaks and America-hating lunatics." Miller urged voters to "send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future."

It’s not hard to see why Miller has a target on his back.

But imagine that Miller, who also urged his boss to wind down the Iran war, never joined the administration. Wouldn’t Trump still have pursued all these tough policies, starting with mass deportation? Clearly, it’s the commander-in-chief who decides.

TRUMP ‘HOLDS ALL THE CARDS’ IN WAR AGAINST IRAN’S REGIME, WHITE HOUSE SAYS

Other top aides and Cabinet secretaries have certainly been raked over the coals.

The media weren’t kind to Karl Rove, dubbed "Bush’s brain," the strategist who was investigated in a CIA leak case but never charged.

Some were accused of being too close to the industries they regulated. Ronald Reagan’s Interior secretary James Watt ripped the environmental movement as a clash between "liberals and Americans," and the Sierra Club collected more than 1 million signatures seeking his ouster.

But none of them were pummeled with the fierce intensity that has enveloped Miller.

As for the coming investigations, Todd Blanche announced that "the chief of staff already has a lawyer. The attorney general of the United States and the Justice Department." With those words, the AG confirmed again that his department serves as the personal law firm of Trump and his acolytes.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Look, Stephen Miller is a brawler, the opposition party is spoiling for a fight, and that should provide the press and public with plenty of pounding in the political ring. But while Miller is now the most important staffer of Donald Trump’s last two years in office, remember, he is still a staffer.

World.title: Nvidia opens investigation after CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
World.content:
Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The announcement followed recent reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. The two are not related.

A person familiar with the matter told NBC News late Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had a relationship with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

“The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement.

“A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency.

Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.”

Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears.

China has long sought to become a global leader in AI. President Xi Jinping set a 2030 deadline to surpass the capabilities of American AI systems.

Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI.

In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology.

Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. That’s up more than 500% over the last five years.

World.title: Trump says deportations were ‘too tough’ and hurt him in midterms
World.content:
President Donald Trump conceded that his immigration policies were “too tough,” saying in an interview on CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday that mass deportations hurt him during the midterm elections.

Trump said his policies had been overly harsh in removing undocumented immigrants who hadn’t committed crimes.

“I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally,” Trump said in the interview, which was recorded Friday.

He added that “a large group of people” think immigrants who are “good people, working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel or doing something ... and, in some cases, paying taxes,” should be “allowed to stay.”

Trump pointed to immigration as one of the areas in which he wanted to work with Democrats, saying yes when he was asked whether a deal could look like the creation of legal status for undocumented workers.

He said, however, that people “on the sort of pretty far right ... would like everybody taken out,” saying some of them were in his administration. Trump on Friday promoted Stephen Miller, who conceived of the mass deportation policy enacted since Trump returned to office, to White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump also blamed “bad messaging” for Republicans’ crushing midterm losses last week and downplayed the Iran war’s impact on economic woes.

“I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time,” Trump said, adding that the media did not cover “positive news for me. So I have to do it myself. I have to get it out there.”

Pressed by CBS News’ Ross Douthat about what the “bad message” was, Trump said, “We couldn’t get the word across.”

The White House has mostly been without a press secretary since late August, after Karoline Leavitt left the administration. Katie Zacharia briefly replaced Leavitt, but she left after just five days.

Trump also commented on his business dealings in the interview when Douthat asked about his net worth’s having increased by nearly $3 billion since he returned to office, prompting him to initially say, “So did everyone’s.”

Trump’s net worth is $7 billion, according to Forbes. It reported that the amount went up by $2.7 billion since he was elected in 2024 for a second term. Trump’s financial disclosure forms show he has made $1.4 billion in cryptocurrency earnings.

“I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don’t care. I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know,” Trump said. He added that one of his sons “watches over money,” adding that the two do not discuss finances.

Trump’s sons founded a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, two years ago. Trump himself is a co-owner, and investors include Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family and national security adviser for the United Arab Emirates.

“I think if I told you that story and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part-owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say, ‘That sounds corrupt,’ right?” Douthat said, asking Trump how his stake in the company is different.

“Because I know nothing about it,” Trump answered, adding that he did not know when he was pressed about whether foreign investors in the company believe they are buying influence.

World.title: Hakeem Jeffries says he’s a ‘hard yes’ on impeaching Pete Hegseth
World.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week.

Asked in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” he added.

Jeffries’ support is a major endorsement of impeachment efforts against Hegseth and signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote on the measure. The impeachment push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust Hegseth after voters have given low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which factored into the midterm election results.

Asked on ABC News whether Jeffries believed all other House Democrats would support the impeachment resolution, he said they would “have that conversation Tuesday morning.” The House is back in session this week, and the impeachment resolution is expected to be filed early this week, with a vote to follow.

Massie has been a vocal critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran. He previously filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth in September, but Republican leaders canceled planned votes, and the House left early, pushing the vote to after the election.

NBC News reported last week that President Donald Trump has told allies that he was considering replacing Hegseth. Trump, though, has publicly denied that he plans to replace Hegseth, telling reporters last week that he was “doing a very good job.”

At the same time, Hegseth has forcefully pushed back on Massie’s impeachment plans, referring to Massie in a social media video last week as a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in the video. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Massie, though, said on social media last week that his “Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress.” Democrats, Massie said, would “have hearings & trials.”

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., also introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth in April. In a post sharing Jeffries’ comments Sunday, Ansari said that Hegseth “must be held accountable.”

“Let’s get this to the floor and voted on this week,” she said in the post.

World.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC head Dana White press secretary
World.content:
President Donald Trump said he was joking when he offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, putting an end to more than 24 hours of speculation about whether the announcement was serious.

“I will tell you, I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea, and there’s only one Dana. He’s great,” Trump told reporters Sunday evening on the tarmac in Palm Beach, Florida.

Trump sent out a surprise post Saturday on Truth Social saying he had offered White the job. The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left the role after just five days last month.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote.

Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.”

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

White said at a boxing event in London on Saturday evening that he was heading to Washington that night and had a meeting scheduled with Trump on Monday.

Trump told reporters that the meeting Monday was still on but that it was unrelated to the press secretary position.

“So he’s actually coming tomorrow,” Trump said Sunday night. “Of course, I was kidding. ... But Dana is actually coming tomorrow, actually, for other reasons. I think he was going to be in Washington, so he’s going to come over and see me.”

When Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Saturday, it was unclear whether his offer was a serious one.

Shortly after Trump posted, White posted on Instagram what appears to be an AI-generated image of himself behind the lectern in the White House briefing room, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”

White also added a screenshot of Trump’s post to his Instagram Story.

Trump and White have long been friends, and Trump has attended many UFC fights while he has been in the White House.

White this year also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the U.S.’ 250th birthday.

Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July.

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt, who had been White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family.

The White House had another staff shake-up Friday, when chief of staff Susie Wiles said she would step down. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.

Wiles’ departure made her the seventh woman to leave the Trump administration this year. So far, all of them have been replaced by men, except Zacharia and Leavitt, as a press secretary has not yet been named.

World.title: Gunman with far-right views who killed 6 in Poland shooting rampage dies in hospital
World.content:
The man who opened fire in a public square, killing six people in a suspected far-right terror attack in Kraków, Poland, has died, police said early Monday.

The man, 24, was shot by police during Saturday’s midday rampage in Main Market Square, the historic center of Poland’s second-largest city.

More than a dozen others, including two police officers, were injured. The two officers were in “serious” condition, regional official Krzysztof Jan Klęczar said Sunday.

The gunman “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence,” Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said on X.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said he used an automatic rifle to carry out the attack and that he “was fascinated by far-right ideologies.”

However, officials appeared to backtrack from the earlier comments as nationalist opposition politicians questioned the grounds on which the interior minister had said far-right ideology was the motive.

“Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are some initial indications,” government spokesman Adam Szlapka told TVN24.

Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said on Monday that despite the death of the shooter, the investigation will continue, aiming to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group.

“Evidence is being collected, but I will not show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” Zurek told Radio Zet.

A man and two women, believed to be the shooter’s parents and sister, were also found dead in an apartment in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie, a city about 93 miles northeast of Kraków, according to Andrzej Fijołek, deputy inspector of Police National Headquarters. The suspect faced murder charges in those killings, as well, Żurek said Sunday.

Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, authorities said. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.

The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.

Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The attack took place in Kraków’s popular commerce and tourist destination.

“We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” Marie-Ange Collaer, who was visiting with her family from Brussels, wrote on Facebook.

World.title: They’re last place in their own division — and a legitimate Super Bowl contender
World.content:
The Green Bay Packers remained in last place in the NFC North despite beating the New England Patriots on Sunday. But that doesn’t mean anyone will be eager to play them anytime soon.

The Packers dismantled the Patriots in their Week 9 matchup, winning 45-27 in a dominant showing. Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love had an MVP-level performance, completing 23 of 29 passes for 372 yards and three touchdowns. The Packers’ defense also played well, picking off Drake Maye three times.

“That was a total team victory,” Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur said postgame. “Each phase contributed in a large way.”

Playing in a division in which every team has at least six wins has the Packers at the bottom of the NFC North. Yet they are every bit as dangerous, if not more, than some of the teams ahead of them.

Love is a major reason Green Bay should be taken seriously as a Super Bowl contender. Playing behind a questionable offensive line, Love entered Sunday ranked 10th in QBR and has been the league’s top deep-shot thrower. He entered Sunday first in passes of both 20-plus yards and 40-plus yards, and he carved New England up with big play after big play.

Love completed a 49-yard pass on the Packers’ second drive, a 43-yard pass on their third drive and then a 23-yard strike, followed by another 43-yard shot, on Green Bay’s final touchdown drive before halftime. Coupled with Maye’s turnovers, Love’s passing pushed the Packers to a 24-7 lead after two quarters.

In the second half, Love completed throws of 28 yards, 33 yards and 39 yards (for a score) before he was ultimately removed from the game in the fourth with Green Bay holding a 45-21 lead.

“I can’t say enough about the play of Jordan Love. He makes my job a hell of a lot easier,” LaFleur said. He added, in regard to his quarterback’s deep passing, “Those are low-percentage throws in theory, but he’s making them look high-percentage.”

World.title: Joe Biden to scale back book tour as cancer ‘slows me down’
World.content:
Former President Joe Biden signaled he will have to scale back the tour to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise me, America,” as he continues to undergo treatment for cancer.

“Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote in a lengthy post on X on Sunday. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

As a result, Biden said he would no longer “be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves.”

Months after leaving office in January 2025, Biden, 83, announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment.

Last year, his office also shared that he had undergone surgery to remove cancerous skin cells.

The memoir is due out on Nov. 17 and details his four years in the White House, including “the decisions I made, and why I made them,” he wrote. “More than anything, it’s about my faith in the American people and the great American experiment in self-governance and democracy.”

Joe Biden and his son Hunter Biden at the White House in 2024. Demetrius Freeman / The Washington Post via Getty Images file

In August, his son, Hunter Biden, told the BBC in an interview that his father’s cancer had spread to other parts of his body and was causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues.

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told the BBC in August. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

“It’s really sad to watch,” he added.

Former first lady Jill Biden also previously told NBC News: “I think Joe will live with cancer till the rest of his life.”

Biden was the oldest man to serve as U.S. president and his age and health were a source of concern for much of his time in office.

The memoir of the 46th president delves into “his campaign, his presidency, his decision to run again,” according to the publisher, Hachette Book Group. It also “reveals the deeply agonizing calculation behind his decision in the summer of 2024 to step aside from the presidential race and to put his party and the nation before his personal ambitions.”

Biden suspended that re-election bid and ultimately endorsed his vice president, Kamala Harris, after mounting pressure to step aside. Biden has frequently defended himself against accusations about his mental acuity and memory.

Biden said in the post Sunday that his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment,” and thanked the public for their prayers and well wishes as he vowed to keep fighting.

World.title: Man who carried out mass shooting in Poland has died, police say
World.content:
The 24-year-old who opened fire in a busy city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in a hospital Monday morning, police said.

The attacker, who has only been identified as a Polish man, was wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest when he drove into the Main Square in Krakow's Old Town and opened fire. The location is a major tourist destination in Poland's second-largest city, and several foreigners were among the dead and wounded.

Police said the man initially continued firing even after he was wounded by police officers. He had been in critical condition since the attack and had been operated on multiple times. He died at 4:30 a.m. in the hospital, authorities said.

"We are first of all investigating if he was inspired by anyone, if someone helped him," Eryk Stasielak from the Krakow branch of the national prosecutor's office told The Associated Press. "We have secured his electronic devices and we will try to open them and get to the contents."

Poland was in the second of two days of national mourning on Monday.

Investigators recovered nearly a dozen firearms from both scenes. Poland's interior minister initially said over the weekend that the gunman held possible far-right extremist views, but he appeared to backtrack on Monday, declining to offer any possible motive until "the matter is fully clarified."

Prosecutors on Sunday announced the beginning of an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, saying the act constituted "a terrorist offense."

Police officers work next to Krakow's Main Market a day after a gunman opened fire, killing six people and wounding around a dozen others in the historic center of Poland's city of Krakow, Nov. 8, 2026. Wojtek RADWANSKI/AFP/Getty

Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, authorities said. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.

Five foreigners were among the wounded, from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

Two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital Monday. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon after being in comas.

"If it weren't for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday.

Officials launched an appeal for blood donations for the benefit of the most seriously wounded officer.

The bodies of three people — the assailant's sister, mother and father — were found at the man's house in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 93 miles northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds, authorities said.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the gunman held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

He said the assailant's father owned over 10 guns legally and that the attacker also owned guns. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found in the possession of the man in Krakow or in his car.

Poland mourns the victims

On Sunday night, mourners laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city's central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief.

"I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety," Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. "In a situation like this, it's all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid."

St. Mary's Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary's Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight Saturday into Sunday in tribute to the victims. It is the first time the call has been missed since World War II.

"I'm absolutely devastated," Weronika Filar, 27, a Krakow resident, told Agence France-Presse on Sunday.

"It's one of the safest places on Earth genuinely ... I did not expect anything like this to happen to us," she said. "Our city will never be the same."

People placed candles at the main market square on Nov. 8, 2026, after yesterday's deadly shooting in the Main Market Square in Krakow, Poland. Omar Marques / Getty Images

"We've heard of various incidents of this sort happening elsewhere in Europe," Krzysztof Stepien, a 28-year-old part-time city guide, told AFP.

"Nothing like this has ever happened here, and I hope it never will again," Stepien said.

American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the "beautiful city" during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital.

"I'm Polish, my parents were from here," she said. "I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too."

The European flags were flying at half-mast outside the European Commission headquarters in Brussels on Sunday.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October, three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects.

People placed candles at the main market square on Nov. 8, 2026, after the deadly shooting in the Main Market Square in Krakow, Poland. Omar Marques / Getty Images

The Krakow shooter's military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.

"We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland," Rekawek said.

World.title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese espionage concerns
World.content:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations that he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.

The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

Jensen Huang, in a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he said.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.

John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday that, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."

A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.

Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.

Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

World.title: OC fishermen find cruise ship employee treading water miles off coast
World.content:
Two Newport Beach fishermen found a Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast while returning home from a fishing trip near Catalina Island on Friday.

Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were fishing for marlin in the morning. By noon, they had rescued the 37-year-old man who had been treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Garrett said, recalling the moment the boat's captain spotted the man in the water.

"Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up," Norton said. "He was in total shock."

Garrett said when the man came to, he told them he was a pianist on the 14-deck Royal Caribbean cruise ship called the "Ovation of the Seas," which was en route to Ensenada, Mexico out of Long Beach.

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

After pulling him from the water, the crew put out an emergency maritime call, and a group of Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda said. They believe he may have gone overboard from the ship about nine hours before he was found, at around 2:30 a.m.

The man, who still hasn't been identified, was hospitalized after the ordeal and is expected to survive, according to the U.S. Coast Guard, which is investigating the incident and how he went overboard.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said. "A different year, no way he makes it."

In a statement to CBS LA, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson shared, "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

World.title: Trump says he was kidding when he offered UFC CEO press secretary role
World.content:
President Trump says he offered the open White House press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White, only to reveal a day later that he "was kidding."

The president said Saturday in a Truth Social post, "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."

"I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," he said in reference to UFC fighters. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left."

On Sunday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I was kidding, of course."

"When you look at the fighters that I put in, that's why I said some don't come from parts unknown. They come from a lot of areas and very rough areas. But he is a very capable guy," he said. "Of course, I was kidding, and you can see because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants that they're all going to come with him. But it was just a little fun."

On Saturday, White added to the confusion on whether he had accepted the position by sharing an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, "On to the next chapter."

During a news conference for a boxing event in London Saturday that White was promoting, White was asked about Mr. Trump's social media post.

"I'm flying to Washington, D.C., right now," White said with a smile and a chuckle. "… I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday. So I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Reporting from at least one media outlet had suggested that the post may have been made tongue-in-cheek. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the UFC for additional comment but received no response.

Mr. Trump confirmed on Sunday he's meeting with White on Monday but didn't disclose the reason.

Dana White, president of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) and President Trump during an event in Las Vegas, Nevada, on Aug. 5, 2026. Ian Maule / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The president's remarks come days after Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the House and the Senate.

The press secretary role has been vacant since Oct. 16, when conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was removed from the job after just five days. Zacharia was Mr. Trump's pick to fill the role after Karoline Leavitt stepped aside in August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her young family.

As the chief of Ultimate Fighting Championship, running a global league valued at more than $15 billion, White has been a longtime supporter of Mr. Trump and attended his inauguration. The White House also hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship in July on the South Lawn to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. The event coincided with Mr. Trump's 80th birthday.

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Mr. Trump said in his post.

In an interview with "60 Minutes" last September, White described his relationship with Mr. Trump, saying that when they get together for dinner, they "don't talk politics."

"We talk about … goofy guy stuff that all guys talk about. You know what I mean?" Dana said. "… We talk about 'Rocky' movies. We talk about different fights that have happened."

World.title: Le Pen says France "least racist" country, floats expelling migrants
World.content:
A stagnating economy has fueled protests across France in recent weeks — and is driving support for extremist politicians.

One person who may benefit from the strife in the streets: Marine Le Pen, the longtime face of far-right populism in Europe. Despite three failed attempts at the French presidency – and a conviction for embezzlement, which she has appealed — she's now leading the polls in France's presidential race that will happen in the spring.

Since the protests began, polls show that Le Pen's popularity has ticked up.

In an interview with 60 Minutes, Le Pen blamed economic difficulties and rioters from "the extreme left" for protests that have left 2,500 businesses damaged and 1,500 police injured.

On the larger problems facing France, Le Pen, as she has for many years, pointed to immigration, arguing for expelling immigrants who don't assimilate while insisting that France is "the least racist" country in the world.

"When you take in too many immigrants, you create the conditions for destabilizing your society," Le Pen said in an interview. She said immigrants are more likely to be unemployed than French citizens, and as a result, "we can no longer import unemployed people."

60 Minutes contributor Trevor Phillips told Le Pen that people in immigrant communities would argue the high immigrant unemployment rate is because of discrimination in France.

"No, that doesn't exist," she said. "You're not going to import those ideas here."

Le Pen repeatedly asserted "there's no discrimination in France" and called it "the least racist" country in the world. She said the French see things differently than Americans: "We believe someone who comes to immigrate to our country must blend into the national community. You have something more like a layered cake: each community can live alongside the others while keeping its own customs. That is not how we see things."

When asked whether she would argue for the remigration of immigrants who "aren't adopting the French way," Le Pen said: "If someone comes and says, 'I hate you, I despise your culture, I don't want to respect your laws,' well, we say to him, 'Listen, sir, the door is wide open.' And we might even, for that matter, force you to leave."

Phillips noted that 20 years ago, the French would refer to Le Pen's political party as extremist. He asked: Have the French people changed, or has she?

"I will not allow people to say that France has become extremist," she said. "Over time, French people have got to know me. Has France changed? I think it's the end of a chapter. It's the end of a world, a world built on unrestrained globalization."

World.title: Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money
World.content:
Democrats won big on issues like immigration. But ICE still has the money

toggle caption i Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images

In the days leading up to the midterm elections, hundreds of people left their "I voted" stickers on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a Houston man killed by federal immigration agents earlier this year.

"The fact that people were thinking of my dad and thinking of other immigrants — that just means the world to me," said Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, told NPR.

Those votes resulted in a seismic political shift in Texas: for the first time, a Latina, Democrat Gina Hinojosa , will be governor. Texans also elected the state's first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 40 years, and the Texas House of Representatives flipped .

Sponsor Message

"Unfortunately, Texas has become like the epicenter of ICE enforcement and like gross violence against immigrants," Ronaldo Salgado said. "Well, the voters have spoken — incoming lawmakers now have a duty to listen to us."

The political fallout

Immigration policy was one of the top issues on voters' minds this election, according to exit polling . Artemio Muñiz of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans, told NPR "with these anti-immigrant-type policies, I think the Hispanic community got fed up."

That seems more true than ever in the counties along the U.S.-Mexico border, which flipped Democratic after supporting Trump in 2024.

"I think the message is clear from the Texas Hispanic community that the only acceptable or effective Hispanic outreach from the Republican Party in Texas is one that includes a reasonable solution for immigration," Muñiz said, suggesting the solution should include secured borders and a legal pathway for undocumented immigrants who have been in the U.S. for decades.

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images North America

In Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing calls to end the state's partnership with ICE.

"That's something that can happen on day one," said César Espinosa, the executive director of the Houston-based advocacy organization FIEL. He said his group would also like to see Hinojosa and the Texas legislature to push for driver licenses for undocumented immigrants. Already, Houston's mayor is reducing his police department's cooperation with ICE.

Sponsor Message

Nationwide, immigration advocates say they want to see ICE defunded, or severely restricted.

"We demand that the incoming Congress hold ICE accountable", says Murad Awawdeh of the New York Immigrant Coalition.

What could the new Congress actually do?

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become the next chair of the House oversight committee, had two words of advice for Republicans on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has promised to look into several issues, including ICE accountability.

ICE is the highest funded federal law enforcement agency in the U.S. Congress essentially gave immigration enforcement a blank check in 2025 and in 2026 they awarded ICE and Customs and Border Patrol around $240 billion.

toggle caption i Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

It's enough funds to run the mass deportation operation for the remainder of Trump's term.

Congress could claw back that money. And lawmakers are already eyeing more stringent oversight.

"We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities (have) killed individuals … assaulted individuals … have incarcerated individuals," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is likely to chair the House Homeland Security Committee. "That system has to have accountability for the men and women who work in it."

He said he'd like to legally require policies, like requiring the use of body-worn cameras for federal immigration agents and banning them from wearing face coverings.

The major hurdle is President Trump: following the midterm election results the President said he would welcome the nickname "Mr. Veto."

Another possible indication of how the administration will be seeing immigration enforcement moving forward came Friday, a few days after the midterm elections. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller was promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller's central project in government has been immigration control and mass deportations. Miller is considered the architect of the first Trump administration's child separation policy, and as NPR reported, was deeply involved in the project of turning large warehouses into immigration detention centers.

Sponsor Message

Naureen Shah at the ACLU says she thinks one of the most powerful things that could happen to change ICE behavior is Congressional oversight via subpoenas.

"ICE has to be afraid," she said. "They have to be afraid of losing their funding, they have to be afraid of being subpoenaed and asked extremely hard questions before a live audience of the American people."

The Trump Administration vows that "Deportations will continue".

The day after the Midterm elections, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin posted a three-word tweet : " Deportations will continue ."

Vice President JD Vance took to X to share his thoughts on the Republican Party's big loss. He said he believes it is due to voter's concerns over the economy, inflation and the war with Iran. He left immigration enforcement off that list.

He did, however, say he is open to changing enforcement tactics by focusing more on businesses that hire undocumented workers. But he said immigration amnesty is not the solution.

Shah of the ACLU says she believes ICE enforcement and the current state of the economy are inextricably linked. "What's really clear is that the stories of life becoming harder for everyday Americans are actually also stories about ICE's impact. People are afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to go to work. It impacts our schools, our teachers. It impacts the labor force when people aren't showing up for their jobs. So Democrats have an opportunity through their oversight device to tell a story about how to make everyday life more affordable for all Americans."

Could we see more oversight on ICE detention facilities?

toggle caption i Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

The Trump administration has spent billions of dollars to expand ICE detention facilities — many of which have faced criticism and protest over dire conditions. There have been a record number of deaths in detention since the start of Trump's second term.

Sponsor Message

The day after mid-term election results the two major private detention center companies that contract for ICE, CoreCivic and the GEO Group , had their quarterly investor calls.
