The main question asked by investors at the CoreCivic call was: how will the result of the midterms affect ICE operations?

CoreCivic President Lucibeth Mayberry optimistically, pointing out that "[ICE] have again began increasing enforcement activity. They have the secure funding to do so." But then she offered a word of advice to ICE about purchasing new detention centers: "we would urge the ICE administration to move quickly."

World.title: Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
World.content:
Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Associated Press

Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for the industry's ties with the Trump administration when they take over Congress in January. In anticipation, many are hiring former Democratic lawmakers and aides to make their case to the incoming House and Senate majorities.

Among the latest to make that move is Palantir, which has hired former Sen. Jon Tester, a colorful Montana Democrat who's also an organic farmer.

"My agreement with Palantir is advisory in nature, it is not lobbying," Tester, who lost reelection to the Senate in 2024, told NPR in an interview.

The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term. Palantir — named by billionaire founder Peter Theil after the mythical "seeing stone" from J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings — has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants.

Sponsor Message

"Perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general," said Tester. "But the fact is, I think Palantir has got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it."

Palantir has long denied claims it aids mass surveillance on the American public — saying it doesn't gather or manipulate data at all, but instead creates tools for government agencies and private companies to organize and optimize their own information. The company has said it is committed to "protecting privacy and upholding liberal democratic values."

Earlier this year, while in the minority, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., along with 30 other Democratic lawmakers demanded answers about Palantir's contracts with the Department of Homeland Security and whether its tools are part of efforts by the federal government to surveil Americans. Palantir denied the accusation and said it is "neither conducting nor enabling mass surveillance of American citizens," but Wyden wasn't fully satisfied with its response, according to his Senate office.

"Senator Wyden has a number of questions about Palantir's work to facilitate the Trump-Vance abuse of government data that he intends to ask again as chairman of the Finance Committee," Wyden's staff wrote in a statement to NPR. "If Palantir is not responsive next year, compulsory processes will be on the table."

Sponsor Message

It's not a coincidence that tech companies are turning to Democrats to help burnish their reputation, said Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former State Department official.

"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Ibrahim said.

During Trump's second term, Palantir's CEO and co-founder Alex Karp — a self-described liberal — has been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration and AI.

"I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope many," Karp said in an interview with Axios in 2025 specifically referencing his support for much more restrictive immigration policies. "You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private."

During his 18 years in the Senate, Tester was an outspoken critic of the PATRIOT Act that passed shortly after the 9/11 attacks that expanded the Justice Department's surveillance powers. When asked whether his concerns over government surveillance remain and whether he has the same concerns with his new employer, Tester said Palantir is different and that the company doesn't build "big databases" or trade in private data.

"I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy."

Last year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products.

Valued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.

Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.

The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment."

Sponsor Message

"It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward."

World.title: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
World.content:
Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage

toggle caption i Chris Machian/KFF Health News

Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."

Sponsor Message

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."

Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.

Sponsor Message

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.

"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.

Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.

Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.

The high price of cutting benefits

About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.

toggle caption i Chris Machian/KFF Health News

To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.

Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.

The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.

Sponsor Message

One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.

"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.

Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."

Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.

Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."

Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."

"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."

Confusion and longer wait times

The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.

Sponsor Message

As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."

State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.

Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.

"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.

"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.

Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.

McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.

His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.

"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."

When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.

Sponsor Message

Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.

McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."

"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."

Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.

The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.

Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.

He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.

"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.

toggle caption i Chris Machian/KFF Health News

The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.

Sponsor Message

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.

"We definitely had fun"

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.

"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.

Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.

"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.

Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."

"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.

CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.

In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.

"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.

Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.

"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.

Sponsor Message

Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.

"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.

Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.

Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.

In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.

Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.

"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."

Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."

Dropping Medicaid enrollment

As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.

Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.

Sponsor Message

As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.

Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.

McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.

"The cancer has grown so much," he said.

He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Supreme Court weighs effort to shield federal law enforcement as ICE complaints rise
World.content:
Supreme Court weighs effort to shield federal law enforcement as ICE complaints rise

toggle caption i J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Five years ago, a gang riot broke out inside a federal prison in Hawaii.

Kekai Watanabe was beaten with a makeshift weapon known as a "lock in a sock."

When he complained about serious back pain, a nurse told him to "stop being a cry baby."

Seven months later, doctors diagnosed Watanabe with a fractured tail bone, and he sued the nurse for violating his Eighth Amendment right against cruel and unusual punishment.

On Monday, the Supreme Court will hear his case, which could determine whether federal law enforcement officers can be held to account when they violate constitutional rights. The claim by Watanabe, now 40, echoes far beyond the walls of prison — and into American streets where immigration officers have been accused of beating and running over migrants.

"What's at stake here is whether, basically, we as a country are going to hold federal law enforcement officers accountable when they violate clearly established constitutional rights," said Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, who filed a "friend of the court" brief in the case. "I mean, it really is, I think, that stark."

Sponsor Message

It's already difficult for these claims to proceed, because the court requires people to show the facts in their cases are identical to precedent. In the federal prisons, the landmark case dates to 1980. The prisoner in that lawsuit died from untreated asthma. The nurse's lawyers say Watanabe, the inmate from Hawaii, survived the gang attack in 2021, so his case is different enough that it should be dismissed.

Mary Hampton Mason worked at the Justice Department for nearly 35 years, in an office that evaluated these kinds of legal claims. Mason said rogue officers are rare, and problems are typically systemic.

"It's a result of agency culture, it's a result of training, it's a result of all sorts of things, but these failures are really institutional," Mason said.

The Supreme Court created a right to sue federal officers for wrongdoing in a 1971 case known as Bivens. But Mason said that precedent has been hollowed out for years, and the court should finally overrule it because it gives plaintiffs false hope.

"In fact in the last 20 years, I'm only aware of one Bivens case that has resulted in a judgment for the plaintiffs that … didn't get reversed on appeal, and that's in thousands and thousands and thousands of cases filed," she said.

Sponsor Message

But supporters of the prisoner say that number doesn't account for settlements or how these lawsuits can deter other bad behavior. If individual federal officers and agents can be on the hook financially, the argument goes, they could think twice before breaking the law.

"That's why damages are so important," said Gregory Cui, an attorney at the MacArthur Justice Center, a civil rights legal organization. "Because they're a way to try to fix things, to give a person the means to pay for medical care or rebuild their life."

In a "friend of the court" brief, Cui reported that the grievance process for people inside federal prison almost never works for inmates, who succeed just 1% of the time in changing things such as access to medical care or better conditions behind bars.

Cui and other legal experts said the Supreme Court agreed to hear this case at a time when abuses by federal immigration agents and others are in the spotlight. Now, they said, is the wrong time for the court to eliminate one of the few avenues of accountability for those errant officers.

"A world with no Bivens is a world in which federal law enforcement officers would enjoy absolute immunity, where no matter how egregious their conduct is, no one can hold them liable," said Vladeck, of Georgetown Law Center. "As alarming a prospect as that may have been five years ago, it should be an especially terrifying one today, and it ought to be one that even this Supreme Court is worried about endorsing."

Both sides agree Congress has the power to weigh in and give people whose rights have been violated by federal officers a clear way to sue. But so far lawmakers have not advanced legislation to hold those people to account.

World.title: Democrats won big. Can they lower your grocery bill?
World.content:
Democrats won big. Can they lower your grocery bill?

toggle caption i Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

It's been a feature of campaign ads and stump speeches for months: grocery prices are out of control.

Affordability concerns, including high food costs, were top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, as the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran continued to drive up prices. That economic strain helped Democrats win control of both houses of Congress on Tuesday.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority would make tackling high prices a priority come January. "It was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one," he told NPR on Friday.

Sponsor Message

The question is how Democrats will do that with President Trump still in the Oval Office, willing to wield his veto pen. Senate Democrats won't have a filibuster-proof majority, and Trump may have little appetite to roll back his signature tariffs or reverse course on the Iran war, two of the main causes of high food prices.

Lael Brainard, who leads a public policy group called The Kitchen Table Project, said Americans are nevertheless expecting relief from Washington — and quickly.

"They are feeling like they are getting squeezed by high prices that don't need to be that high," she said.

What Democrats plan to do to lower food prices

Despite the political hurdles, Democrats said they intend to move ahead with plans to cut grocery bills, including by rolling back Trump's tariffs. Those tariffs have not only raised the cost of certain foods and drinks imported to the U.S., but also created other pressures on the food industry by making it more expensive to import things like machine parts and packaging.

The Iran war has led to a surge in energy prices, which has made it more expensive to transport just about everything. Fertilizer costs also grew when the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off a significant portion of the global fertilizer trade.

But getting Trump to backtrack on tariffs or the Iran war — or his immigration crackdown, which has led to labor shortages on U.S. farms — could prove tricky for Democrats.

"I think the president would certainly want to find ways to reduce the cost of groceries. Democrats [also] see that in their interest," said Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick. "The mechanisms, the tools, the levers that would be most readily available to do that — there's quite a bit of distance between the president and Democrats that'll be taking over both the House and the Senate."

Sponsor Message

Several incoming Democratic senators also floated other proposals during their campaigns that aim to make groceries more affordable.

James Talarico of Texas said he would push back against "attacks" on the federal food assistance programs WIC and SNAP, the latter of which is undergoing a major overhaul by the Trump administration and has seen a precipitous drop in participation since last summer. Kansas' Adam Hamilton announced his support for a national ban on "dynamic pricing" in grocery stores. And multiple candidates, including Roy Cooper of North Carolina, vowed to block food industry mergers they say would raise consumer prices.

Democratic governors take a piece of the affordability pie

Beyond the blue wave in Congress, Democrats also made gains in state capitals across the U.S. on Tuesday. At least 28 states will have Democratic governors beginning next year, and ten state legislative chambers flipped to Democrats, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Incoming state governors have floated their own ideas for how to give residents relief in the grocery aisle.

Keisha Lance Bottoms proposed allowing municipalities in Georgia to suspend or fully eliminate their local sales tax on groceries, baby formula, diapers and more. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, promised to outlaw "predatory surveillance pricing" and price gouging in grocery stores. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland said the state would explore a policy similar to one in Albuquerque that temporarily waives permitting fees for markets that sell healthy and affordable food in so-called "food deserts," the Albuquerque Journal reported .

World.title: On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy
World.content:
On wild Cumberland Island, a land swap proposal stirs controversy

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

CUMBERLAND ISLAND, Ga.— Wild horses, feral hogs and deer roam free on this 18-mile barrier island, one of the largest and most ecologically diverse along the Atlantic coast. The landscape includes salt marshes, maritime forests, and an expansive stretch of pristine, untouched beach only accessible to the public by ferry.

Since 1972, the National Park Service has managed Cumberland Island National Seashore, including roughly 9,800 acres of wilderness designated by an act of Congress which stated that "the seashore shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state."

But there's more on this island than federally protected wilderness. Visitors also can find Native-American relics, remnants of Spanish missions, the ruins of ante-bellum plantations, and opulent homes built by the wealthy Gilded Age industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy, who had 9 children.

Sponsor Message

Descendants of the Carnegies still live or vacation here on private property, and the park service has proposed a land swap with them that would allow for new construction. That possibility is creating tension between the many stakeholders who all have differing views of what it means to preserve the island they hold dear.

Park superintendent Melissa Trenchik has been defending the plan, giving media tours to an area under a grove of huge live oak trees on Cumberland's west side, which overlooks an expansive salt marsh and Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay on the horizon.

It is currently parkland, which under the proposal would be handed over to two branches of Carnegie descendants for the construction of up to eight new private homes.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"They obviously want to be with this incredible view," Trenchik told Georgia Public Broadcasting ' s Jillian Magtoto, as they stood on the edge of a maritime forest looking out over the Cumberland Sound.

The idea, Trenchik said, is to consolidate private ownership on the west side of the island, so the park can better interpret natural and cultural resources on the Atlantic beachside of Cumberland, including sensitive coastal and wilderness areas where the government could then prohibit development. The park service received more than 12,500 public comments on the proposal.

Sponsor Message

"Right now, if we do nothing, development is possible," she said of the private land the park service seeks to acquire.

Trenchik said the eight new "modest" homes would be subject to permanent conservation limits and could not exceed 35 feet in height. Critics, however, say the 15,000-square footage allowance, including driveway and outbuildings, is anything but modest.

"We're swapping for McMansions," said Joseph Manning, an attorney with Defenders of Wildlife, a Washington D.C. based conservation group fighting the deal.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

Manning sees what's happening on Cumberland as the latest attempt by the Trump Administration to privatize public lands, pointing to other attention-grabbing headlines about a baseball park in Grand Teton, a land exchange in Yosemite , and repeated shrinkage of Bears Ears National Monument.

"Possibly the universal theme among all of these parks and refuges land exchanges that we're seeing is that they are not being done to expand public access," Manning said. "They're being done to benefit a particular special interest or just a handful of individuals or families, as is the case at Cumberland Island."

Barclay McFadden is a great-great-grandson of Thomas Carnegie, the brother of Pittsburgh steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.

"The hysteria about mansions and the Gilded Age and all that is so unfounded," McFadden said. "We love our island."

McFadden, who is involved in one of the land deals, said he's hurt by the way the debate over the land swap paints his family as modern-day robber barons without taking into account their history on the island.

"Five generations have been buried there. We have a family cemetery. It's still there. That's where I'll go," he said. "For our children and our grandchildren, it's a sacred place."

The land swap will allow them to build homes for those younger generations, McFadden said.

"We have been wonderful stewards of the island, and we have taken care of the island," he said, pointing out that his grandmother's generation had the opportunity to sell their property to developers in the 1970's. "They protected the island from turning into a golf course."

Sponsor Message

His cousin Jamie Ferguson, who is not directly involved in the current land swap proposal, said he trusts the Carnegie descendants' legacy of protecting what's special here. He jointly co-owns (with about 40 others) a Carnegie mansion here, now operated as a bed and breakfast – the Greyfield Inn.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"It's kind of like a live oak family tree - it's really widespread," said Ferguson, the family's unofficial historian. "The common thread we have though is this place."

He said his grandmother was adamant that the land remain in the family, even when other Carnegie descendants donated property to the National Park Service.

One advantage Ferguson sees to the land swap is greater visitor access to what he calls the "most important historical monument on Cumberland," a site known simply as The Chimneys. The remnants of about two dozen brick and tabby chimneys are lined up in rows under Spanish moss draped oak trees. It's where enslaved workers lived on an old sea island cotton plantation that pre-dated the Carnegies.

Ferguson points out the National Park Service is tasked with not just preserving the island's natural history, but also its cultural history.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"Like it or not, we're part of that cultural history," said Ferguson. "And I don't mean that in a bad way. I mean, I believe that we're a part of that cultural history, and that comes with some responsibility too."

There are a few other private homes on Cumberland that are not owned by Carnegie descendants. Naturalist Carol Rucksdeschel lives in one of them. After living on the island for more than 50 years, she's still excited each day at what she discovers.

"God look at that - that's so beautiful," she said one recent day, spotting a pair of wood storks descending into the marsh grass.

At 85, Ruckdeschel still surveys Cumberland Island every Friday morning, combing the beaches looking for stranded sea turtles and new nests. The ecologist has emerged as one of the main voices opposing the land swap, which she worries is the "first nose under the tent" towards greater development on the island.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"This plan to me is a real affront to the American people, but it's also an insult to the Park Service," Ruckdeschel said. "It's not what they're supposed to be doing. They're supposed to be protecting this place."

Sponsor Message

She's also not happy that the park service plans to double daily visitation to Cumberland, up to 700 visitors a day.

Ruckdeschel, who is involved with the conservation group Wild Cumberland, said she's friends with Carnegie descendants and acknowledges their love for the island. Still, she said, more homes and more people will disturb what the island should be – a pure primitive wilderness where nature overtakes what humans have left behind.

"It's stepping into its climax stage, which is terribly exciting," Ruckdeschel said of the rewilded maritime forest she's witnessed take over old plantation cotton fields.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"And that's what I would have loved to have seen the whole island do," she said. "And then people die out, places go back to nature and that's it."

World.title: U.N. climate talks begin today. Here are 3 things to know
World.content:
U.N. climate talks begin today. Here are 3 things to know

toggle caption i Burak Kara/Getty Images Europe

For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

Sponsor Message

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

It's all about electrification

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

Sponsor Message

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

Roadmap off fossil fuels

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. is not in the room

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

The Trump administration has reversed action on climate progress, phasing out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind, reducing regulations for greenhouse gases, and halting renewable energy projects.

Last year, some countries told NPR they were happy that the Trump administration was not at the climate talks. "Generally, it's a good thing they're not here because we have less recalcitrants to deal with," Ralph Regenvanu, minister of climate change of Vanuatu, told NPR then.

But some democratic lawmakers will be at COP31, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. Fresh off Democrats' midterm victory sweep, Whitehouse says he and the other lawmakers plan to keep the focus on fossil fuels and a potential carbon pricing mechanism.

Sponsor Message

" It cannot remain free for the fossil fuel industry to pollute if we want to have any chance of a pathway to climate safety," Whitehouse says.

World.title: Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
World.content:
Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect

toggle caption i Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR

It is the final hoorah for the 119th Congress. Republicans have just weeks left in control of the House of Republicans and the Senate. The main thing on the agenda: keeping the federal government open. Funding is set to run out on December 11, when a stop-gap measure passed about a month ahead of the midterms expires.

Any funding extension is all but certain to be done through another short-term bill, known as a continuing resolution. The typical government funding process — 12 carefully negotiated appropriations bills — would take time and political will that lawmakers currently lack.

Sponsor Message

Congress will also need to find a path forward on the National Defense Authorization Act, long considered a must-pass annual military funding package. This year, the bill is quagmired in the unforgiving politics of the Iran war. The conflict is opposed by a majority of Americans — something President Trump has acknowledged was a key force in driving his party out of power.

The House is also likely to vote on an impeachment effort targeting Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a key figure in forcing the administration's release of the Epstein files, the impeachment measure lists a number of charges, including that the administration failed to properly consult Congress on the military campaign.

Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.

With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.

Sponsor Message

Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.

World.title: Veterans, families call for better access to make claims for exposure-related illness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hakan Haytaoglu was a military pilot who worked secret missions for the Canadian Armed Forces during his 35-year career.

At the age of 55, just months shy of retirement, he was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of cancer called neuroendocrine carcinoma.

He sought support through a medical claim to Veterans Affairs Canada, but the claim was denied.

Haytaoglu decided to appeal.

Hakan Haytaoglu was a pilot with the Canadian Armed Forces until his diagnosis with an aggressive cancer. His wife fought for medical benefits and won. (Submitted by Maura-Jo Haytaoglu)

For months, while caring for her dying husband, Maura-Jo Haytaoglu hunted down the evidence he needed to connect his illness to his job.

"I dug and I dug while he was sick in bed," she said. "I sat beside him and I researched and I dug and I put the proper people in my corner that fought for us."

The military pilot who friends and family called Hawk died just a few weeks before his case could be heard before the Veterans Review and Appeal Board in August 2025.

So Maura-Jo did it for him, and won.

"It was the hardest day of my entire life, beyond watching my husband die in my arms," Haytaoglu said.

"It shouldn't be this hard for those who served their country."

Maura-Jo Haytaoglu and husband Hakan as he received chemo treatments following his diagnosis of a rare cancer. He died in July 2025, just a few weeks shy of the appeal of his medical claim. (Submitted by Maura-Jo Haytaoglu)

A new report by the House of Commons national defence committee states there are 2,750 Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces contaminated sites in Canada as of June 2026.

Among 11 recommendations, the report calls for the federal government to make it easier for service members and others exposed to health risks to find the information they need when making medical claims.

CBC News reached out to Veterans Affairs Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces for reaction to the call for more access, and did not hear back in time for publication.

Invisible crisis

The report cites witness testimony by veterans like Erin Zimmerman.

Zimmerman has been helping more than two dozen veterans and their families locate evidence to support appeals for medical claims, including the Haytaoglu case.

Zimmerman says her expertise in research as a civil servant came in handy in her own fight for answers. The 48-year-old mother of four has been diagnosed with a rare form of early-onset Parkinson's disease. She worked at CFB Moose Jaw in sections now an active contamination site, including during one of her pregnancies.

She said she had never been informed of the risks.

Some of Erin Zimmerman's committee testimony was included in the final report released in October. (Submitted by Erin Zimmerman)

Zimmerman is grateful to see her calls for more transparency in the committee report.

One of its recommendations suggests the federal government "proactively inform personnel and families currently and previously living and/or working on Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces sites, bases and wings of environmental risks and assessment results."

"We're in a crisis," Zimmerman said. "But this crisis is an invisible demographic."

Veterans face significant difficulty obtaining reliable information about past toxic exposures, according to Jim Hutton with Veterans with Cancer Inc.

The non-profit works with veterans diagnosed with cancer to establish the connection between their service and their illness to back medical claims.

At the same time, Hutton said, Veterans Affairs does not properly track exposure-related cancer claims.

He said this leads to veterans having to file access to information requests and searching old government records, in multiple databases, to prove the risk they faced while serving their country.

"Veterans should not have to become investigators," Hutton said in an email to CBC News. "That is an unreasonable burden."

The group documented cases where veterans failed to find the evidence they need because historical exposure information is missing, or can't be found in their military service records.

On the upside, once the evidence is found, it can help others who worked alongside that service member. That's what happened in Hawk Haytaoglu's case.

Maura-Jo Haytaoglu said the information used in her husband's successful appeal is now helping the surviving service members that worked with him on a secret mission some 30 years ago.

"Three of them are dead because of cancer, one is battling Stage 4 cancer and one has beat cancer three times," she said.

The surviving members used the precedent in their own claims.

"My husband's legacy lives on because we had the courage to say no, we're not going to accept this."

World.title: Some women in Canada are choosing fertility treatments to avoid passing down genetic mutations to their kids
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After Emma Clayton Jones learned she had a genetic mutation that put her at higher risk for some cancers, she started thinking about freezing her eggs.

"I've always known that when I want to start a family, there would be the option to freeze my eggs and then test the embryos," she told CBC News.

Clayton Jones has the BRCA 1 mutation, an inherited genetic change that raises the lifetime risk of developing various cancers, including breast and ovarian — and she doesn't want to pass it on to her future kids. By freezing her eggs, Clayton Jones can plan ahead by preserving her fertility, and later, creating embryos that will be tested for the same genetic mutation.

"After having a cancer scare myself, I thought, 'If I have the choice and the privilege to not put someone through it, I won't.'"

WATCH | Why are more people in B.C. freezing their eggs?: Why are more British Columbians freezing their eggs? | Duration 9:33 More people are relying on freezing their eggs so they can have children later in life. But at what cost? CBC's Baneet Braich looks into how egg-freezing works, its challenges, and the growing support offered to people hoping to have a family one day.

She isn't alone — more women across Canada are considering freezing their eggs, a procedure that's surging in popularity among those who can afford it.

Experts say most people freeze their eggs to preserve their fertility. After all, people are having children later , for reasons like career ambitions, relationship status and the rising cost of living.

But many women like Clayton Jones are also coming forward, too, hoping to plan their pregnancies in a way that better protects their future children.

Ethical concerns

Egg freezing isn't absolutely necessary to pursue genetic testing, as it is the embryos, not the eggs themselves, that get tested. But it's a common path for women who have concerns about passing down health issues and who are unsure of when they want to have children. Once they are ready, they will often begin in vitro fertilization, or IVF.

"Testing embryos for genetic abnormalities is a safer and more reliable option, particularly given that sperm can also carry abnormalities," said Judith Daniluk, a University of British Columbia professor who specializes in women's fertility.

Experts warn there are some ethical concerns with genetic testing — particularly if it's done for reasons other than potential health issues, like sex selection. There are also some religious groups who believe that genetic testing is always morally wrong.

"Some disability advocates are also concerned about the slippery slope of trying to eliminate normal diversity within the human species," she said, "as well as further stigmatizing those with disabilities."

'Overall, it is still an uphill battle to make it accessible to anyone who wants to do it,' Dr. Sony Sierra said of fertility treatments and access to them. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Notably, it's a criminal offence in Canada to choose an embryo based on sex, unless it's to prevent a sex-linked illness, or to pursue so-called "designer babies," which have genetic traits selected for them that their parents consider desirable. Anyone found guilty faces a fine of up to $500,000 and up to 10 years in prison, though there have been no documented convictions of elective sex selection in Canada.

But in the U.S., where elective sex selection is legal, genetic testing has allowed people to choose whether their embryo will develop into a boy or a girl, said Caitlin Dunne, a reproductive endocrinologist and infertility specialist at the B.C.-based Pacific Centre for Reproductive Medicine.

Still, genetic testing for health reasons is legal in Canada. But fertility treatments aren't cheap. When it comes to egg freezing, doctors who spoke to CBC News said that one cycle typically costs around $8,000, with another $2,000 to $8,000 for medication.

Patients often need two or three cycles to increase their chances for pregnancy, and there are additional costs associated with storage.

Public funding for fertility treatments, such as in vitro fertilization, or IVF, varies from province to province and generally doesn't cover elective egg freezing. But increasingly, workplace benefits will cover a cycle, or at least the medication required for it.

Clayton Jones said she's still trying to figure out the costs.

A still image of Dr. Sierra's egg freezing clinic. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The 32-year-old says she's thinking about pregnancy in the "next couple of years," but wants to balance her expectations with the cost of the procedure.

"It seems like it's going to be a bit of a patchwork of expenses. I'm trying to get to the bottom of how much to actually budget for something like this."

Fertility a 'public health concern' affecting many

"The egg freezing is more precipitated for me by the idea that I'd like to do the genetic testing of the embryos," Clayton Jones said. "I feel a tiny crunch of pressure related to the BRCA gene, but I am also trying to be cost-conscious."

Dr. Sony Sierra, Toronto-based medical director of Evolve Egg Freezing Clinic, told CBC News that elective egg freezing has become more popular and accessible because public discourse and celebrity stories have made it mainstream — but there is still a long way to go.

"Overall, it is still an uphill battle to make it accessible to anyone who wants to do it," she said, adding she hopes that improves over time.

Dunne says she also hopes fertility treatments will become more accessible as more people become informed.

"Look at your nieces or employees, sisters, aunts, people with ovaries. There are all kinds of people around you dealing with infertility or concerns. It truly is a public health concern that touches so many."

World.title: Suspicious tree removal and permits linked to Toronto developer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto developer is facing new accusations of illegal tree removal at a residential property in the city's west end.

Modcity has faced numerous similar accusations in the past, and as of early September, the city had 10 open investigations related to the company.

Now, four more trees have been cut down without permits at a property connected to the company. This time, in the Long Branch neighbourhood of Etobicoke.

The affected trees include one that the city and locals previously fought to protect. The white fir towered above a two-bedroom bungalow, and had been the subject of neighbourhood walking tours.

"It was the epitome of the perfect tree," said neighbour Sherry McCutcheon.

Without it, the area is "bare … it's drab, it's very dreary looking now."

The loss of the white fir was "disturbing," said neighbour Randy McWatters, who says he remembers when it was not much taller than him. He'd watched it "grow and grow" for more than five decades, he said.

Several years ago, Randy McWatters was involved in a successful neighbourhood campaign to save the white fir at 65 Fortieth St. (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)

The incident also involves allegedly fraudulent tree removal permits.

The pattern of alleged wrongdoing is prompting calls for a harsher crackdown by the city and province. Modcity denies any wrongdoing.

Property tied to developer

The four trees were cut down at 65 Fortieth St. on Oct. 24. Property records show that was one day after the property changed hands, having been bought by a company directed by two of Modcity's co-founders: Ron Sheinin and Rohan Sadana.

CBC Toronto obtained photos of apparent removal permits for three trees in the backyard, which were posted at the property the day the trees were cut down. While the supposed permits have the City of Toronto letterhead, and list the address of the property, the city confirmed to CBC Toronto it did not issue them.

If the documents were forged, that would be a crime, says Amber Morley, the local city councillor.

"That needs to be fully investigated to the full extent of the law."

Morley says her office is working with city departments to explore options. The city confirmed it is investigating to determine if there were bylaw violations.

A violation could lead to proseuction, said media relations manager Kayla Lewis in an emailed statement.

City councillor Amber Morley says the possibility that forged permits were used must be 'fully investigated.' (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)

Sheinin and Sadana did not answer detailed questions from CBC Toronto, including whether they posted or authorized the posting of fake permits, or whether they authorized the removal of trees without city approval.

In an email, Sadana said they "strongly dispute" allegations of wrongdoing.

Several neighbours told CBC Toronto they saw Sheinin and Sadana at the property while the trees were being removed. A photo taken that same day also shows a car parked across the street with a Modcity vanity licence plate. The registered owner is a numbered company, of which Sheinin is the president and sole director.

Loss of beloved tree

The city and community had previously fought to protect that large white fir.

In 2018, the previous property owner applied to sever the property, with a plan to tear down the existing house and build two new ones. Toronto's committee of adjustment approved the application, despite objections from the city's urban forestry department.

The city ended up appealing the decision to the Toronto Local Appeal Body (TLAB), on the basis that the variances would require the removal of a healthy tree. The appeal was successful, with the TLAB issuing its decision in 2022.

Danijela Puric-Mladenovic of the University of Toronto says municipal bylaws aren't a strong enough tool to deter some developers from breaking the rules. (Sarah MacMillan/CBC)

It was a "nice tree, beautiful. And everybody commented on it all the time. So I'm sorry to see it go," said McWatters, who advocated to save the tree, including by gathering signatures from neighbours.

Danijela Puric-Mladenovic, an assistant professor in forestry at the University of Toronto, says losing large trees like that one is significant for the local environment.

"Whatever we plant will never reach the canopy that we used to have," Puric-Mladenovic said, "because there is no growing space. With those new developments, there is little place left for larger trees to develop."

Modcity is facing four charges related to tree bylaw offences, which are currently before the courts, and several other noise bylaw-related charges.

The maximum fine for each offence is $100,000. However, under provincial legislation, the city cannot deny a developer a building permit on the basis of violating its tree bylaws.

Speaking generally, Puric-Mladenovic argued the potential fines aren't a strong enough deterrent, when compared with potential developer profits.

"Even if they don't follow the rules, they know that that's not going to hurt them," she said.

Last year, the city asked the province to change the law, so that not complying with its tree bylaws would be grounds for denying a building permit.

The Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing has not responded to emails from CBC Toronto.

World.title: Critics warn of health data privacy concerns as Ottawa ramps up AI strategy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Should a private company handling your personal health data be able to claim it has a “legitimate interest” that allows it to collect and use your information without your consent?

That’s just one of the concerns critics of Canada’s proposed privacy legislation are flagging in a recent commentary published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ).

This summer, the federal government announced an update to Canada’s private-sector privacy laws that would recognize privacy as a fundamental right, strengthen transparency around automated decisions by systems including AI, and allow individuals to request their personal information be deleted in certain circumstances.

Touted as a “key element” for Canada’s AI for All strategy, the federal government said in the announcement that the proposed bill will “ establish clear guardrails to protect Canadians’ personal information in a rapidly changing digital world.”

But in the commentary, health researchers say Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, “contains critical gaps that leave sensitive health data exposed.”

Under the proposed law, private sector companies would be allowed to “collect, use or disclose an individual’s personal information without their knowledge or consent” provided they have a “legitimate interest” that outweighs any “reasonably foreseeable” harm to that individual.

“What's concerning about this is it's the company that's making the decision,” said Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a clinician scientist at Women’s College Hospital in Toronto, and co-author of the CMAJ commentary.

Dr. Sheryl Spithoff at Women's College Hospital says there should be more guardrails in place when it comes to privacy regulation and sensitive health data. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

“It gives these companies significant discretion over using patient or individual data without consent.”

What is a ‘legitimate interest’?

Companies are required by the bill to document their legitimate interests, carry out privacy impact assessments to judge the risks to individuals and be able to provide this information on request. But Spithoff says companies should be required to inform regulators from the start and that this “legitimate interest” clause should only be for rare instances.

“Also there should be higher standards for sensitive information like personal health information,” she said.

The CMAJ commentary pointed out that the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation requires a high bar of proof and specifies that “legitimate interest” does not take precedence over the “fundamental freedoms and rights” of the data owners in question. Bill C-36 doesn’t provide these kinds of guardrails.

When CBC News asked AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office what counted as a “legitimate interest” and what safeguards were in place to prevent private health data from being sold to private-sector companies, the minister’s office repeated the definition given in the bill.

“Organizations relying on this exception would be subject to safeguards, including requirements to assess privacy risks and take steps to mitigate them,” the minister’s office said in a statement, without expanding on what those safeguards were.

WATCH | AI Minister Evan Solomon champions updating privacy laws: 'The moment is here' to modernize Canada's privacy laws: AI minister | Duration closed caption 1:29 Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act will help keep Canadians safe in the digital age. 'I think it's a common-sense approach to what Canadians and what average folks want from their digital media,' Solomon said on Monday about the new bill. 'They want some control over their personal information.'

Data sold to pharmaceutical companies

Last year, a study Spithoff worked on found that millions of Canadians’ health data, including details about their medical history and prescriptions, was being stripped of identifying material and then sold to pharmaceutical companies .

At the time, study authors warned that while this sharing of info could lead to better patient care, it also opened up the risk that private pharmaceutical companies could use this information to put their economic interests above the interest of patients and drive up prices.

Other jurisdictions are tackling similar privacy problems.

Earlier this year, a class-action lawsuit was launched against Chicago-based Tempus AI, alleging that after the company acquired a genetic testing firm, Ambry Genetics, they compelled the firm to hand over patients’ genetic and clinical data, trained their AI systems on it and sold that data to pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies without patients’ consent or knowledge.

Bill C-36 requires that personal information be "de-identified" by modifying personal details, like names and health card information. But researchers are concerned about the potential for re-identification as AI tools advance, where sensitive information could be linked back to specific individuals.

Teresa Scassa, the Canada Research Chair in Information Law at the University of Ottawa, says there's an increasing risk of de-identified data being traced back to individuals as AI tools grow more advanced. (CBC)

“There are very real concerns that nothing can be properly or fully anonymized anymore … with the amount of other data that's available and the power of AI technologies,” said Teresa Scassa, the Canada Research Chair in Information Law and Policy at the University of Ottawa and another author of the CMAJ commentary.

Scassa says that de-identified or even anonymized data can allow for correlations and links to be drawn that can affect individuals negatively even if they are not identified in those data sets.

She says individuals can be “profiled as somebody who is at a high risk of having a particular medical condition which would be expensive to treat, and therefore they might not be eligible for [types of] insurance.”

Under the proposed bill, deliberately re-identifying personal information would be an offence, but Scassa noted that this could be hard to prove.

Experts caution that even fully anonymized datasets can contain and amplify biases present in the health-care system, potentially putting patient information at risk. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

Anonymized data still carries risk

Critics are also concerned that the proposed legislation only covers information that has been de-identified — there’s no protection for what’s known as anonymized data.

According to the bill, de-identification means “modify[ing] personal information so that an individual cannot be directly identified from it, although a risk of the individual being identified remains.” Anonymized data, as defined in the bill, is data that has been “irreversibly and permanently” stripped of personal information so there is no “reasonably foreseeable” risk an individual can be identified.

But experts warn anonymized data still contains risks, and say it’s the very data used to train AI systems.

“There are risks to the use of the information in artificial intelligence systems and we have no means of governing it,” said Scassa.

The commentary explains that anonymized data, which would fall outside of the scope of the law, often reflects societal biases that, when incorporated into AI systems, can lead to discrimination against people with shared characteristics.

WATCH | How could AI be applied in hospitals?: Could AI help manage overcrowding in N.B. hospitals? | Duration closed caption 3:09 Researchers at the Université de Moncton believe artificial intelligence is the answer to improve the way patients are processed in and out of hospitals, which could reduce overcrowding in acute care beds.

Authors provide an example of this discrimination in the U.S. when a widely used algorithm to allocate hospital resources was found to allocate fewer resources to Black people than white people.

“[Researchers] found out that it was because the algorithm was relying on past use of health system resources to allocate future resources,” said Spithoff.

Health data benefits

While experts say there are legitimate concerns over the use of sensitive health data, some other physicians are highlighting that when used safely, this information can be crucial in advancing health-care research.

Dr. Amol Verma is a physician and scientist at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto who leads a hospital research network called VITAL, which enables access to de-identified hospital data for health-care organizations nationally.

Dr. Amol Verma, with Unity Health Network's generative AI program, is pictured at St. Michael's Hospital, in Toronto, on Sept. 11, 2024. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

He says his network works with hospitals and with AI tools to make health data usable for research and innovation while still protecting patient privacy.

“We've been able to improve the efficiency of hospital care, reducing the time people spend in hospital safely, without causing increased risk to patients,” Verma said.

Verma said that concern over privacy is not necessarily a constraint on innovation.

“I think the only way we can have innovation around data in our health-care system is hand-in-hand with innovation and privacy protection.”

World.title: Canada heads to UN climate summit in Turkey with finance, fossil fuel transition on the agenda
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada heads to the UN's annual climate summit, COP31, defending its fossil fuel expansion at home while seeking influence on clean energy, climate finance and the global transition away from fossil fuels.

With the U.S. retreating from international climate diplomacy, Canada has an opening to play a larger role in the negotiations. But experts say recent climate-policy rollbacks at home could complicate its efforts to do so.

"We feel like Canada's credibility is on the line," said Pratishta Singh, international diplomacy manager at Climate Action Network Canada, a non-governmental group.

"Canada cannot position itself as a climate leader internationally while … doubling down on fossil fuel infrastructure."

The UN summit runs from Nov. 9-20 in the resort town of Antalya, Turkey. It is the first since the U.S., under President Donald Trump, pulled out of the Paris Agreement on climate change, although his administration largely boycotted the previous COP30 summit as well.

That withdrawal could leave more room for so-called middle powers such as Canada, which has historically supported international climate diplomacy and co-operation.

Canada does not appear to be shying away from the UN process despite its recent climate-policy rollbacks. A significant diplomatic contingent, led by federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, will attend COP31, along with a dedicated Canada Pavilion hosting side events involving government, think tanks and NGO groups.

WATCH | The need for fossil fuel transition: Will we ever be off fossil fuels? Should we be? | Duration closed caption 4:12 Is ditching oil the only way to save the planet? Not entirely, the science says, as long as the world hits carbon-neutral by 2050. The CBC's Johanna Wagstaffe breaks down what "net-zero" actually looks like and whether a sustainable future can function with oil still in the mix.

"I do think that there will be some heat from groups about the stepbacks on some of the climate policies that we've seen over the past year. So, I think it'll be up and down," said Philip Gass, who leads research on Canadian energy at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, a climate and energy policy think tank.

"Depending what the topic of the day is, it might be a little bit rocky for Canada."

Fossil fuel transition

Brazil, which hosted last year's climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belém, proposed a roadmap for countries to transition away from fossil fuels. The plan would help countries establish targets to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels and replace them with clean sources of energy.

But reaching an agreement among the more than 180 countries proved elusive. Decisions at UN climate summits require consensus among participating nations, and a smaller coalition of countries willing to move ahead, including Canada, met in Colombia in April to discuss the issue separately.

What this coalition of countries now wants is concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels, not just resolutions or promises. They want countries to set specific dates and targets for ending the use of oil, gas and coal, along with a formal mechanism through which developing countries can apply for financial or technical assistance to aid their own transitions.

This could put particular pressure on countries such as Canada, which has a large oil and gas sector.

Gass says the federal Canadian Sustainable Jobs Act, passed by the Justin Trudeau government in 2024, is "aligned with a lot of the principles of just transition" away from fossil fuels.

But Canada's continued expansion of fossil fuel production complicates its position, he said.

"It would be very hard, for example, for Canada to look to lead a process being a fossil fuel producer that has expanded fossil fuel production this year," Gass said.

"That doesn't mean they can't be constructively involved in the discussion."

Singh said Canada needs to match its words at international conferences with "serious domestic implementation" of the sustainable jobs law to be taken seriously by other countries.

Earlier this year, the federal government released a strategy that was criticized by the NDP and labour experts for not doing enough for workers. The sustainable jobs strategy acknowledges that global efforts to reduce emissions will reshape industries, and the government says Canada must ensure the shift improves job quality and supports growth.

Clean electricity

Canada can point to its investments in clean electricity as evidence of its climate ambitions.

The federal government announced major investments in electricity production in the budget released last week. It has now proposed more than $100 billion in various commitments to boost clean electricity projects over the next three decades.

Julia Levin, who studies national climate policy at the advocacy group Environmental Defence, said the funding announcements were "positive, but underwhelming."

She pointed out that the government has weakened federal clean electricity regulations, allowing more electricity to be generated from natural gas, a fossil fuel.

But Canada's recent investments, including a major push for nuclear energy, could give it some clout at COP31. The summit's presidency wants countries to work toward an ambitious new electrification target: increasing the global share of final energy demand met by electricity from just over 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

Meeting that target would require countries to significantly scale up clean electricity production, which aligns with what Canada is trying to do.

WATCH | Carney's electrification ambitions: Carney announces national strategy to double Canada's electricity grid by 2050 | Duration closed caption 6:47 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Powering Canada Strong, a new national strategy aimed at doubling Canada's electric capacity by 2050 and lowering electricity costs for seven in 10 households by expanding the role of natural gas in the country's energy mix. The plan will be fine-tuned during four months of consultation with provinces and stakeholders.

Climate finance

Finance for developing countries, a longtime sticking point in climate negotiations, has become an even bigger problem since the U.S. largely shut down its foreign aid agency . Aid budgets have declined in other high-income countries as well.

Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is leading Canada's delegation to the COP31 summit in Turkey. Canada is expected to focus on issues like climate finance and clean energy. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Canada announced about $5.9 billion in climate finance over the next five years in the spring economic update earlier this year, with a goal of mobilizing a total of $13 billion using private sources.

"Canada is one of the few Global North countries who have actually pledged, post 2025, international climate finance," Singh said.

But details about how that funding will flow still need to be announced, which Singh said she hopes will happen at COP31.

The federal government has said one of its top priorities at the conference will be to "mobilize climate finance at scale from public and private sources."
