World.title: “Neurotics Anonymous” – a Film Honoring the Role of Movies in Our Lives
World.content:
The Cuban film Neurotica Anonima at the La Rampa Theather in Havana.

By Irina Pino

HAVANA TIMES – Last Saturday, I watched the Cuban film Neurótica Anónima [“Anonymous Female Neurotic”] at Havana’s “La Rampa” movie theater. The film is directed by Jorge Preugorría, who is also an actor, and stars Mirtha Ibarra, the former muse and wife of film director Tomas Gutierrez Alea. The production is an adaptation of a play written by Ibarra and produced in Spain, where it enjoyed great success.

The plot centers on an usher at the [fictitious] Cine Cuba movie theater and is clearly an allegory of the country’s destruction. Together with the other movie theater employees, Mirtha Ibarra’s character is informed in a meeting of the theater’s imminent closure, due to the danger of the entire building collapsing. The employees are told they’ll be reassigned to other venues to continue their jobs.

The first of the group to react is Iluminada, the character Mirtha Ibarra interprets. She protests vehemently, since she loves this site where she has worked for many years. The other employees join her. Then, the projectionist has the idea of making a documentary to save the locale.

They fan out to the street to collect opinions. Most of those they interview agree that movie theaters are dying: people don’t go, due to the lack of transportation and a preference for the ease of watching at home.

That’s actually a reality here. Only two movie theaters are still functioning in Havana – La Rampa and Yara, each offering two shows on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Those that are left from “Project 23” (which included several other theaters on 23rd Street in Havana) are subject to blackouts, making attendance at these theaters very risky.

The neighborhood movie theaters no longer exist, buried by disinterest and destruction. None of the government organizations has been interested in preserving them. This has contributed to people losing the habit of enjoying the cinematic arts in a darkened hall.

But back to the plot of Neurótica Anónima. It’s a bit fantastical, with elements borrowed from “Moscow Doesn’t Believe in Tears”, “Thelma & Louise”, “Throne of Blood”, and “The Passion of Joan of Arc”, as well as “Strawberry and Chocolate” and “To a Certain Extent”—both of the latter starring Cuban actress Mirna Ibarra.

These cinematic winks have their own beauty and are welcomed by the film buffs who detect them, for their artistic value and the feelings they evoke. This technique isn’t new – right now I’m recalling “Stardust Memory”, one of my favorite Woody Allen films, which echoes scenes from Federico Fellini’s “8 ½”.

But in this film, something very peculiar is happening: the protagonist is suffering from a neurosis that causes her to imagine herself playing the heroines from all these films. Her experience is vivid.

The sub-plot involves her real life as a couple. Her husband is an alcoholic who spent three years in prison for a crime at the foreign company where he worked. He now earns money renting out their patio for religious rites where animals are sacrificed, something Iluminada finds intolerable, along with his addiction.

I want to highlight one amusing scene, where she goes to a Research Center for Control of Neurosis. The Center has a series of different treatment rooms for different disorders. It makes me think that Cuba has us suffering from so many kinds of disorders that it would be very difficult to enumerate all of them.

In general, the film features a cast of outstanding actors and actresses, some of them now passed. Mirna Ibarra gives freshness and credibility to her character.

This feature film comes short of being memorable, nor is it as critical as other Cuban films. However, it still represents an interesting option for admirers of cinema from our island.

Read more from the diary of Irina Pino here on Havana Times.

World.title: Lost savings and broken trust: life for those hit by Ueno Bank’s closure
World.content:
Lost savings and broken trust: life for those hit by Ueno Bank’s closure

9th Monday, November 2026 - 03:07 UTC Full article

Marlyn López, a 43-year-old university lecturer, lives in Piribebuy, about 75 kilometres from Asunción

For nearly three million Paraguayans, November 3 began with a message on their phone screens: “We cannot display your balance.” Early that morning, Paraguay’s Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over a critical solvency problem and froze its deposits. A week later, with President Santiago Peña removed from office and in pre-trial detention, many of those affected still have no access to their money and say they have also lost faith in the country’s institutions.

Marlyn López, a 43-year-old university lecturer, lives in Piribebuy, about 75 kilometres from Asunción. That morning she was about to buy fuel using the bank’s app, where she kept her newly paid salary and some savings, about 24 million guaraníes, or roughly US$3,800. She had only 30,000 guaraníes in cash, about US$5. “I was left with nothing, like nearly three million people,” she told El País. She has survived thanks to colleagues who transferred money to her without being asked. The authorities say they have paid an advance to half of the depositors, but she has yet to receive any notice. “I have not only lost money. I have also lost faith in the authorities, in the state institutions that should have supervised the financial system. I believed them when they said everything was fine,” she said.

Peña had repeatedly defended the soundness of the bank, in which he was once a shareholder, and blamed allegations of irregularities on campaigns by some media outlets. Prosecutors are investigating an alleged scheme of unsecured loans to companies of the Vázquez Group, the bank’s owner, which held some US$850 million in public deposits.

Rubén Causarano, 48, is a blacksmith, mechanic and beekeeper who sells food from a cart on an Asunción street corner. He had about 5 million guaraníes, roughly US$800, in Ueno, and that Tuesday he needed to send money to his daughter so she could travel to her studies. Since he always paid by card or transfer, he had no cash: he broke open the piggy bank where his daughters saved coins so he could buy fuel and drive her to the bus. He then worked for hours repairing vehicles to get paid in cash. “I’m left with the fear that they’ll screw us again. We’ll have to go back to our grandmothers’ old tradition of keeping our money under the mattress,” he said.

“These politicians are crooks; it can’t be that out of greed they have left half the country without money for daily life, without food, without medicine,” added Causarano, who has also yet to be told when he will be repaid. “Now the president has been kicked out, several of them are in jail, but those who take their place are just as crooked. How can we believe them?”

The new president, Pedro Alliana, has promised that everyone affected will recover their savings. Customers with small balances have begun to be repaid, and repayments will be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about US$19,300.

World.title: Leo XIV, before Milei: “The economy must serve the person”
World.content:
Leo XIV, before Milei: “The economy must serve the person”

9th Monday, November 2026 - 03:00 UTC Full article

Leo XIV referred to “families who carry the burden of uncertainty”, those looking for work, the elderly and those who, even while working, struggle to meet their household needs

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday, the first papal visit to Argentina in 39 years, and in his first address to the authorities, with President Javier Milei at his side, said that “the economy must be at the service of the person, and not the person at the service of the economy”, urged those in authority to “recognise the limits of power” and called for “special attention” to the sick and people with disabilities.

The pontiff arrived from Montevideo and was greeted at the foot of the plane by Milei, with whom he held a 30-minute private meeting at the Casa Rosada. At dusk, at the Palacio Libertad, before national and provincial authorities, religious representatives and diplomats, the Pope championed a democracy strengthened “by a willingness to listen, care in the use of words, the patient search for agreements and the ability to recognise in those who think differently a compatriot with whom one shares a common destiny”. “Those who exercise authority also have a duty to act prudently, recognise the limits of the power entrusted to them and direct their decisions towards the good of the whole community,” he added.

Leo XIV referred to “families who carry the burden of uncertainty”, those looking for work, the elderly and those who, even while working, struggle to meet their household needs. “A nation must ask itself seriously where it has failed when its young people must leave their land to fulfil their dreams,” he said, calling for “particular strengthening of education, vocational training, universities and research”. Reiterating his opposition to abortion, legal in Argentina since 2020, he also called for “special attention in illness, dependency and disability”.

The Pope did not mention Milei or the government, but several passages were read by the Argentine press as allusions to criticism of the president over his cuts to education, disability and pensions and the tone of his attacks on opponents. Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy has been one of the most critical voices against the government’s austerity policies.

Milei, who spoke before the Pope, gave a restrained speech, far from his usual tone. “I am pleased to see the entire political spectrum here, showing that there are reasons and occasions that go beyond our differences,” he said, and described Pope Francis, whom he had harshly criticised in the past, as “the most important Argentine in history”. Francis, who died last year, never returned to his country during his pontificate.

Authorities expect some seven million people to take part in the Pope’s events in Argentina, supported by more than 25,000 volunteers. On Monday, a national holiday, Leo XIV will visit the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities in Claypole, celebrate Mass at the Monument of the Spaniards in Palermo, and meet trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina.

World.title: Leo XIV leaves Uruguay urging Catholics to reach out to “those who have drifted away”
World.content:
Leo XIV leaves Uruguay urging Catholics to reach out to “those who have drifted away”

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 20:16 UTC Full article

Leo XIV’s was the first papal visit to Uruguay in 38 years, since John Paul II’s in 1988

Pope Leo XIV ended his visit to Uruguay on Sunday with a Mass before some 30,000 faithful in the city of Florida, where he urged Catholics to reach out to those who have drifted away from the Church in South America’s most secular country, before flying to Buenos Aires, the second stop on his regional tour.

“We cannot always wait for those who have drifted away to return on their own. Uruguay, we must set out! We must enter homes again, draw close to people, listen to their questions and bring them to Christ!” the pontiff said at the most forceful moment of his homily, celebrated before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, on her feast day. “Do not be afraid to say you are Christians,” he added, in a message that also focused on the role of mothers and grandmothers in passing on the faith.

Leo XIV’s was the first papal visit to Uruguay in 38 years, since John Paul II’s in 1988. In just over two days, the pontiff championed humanism and warned about the risks of technology, but also questioned Uruguay’s abortion and euthanasia laws in his speech to the authorities in Montevideo. On Saturday he celebrated Mass before some 30,000 faithful in Paysandú, where he praised mate as a symbol of unity and the bridge linking the city with Argentina as a call to dialogue; he visited the Casavalle neighbourhood and the Catholic University, and led a vigil before some 60,000 people at the Centenario Stadium.

The visit made the faith of some political leaders visible. “We must take care of the body but also of the soul,” said Fernando Pereira, president of the ruling Broad Front. Juan Martín Fernández, president of the Christian Democratic Party, said the Pope “has stood up to leaders like Donald Trump and has questioned Israel over Gaza” and has endorsed “the option for the poor”. “Uruguay is the most secular country, but we have his presence at the traditional pilgrimage of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, and it is something that happens very rarely,” said Florida’s mayor, Carlos Enciso.

In Buenos Aires, the Pope is due to pay tribute to General José de San Martín, meet President Javier Milei at the Casa Rosada and address the authorities at the Palacio Libertad. It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987.

World.title: Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 01:53 UTC Full article

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator

Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña, removed from office by the Senate on Friday, and requested his pre-trial detention in the case over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which froze the savings of nearly three million customers. A judge must rule on the request. Prosecutors also charged former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, who is in custody.

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator. Carvallo, who had been Ueno’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration. According to prosecutors, between 2023 and 2026 the bank received large deposits from public bodies and the pension system while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies linked to its owners, the Vázquez Group. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The former president, who had been placed under house arrest after his removal, was moved overnight to the barracks of the Presidential Escort Regiment, responsible for presidential security, after protesters threw stones at police and tore down fences near his residence in Asunción. Police dispersed the protest. Dictator Alfredo Stroessner took refuge in the same barracks in 1989 during the military coup that toppled him.

The new president, Pedro Alliana, began his term with cabinet changes. He appointed Ariel Martínez as interior minister, a post he held under former President Horacio Cartes (2013-2018), and Juan Carlos Baruja, also close to Cartes, head of the ruling Colorado Party, as public works minister. Alliana said he would suspend foreign travel to focus on the crisis and promised that all those affected would recover their savings.

Customers with balances of up to about US$1,500 have begun recovering their money, and payouts will later be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes or US$19,300. Banks will open exceptionally on Sunday so that those affected can open accounts and complete the necessary procedures.

Tension remains high. Protesters and the opposition accuse Alliana of failing to act in time to prevent the bank’s collapse and are also demanding his removal and early elections in early 2027.

World.title: Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing
World.content:
Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, will visit the Falklands and South Georgia from Monday, November 9, the day before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s case against the Sea Lion oil project, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment. The Princess, who will travel with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, will begin with a series of engagements in the Falklands: she will meet members of the community, visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse, Tussac House and the newly completed Falkland Islands National Sports Complex, and attend a reception at Government House in Stanley.

In South Georgia, a territory with no permanent civilian population, she will see the Trust’s work, meet British Antarctic Survey staff and members of the territory’s government, and commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922), who sailed some 1,500 kilometres in a lifeboat to the island to seek help for his crew, trapped by ice in Antarctica.

The palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit. Its timing, however, coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands: the Hamburg tribunal will hear Argentina and the United Kingdom on November 10 and 11, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on November 12, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: “They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets
World.content:
“They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:50 UTC Full article

Many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums

Thousands of Paraguayans celebrated in Asunción on Friday as the Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office, but the joy turned almost immediately to anger among those who wanted a complete change of government. “Out with them all,” hundreds of protesters chanted outside Congress as Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as the new head of state.

Celebrations erupted at the news that Peña, 47, was leaving office without immunity and, hours later, was placed under house arrest accused of breach of trust over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which had more than 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people. But many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums. “If the same people stay, there is no change”, “We want jail” and “Where is the money?” read the signs.

“The people are staying here until they all go,” Celicia Lugo told the EFE news agency, adding that Peña and Alliana “are the same”. “The incoming government is more of the same, because only Peña will be gone, the rest will stay,” said Milda Cuevas, who celebrated the removal and demanded that the former president “be tried” and “go to prison”. For Andrea Gutiérrez, Ueno “was just one example” of what she sees as the ongoing plundering of citizens.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday, when the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank, which had received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, and froze its deposits. Those affected include some 32,000 pensioners of the Social Security Institute, according to EFE.

In an attempt to contain the anger, Alliana announced after being sworn in that those affected by the bank’s closure “will be fully compensated”, without saying how. The legal deposit guarantee covers up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor.

World.title: Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia
World.content:
Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:30 UTC Full article

Photo: AFP

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Montevideo on Friday, the first stop on his South American tour, and in a speech to Uruguayan authorities praised Mercosur, peaceful coexistence and care for the environment, but also defended life “even that which is still growing in the mother’s womb” and questioned euthanasia, in a country where both are legal and which is considered the most secular in the region.

The pontiff’s plane landed at 4.19 p.m. at Carrasco airport, where he was met by President Yamandú Orsi and the Cardinal Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla. Leo XIV travelled in the popemobile along the waterfront promenade to Plaza Independencia, accompanied by some 3,000 volunteers, received the key to the city and visited the Cabildo and the Cathedral. Orsi welcomed him to a region “where there are no wars between countries”, called him “dear friend” and noted that in Uruguay former presidents sit together “in peace and joy”. Former presidents Julio María Sanguinetti, Luis Alberto Lacalle Herrera and Luis Lacalle Pou attended the ceremony, along with Lucía Topolansky, widow of former president José Mujica.

In his speech, the Pope took up Francis’s ideas on the common good and care for natural resources, and praised the transformation of Uruguay’s energy mix. He stressed the importance of peace and dialogue in resolving differences and praised the role of Mercosur, the bloc Uruguay forms with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. “Coexistence between people of different origins and traditions is also part of Uruguay’s history,” he said.

Leo XIV also addressed the most sensitive issues for the country. He defended life from conception, a reference to abortion, legal in Uruguay since 2012, and to euthanasia, approved in 2025. “Everyone deserves to receive [care] until the natural end of life,” he said. He also referred to the high suicide rate: “No one should feel like a stranger among their own or think that their absence matters more than their presence.” And he said secularism does not mean religion must be confined to private life.

Uruguay separated Church and State in its 1919 Constitution. Only 36% of Uruguayans describe themselves as Catholic, according to Latinobarómetro, and one in ten of those consider themselves practising. A survey by Usina de Percepción Ciudadana found that 37% of Uruguayans attach importance to the visit and 63% little or none.

On Saturday the Pope will celebrate Mass in Paysandú, visit the Montevideo neighbourhood of Casavalle and the Catholic University of Uruguay, and lead a vigil at the Centenario Stadium. On Sunday he will celebrate Mass in Florida, before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, and travel to Buenos Aires. After Argentina and Peru, he will return to Rome on November 16.

World.title: Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office
World.content:
Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:17 UTC Full article

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours

Paraguay’s Senate on Friday removed President Santiago Peña from office in an impeachment trial for “poor performance of his duties” over the collapse of Ueno Bank, and hours later prosecutors ordered him placed under house arrest over alleged economic crimes. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in before Congress that night as the new head of state and will serve out the term until August 15, 2028.

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours. With it, Peña loses the lifetime Senate seat and parliamentary immunity he would have obtained had Congress accepted the resignation he tendered on Thursday, which was never considered. Thousands of savers gathered outside Congress celebrated the decision.

Prosecutor Christian Benítez said Peña will remain detained at home until he is placed at the disposal of the Specialised Unit for Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption. According to La Nación, prosecutors are investigating him for alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and self-serving administration. The order also covers former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to the Associated Press. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The Senate rejected the 72-hour extension the president had requested to prepare his defence. Peña, who had said on Thursday that he would appear, ultimately did not attend and sent his lawyers, Adolfo Ferreiro — who in 2012 defended President Fernando Lugo, also removed through impeachment — and Ricardo Preda. Both argued they had not had enough time to prepare a defence and that the trial was moot after the resignation, arguments the Senate rejected.

“I submitted my resignation to avoid further harm to the country and help restore calm to Paraguay. I do not want my presence to be a cause of further division or instability,” Peña wrote in a farewell message. “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.”

Alliana, 52, born in Pilar, a former governor of Ñeembucú department and former president of the Colorado Party, was sworn in minutes after the removal. Antonio Barrios took over as vice president, according to ABC Color. The opposition accepted the succession, albeit with reservations. “We accept this situation to ensure institutional continuity for the country,” said opposition senator Rafael Filizzola, who called Alliana “complicit” in what happened. Alliana had publicly distanced himself from Peña on the eve of the bank takeover and is expected to make changes to the government and the Central Bank.

The fall of Peña, a 47-year-old economist who took office in August 2023 with a modernising message, unfolded in just four days. On Tuesday, the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over insolvency and irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, freezing the deposits of nearly three million customers, about 60% of the adult population, as well as hundreds of millions of dollars in public and pension funds. Carvallo had been the bank’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, and Peña himself was a shareholder in the bank’s holding company until April 2025. On Thursday, the Colorado Party withdrew its support, led by its president, former President Horacio Cartes, who backed the impeachment.

World.title: How Mexico’s longest dictatorship planted the seeds for a revolution
World.content:
In the last decades of the 19th century, Porfirio Díaz dominated public life in Mexico, sometimes as the power behind the throne but usually as the country’s president. Díaz’s rule, remembered as the Porfiriato, began with the Plan of Tuxtepec, launched 150 years ago in 1876.

It was during Díaz’s rule that capitalism became firmly rooted in Mexico, with railroads unfurling across the country, national products making millionaires out of Mexican businessmen on the world market and native elites fervently embracing European trends, leaving marks like the Palacio de Bellas Artes and Teatro Macedonio Alcalá on national cityscapes. But it was also the dizzying speed and unevenness of this development — which stripped rural communities of their communally-held lands and enslaved Indigenous people on henequen plantations in Yucatán — that planted the seeds of the cataclysmic Revolution of 1910.

The Tuxtepec Revolution ended what is remembered as the Restored Republic, or the nine years of republican rule following the end of the French Intervention. To make sense of Díaz’s revolt, we need to understand the politics of the Restored Republic itself. After the civil war of the 1860s, the Conservative Party was discredited for its collaboration with the French, and liberalism was in practice the only game in town, which meant that politics broke along factional lines within the Liberal Party.

Díaz had made his name fighting against the Santa Anna dictatorship and later the conservatives and their French allies, and during the Restored Republic — as the period between 1867 and 1876 is called — he was the figure most associated with the populist, mass-politics wing of the liberals. On the other side of the political spectrum was Díaz’s fellow Oaxacan and old mentor, Benito Juárez.

How do you solve a problem like Benito Juárez?

In 1867, Juárez had already served two terms as President of Mexico. Supreme Court chief justice following the Ayutla Revolution, Juárez first rose to the presidency in 1858 not by election but as constitutionally designated successor to President Ignacio Comonfort, whose self-coup in January 1858 marked the start of the Reform War, a three-year civil war between liberals and conservatives.

Juárez led the liberals to victory and won reelection in June 1861, just in time to see the Conservatives play the ace up their sleeve, reopening the civil war by bringing in Archduke Maximilian of Austria to rule Mexico as emperor, supported by French bayonets. With Juárez and his government-in-exile — the “Nomad Republic” — leading the war effort as they wandered across the country, the liberals again beat the Conservatives and their European allies in 1867.

By the time he entered Mexico City in triumph in July of that year, Juárez had already been in power for nearly a decade, and he announced his intention to run for the presidency again in October. Already, he faced opposition from fellow liberals who felt that with the civil war over and the French expelled, a third term was unjustifiable.

Particularly concerning for the anti-reelectionists were Juárez’s stated plans for governing. The Constitution of 1857, which had lit the fuse of civil war years earlier and which Juárez himself had an important part in writing, established a notably weak executive branch and placed virtually all power with the national legislature.

Juárez understood that the Constitution would need to be reformed if the country was to advance according to his vision. That meant giving the executive the veto it lacked and dividing the unicameral legislature into a senate and chamber of deputies, and there was little chance Congress would vote to limit its own power. So Juárez circumvented it, calling a national plebiscite to ratify his proposed changes.

Porfirio Díaz, unable to accept this kind of change to the Constitution he had fought to establish and defend, decided to run against the man he had fought under. He gathered around himself some of the country’s leading lights, intellectuals like Ignacio Ramírez, Guillermo Prieto and Vicente Riva Palacio, not to mention broad support from the masses.

Díaz was a popular and respected war hero, but Juárez swept the election anyway, winning 72% of the vote, although the Senate ratified his victory at the price of not passing his constitutional reforms. Díaz resigned from the Army and returned home to Oaxaca, where he dedicated himself to business and to cultivating his prestige.

In 1871, Juárez decided to stand for a fourth term as president, a decision so controversial that not only Díaz but Juárez’s close ally Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada decided to run against him. In the elections that summer, Díaz came in second. Juárez won 48% of the vote, the most of the three candidates, but short of the 51% needed to win. It was up to Congress to choose a winner, and they chose Benito Juárez.

That same year, Juárez and Díaz ran against each other once again, and again Juárez won; this time, though, a third candidate had been in the mix, and no one had a majority of the votes. It was up to Congress to choose a winner, and they chose Juárez. Díaz and others who believed that Juárez was becoming an autocrat responded by rebelling against his government under the Plan of Noria.

The rebellion went on for half a year before Juárez’s sudden death by heart attack took the wind out of Díaz’s movement. His successor, Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, pardoned the rebels and politically neutralized Díaz, who eventually settled across the border in Texas. Lerdo de Tejada pursued the same centralizing policies that the former president’s enemies had called autocratic. This undermined Lerdo de Tejada’s own government.

The straw that broke the camel’s back was the president’s September 1875 announcement of his intention to stand for reelection the next year. In March 1876, a group of pro-Díaz military officers and intellectuals proclaimed the Plan of Tuxtepec in the Oaxaca town of Villa de Ojitlán, declaring Lerdo de Tejada’s government illegitimate and calling for the end of reelection for the presidency and governorships. It invited Díaz to lead the rebellion.

The meaning of the Tuxtepec Revolution

Looking back a century and a half and through the lens of all the classroom days, novels and popular songs that help shape a country’s memory, it’s easy to see history as a clash of giant individuals fighting for reasons of personal ambition. We miss a great deal, however, if we read the Tuxtepec Revolution as a grasping, ambitious Díaz versus the noble Juárez — or vice versa, as power-hungry Juárez against champion-of-the-masses Díaz. Indeed, much of the tragedy of Díaz’s struggle against Juárez, and later Lerdo de Tejada, is that the commanders on both sides had an outstanding history of patriotic service, fighting against French occupiers and the old feudal order to make Mexico a more democratic country.

In some ways, their positions even intermingled: In 1867, it was Díaz who stood for respecting the tedious mechanisms for reforming the Constitution; Juárez wanted to submit the document to the will of the whole country. Who here was the populist? And when Díaz — the anti-reelectionist, the federalist — finally won power, he did just as Juárez and Lerdo de Tejada had done: He centralized power and perpetuated himself in it.

It would be an easy cliché to explain this turn by saying that power corrupts. Harder to wrestle with, but maybe more illuminating, would be to consider whether it was something about Mexico itself — about the reality of the country — that made these two men, with their democratic bona fides, govern as they did.

It may be more fruitful to read the Tuxtepec Revolution as a continuation of the struggle between centralism and federalism that had characterized Mexican politics since the country’s earliest days of independence. Díaz’s partisans were largely regional leaders who stayed in power by remaining closely attuned to the concerns of the communities and areas they represented.

Although these men were military commanders, imagining them as the kind of professional military men who overturned governments in 20th-century Latin America — or indeed, who would later keep Díaz in power as his dictatorship stretched on — is a misstep too, given that they rose as the elected leaders of their hometown militias.

Diego Levin is a historian and researcher.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Government clarifies 59 million liters of fuel were not stolen, just logistically misplaced
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Federal law enforcement authorities clarified Thursday that 59 million liters of gasoline seized during what was initially celebrated as the largest fuel-theft bust in Mexican history were not actually stolen, but had simply been misplaced in a series of administrative oversight errors spread across ten industrial storage tanks.

The announcement comes nearly two months after joint state and federal forces executed a high-profile raid on a fuel terminal in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato, triumphantly declaring a decisive victory against huachicoleros, or fuel thieves.

“Upon closer examination of the terminal’s filing cabinets, we determined that all 59 million liters were, in fact, accounted for on paper, though regrettably filed under ‘miscellaneous liquid assets’ rather than active inventory,” said a spokesperson for the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR), who requested anonymity to speak on the logistical mix-up. “It was less an act of organized crime and more an issue of an intern mislaying a very large set of clipboards.”

According to officials, the initial confusion arose when law enforcement agents arrived at the facility and discovered tens of millions of liters of petroleum sitting in industrial containers without an immediate, visible paper trail attached to the side of the tanks.

The government praised the terminal’s operating company for its swift cooperation in resolving the discrepancy by presenting the missing permits shortly after the raid concluded, effectively reducing the historical law enforcement operation to a routine inventory audit.

“We are pleased to report that the energy security of the nation was never compromised by illicit cartels, but rather momentarily obscured by a localized filing error,” the spokesperson added, noting that the federal agent who authorized the initial raid has since been reassigned to another state.

At press time, federal officials confirmed that while no arrests had been made, the 59 million liters of fuel have been safely returned to their original status of existing quietly in Guanajuato until further notice.

World.title: An early flu outbreak is hitting the US West Coast. Here’s what it means for Mexico
World.content:
This time of year, travel from the U.S. changes from family vacationers to snowbirds heading south to Mexico for warmer weather and tourists wanting to experience Día de Muertos. But this year, travelers from the West Coast may bring an unwanted illness along for the ride.

The flu season started prematurely in the U.S., unexpectedly hitting the states bordering the Pacific Ocean sooner than usual. The early arrival is driven by a mutated influenza A strain. Over the summer, Mexico saw a surge of off-season flu that was mostly influenza B, and as of early October, Mexico’s Health Ministry had not detected this new mutation. As travelers decide whether to mask up for their flights, they should also consider extra precautions before crossing the border this year.

What’s different this year

In the U.S., flu season typically starts in the south in places like Florida, where the virus arrives from the Southern Hemisphere. The flu then spreads throughout the rest of the country during the fall and winter months. But this year, Western states along the Pacific Ocean, including Hawaii, are seeing flu levels that are normally seen in December or January. For example, Hawaii’s most recent positive flu test rate is 27.1%, significantly higher than the 5.6% rate for the same time last year. Both California and Washington have positivity rates above 11%.

The flu strain affecting these states appears to come from Asia and is a mutated version of the H1N1 virus. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A, and the current G155E mutation can evade a person’s existing immunity. Japan first detected this H1N1 mutation in May and is now seeing surges spreading rapidly among children, leading to school closures. The H1N1 virus first emerged in 2009 in La Gloria, Mexico, and created a pandemic that mostly affected children. At this time, no G155E mutation has been identified in Mexico.

Who’s most at risk

Teens and young adults appear to have a weaker antibody response to the G155E mutation. This means the virus may spread more easily past their body’s existing immunity. So far, there is no evidence that the mutation causes a more severe illness.

Those most at risk for severe illness are the same as with prior flu seasons and have priority for free flu shots in Mexico. This includes:

Children 6 to 59 months of age

Adults age 60 and older

Pregnant people

People ages 5 to 59 who have chronic health conditions, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, cancer or HIV

Healthcare workers

Other groups considered at higher risk, but not a priority for free flu shots, include:

People with disabilities

Individuals living in long-term care facilities

People with weakened immune systems

The cross-border risk

The U.S. accounts for 67.1% of international travel into Mexico, with 19 million visitors expected this year. Border crossings begin to increase in late October, driven by cultural tourism around Día de Muertos. Travel levels remain high through January because of holidays, family vacations and snowbirds escaping the cooler winter weather in the north. This travel peak coincides with the same timeframe for higher flu levels.

Health officials in both Mexico and the U.S. are urging everyone to vaccinate early. This is because it takes about two weeks for the body to develop immunity after vaccination. For the best protection for yourself and those around you, now is the time to get your shot and build immunity before holiday travel and celebrations.

Protecting yourself in Mexico

Mexico administers 30 million flu vaccines annually to prevent influenza and related complications. The Health Ministry launched the National Vaccination Campaign for the 2026-2027 fall and winter season on Oct. 12, and it runs until March 31, 2027. This year’s goal is to reduce and prevent respiratory illness complications during the cold and flu season by administering more than 50 million doses of vaccines against COVID-19, influenza and pneumonia.

Additionally, for the first time, the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine is available to pregnant women between 32 and 36 weeks’ gestation. This intervention aims to protect the unborn child from the virus during the first few months of life. RSV is a common virus that typically causes mild, cold-like symptoms. However, infants and older adults with certain risk factors are more likely to develop severe illnesses or need hospitalization.

Free vaccination clinics are available across Mexico in local health clinics and gathering places. The Secretaría de Salud has an interactive map to help locate a clinic near you at dondemevacuno.salud.gob.mx, or you can call the toll-free number 079 for information about available sites. If you are not in a priority group for a free vaccine, you can purchase vaccines at private pharmacies and hospitals.

Leanna Coy is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Mexican caves: What you need to know before you step into one
World.content:
If you hike in Mexico long enough, sooner or later you’re likely to find yourself standing in front of a cave entrance, wondering if you should venture inside.

Whether invited by locals or entirely on your own, here are a few thoughts from someone who has spent many hours underground in Mexico.

Bags of golden coins

All over the world, people find caves enticing, but even more so in Mexico, which has a long history of colorful bandidos who, we are told, could think of no better place to hide their stolen coins and bars of bullion than a cave.

This stubbornly held belief has given rise to treasure-in-cave stories that I have heard again and again.

“This cueva has a small entrance, but after you crawl a while, it opens up into a huge room as big as a cathedral and then there’s a long tunnel that goes all the way through the mountain to the other side … además,” the storyteller often says, adding, “I was told that a guy went inside this very cave years ago and came upon bags filled with doubloons, but just when he was going to carry one away, a voice boomed out: ‘Todo o nada,’ meaning either you take all of it at once or you get nothing.”

Inevitably, these stories say that the beguiled explorer never made it out — but that has not discouraged countless treasure hunters from digging countless holes in just about every cave in the country.

Crystals 14 meters long

A more aesthetic sort of treasure does actually lie much deeper inside many caves: beautiful, delicate stalactites, stalagmites, aragonite crystals, and bizarre formations called helictites, which look like stalactites that have decided to defy gravity, pointing every which way.

But the most stupendous cave formations of all are the famed selenite crystals of Mexico’s Naica Cave: up to 14 meters (about 46 feet) long and 4 meters (about 13 feet) thick.

North America’s deepest cave

Equally exciting is the unbelievable size of Mexico’s cave systems.

In 1965, students in Austin, Texas, asked their geology teacher where they could find the deepest cave in North America.

The answer turned out to be Oaxaca, Mexico, and led to the discovery of Sistema Huautla. At 103.4 kilometers (64.2 miles) long and 1,560 meters (5,118 feet) deep, it’s currently recognized as the deepest cave in the Western Hemisphere.

At the same time, exploration of Mexico’s cenotes has led to the discovery and mapping of 2,096.4 kilometers (1,302.6 miles) of wet and dry caves on the Yucatán Peninsula. If these huge systems are eventually linked up, Mammoth Cave in Kentucky will have to cede the title of “Longest Cave in the World” — 686 kilometers or 426 miles — to Mexico.

No wonder speleologists widely consider Mexico the new frontier in underground exploration, where one can experience the exhilaration of being the first person to step into a passage.

Which, when standing before the entrance to a Mexican cave, prompts the question: Should you go inside?

‘Thank God for my helmet!’

Consideration No. 1: Unless we are talking about a commercial cave, you need to have the proper equipment for going underground. Experienced cavers always carry a minimum of three sources of light, for example, a headlamp and two flashlights, each with spare batteries. Serious cavers also use helmets. They not only protect you from collisions with stalactites or low ceilings, but also make all the difference should you trip and fall. “Thank God for my helmet!” is one of the most often spoken phrases (in every language) beneath the surface of the Earth.

Consideration No. 2: Many caves flood during the rainy season. To appreciate the consequences, see “The Rescue,” National Geographic’s 2021 documentary on what happened to 13 boys when a cave flooded in Thailand.

So, if it’s the dry season, you’ve got the right equipment, and you are accompanied by experienced espeleólogos. But are you clear to crawl into a Mexican cave?

Invisible spores

Hold on. There are still a few more considerations. The most serious is Histoplasma capsulatum. This is a fungus that grows on bat guano and continuously produces tiny spores, invisible to the eye. Once you breathe them in, they lodge in your lungs, and your body fights them, subjecting you to nonstop coughing, fever and chest pains — if you are lucky.

Some years ago, 17 people went to visit a small, dusty cave in Jalisco, all of them wearing face masks. After the typical histo incubation period of 11 days, all of these individuals were feeling bad, and ended up at the IMSS medical center in Guadalajara. After hours of studies, they were told to report back the following morning.

“But what about the medicine? What do we take?”

“There is no medicine. Just relax at home for two weeks and you’ll be okay.”

“But why do we have to come back tomorrow?”

“Oh, it’s because we’ve never had 17 people with histo all here at the same time. This is very exciting for us!”

Bad air

Another complication you could run into in a wild cave is “bad air.”

At low spots, carbon dioxide — which is invisible and odorless — can accumulate. If this lake of CO2 is deep enough and you step into it, you will first find yourself panting heavily as if you were running a marathon. Should you find yourself in this situation, you have about two minutes to get yourself out of there.

On top of all that, we have slight inconveniences such as low, tight crawl-ways half-filled with mud, guano and bat urine … and then there are the frequent encounters with rabies-carrying vampire bats (usually harmless unless you try to sleep in the cave). Perhaps you can see why some people in this country consider cueveros “locos.”

So, finally, should you or should you not crawl into that enticing Mexican cave?

We’ve given you (just about) everything you need to know. But the decision is ultimately yours.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: INE crisis deepens, economy gains momentum and Latino voters reshape US midterms
World.content:
Plan Michoacán progress report

Wednesday’s mañanera was devoted to progress on Plan Michoacán, the federal response to Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s killing in November 2025. Sheinbaum said the plan is 67% complete, with 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” finished. Planned investment through 2030 has more than doubled from the original 57 billion pesos to 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion), and 72.43 billion pesos has been spent.

Cabinet members each highlighted a piece of the plan. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said 115 “Well-being Fairs” across all 113 municipalities helped residents complete more than 1.1 million administrative procedures, and that 673 firearms were exchanged for cash. The government, together with the private sector, is investing more than 41 billion pesos in six highway projects covering 411 kilometers, and work on the 9.3-billion-peso Bajío Industrial Park in Zinapécuaro starts this month. Other officials cited scholarships for 795,000 students, 177,000 people aided by the Sembrando Vida reforestation program, electricity coverage reaching 99.99% of homes and a new addiction-treatment hospital in Apatzingán. Tourism is up 10.1% through August. Mexico News Daily noted that not all the investment cited is directly tied to Plan Michoacán funding.

Security was left for a separate update next Tuesday. Homicides in the state fell 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026. At the Uruapan march, Quiroz demanded an “exhaustive” and “independent” investigation into Manzo’s killing, noting that more than 30 people have been arrested, including seven of his bodyguards. She hasn’t decided whether to run for governor.

Banxico surprises with rate cut

The central bank lowered its benchmark rate 25 basis points to 6.25% in a split vote, though 30 of 36 institutions surveyed by Citi expected no change. Banxico raised its fourth-quarter headline inflation forecast from 3.5% to 3.7% and signaled it would hold the rate “for an extended period.” The dollar hit 18.96 pesos before closing at 18.75.

Mexican judge faces extradition

Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexico City district judge, was arrested in Colombia on Nov. 1. U.S. officials accuse him of accepting a US $2 million bribe to help free Andrew Clark, second-in-command to ex-Olympic snowboarder Ryan James Wedding’s trafficking organization. Benítez is the first Mexican federal judge indicted by the United States, and he faces nine counts, each carrying up to 15 years. Separately, Édgar Aarón Vázquez, leader of the New Empire Cartel and accused of protecting Wedding, was killed Thursday in a confrontation with police in the State of Mexico.

Phone-free schools

Starting Tuesday, cell phones and tablets are restricted during classes and recess at public and private primary and secondary schools nationwide. High schools will set their own rules with their school communities. The Education Ministry’s slogan was “Turn off the screen and turn your imagination on!”

The rules follow a Sept. 18 decision by the National Council of Educational Authorities, in which officials from all 32 states agreed to the measures. Education Minister Mario Delgado said the goal is to boost focus, encourage socializing in schoolyards and hallways, and promote responsible technology use. The guidelines grew out of expert presentations on the addictive nature of certain algorithms and forums with parents and educators. According to Delgado, 81% of 565,000 educators surveyed backed guidelines for safe device use.

Papal visit confusion

A comment by the Vatican’s new communications chief about the pope visiting “Our Lady of Guadalupe” set off reports of a 2027 Mexico trip. Televisa’s Vatican correspondent Valentina Alazraki reported that a Vatican spokesperson clarified the comment referred to a parish in Casavalle, Uruguay. Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada said she had no confirmation, and Alazraki reported that Leo XIV wants to come but “there is only the intention.”

Mexican-American María Montserrat Alvarado took office as the Vatican’s communications chief on Sunday. The 39-year-old Mexico City native, raised in Miami, is the first laywoman to lead a ministry-level Vatican department.

Mexico’s economy gains momentum

The MND Economy Index™ hit a record 74.5 out of 100 for August, half a point shy of “strong.” Mexico-Canada trade rose 18.3% in the first eight months to 34.42 billion Canadian dollars, while Mexico’s trade surplus with the U.S. jumped 26.1% through September to a record US $184 billion, driven largely by AI-related equipment purchases.

2026 annual growth forecasts improved in both Banxico (1.5%) and Citi (1.8%) surveys.

Mexico City weighs tougher penalties for animal poisoning

After four dogs died from poisoned meat in Condesa’s Parque España, lawmakers proposed tougher penalties. Labor Party lawmaker Diana Barragán’s bill would allow three to nine years when poisoning kills an animal, and other proposals would bar convicted abusers from acquiring animals. A 58-year-old suspect is jailed pending trial.

Travel headlines

Looking ahead

Banxico and Citi both predict Mexico’s economy will grow about 1.8% to 1.9% in 2027, with year-end 2026 inflation near 3.9%. Banxico has signaled it plans to hold its rate steady for an extended period.

One sector that will shape that outlook is data centers. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said last week that companies have announced more than US $8 billion in data center projects, led by Querétaro, with Guanajuato and Nuevo León also drawing investment. Sheinbaum has said Mexico needs data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but not necessarily to become a hub for the rest of the world, given their energy and water demands.

Data centers were also a hot topic in the U.S. midterms. The Associated Press reported that a campaign season filled with outrage against them ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the facilities. Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governorship, campaigned on a moratorium on new data center construction. Whether the issue crosses the border is an open question as Mexico heads to its own midterms on June 6, 2027.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: Is the beach the real Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — explores whether living in a beachfront community really qualifies as an authentically Mexican experience.

About 15 years ago, when I had my first online job, one of my supervisors lived in Los Cabos. She very much enjoyed telling people “what it was like in Mexico,” and was proud of her knowledge.

“Well, in my experience here, that’s not a problem at all!” she’d say when one of the many other Mexican residents would casually bring up an issue. “Things are pretty easy in Mexico, you know. All you have to do is …”

A friend of mine who worked with me and lived in Mexico City would privately express her annoyance to me. “That’s easy to say if you live in a gringo paradise with low population density. I’d love to see this ‘Mexico genius’ get by in my own barrio.”

Even in Xalapa, where spotting a foreigner is like stumbling upon Waldo, I’ve been on the receiving end of this kind of annoyance. “You live in a bubble in Xalapa; that’s not the real Mexico!” a friend of mine once insisted. She herself had lived for years in a tiny town outside of a fairly dinky and unglamorous city. I rolled my eyes and let it go; it wasn’t something I cared to debate.

Besides, if that was “the real Mexico,” I’d happily leave it all for her.

Where is the real Mexico, and how do I get there?

Chances are that you clicked on this article primed for a debate. It’s a sensitive topic, especially among those of us who consider Mexico home and ourselves to be fully integrated. Whether we foreigners live in beach towns or tiny towns, everyone’s surely got an opinion!

So what is the measuring stick that people use to define the “real” … any place, actually? Because this tendency isn’t at all unique to Mexico.

Think of every Hallmark rom-com you’ve ever seen: a high-powered and glamorous businesswoman travels from her sleek New York City apartment back to her home for the holidays. It’s always a small town in the U.S. Midwest. Everyone knows each other, and her high school sweetheart is there, handsome and single, or perhaps widowed.

That small town? That’s the “real” America, the movie says. Not like New York City, which was actually established first. Similarly, people in Mexico — especially foreigners — often have some strict ideas about what counts as “authentically Mexican.”

I suspect, actually, that Mexicans do not have conversations about this, which is telling: they have nothing to prove. They’re Mexican, and wherever they live in the country is “really” Mexico, period.

Not all beaches are developed equally

Still, beach communities receive special scrutiny. Not all beach communities are alike, though. Living in Cancún or Los Cabos, for example, is very different than living in Chachalacas, Veracruz.

Cancún and Los Cabos are full of fancy beach resorts and the kind of development that could attract royalty. Everyone who works there has to speak at least some English.

Chachalacas is a tiny town that only recently got paved roads. Its fanciest hotels are fancy simply because they have in-room air conditioning and a pool. English can most certainly not be counted on, and beach parking is on the sand … or you can take a bus from a small, unfancy town nearby. Bathrooms are bare toilet seats in the middle of small wooden shacks; 1 star for sure. To flush the toilet, there’s a large tub of water outside and a bucket. But boy, is the seafood good!

So here’s the question: Is Chachalacas more real than Cancún? It’s hard to argue that they share much in common besides the beach. Or perhaps it’s the presence, or not, of foreigners in a place, be it the beach or somewhere else. Does the fact that one might look around and see a sea of one’s paisanos make it less authentic? For some, I think it absolutely does.

We were in the real Mexico all along

And of course, the question might not even be a consequential one. People live where they want to live. Does it matter if they’re adapting or not? Do people even care if where they’re living is authentic in a stranger’s view? But no matter where you are, if you live on or near the beach, expect to get side-eyed when you talk about your knowledge of Mexico.

The word “beach” is practically synonymous with “vacation,” which explains a lot. You hear it in our language: “Time to leave the beach and get back to the real world.” This is a sad phrase to me, since it separates the real world from the kind of world that you’d actually like to live in. So perhaps the rest of us are just jealous?

My daughter has an educational book about sex. It spends some time talking about the differences between boys and girls. It does a good job of emphasizing that things like haircuts and clothing are pretty much never exclusive to one sex. “There are all kinds of different ways to be a boy,” it says, and “there are all kinds of different ways to be a girl.”

This, I believe, is the correct attitude to have with most things. Like everywhere else, Mexico is a very diverse place. There are as many different ways to “be Mexico” as there are different ways to be Mexican.

So wherever you are, maybe don’t worry about it too much. If someone wants to challenge you on it, like my friend above, shrug your shoulders and suggest a Tex-Mex style margarita, or maybe a caguama … you know, depending on where you are.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: South Sudan Election Talks Set to Resume
World.content:
The bridge over the Nile at Juba, South Sudan’s capital. Undated photo: Rod Waddington, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

South Sudan’s political parties are due back at the table in Juba on Monday 9 November 2026 to finalise resolutions from a national dialogue that opened in late September. The ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) said in a statement that the plenary session will discuss and finalise proposed resolutions and a joint communiqué, meaning a shared closing statement; we have not independently confirmed that the session opened.

For US readers, the outcome matters because it shapes whether the world’s youngest country, independent since 2011, holds its first general elections on Tuesday 22 December 2026. A disputed or delayed vote in an oil-exporting, aid-dependent state raises the risk of fresh fighting and fresh humanitarian demands.

What Parties are due to resume the Juba inter-party dialogue on Monday 9 November, the SPLM says.

Who The SPLM says Secretary-General Akol Paul Kordit prepared the session and Kiir will help set the closing date.

The deadline General elections are scheduled for Tuesday 22 December 2026, the first since independence in 2011.

The dispute Critics call it government-controlled; Riek Machar, founder of the opposition SPLM-IO, remains detained and on trial.

What to watch Whether a joint communiqué is adopted and whether it keeps the 22 December election date.

What Is Planned in Juba on Monday

SPLM Secretary-General Akol Paul Kordit met senior party officials and representatives of other political groups earlier this week to prepare the resumption, the party said. The meeting agreed that the plenary would discuss and finalise proposed resolutions and a joint communiqué.

The date of the closing ceremony will be set in consultation with President Salva Kiir once the resolutions are adopted, the SPLM said. The party’s own statement is the only account so far, so this report stays marked as reported, not confirmed.

How the Dialogue Began

Kiir opened the dialogue in Juba in late September, just days after he dissolved the power-sharing transitional government, formed under the 2018 peace deal, on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Kiir told the gathering it “is not a place for negotiations and disagreements”.

The gathering brought together parties based in Juba and other stakeholders. Major opposition groups, including those linked to Machar, rejected the government’s approach.

In plain English: South Sudan’s parties are meeting again to agree a joint statement before an election that the government says will go ahead and that critics doubt can be credible.

Why Critics Are Doubtful

The SPLM-IO (SPLM in Opposition), the movement’s opposition wing, rejected the Juba-led dialogue in August and asked for regional or international mediation. The United People’s Alliance, an opposition coalition, also rejected it.

Machar, who founded the SPLM-IO, remains in detention and on trial. Cabinet Affairs Minister Martin Elia Lomuro said in August that there will be no extension of the transition, so in our assessment the dialogue has little room to change the calendar.

A busy street at Gudele in Juba, photographed in January 2024. Photo: MakurProTyler, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What It Means for You

Investors and aid groups should read the final communiqué for one signal: does it keep 22 December, or open a door to delay? In our assessment, a text that holds the date raises security and logistics risks in Juba, while a text that allows delay is likely to start a new fight over who governs once the current mandate ends.

Americans with travel plans should check the US State Department travel advisory before any trip. Our guides to the South Sudan election and South Sudan’s geopolitics set out the background.

What Is Not Known

We do not know whether the session opened as planned, which parties will attend, or whether the SPLM-IO and other holdouts will return. We found no published attendance list.

It is also unclear whether the communiqué will address the election date directly. Related developments are in our reports on the Cabinet’s Russia partnership and the UN warning on a coup.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is South Sudan’s election?

General elections are scheduled for Tuesday 22 December 2026. They would be the first since independence in 2011.

Who is Riek Machar?

Riek Machar founded the opposition SPLM-IO, the opposition wing of the SPLM. He remains in detention and on trial.

What is the inter-party dialogue?

It is a forum launched by President Salva Kiir in late September 2026 for Juba-based parties and other stakeholders. It is meant to prepare the elections, though opposition groups say the government controls it.

World.title: Eritrea’s Isaias Meets China’s Horn Envoy
World.content:
A main avenue in Asmara, Eritrea’s capital, photographed in 2015. Photo: Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Eritrea’s President Isaias Afwerki met China’s special envoy for the Horn of Africa, Hu Changchun, in the capital Asmara on Thursday 5 November 2026. The talks centred on bilateral ties and regional developments, and Hu restated Beijing’s support for Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

For US readers, the meeting shows China courting a government that sits on the Red Sea, the shipping lane that links Asia to Europe through the Suez Canal. Eritrea is also locked in a tense standoff with its much larger neighbour Ethiopia, which is why the wording of China’s message matters.

Who President Isaias Afwerki of Eritrea and Hu Changchun, China’s special envoy for Horn of Africa affairs.

When and where Thursday 5 November 2026, early evening, at the Denden Guest House in Asmara.

What China said Beijing stressed respect for Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Prediction markets Polymarket puts a 12.5% chance on Eritrea invading Ethiopia by 31 December (9 November, 3:32 a.m. ET).

What to watch Liu Xianfa, China’s Special Representative on African Affairs, is due in Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt this month.

What Was Said in Asmara

Isaias received Hu Changchun, China’s Special Envoy for Horn of Africa Affairs, at the Denden Guest House in the early evening of 5 November. Eritrea’s Ministry of Information, which published the account, said the extensive talks centred on bilateral ties and current developments in the region.

Hu reiterated the position of the People’s Republic of China on the imperative of respecting Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. The published account does not say whether Ethiopia was named, and it lists no agreements.

A Visit Announced Days Earlier

China’s Foreign Ministry said on Monday 2 November that Hu would visit Eritrea in early November. Spokesperson Mao Ning described it as part of a round of envoy visits to the Middle East, the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, aimed at promoting peace talks and easing tensions.

The same announcement named Liu Xianfa, China’s Special Representative on African Affairs, for Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early and mid-November. Hu had last met Isaias on Friday 10 April 2026, when China said it would deepen what it calls the China-Eritrea strategic partnership.

In plain English: China sent a diplomat to tell Eritrea’s president it respects his country’s borders, while another Chinese envoy is due in Ethiopia, Eritrea’s rival.

Why Sovereignty Is the Key Word

Ethiopia has had no coastline since Eritrea became independent in 1993, and its leaders have said publicly that they want sea access. Eritrea reads that demand as a threat to its territory, and our report on Eritrea’s list of Ethiopian war threats shows how sharp the quarrel has become.

By restating respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, Beijing tells Asmara it does not back changes to borders by force. It does not publicly take a side, and with a second envoy due in Ethiopia this month, China keeps a line open to both capitals.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction platform, prices a contract on whether Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 December 2026 at 12.5%, as of 9 November, 3:32 a.m. ET. About US$64,000 has been traded on that contract.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

Shippers, oil investors and anyone watching Red Sea insurance costs follow this corner of the world because a war on the Eritrean coast would add risk to a route already under strain. A diplomatic track that keeps both sides talking, even through third parties, lowers that risk, although one meeting proves little by itself.

Americans thinking of travelling to Eritrea or Ethiopia should read the current State Department advisory first. Our guide to Eritrea and its neighbours and the profile Djibouti in Africa give the map behind the story.

What Is Not Known

The Eritrean account does not say whether Hu raised Ethiopia or offered to mediate. We found no Chinese Foreign Ministry readout of the 5 November meeting as of Monday 9 November 2026.

It is also unclear what Isaias said, since the account quotes only Hu’s position. For his other foreign contacts this autumn, see our report on Isaias and the Russia-Africa summit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Hu Changchun?

Hu Changchun is the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s special envoy for Horn of Africa affairs. He met President Isaias Afwerki in Eritrea on Friday 10 April 2026 and again on Thursday 5 November 2026.

What did China say about Eritrea’s sovereignty?

Hu reiterated China’s position on the imperative of respecting Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Eritrea’s Ministry of Information published that account of the meeting on 5 November 2026.

Is China sending envoys to Ethiopia too?

China’s Foreign Ministry said on 2 November that Liu Xianfa, its Special Representative on African Affairs, would visit Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early and mid-November. The ministry gave no exact dates.

World.title: IMF to Review Ethiopia’s New Forecast Model
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · IMF · ECONOMIC FORECASTING

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global lender to governments, plans to review with Ethiopian officials how far a new economic forecasting model has got and when it will be fully in use. The model was due to be finished in September 2026, and the review is reported to be part of talks due this month.

This matters to readers in the United States because each payment from the IMF’s US$3.4 billion loan programme for Ethiopia rests on the government’s numbers. Better forecasts make it easier to judge Ethiopia’s debt sustainability while it restructures its debts.

What the New Model Is

Ethiopia’s Ministry of Finance asked the IMF in October 2024 for help to upgrade how it forecasts growth, inflation and public finances. The plan is to replace the ministry’s older framework with the Comprehensive Adaptive Expectations Model (CAEM), a toolkit tailored to Ethiopia’s data and institutions.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A scoping mission in May 2025 reviewed current practice at the finance ministry, which works with the planning ministry and the National Bank of Ethiopia (the central bank). The roadmap foresaw about seven IMF advisory missions, roughly two to three months apart, as reported.

A separate IMF report, published on 16 July 2025, covered the central bank’s own forecasting system after a mission in Addis Ababa from 4 to 8 November 2024. It found that forecasting models and a dedicated team were in place, and it recommended more nowcasting models, which estimate the present from early data, plus a structural macro model and a structured forecasting process.

A street in Addis Ababa with new office towers, near the ministries that run the federal government. File photo, Rio Times library

Why the Schedule Is in Question

The September 2026 target has passed, and we found no announcement that the model is complete. The IMF has not said publicly whether the model is finished.

Ethiopian coverage says the IMF will discuss the timeline for full implementation with the authorities, which is reported, not confirmed. The same coverage says data gaps remain, especially how often national accounts and production figures are published.

The plan is also to link the model to a debt dynamics tool, a calculator that tracks how debt grows under different assumptions. Debt sustainability is a central question for Ethiopia, so the link is the part investors are most likely to watch.

The Programme Behind the Talks

The IMF’s board completed the fifth review of Ethiopia’s four-year Extended Credit Facility, the Fund’s concessional loan programme, on 1 July 2026 and released about US$464 million. Total payouts reached about US$2.647 billion of a programme approved on 29 July 2024 and worth about US$3.4 billion.

The IMF projects average inflation of 11.7% in the 2025/26 fiscal year and 12.3% in 2026/27, with real growth of 7.8% and 8.2%. Our report on the review talks that slipped to November explains the timing.

What It Means for You

For lenders and bondholders, the model is a plumbing upgrade with real consequences. Debt-sustainability maths is only as good as the growth, inflation and revenue forecasts that go into it.

For readers following Ethiopia’s reforms, a delay would not stop the programme by itself. It would, however, leave the government with the older tools while it liberalises the birr, the national currency, and faces a heavy repayment calendar, as our note on the central bank’s rate hold shows.

What Is Not Known

It is not confirmed whether the model was finished in September 2026 or what the new date is. The date of the November talks, and an IMF board decision reported for early 2027, have not been confirmed by the Fund.

More coverage sits on our Ethiopia hub. For the wider economy, see the GDP rebasing explainer.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Comprehensive Adaptive Expectations Model?

It is a forecasting toolkit that Ethiopia’s finance ministry is building with IMF help. It is meant to show how growth, inflation, public finances and trade affect one another.

Why does the IMF care about Ethiopia’s forecasts?

Each review of Ethiopia’s IMF loan programme releases money only if targets are met. Those targets rest on the government’s own projections.

Was the model finished in September 2026?

That is not confirmed. September 2026 was the target, and the IMF is reported to be reviewing the schedule.

How much has the IMF paid Ethiopia so far?

About US$2.647 billion of a programme worth about US$3.4 billion. That followed the fifth review on 1 July 2026.

Sources: International Monetary Fund, press release 26/235 on the fifth review of Ethiopia’s Extended Credit Facility, 1 July 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/07/01/pr26235-ethiopia-imf-completes-5th-review-under-ecf-arrangement); International Monetary Fund, Technical Assistance Report 2025/070, Forecasting and Policy Analysis System scoping mission, 16 July 2025 (imf.org/en/publications/technical-assistance-reports/issues/2025/07/16/the-federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia-technical-assistance-report-forecasting-policy-568688). The model project details come from Ethiopian coverage and are marked as reported.

World.title: World Bank Cites Addis Ababa City Borrowing
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · ADDIS ABABA · CITY FINANCE

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, is one of the few cities in Sub-Saharan Africa outside South Africa that pay for large public works with long-term borrowing, according to coverage of a new report by the World Bank, the global development lender, on African cities. We could not open the report itself, so every figure from it below is marked as reported, not confirmed.

This matters to readers in the United States because Ethiopia is restructuring its foreign debt, and how its biggest city borrows is a useful test of whether public borrowing can work there. The capital also won a United Nations award on 31 October 2026 for its urban renewal.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Key Facts The report A World Bank report on African cities is said to single out Addis Ababa’s long-term city borrowing.

The claim Addis Ababa is described as one of few Sub-Saharan cities outside South Africa borrowing this way.

The spending The city is said to spend about 50% of its budget on capital projects (reported, not confirmed).

The award UN-Habitat, the UN’s cities agency, named Addis Ababa a 2026 Shanghai Award winner on 31 October.

The backdrop The IMF, the global lender to governments, welcomed a deal in principle with Ethiopia’s dollar bondholders.

What the World Bank Report Is Said to Say

The report describes long-term contractual borrowing as a way for a city to pay for foundational infrastructure, meaning the basic physical works a city runs on. It is said to call Addis Ababa a rare example in Sub-Saharan Africa outside South Africa of a city that has used this tool on a meaningful scale.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Coverage of the report says the city routinely spends about 50% of its budget on capital projects, peaking at 56% in the 2022/23 fiscal year. We could not check these percentages against the report, so treat them as reported, not confirmed.

The report is said to note that local budgets in the region mostly go on salaries and running costs. By that yardstick, a city that puts half its budget into building would stand out.
