Why the City Can Borrow

The report is said to credit two things: high fiscal autonomy, meaning the city decides much of its own spending, and steady backing from the federal government for municipal borrowing. It also points to the city’s weight in the economy and its role as the federal capital and the seat of the African Union, the continental body.

Whether other African cities could copy this mix is not something the coverage answers. Cities that depend on national transfers for most of their income would start from a very different place.

The Award Behind the Headline

UN-Habitat, the United Nations agency for cities, announced on 31 October 2026 in Fuzhou, China, that five cities had won the 2026 Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities, known as the Shanghai Award. They are Addis Ababa, Santiago de Cali in Colombia, Istanbul, Jingdezhen in China and Katowice in Poland.

UN-Habitat recognised Addis Ababa for an integrated approach that combines adequate housing, green infrastructure, river restoration, safe and accessible mobility and participatory governance. The 2026 cycle drew 92 applications from 34 countries.

The National Debt Backdrop

Ethiopia is still restructuring its foreign debt, the process of agreeing new repayment terms with lenders. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global lender to governments, said on 1 July 2026 that it welcomed progress with official creditors.

It also welcomed an agreement in principle with holders of Ethiopia’s Eurobonds, which are bonds sold abroad in dollars. City borrowing is a separate matter, and the coverage gives no dollar amounts for what Addis Ababa owes.

Our earlier piece on Ethiopia’s bond exchange covers the market side. The GDP rebasing explainer shows why the size of the economy is itself under review.

What It Means for You

For investors, a city that borrows on long contracts is a different credit story from a national government that is restructuring its debt. Any investable product would need audited figures for the city’s debt, and none were given in the coverage.

For readers with ties to Ethiopia, the practical signal is modest. Cities with predictable budgets are better placed to finish housing, transport and water projects.

What Is Not Known

We could not open the report, so the 50% and 56% figures, the list of reasons and the claim about “few cities” rest on coverage of it. The size of the city’s debt, its lenders and its repayment terms were not given in that coverage.

More coverage sits on our Ethiopia hub. The central bank rate decision shows how tight money is for borrowers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Ethiopian city won a 2026 Shanghai Award?

Addis Ababa. UN-Habitat announced on 31 October 2026 that it was one of five winners.

Does Addis Ababa borrow for infrastructure?

A World Bank report is said to describe it as one of few Sub-Saharan cities outside South Africa doing so on long-term contracts. We could not confirm this against the report itself.

How much of the city budget goes on construction?

Coverage of the report puts it at about 50% in a normal year and 56% in the 2022/23 fiscal year. These figures are reported, not confirmed.

Is Ethiopia restructuring its national debt?

Yes. On 1 July 2026 the IMF welcomed progress with official creditors and an agreement in principle with Eurobond holders.

World.title: Who Runs Ethiopia’s Army and Foreign Policy
World.content:
File photo. Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia's prime minister, speaking at the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, 2019. Photo: Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

ETHIOPIA · POLITICS

Key Facts The country Ethiopia, Africa’s second most populous nation, hosts the African Union, the continent’s 55-nation bloc.

What happened Parliament approved Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s cabinet on Thursday 8 October 2026: 22 ministers plus a deputy.

Defence and diplomacy Mohamed Idris, formerly Minister of Peace, now runs defence; Gedion Timothewos keeps foreign affairs.

The US link The US rates Ethiopia Level 3 (Reconsider Travel) and bars it from AGOA, a US duty-free trade programme.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction market, gives about 13% for Eritrea invading Ethiopia by 31 December (9 November, 3:20 a.m. Eastern).

Ethiopia’s new government has put a former peace minister in charge of the army and kept the same foreign minister, while Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed presses for a sea outlet on the Red Sea. For US readers, these two men shape how Addis Ababa deals with Washington, Beijing and its neighbours.

Parliament approved the cabinet on Thursday 8 October 2026. Our full list of Ethiopia’s ministers has every name, and our guides explain what the posts can decide and what the economic team means for investors.

What Happened

Ethiopia’s House of Peoples’ Representatives, the elected lower house of parliament, unanimously approved Abiy’s nominees on Thursday 8 October 2026. The list has Deputy Prime Minister Temesgen Tiruneh and 22 ministers.

Who Now Runs the Army

Idris spoke at the 119th Defence Forces Day ceremony in Addis Ababa on Sunday 25 October 2026, held under the theme “Army of Victory”. He called the national army a pillar of public confidence and a shield for the country in difficult times.

Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, the army’s chief of general staff, attended the ceremony along with foreign military attachés and diplomats. The ceremony took place at the Armed Forces General Headquarters.

On Tuesday 3 November 2026 Idris met China’s ambassador to Ethiopia, Chen Hai, in Addis Ababa. They agreed to deepen military ties and discussed cooperation on the defence industry, technology transfer and training, but no signed deal or sum was announced.

Who Speaks for Ethiopia Abroad

Gedion Timothewos keeps the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, so Ethiopia’s diplomatic line is unchanged. On Monday 5 October 2026 Abiy repeated that landlocked Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.

Eritrea, the neighbour to the north that holds the Red Sea coast, has rejected the claim. On 9 October 2026 its information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, accused Ethiopia of an “unprovoked war of aggression” and of wanting the port of Assab.

Habtamu Itefa, the minister of water and energy, oversees the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydropower project, on the Nile. Egypt and Sudan, which depend on the river, dispute how Ethiopia runs the dam.

The Washington Connection

Gedion met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington on Monday 11 May 2026, during the US-Ethiopia Bilateral Structured Dialogue, a formal framework for talks between the two governments. Rubio said they discussed expanding the security partnership and increasing commercial opportunities between the two nations.

Ethiopia has been excluded since 1 January 2022 from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), the US programme that gives African exports duty-free access. Restoring it needs a separate decision by the US administration, and none has been announced as of 9 November 2026.

The US State Department rates Ethiopia Level 3, Reconsider Travel. The US Embassy’s security alerts of October and November 2026 tell Americans not to travel to the northern Amhara, Tigray and Afar regions, and our travel guide for Americans has the details.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users bet real money, gives about 13% for Eritrea invading Ethiopia by 31 December 2026, in a market with US$123,462 traded across all deadlines. The figure was read on 9 November 2026 at 3:20 a.m. Eastern Time.

These prices are bets, not polls or forecasts by officials. Our Ethiopia geopolitics guide covers the neighbours behind them.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US investors, Ethiopia is a frontier market where the defence and foreign ministers help set the risk, since a clash with Eritrea would threaten the region’s trade routes. Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa’s team matters more for debt and tax questions.

Travellers should follow the US Embassy alerts and avoid the three northern regions, because the cabinet change does not alter the Level 3 rating. Companies hoping for AGOA access should expect no quick change, since that decision sits in Washington.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Idris will change military policy, because the government has announced no new defence strategy. It is also unclear whether the talks with China will lead to signed deals.

No US decision on Ethiopia’s AGOA status has been announced. Whether the Red Sea dispute with Eritrea stays diplomatic is also open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Ethiopia’s New Defence Minister?

Mohamed Idris, who had been Minister of Peace since November 2024. Parliament approved him on Thursday 8 October 2026.

Who Is Ethiopia’s Foreign Minister?

Gedion Timothewos kept the post in the cabinet approved on 8 October 2026. He met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 11 May 2026.

Is Ethiopia Safe for American Travellers?

The US rates Ethiopia Level 3, Reconsider Travel, on the State Department scale. The US Embassy advises against travel to the northern Amhara, Tigray and Afar regions.

Can Ethiopia Export Duty-Free to the US?

No. Ethiopia has been excluded from the AGOA trade programme since 1 January 2022, and no restoration has been announced.

World.title: Report Says Miller Pushed Agencies on Somalis
World.content:
Analysis: United States

Key Facts Who. Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff (the president’s top aide), and Minnesota’s Somali community.

What. A US news investigation says Miller’s orders reached five or more agencies; the White House cites fraud.

Why it matters. The reported orders touch food aid, health services and money sent to relatives in Somalia.

What is next. Miller starts on Monday 9 November; a US Treasury order on reporting large overseas money transfers runs to early February 2027.

As of. 9 November 2026, 08:00 GMT

A US news investigation reports that Stephen Miller spent a year pressing federal agencies over Minnesota’s Somali community. The White House says the aim was fraud, and Minnesota’s Feeding Our Future child-meals fraud case shows that some fraud was real.

What the Investigation Reports

Stephen Miller was until now deputy chief of staff and a leading figure in President Trump’s immigration policy. Trump named him chief of staff (the president’s top aide) on Friday 6 November 2026, replacing Susie Wiles, the outgoing chief of staff.

He takes over on Monday 9 November, days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the 3 November midterms. A US news investigation published on Friday 6 November, based on a recording of a December 2025 White House call, reports on his past year.

The Rio Times has not heard the recording, and no second outlet has independently confirmed it. We therefore present everything from it as reported claims, not as our own findings.

On that call, the report says, Miller asked administration officials about fraud linked to immigrants, Minnesota and the state’s Somali population nine times in about ten minutes. When an official described a fraud case in Florida, the report says he cut in.

When told of a criminal investigation in the Eastern District of Virginia, a federal prosecutors’ region, he reportedly answered, “I hear you, but that’s a long way off from Minneapolis.” The report says Miller seemed uninterested when fraud cases did not prominently involve immigrants.

The investigation also says Miller’s directives on Minnesota fraud reached at least five federal agencies in the past year. They touched access to food aid and health services, and how Somalis and others send money to relatives abroad.

Two administration officials told the investigation that some colleagues wanted a broader approach to fraud. One of them said the focus was on “the specific population of immigrants” rather than fraud in general and called the campaign “inane”; a separate source close to the White House called it “a passion project for him”.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Public Record Shows

Feeding Our Future, a Minnesota non-profit, defrauded a federal child-meals programme during Covid, in a scheme prosecutors put at about US$250 million. Its leader, Aimee Bock, was sentenced on Thursday 21 May 2026 to 500 months (about 41 years 8 months) in federal prison.

A White House official says the Somali population was “a large part of the massive fraud in the state”, and we have not found an official count of defendants by origin. We cannot verify the White House’s description of how large that share was.

Most Somali Minnesotans are not accused of anything. Individual defendants are not a community, and the crimes of some people say nothing about their neighbours.

On Friday 7 August 2026 the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the US Treasury’s financial-crime unit, renewed an order for 180 days. It requires certain banks and money-transfer firms in Hennepin and Ramsey counties, which cover Minneapolis and St Paul, to report international transfers of US$3,000 or more.

Treasury says part of the money diverted in Minnesota’s fraud schemes was laundered overseas. The renewed order runs from 11 August 2026 until about early February 2027.

The north front of the White House in Washington, July 2007. Photo: Ad Meskens / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

What the White House Says

A White House official told the investigation the call “was focused on rooting out fraud in Minnesota”. The official added that there is “no denying the Somali population was a large part of the massive fraud in the state”.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said President Trump has launched “an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government”. Those are the administration’s own words, and readers can weigh them against the court record above.

Why It Matters Beyond Minnesota

Minnesota is home to the largest Somali community in the United States. Earlier this autumn, Minnesota leaders rebuked Trump’s 8 October post on Somalis.

Remittances, the money Somalis abroad send home, are a major pillar of Somalia’s economy. World Bank data put them at roughly 18% of Somalia’s GDP in 2024 (the value of everything the country produces) in recent years.

That is why rules on money transfers matter far beyond Minnesota, although no figures yet show any effect on flows. Our explainer on who wants what in Somalia gives the wider political picture.

Washington’s attention to the country is not new, as our report on Somalia on the US Coast Guard port-risk list shows. Both pieces help place the Minnesota story in a wider frame.

What It Means for You

If you are a Somali American, the reported focus may bring closer scrutiny of benefits and of money sent to family, and banks in two Minnesota counties already report transfers of US$3,000 or more. If you send money to Somalia, ask your provider whether a reporting rule applies where you live.

If you are a US reader, the story shows how a single fraud case can shape the priorities of federal agencies. The outcome will depend on what Miller does in his new role.

What Is Not Known

We do not know whether the recording is authentic in full, because we have not heard it. We also do not know what the five agencies actually changed.

It is unclear whether the pressure continues under Miller’s new role. The effect on remittance flows is unknown, because no figures exist yet.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the federal department for border and immigration enforcement, published a notice on 14 January 2026 ending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somalia from 17 March 2026. TPS lets people from crisis countries stay legally, and we have not confirmed the current legal status, because court action has been reported.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the investigation say Miller did?

It reports that Miller’s directives on Minnesota fraud reached at least five federal agencies in the past year. They touched food aid, health services and how people send money abroad.

What does the White House say?

A White House official says the call was focused on rooting out fraud in Minnesota. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis says President Trump has launched “an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government”.

What is the US$3,000 transfer rule?

FinCEN renewed an order requiring certain banks and money-transfer firms in Hennepin and Ramsey counties to report international transfers of US$3,000 or more. It runs until about early February 2027.

World.title: Kenya Opposition Sees Ruto Warning in US Vote
World.content:
Politics: Kenya

Key Facts Who. Ndindi Nyoro, a Kenyan opposition lawmaker and former ally of President William Ruto, links the US vote to Kenya.

What. Democrats, the US opposition party, won both chambers of Congress in the 3 November midterm elections.

Why it matters. Kenya’s inflation hit 7.3% in October, the highest since July 2023, just under the government’s 7.5% ceiling.

What is next. Kenya votes on 10 August 2027, with a second-round runoff if no one wins outright.

As of. 9 November 2026, 08:00 GMT

Kenya’s opposition says the Democratic sweep in the US midterms, a campaign centred on living costs, is a warning for President William Ruto. Kenya’s own election is nine months away, and prices are rising.

Ndindi Nyoro, an opposition lawmaker and former ally of Ruto, argues that cost-of-living anger that swung American voters can swing Kenyan ones too. His case is a campaign argument; Kenya’s inflation figures are real, but no poll links them to the US result.

The US midterms are congressional elections held halfway through a president’s term. Kenya votes for a president on Tuesday 10 August 2027, about nine months (274 days) from 9 November 2026, and the field of challengers is still forming.

What Happened in the US Vote

Democrats won control of both the US Senate and the US House of Representatives on Tuesday 3 November 2026, ending Republican control of Congress. That creates divided government for the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

Democrats flipped about seven Republican-held Senate seats, in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. A few races, including Alaska and Mississippi, were still uncalled on 4 November, and we have no verified final seat count.

The campaign centred on Americans’ frustration with the high cost of living, and it was at the heart of Democratic messaging. Trump has said he would veto Democratic legislation, though he has also predicted the two sides will work together after a few months.

Trump’s White House reshuffle began soon after the vote. He named his deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, as chief of staff on Friday 6 November.

Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Why Nyoro Sees a Warning for Ruto

Nyoro is the Member of Parliament for Kiharu, a Kenyan constituency, and leads the People’s Party of Kenya, an opposition party. He broke with the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA), the party he once shared with Ruto’s camp.

At a party event on about 5 November 2026, he said the 2027 election could end Ruto’s presidency. He pointed to US voters switching sides, even in areas that backed Trump, as proof that discontent over economic pressure and unmet expectations can change results.

Nyoro has called for the opposition to unite behind a single presidential candidate to avoid a runoff, a second round of voting. Opposition unity is untested, and the field is still forming.

Nyoro’s argument is that the frustration which moved American voters can move Kenyan ones. It is a political claim, not a forecast.

Kenya’s constitution requires a presidential winner to take more than 50% of votes, and at least 25% of the vote in each of more than half of the 47 counties, which means 24 counties. Otherwise a runoff follows.

Nairobi’s skyline at dusk, with the Kenyatta International Convention Centre tower at centre.

The Cost of Living Behind Both Votes

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), the official statistics agency, reported on Friday 30 October 2026 that annual inflation reached 7.3% in October. That is up from 6.8% in September and the highest since July 2023, as our October inflation report showed.

Inflation is the pace at which prices rise over twelve months. At 7.3%, a basket of goods that cost 100 a year ago now costs about 107.

Transport prices rose 17.1% year on year, and food and non-alcoholic drinks rose 10.2%. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels rose 3.7%.

Diesel cost 32.5% more than a year earlier, and petrol cost 22.8% more. Both rose far faster than overall inflation of 7.3%.

Non-core inflation, which covers food, fuel and energy, was 15.1%, up from 14.0%. That is more than double the headline rate of 7.3%.

Core inflation, which strips out the most volatile prices, was 4.3%, up from 4.0%. It stayed well inside the government’s band.

The government’s inflation target is 5% with a band of 2.5% to 7.5%, set by the National Treasury, Kenya’s finance ministry, and pursued by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK), the monetary authority. At 7.3%, inflation sits just under the top of that band.

The gap between core and non-core readings shows that food and fuel are driving the pressure. Core inflation, at 4.3%, sits well below the headline rate of 7.3%.

The Strongest Counter-Argument

A midterm is a verdict on a sitting president, while Kenya’s vote is a presidential race, so the comparison is political, not mechanical. Ruto is not on any ballot until 2027.

Opposition parties are still working toward a single candidate, and a divided field can split the opposition vote. A runoff is required if no candidate clears the constitutional thresholds.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the signals to watch are inflation, now near the government’s ceiling, and whether the opposition unites behind one candidate. A runoff would add a second round of uncertainty.

For travellers, the election is nine months away, and we have no verified travel advisory linked to this story. Petrol costs 22.8% more than a year ago.

For US policy readers, the story shows how cost-of-living anger is read across borders. Our explainer on who runs Kenya is a good start.

What Is Not Known

No independent Kenyan opinion poll in our sources shows how the US result moves Kenyan voters. Nyoro’s reading is his own.

Whether the opposition will unite behind one candidate is open. The final House seat count in the US is also unverified.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Nyoro say about the US vote?

Ndindi Nyoro said on about 5 November 2026 that the 2027 election could end Ruto’s presidency, citing US voters switching sides. That is his opinion, not a forecast.

When is Kenya’s next election?

Kenya votes on Tuesday 10 August 2027. A presidential winner needs more than 50% of votes and at least 25% in 24 of 47 counties, or a runoff follows.

How high is Kenyan inflation?

Annual inflation was 7.3% in October 2026, up from 6.8% in September, the official statistics agency said. The Central Bank of Kenya targets 5%, within a band of 2.5% to 7.5%.

World.title: Algeria Sends Envoy to Niger and Chad
World.content:
File photo, 2006. Boulevard Mali Bero in Niamey, the capital of Niger, seen from the Grand Mosque. (Photo: Roland Huziaker, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Algeria’s foreign minister took personal letters from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune to the leaders of Chad and Niger on 3 and 4 November 2026, as the two neighbours trade accusations over a deadly drone strike. Nobody has called it mediation, but the timing suggests Algiers wants to cool a dispute that could unsettle the Sahel, the arid belt south of the Sahara.

For US readers, a rift between two Sahel governments matters because both fight armed groups and sit on key trade and smuggling routes. Niger is also one of the world’s uranium producers.

Who: Algeria’s Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, Niger’s General Abdourahamane Tiani and Chad’s President Mahamat Idriss Déby.

Algeria’s Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, Niger’s General Abdourahamane Tiani and Chad’s President Mahamat Idriss Déby. What: Attaf took Tebboune’s letters to Chad’s capital on 3 November and Niger’s capital on 4 November.

Attaf took Tebboune’s letters to Chad’s capital on 3 November and Niger’s capital on 4 November. Trigger: Niger blames Chad for a 24 October drone strike that killed two civilians.

Niger blames Chad for a 24 October drone strike that killed two civilians. Denial: Chad says it did not order or support any strike and backs an international inquiry.

Chad says it did not order or support any strike and backs an international inquiry. As of: 9 November 2026, 09:00 GMT.

What Algeria Did

Ahmed Attaf, Algeria’s foreign minister, travelled as Tebboune’s special envoy and was received by Chad’s President Déby in N’Djamena on Tuesday 3 November 2026. The next day, Wednesday 4 November, he travelled to Niamey, Niger’s capital, with a written message for General Tiani.

Tiani leads Niger’s military government, and Algeria is its northern neighbour. The contents of both letters have not been published, and Algiers has not described the trip as mediation.

Algeria has a stake in calm, because it shares a long desert border with Niger. Tension between Niamey and N’Djamena adds risk along the same smuggling and security routes.

Avenue Alifa Zezerty in N'Djamena after rain, August 2024. The capital holds most of Chad's formal economy and services. Photo: Korom10, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Dispute Began

Niger’s government said a drone struck a mountainous area of its Agadez region, in the north, in the early hours of Saturday 24 October 2026. It said two civilians died and accused Chad of launching the strike with French support, and it summoned Chad’s ambassador.

On Monday 26 October Niamey demanded an end to what it called hostile acts, and said it would take the case to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, the two main bodies that handle threats to peace. Our earlier report on the accusation covers the first reactions.

On Tuesday 27 October Chad’s government spokesperson, Gassim Chérif Mahamat, said N’Djamena had not ordered, carried out or backed any air operation against Niger from its territory. He asked Niamey to show its evidence, called for an international inquiry, and said armed Chadian rebel groups are present on Nigerien soil, a concern Chad says it has raised repeatedly.

In Plain English

A special envoy is a senior official sent with a personal message from a head of state. Mediation means a neutral country helps two sides talk, and Algeria has not said it is doing that.

Niger’s government is run by soldiers who seized power in 2023. Chad’s leader Mahamat Idriss Déby took power in 2021 after his father’s death and won a presidential election in May 2024.

What Is Not Known

Nobody has published evidence of who flew the drone, and both sides rely on their own accounts. The content of Tebboune’s letters and any proposals for talks remain private.

It is also unclear whether Tiani and Déby will speak directly, or whether either side asked Algeria to step in. No border closure or other new measure has been announced.

What It Means for You

Investors and aid groups with Sahel exposure should watch for a direct call between the two presidents, which would signal the row is cooling. A first meeting of ministers, or an international inquiry into the strike, would be a further sign.

Our guide to Chad and the Sahel sets out the borders, trade and refugee flows at stake, and our guide to Algeria’s geopolitics explains Algiers’ regional role. We also reported on French fighter jets due back in Chad, and Niger accuses France of backing the strike.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Algeria officially mediating between Niger and Chad?

Not officially. Algeria’s foreign minister delivered letters from President Tebboune to both leaders, but no one has announced a mediation mandate or its content.

What caused the Niger-Chad tension?

Niger says a drone strike on 24 October killed two civilians in its north and blames Chad, with French support. Chad denies it and has asked for evidence and an international inquiry.

Who is Abdourahamane Tiani?

General Abdourahamane Tiani leads Niger’s military government, which took power in a July 2023 coup. The Algerian envoy travelled to Niamey to see him on 4 November.

Why does the Niger-Chad dispute matter outside Africa?

Both countries sit in the Sahel, a belt of states fighting armed groups south of the Sahara. Niger is also a uranium producer.

World.title: Diesel Up 17% as Costa Rica Prices Rise for a Second Straight Month
World.content:
Costa Rica’s cost of living is climbing again. Consumer prices rose 0.39% in October, and the year-on-year rate reached 0.55%, the second straight month above zero after 16 months of annual declines, according to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC).

That October jump compares with 0.11% in September and 0.19% in October 2025. The interannual rate also climbed from 0.34% a month earlier. Transport drove most of the increase. INEC reported that the transport division rose 1.71% in a single month and accounted for 0.30 percentage points of the overall index, with diesel up 17.39%, gasoline up 3.10%, taxi fares up 5.73% and bus fares up 2.02%.

Nelson Castillo Mendoza, coordinator of the INEC price index unit, said the main upward pressure came from fuel and public transport fares. He noted that those prices are set by the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep) and moved in line with international fuel prices during the month.

The rise follows September’s warnings of higher fuel prices as oil climbed back above $100 a barrel. Regulated goods and services rose 1.99% in October, according to INEC data, while unregulated items rose just 0.16%. Energy prices as a group rose 2.75%. Entertainment also cost more. The recreation, sport and culture division rose 0.96%, which INEC attributed mainly to higher ticket prices for events. Eggs rose 4.09%.

Some grocery staples moved the other way. Onions fell 10.73%, potatoes 3.50%, ground beef 2.44% and chicken breast 1.73%, and food and non-alcoholic beverages as a whole rose only 0.09%. Of the 293 goods and services in the basket, 45% rose, 33% fell and 22% were unchanged, with 10 of 13 spending divisions moving higher.

The longer view still shows Costa Rica with unusually low inflation. Cumulative inflation from January through October was -0.01%, essentially flat, compared with a 1.77% decline over the same period of 2025. Full-year 2025 inflation was -1.23%.

That keeps Costa Rica well below the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) target of 3%, with a tolerance band of one percentage point in either direction. The October reading sits 1.45 points below the bottom of that range, and inflation has now been below target for 42 consecutive months. The last time it was inside the band was April 2023.

The BCCR expects that gap to close. In its October Monetary Policy Report, the bank projected headline inflation near 2.7% in the second half of 2027, higher than its July forecast, and tied the revision to expected higher hydrocarbon prices. It kept its monetary policy rate at 3% and said it would adjust its stance if conditions or risks change.

The central bank listed extreme weather, including El Niño, geopolitical conflict and higher oil and grain prices among the risks that could push inflation up faster. A stronger colón and weaker global growth were among the factors that could hold it down. For households, the October figures arrive alongside other pressures. Earlier this month, INEC data showed unemployment climbing to 6.5%, while the exchange rate has left dollar earners with fewer colones than in January.

Rents have also been outpacing general inflation for months. The return of rising prices ends a long stretch of falling prices in Costa Rica. Whether the shift becomes a steady climb back toward target or a short fuel-driven spike will depend largely on oil markets and on the next round of regulated price adjustments, which anyone who fills a tank, rides a bus or takes a taxi in Costa Rica will feel first.

World.title: Alcaraz Wins First Paris Masters Title Ahead of ATP Finals
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz won his first Paris Masters title Sunday, beating American Ben Shelton 7-6 (5), 7-5 to claim his fifth trophy of the season and strengthen his late-season run ahead of the ATP Finals. The 23-year-old Spaniard needed one hour and 57 minutes to finish the match, adding a ninth Masters 1000 title to his career collection. The victory also reversed the outcome of their U.S. Open quarterfinal in September, when Shelton won in five sets.

Alcaraz heads toward the season-ending tournament in Turin with consecutive titles in Vienna and Paris. His latest win was the 29th tour-level title of his career, continuing a recovery from the right wrist injury that interrupted his season. Shelton made him work for it. The American created six break-point opportunities in the opening set but could not convert any of them. Alcaraz escaped a particularly difficult service game early on, saving four break points to keep Shelton from taking control.

The first set remained on serve through 12 games. In the tiebreaker, Alcaraz held his nerve and closed out the set after 65 minutes when Shelton sent a forehand long. The American broke through in the second set, but Alcaraz recovered the break and put the pressure back on his opponent. With Shelton serving at 5-6 to force another tiebreaker, the Spaniard earned two championship points.

He converted the second, finishing an exchange at the net with a backhand winner before celebrating with his team. “It is something I have been chasing for a long time,” Alcaraz said during his on-court interview. Paris had remained a gap in a Masters 1000 record that already included victories on clay and outdoor hard courts. He has now won seven of the nine tournaments in the category, with Canada and Shanghai the only titles missing.

The result also made him the third player to win a Masters 1000 title in five consecutive seasons since the series began in 1990, joining Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic. For Alcaraz, the significance extends beyond another trophy. After returning from injury, he has won titles in Tokyo, Vienna and Paris, building a strong finish to a season disrupted by months away from competition.

His next stop is the ATP Finals, scheduled for November 15-22 in Turin, Italy. Alcaraz arrives with 19 wins from 21 matches since his return, giving him a strong recent record to carry into the season’s final ATP Tour event.

World.title: Bird Watching Helps Older Adults Stay Sharp, and in Costa Rica It Costs Almost Nothing
World.content:
In nursing homes from Connecticut to Bavaria, caregivers have found an unlikely ally against loneliness, agitation and memory loss among older adults. It does not come in a pill bottle. It perches on a feeder outside the window.

Bird watching is now being used deliberately as therapy for older people, and the results have been strong enough to draw researchers’ attention. In Costa Rica, which has more than 940 recorded bird species and a yigüirro singing in nearly every backyard, the same benefits are within reach of any family at almost no cost.

One of the best-known programs, Bird Tales, began in Connecticut in 2011, when dementia care specialist and registered nurse Randy Griffin teamed up with Audubon educator Ken Elkins. Their sessions combine photographs, feathers and plush birds that play real bird calls with feeders installed outside care home windows.

The four Connecticut nursing homes that piloted the program reported needing less medication to calm agitated residents. When the Bird Conservancy of the Rockies later brought Bird Tales to care facilities in the Denver suburbs, an activities director at one of them said residents stayed calm for hours after a session, even when they could not remember it had happened.

The strongest evidence comes from Germany. Since 2017, the Bavarian bird protection society LBV has set up feeding stations in nursing homes across the state and given staff and residents the materials and guidance to look after them.

Researchers at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt followed 1,684 residents with varying degrees of impairment and published their findings in the Journal of Environmental Psychology in 2023. The team, led by psychologist Elisabeth Kals, reported that regular bird watching particularly supported residents’ cognitive abilities, mobility and social wellbeing.

The LBV has since adapted the program for older people living at home, with training for relatives and volunteers. In Britain, a weekly dementia-friendly birdwatching group for people living with dementia and their carers meets at the RSPB’s Sandwell Valley nature reserve on the edge of Birmingham.

Why does it work? Birds offer something new every day that still follows a predictable rhythm. They engage sight and sound, and they give people something to talk about. Perhaps most important, they hand people a small responsibility. Specialists in elder care have long warned that care settings can breed dependency and helplessness. Filling a feeder each morning is a modest task, but it is one that belongs to the resident.

The Tico Times could find no structured program of this kind in Costa Rica’s hogares de ancianos, care homes, or in its day centers for older adults. Occasional activities show the interest is there, such as a November 2024 birding walk for older adults led by tourism students at the Costa Rica Institute of Technology’s San Carlos campus.

But families caring for an older relative at home do not need to wait for an institution. Nearly everything required is already growing in the garden or sitting in the kitchen. Start with the right spot. Choose a window, porch or balcony where your relative already spends much of the day, ideally one facing a tree, hedge or patch of garden.

Then put out fruit. A ripe banana, papaya or plantain peel set on a board, a flat stone or a fence post will draw blue-gray tanagers (viudas), kiskadees (pecho amarillos) and yigüirros within days. Skip bread, rice, salty leftovers and honey, which are poor food for birds. Replace the fruit every day so it does not spoil or attract rats.

A shallow dish or old plate of water draws just as many visitors, and watching birds bathe is often the highlight of the day. Change the water daily, because standing water breeds the mosquitoes that spread dengue every rainy season. For hummingbirds, skip the store-bought feeder and plant flowers instead. Cuttings of rabo de gato, heliconia and other tubular flowers can usually be had free from a neighbor, and they root easily in Costa Rica’s climate. Flowers need no cleaning and give hummingbirds natural nectar.

Technology helps too. The free Merlin Bird ID app from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology identifies birds from a photo, and its Sound ID feature recognizes many common species from a song picked up by a phone’s microphone. Download the Costa Rica bird pack and the field guide works offline.

For someone with poor eyesight or who is confined to bed, recordings of familiar songs can stand in for the birds themselves, much as the singing plush birds do in Bird Tales. For many Costa Ricans, the song of the yigüirro, the national bird, whose singing traditionally announces the arrival of the rains, carries a lifetime of memories.

The routine matters more than the equipment. Let your relative put out the fruit each morning, even if that only means handing a banana to a caregiver. Keep a notebook or calendar where they record the date and the birds they saw. Naming, counting and remembering are exercise for the mind. Grandchildren can send photos of the birds in their own yards. That turns a phone call into a conversation about who came to visit today rather than a review of aches and pains.

A few cautions apply. Keep feeding spots away from places where cats can hide. Never trap or cage wild birds, which Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law prohibits and which defeats the purpose entirely. For anyone living with dementia, a safe chair and the same routine each day are part of the benefit. Repetition is not a problem to be solved.

None of this replaces medical care, and families should keep working with doctors on any treatment plan. But in a country whose population is aging quickly, and where many families care for parents and grandparents at home, a banana on a fence post may be one of the most affordable tools available.

The birds are already here. All they need is an audience.

World.title: How Living in Costa Rica Changed the Way I See the World
World.content:
When speaking of the 1980s and 90s, I like to refer to it as the previous century. “In the previous century, we didn’t have high speed internet,” I might say. It lends a sort of historical ring to it, like a time and place long ago and far away. In a sense, it was a long way back. Last night, I laid in my bed and watched the last innings of the final game of the baseball World Series on my cell phone. I couldn’t have done that in the previous century. Times change, things evolve. People too– we change and evolve with the passing of the years as well.

This is relevant to me because I recently reread articles I wrote back in the 1990s about my life in Costa Rica. I was younger then, less patient, more ready to criticize and lampoon Tiquicia. I wrote a column, for two different monthlies that catered to the expat communities here. I was, to put it bluntly, a smart ass.

I cringed while reading some of my more pointed articles. At the time I was writing from the point of view of an American who was frustrated with the things we took for granted up there. Down here, the telephone company was still a monopoly. Cell phones were rare and the still in demand landline phones always had a long waiting list.

Many heavily traveled roads and streets were dirt, which meant dust in the summer and mud and potholes in the rainy season. Cops were either apathetic and poorly trained or corrupt predators, using the badge to solicit bribes. I ridiculed shopkeepers who whipped out their calculators for the simplest addition. The local customs, the local diet, all was fair game. My audience, which consisted mainly of other impatient expats like myself, ate it up.

I was in the early years of my second marriage– to a Tica– and the only time I wrote without a condescending voice was the occasional article about home and family life. Otherwise, I felt like my marriage to a local somehow gave me a free pass to be a self-appointed expert on everything that Ticolandia lacked.

A Tico friend who was fluent in English read my stuff and wasn’t overly offended, mainly because he shared my acerbic sense of humor. He suggested that I turn the tables, and write something from the point of view of a Costa Rican fed up with Gringo arrogance. So I did. I wrote from the perspective of a fictional brother-in-law.

I have numerous brothers-in-law, but none speak English well enough to write like my imaginary cuñado. I laid it on heavy, with over the top mentions of fat, aging gringos, their tongues coated blue from sucking on tablets of viagra, chasing girls young enough to be their granddaughters.

My narrator bragged about all the naive, panting young gringas he happily bedded and then dropped when the next Latino hungry candidate caught his eye. It was a 600 word middle finger in the face of the expat community. I had hoped it would be taken in jest, but I was wrong. One retired military vet angrily asked where my make believe brother-in-law lived, because he was ready to punch him out. Another reader greeted me with a frown and said that visiting tourists would read it and never want to come back. The response was so overwhelmingly negative that I found myself avoiding people on the street until the next edition of the monthly came out.

Imagine writing something and then hoping people did not read it. That month was a turning point in the way I looked at the place I had chosen to live. Just because most Ticos would not be able to read my articles did not make them any less nasty. It was a bit like making faces at a blind person.

I began to write from a more objective and empathetic viewpoint, with an eye toward getting to know the culture and the history. I mined my wife and her family for material– not for laughs but for honest appraisals of their lives and how they differed from my own. I sometimes made myself the butt of the joke and discovered it was okay to laugh at my own occasional ineptitude when it came to adapting to my surroundings.

And so it has followed all these years later. I am no longer an outsider, looking in, ready to ridicule. I am as much Tico as Gringo, on the inside now, where the viewpoint is completely different

World.title: Costa Rica Heads to Ecuador and Argentina Without Keylor Navas
World.content:
Bryan Ruiz will take Costa Rica into its toughest test of the year without Keylor Navas. The veteran goalkeeper was left out of the 23-man squad Ruiz named Friday for friendlies against Ecuador and Argentina, his first matches since the federation confirmed him as permanent head coach.

Costa Rica plays Ecuador on Friday, Nov. 13, at the Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa in Quito, with kickoff at 6 p.m. Costa Rica time (7 p.m. ET). It then faces Argentina on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at the Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. Ruiz said in television interviews last week that Navas has a minor problem in one knee that requires a medical procedure and about 10 days of rest. The coach said the Pumas UNAM goalkeeper had offered to join the squad anyway, but that his priority was for Navas to recover properly.

Without Navas, the job in goal falls to Patrick Sequeira of Portugal’s Casa Pia, Abraham Madriz of Saprissa and Bayron Mora of Alajuelense. Ruiz has said he wants to use the window to evaluate which goalkeepers he can count on for the World Cup cycle ahead. Two other players are out injured. Defender Jeyland Mitchell of France’s Strasbourg and striker Alonso Martínez of New York City FC were both ruled out with physical problems.

The headline return is Manfred Ugalde. The Spartak Moscow striker is back after serving a suspension and has scored 10 goals this season, six in the Russian league and four in the cup. Copenhagen defender Kenay Myrie also returns to the squad. The group leans heavily on the domestic league, with 16 locally based players and seven playing abroad. Alajuelense has eight players, more than any other club. The squad has an average age of 25.8, and nine players are under 23.

Argentina, runners-up at the 2026 World Cup, will be playing its first matches since Lionel Messi’s farewell from the national team on Oct. 6 against Benin. Coach Lionel Scaloni has named a 28-player squad and will face Uruguay at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires on Nov. 13 before hosting Costa Rica in Córdoba.

The Ecuador match brings its own challenge. Quito sits at roughly 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level, among the highest capitals in the world, and the match will be Ecuador’s first at the Atahualpa in more than nine years. The two teams have met 12 times, with Ecuador winning six and five ending in draws. Costa Rica’s only win came in their first meeting, in 1992. Ruiz took over as interim coach in late September after the federation fired Fernando Batista. He won both of his Nations League matches, beating Nicaragua 3-0 and Haiti 2-0, before being given the job permanently in October.

The squad begins training Monday, Nov. 9, and travels to Quito on Wednesday, Nov. 11, flying on to Córdoba the day after the Ecuador match. Four more players, Alberth Barahona of Saprissa, Claudio Montero and Geancarlo Castro of Cartaginés, and José Vega of San Carlos, will train with the group through Nov. 11 but are not part of the 23.

Goalkeepers: Abraham Madriz (Saprissa), Bayron Mora (Alajuelense), Patrick Sequeira (Casa Pia, Portugal).

Defenders: Aarón Salazar (Alajuelense), Alexis Gamboa (Alajuelense), Diego Mesén (Cartaginés), Francisco Calvo (Nacional, Uruguay), John Paul Ruiz (Alajuelense), Joseph Mora (Saprissa), Juan Pablo Vargas (Puebla, Mexico), Kenay Myrie (Copenhagen, Denmark), Yerlan Sosa (Alajuelense).

Midfielders: Andrey Soto (Saprissa), Celso Borges (Alajuelense), Douglas López (Cartaginés), Gabriel Leiva (Sporting), Gian Mauro Morera (Cartaginés), Roan Wilson (Alajuelense).

Forwards: Carlos Mora (Universitatea Craiova, Romania), Josimar Alcócer (Sparta Prague, Czech Republic), Josimar Méndez (Sporting), Kenyel Michel (Alajuelense), Manfred Ugalde (Spartak Moscow, Russia).

Both matches will be Ruiz’s first against South American opposition as Costa Rica’s coach, and the trip to Córdoba gives his young squad a measure of how far it has to go.

World.title: Two Bull Sharks Found Dead in a Guanacaste Estuary They Had Never Been Known to Enter
World.content:
Two bull sharks, rays, pufferfish and several other fish species have been found dead in an estuary at Playa Langosta, just south of Tamarindo on Guanacaste’s northern Pacific coast, and environmental authorities are now investigating what killed them. The sharks drew the most attention. There had been no previous record of bull sharks entering this estuary, according to reports from the community.

The animals were found in the San Francisco Estuary at Playa Langosta, not the better-known Tamarindo Estuary that separates Tamarindo from Playa Grande. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) said it viewed the deaths with concern and that the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), working with other competent institutions, will investigate the causes.

The ministry said the assessment will examine the natural closure of the estuary’s mouth, water quality, and possible effects of changing conditions linked to El Niño, including warmer water and shifts along the coast. The mouth of the estuary closed naturally about a week before the discovery, after sand built up where it meets the ocean.

The Tamarindo Integral Development Association (ADIT), which alerted SINAC and requested attention to the case, said the agency attributed the changes at the beach to strong tides and sand accumulation at the outlet. The association has also filed a complaint over the deaths.

Estuaries depend on a steady exchange of water. Seawater pushes in on high tides while rivers bring fresh water from inland. When river flow is too weak to keep the mouth open, a sand bar can form and cut that connection, trapping water and wildlife inside. One hypothesis is that the animals became trapped behind the sand barrier. Even at high tide, the water may not have been deep enough for them to cross back to the sea.

Another possibility is a sharp drop in dissolved oxygen, which can be fatal to fish and other aquatic species in enclosed water. Bull sharks are among the few shark species that tolerate fresh and brackish water, and they are a familiar presence along Guanacaste’s coast, where the species is celebrated each year at the Bull Shark Festival in Playas del Coco.

MINAE stressed that none of these explanations has been confirmed and said it would be premature to attribute the deaths to any specific cause before a technical assessment is complete. The closure comes during a dry year on the Pacific side, as El Niño drought conditions grip Guanacaste. Authorities are also monitoring the estuaries at Avellanas, Bejuco, Ostional, Junquillal and Bongo-Ario, some of which have closed naturally as well.

MINAE asked the public not to alter the estuary mouth without authorization from environmental authorities while the assessment is underway. ADIT likewise urged residents not to dig or bring in machinery to open it, and asked the community to report any new incidents at 8704-6444.

SINAC said it is continuing to monitor the site and other stretches of the coast as the investigation proceeds.

World.title: French Woman Found Shot Dead Inside Her Guanacaste Home
World.content:
A 64-year-old French woman was found dead with a gunshot wound to the head inside her home in Cabo Velas, Santa Cruz, on Friday morning, according to the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). The OIJ received the report at 8:04 a.m., after a worker employed by the woman discovered her body inside the house in the area known as Lomas de Matapalo. The agency identified the victim by the name Bourgeus.

Agents from the OIJ’s Santa Cruz regional office carried out a preliminary examination at the scene and determined that she had a gunshot wound to the head. Authorities are treating the case as a possible homicide. The body was sent to the Judicial Morgue, where an autopsy will establish the cause and manner of death. As of Sunday morning, the OIJ had not publicly reported any arrests, named a suspect or described a possible motive.

Cabo Velas is a coastal area on Guanacaste’s northern Pacific coast that takes in the beach communities of Flamingo, Potrero, Brasilito and Conchal, along with residential developments and vacation rentals in the hills behind them. The case is the second death of a foreigner under investigation in the district in recent months. In August, the OIJ treated the death of a 75-year-old U.S. citizen found in Cabo Velas as an apparent homicide possibly linked to a robbery at the property. In June, a German resident was found stabbed to death on a farm elsewhere in the canton of Santa Cruz.

Elsewhere in Guanacaste, a 22-year-old woman suspected in the killing of an American businessman in Playas del Coco was ordered held in pretrial detention for one year in October while prosecutors build their case. The OIJ asks anyone with information about the case to contact its confidential line at 800-8000-645. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Costa Rica’s First Female Extradition Suspect Faces Legal Battle Over Transfer to United States
World.content:
The first Costa Rican woman ordered extradited to the United States will not be handed over for now. Defense attorneys for Shirley Gómez, known as “La Güera,” and her partner, Frankin Viveros, have appealed a San José Criminal Court ruling that authorized their surrender to U.S. authorities. The appeal suspends the transfer while a higher court reviews the case.

The court approved the extradition of both on September 14. They are wanted by the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona on charges of international cocaine trafficking and conspiracy to distribute cocaine knowing it would be imported into the United States. The defense filed its challenge within the three-day deadline set for appeals.

Neither has been convicted, and the U.S. allegations have not been tested at trial. Gómez, 39, is the only Costa Rican woman to face an extradition proceeding since the country began allowing the surrender of its own citizens in 2025. Viveros, 50, was born in Colombia and later became a naturalized Costa Rican citizen.

The appeal centers on retroactivity. The defense argued that applying the reform to Article 32 of the Constitution would be a retroactive use of the law, because the conduct attributed to the couple began in July 2024. That was nearly a year before the amendment took effect on May 28, 2025.

The judge rejected that argument. The ruling held that international drug trafficking is a continuing offense. It also found that the U.S. filings describe alleged activity lasting until October 1, 2025, well after the reform came into force, so the new extradition framework applies.

The defense also challenged the role of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). It argued that DEA agents made undercover drug purchases in Costa Rica without a formal international cooperation agreement approved by the Foreign Ministry. The judge ruled that the validity of that evidence is for the courts in Arizona to decide at trial, not for an extradition proceeding.

The retroactivity question has already produced split outcomes. In February, the Criminal Sentencing Appeals Court in San José upheld the extradition of former security minister and magistrate Celso Gamboa Sánchez and of Edwin López Vega, known as “Pecho de Rata,” because their alleged conduct extended past May 28, 2025.

In the same ruling, the appeals court blocked the extradition of a third suspect, Jonathan Álvarez Alfaro, after finding that all the acts attributed to him took place before the reform. Gamboa and López Vega were flown to Texas on March 20, becoming the first Costa Rican nationals extradited in our history.

So far, cases where the alleged conduct runs past the May 2025 cutoff have held up on review, and cases where it ends before that date have not. The Gómez and Viveros appeal will test how the courts treat an investigation that began in mid-2024 and continued into late 2025.

According to the U.S. indictment cited in the extradition ruling, Gómez and Viveros acted as local leaders of a trafficking network with links to Colombia, Panama and Mexico. U.S. prosecutors allege that the couple received cocaine flights from Colombia about every two weeks and ran safe houses used by the organization.

The indictment links the network to the seizure of 273 kilograms (602 pounds) of cocaine hidden in two vehicles in August 2024. U.S. prosecutors identify Óscar Enrique Virula Arredondo, a Guatemalan national based in Panama, as an alleged organizer of shipments by speedboat and aircraft. Six alleged leaders of the network were indicted on October 1, 2025.

U.S. filings state that DEA informants recorded negotiations on video and made controlled drug purchases in San José and in Cali, Colombia. None of these allegations has been proven in court. Costa Rican authorities arrested Gómez and Viveros on March 13, 2026, in an operation coordinated with the DEA. Viveros is held in the maximum-security unit at La Reforma prison. Gómez is held at the Vilma Curling Rivera women’s prison.

If the appeal fails, the handover would still not be immediate. In the Gamboa case, the appeals court made the transfer conditional on formal U.S. assurances that neither man would face life imprisonment or a sentence longer than 50 years, the maximum allowed under Costa Rican law. No date has been announced for a ruling on the new appeal.

The decision will help define how far Costa Rica’s 2025 extradition reform reaches, especially in long-running trafficking investigations that began before citizens could be surrendered abroad. Other extradition cases involving Costa Rican citizens are still before the courts.

World.title: Lemonal stevedore slapped with additional charge of damage to property, allowed to remain on previous bail
World.content:
Lemonal stevedore slapped with additional charge of damage to property, allowed to remain on previous bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-seven-year-old Jerry Malique August, a stevedore of Lemonal Village, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, where he was charged with damage to property in connection with an incident for which he had previously been charged with aggravated assault.

August appeared before a magistrate in Court #5, represented by attorney Oscar Selgado, and pleaded not guilty to the new charge.

Prosecutors allege that on August 24, 2026, in Bermudian Landing Village, August damaged a four-door Chevrolet Cruze valued at $3,000.

During the arraignment, the magistrate raised the issue of bail, prompting Selgado to explain that his client had already secured High Court bail in connection with an aggravated assault charge arising from the same incident.

Selgado argued that requiring August to obtain bail again would be unfair, particularly since both charges originated from the same circumstances.

The prosecutor agreed with the submission, and August was allowed to remain on his existing bail without having to secure a new bail arrangement.

August had previously been remanded to the Belize Central Prison following his arraignment on the aggravated assault charge before successfully obtaining bail through the High Court.

His next court appearance is scheduled for November 13, 2026, when he is expected to receive disclosure in relation to both charges.

World.title: ‘Our lives were shattered’: Family of slain police officer Arsenio Cus delivers emotional statement as Khris Rosado awaits sentencing
World.content:
‘Our lives were shattered’: Family of slain police officer Arsenio Cus delivers emotional statement as Khris Rosado awaits sentencing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An emotional victim impact statement from the sister of Police Constable Arsenio Cus brought the devastating consequences of his death into focus in the High Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, as businessman Khris Rosado continued to await sentencing for the fatal traffic accident that claimed the officer’s life.

Rosado, the owner of Thirsty Thursday nightclub, previously pleaded guilty to causing death by careless conduct in connection with the July 28, 2025 collision on the Philip Goldson Highway.

During Friday’s proceedings before Justice Derick Sylvester, Cus’s sister, Paulina Cus, described the profound grief and emotional trauma her family has endured since losing her brother more than a year ago.

“Our lives were shattered. His death left a void that altered our future,” she told the court, describing how the tragedy had changed their family forever.

She recalled how her brother was always willing to help his family, including providing financial assistance during the COVID-19 lockdowns.

Paulina also spoke about the trauma of seeing her brother’s lifeless body in his police uniform and the painful experience of identifying him for a post-mortem examination.

“Do you know what it was to identify your own brother for a post-mortem?” she asked.

She described suffering flashbacks and lasting emotional distress, while reflecting on the birthdays, holidays and family gatherings that her brother would never again share with his loved ones, including his daughters.

The emotional testimony also appeared to affect Rosado, who was visibly moved as he listened to the family’s account of their loss.

Justice Sylvester subsequently adjourned sentencing until Monday, November 9, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Rosado pleaded guilty on June 16, 2026, to causing death by careless conduct following the fatal collision between Miles 6 and 7 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

Cus, 38, of Silver Creek Village, was riding his motorcycle from Ladyville toward Belize City when a vehicle entered his lane and struck him, causing severe injuries. He subsequently died from multiple blunt force traumatic injuries.

Police later located Rosado at his Ladyville residence, where investigators found a damaged 2009 Honda Ridgeline pickup truck believed to have been involved in the collision.

Forensic testing subsequently linked blood recovered from the vehicle to the deceased officer.

Rosado’s sentencing has been postponed several times since his guilty plea, including an October 1 adjournment.

The family now awaits Monday’s proceedings, when Justice Sylvester is expected to deliver his sentence.

World.title: Garrick Hemmans remains behind bars as firearm assault trial set for March 2027
World.content:
Garrick Hemmans remains behind bars as firearm assault trial set for March 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-five-year-old Garrick Hemmans, also known as “Tamalito,” remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison after appearing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, in connection with allegations that he fired several shots at a man in August.

Hemmans, who remains unrepresented, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2, where he was provided with 19 pages of disclosure and 12 photographs as evidence in the case.

The magistrate advised Hemmans to familiarize himself with the disclosed material and prepare for his trial, which has been scheduled for March 10 and 11, 2027.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Hemmans was arraigned on August 28, 2026, on a charge of aggravated assault with a firearm upon 32-year-old technician Emory Williams. He pleaded not guilty and was denied bail due to the firearm-related nature of the offence.

The charge stems from a shooting incident on Rio Bravo Crescent in Belize City on August 25, 2026.

According to police, Williams was standing outside a residence around 7:28 p.m. when a maroon Nissan Murano approached from the direction of Tapir Street.

Williams alleged that Hemmans, who was seated in the front passenger seat, pulled out a firearm and fired several shots in his direction.

Fearing for his life, Williams reportedly ran behind a concrete fence and escaped without injury. The vehicle then sped away toward Fabers Road Extension.

Police processed the scene and recovered two expended 9mm Aguila shells and a bullet fragment.

Investigators subsequently located the Nissan Murano parked outside a residence on Jimmy Dyer Street, where another expended 9mm shell was reportedly discovered on the front passenger seat.

The vehicle was impounded, and Hemmans was detained later that night before being formally charged.

Hemmans remains on remand pending trial.

World.title: Devaun Garcia, previously freed of murder charge, granted $6,000 High Court bail in ammunition case
World.content:
Devaun Garcia, previously freed of murder charge, granted $6,000 High Court bail in ammunition case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-one-year-old Devaun Garcia, who previously walked free from a murder charge after the prosecution discontinued its case, has been granted $6,000 bail by the High Court in connection with the alleged possession of three live rounds of ammunition.

Garcia appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, November 6, 2026, represented by attorney David McKoy, who argued that his client deserved bail, particularly since his two co-accused had already been released.

The prosecution raised no objection to bail, and Justice Nanton granted Garcia bail of $6,000, with two sureties of $3,000 each, subject to several conditions.

Garcia must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Monday and Friday, observe a curfew between 11:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m., surrender his travel documents and refrain from contacting prosecution witnesses. He is also prohibited from leaving Belize without permission from the High Court.

The charges stem from an August 2 incident on Caesar Ridge Road in Belize City, where Garcia, along with 19-year-old Esmond Austin and 19-year-old Isani Conorquie, allegedly possessed three live 9mm Aguila rounds without a firearm licence.

According to police, officers responding to reports of an abandoned vehicle near the Yabra Bridge discovered a damaged black Ford Escape. During a search of the vehicle and surrounding area, officers reportedly recovered three live rounds of ammunition.

Police further allege that Garcia attempted to interfere with the investigation by grabbing ammunition from the vehicle and throwing it toward a nearby canal. The ammunition was subsequently recovered, and Garcia was additionally charged with obstruction.

All three men appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on August 3 and were initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Garcia has previously faced several serious criminal allegations. In April 2025, he and George Hyde were freed from a murder charge involving the 2021 killing of 18-year-old Eaton Thompson of Mahogany Heights after the prosecution entered a nolle prosequi when its main witness could not be located.

In February 2026, Breaking Belize News reported that Garcia was remanded on firearm and ammunition charges following an incident in which police allegedly used drone surveillance to track a suspect who discarded a loaded 9mm pistol. Garcia had also previously secured bail in connection with an armed robbery allegation involving the BelChina Bridge.

Garcia maintains his innocence in the latest ammunition case, claiming that the bullets were planted by police.

His next scheduled appearance in the Magistrate’s Court is December 9, 2026.

World.title: Ector Soler to stand trial for manslaughter in fatal Ladyville motorcycle collision
World.content:
Ector Soler to stand trial for manslaughter in fatal Ladyville motorcycle collision

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-nine-year-old Ector Danielo Soler has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for manslaughter by negligence in connection with a fatal motorcycle collision that claimed the life of 40-year-old Celia Josefina Carballo Pleitez De Lazaro in May 2025.

Soler, a maintenance worker of Airport Plaza and resident of Ladyville, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, where his preliminary inquiry concluded through a paper committal.

He was informed that his case would proceed to the January 2027 session of the High Court, expected to commence in mid-January.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Soler was arraigned on September 26, 2025, on three indictable traffic offences: manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, and driving without due care and attention.

The charges stem from a collision on May 25, 2025, between Miles 9 and 10 on the Philip Goldson Highway in Ladyville.

According to police investigations, 24-year-old Francisco Cortez was travelling southbound on a green Lifan motorcycle with his common-law wife, Celia, riding as a passenger.

The couple had reportedly stopped to purchase food near the Lord’s Bank junction and were returning to their home on Baltimore Road.

As Cortez approached the intersection with Marage Road around 8:00 p.m., he reportedly activated his left indicator and slowed down to make a turn.

Police allege that a red Ducati Monster motorcycle driven by Soler collided with the rear of Cortez’s motorcycle, throwing all three individuals onto the pavement.

Cortez and Soler sustained injuries, while Celia, a Guatemalan national, was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Following an investigation, the case file was submitted to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, which directed police to charge Soler.

Soler was initially granted bail of $7,000 following his September 2025 arraignment.

He will now face trial in the High Court, where the prosecution will be required to prove its case.

World.title: 19-year-old charged in $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion granted $8,000 High Court bail
World.content:
19-year-old charged in $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion granted $8,000 High Court bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nineteen-year-old Adam Abraham Reynolds, accused of participating in a violent home invasion in Burrell Boom Village in which a businessman was tied up at gunpoint and robbed of nearly $90,000 in cash and valuables, has been granted bail by the High Court.

Reynolds, a labourer of Vista Del Mar, Ladyville, appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, November 6, 2026, after spending 16 days on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

His attorney, Norman Rodriguez, successfully applied for bail after the prosecution, representing the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, raised no objection.

Justice Nanton granted Reynolds bail in the sum of $8,000, with two sureties of $4,000 each, subject to several conditions.

Reynolds must report to the Burrell Boom Police Station every Friday, surrender his travel documents, refrain from contacting the complainant directly or indirectly, and remain at least 100 yards away from him. He must also attend all scheduled court appearances and avoid being arrested and charged with any new offences while on bail.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Reynolds was charged with aggravated burglary following an October 14 home invasion at El Chiclero Resort in Burrell Boom Village.

Police allege that four men entered the residence of a 53-year-old businessman around 4:50 a.m., assaulted him, restrained him with duct tape and ransacked his home.

The intruders reportedly escaped with $30,000 in cash, gold chains valued at $12,000, electronic equipment and a 2017 Toyota Rush SUV valued at $45,000. The total value of the stolen property was estimated at $89,900.

Police subsequently located the stolen SUV in Santa Familia Village, Cayo District, on October 15. Investigators allege that Reynolds was inside the vehicle when officers approached, but he sped away before crashing and abandoning it.

Reynolds later surrendered to police in the presence of an attorney on October 19 and was arraigned the following day.

His next court appearance is scheduled for December 9, 2026.

Reynolds remains accused of aggravated burglary and has not been convicted.

World.title: Belize Zoo becomes a classroom for young conservationists
World.content:
Belize Zoo becomes a classroom for young conservationists

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Students from St Martin de Porres School traded their classroom for the Belize Zoo last week, spending a morning learning about conservation through games, interactive booths and hands on activities.

The event took place ahead of the evening celebration of Voices of the Corridor, which marked the completion of a key link in the Maya Forest Corridor.

Students explored aquatic ecosystems with the Savanna Field Station and the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS). They learned about the work of conservation rangers and field enforcement with WCS and Monkey Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, and got a closer look at biodiversity monitoring through camera trapping and bird observation.

Other booths focused on the dangers of fire and how teams protect the Maya Forest Corridor, as well as the role of sustainable agriculture in keeping landscapes healthy. Those activities were led by WCS, the Belize Maya Forest Trust, the Foundation for Wildlife Conservation, the Savanna Field Station and the Ministry of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining.

Organizers said the day gave students an introduction to the people, knowledge and daily work behind conservation in Belize.

World.title: Happy birthday, Shyne: Belize’s comeback king turns 48
World.content:
Happy birthday, Shyne: Belize’s comeback king turns 48

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Today, Belizean rapper and former politician Moses “Shyne” Barrow turns 48.

Like him or hate him, few Belizeans have lived a story quite like his.

Born in Belize City on November 8, 1978, Shyne grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and burst onto the hip hop scene in the late 1990s with Bad Boy Records. His debut album went platinum and made him one of the most talked about young voices in the music industry.

Then it all came crashing down. Shyne was convicted in connection with a 1999 New York nightclub shooting and spent close to a decade in prison. After his release, he was deported to Belize in 2009.

Many would have given up. Shyne didn’t.

He rebuilt his life at home, entered politics and in 2020 won the Mesopotamia seat in Belize City. He went on to become Leader of the UDP and Leader of the Opposition. Even after losing his seat in the 2025 general election, he has kept pushing forward.

This year, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso declared April 25, 2026 as “Shyne Day” in Brooklyn and presented him with the Key to Brooklyn. He has also told his story in the Hulu documentary The Honorable Shyne, carrying Belize’s name to audiences around the world.

Happy birthday, Shyne.

World.title: Warning!
World.content:
PASCOE...find something more productive, even going into farming yourself, it will be in your best interest (Photo: JIS News)

SENIOR Superintendent of Police (SSP) Oral Pascoe is urging agricultural thieves to abandon their criminal activities and find legitimate employment, warning that the police intend to intensify their crackdown on offenders amid an increase in large-scale livestock theft across Jamaica.



His warning comes as the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Agricultural Protection Branch (APB) is reporting 1,424 arrests for agriculture-related offences islandwide so far this year, a more than 600 per cent increase from the approximately 200 arrests during the corresponding period in 2025.

“My warning to the thieves is that they need to change the profession of stealing agriculture produce for a living, because we are sharpened and we are determined to ensure that the farmer benefits from what they do,” Pascoe declared on Sunday in an interview with the Jamaica Observer.

“We have zero tolerance, and we’re going to ensure that once we identify you as a larcenist, and you prey on farmers, we’re going to put you on our monitoring list, and we’re going to target you for snap raids and other operational activities to ensure that you do not carry out those offences,” he charged.

Pascoe, head of the APB, disclosed that the increase is consistent with a seasonal trend in which the demand for meat rises ahead of the Christmas period, with some farmers losing dozens of animals in a single incident.

“Traditionally in Jamaica, in the Yuletide, meaning from about September, accelerating in October to December, there’s a spike in the demand for meat and, of course, our local goat and beef is preferred,” he explained.

He said that, while thieves would usually target one or two animals at a time, the police are now encountering cases involving significantly larger numbers.

“We have about three or four instances where they stole about 40 goats, 30 goats, [animals] in large numbers. Normally, they steal one or two during the year, but…the value of what they steal in terms of livestock is a lot larger,” he noted.

Pascoe further disclosed that the police have received approximately 230 reports of praedial larceny up to the end of September, with that figure climbing to just over 250 following an increase in incidents during October.

He identified Manchester, Clarendon, St Elizabeth, St Mary, St Catherine, and St Thomas among the parishes most affected, noting that the highlighted areas account for approximately 70 to 80 per cent of reports islandwide.

The senior officer said that some of the thefts were not necessarily being committed by individuals acting alone, but by organised criminal groups.

He pointed to incidents in Colbeck, St Catherine, where several animals were reportedly being stolen nightly, forcing the police to intensify their presence.
