World.title: Disposable: The ordinary people doing Russia’s dirty work
World.content:
The life Vasilij Kovacs knew ended with a bang. It was late afternoon on March 1, 2025, when an armored vehicle smashed through the metal gate of the old farmhouse where he lived southeast of the Latvian capital, Riga.

Masked men emerged with their guns drawn. They belonged to Latvia’s State Security Service, the country’s counterintelligence agency. The officers searched the property, seizing several mobile phones, SIM cards and documents, along with a pistol with its serial number filed off, a bayonet from an AK-47 and a cellphone jammer, according to a search report later filed by the authorities. They arrested Kovacs, a Ukrainian man in his 60s who has lived in Latvia for more than 30 years.

In March, Kovacs was transferred to stand trial in Lithuania, where he is accused of planning terrorist attacks, alongside four alleged accomplices. Five others face trial in Warsaw. Lithuanian and Polish prosecutors accuse the ten men of planning and carrying out arson attacks involving cargo parcels across several European countries on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU.





One of those incidents made headlines across Germany. In the early hours of July 20, 2024, a parcel caught fire at Leipzig Airport just before it was due to be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane. The flames engulfed an airfreight container. It was probably only because the aircraft was delayed that the fire did not break out on board.

All ten men say they did not knowingly work for Russian intelligence and say they are innocent of the terrorism charges. According to investigative files from the Office of the Prosecutor General of Lithuania, Kovacs is an example of an increasingly common category of Russian intelligence asset — the kind Western intelligence agencies call “low-level agents,” or, more tellingly, disposable agents.

The 63-year-old Ukrainian national is alleged to have been a small cog in a much larger machine. Investigators say he transported massage pillows modified to be able to conceal incendiary devices from Latvia to Lithuania.

The aftermath of the parcel fire in Leipzig, as seen in the investigation files. | WELT

With its own officers finding it harder to operate in Europe since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the GRU increasingly relies on intermediaries to recruit people through messaging services such as Telegram, according to investigative files from Lithuania’s State Security Department obtained by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, of which POLITICO is a part of.

Often motivated by money, these disposable agents carry out individual assignments: Take a photograph. Mail a parcel. Move something from A to B. Sometimes the tasks are far more dangerous. Recruits may know little about the wider operation. Anyone who gets caught can be replaced.

Much has been written about these agents and the shadow war unfolding across Europe. But one perspective is usually missing: Who are these people? How did they become pawns in a new Cold War that is growing increasingly hot? Are they simply perpetrators — or are they victims, too?





For this article, we spoke to Kovacs several times, interviewed his daughter and examined thousands of pages of investigative records. Together, they reveal a sabotage network where meticulous intelligence planning goes hand in hand with human incompetence, and in which ordinary people are, well, disposable.

The GRU, contacted through the Russian government’s Press Service, did not reply to a request for comment.

The courier

The entrance to the prison where Kovacs has been held on remand for more than a year sits beneath a rusting metal roof. A Lithuanian investigating judge has authorized us to interview him, but when we arrive in September 2026, prison officers refuse to let us in. We need a separate document from the prison administration, they explain. We submit the additional paperwork but eventually have to leave.

A few days later, Kovacs calls from prison. He is allowed around 20 minutes on the phone each day, time he usually reserves for his family. But over the following weeks, he calls us repeatedly. “I also want to know how I ended up in here,” he says. He insists this is about justice, not himself. “I don’t value my own life particularly highly,” he says. “I’m not going to tell you how many times people have tried to kill me.”

There’s a lot about what Kovacs says during our conversations that’s unclear. But on one point, at least, his account and the investigators’ findings agree: He transported a package. Where they disagree is whether he knew what was inside it, what it was intended for — and who was behind the operation.

Vasilij Kovacs, during the first hearing of his trial in Vilnius on April 17, 2026. | Mindaugas Kulbis/AP via Belga

According to the Lithuanian investigative files, Kovacs’ involvement in the affair began on June 27, 2024, when someone contacted him on Telegram with a request.

He barely knew the man, but the two had been introduced by a mutual friend: Andrei Baburov, a former Russian submarine commander who was also the godfather of Kovacs’ 11-year-old son. The two men had met through their shared passion for the sea. Kovacs is a sailor who occasionally earns money delivering yachts for their owners. He says he first met Baburov while transporting a yacht between St. Petersburg and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

The request sounded harmless. A courier had fallen ill, and Kovacs was asked to collect a package and take it urgently to Vilnius, nearly four hours away by car. He agreed, collecting the package from a locker outside a supermarket in Riga using a code sent to him on Telegram by the man Baburov had introduced him to. He insists he was not paid. “If I’m helping someone I know, I do it for free,” he says.





That same day, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew. His contact on Telegram directed him to an underground parking garage. Kovacs parked outside, left the vehicle unlocked and walked away with his nephew. When they returned, the package had disappeared from the trunk. Kovacs says he had gone to buy a charging cable for his phone.

For Kovacs, that part of the job was done. But for the operation investigators have attributed to the GRU, things were only just getting started.

Burning parcels

Lithuanian investigators overseen by the Office of the Prosecutor General have reconstructed the movements of the devices used for the operation in painstaking detail, questioning witnesses and suspects, reviewing surveillance footage and digital evidence and analyzing DNA traces. The resulting files from the criminal investigation, compiling information from agencies in Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Estonia, the U.K. and Germany, run at around 8,000 pages. They reveal a convoluted journey through the Baltic states, involving a succession of intermediaries, missed connections and improvised plans.

The man believed by Polish and Lithuanian investigators to have collected the package from Kovacs’ car was another Ukrainian, a trained chef who had spent five years in a Russian penal colony after being convicted of rape. By the summer of 2024, he was living in Poland and receiving instructions through Telegram from a handler who promised him €4,000 a month.

A photograph from the investigation files shows Vasilij Kovacs, center, with his nephews. | WELT

The following day, the chef allegedly took the massage pillows to a holiday apartment rented under a false name. He also had tubes of cosmetics filled with potentially explosive nitromethane. A video filmed inside the Airbnb apartment and later found on a suspect’s phone shows four boxes containing the massage devices and cosmetic products.

According to the Lithuanian investigative files, another intermediary was supposed to come and get the devices but could not find the entrance to the apartment complex. The chef’s handler changed the plan and ordered him to activate the ignition devices himself. The chef refused, according to an indictment filed by Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, obtained by the Global Reporters Network. The operation had to be reorganized.

Over the following days, the boxes passed through several more hands. At one point, Lithuanian investigators lost track of them altogether. They suspected they might have traveled through Moldova. On July 13, 2024, they resurfaced in Riga, where Kovacs was drawn into the operation for a second time.





Once again, according to his account, Kovacs received a Telegram call from the acquaintance he barely knew. This time, he said, he thought he could hear Baburov in the background. He was asked to transport another shipment to Lithuania, described as “high-quality massage pillows.” On July 17, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew.

There, another man collected his package and drove it to Kaunas, where on July 18 a Ukrainian who had traveled from Poland to Lithuania retrieved it. He, too, had a criminal past, having been convicted in Poland of cyber fraud and money laundering. His instructions came from a Telegram contact calling himself “Warrior.”

The Ukrainian packed four parcels containing the massage devices, tubes of potentially explosive cosmetics and various sex toys investigators believe were included as a distraction. He activated a timer and handed the parcels to the man who had previously failed to find the entrance to the holiday apartment. That afternoon, the man dropped off two parcels at a DHL office in Vilnius. They were addressed to Wimbledon in London and to Birmingham.

Top left, the charred massage pillow that caught fire in Leipzig. Next, four parcels marked with their destination cities in the trunk of a car, in a photograph taken by one of the accused; a Lithuanian intermediary dropping off the parcels at a DHL branch; and the fire at the DPD warehouse in Birmingham on July 22, 2024. | WELT

At 3:17 a.m. on July 20, customs officers in Leipzig inspected the parcel bound for London. They found nothing suspicious. The parcel was due to be loaded onto a plane to London. But at 5:45 a.m., it burst into flames while still on the ground. An expert report commissioned by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office, dated August 30, 2024, offered a terse assessment: “Fire caused by deliberate action: plausible.”

Two days later, the second parcel caught fire in a warehouse in Birmingham. That shipment, too, had previously been inspected by customs officers in Leipzig. They had found nothing.

The Ukrainian man also sent two other parcels to Poland through the DPD shipping service. In the early hours of July 21, one of them burst into flames inside a truck near Warsaw. Polish investigators recovered the other intact.

The Kremlin’s recruits

For investigators, the parcel operation is a case study in how Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, now organizes its operations in Europe. “The July 2024 incident fully corresponds to the modus operandi favored by the GRU in recent years when planning and conducting operations,” according to a report by Lithuania’s State Security Department, also known as the VSD, obtained by the Global Reporters Network.

For years, the GRU sent its own officers abroad to carry out covert operations. But that became increasingly difficult after the failed assassination attempt against former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal in Britain in 2018 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years later. Now, the GRU leaves the dangerous work to others, increasingly relying on recruits directed through multiple layers of intermediaries.

At the top of the chain are still Russian intelligence officers. The Lithuanian report identifies Denis Smolyaninov, who, according to a decision to sanction him by the Council of the European Union, recruited operatives for sabotage missions in Europe through social media. The VSD considered it highly likely that Smolyaninov and two other GRU officers were involved in the parcel operation. Smolyaninov did not reply to a request for comment sent via the Russian Press Service.





The Lithuanian investigative files offered an unusually detailed picture of how the system worked. One of the alleged organizers was Andrei Baburov, the former submarine commander and godfather of Kovacs’ son. He allegedly coordinated the transport of the modified massage devices from Russia, drawing on old contacts, including former naval comrades and acquaintances in the Baltic states. Baburov did not reply to a request for comment.

Such personal connections are typical, according to the VSD. Recruits are often linked through “family or social ties,” the Lithuanian report says. Many have financial problems, no jobs or criminal records. They are recruited for individual assignments and do not necessarily know what lies behind them. The less they know, the less they can reveal if they are arrested. And anyone who gets caught can be replaced. “Their main motivation is the desire to make money quickly,” the report states.

Two years after the parcel attacks, operations of this kind had become a growing concern for European security agencies. In August 2026, two explosive-laden drones detonated at Leipzig/Halle Airport, while a third crashed into a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Among the suspects was a longtime acquaintance of Smolyaninov.

Shortly afterward, two Bulgarians allegedly threw incendiary devices near defense companies in Munich. Investigators suspected the GRU was behind the incident. In Romania, a fire broke out next to an arms factory. Starlink installations were set ablaze in Poland and Bulgaria, leading to further arrests. The GRU has seemingly turned the disposable-agent model into a mass-production operation.

Disposable

On the phone, Vasilij Kovacs sounds agitated. Speaking rapidly in Russian, he tries to explain himself, only to circle back over the same ground. “It was a crime committed so that it would be solved,” he says.

In Kovacs’ trial, the witnesses for the prosecution have already testified and the defense is preparing to call its own. With hearings scheduled well into January, a verdict is a long way off. Kovacs sees himself as the victim of a conspiracy. He believes the Russians deliberately drew him into the affair to make him, a Ukrainian citizen, a convenient villain. European investigators, he argues, only identified the most obvious participants without pursuing the people truly behind the operation.





He says it was Baburov who lured him into the trap, but he does not believe his former friend worked for the Kremlin. “They threw him away, too,” Kovacs said. Baburov, he says, was an opponent of the Russian government.

Kovacs is reluctant to answer questions about himself. Asked about his background, he says he was born in western Ukraine and had worked as a businessman. Had he worked at sea? “I’m just an amateur.” Then he interrupted: “But let’s move away from talking about me.”

He prefers to discuss what he sees as inconsistencies in the investigation. The weight of the massage pillows he transported does not match the weight of the parcels eventually shipped, he says. In his cell, he has filled a sheet of paper with tightly packed notes. Why are key figures behind the operation standing trial in Warsaw rather than Vilnius? What information was being withheld from the Lithuanian court? If the cargo had passed through Moldova, why was it not inspected at the border?

Kovacs, center, and other suspects, during their first hearing in Vilnius on April 17, 2026. | Mindaugas Kulbis/AP via Belga

Other questions he’s less eager to address. What about the pistol with its serial number filed off, or the cellphone jammer found at his home? He was only renting the property, he says. They did not belong to him.

A photograph from the opening of his trial shows Kovacs sitting in the dock, unshaven, wearing a baseball cap beneath a hood. He looks tired. In another photograph, taken before his arrest, he sits on a motocross bike with his grandson perched in front of him, showing the boy how to hold the handlebars. He’s wearing the same cap, but with the bill turned backward. He looks carefree, almost boyish.

Viola Lisija, Kovacs’ 37-year-old daughter, knows the man in that photograph better than almost anyone. “He may be the person I’m closest to in my life,” she says. On the day he was arrested, she was supposed to meet him. She was at a playground in Riga with her son, now 7, when she learned what had happened. “My son loves his grandpa very much,” she says.





Her father had arrived in Latvia as the Soviet Union was collapsing. He initially worked in forestry before going into business, buying and selling forest land and acquiring stakes in Russian companies, including a shoe factory and an ice cream manufacturer. “Those were probably his best years,” Lisija said.

Around 2014, Russian authorities accused Kovacs of being a Ukrainian spy, according to his daughter. He was forced to stop traveling to Russia and give up his business interests there. Back in Latvia, he occasionally earned money sailing yachts from one port to another for their owners.

His background may help explain why Kovacs was of interest to the people behind the parcel operation. He had contacts in Russia, traveled between the Baltic countries and occasionally took on assignments. His daughter believed his previous troubles with the Russian authorities might also have made him a target.

Kovacs and his grandson, before his arrest. | Vasilij Kovacs

Yet parts of her father’s life remained a mystery even to her. Had he ever moved in shady circles? “I really don’t know,” Lisija says. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, she noted, entrepreneurship and organized crime were often intertwined. Her father came from a different era. She says she never saw her father with a gun. “There were never any stories that made me think: Aha, he’s disappearing at night or doing something strange.”

Kovacs is struggling in prison. He has high blood pressure and complains of headaches. His family, too, is close to breaking point. Lisija’s son misses his grandfather. Every other day, the boy asks about him. She tells him Grandpa is at sea.

“I tell him he’s enjoying life to the fullest,” Lisija says. “I say, ‘He loves the sea, he’s a captain, and he’s off on long voyages around the world.’”

For now, at least, the boy believes her.





Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Artur Weigandt is a freelance journalist based in Prague.

The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: Marine Le Pen is coming after Kaja Kallas
World.content:
The comments reveal growing tensions over the EU’s power as nationalist parties from France to Germany and Poland seek to wrest power back from Brussels, with foreign policy among their top targets. They also put extra pressure on Kallas and the European External Action Service, which has been locked in a protracted turf war on foreign policy with the European Commission headed by Ursula von der Leyen.

The view inside the National Rally is that the EU’s diplomatic service is not only a waste of taxpayer money but also gets in the way of European nations being able to flex their muscles on the world stage.

One example is Ukraine, on which Kallas and Le Pen are deeply divided — although they have not clashed publicly. The former Estonian prime minister is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s fiercest critics and a staunch supporter of Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while Le Pen is pushing for an international peace conference to settle the conflict and says Europe has run out of money to give to Kyiv.

Kallas has “used very warrior-like language on Ukraine,” said National Rally MEP Jean-Paul Garraud. “We support Ukraine but if we expressed ourselves like that we would be in total war” with Russia, he said.

Le Pen has directed her most vicious attacks against von der Leyen, who has long been accused by the far right of exceeding her powers. But it’s Kallas and the EEAS that risk becoming collateral damage under a far-right presidency in France.

Le Pen is the front-runner ahead of next year’s presidential election. In a recent visit to Brussels, she vowed to downsize the European Union if she comes to power.

World.title: Polanski will struggle to end the Greens’ bitter Zionism fight
World.content:
Polanski meanwhile told the BBC in October that he would not seek to overturn the motion himself — and that he would not be able to even if he wanted to.

Polanski’s current stance — making amendments to the motion at the first available opportunity in 2028 — remains unchanged, a Green Party official told POLITICO. They stressed that his support for governance changes is geared towards a long-overdue rule update rather than this specific policy.

But Green MPs hope to use the pressure of public interventions to get results sooner. Adrian Ramsay, a former leader of the party, has said Polanski’s “strong communication and motivational skills” have shifted the dial on the climate and cost-of-living — and implied they could do so here.

From left: Councilor Asma Alam, MP Hannah Spencer and Polanski. They pose for a picture in Stockport, England on Jan. 30, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

That has, in turn, prompted pushback from defenders of the Green Party’s structure. “Some of these people wrote the job role of leader, and now they’re expecting someone to do it very differently from how they designed it,” said Rouxel, the former deputy chair of the party’s executive committee. Polanski, he said, simply does not have the power to intervene in democratic processes.

Pressing for an overhaul

MPs are forging ahead anyway. Ramsay told POLITICO the proposals set out by a working group on party governance had a “good chance” of being heard at the party’s next conference in spring.

“I’ve spoken to some of the people on the working group who are determined to do that. The bigger question is whether there can be movement on the motion itself in that time period, which is harder but essential,” he added.

World.title: The Kremlin call: How talking to Putin exposed Europe’s deepest rift over Ukraine
World.content:
The leaders of Finland and Norway were slammed for reaching out to Russia — but Europe still can’t find a better way to influence Donald Trump’s peace talks.

Beneath the chandeliers and oil paintings of his Presidential Palace, Finland’s president Alexander Stubb sat down next to his old friend Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian prime minister, to call Vladimir Putin.

They hoped such a dramatic and direct intervention with Russia’s leader would demonstrate European resolve.

Instead, the conversation on a damp autumn morning in Helsinki triggered the biggest rift among Nordic allies since Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — and exposed Europe’s wider divisions over how to deal with Moscow at a pivotal moment in the push for peace.





As Russian and Ukrainian negotiators prepare for talks with Donald Trump’s envoys in Abu Dhabi this week, the fallout from the call is still reverberating across Europe. Governments are arguing over who should represent Europe in future negotiations and remain divided over a question at the heart of the debate: Does engaging Putin help deliver peace, or simply reward aggression?

Underlying European anxiety is another dilemma: Can America be trusted to broker a fair deal for them and most of all for Ukraine?

EU leaders will grapple with these questions at an informal summit in Dublin this week. Few involved expect them to agree.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his U.S. counterpart Donald Trump in New York, on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images

In an interview with POLITICO in Oslo, Støre explained why he and Stubb decided to call a leader waging hybrid warfare on Europe and killing Ukrainian civilians with daily drone and missile strikes.

“We work closely with our European partners in supporting Ukraine, but the only voice reaching Moscow comes from Washington,” Støre said. “And you know, we have good and open relations with the American negotiators, with the American administration, but this [war] happens in Europe. And living month by month, thinking that this war will end by Europe not talking to Moscow, I think, is an illusion.”

Other countries sharing a border — and a history — with Putin’s Russia profoundly disagree.





“Europe should not be in a mediator’s position,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO in another interview. “You should not take the role of trying to please the dictator.”

Based on interviews with politicians, diplomats and officials, many granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, this is the inside story of a phone call that shook Europe.

The Trump shock

Europe has struggled for influence over the stop-start Ukraine peace process ever since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, promptly picked up the phone to Putin and ended U.S. financial assistance to Kyiv.

Trump’s interventions shattered the transatlantic consensus built under his predecessor Joe Biden, offering Putin the prospect of an advantageous ceasefire and a return to the international fold.

The U.S.-Iran war this year interrupted momentum but Trump returned to the topic of Ukraine again in October, criticizing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for continuing to attack Russian energy infrastructure, while declaring that Putin’s side had been “fine”.





Fearing the negotiations were drifting toward collapse, Stubb and Støre intervened. Støre hosted Zelenskyy and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo in an attempt to repair relations. Stubb, who also attended, declared the meeting on Oct. 20 had put the peace process “back on track.”

But 24 hours later, Witkoff again stunned European leaders by meeting Putin in St. Petersburg and praising him as a “humanitarian.”

After consulting Zelenskyy, the two Nordic leaders concluded they could not leave Trump, Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner as the only Western figures speaking directly to Putin.

Old friends

Stubb and Støre have known each other for years and worked closely on Russian affairs when they both served as foreign ministers. They talk and text frequently — and like to pair up on key files despite coming from different political backgrounds.

They had quietly explored the idea of a joint call to the Kremlin for months and concluded that reviving momentum would be critical ahead of renewed negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

Europeans, many officials privately acknowledge, no longer trusted Washington to defend either Europe’s interests or Ukraine’s.





“We have to ask the question in Europe if we feel that someone else should have the contact and the discussion on our behalf,” one EU government official said. “Is the feeling that the U.S. should own our objectives?”

“It’s important that Donald Trump is not the only leader from the West who talks to Putin,” another senior European official said. “We need pro-Ukraine leaders putting their messages to Putin too.”

So, almost five years after Russia’s diplomatic isolation began, Stubb and Støre decided to call the Kremlin. The Nordic team reached out to Putin’s officials and agreed parameters for the conversation. Each side would take turns to deliver their prepared messages, without interruption from the other.

Omens in oils

Some of the omens were inauspicious from the start.

As the leaders sat next to each other at the long cabinet table in Stubb’s plush presidential salon on Oct. 27, two large, gilt-framed oil paintings loomed over them, depicting battle scenes from the Crimean War. One canvas shows an Anglo-French naval force retreating under fire on Finnish territory, a reminder of an era two centuries ago when Finland itself was part of the Russian Empire.

According to some accounts, Putin shared his own keen interest in Russia’s past with the two Nordic leaders — delivering a lengthy lesson on Slavic history and the origins of the war in Ukraine.





One senior official familiar with the matter said Stubb and Støre listened patiently during the 90-minute conversation. Other European officials briefed on the call denied that Putin had given the two leaders a history lecture at all, and suggested this claim was Russian spin aimed at humiliating the Europeans.

Støre himself said: “I was present. He didn’t.” Putin has well-worn arguments about the origins of the war, he added. “But in all fairness, he can give his explanation, and we respond to that.”

For their part, the Nordic pair first gave Putin Zelenskyy’s messages — that territorial boundaries can only be discussed at leader level, face to face, and first there must be de-escalation measures. Stubb and his friend then turned to the matter of Baltic Sea security and the need to keep the waterway open for trade.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting of the Council on Interethnic Relations in Moscow on Nov. 3, 2026. | Sofia Sandurskaya/Sputnik via Getty Images

One reason for holding the call was to try to judge Putin’s state of mind, according to officials. The Norwegian leader said Putin was “rational” and “professional” on the phone. “His arguments were perfectly clearly transmitted.”

Putin took the idea of talks in Abu Dhabi seriously and told the Nordic pair he would instruct his negotiators to prepare for the meeting to explore if progress is possible. “The fact that he picks up that phone, that we have, you know, other ways of reaching, I think that signals, at least that there’s a readiness to sit down.”

But afterwards, Støre was still not convinced that Putin was genuinely open to a deal. Despite their efforts, the Norwegian and Finnish team do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi.

Baltic backlash

When Stubb’s office announced the surprise call had happened, the diplomatic blowback played out live in public.

By coincidence, the leaders of Denmark and Sweden, among others, were already gathered in Helsinki for a Nordic Council meeting. Confronted by TV crews, they made little effort to hide their irritation.





“I’m very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative,” Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told broadcasters. “I think we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement”. Lithuania also criticized the move.

In private, some diplomats were even harsher. “There are too many middle-aged men who want to end up in the history books having solved this war,” one EU diplomat said. “Putin is just gaining from opening up a more normalized dialogue with the rest of the world — and continuing to bomb and kill innocent people in Ukraine.”

European Council President António Costa, Zelenskyy and Danish PM Mette Frederiksen on Oct. 16, 2026 in Brussels. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga via Getty Images

Their complaints were not simply over the decision to engage with Putin, but that Stubb and Støre had not properly coordinated with allies beforehand.

Officials familiar with the preparations for the call deny this, insisting that Frederiksen and others including the leadership in France, Germany, and the U.S. were told about the call before it happened. It may just have been that Frederiksen expected more advance warning, and a genuine say over the plan. She said her Finnish and Norwegian counterparts had failed to coordinate the call with “the rest of us.”

Moscow endorsement

Støre is defiant. “She is right, because I did not ask — we did not ask for permission,” he told POLITICO. “We consult each other in the Nordic family, but it is not a mechanism which is that, you know, doing this requires a yes from all the Nordics or from 27 Europeans or beyond.”

Privately, some officials think Støre aggravated the wound in the immediate aftermath, when he pointed out that the EU had been divided on Russia since the war began. “It’s true — it’s just not his place to say it,” one official said. “Norway is not in the EU.”





Stubb and Støre say they never sought to speak for anyone other than the countries they lead, which both border Russia. They talked to Zelenskyy at length before the call to agree what to say to Putin and then briefed him again afterwards.

They had hoped their initiative would bolster Zelenskyy. Instead, the backlash became so intense that the Ukrainian leader stepped in to defend them. “They truly help us,” he said.

The two Nordic leaders also won an endorsement from Moscow. “I believe it was the right thing to do,” Putin said. “After all, there are some people in Europe who do not want to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia … but seek to establish some kind of constructive dialogue.”

Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre welcomes Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Oslo on Oct. 8, 2026. | Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB via Getty Images

Putin’s comments are unlikely to soothe lingering resentments between Nordic neighbors. As one official put it, there may be some lasting “family trauma” for those regional leaders who were not included in the Putin call plan.

For all the northern angst, the episode also exposed a harder truth for Ukraine and its supporters. Despite Trump’s midterm election defeats, he is still dictating the pace of talks. Europe, meanwhile, has no one to match America’s booming voice when it matters in the room.

Clea Caulcutt, Hans von der Burchard, Veronika Melkozerova and Laurens Cerulus contributed reporting.

World.title: Storm killed five in Gaza as sandstone slab collapsed onto tents
World.content:
Tents located near an elevated soil mound were crushed reportedly due to the storm's heavy rains, killing five people in the central Gaza Strip.

 

"A sandy embankment collapsed onto tents housing displaced people at a shelter centre south of Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip," said Mahmud Bassal, spokesperson for Gaza's civil defence.

"Rescue teams are continuing to search for missing people," he said. A video circulating on social media showed dozens of men at the scene, some trying to lift a large stone slab while others dug beneath it with shovels.

tents buried under rocks and earth a day after a large sandstone slab collapsed at a displacement camp in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Monday, 9 November 2026. AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana

The agency further warned "displaced people against setting up tents or remaining near sand masses and elevated soil mounds, particularly during periods of rainfall, as these pose a real threat to their lives" and called on humanitarian organisations to provide the necessary equipment.

Hundreds flee camps after 70,000 tents flooded

Thousands of displaced people had their tents flooded by the heavy rain on Saturday, leaving them without shelter in war-devastated Gaza.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said that about "70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day" of rains.

It also noted the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries," some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A Palestinian child sits beside a pool of rainwater at a camp for displaced people in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, Saturday, 7 November 2026. AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana

During the weekend, hundreds of displaced families started fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and other parts of the territory after floods destroyed their shelters.

A fragile ceasefire came into effect in Gaza on 10 October 2025, after two years of war that erupted following the unprecedented attack carried out by Hamas on Israel on 7 October 2023.

The war left most of the population displaced and often living in tents or other makeshift shelters as bombs destroyed huge swathes of the territory.

The Israeli army continues airstrikes and ground operations in spite of the ceasefire agreement reached with Egyptian, Qatari and US mediation.

World.title: Nvidia stock slides as company probes claims CEO was foreign intelligence target
World.content:
Nvidia stock was down 4.51% ahead of the US markets opening, as the company announced that its board had launched an "independent investigation" following reports that founder and CEO Jensen Huang may have been targeted in a foreign intelligence effort.

 

"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," an Nvidia statement said on its website.

The company further highlighted that the board prioritises US national and economic security, which it said is "paramount to the interests of Nvidia" and its shareholders.

Related Tech stocks recover after midterms rout as Nvidia takes centre stage

"While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information," the company also noted.

"Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.

"The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate," Nvidia concluded.

Meanwhile, China denied on Monday there was a spy plot attempt to ensnare the Nvidia CEO, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Related Nvidia investigates its own CEO Jensen Huang over affair with alleged Chinese spy

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, commented on the claims and potential market impact: “How boards view undisclosed CEO romantic relationships often depends on who is involved. Relationships with colleagues can raise conflicts of interest and favouritism concerns, while those outside the company are usually private unless they pose security, reputational or company-resource risks.

“Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is in a precarious position, and the dial on his situation currently sits at ‘highest risk’. Personal scandals never sit well in the corporate world, let alone ones where the CEO is being investigated for an affair with a suspected foreign spy," he said in a note sent to Euronews Business.

“Given pre-existing sensitivities around China accessing US technology, and various export restrictions already in place, Nvidia’s situation is going to be treated with intense scrutiny. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Jensen Huang step aside on a temporary basis while an investigation takes place.

“Even if Jensen Huang is found not to have discussed any confidential information with the woman in question, the affair is not a good look for a company that prides itself on family-based cultural values. It’s plausible that Jensen Huang might decide to step down as CEO if he thinks the incident has tarnished the company’s reputation, as well as his own. Or the board might decide he has to go," he added.

“Yet one could see why Nvidia’s board might be keen to back Jensen Huang and not lose him. He has been the architect of Nvidia’s success, making it the go-to place for advanced AI chips, and making shareholders seriously rich along the way. He is the face of Nvidia, and many shareholders big and small might prefer him to stay put if it means a continuation of the current strategy,” Coatsworth concluded.

World.title: A Portuguese chef’s journey from Vila do Conde to Macao
World.content:
“Macao got recognised in 2017 by UNESCO as a ‘Creative City of Gastronomy’, so I think it’s the right place if you want to open a restaurant, a takeaway shop,” says Cristiano Tavares, Founder, Macalhau & Executive Chef, Vic’s Restaurant.

 

The chef from Vila do Conde in northern Portugal arrived in Macao in 2012. He opened Macalhau, a takeaway serving as a homage to his grandfather, a codfish fisherman, then brought the ice cream brand Gelados de Portugal to the city. “Opening Macalhau was quite easy,” he says.

Now executive chef at Vic’s, Rocks Hotel, he has recreated the local dish Minchee with codfish. His message to Macao is one of gratitude: “I always knew my purpose here was to give back to this community, to this region that gave me this opportunity.”

World.title: 007 casting shock: Two new A-listers could play James Bond after 'secret screen tests'
World.content:
Every week brings a new rumour and supposed "confirmation" regarding the identity of the actor who will portray the seventh James Bond.

 

Will it be Callum Turner, who recently got Pierce Brosnan's seal of approval?

Could the role go to Jack Lowden, who has been a longtime favourite for the role?

Or will Josh O'Connor nab the role at the last minute?

While many were seeing this as a three-way race, surprising reports emerged this weekend that two more stars have auditioned for Bond - and they are easily the most high-profile actors to do so.

When the shortlist was announced, there was mention of a mysterious fourth candidate – and that unknown auditionee happens to be two actors, who have shaken up the casting race.

According to both Deadline and Variety, Nicholas Hoult and Robert Pattinson have had secret screen tests for Bond.

Nicholas Hoult (left) and Robert Pattinson (right) AP Photo

Hoult, 36, is best known for his roles in the X-Men franchise, Mad Max: Fury Road, Nosferatu and Superman, playing the evil Lex Luthor in the latter and in the upcoming sequel Man Of Tomorrow.

As for Pattinson, 40, the actor needs little introduction. Following his star-making turn in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and the Twilight franchise, he has gone from strength to strength with roles in The Lost City of Z, High Life, The Lighthouse and Tenet. He is also the current Batman, having debuted as the Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves' The Batman in 2022. He is currently filming the sequel.

This year has been a particularly busy (and productive) year for Pattinson, as he starred alongside Zendaya in The Drama, played Antinous in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, and portrayed American TV presenter Chris Hansen in Primetime. He will next star in Dune: Part Three, which is directed by none other than Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve – the director of the upcoming James Bond film. Many see this as an indication Pattinson has an advantage and is the new frontrunner to play 007.

Considering both Hoult and Pattinson are already two of Hollywood's established leading men, the news of their inclusion in the Bond race comes as a surprise.

The role of Bond usually makes the star, and rising performers are usually favoured. Sean Connery was a relative unknown before Bond; George Lazenby had never acted outside of a few ads; Roger Moore was a household name thanks to The Saint but hadn’t had a huge break on the big screen; Timothy Dalton had a great stage career but was not an established movie star; Pierce Brosnan was a Bond hopeful for years but remained best known for his role as Remington Steele in the TV show of the same name... Only Daniel Craig had some major big screen credentials with memorable roles in Road To Perdition, Layer Cake and Munich... However, it was Casino Royale that made him a bona fide leading man.

With this in mind, and the fact that already established stars command higher salaries, many thought that Amazon would be banking on a relatively unknown actor in his late 20s or early 30s rather than someone who is already in demand.

The recent news of Hoult and Pattinson's screen tests now give weight to the counter argument that Amazon, who took creative control of the Bond franchise last year from long-serving producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, may buck the trend and cast a more known actor. However, this would mean that the public won’t be discovering a “new” performer and will have to work harder to dispel memories of other high-profile roles.

Speaking to The Independent earlier this year about the casting process, retired casting director Debbie McWilliams – who helped cast Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Criag as Bond - said that “it is absolutely essential that [Bond] retains a total enigma,” adding: “We want to know as little about them personally as possible, because that’s what spies are."

“We don’t need to know where he goes shopping or who his parents are, or where he lives… He’s licensed to kill, and we have to believe that he can do that. If you don’t, then you’ve lost the audience.”

So, could the current Batman also be the next James Bond?

The internet seems pleased about the possibility - frequently pointing out that Pattinson's role in Tenet was akin to an audition tape for Bond.

Check out some of the reactions below:

Not long to find out now... While an exact timeline for finalizing casting is not known, Bond 26 producer Amy Pascal revealed in August that "the end of the year is a good bet" for the official announcement.

“We are being really, really methodical," said Pascal in August. "Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring, exciting and different.”

Bond 26 will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who recently teased at the LACMA Art + Film Gala that he would not be commenting on the casting, but that he was "having a great time".

He said on stage at the event (as per Variety): “For many years, LACMA has been a temple for me. Tonight feels like home, and to express my gratitude. With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond..." Villeneuve then said: “The actor who will play the next James Bond is… And I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack."

Bond 26 is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight and it will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson.

Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028 at the earliest.

World.title: Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon highlights record China presence and robot speakers debut
World.content:
The tenth edition of the Web Summit (source in Portuguese) in Portugal, which starts today and runs until next Thursday, once again brings the technology world together in Lisbon, but 2026 marks a new era in the event's history, with the shift to physical Artificial Intelligence (AI).

 

For the first time, humanoid robots will take on the role of official speakers, showcasing China's cutting-edge approach. The country built these machines and is bringing the largest delegation it has ever sent to this technology conference.

Riding on the presence of Chinese companies, the focus of the talks will no longer be only on software that creates texts and images, but also on autonomous agents that interact directly with the public.

One of the robots on show, developed by Galbot, has wheels and two arms and is capable of carrying out real work shifts in shops, pharmacies and factories.

The automatons will make their first appearances on the opening night and, over the four days, as well as taking part in talks, they will give practical demonstrations at the brand stands set up at the Feira Internacional de Lisboa (FIL) and the MEO Arena. The Ministry of Commerce and the Cyberspace Administration of China are also sending delegations.

The Web Summit programme looks at the use of AI agents, technology-supported scientific research, the challenges of digital regulation and the reshaping of work models.

The organisers expect to welcome close to 70,000 participants, including 900 speakers and more than two thousand startups. The doors open at 16:30, with the first speeches on the main stage starting at 18:00, and the opening session led by the Minister Adjunct and for State Reform, Gonçalo Matias.

Portuguese-speaking delegation

Around 300 Brazilian startups will be present at the venue, 100 of them as part of the mission organised by Sebrae and ApexBrasil. On Tuesday, these institutions will announce up to 20 startups selected for an incubation programme in Lisbon, starting in March 2027.

This will be a way of bringing Brazil's technology ecosystem closer to European investors who operate in international markets.

Portugal, for its part, is sending 78 companies to this year's Web Summit, mainly from the AI and health technology sectors.

Web Summit in Lisbon until at least 2028

Paddy Cosgrave, chief executive and co-founder of Web Summit, has not revealed whether the event will stay in Portugal beyond 2028, when the 110 million euro contract signed with the Portuguese government and Lisbon City Council comes to an end.

In an interview with the newspaper Expresso last week, Cosgrave said that he is in negotiations with most major European cities and expressed his intention to make the announcement at the 2027 edition.

The limitations of the Lisbon venue will be a factor to take into account. "We have been at the limit of capacity for years and we have built 30,000 square metres of temporary structures", he said.

World.title: Russia: HIV spreads beyond risk groups in 27 regions, epidemiologists say
World.content:
In 27 Russian regions, there is a generalised HIV epidemic. This was reported by the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor. Scientists use this term for the stage when the human immunodeficiency virus spreads in the general population rather than only among risk groups.

 

In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women. The situation is most serious in the Kemerovo, Irkutsk and Sverdlovsk regions.

And although, according to the Central Research Institute for the Prevention and Control of AIDS, 45,000 new HIV cases were detected in Russia in 2025, which is 13.4% lower than in 2024, last year a record was set for the number of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical institutions, according to statistics compiled by the specialist portal Medvestnik.

Experts record the highest level of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical facilities in 15 years

These are the highest figures in the past 15 years. Clusters of viral hepatitis C and mixed HIV plus hepatitis infections predominate, said Yelena Igonina, head of the Department for the Epidemiological Wellbeing of the Population at Rospotrebnadzor. In 2025, eight clusters of infection were recorded in healthcare facilities in Russia, with 104 patients infected.

According to Rospotrebnadzor, investigations continued in 2026 into 11 clusters of infection in the territory of ten regions of Russia, where the spread of HIV and hepatitis in medical organisations is suspected. In Moscow, an investigation is underway into a cluster in which 22 cases of viral hepatitis C have been identified.

One of the largest confirmed clusters in the past two years was the infection of 82 people in a sanatorium in Kabardino-Balkaria. While receiving medical care, 76 patients contracted viral hepatitis C and six were found to have mixed infections. In oncology hospitals in Kamchatka Territory and Buryatia, 147 and 42 patients, respectively, were infected with hepatitis. Another three hepatitis C clusters were identified in dialysis centres in the Samara and Kursk regions, where 26 people were affected.

Experts describe violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules as the main cause of the infections, including the use of single-use catheters or glucometers on several patients. In such situations, the source is usually patients with undiagnosed infections.

Yelena Igonina notes that these "systemic and gross violations" have become entrenched in today’s Russia. Although simultaneous testing for hepatitis C antibodies and RNA covers blood, component, organ and tissue donors well, testing for RNA among other categories that should be tested, namely dialysis, haematology and transplant patients, contacts in hepatitis clusters, children under one born to mothers with HIV and patients with immunodeficiency, is significantly lagging behind.

In addition, for the first time in six years, two cases of HIV infection via transfusion of blood components were identified in 2026, the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor added.

When hospitals receive large numbers of people with undiagnosed infections, international HIV consultant Aleksei Verter told Current Time, this means that "the infectious process in the country is latent, hidden" and a great many people do not know they are infected.

Despite lower mortality, the number of people living with HIV is rising

Despite a decline in HIV incidence and mortality in Russia in recent years, the number of people infected continues to grow, Medvestnik’s authors note. Statistics show that for each death there are one and a half new infections, that is, the number of people "living with HIV continues to grow constantly", explains Natalya Ladnaya.

The decline was preceded by a long period of rising incidence, but in the past three years rates of morbidity and mortality among people with HIV have been falling and, according to her preliminary data, this trend will continue in 2026. At the same time, the expert is convinced that there is no reason to rest on one’s laurels, since "the dynamics can change rapidly".

In recent years, the number of deaths from HIV in Russia has been between 30,000 and 34,000 per year. This is an extremely high figure, stresses the head of the research department for the prevention and control of AIDS at the Central Research Institute of Rospotrebnadzor. "Among all the countries in the world there are only 15 where more than 15,000 deaths of people with HIV are recorded, including Russia." "The highest HIV incidence rates per 100,000 population in the European region are in Russia, Ukraine and North Macedonia", says Central Research Institute of Epidemiology director and Rospotrebnadzor academician Vasily Akimkin.

HIV infection has become the leading cause of death among Russians of working age. Among men aged 40 to 49, more than 3% are affected by the virus, clarifies Natalya Ladnaya, while the average age of those infected in Russia has increased over the past 15 years from 32 to 44. It is also noteworthy that two-thirds of new HIV transmissions occur through heterosexual contact.

More than 1.232 million people with a confirmed HIV diagnosis now live in Russia, which is 0.8% of the country’s population, Akimkin adds. Rospotrebnadzor has warned that if current approaches to prevention and treatment remain unchanged, the number of people living with HIV in Russia could reach 1.47 million by 2030, according to the agency’s mathematical model. Under this scenario, the annual number of new cases will be between 31,000 and 51,000, and the number of deaths included in the model could rise to 51,000 a year, which is linked, among other things, to population ageing.

In the past seven years, the main causes of death among children with HIV have also changed. An increase in mortality in this group of patients was recorded in 2025 in all federal districts except the Central and Ural districts.

According to an analysis by several Russian media outlets, Rospotrebnadzor and the Health Ministry calculate figures differently. Rospotrebnadzor’s data are more complete, as they are based on laboratory notifications of every positive immunoblot. The Health Ministry’s data are based on the number of people who have been registered for regular follow-up care. As a result, the overall gap between the total number of people with a confirmed diagnosis, 1.23 million according to Rospotrebnadzor, and those actually under medical supervision, 846,500 according to the Health Ministry, amounts to 385,555 people.

600,000 infected people

Only half of people living with HIV in Russia had a suppressed viral load by the end of 2025, said Natalya Ladnaya at the conference "Epidemiological Surveillance of HIV Infection", as quoted by Medvestnik. In practice, this means that at least 600,000 people with HIV "continue to play an active part in transmitting the virus", the expert concludes.

Viral load suppression occurred last year in 77.9% of people with HIV who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and "so far it has not been possible to exceed this level", she says, while WHO standards for keeping the epidemic under control are 95-95-95, that is, 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of them receive ART and 95% of those on therapy achieve suppression of HIV replication.

As for access to medical care for people living with HIV in Russia, 72% of those infected were under follow-up last year. Despite extensive HIV testing, which has increased by 75% over the past decade and reached 54 million tests last year, effectiveness is declining. In the view of the director of the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, approaches need to be adjusted by increasing the share of people at the highest risk of infection, who are insufficiently covered by testing. Their share has now almost halved, from 5.8% in 2014 to 3% in 2023.

But the effectiveness of the work is declining, meaning there are more tests, but testing is increasingly carried out among people with a lower probability of having HIV.

Chronic underfunding by the state

The fact that the burden of HIV infection is not decreasing even as incidence falls is reflected in healthcare spending, stresses Natalya Ladnaya. In 2025, spending related to HIV infection was estimated at 279 billion roubles.

In the expert’s view, there is no reason to expect the situation to change; on the contrary, the spread of the virus may intensify among traditionally vulnerable population groups and among people living in regions bordering Ukraine that are characterised by high levels of migration. According to Rospotrebnadzor, incidence and mortality may also rise in the Far Eastern, Southern and North Caucasian federal districts.

Bloggers have also spoken about the spread of viruses, including HIV, among those fighting against Ukraine. According to Anastasia Kashevarova, the Russian authorities should "seriously think about it, there is a threat of an epidemic of socially dangerous diseases", since hepatitis, HIV and tuberculosis are currently spreading in the army and to frontline regions, but "will then spread further into the interior of Russia".

The Insider previously reported that after Russia’s occupation of parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions, patients with HIV faced shortages of life-saving medicines. The Russian Health Ministry did not include them in centralised drug procurement, and some patients were given medicines past their expiry date.

According to observers, the fact that the healthcare budget is shrinking and all funds are going to the war helps explain, among other things, shortages of sterile consumables in state hospitals.

Other Russian media emphasise that most donors financing HIV prevention programmes for the general population and vulnerable groups have left Russia. The country itself does not adequately fund these projects, says Evgeny Pisemsky, editor-in-chief of the queer media outlet "Parni+", quoted by Current Time. With 45,000 new HIV cases detected in 2025, the draft Russian budget for 2027 provides for additional funding for medicines for only 30,000 new carriers of the virus.

World.title: Why airlines are upgrading premium offerings in bid to boost profits
World.content:
Airlines are betting that more passengers will pay for an upgrade to their flight experience, with some carriers fitting roomier seats, bringing in Michelin-starred chefs to design onboard menus and also investing in elite airport lounges.

 

Some airlines envisage up to 70% of passengers paying for enhanced options, if not first-or business class. That shift could mean fewer standard economy seats on many flights.

The war in Iran has pushed up jet fuel costs, but airlines see premium travel as a way to boost profits over the long term.

Business class seats can each take up floor space equivalent to four basic-level seats, but can be priced five or six times higher, said Volodymyr Bilotka, a professor at Purdue University and a specialist in aviation economics.

"Airlines have traditionally been investing quite a lot into the premium offerings because the profit margins are significantly higher," Bilotka told the AFP news agency.

In the most recent quarter, American Airlines said premium revenue increased 18.5% year-over-year, four points better than the main cabin. American executives said the boost has been a bright spot in a travel market complicated by the jet fuel spike.

"Premium products generate roughly half of the company's ticket revenue on approximately 30% of seats today," American said.

Besides the traditional differentiation between the main cabin and business class, customers may now pay as much as $200 (€179) for more legroom or the ability to sit at the front of the plane and disembark first.

Premium's steady growth

Since 2020, the number of premium seats on US flights has risen 33%, more than double the growth of mainline seats, according to travel news site Skift.

United Airlines more than doubled its premium-seat capacity between 2015 and 2026, the airline told AFP, adding that it plans additional options.

Launching in 2027, United’s new “Relax Row” will allow passengers in economy class to turn a row of three seats on some wider Boeing planes into a couch they can sleep or lounge on after takeoff.

United has also unveiled its new Economy Plus option that allows customers to forgo having a passenger in the dreaded middle seat. It plans to begin this option on some flights at the end of 2026.

‘More premium experiences’

JetBlue announced the launch of BlueFirst, a new first-class service on domestic flights. "Customers are increasingly looking for more premium experiences," said JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty.

Meanwhile, Delta has invested in Delta One, a revamped luxury option, with premium wine, "top-of-the line" food like the Wagyu burger and larger screens for entertainment.

To assist with the menu, Delta partnered with Simon Hulstone, chef of Michelin-starred restaurant The Elephant in Torquay, UK, and Andrea Robinson, an award-winning sommelier.

The company plans the service for new Airbus A350-1000 planes, with about 150 premium seats and 161 seats in economy.

"Twenty years ago, 90% of the seats were main cabin," said Ekrem Dimbiloglu, Delta's managing director for onboard strategy and experience, adding that the share of premium seats could soon represent as much as 70% on some Delta flights.

In October, British Airways announced that the top level of the two-tier A380 would be entirely composed of premium seats. Then this month, Singapore Airlines revealed that it is investing €1.4 billion to upgrade its luxury long-haul cabins – including the largest double bed in commercial aviation in first class.

Some airlines already offer services without any economy seats, such as all-business class carriers BeOnd and La Compagnie, while Jet2 recently announced a new charter service which will use a specially configured Boeing 737-800NG with 76 business class seats.

A rise in premium amenities

Consultancy Cirium estimates that premium seats among the 42 carriers in the three major airline alliances (SkyTeam, Oneworld and Star Alliance) and Middle East carriers now represent 19% of total volume compared with 17.1% in 2019.

Other new options include giving customers choice among meal options prior to boarding and free wifi. There have also been a slew of announcements of new and beautified airport lounges, including by Southwest Airlines, which was once known as a discount carrier.

But the increasing tendency of airlines to market to customers who can afford premium amenities could open the door to a discount carrier, although higher fuel costs have added to the challenges facing all airlines.

World.title: EU to send joint team to Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi
World.content:
The European Commission and the European Council will send a joint team of senior officials to the round of trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi that the United States will host between Ukraine and Russia.

 

The negotiations will unfold over two days: 10 and 11 November.

"The EU will be present alongside our partners," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday morning after speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"Freedom of navigation in the Black Sea must be restored and preserved. I reiterated my support for his (Zelenskyy's) call for a ceasefire covering food and energy infrastructure."

A spokesperson for the European Council also confirmed the participation.

The institutions will be joined by the E3: France, Germany and the United Kingdom.

The EU team will be led by Bjoern Seibert, von der Leyen's chief of cabinet, and Anna-Maria Boura, chief foreign policy advisor to European Council President António Costa.

Both institutions previously indicated their willingness to engage directly with the Russian delegation, something that has never happened in the context of the peace talks.

At this stage, however, it is not clear if this face-to-face will happen.

Jared Kushner, the US special envoy, said last week that the multilateral format would be organised "if progress is made", though he did not say whether this would be in Abu Dhabi or elsewhere at a later date.

Kushner's long social media post laying down principles to reframe Europe's security architecture after the war has triggered pushback among allies, with Zelenskyy calling it "dangerous". European officials believe the discussion is premature and misguided given that Russia is yet to make a single concession at the negotiating table.

The confirmation of the EU team comes after Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent a scathing letter to Costa complaining about the "disarray" in diplomatic formats and demanding the appointment of a special European envoy.

In his reply, Costa agreed to put the issue on the table at this week's informal summit in Dublin, Ireland, which will take place right after the Abu Dhabi meeting.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski agreed with Meloni and warned that Eastern European's interests should be considered.

"The last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the East Europeans," Sikorski said from Warsaw.

The Abu Dhabi talks will mark the resumption of trilateral peace negotiations since February, when the war on Iran abruptly shifted Washington's focus.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, together with Kyrylo Budanov and Sergiy Kyslytsya, head and deputy head of the president's office; and Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the ruling party in the Parliament.

The Russian delegation will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, aide to President Vladimir Putin, and Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.

The US will be represented by special envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner.

World.title: Turkey pushes for transition at COP31 as coal burns
World.content:
The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.

As Turkey welcomes delegates to the 2026 UN climate talks in Antalya and pushes for cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, it can point to surging renewable energy capacity at home.

The COP31 host has approved more than 33 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage projects since 2022 that can power over 27 million homes.

Among the largest battery project pipelines in Europe, this storage will complement fast-expanding wind and solar energy that today provides 22% of electricity in Turkey, up from 4.5% a decade ago.

Yet this clean energy upswing is a long way from compensating for the country's overreliance on fossil fuels.

Turkey's coal-fired electricity generation increased by roughly one-third in the last decade, and in 2024 overtook Germany and Poland, which previously had the highest coal power capacity in Europe before it began to decline.

UN climate summit opens amid worsening climate crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Coal undermining climate ambition

Turkey is among the few industrialized countries that has yet to commit to a phaseout date for coal — the fossil fuel with the highest planet-heating emissions.

Yet at the same time, "coal's position in the electricity market in Turkey is increasingly precarious," Efe Baysal, Turkey team lead at global environment network, 350.org, told DW.

He points to high local community opposition to coal projects on environmental grounds or due to lack of financial viability. According to German nonprofit climate campaigners, Beyond Fossil Fuels, some 97% of new coal projects have been cancelled in the last decade in Turkey, in what it calls "a global record."

"Turkey's coal project failure rate is the final nail in Europe's coal coffin," said Kasia Szeniawska of Beyond Fossil Fuels in a statement earlier this year. "Coal power is finished: it's financially risky, increases costs for billpayers, harms people's health, and sabotages climate goals."

But in June, Turkey announced plans to expand one of its largest coal plants and near double its capacity.

COP31 host Turkey still relies on coal for electricity and has no plans to phase it out Image: Omer Urer/AA/picture alliance

The move underlines Turkey's "conservative energy policy" and "highly insufficient" climate goals, said Umit Sahin, head of the climate change program at the Istanbul Policy Center, a global research institute.

Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to keep rising until 2038, meaning it will struggle to meet its plans to reach net zero by 2053, notes Climate Action Tracker, a climate research think tank.

Push for electrification, energy independence

Aside from climate concerns, Turkey's high dependence on imported fossil energy makes it extremely vulnerable to volatile global oil and gas markets. The nation currently imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of crude oil and 60% of its coal — which together make up a "lion's share" of Turkey's energy capacity, said Baysal.

It is partly this dependence that has inspired Turkey's push for greater electrification at the COP31 climate conference.

In September, the country launched the "35x35" global electrification pledge, which aims to increase electrification of world economies from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The goal is for electrification to replace fossil fuels, including in transport, buildings and industry, and preferably using clean energy, though this is not mandatory —heat pumps, for example, emit fewer greenhouse gases than gas boilers, even when the electricity is generated using fossil fuels.

The pledge complements existing UN climate goals of doubling energy efficiency and tripling renewables to keep temperature rise in line with the Paris climate agreement.

Turkey's mining threatens ancient olive grove heritage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey COP31 President Murat Kurum will promote the 35x35 pledge in Antalya on both climate and energy security grounds.

"[The war in the Gulf] has shown us, once again, that fossil fuels do not guarantee energy supply security," he said earlier this year at a UN climate meeting in Bonn, Germany. "Investment in alternative energy sources, in particular to support energy diversity, means stability, resilience and clean development."

But despite the rhetoric, Climate Action Tracker says that under Turkey's National Energy Plan, the COP31 host is only on track to electrify around 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.

Can renewables expansion turn the tide?

Turkey is one of numerous Mediterranean countries facing extreme climate impacts like wildfires and record heat, in addition to recent severe and deadly flooding.

Torrential rainfall caused severe flash floods in Istanbul in October Image: Adem Kutucu/Anadolu/IMAGO

As it hosts this year's climate summit, the country has a great opportunity to hasten the energy transition, said Baysal, especially since it receives nearly double the annual sunlight of Germany.

Turkey is already starting to realize some of this potential, with one analysis showing the country produces more solar module manufacturing capacity than several major European countries combined.

Solar increased from around 0.1% of total installed electricity capacity in 2014 to almost 21% at the beginning of 2026, according to Turkey's resources and energy ministry.

The COP31 host can reduce its emissions 35% by 2035 if 10 GW of solar and wind is added each interim year — as opposed to the government's target of 8 GW — noted Umit Sahin. This goal will be helped by fast-expanding battery capacity, he said.

"But if you don't phase out coal, your emissions cannot go down," he added.

Meanwhile, the COP presidency could be a "turning point" and "a very important step for Turkey," said Sahin.

If the country wants to show climate leadership, and reduce energy dependency, it will need to embrace a "progressive climate policy" that promotes a full energy transition, he added.

Serdar Vardar and Jonathan Rampley-Sturgeon contributed reporting to this article.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker
