Six people have been killed and many more injured after a man opened fire from a moving vehicle in the historic centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, today. Police have apprehended the perpetrator. The interior minister says that the incident is being treated as a terrorist attack, and that preliminary indications suggest the perpetrator had “very radical far-right” views. Police later discovered three further dead bodies in the suspect’s home, who are believed to be his parents and sister. 📌Premier przekazał, że policja, służby specjalne, prokuratura zrobią wszystko, żeby jak najszybciej przekazać informacje opinii publicznej o powodach (strzelaniny – PAP) – powiedział w sobotę na briefingu premier Donald Tusk. 📌- Prawdopodobnie w domu zamachowca są nieżywi… pic.twitter.com/gnV7c1TALa — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) November 7, 2026 At around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday, a man who had driven onto Kraków’s market square – a large public space filled with tourists and locals – “began firing at random people from his car”, said police. They later confirmed that six people – four women and two men – have died and 15 were injured. Three of the deceased have been identified as Polish women, and one other as a British man. The two other victims have not been identified at the time of writing. The police also revealed that there is only one suspected perpetrator, that he is a Polish citizen, and that he has been detained and transported to hospital. ~aktualizacja Zmarła kolejna z osób poszkodowanych w zdarzeniu na Rynku Głównym w Krakowie. Na ten moment nie żyje 6 osób. 4 kobiety i 2 mężczyzn. pic.twitter.com/yK6a7fSj2P — Małopolska Policja (@kwpkrakow) November 7, 2026 Footage from Republika, a TV station that had been present in the city centre to report from an anti-government protest that was taking place today, showed paramedics appearing to treat victims on the square. The station also broadcast footage showing the car from which shots were fired driving through a street that leads away from the square. A police car can be seen behind it and the apparent sound of gunfire can be heard. Moment ucieczki czarnego Subaru w Krakowie, widać, że sprawca strzela z samochodu do ludzi… pic.twitter.com/VfWYtx8PYX — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 7, 2026 Further videos and photos shared on social media show the alleged perpetrator being apprehended by a police officer, with both men injured and requiring medical treatment. The suspect is wearing a military-style uniform, including some kind of helmet and face covering, while what looks like an AR-15-style rifle can be seen on the ground alongside him. A spokeswoman for provincial police headquarters in Kraków, Katarzyna Cisło, later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that police officers had fired at the suspect, who had returned fire. Two police officers were injured during the incident, with one undergoing surgery and described as being in critical condition. 🔴Strzelanina w Krakowie. Jest nagranie z momentu zatrzymania zamachowca pic.twitter.com/2EXVvLEoRY — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 7, 2026 A spokesman for national police headquarters, Andrzej Fijołek, told TVN that the suspect is a 24-year-old from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a small town in southeastern Poland. Fijołek revealed that the man has a firearms licence and had used an AR-15 rifle during the incident, which he fired randomly while driving the car. “I can confirm that his attire indicates he was well-prepared, well-armed and knew what he was doing,” he added. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced that, contrary to some rumours on social media, the suspect is not and has never been a member of the Polish military. Stanowczo dementuję informacje pojawiające się w przestrzeni publicznej, że zamachowcem, który dokonał dziś ataku w Krakowie był żołnierz Wojska Polskiego. Mężczyzna nie był i nie jest żołnierzem WP i nigdy nie mial nic wspólnego z wojskiem. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 7, 2026 On Saturday evening, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński confirmed that “we are dealing with a terrorist attack”. He praised “police officers’ swift response for preventing a much larger massacre”. Kierwiński said that the perpetrator is currently in critical condition in hospital. He added that the information obtained so far suggests that the attacker had “very, very radical views” and “may have been fascinated by far-right ideologies”. However, the interior minister emphasised that investigations are still ongoing. Subsequently, Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed that three further bodies – of two women and one man – had been found at the suspect’s home. He said they were likely his close family members. Minister @MKierwinski na konferencji w Krakowie: 💬 Sprawca mógł być zafascynowany ideologiami skrajnie prawicowymi. Ten wątek będzie jednak szczegółowo weryfikowany. Czynności prowadzą funkcjonariusze @PolskaPolicja, jak i @ABW_GOV_PL – na miejscu zdarzenia oraz w domu rodzinnym… pic.twitter.com/PppmMPmWYW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) November 7, 2026 Gun violence in Poland is extremely rare, and this kind of mass shooting incident is unheard of. The country also has one of the lowest rates of gun ownership in Europe, though a record number of licences, 50,709, were issued last year. Kraków is by far Poland’s biggest tourist destination, receiving over 16 million visitors last year. The historic city centre, which is a UNESCO-listed World Heritage Site, would have been filled with locals and tourists on a Saturday afternoon. The market square itself, surrounded by historic townhouses, is the heart of the city’s life, filled with restaurants, cafes and bars, as well as St Mary’s Basilica, the famous Cloth Hall (Sukiennice), and the old town hall tower. Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. The city's food and drink was rated as better than in Paris and Rome, while it also scored top marks for accommodation, ease of getting around and value for money https://t.co/U1P1QkQCm4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 19, 2025 President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, Poland’s eastern neighbour, expressed his condolences and declared that his country “stands in solidarity with Poland”. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also sent messages of condolence. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, expressed his sorrow at the “savage and murderous attack” in Kraków and declared that “America stands with Poland at this dark hour”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Credit rating agency S&P has revised Poland’s outlook to negative, saying that the country has seen “one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally” and that “political polarisation hinders fiscal consolidation”. It also lowered the country’s long- and short-term local currency ratings. S&P’s decision follows similar ones by the other members of the big three rating agencies. Fitch has had Poland on negative outlook since last year, while Moody’s cut the country’s credit rating in September this year to its lowest level since 2002. In a statement issued on Friday evening, S&P said that its “negative outlook reflects the risk that elevated budgetary deficits and rising government debt could constrain policy flexibility in the face of future shocks”. “This could expose Poland to shifts in investor sentiment or necessitate a sharp fiscal adjustment that would weigh on economic growth,” they added. 🚨Bardzo źle to wygląda! S&P o finansach Polski: „Takie pogorszenie sytuacji budżetowej należy do najpoważniejszych na świecie”. Dług netto ma wzrosnąć o ponad 20 pkt proc. PKB w 5 lat i przekroczyć 70% PKB w 2029 r. S&P obniżyła rating długu w PLN i perspektywę do negatywnej. — Piotr Nowak (@PiotrNowak_PL) November 7, 2026 Poland has struggled with ballooning budget deficits in recent years, driven by a rapidly expanding defence budget in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and longer-term increases in social spending. Last year’s deficit, at 7.3% of GDP, was the second-highest in the European Union. This year it is forecast to drop slightly, to 6.7%, according to recent finance ministry projections. But next year’s budget foresees a deficit of 7.1%. Those figures are much higher than those the government pledged to reach when, in 2024, Poland was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. For example, the deficit was supposed to fall to 3.7% of GDP in 2027. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has cut Poland’s rating from A2 to A3. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level was 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland since 2016 https://t.co/qUAEouqhlx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 19, 2026 S&P says that it projects Poland’s net debt exceeding 70% of GDP by 2029. That rise of “more than 20 percentage points over five years marks one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally”. The agency notes that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in 2027, making any “meaningful consolidation unlikely” before then. Moreover, the veto power of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki means the government “faces constraints in advancing its legislative and fiscal consolidation agenda”. Pointing to the ongoing crisis around the constitutional court, S&P also warns that “renewed institutional tensions could weigh on policy predictability”. However, the agency notes that Poland’s economy remains “resilient”, with real GDP growth projected to average around 3% between 2027 and 2029. It also points to the fact that the country has seen a peak in EU-funded investment this year, while exports have picked up. As well as shifting Poland’s overall outlook to negative, S&P downgraded its local currency ratings – meaning its assessment of the country’s willingness and ability to service debt denominated in domestic currency – from A/A-1 to A-/A-2, the same level as its foreign currency ratings. “Our fiscal projections are now weaker than previously envisaged, and we note a track record of recent fiscal slippages amid a challenging policy environment, which underpin our assessment of Poland’s reduced fiscal flexibility,” wrote the agency. Finance minister Andrzej Domański acknowledged S&P’s decision to lower Poland’s outlook to negative in a social media post. However, he pointed to the section of the agency’s report in which it said that the government is constrained by presidential vetoes. Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year, including several fiscal measures. “Despite the presidential vetoes, we will continue taking steps to strengthen the country’s finances,” wrote Domański. 🇵🇱 Agencja S&P utrzymała rating Polski na poziomie A-, obniżając jednak jego perspektywę do negatywnej. W uzasadnieniu decyzji czytamy wprost: „Rząd premiera Donalda Tuska napotyka ograniczenia w realizacji swoich planów legislacyjnych i konsolidacji finansów publicznych ze… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) November 6, 2026 However, Nawrocki notes that the ballooning budget deficits preceded his coming to power, and has blamed the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk for overseeing budgetary “chaos” and causing “a deep crisis of credibility”. In response to S&P’s announcement, Marcin Ociepa, deputy head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of “trying to shift responsibility for Poland’s credit rating downgrade [sic] onto the president”. “Any family that managed its finances the way Donald Tusk manages our country’s finances would drown in debt and go bankrupt,” wrote Ociepa. “That is exactly what awaits Poland if this government remains in power.” ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: 2,000-year-old Vandal artefacts anonymously handed to Polish museum
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland. The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery. The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary. The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground. They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position. The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken. Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered. The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice. “We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.” The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts. The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów. The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC. They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period. Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish deputy PM proposes “constitutional reset” to resolve crisis around top court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court. The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president. To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament. Deeskalacja sytuacji wokół Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jest konieczna aby przywrócić obywatelom niezależny sąd konstytucyjny. Apelują o to przedstawiciele organizacji społecznych, Rada Przedsiębiorców, Naczelna Rada Adwokacka, Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka i Episkopat Polski.… pic.twitter.com/3RCsKRlSiM — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 5, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court. They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court. Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023. As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges. The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate. Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised. Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in. That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”. Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges. The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions. The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined. 💬 336 głosów posłów i senatorów. To wykracza poza większość jakąkolwiek koalicyjną dzisiaj sformułowaną – @KosiniakKamysz w Warszawie pic.twitter.com/iLUuM5TSxQ — 🍀 PSL (@nowePSL) November 5, 2026 Whereas TK judges currently all serve nine-year terms, under Kosiniak-Kamysz’s proposal, five of the judges would serve three-year terms, five of them six-year terms, and the final five would serve for nine years. Unlike now, the new judges would not have to swear their oath before the president, but before parliament. Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.” The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz’s plans would require changes to Poland’s constitution, which specifies the manner in which TK judges are chosen. A constitutional amendment requires the support of a three-fifths majority in the Sejm and a simple majority in the Senate. It does not need presidential approval. PSL itself has only 28 members of the 460-seat Sejm and four senators. Kosiniak-Kamysz acknowledged that “it won’t be an easy road” to win the necessary support for his idea. He appealed not only to his fellow ruling parties, but also to opposition groups that have expressed their backing for a constitutional reset, such as the centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). On Thursday evening, one of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a photo of himself meeting Kosiniak-Kamysz, with the caption: “It’s going in the right direction”. However, some voices within the ruling coalition expressed scepticism towards the idea. Borys Budka, a former leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which is the largest governing party – said it was “hard to imagine changing the constitution alongside someone like PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński”. Tomasz Trela of The Left (Lewica) likewise said that, “if anyone thinks The Left will change the constitution arm in arm with PiS, they’re mistaken”, reports Polsat News. Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year. The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM — Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026 The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022. The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items. Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours. “This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs. “Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.” The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%. The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition. In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs. The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers. China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods. Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office. 🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place. The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”. “This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency. World.title: Prague Ice Rinks Guide This Winter: Opening Dates, Prices and Locations
World.content:
As temperatures fall, public ice rinks are beginning to reopen across Prague for the 2026–27 winter season.

Several districts have already confirmed opening dates, while others are still finalising their winter programmes. From free skating in Smíchov to rinks beneath the Žižkov Television Tower and on the Letná Plain, residents and visitors will have plenty of options in the coming months.

Here is what has been announced so far.



Prague 1

The Na Františku ice rink is scheduled to open on November 13. Public skating will begin at 8 a.m., with closing times varying between 6:30 p.m. and 8:30 p.m., depending on the day. Skate rentals, refreshments and a heated tent will be available.

A second rink is expected to open on Wenceslas Square on November 28. It will operate daily in four sessions between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m.

A two-hour ticket will cost 200 CZK for adults and 100 CZK for children under 15. Visitors will be able to rent skates and helmets, while skating aids for children, skate sharpening and storage facilities will also be available.

It remains unclear whether the rinks at Ovocný trh and Čapadlo will return this winter.

Prague 2

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 2.

The rinks at Havlíčkovy sady, also known as Grébovka, and Svatopluk Čech Park are scheduled to open on November 20. A third rink, located in Folimanka Park beneath the Nusle Bridge, is expected to follow on December 1.

All three venues are expected to operate daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., the ice will be reserved for kindergartens and primary schools in Prague 2. Public skating will take place in the afternoons and throughout weekends.

On December 24 and December 31, the rinks will close at 3 p.m.

Prague 3

Prague 3 will again operate two public ice rinks.

Both are scheduled to open on November 14. One will be located in Mahlerovy sady, beneath the Žižkov Television Tower. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 50 CZK for children.

The second rink will return to the Pražačka sports complex. It will be open from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends. All-day admission will cost 120 CZK for adults and 80 CZK for children.

Skate rentals and refreshments will be available at both locations.

Prague 4

So far, one public ice rink has been confirmed in Prague 4.

The rink near the Prague Congress Centre, close to Vyšehrad metro station, is scheduled to open on November 13. It will operate from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. during weekends.

Admission will cost 120 CZK per hour for adults and 80 CZK for children. Skate rentals and refreshments will also be available.

The opening date for the public rink in Podolí has not yet been announced.

Prague 5

Residents will once again be able to skate for free at the Aréna sportu on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 13, with the official launch of the winter programme planned for the afternoon of November 20.

The venue will also host several themed events during the season, including St. Nicholas on Ice, a superhero-themed skating event and a Valentine’s Day programme.

Prague 6

Two Prague 6 locations are expected to offer outdoor skating this winter.

The rink in Ořechovka is provisionally scheduled to open around November 20, although the final date has yet to be confirmed.

At Vypich, a trial operation is expected to begin on November 27. The official opening is planned two days later and will coincide with the lighting of the local Christmas tree.

Prague 7

The ice rink on the Letná Plain is scheduled to open on November 14 and remain in operation until March 7, 2027.

It will be open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 120 CZK for children under 15.

Children under 15 who live in Prague 7 or attend school in the district will be able to skate free of charge.

Prague 8

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 8.

On November 17, rinks are scheduled to open in Libeňské podzámčí and near the Krakov Cultural Centre in Bohnice. A third location near the Ládví swimming pool is expected to open on November 20.

Further information on admission and operating hours is expected to be announced by the district.

Prague 9

The rink in Park Přátelství in Střížkov has already opened for the season.

It has been operating since November 5 and is open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Morning hours are reserved for schools, while skate rentals are available to visitors.

Another rink will open in Zahrádky Park on December 5. It will also operate daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.

On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., schools will be able to reserve the ice. Visitors will have access to skate rentals and refreshments from Café Park Zahrádky.

Prague 10

Prague 10 will again open a public ice rink in Heroldovy sady in Vršovice.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 29, 2026, and is expected to remain in operation until February. The final closing date will depend on weather conditions.

With opening dates spread throughout November and early December, Prague’s winter skating season is now gradually getting underway. Several districts are still expected to release further details, and visitors should check local announcements before heading to the rink.

World.title: St. Martin’s Day 2026 in Prague: Where to Enjoy Traditional Goose
World.content:
St. Martin’s Day, which Czechs celebrate on November 11, is a holiday of good food and drink. Autumn slowly alternates with winter, and it begins to snow.

In the past, the economic year was ending at this time, and the landowners were preparing a feast for their people as a form of thanks, when they were also paid out their wages.

St. Martin’s Day in restaurants

You can be sure that almost every restaurant around mid-November will be offering its visitors a special St. Martin’s Day menu. What does it feature?

According to a tradition that has lasted for several centuries, geese were always roasted in the autumn, fresh cabbage was processed, and wine or beer was drunk. And today’s restaurants and pubs remain faithful to these basic ingredients.

Typically, you will be served liver pâté as an appetizer, followed by a strong broth with liver dumplings and noodles, which the chefs usually leave to simmer overnight, with the main course being roast goose with red or white cabbage and dumplings.

Where to taste St. Martin’s menu?

Restaurant Salabka (November 6 – 14): Choose from 3 to 5 courses featuring seasonal autumn ingredients and contemporary gastronomy. Available from November 6, alongside the regular autumn tasting menu.

More info here.

Restaurant Obecní dům: (November 7–11): Enjoy a festive menu combining traditional roast goose with creative starters, including smoked duck and goose prosciutto carpaccio. A special St. Martin’s brunch takes place on November 8, while the restaurant’s beer hall joins the celebrations from November 9 to 15.

More info here.

Restaurant Masaryčka: Here the highlight is a tender goose leg confit with caraway, served with braised red cabbage, plums and assorted dumplings (499 CZK). Alternatively, guests can enjoy homemade potato lokše filled with pulled goose meat, onion cabbage and apples (359 CZK). To finish on a sweet note, the menu offers apple strudel with vanilla sauce, walnuts, honey and cinnamon crumble (149 CZK).

More info here

Restaurant Deer: a special four-course menu by chef Lubomír Dolejš, available until November 11. The menu features goose breast, traditional goose soup (kaldoun), confit goose leg with cabbage and bread dumplings, followed by miniature St. Martin’s pastries. The full menu costs 1,295 CZK per person, with individual dishes also available.

More info here

Le Petit Beefbar at the W Hotel: the “Made the List – Holiday 2026 Edition” program features everything from St. Martin’s goose and Advent brunches with oysters and champagne to Christmas dinners at Le Petit Beefbar au Grand Café, culminating in a New Year’s Eve celebration. Starting November 11, the restaurant will host “St. Martin’s Week,” serving slow-roasted goose with all the traditional sides during dinner service.

More info here

World.title: Prague Welcomes Tea Experts and Producers from Around the World
World.content:
Prague will welcome tea producers, experts and enthusiasts from around the world next weekend as Euro Tea Expo returns to the Czech capital for its second edition.

The two-day event, taking place on November 14 and 15, will bring together 37 exhibitors and focus on tea traditions from different parts of the world.



This year’s theme is “Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding.”

One of the main guests will be Master Lin Zhenchuan, a recognised inheritor of the traditional Fuding white tea-making techniques and founder of PINPINTEA.

Fuding white tea production is listed as part of China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage.

With more than 30 years of experience, Master Lin will introduce visitors to the craftsmanship and history behind Fuding white tea through presentations and guided tastings. Guests will also be able to compare fresh and aged white teas and learn more about the ageing process.

The programme will feature demonstrations and presentations covering several tea traditions, including a traditional Shē ethnic group white tea performance, Sichuan gaiwan tea culture and long-spout teapot demonstrations.

Visitors can also learn about Kenyan tea, Japanese hojicha, ancient tea trees in Guangxi and the connection between tea and wellbeing. Beyond tea, the programme includes Taiji sessions, a tea and Taiji performance, and a Japanese Nerikiri confectionery workshop.

Organisers say this year’s edition will also expand beyond tea. Five European vegan brands will present plant-based products and sustainable lifestyle concepts as part of the event.

The first Euro Tea Expo was held in Prague in 2025 and brought together 33 exhibitors from 15 countries, attracting around 960 visitors. The organisers say the event aims to further strengthen connections between tea producers, professionals and consumers across Europe.

Event information

Dates: November 14–15, 2026

Opening hours: 10:00–18:00

Venue: U Slavie 1540/2a, Prague 10 – Vršovice

Theme: Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding

Exhibitors: 37

World.title: Canva Closes Prague Office as More Than 1,200 Jobs Are Cut Worldwide
World.content:
Canva is shutting down its Prague office, leaving only six employees from a workforce of around 50 as part of a company-wide restructuring affecting more than 1,200 people.

According to a former employee familiar with the situation, staff first received a company-wide email from Canva CEO Melanie Perkins outlining major changes.

Around 20 minutes later, employees whose positions were being eliminated received individual notifications.



Those affected were reportedly given about a week to collect their belongings. Access to most internal work systems was cut immediately, with employees retaining access only to services such as Slack and email.

The Prague closure comes during what has been described as the largest restructuring in Canva’s history and the company’s first major round of mass layoffs.

The changes are expected to affect 1,271 employees, equivalent to roughly 22 percent of the company’s workforce.

Prague Staff Point to Structure and AI Costs

A former member of the Prague office said two factors appear to have contributed to the decision.

The first is the company’s organizational structure. Responsibilities were divided across several layers, making communication and decision-making more difficult. The problem was further complicated by the ten- to eleven-hour time difference between Central Europe and Sydney.

The second issue, according to the former employee, involves the cost of artificial intelligence.

Canva has invested heavily in AI tools and technology, initially facing significant costs associated with computing power. Over the past month, the company has begun introducing its own models, although it remains unclear how much this could reduce the cost of processing graphics and other AI-related tasks.

The company has integrated tools and services linked to platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude. At the same time, users are increasingly able to generate images, designs and other visual content directly through competing AI systems without relying on Canva’s traditional platform.

World.title: No Price Cap, No Limits: Tourist Charged CZK 8,000 for a 3 km Taxi Ride
World.content:
Prague received 70 complaints from taxi passengers during a three-week period when the city’s maximum taxi fares were temporarily not in force, according to information published by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators.

The complaints included several cases involving foreign visitors who were charged thousands of crowns for relatively short journeys. In one of the most extreme cases, a passenger paid CZK 8,096 for a 3.2-kilometre trip from Duplex Club to Na Františku Hospital.

Another passenger was charged CZK 9,955 for a journey through Prague but was reportedly unable to provide the exact route when filing a complaint. The published list of cases shows that, with one exception, the complaints involved foreign tourists.



Among the other reported fares were more than CZK 7,500 for journeys of around 15 kilometres between central Prague and Václav Havel Airport.

According to the list, a passenger travelling from the city centre to the airport paid CZK 7,560 for a 15-kilometre journey. A similar trip from Smetana Embankment cost CZK 7,554.

The issue was highlighted by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators, which asked Prague City Hall how many complaints had been submitted during the period when fare limits were not being applied.

“There were 70 in total. Some of them really did not hold back,” Štěpán Hradečný, speaking on behalf of the chamber, wrote on Facebook.

Prague City Hall confirmed that the complaints related to the period when taxi price regulation was temporarily absent.

“These complaints relate to a period when taxi price regulations were not in effect. When prices are not regulated by the city, the only regulator is the market itself,” City Hall spokesperson Vít Hofman told *Blesk*.

The situation followed the removal of Prague’s maximum taxi fare limits on September 30. According to Prague Deputy Mayor for Transport Jaromír Beránek of the Pirate Party, the move was not intended as a political decision by the city’s leadership.

Beránek said he had asked the relevant department to prepare materials for a discussion on taxi fare regulation. Instead, the preparatory process resulted in the limits being removed altogether.

The price caps remained absent until October 20, leaving a 21-day period during which taxi fares were not subject to the city’s maximum limits.

World.title: Two-Michelin-Starred Austrian Chef Comes to Prague for Exclusive Dinner
World.content:
Prague’s Zlatá Praha restaurant will host an exclusive four-hands dinner bringing together two-Michelin-starred Austrian chef Andreas Döllerer and Maroš Jambor for one evening of contemporary fine dining.

The special collaboration will see the two chefs create on November 22 a bespoke menu combining their individual culinary styles, seasonal ingredients and modern interpretations of gastronomy.



Based in Golling, Austria, Andreas Döllerer is one of the country’s most acclaimed chefs.

His restaurant, awarded two Michelin stars, is known for its distinctive approach to Alpine cuisine, which reinterprets traditional regional ingredients and culinary influences through contemporary techniques.

For the occasion in Prague, Döllerer will join forces with Maroš Jambor, creating a menu that brings together their respective approaches to fine dining.

The four-hands concept offers guests the opportunity to discover the work of both chefs through a single, specially designed dining experience.

The exclusive menu is priced at CZK 6,000 per person and includes a welcome drink and water. Guests can also opt for a wine pairing at an additional CZK 2,500 per person.

The event requires full prepayment. Reservations are available online.

World.title: American Man Suspected of Racist Assault at Prague’s Želivského Stop
World.content:
Police are investigating an alleged racist assault at the Želivského tram and metro stop in Prague’s Vinohrady district after an English-speaking man reportedly attacked a passerby and damaged his phone.

The suspect has since been identified, although police have not confirmed reports linking him to an American previously detained in Russia.

The incident took place on the morning of November 4 on Vinohradská Street, close to the Želivského stop.



According to the victim, an Arab man who has lived in the Czech Republic for several years, the confrontation began when a stranger started shouting racist remarks in public.

The man allegedly called for the deaths of Black people, Jews and Arabs.

The victim challenged the statements, telling the stranger that racist abuse and threats against people because of their background were unacceptable.

He then began recording the encounter on his mobile phone, fearing that the situation could turn violent.

“I started recording in case I was attacked—and, unfortunately, that is exactly what happened,” he later wrote in the Facebook group Vinohradská parta.

Footage of the confrontation shows the alleged attacker directing insults at the victim. At one point, he raises his phone and says, “Hello, Trump?” He also appears to threaten the other man with death before the confrontation turns physical.

The suspect then allegedly grabbed the victim’s mobile phone and threw it into the road. According to the victim, the device was struck by a passing truck. Although he managed to recover it, the phone was damaged.

The victim said he had reported the incident to the police and called on local residents to help identify the alleged attacker.

“I am dealing with this through the police, but the perpetrator has vanished. Let’s find him and show that violence and racism have no place in Vinohrady,” he wrote.

The original Facebook post containing the video was subsequently removed. The victim suggested that its disappearance might have been connected to the ongoing police investigation.

Police later confirmed that they were dealing with the case as a suspected criminal offence.

“We are handling the matter as a suspected criminal offense, and we have identified the suspect,” police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech tabloid Blesk.

Suspect reportedly linked to Russia

The investigation has also raised questions about the man’s identity.

The suspect could be an American citizen who previously faced criminal proceedings in Russia and was ordered by a Russian court to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The man was reportedly accused of assaulting a female police officer in Russia. Media reports have also suggested that he holds Czech citizenship and travelled from Russia to Prague, where he is currently staying.

However, Czech police have not confirmed whether the individual identified in connection with the Želivského incident is the same American mentioned in the Russian case.

World.title: Fake Apartments and Rental Scams Target Students in Prague, Police Warns
World.content:
Prague Police are warning about a growing number of rental fraud cases, with international students among the groups most vulnerable to fake apartment listings.

Leaving everything you know behind is the beginning of a new chapter. A new city. A new home. A new life.

After weeks of searching, you finally have the keys to your apartment in Prague. You climb the stairs of an old building, find the right door and put the key in the lock.

But it will not turn.

You try again. You check the address, look at the contract and reread your messages with the supposed landlord. Everything appears to be in order, except for one crucial detail: the apartment was never yours.

The address exists. The building is real. But the home you thought you had rented does not belong to you.



A Key That Opens No Doors

Rental scams are an increasingly common problem in Prague’s housing market, with international students among the most vulnerable targets.

Many arrive in the Czech capital without knowing the local rental system or having the opportunity to view an apartment in person. The pressure to secure accommodation before the start of the academic year can also make students more vulnerable to convincing-looking fraudulent listings.

In 2024, Czechia ranked ninth among Erasmus+ programme countries for incoming higher education mobility, with approximately 17,000 arrivals, according to Dům zahraniční spolupráce.

The growing number of international students in Prague has also increased the demand for accommodation.

Charles University, one of the city’s largest universities, has repeatedly warned prospective international students about rental fraud. According to its 2024 annual report, the university had 11,455 international students from 139 countries, out of a total student population of more than 54,000.

The university advises students to watch out for several warning signs, including requests for deposits or other payments before a contract has been signed, pressure to finalise an agreement unusually quickly, and landlords who claim to be living abroad.

Offers that appear too good to be true should also raise suspicion.

Three Cases, Nearly CZK 150,000 in Losses

Prague Police have also warned about an increasing number of rental fraud cases involving apartments.

In mid-January, three cases were reported within a single week, resulting in combined losses of nearly CZK 150,000, or approximately €6,000.

One increasingly common method involves collecting deposits from prospective tenants for apartments that are never actually rented out. In some cases, fraudsters advertise properties they do not own or have no right to rent.

Police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspect involved in the January cases may be connected to other similar incidents, meaning the number of victims could be higher.

For international students, the consequences can be particularly severe.

Police and universities therefore advise prospective tenants to verify listings carefully, avoid sending money before signing a contract and viewing the property, and remain cautious of unusually cheap offers or landlords who create pressure to pay quickly.

World.title: PM Magyar: Viktor Orbán’s brother has been detained on human-smuggling suspicion
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said that former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s brother, Áron Orbán, was detained on suspicion of human smuggling, citing press reports. However, authorities have not yet confirmed his alleged detention or the specific grounds for it.

The announcement came on Monday, after the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) carried out a joint operation in Budapest and two locations in Pest County. According to the authorities, several people were detained, and searches were conducted at multiple properties as part of two parallel criminal investigations. Further details were expected later in the day.

Magyar made the claim in a Facebook post, but did not provide further information. The Kontroll news site reported that Áron Orbán could be among those affected by the operation. The NVVH’s president, Anna Róza Unger, declined to confirm or deny reports that counter-terrorism officers had visited a property in Fótliget linked to one of Áron Orbán’s companies. She told Telex that the office had carried out further investigative measures in the case involving him and would provide more information later.

The investigation into alleged visa dealings

Áron Orbán’s name had previously emerged in an investigation into suspected abuses involving work-related residence permits for foreign nationals. According to earlier reporting by Telex, business interests linked to him may have helped Vietnamese applicants travel to Hungary. His company, Multi Shoot Zrt., reportedly enrolled Vietnamese applicants in a two-day life-saving course at the University of Pécs, which could have helped them obtain Schengen visas. The report also said that Áron Orbán had approached a government commissioner to help speed up certain visa applications.

In September, the NVVH announced that it had taken over the investigation. According to the office’s account of the suspicion, a group closely connected to senior political figures allegedly offered to secure work-related residence permits for clients in exchange for payment. The office said the case concerned suspected influence peddling and other offences.

In April, the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office reported that four people had been questioned as suspects in a related case involving the recruitment and employment of foreign workers. Two were taken into custody, with a court subsequently ordering their pre-trial detention for one month. Prosecutors said the suspects had allegedly invoked trusted connections with influential public officials while promising to arrange residence permits smoothly. They were accused of dividing €17,000 received in advance from a business owner.

The NVVH’s September announcement described the wider investigation as examining whether people with political connections had used their relationships to obtain preferential treatment in official procedures.

Viktor Orbán: I’m the target; my brother’s just a pawn

“Today, the government is due to answer to the National Security Committee regarding the spy scandal. This ‘settling of scores’ is a diversionary tactic. What is happening in Hungary is not accountability, but a settling of scores. Whenever the government faces something embarrassing, the ÁVH steps in. In this dirty game, the aim is to eliminate political opponents and establish a one-party system. I am the target; my brother is merely a pawn,” Viktor Orbán reacted on Facebook.

World.title: Fidesz support plunges in latest poll, Tisza consolidates its lead: Former governing party now “middle tier”
World.content:
Hungary’s governing Tisza Party has strengthened its position in the latest Medián opinion poll, while support for opposition Fidesz has fallen sharply. The survey, conducted in early November, puts Tisza at 55% among the entire population, compared with just 16% for Viktor Orbán’s party.

According to results reported by HVG and covered by Telex, the gap is even wider among certain voter groups. Among decided voters who say they are certain to vote, Tisza leads Fidesz by 68% to 20%.

Compared with Medián’s September survey, Tisza gained one percentage point among the entire population, three points among voters with a party preference and four points among decided voters certain to cast a ballot.

Fidesz, meanwhile, lost six percentage points among both the entire population and voters with a party preference, and seven points among certain voters.

The party reportedly suffered its biggest losses among people with lower levels of education, Budapest residents, men and those aged 50–64.

Mi Hazánk also benefits from Fidesz’s decline

Not all of Fidesz’s lost support appears to have shifted to Tisza. The opposition Mi Hazánk party has also gained ground, while the number of undecided voters has increased.

Mi Hazánk now stands at 9% among the entire population and 11% among both voters with a party preference and those certain to vote.

Political analyst Gábor Török commented on the figures, saying that Fidesz and Mi Hazánk had, for the first time, entered the same league. He described both as parties of the political middle tier, following Mi Hazánk’s rise and Fidesz’s decline.

Did you read this? Tisza keeps a firm grip on the lead as Hungarians give economic policy a thumbs-down

Most Hungarians say the country is heading in the right direction

The survey also asked respondents how they viewed the overall direction of the country. A clear majority, 59%, said things were fundamentally moving in the right direction, while 32% believed Hungary was heading in the wrong direction.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar also reacted to the findings. He said Fidesz, which he described as Viktor Orbán’s once-dominant party, had fallen to a level of support not seen in 30 years. Magyar added that, if an election were held today, Tisza would win all 106 individual parliamentary constituencies.

“Thank you for your tremendous trust! We shall continue on the path of political transition, working towards a Hungary that functions effectively and treats its people with humanity,” he wrote. “Just as a point of interest, I would like to point out that TISZA was in a better position in April 2024, when we took over the party and the first survey was carried out, than Fidesz is now,” he added.

World.title: Wizz Air sued by pilots and cabin crew – Cases could affect all Hungarian workers
World.content:
Wizz Air is facing two separate lawsuits brought by its pilots and cabin crew over the calculation of their pay during annual leave and sick leave. The cases have now reached Hungary’s Constitutional Court, as the Budapest Court of Appeal has raised concerns that the relevant labour legislation itself may violate the Constitution or international agreements.

According to documents obtained by 24.hu, the Budapest-Capital Regional Court ruled in favour of the employees in both cases at first instance, ordering the airline to pay the outstanding amounts and late-payment interest. Wizz Air appealed both decisions. The Court of Appeal subsequently suspended the proceedings and referred the legal questions to the Constitutional Court.

The stakes extend beyond the airline, as a ruling could have implications for employers and employees across Hungary.

HUF 73.5 million in disputed payments

The first lawsuit was brought by 12 Wizz Air pilots, who are seeking nearly HUF 67 million (approx. EUR 184,600) in gross outstanding absence pay, plus interest. They argue that between 1 August 2021 and 31 December 2023, the airline calculated their holiday pay at a significantly lower rate than their remuneration for days actually worked.

A separate case involves seven cabin crew members, who are claiming approximately HUF 6.5 million (approx. EUR 17,900) in gross outstanding payments, plus interest, over the calculation of their pay during annual and sick leave.

The disputes concern távolléti díj, the Hungarian legal concept of absence pay. It is intended to ensure that employees receive appropriate remuneration when they are away from work for legally recognised reasons. However, the calculation of this payment under the current rules may exclude certain components of an employee’s usual earnings.

The cases cover the period from 2021 to 2023 because, according to court documents cited by HVG, Wizz Air changed its calculation practice from 1 January 2024, when it began including the disputed pay components for both groups of employees.

Why the Constitutional Court’s decision matters

The Budapest Court of Appeal believes the issue may not be limited to Wizz Air employees. Under the current Labour Code, certain elements of a worker’s remuneration may not be taken into account when calculating absence pay, even if they make up a substantial part of their usual earnings.

This could mean that employees receive considerably less money when they take their legally protected time off. The court has therefore questioned whether the relevant provisions are compatible with constitutional requirements and international agreements.

If the Constitutional Court finds that the rules are unlawful, the consequences could extend to the wider Hungarian labour market, potentially affecting how employers calculate holiday and sick-leave payments.

World.title: Main railway line upgrade reaches busy Budapest station – Speed restrictions to be lifted
World.content:
Renovation work on one of Hungary’s busiest railway lines has reached Kőbánya-Kispest station, where tracks and platform canopies are being upgraded. The works are also expected to remove several existing speed restrictions, helping to shorten journey times and reduce delays.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced on Sunday that MÁV specialists would work at the station between 4 November and 1 December as part of a maintenance programme launched in the summer on the Budapest–Cegléd railway line, also known as line 100a. Earlier stages covered the section between Pilis and Albertirsa stations, as well as Albertirsa station itself.

According to the minister, nearly 80 railway workers and heavy machinery are involved in the project. The fourth and fifth tracks at Kőbánya-Kispest are being rebuilt, while new track switches, connecting track sections and a level crossing are also being constructed.

The works require around 6,000 tonnes of crushed stone, the movement or replacement of several hundred metres of rails and the installation of 1,250 reinforced concrete sleepers. The station’s platform canopies are also being renovated.

Faster trains expected after the works

One of the main benefits for passengers will be the removal of speed restrictions on four shorter sections of the line. Trains currently have to slow down to 20 or 40 km/h in these areas because of track conditions.

The original permitted track speed of 80 km/h is expected to be restored during follow-up track adjustment works scheduled for 10–13 December, Vitézy said. This should mean shorter journey times and fewer delays caused by infrastructure problems.

The minister stressed that introducing new trains alone is not enough to improve railway services: the tracks themselves also need proper maintenance.

Timetable changes affect Budapest commuters

Passengers should be aware that the construction work is temporarily affecting train schedules. According to HVG, the Tokaj and Nyírség InterCity services have returned to their usual routes, but several other InterCity trains leave Budapest’s Nyugati railway station eight minutes earlier than before.

Suburban services are also operating according to modified timetables, while replacement buses are running instead of some late-night and early-morning trains. Special timetables apply on 21–22 November and 28–29 November.

Vitézy advised passengers to check their journeys in the MÁVPlusz app before setting off. He also thanked local residents for their patience, particularly because some of the construction work takes place at night.

World.title: Man who doused Hungary’s PM with wine at festival apologises – Here’s how Magyar reacted
World.content:
The man who poured wine over Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar at a festival in Szekszárd in September has apologised in a letter. Magyar confirmed on Sunday that he had received the apology and said he considered the matter closed, adding that he would not initiate legal proceedings.

The prime minister shared the letter on social media, along with a brief response thanking the man for the gesture. The letter, dated 25 September, acknowledges that the incident was wrong and that the writer takes responsibility for his actions.

“Looking back on what happened, I realise that my actions were unworthy both on a human level, towards you personally, and of the basic respect that people should show one another in public life,” the man wrote.

He also said that disagreements and the emotions they can provoke should only be expressed in a civil and respectful manner. In the letter, he apologised for creating an unpleasant situation and disturbing the prime minister’s peace.

Magyar responded: “Thank you for the gesture. As far as I am concerned, the matter is closed; I will not initiate proceedings. Go, Szekszárd!”

What happened at the Szekszárd festival?

The incident took place on 19 September, during the Szekszárd Harvest Festival. Magyar had stopped at the event while travelling home from a campaign visit to Pécs.

According to reports and footage of the incident, the prime minister was standing at a food stall when a man approached from a short distance and threw the contents of his wine glass over him. Security staff subsequently escorted the man away from the scene.

Magyar commented on the incident shortly afterwards, suggesting that the man had been bothered by the cheerful atmosphere but had not been brave enough to confront him face to face.

The man’s wife later told Hungarian media that her husband felt bad about what had happened. The apology now published by Magyar formally acknowledges responsibility for the incident, while the prime minister’s response indicates that he does not intend to take the matter further.

World.title: Budapest apartment gutted by fire, 15 residents evacuated from smoke-filled building
World.content:
A flat was gutted by fire in a four-storey residential building in Budapest’s District III on Sunday, filling the entire building with smoke. Firefighters evacuated 15 residents, including some who had to be brought outside using rescue masks.

According to the National Directorate General for Disaster Management, the fire broke out in a flat on Pozsonyi Street. Budapest’s professional firefighters arrived at the scene in large numbers and extinguished the flames using water jets.

Under the direction of the disaster management operations service, firefighters also dealt with remaining hot spots and inspected and cooled the building’s external façade and roof.

Residents evacuated, gas supply suspended in five flats

Fifteen people were evacuated from the building. Some residents were taken outside wearing rescue masks, while an ambulance was also dispatched to the scene.

A heated emergency bus was provided for residents while the situation was being dealt with. Gas utility specialists inspected the building, but the gas supply was not restored to five flats.

The local municipality is arranging temporary accommodation for the owner of the flat affected by the fire, while eight other residents are making their own arrangements for temporary housing.

The disaster management authority shared footage of the incident on its social media page, showing the emergency response in the residential area.

Fatal fire in Budapest in October

According to a report by Origo, a fatal fire broke out almost two weeks ago on Szeréna Road in District II: the 80-square-metre property was completely engulfed in flames by the time emergency services arrived at the scene. The body of the doctor who lived there was found inside the flat.

World.title: Hungarian defence minister’s warning: European plane bomb threats could be coordinated
World.content:
Hungary’s Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi has warned that the recent wave of bomb threats targeting passenger aircraft across Europe could be part of a coordinated campaign aimed at disrupting air travel and testing security systems. He also explained why Hungarian Gripen fighter jets are scrambled during such incidents and under what circumstances they could use weapons.

In a Facebook post on Sunday, the minister pointed to the unusual frequency, geographical spread and timing of the threats. On one recent day, Hungarian authorities ordered three separate alerts within a few hours, while similar incidents were reported in other European countries.

According to Ruszin-Szendi, the pattern raises the possibility of coordinated action. If that is the case, the objective may not necessarily be to cause direct physical damage, but rather to disrupt European aviation, create uncertainty and undermine public confidence, while testing how quickly national and allied security systems respond.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Why are Hungarian Gripens scrambled?

The minister stressed that the role of the Hungarian Air Force’s JAS-39 Gripen fighter jets goes beyond simply escorting threatened passenger aircraft.

Their tasks include identifying the aircraft, checking its position and monitoring its movements. This can be particularly important if a plane unexpectedly deviates from its declared route, fails to follow air traffic control instructions or behaves in a way that could pose a threat to the population or critical infrastructure.

Ruszin-Szendi also highlighted that the Gripens are armed combat aircraft. Under the appropriate legal and military conditions, and with the necessary authorisation, they can use force against an immediate threat from the air.

However, he emphasised that a bomb threat or an unexpected change of flight path alone does not justify the use of weapons. Any such decision is subject to strict legal, operational and command requirements.

More details: Hungarian Gripen jets scrambled 3 times over bomb threats to passenger planes

The security lessons of 11 September

To explain why such capabilities are necessary, the minister referred to the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States, when hijacked passenger aircraft were used as weapons. The attacks demonstrated how a civilian plane could become a serious threat to human lives and national security.

Ruszin-Szendi said Hungary maintains continuous air defence readiness as part of NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defence System. Hungarian Gripen pilots and the military personnel supporting them remain on standby around the clock to protect the country’s airspace.

He described the fighter jets’ take-offs not as a show of force, but as evidence of a defence capability that operates continuously and can respond when an aircraft presents a potential threat.

The minister also stressed the importance of rapid decision-making, preparedness and cooperation with NATO allies in responding to both conventional military threats and more difficult-to-identify hybrid challenges.

World.title: Hungary expands energy cooperation with Poland and Czechia in new regional agreement
World.content:
Hungary has expanded its regional energy cooperation with Poland and Czechia, which have joined a broader coalition involving Italy and several Central and Southern European countries. The agreement was signed in Zagreb, where energy ministers also discussed access to Black Sea natural gas, supply diversification and Hungary’s planned green energy investments.

Hungary’s Minister of Economy and Energy, István Kapitány, announced the development in a Facebook video on Sunday. According to his statement, the discussions focused on strengthening energy security by giving participating countries access to more supply sources and transport routes.

The expanded cooperation brings two more members of the Visegrád Group (V4) into the initiative. Poland and Czechia join Hungary, Croatia, Romania and Italy in a regional framework intended to improve energy market integration.

One of the key topics was diversifying gas procurement routes. Hungary aims to work more closely with Croatia and Romania to secure access to alternative energy sources, including natural gas extracted in the Black Sea region.

“Our goal is for Hungary to obtain energy from an increasing number of sources, safely and at affordable prices,” Kapitány said.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Hungary eyes Black Sea gas supplies

During the meeting in Zagreb, Kapitány also held separate talks with Romania’s new energy minister. The two sides reviewed how Hungary could play a more active role in purchasing natural gas produced in the Black Sea and facilitating its transport to the region.

The Black Sea is expected to become an increasingly important source of natural gas for Central and South-Eastern Europe as new production projects are developed. However, access to these supplies also depends on available infrastructure, transport capacity and agreements between the countries involved.

Kapitány described his discussion with his Romanian counterpart as constructive and said the two ministers would continue their talks in Bucharest in two weeks.

The Zagreb meeting also covered Hungary’s major energy development projects, particularly its efforts to expand green energy capacity.

For Hungary, closer cooperation with neighbouring countries could help diversify its energy imports and reduce reliance on individual supply routes. This agreement shows a stronger regional approach, although its practical impact will depend on the projects and supply arrangements that follow.

World.title: Polish Mass Shooter Dies of Injuries; Motive Remains Unclear
World.content:
A gunman who killed six people in Krakow and injured many more has died of his injuries in hospital, Polish police said on Monday, as prosecutors continue investigating Saturday’s mass shooting in Krakow in an attempt to establish what motivated the 24-year-old.

The shooter, identified in the foreign press as Michal Oksinski, killed six people in the southern Polish city and is believed to have murdered three family members earlier that day. Investigators said on Sunday they had found no letter or other document explaining the Polish man’s actions, either on him or in his car.

“We’ll see what the examination of his phone and electronic devices seized from his family home reveals,” prosecutor Eryk Stasielak said. Justice Minister and Prosecutor General Waldemar Zurek added that investigators had obtained “certain symbols associated with the suspect” and “some evidence that sheds more light on this whole tragedy”, but declined to elaborate, citing ongoing investigation.

At an evening press conference on Saturday, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that, according to preliminary findings, the gunmen had acted alone, held “very, very radical views” and was “fascinated by far-right ideologies”. Prosecutors, however, said on Sunday that searches had uncovered no evidence of active political or extremist involvement. Kierwinski’s remarks drew criticism from right-wing lawmakers, and on Sunday he clarified that the motive was still under investigation.

The attack, Poland’s deadliest mass shooting since World War II, took place shortly after 15:00 on Saturday, when the gunman drove onto Krakow’s historic Main Market Square, normally closed to traffic, and opened fire on pedestrians from his car. Wearing a bulletproof vest, military-style helmet and tactical equipment, he sent people fleeing into nearby restaurants, cafés and building entrances.

The six fatalities were: three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, a Polish man of about 50, a 32-year-old British citizen and a 51-year-old Austrian woman. Fifteen others were wounded, including five foreign nationals from Austria, Portugal, Germany, Britain and Russia.

Police responded within minutes. The first emergency call came at 15:00, with municipal guards arriving within two minutes and police firing their first shots at the attacker by 15:03. Officers exchanged fire with the shooter before disabling him. Two policemen were wounded in the exchange, and one remained in serious condition on Sunday, although officials said his health had improved. Both are being hailed in Poland as heroes.

“In the face of the tragedy in Krakow, we saw the best in people: the courage of police officers, the dedication of paramedics and the selfless help of ordinary people who rushed to save others,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X.

Family killings and firearms

Following the attack, police discovered three bodies at the shooter’s family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski: his parents and 21-year-old sister Magdalena, who studied painting at Krakow’s Academy of Fine Arts and had returned home for the weekend. Investigators believe he killed them before driving more than 160 kilometres to Krakow in his father’s car. Two family cats were also shot dead.

The gunman worked as a turner at a local refractory materials plant, had no criminal record and was not known to the police. He held a valid firearms license and used a civilian version of an AR-15 rifle in the Krakow attack.

His father, a sport-shooting enthusiast, was also a licensed gun owner. Between them, father and son held permits for 11 firearms. Investigators are examining which weapons were used in the attacks. Authorities believe the gunman acted alone.

Mass shootings are exceptionally rare in Poland, and Saturday’s killings were unprecedented in scale in the country’s postwar history. Other recent attacks were of political background and include the 2010 shooting at a Law and Justice party office in Lodz, which left one person dead, and the fatal stabbing of Gdansk mayor Pawel Adamowicz at a charity event in 2019.

The Krakow attack follows three unrelated stabbing incidents at schools across Poland, which took place within the space of one week in October. It also comes amid growing civilian gun ownership, with registered firearms more than doubling over the past decade to exceed 400,000 in 2025. A report published in May by Poland’s Supreme Audit Office (NIK) warned of serious gaps in firearms oversight, including the absence of mandatory periodic medical and psychological assessments for people holding sporting, hunting and collecting licences, which are generally issued indefinitely.

Poland declared two days of national mourning on Sunday and Monday. In Krakow, the hejnal – the trumpet call played every hour from the tower of St Mary’s Basilica at the Main Square, which is one of the symbols of the city – fell silent for the first time in 87 years.
