World.title: Bye-Bye Serbia’s SPS, the Socialists Who Weren’t
World.content:
There are two untrue things one might have said about the Socialist Party of Serbia: that it was socialist, and that it was a party.

The founding of the SPS was auspicious: it inherited from the League of Communists of Serbia a large membership, considerable property, and formal and informal control of nearly every institution in the state.

Born as a party of power, it held nearly absolute power until it was removed in 2000, and acted like a party of [secondary] power afterwards.

If we want to talk about the SPS’s ideas, it never had many; the party was happy to parrot some slogans from the state socialist period to satisfy a part of its electoral base, and [like other parties in Serbia], to borrow most of its programme from Vojislav Seselj’s Serbian Radical Party, SRS, to [de]mobilise the rest.

What it had instead was a structure that became the foundation for how power would be exercised in Serbia in the coming decades: privatise public property to your wealthier supporters and hire the rest; marginalise alternatives while promoting fear; and maintain control over the media, the police and intelligence services, and the grey economy.

World.title: Kosovo Fortress Faces Uncertain Future After Flawed UNESCO Restoration
World.content:
A herd of unattended goats grazes freely beneath the walls of the fortress of Novoberde/Novo Brdo. One of Kosovo’s best-known cultural heritage sites, the fortress has been closed to visitors for more than eight years after its walls began to collapse less than two years after a major UNESCO-led renovation project.

Last month, shortly after approving a conservation project for the fortress, Kosovo’s Ministry of Culture took “emergency measures” to secure the medieval fortress and prevent further collapse.

Novoberde/Novo Brdo, 35 kilometres southeast of Pristina, was established near silver and gold mines in the medieval period. Mining and trade connected it to other regions, transforming it into an economic and commercial hub that drew Saxon miners and spurred the construction of the significant fortress.

World.title: ‘We Could Have Waited’: Caesareans the Norm for Pregnant Women in Greece
World.content:
Ioanna Vasilaki, an independent midwife and president of the Association of Independent Midwives of Greece, EAMME, said doctors will sometimes suggest inducing labour so the baby can be delivered during his or her shift. Often this ends in a C-section.

A third of respondents said their labour was induced; a quarter of these women said they were not told why.

Half who underwent C-sections said it was conducted as an emergency procedure.

Gourounti said it was “quite strange that when you go to give birth, one in two women ends up having some kind of difficulty or medical issue that arises during labour, necessitating an emergency C-section”.

According to Giorgos Daskalakis, professor of obstetrics and gynaecology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and director of the first obstetrics and gynaecology clinic at the public Alexandra Hospital, some doctors in public hospitals outside Greece’s main urban centres work too many shifts, “so it is extremely difficult for them to spend too much time performing normal deliveries on women”.

Midwives say that often epidurals are not provided to women giving birth vaginally because there aren’t enough anaesthesiologists in Greece.

According to a report in the Greek newspaper Kathimerini in 2024, there are roughly 1,000 anaesthesiologists in Greece. The Hellenic Society of Anaesthesiology puts the figure at 750, in a country of some 10.5 million people. That’s far fewer than global healthcare bodies recommend.

“If you pay,” said Kentrifylli, “if you find a hospital doctor and they see you privately in their office and take you to the emergency room without it being time for you to give birth and put you in a labour induction position, then you will have the option of an epidural.”

Daskalakis said that issues with the legal framework in the event of alleged malpractice are also driving doctors to err on the side of caution by recommending C-sections.

“Consequently, every time a complication arises, the simple question asked is: ‘If a C-section had been performed, would things have turned out differently? Would it have been better?’ And the inevitable answer is that a caesarean section would obviously have led to a better obstetric outcome. Terrified of legal repercussions, doctors are highly susceptible to performing a C-section just to get through the process easily.”

In mid-2024, a law was passed allowing for the creation of Natural Birth Centres within public hospitals and independent institutions, where midwives would oversee deliveries. Amid what midwives say is resistance from obstetricians, no such centre has been opened in the public health system. One private centre was opened, but it closed in January this year, citing financial constraints.

Daskalakis is not enthusiastic about such birth centres. Instead, to encourage natural childbirth, he says staffing should be approved, uniform protocols introduced, and public awareness raised.

Financial incentives?

Daskalakis also argues for bonuses for hospitals that cut their own rate of C-sections.

“The money won’t go into someone’s pocket,” he said. “It will go to the hospital, which will automatically have an incentive to monitor the process because it will receive a bonus.”

Mouzalas, however, said the way a birth is handled should have nothing to do with “economic or ideological” considerations. “It should be related exclusively to scientific reasons”.

In 2017, the WHO proposed the use of the Robson classification as the global standard for assessing and comparing C-section rates across healthcare facilities.

The Robson classification was applied for the first time in 2019 by scientists in Greece to identify trends in caesarean births by examining 8,572 women in a private health facility. Just under 61 per cent of births were caesareans, 34.6 per cent were induced, and 30.7 per cent were births after a previous C-section.

However, in Greece, there is a complete absence of any oversight mechanism for C-sections.

“There is no system in place to require every hospital and every physician to provide a substantiated explanation as to why they deemed a C-section necessary,” said Gourounti, who expressed doubts regarding the widespread application of the Robson classification system in Greece.

“Each hospital and each doctor must provide a substantiated explanation as to why they deemed the choice of a caesarean section necessary,” she said.

Professor Athanasiadis told BIRN that the Robson classification is used in all Obstetrics and Gynaecology departments of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, as well as at the Aretaieion and Alexandra public hospitals in Athens, though he stressed he cannot speak for all Ob-Gyn departments across Greece.

According to him, the Robson classification serves as an “internal audit” tool that helps refine clinical practice and reduce unnecessary C-sections. He also underlined that the Robson system can be implemented in public hospitals, but not in private ones, which do not have a departmental structure but instead rely on collaborating private physicians.

The role of the midwife

World.title: Week in Review: Between Hope and Apathy
World.content:
Bulgaria has a newly elected president – government-backed candidate Iliana Iotova. In the November 1 run-off for the presidency, she won 57.6 per cent of the votes cast to her challenger Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 per cent.

Yet unlike their neighbours in Serbia, who voted in record numbers in recent elections, Bulgarians voted in record low numbers. Only 29.1 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots in the run-off, slightly more than in the first round. Our analysis looks at why many Bulgarians are tuning out of politics altogether.

World.title: With Change of Power, Serbia Can Reinvigorate EU Accession Bid
World.content:
“Catastrophic” - that’s how Dragana Djurica describes the current state of Serbia’s European Union accession process.

On Wednesday, the bloc’s executive arm, the European Commission, delivered its annual assessment of the progress made - or not - by countries bidding for membership. One of the main takeaways was the substantial progress made by Montenegro; another was the dramatic backsliding by Serbia.

“This is not a progress report, as it is officially called, but a report on backsliding,” said Djurica, head of the European Movement in Serbia, an NGO that advocates for Serbia’s EU integration.

“It is one of the most critical, and I would even say the worst, reports Serbia has received from the European Commission since the start of accession negotiations.”

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
As is traditional, a Remembrance Sunday service was held at the Commonwealth War Graves cemetery in Bulgaria’s city of Plovdiv on November 8.

Remembrance Sunday, held annually on the Sunday closest to Remembrance Day on November 11, commemorates and honours the dead in the wars of the 20th century. The November 11 date arises from the anniversary of the Armistice at the close of the First World War.

In Plovdiv, the service was led by British ambassador Nathaniel Copsey and Father Patrick Irwin, and attended by military veterans from Britain and the Commonwealth, as well as members of the public.

The Lesson was read by Lieutenant Colonel Matthew Walker, and 10-year-old Charles Copsey delivered the Exhortation:

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old,

Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn.

At the going down of the sun, and in the morning,

We will remember them.”

(Photos: Clive Leviev-Sawyer)

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
Hundreds of bags of red pepper have washed up on the beach near the village of Sinemorets on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, Tsarevo municipality’s mayor Marin Kirov said on November 8.

Officials from the Regional Inspectorate for Environment Protection and Water in Bourgas and the Basin Directorate are taking samples of the sea water near Sinemorets to determine if there is any pollution.

According to the Bourgas district administration, the cargo was likely transported in a shipping container that opened at sea and currents carried the sacks to shore.

The incident also follows recent incidents of drones sinking or severely damaging merchant ships off Bulgaria’s coast, in attacks widely blamed on Russia.

The results of the checks on the sea water are expected next week. However, reaching the beach is a serious challenge for the inspectors themselves, as they have to walk nearly two kilometres through difficult terrain.

Kirov, in a post on Facebook, said that although though the beaches are exclusive state property, “we fully recognise the gravity of the situation regarding the hundreds of sacks of red pepper found on an undeveloped beach in Sinemorets”.

He said that the municipality was in constant contact with the district governor, and would assist in the cleanup of the beach.

“Naturally, I would like to make a point: such incidents are likely to become more frequent, and a formal mechanism for cleaning the coastline needs to be established,” Kirov said.

“Should this recur—given that the sea frequently washes various types of cargo onto our beaches and rocky shores—the state must allocate funds to the Bourgas district administration to cover these cleanup operations,” he said.

(Photo via Kirov’s Facebook page)

World.title: Bulgarian Navy team destroys Russian drone found near Shabla
World.content:
A Bulgarian Navy team destroyed on November 6 a drone – identified as a Russian Gerber-2 – that had been found near Shabla on Bulgaria’s northern Black Sea coast, according to a statement by the Defence Ministry.

At 10am, a signal was sent by the operational duty officer of the Ministry of Interior about the presence of a drone in the area of the beach north of the lighthouse on Cape Shabla, the ministry said.

A specialist team from Varna Naval Base established that the aerial drone probably fell into the sea and was subsequently thrown ashore.

According to the Defence Ministry, there were no inscriptions on its hull and it was classified as a Russian Gerber – 2. This contradicts earlier media reports that the drone was marked as a Shahel, a type that is of Iranian manufacture and which is used by Russia.

The drone was destroyed on site, with strict observance of all safety measures. It was established that it did not carry an explosive, the Defence Ministry said.

The incident is the latest of more than 100 in which drones or parts of drones have been found in Bulgarian waters or on beaches since the beginning of 2026, against the backdrop of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

(Photo: Ministry of Defence)

World.title: Two aircraft land at Sofia Airport following latest bomb threats – report
World.content:
Two civilian aircraft that were travelling from London and Brussels landed at Vassil Levski Sofia Airport on November 6 following e-mailed bomb threats, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) said, citing the Transport Ministry.

The aircraft were checked by Border Police teams and no explosive devices were found, BNT said.

The planes landed without any problems.

This is the latest of a succession of disruptions of flights in Europe because of e-mailed bomb threats. On November 5, three aircraft that were the subject of bomb threats landed at Bulgarian airports – two in Sofia and one in Plovdiv.

Director of Air Traffic Management Ivan Dyaksov told Nova Televizia on November 6 that the e-mails were sent by “unknown organisations” whose goal is to sow discord.

There have been at least 24 such cases across Europe in the past week,” Dyaksov said.

National security expert Colonel Assen Peychev told Nova TV: “There are two countries in the world that have an interest in destabilising Europe – Russia and Iran”.

“They aim to both drain resources and test how Nato countries react,” cybersecurity expert Lyubomir Tulev said.

(Photo: Sofia Airport)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Dr. Konstantin Trenchev, founder and honorary president of the Podkrepa labour confederation, has died at the age of 71 after a short illness, Podkrepa said on November 6.

“There are individuals whose names remain inextricably linked to a certain historical era,” Podkrepa said.

“For the Bulgarian independent trade union movement and the democratic changes after 1989, this name is Dr. Konstantin Trenchev.”

A doctor by profession, a public figure, a dissident by conviction and a leader by vocation, Trenchev was the man who, in 1989, laid the foundation for the first independent trade union in Bulgaria – Podkrepa, the statement said.

At a time when free association was impossible and the protection of human and labour rights was subordinated to state power, he chose the most difficult path – to oppose the system and give hope that free trade unionism was possible, it said.

The creation of Podkrepa was not simply the establishment of a new organisation, the labour confederation said. “It is an act of civic courage and protection of the dignity of Bulgarian workers”.

Because of this activity, Dr. Trenchev was subjected to repression, was arrested and spent several months as a political prisoner.

“Instead of being crushed, he became one of the symbols of the struggle for democracy, freedom of speech and the right to independent trade union association.”

After the fall of the communist regime, he became one of the founders of the Union of Democratic Forces and participated in the processes of democratic transition in the country, including in the National Round Table between the ruling party and the opposition.

After the democratic changes, Trenchev devoted more than a quarter of a century to building Podkrepa.

Thanks to his efforts, Podkrepa became the first Bulgarian trade union organisation accepted into the international and European trade union family.

He was the first Bulgarian elected as Vice-President of the European Trade Union Confederation, as well as as Vice-President of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions – “a recognition not only of his personal authority, but also of Bulgaria’s place in the European social dialogue”.

In 2015, after 26 years at the helm of Podkrepa, he handed over the leadership to the next generation of trade union leaders and was elected honorary president of the confederation – recognition for his exceptional contribution to the development of the organization and the Bulgarian trade union movement, Podkrepa said.

(Photos via the Podkrepa website)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Bulgaria had the third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in the European Union in September 2026, according to figures released on November 6 by EU statistics agency Eurostat.

Among EU member states for which data are available, the highest annual increases in the total retail trade volume were recorded in Cyprus (7.6 per cent), Sweden (6.9 per cent) and Bulgaria (5.7 per cent).

The largest decreases were observed in Germany (-2.4 per cent), Romania (-2.3 per cent) and Spain (-1.5 per cent).

In September 2026, compared with September 2025, the calendar adjusted retail sales index increased by 0.4 per cent in the euro area and by 0.9 per cent in the EU, Eurostat said.

(Photo: Ngaulin)

World.title: NSI poll: Consumer confidence in Bulgaria plummets
World.content:
A regular three-monthly poll by the National Statistical Institute (NSI), the results of which were released on November 6, shows that consumer confidence in Bulgaria has dropped by 6.9 percentage points.

The NSI found it to be slightly down in February. This was followed by a downturn in May, then an improvement in the poll reported in August.

In October 2026, there was decreased confidence among both urban and rural dwellers, by 5.3 and 11 percentage points, respectively, the NSI said.

Those polled were more pessimistic in their views of the economic situation in Bulgaria over the past 12 months and the coming 12 months.

Compared to July, their assessments and expectations about the changes in the financial situation of their households were also more negative.

In October, consumers’ assessments about the change of consumer prices over the past 12 months were more unfavourable. However, inflation expectations over the next 12 months were less intense, the NSI said.

While overall expectations were that unemployment in Bulgaria would slightly decrease over the coming 12 months, those living in cities expected that it would increase.

Most consumers saw the current economic situation in Bulgaria as unfavourable for savings.

Their attitude regarding intensions of spending on major purchases of durable goods and home improvements over the next 12 months was also negative, the NSI said.

World.title: Bulgarian sculptor and former Speaker of Parliament Vezhdi Rashidov dies
World.content:
Renowned sculptor and former Speaker of Bulgaria’s National Assembly Vezhdi Rashidov has died at the age of 74, it was confirmed on November 6.

Rashidov was born on December 14 1951 in Dimitrovgrad.

In 1970, he graduated from the Iliya Petrov Art School of Fine Arts in Sofia, and in 1978, he graduated from the Sculpture Department at the National Academy of Arts in Sofia.

From 1978, Rashidov participated in national and international exhibitions, biennials and symposiums.

He presented his works at the International Sculpture Biennale in Ravenna and the World Art Fair in Basel.

Among his solo exhibitions are those at Unesco in Paris in 1989, in Tokyo in 1992 and at the Oscar Wilde Museum in Dublin in 2006. In addition to sculptures, he exhibited drawings and watercolours.

Among his awards are the Vatican’s Dante Alighieri Gold Medal in 1981, the first prize at the International Biennial of Humor and Satire in Gabrovo in 1983, and the Vera grand prize for sculpture at the “Traditions and Modernity” International Festival in Moscow in 2009.

Rashidov was awarded the Order of the Stara Planina with Ribbon and is a Corresponding Member of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. He was an honorary citizen of Sofia, Dimitrovgrad, and Kurdzhali, among other cities. His works are held in Bulgarian galleries and in collections abroad, including the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, the Pushkin Museum in Moscow, and the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

Rashidov was Minister of Culture in the first and second Boiko Borissov governments. He held the post from July 27 2009 to March 13 2013 and from November 7 2014 to January 27 2017.

Rashidov was a member of parliament in seven parliaments. On October 21 2022, he was elected Speaker of the 48th National Assembly and held the position until the end of his term in February 2023.

In the 49th National Assembly, he was an MP from Borissov’s GERB-UDF. On September 1 2023, his resignation was approved by Parliament.

World.title: Research: Vučić Falling is More Important Than Price Increases and Protests for Croatia
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Research has discovered that Aleksandar Vučić falling in Serbia is more important than the price increases and protests within Croatia.

The defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the elections over in Serbia was the most important topic for Croatians in the past month, ahead of inflation and price increases, shows the new CRO Demoskop. Index reports that the defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the parliamentary elections in Serbia was declared the most important topic of the past month by 21.9 percent of respondents. Inflation and price increases took second place with 14.3 percent, while street protests in several European cities were singled out by 12.4 percent of citizens.

The death of Goran Bare and Mišo Kovač was an important topic for 11.9 percent of respondents. The Nazi rampage by part of Torcida fans, arrests and threats to journalists was singled out by 9.9 percent. Problems with the remediation of illegal waste in Gospić and protests against the incineration of waste in Koromačno received 4.7 and 4.4 percent respectively.

If elections had been held at the beginning of November, HDZ would have won 24.9 percent of the votes, and SDP 17.5 percent. HDZ fell by 0.1 percentage points compared to October, while SDP lost two points and recorded the lowest support in the current term. In the last year support for HDZ has fallen by five, and for SDP by six percentage points.

This is at the same time HDZ’s weakest result since Andrej Plenković began his third premiership in April 2024. Among the four leading parties support in one month fell by a total of 2.7 percentage points, and around three quarters of that drop falls on SDP. Možemo is in third place with 13.6 percent, and Most in fourth with 9.4 percent. Those parties also recorded a slight drop, by 0.2 and 0.4 percentage points respectively. Undecided voters stand at 18.8 percent, compared to 15.6 percent in October. The research was conducted by the agency Promocija plus on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The sampling error for party ratings is ±3.53 percentage points, with a confidence level of 95 percent. The data source is CRO Demoskop for RTL.

World.title: Will New Dawn in Serbia Result in a Change of Relations With Croatia?
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Will the new dawn in Serbia after the removal of Aleksandar Vučić finally result in a long-awaited change of relations with Croatia?

The fact that a new group of people with fresh policies will finally lead Serbia does not necessarily mean that it will totally abandon its old, poisonous national priorities. Zlatko Crncec reports for Novi list that the new political ruling elite in Serbia is encouragingly announcing a radical break with the foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. However, as in everything else, much, if not almost everything, remains rather unclear.

Both when it comes to who will make up the future Serbian Government, and what exact policy they will pursue. Because the fact that a new team is coming to the head of Serbia does not necessarily mean that it could abandon old national priorities. Between good-neighbourly relations, the protection of Serbs in the region, the constitutional issue of Kosovo and the attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, space opens up for serious political uncertainties.

It is still not clear whether the victory of the Student List “Students are Winning” also means a real change in Serbia’s attitude towards neighbouring countries. Or will only the way in which the previous national and foreign policy goals are presented to the public change?

neighbourly relations…

This is especially important for Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Kosovo. These are the countries towards which Aleksandar Vučić’s policy, in various forms and intensities, has for years been burdened by unresolved issues from the past, national pretensions, the instrumentalisation of the position of Serbian communities and occasional political crises. The programme of the list and the public appearances of its leader Ilija Srdanović point to several important conclusions. First, the new political structure wants to distance itself from the personalised foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. Second, it does not intend to abandon traditional Serbian state priorities, especially when it comes to Republika Srpska and Kosovo. Third, it is trying to find a language that would simultaneously satisfy pro-European oriented citizens, the nationally sensitive part of the electorate and international partners. Precisely in that combination lies the greatest unknown of the new policy.

For Croatia the most important message is the one that the leader of the Student List Ilija Srdanović expressed immediately after the election victory. He announced that relations between the two countries will be based on good-neighbourliness, and not on a policy of confrontation. “Croatia will not be in any other status there except good-neighbourly relations,” Srdanović emphasised. In doing so he attributed responsibility for the deterioration of relations to the previous Serbian president. He spoke about the policy of one man who “set two peoples against each other”, emphasising that foreign policy should in the future be conducted by the government of Serbia, and not by an individual. Namely, in Serbia the government has greater powers than the president, but it is allowed that he can be a member of a party.

Vučić, at least for the largest part of his mandate, was also the president of the ruling SNS and in that way was able through party discipline to be at the same time the strongest political figure in Serbia. Therefore what Srdanović stated can still mean some progress. Vučić’s Serbia often used the Croatian state as a foreign policy opponent, and Croatian authorities as a convenient argument in domestic political showdowns.

Accusations about Croatian influence on the Serbian opposition, alleged interference in internal affairs and acting against Serbian national interests were part of everyday political life. Srdanović’s message suggests that such a practice could be abandoned. However, it is important to pay attention to his statement about Croatia, and for now much clearer regarding mere political tone than when it comes to concrete moves. Besides, at this moment it is still not clear whether Srdanović, although he was first on the list, will even be a member of the new Serbian Government. If he will be, it isn’t clear which portfolio he could take over.

minority rights

The more extensive Student List programme shows that a good-neighbourly policy does not mean abandoning issues that have traditionally burdened relations between Belgrade and Zagreb. In the part of the programme that relates to the position of Serbs in the region, the list particularly emphasises the rights of Serbs in Croatia, the preservation of their national, cultural and linguistic identity, the position of returnees, what it calls the selective application of law in certain court proceedings, and the conditions for the dignified marking of grave sites.

In doing so it invokes United Nations Security Council Resolution 1120, the Erdut Agreement and the bilateral agreement from 2004 on the protection of the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia, and of the Serbian and Montenegrin minorities in Croatia. That part of the programme deserves a certain amount of attention. It shows that the Student List does not intend to abandon an active policy of protecting the Serbian minority outside the borders of Serbia. That in itself, of course, is not at all disputable. The protection of minority rights is a legitimate obligation of every democratic state, and Serbia and Croatia have bilateral agreements precisely so that those rights would be protected. However, a problem arises if minority issues are turned into an instrument of political pressure on a neighbouring state. Which Vučić abundantly used. Therefore for Croatia it will be important how Belgrade will concretise its demands.

Will it be a matter of institutional cooperation, exchange of information, solving the problems of returnees, protection of cultural heritage and equal treatment by judicial bodies, or will space again be opened for political accusations and unilateral interpretations of history? Particularly interesting is that the programme at the same time mentions the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia. Which are far from what the Serbian minority has in Croatia.

However many shortcomings the model of electing three Serbian deputies in a special electoral unit has, the fact that Croatia nevertheless applies it speaks of the fact that it wants transparent and good relations. On the other hand, in Serbia there is no mechanism that would guarantee that Croats have their guaranteed representative in the National Assembly. The announcement that the Student List could work on that gives the possibility for a different and better model of mutual relations, instead of constant political competition around the position of Serbs in Croatia. If Belgrade is going to advocate for the rights of Serbs in Croatia, it should at the same time show readiness to protect the rights of Croats in Serbia without political calculations, including their cultural autonomy, representation and the possibility of participating in public life.

war crimes

The second major issue remains the wartime past and open questions from the 1990s. Srdanović has in previous appearances emphasised that the new generation does not want to be burdened by responsibility for events from a time in which its members did not participate. Such a position is politically understandable, but it is not sufficient for things to move from a standstill. In that sense more important than statements about a new beginning will be whether the new authorities will open space for a more serious attitude towards the missing, war crimes, archival material and compensation for victims. In the political confusion that currently reigns in Serbia, it is impossible to extract anything more than these genuinely encouraging wishes that Srdanović expressed in the above-mentioned and in several other public appearances.

the attitude towards srebrenica…

Bosnia and Herzegovina is perhaps the politically most sensitive issue in the entire regional agenda of the Student List. In an interview for Radio Free Europe Srdanović very clearly said that the new authorities will continue cooperation with Republika Srpska. “The continuation of cooperation with Republika Srpska is in the interest of the citizens of Serbia and the citizens of Republika Srpska,” Srdanović said.

To the question of whether Belgrade will encourage the authorities of Republika Srpska to solve problems with the institutions of the central government in Sarajevo, he answered that they will advocate for open dialogue and finding common solutions for all citizens of BiH and Republika Srpska.

Whatever that means.

The Student List does not question the special relationship of Serbia and Republika Srpska. It does not announce its reduction, redefinition or the withdrawal of Belgrade from political and institutional relations with Banja Luka. Another possibility is a change in the way that relationship is realised. Srdanović speaks of dialogue, common solutions and the interests of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which can be read as a distancing from the policy of constant conflicts between Republika Srpska and the state institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the programme does not give a precise answer to the question of how the Student List imagines the relationship of Belgrade towards the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serbia has special ties with Republika Srpska, which also stems from its constitutional and political framework, but at the same time has the obligation to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The new authorities will have to show whether they can reconcile those two facts without creating additional tensions. Particularly indicative is Srdanović’s answer about Srebrenica. To the question of what position the new authorities will take, he said that the issue of Srebrenica is defined by court decisions, and he mentioned the documents that the Serbian Assembly adopted back in 2010.

World.title: Zadar Airport Smashes Previous Records in 2026
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Zadar Airport has smashed its previous records in 2026 despite having a somewhat weaker October than usual. A brand new route from Zadar to German will also operate next summer.

In the first ten months of this year, almost 80,000 more passengers were recorded by Zadar Airport than in the same period last year. For summer 2027, a brand new Ryanair line to Friedrichshafen has also been announced. as eZadar reports, Zadar Airport has already by the end of October surpassed the number of passengers achieved during the whole of last year. According to official statistics, in the first ten months of 2026 1,714,335 passengers were recorded, or 74,734 more than in the entire record year of 2025. Compared to the same ten-month period last year, traffic rose by 4.89 percent, or by 79,947 passengers. The new annual record was thus set while two months still remain until the end of the year.

8,000 fewer passengers in october

October itself, however, finished in a weaker way than October last year. 95,956 passengers passed through Zadar Airport, while in October 2025 there were 103,829. That is a drop of 7.58 percent, or 7,873 fewer passengers. The number of aircraft in the official records was also reduced: from last year’s 532 to this year’s 499, which represents a drop of 6.20 percent. The October result is thereby the first monthly drop in the number of passengers this year compared to 2025. All previous nine months recorded growth.

a new line for summer 2027

In addition to the traffic results, the question of the director’s mandate is currently topical at Zadar Airport. Josip Klišmanić, who has been at the head of the company since October 2017, had his existing mandate, according to data available at the Commission for Deciding on Conflict of Interest, expire on the 14th of October 2026. The government has proposed his temporary appointment for a maximum of six months, until the appointment of a director through a public tender.

This period of the year is always quieter at Zadar Airport. The direct international connection is reduced to Munich, on Mondays and Fridays. Domestic connections are maintained via Pula and Zagreb. For the next summer season an expansion of the destination network has also been announced. The Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair in the summer flight schedule 2027 will connect German Friedrichshafen with Zadar, whereby Zadar Airport gains yet another direct connection with the German market.

World.title: Church Facade in Croatian Village Gets €466,000 as Youth Leaves and Jobs Remain Scarce
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – A church facade that was allegedly “damaged by birds” in the Croatian village of Gvozd will get €466,000 as local youth leaves permanently and jobs remain scarce.

As much as €466,000 from taxpayer pockets will go to the renovation of the Catholic Church of St. Peter and Paul in Gvozd, a small municipality halfway between Karlovac and Sisak. Paula Hadjur reports for Index that this is an expense that the Homeland Movement (Domovinski pokret) proposed by an amendment to the budget re-balance, and which is only one of the five that the government accepted.

The rapidly emptying old village, in which the majority is Serbian population (62.63 percent according to the last census), a few years ago received its first Orthodox church, while the Church of St. Peter and Paul was built back in 2008. Although it is relatively new, the Homeland Movement in its explanation stated that the church should be renovated due to the damaged facade and “protection from further decay”. The mayor of the municipality Milan Vrga, otherwise a member of the SDSS, found out about the renovation of this church from the media. Given that it is a large investment in a small municipality, Vrga welcomed the expense, regardless of what it related to. “When something is being built, there is labour force and our cafés and shops work more. That is certainly a benefit for the renovation,” he said for Index.

the church renovation has been accepted, but the rest is being waited on

However, the municipality would likely also welcome the renovation of other buildings that suffered due to lack of maintenance or in the earthquake. They are aware of the fact in Gvozd, so they applied for two large renovation projects on the last tender of the Ministry of Construction, for which they are still waiting for a decision on whether they will be accepted. “We have investments, we are in talks with the Ministry of Construction and Minister Branko Bačić so that we would renovate the culture centre that collapsed in the earthquake,” Vrga says. People, like the mayor, welcome this church renovation, but they would welcome the renovation of any sacral building, regardless of the faith. What bothers them is, they tell us, that investments are not being made elsewhere either.

why is there no cash for other projects?

“I have nothing against that, I myself am a believer, but if there is money for something like that, why isn’t there for something else?” local resident Milka Zorić-Dmitrović tells us and gives the example of the former court building that is located in the very centre of the municipality, and which could be renovated. “Why couldn’t that building be turned into a nursing home? We have a majority of older people,” she said. “I have nothing against the church, let it be renovated, but please pull some money for things like this as well.” In general, the residents of Gvozd themselves are of the belief that events, workshops or similar activities do not happen particularly often in their village. “There’s nothing here. There’s a library, but there are no workshops or anything similar there,” Milka also stated.

one of croatia’s most undeveloped municipalities

Dara Gruborović also lives in Gvozd, she went to school there and herself notices that the situation in her place is difficult. This is also confirmed by statistical data because the Government classified Gvozd in the lowest group according to the development index. “There are very few people living in Gvozd. Those who stayed here are old, and all the young ones have left and gone elsewhere. There are no jobs,” she explained. “It would be good if factories were built so that people could work,” she says, and it also saddens her when she sees that children in the village do not have many opportunities. “There are very few children, and none of them socialise with anyone. They have nowhere to go out, it’s sad.”

The bright spot of the municipality, the residents told us, is the non-profit association Suncokret. We could also see their posters in front of the building of the collapsed community centre that the mayor also spoke about, where they also set up boxes with clothing donations for all those who need them. Their activities range from socialising with children who come to them after school and helping residents with filling out forms to the exchange of volunteers from all parts of the world. Two volunteers from Finland were also in Gvozd.

“It’s a very quiet village, they have everything basic that is needed. I like being here for a month, but this is not a place for some activities. If you want to be at peace, it is nice,” Jonathan from Finland said. “I would return here, but I wouldn’t spend too much time, a year or more, because there’s not much to do here, but the people are very nice.”

World.title: Zagreb Engineers Turn a Garage Hobby into a Global Tech Business
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – Zagreb engineers managed to turn a garage hobby into a truly global tech business, and it all started with hiding cigarettes from inspectors…

In a smaller industrial zone in Rudeš, a Croatian technology company has been working on innovative solutions that are used in the products of large global companies, from Europe to the USA. Paula Hadjur reports for Index that Matija Puškar, one of the founders of Byte Lab, revealed more about exactly what their team is engaged in. Their job is not to create finished products, but to develop technological solutions that make them smarter, simpler and more accessible to customers. For example, after receiving a specific request, their team designed a device that measures performances in motocross, which is then placed on the drivers’ helmets.

“we’re currently working on an electronic nose…”

“The most successful path to a good product is to talk to people who are deep in that niche. We’re exclusively an engineering company that carries out their own ideas. Someone has a problem and from that, a technical solution arises,” he explained.

They are currently busy working on a so-called electronic nose, an idea that arose in their innovations department in which an entire team works on all projects that seem interesting and useful to them for companies that have not yet developed those ideas themselves. “The idea evolved to the level that we went to our standard clients and showed them the technology. Some clients said it wasn’t particularly interesting to them, but there were those to whom it was very interesting. For example, that the nose, just from the smell of the coffee, understands which brand it is and how much it is roasted and on the basis of that automatically adjusts the coffee preparation process,” he says.

cooperation with the rest of europe and even the usa

They cooperate the most with the USA, Puškar explained, but also with European countries such as Switzerland, Germany, the Benelux countries and the United Kingdom. They also work with Middle Eastern countries. “That distribution is quite natural. We are part of the EU so we give the greatest value to clients in Europe. Prototypes that are produced today in our ground floor can already tomorrow at 9 o’clock be delivered to them,” he says. However interesting and abstract the innovations are, perhaps the most valuable thing in this story is the way it arose. In a garage in Špansko two friends, still as kids, started learning about electronics over the summer.

“The whole story started 10 years before the company was founded. Danijel Babić and I were kids from Špansko who were playing around with electronics,” he says. The first more concrete projects Danijel and he carried out still during their studies at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing (FER), when they developed a system intended for medical diagnostics, such as gait analysis in persons with amputation, because of which they also received the Tesla’s Egg recognition of the VIDI e-novation competition back in 2007. As their desire for innovations did not diminish even with the years, and the projects became larger and larger, both decided to finally open their company, which somewhat later was also joined by their friend and colleague from FER Ivan Dodig.

“In 2011, we came to the situation that the colleague was finishing faculty, I was in the final year. We saw that we already had some revenues and came to the conclusion that we need to formalise so that the whole story would have its head and tail,” he says.

from smart bikes to electric gas meters…

We also went down into Byte Lab’s production plant. Everything starts from an empty board, Puškar explained to us while he was leading us, on which electronic components are placed that are then soldered in ovens, after which additional controls and correctness tests follow, with the help of human hands. That is how some of their most recognisable solutions arose – electric gas meters, smart bicycles and even devices that track performances of motocross races. “If you do motocross, you don’t know how you’re managing to ride, unless you have a friend who times you while you’re passing. We made a device that tracks the complete analytics of entering corners, jump heights, speed tracking,” Puškar says, and subsequently it was interesting for him to hear from clients that that product was later also used among skiers.

“From the standpoint of data, what’s the difference?” Puškar asks himself.

their first product was a cigarette controller

Today, the Byte Lab team, which achieved around 4.5 million in revenue last year alone, still keeps the first product they ever sold as part of the company, in the drawers of the office in which today they close most of their deals with world-famous brands. “We were making cigarette controllers,” Matija laughs. “Advertising of cigarettes was already banned then, and we got the task to make a controller that by pressing a button opens and automatically closes the shutters under which the cigarettes stand, so that traders would reduce the risk of fines.”

Today, they’re a company with around 90 employees, with their own plant, production and a whole series of long-term partners. But, Puškar says, they never thought that the whole story could reach such proportions. “We like to joke that for us the development of new products is like running is for Forrest Gump: you ask yourself where you’re running, you don’t know, but it doesn’t matter. We love creating something new, we strongly nurture that curiosity and it motivates us. The nicest thing is that we work really broadly, from appliances to medical devices. It’s nice to see your products on shelves in shops, in concert halls and at airports,” he concluded.

World.title: Filipinos Overtake Nepalis as Foreign Workers in Croatia
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – For the first time, Filipinos have overtaken Nepalis as foreign workers in Croatia, according to the latest data issued by the Interior Ministry (MUP).

It’s important to bear in mind that the mentioned data doesn’t show how many foreigners overall are actually working in Croatia, but how many work permits have been issued to them. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that these statistics are also influenced by legal changes that have enabled the issuance of permits for three years instead of one. Despite that, some trends are quite interesting.

According to MUP data, in the first nine months of 2026, 18,712 residence and work permits were issued to citizens of the Philippines, which is 46.1 percent more than in the same period last year, when 12,809 were issued. At the same time, the number of permits issued to citizens of Nepal fell from 24,948 to 17,386, or by 30.3 percent. An even larger drop was recorded among citizens of India, to whom 7,734 permits were issued, which is 37 percent less than in the same period last year, when 12,274 were issued. Filipinos already last year overtook Indians in the number of permits issued, and this year the difference between them has further increased.

filipinos overtook nepalis, but workers from bosnia and herzegovina and serbia still dominate

Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia are still at the top in the number of residence and work permits issued in Croatia. In the first nine months of 2026, 22,565 permits were issued to BiH citizens and 19,886 to Serbian citizens. Nevertheless, a drop was recorded in both groups compared to the same period last year, by 12.4 percent for BiH citizens and 4.5 percent for Serbian citizens.

Although workers from neighbouring countries are still the most numerous according to the number of permits issued, in this analysis we particularly focused on changes among citizens of Asian countries, primarily the strong growth in the number of permits for Filipinos and the drop for Nepalis and Indians.

construction declines but hospitality and tourism rises

The largest number of work permits in the first nine months of 2026 was issued in tourism and hospitality – a total of 48,156, which is 5.1 percent more than in the same period last year. In construction 32,701 permits were issued, or 18.5 percent less than last year. The drop is even more pronounced compared to 2024, when 55,507 permits were issued in that activity. In two years their number decreased by 41.1 percent. Industry is also recording a drop, with 15,121 permits issued, as well as transport and communications with 7,853 permits. At the same time the number of permits in trade rose to 7,752, which is 13.5 percent more than last year.

a drop in the number of permits issued doesn’t mean a drop in foreign worker numbers

In Croatia from January to the end of September this year 124,023 residence and work permits were issued, which is 8.9 percent less than last year and 21.9 percent less than in 2024. Particularly pronounced is the drop in the number of permits for new employment, of which 101,841 were issued in 2024, and this year 48,847, or as much as 52 percent less. However, as we mentioned in the introduction to the text, the number of permits issued was primarily influenced by the amendments to the Law on Foreigners that entered into force in March 2025. They enabled the issuance of residence and work permits for a maximum of three years, instead of the previous one year. The amendments to the law enabled foreign workers under certain conditions to change employers without issuing a new work permit, because of which such changes are not recorded in the statistics of permits for new employment.

That a drop in the number of work permits issued does not necessarily mean a reduction in the number of foreign workers is also shown by data from the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO). At the end of September 2024, 123,836 insured persons from third countries, i.e. countries that are not members of the European Economic Area or Switzerland, were recorded in Croatia. A year later there were 138,114 of them, and at the end of September 2026 146,307. That is 5.9 percent more than last year and 18.1 percent more than two years ago.

Interesting are also the data according to the countries from which the workers come. At the end of September this year 19,978 insured persons with Philippine travel documents were recorded, as much as 44 percent more than a year earlier. At the same time the number of insured persons with Nepalese travel documents fell by 2.5 percent, to 23,787, and those of India by 4.7 percent, to 10,729.

These data confirm that the number of Filipino workers in Croatia is indeed growing strongly, while the number of Nepalis and Indians is decreasing, but significantly more mildly than could be concluded from the statistics of work permits issued.

Although HZMO data give a different picture of the movement in the number of foreign workers from the statistics of permits issued, the fact is that significant changes are also recorded according to them, especially the strong growth in the number of Filipinos. We spoke with economic analyst Predrag Bejaković about the reasons for these changes. “It’s merely a matter of a reshuffling of the entire European labour migration system. After the pandemic several new destination ‘poles’ emerged, and Croatia is one of them, along with Portugal, Lithuania, Romania and Hungary,” Bejaković explains.

croatia was the top destination for nepalis in 2023

“However, back in 2025 the number of first employment permits issued to those workers in Croatia decreased, while the largest share of those permits was issued in Romania. Thus Nepalese workers are increasingly directing themselves towards Romania, and Indian workers towards Portugal, which in 2025 became their leading destination in the EU. Croatia is thereby competing with other countries for the same workers and is no longer the only ‘new’ destination,” he says.

croatia is the second favourite country in the eu for filipinos

Among the reasons for the changes Bejaković singles out stricter conditions for employing foreign workers, competition from other European countries, and the attitude towards foreigners and the lack of an integration policy in Croatia. With Filipinos, Bejaković explains, a more orderly employment system plays an important role. In 2024 Croatia signed a memorandum of cooperation with the Philippines in the field of the labour market, and Philippine institutions strongly regulate the employment of their citizens abroad. According to the analysis Bejaković is working on, Croatia in 2025 became the second most frequent destination for Filipino workers in the European Union. He emphasises that according to the Eurostat category of first work permits Hungary is in the leading place.

why has the number of permits issued for construction decreased?

To the question of how much these changes are connected with demand in individual activities, he replies that sectoral demand plays an important role, but that the drop in the number of permits issued cannot be directly equated with a drop in the need for workers. “The drop in construction could partially be connected with changes in the intensity of structural reconstruction after the earthquake and the dynamics of the investment cycle financed by EU funds, including funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Workers on the reconstruction of buildings damaged by the earthquake received permits without a labour market test and without the opinion of the Croatian Employment Service. If the scope of those jobs is decreasing, the need for employment through that special procedure is also decreasing,” he explained.

Bejaković says that in practice differences can be observed in the employment of Filipinos and Nepalis according to activities, but that more precise data are lacking for reliable conclusions. He notes that employment in tourism and hospitality is facilitated for Filipinos by knowledge of English, experience in those activities and developed employment channels. Nepalis, on the other hand, he says, more often came for physically demanding jobs, so a reduction in demand in construction could more strongly affect their employment.

the influence of legal amendments

As for the influence of the amendments to the Law on Foreigners on the statistics of permits issued, Bejaković explains that two waves of legal changes need to be distinguished, from March 2025 and June 2026.

“Part of the drop is statistical, and not real. If a permit lasts three years instead of one, there is no annual extension so fewer permits are issued for the same number of people. The same applies to a change of employer: a worker who is already here changes jobs with a notification and confirmation, and not with a new permit for new employment. The new law additionally facilitates this. A change of employer is no longer tied to the same occupation, and is possible after six months with the first employer instead of after a year. The drop in the number of permits for new employment therefore does not mean that the number of foreign workers has fallen by that much,” he says.

stricter rules for croatian employers themselves

Bejaković emphasises that the second part of the drop in the number of permits issued is real and intentional, that is, a consequence of stricter conditions for employers, including a minimum inflow of money into the account, a prescribed ratio of domestic and foreign workers, and a check of whether they are actually performing the registered activity. Thereby, according to his words, fictitious employers and part of the agencies were removed from the system. “Can that explain the differences between Nepalis and Filipinos? Partially. Stricter conditions most affect the agency model and smaller employers, and they were precisely the main channel for Nepalese workers in construction. The Filipino channel, with the memorandum and more orderly employment, more easily passes the new procedure,” he says.

the future of employing foreign workers in croatia

Speaking about the future of employing foreign workers in Croatia, Bejaković expects a smaller inflow of new workers, but also a more stable structure, with a larger number of those who will stay longer in the country, change employers and gradually integrate. He adds that the need will not disappear because the demographic picture is relentless. “The long-term question is the sustainability of a model based on low-skilled and temporary work. If we want foreign workers to permanently fill the demographic gap, the focus must shift from the speed of issuing permits to integration, language, housing and the protection of workers’ rights,” he concluded.

World.title: Croatian Promotional Video Starring John Malkovich Wins Award
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The now famous Croatian promotional video starring the one and only John Malkovich has won a prestigious award.

The now globally known video “Croatia – I Hear It’s Beautiful” was awarded at the City Nation Place Awards in London. Croatian islands won gold and Dubrovnik also took home silver at the Wanderlust awards ceremony. 24sata reports some excellent news for Croatian tourism is coming from London, where the prestigious City Nation Place Awards ceremony was held, at which the promotional video “CROATIA – I hear it’s beautiful”, starring John Malkovich, won the main award in the Best communication strategy: tourism category.

This is another in a series of awards won by the promotional video of Croatian tourism, and this time it is an award given by City Nation Place (CNP), a global platform and professional organisation dedicated to the branding and marketing of cities, regions and countries.

“This year we’ve made a significant step forward in presenting Croatia on the international scene, and we are particularly proud of the new promotional film that presented the country from a different, fresh and authentic perspective, as well as the entire campaign ‘Croatia I hear it’s beautiful’. At a time when it seems that almost everything has already been seen and presented, it is important to continuously find new, innovative ways of communication and promotion, create different stories and highlight what makes Croatia special,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

Croatia’s popularity on a global level is also confirmed by the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which are awarded by the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust on the basis of votes from its readers. Precisely the travel lovers and readers of this popular magazine declared Croatian islands the most desirable in the European regions category (gold award), while Dubrovnik was declared the second most desirable European city (silver award)

“We are extremely pleased with this international recognition, which confirm that Croatia has a strong and recognisable tourism story. It is particularly valuable that Croatian islands and Dubrovnik were recognised by the readers and travel lovers themselves. More than 250,000 Wanderlust readers took part in the voting and this year broke the record with as many as 8.2 million votes. The success of the promotional video of Croatian tourism shows that creative, authentic and contemporary communication can further strengthen the visibility of our country on international markets. Our goal is to present Croatia as a diverse and high-quality destination throughout the year, highlighting not only its best-known strengths but also the richness of local experiences, culture, local food and way of life,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Gold for the Croatian islands confirms the allure of Croatia’s island diversity, preserved nature and authentic experiences, while the award for Dubrovnik additionally confirms its international recognisability and rich cultural-historical heritage. Let us add that among others the presentation of the Wanderlust awards was also graced by the presence of Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex.

World.title: First Leg Lengthening Procedure Carried Out in Croatia
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The very first leg lengthening procedure carried out in Croatia has been performed at Zagreb’s Clinic for Traumatology.

A medical team from the Clinic for Traumatology in Zagreb has performed the first leg lengthening operation in Croatia using a new method that does not use an external fixator. Index reports that the procedure was carried out on a 28-year-old patient for whom a six-centimetre difference in leg length had been making movement difficult for years.

Kristina Sambolek (28) has had a shorter left leg since birth due to a hip deformity. She has spent her entire life in and out of hospitals, and numerous operations are behind her. Because of the difference in leg length she walks on her toes and wears shoes with soles of different thicknesses. “The first thing they did to me was literally tie my legs so they were hanging in the air and try that way to set the hips back into the socket,” Kristina described.

“The biggest problem was that on the left side I didn’t have a proper socket at all, nor a joint, so for years they tried to fix that with operations. I have the feeling that I spent more of my childhood in hospital than at home,” she recalled.

slovenia has been using this method for around a decade

Over time, she learned to endure the pain and accepted the limitations, but she never gave up hope of a better life. “I’ve been through operations and I know what awaits me, so I’ve come to terms with the fact that I have to go through this so that it will be easier for me. My wish is to be able to put on high heels and be like a real woman,” she said. The operation at the Traumatology Clinic is the result of international cooperation with colleagues from Slovenia. “This is one of the most favourable methods for lengthening long bones. It is much simpler for patients than external fixators,” said Prof. Dr. Sc. Matej Drobnič, specialist in orthopaedic surgery from Ljubljana. He added that in Slovenia this method has been used for about ten years and that five to six such procedures are performed annually without significant complications. The two-hour procedure in Zagreb is the first of its kind in Croatia.

“It’s a type of brand new technology where a nail is implanted into the bone. The leg then grows on its own, one millimetre a day. The patient will lengthen the leg herself with magnetic stimulation and we expect that in 50 days we will get the 50 millimetres we are planning,” explained Assist. Prof. Dr. Sc. Tomislav Čengić, head of the 3rd Department of Geriatric Traumatology and Hip Surgery at the Clinic for Traumatology.

The new method will enable patients with a difference in leg length to be treated in Croatia, without going abroad. “Three to five patients a year could certainly be found in Croatia for this type of operation. This procedure is significant for us, but also for the entire orthopaedic and traumatology profession in Croatia,” emphasised Assoc. Prof. Dr. Sc. Srećko Sabalić, head of the Clinic for Traumatology. Assist. Prof. Čengić emphasised that the success is the result of teamwork. “The entire clinic team took part in the procedure, from anaesthesiologists, scrub nurses, technicians to radiology engineers,” Čengić said. For the patient the operation means a step towards easier walking, and for Croatian orthopaedics the introduction of a modern treatment method.

The operation was performed by Assist. Prof. Tomislav Čengić, Prof. Matej Drobnič, Dr Danijel Jurković and Dr Fabijan Čukelj. Also in the team were anaesthesiologist Dr Ajša Muratović, scrub nurses Martina Stivičević, Tihana Krusha and Barbara Funtak, and radiology engineer Dubravko Kamenar.
