World.title: Kaarel Vanamölder and Madli Vanamölder: Praise tools!
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is just another tool, much like the power tools that transformed construction or word processors that revolutionized writing. Rather than demonizing AI, we should learn to use it skillfully and take responsibility for the results, write Kaarel Vanamölder and Madli Vanamölder.

A circular saw really is an absolutely marvelous tool. Especially a cordless one! You simply place it (6,000 revolutions per minute at no load!) on a wooden beam, pull the trigger and in an instant you have a straight, clean cut. A cordless drill or screwdriver is every bit as amazing!

Just imagine if our ancestors had had tools like these ... No more hammering three-inch square nails into floorboards or cursing, generations later, as you struggle to pull them out. Instead, you'd simply grab a Torx T25 bit and, with a satisfying whir, a hot screw lovingly driven into the board by your great-great-grandfather would come rising out. Alongside the fanciful thought experiment "What if Lembitu had had a machine gun?" we might just as well, or perhaps even more aptly, ask: "What if the builders of St. Olaf's Church tower had used cordless drills?"

A cordless drill, circular saw or any other power tool primarily increases productivity: the job gets done faster than with hand tools, which require care, experience and manual skill on the one hand and constant maintenance on the other.

Picture a perfectly ordinary wooden house built a century ago: fastening all the boards to its walls required thousands of nails and, above all, skill. There was no time to keep tapping away at a single nail indefinitely. It had to be driven home with no more than a couple of precise, powerful blows. Then on to the next one. And the next.

People may have had more time back then than we do today (there were no unanswered emails or online meetings after all), but time was still money and the house had to be finished by the deadline. Master hammerers were probably just as sought-after as plasterers, painters and stove builders.

A carpenter's tools — augers, chisels, planes, saws, axes and the like — had to be impeccably sharp. Only then could cuts be clean, precise and require minimal effort. The same applied to all tools. My late grandfather had several scythes, each suited to a different type of vegetation. As he mowed, every so often you would hear that distinctive "shhk-shhk-shhk" as he honed the blade again and again with astonishing speed and skill. The work took time, but it was efficient and produced good results. Of course, nothing as consistently immaculate as a lawn kept in a perpetual crew cut by a robotic mower on constant patrol.

Machines and standards

Power tools make it possible for even amateurs to manage construction work reasonably well. Of course, compared with a skilled tradesman, they spend considerably more time fumbling around, figuring things out, experimenting and making incorrect cuts. Meanwhile, a true professional starts by switching on a teal Makita jobsite radio (tuned to Star FM) and gets down to work without making a fuss. And let's face it: ultimately, the proof is in the workmanship. A professional builder will generally produce better results than an amateur, even if they use exactly the same tools.

"A professional builder will generally produce better results than an amateur, even if they use exactly the same tools."

Changes in technology also transform construction methods and standards. In the age of our ancestors' craftsmanship, joinery techniques reigned supreme, with an astonishing variety of joints and applications. Even today, you can come across strangely therapeutic videos on social media showing how several pieces of wood are joined into a single structure through skillful sawing and chiseling, in ways that seem incomprehensible at first glance.

Traditional wood joints can also be made using modern specialized machinery, but nowadays structural elements are predominantly connected using metal brackets and plates, joist hangers and, of course, screws (cordless drill!). It's simply faster and more efficient. Admittedly, a carefully finished traditional wood joint is undoubtedly more aesthetically pleasing, but structures held together with screws are generally covered with standard-sized construction panels anyway.

Machines impose standardization. Even the thickest, most gnarled tree trunk can be effortlessly turned into, say, 50-by-150-millimeter lumber, cut to lengths of 3,600, 4,200 or 4,800 millimeters, at an electrically powered sawmill. The wall framing built from this lumber accommodates precisely the right amount of mineral wool insulation (610 by 1,220 by 50 millimeters).

Once you understand the standards and how they fit together, a building goes up almost effortlessly, like a construction kit. One side effect, of course, is that buildings and rooms constructed this way tend to look alike, with the same proportions — all dictated by the standards.

Progress and the alternatives

In 1903, Matthias Johann Eisen (1857–1934) published his famous short story "Tallinn in the Year 2000." In it, the first-person narrator accidentally travels a century into the future through the Baltic Station. A "kind gentleman" he happens to meet introduces him to this new world. It is a fascinating text that offers a glimpse into what modernity meant at the beginning of the 20th century.

The main themes are speed and reduced effort: nobody travels by horse-drawn carriage anymore, self-propelled vehicles have taken over, an elevator takes people up to Toompea, newspapers are published three times a day and an express train can get you to Pärnu in an hour. Not to mention the airship.

The age of bicycles is over: "Who would want to tire their legs anymore when self-propelled vehicles take all the effort out of traveling? Bicycles are now used only by the very poor, such as servant girls, manual laborers and so on." Speed and efficiency were the goals humanity pursued back then and, broadly speaking, remain so today. In every sphere of life, not just construction.

There have always been those who branch off from the mainstream or even head in the opposite direction. The widespread introduction of machinery during the Industrial Revolution gave rise to the Luddite movement in the early 19th century. Armed with blacksmiths' hammers, desperate former skilled workers who had lost their jobs smashed equipment in factories and workshops because the machines' greater productivity had deprived them of their income, social standing and way of life. The need for skilled craftsmanship declined dramatically and almost anyone could operate a loom. Rapid technological changes came as a shock to traditional weaving communities.

As an alternative to modern machinery, it is possible to preserve and deliberately learn old and disappearing crafts and techniques. Traditional craft technologies offer a wealth of opportunities, from restoring log buildings to practicing craftsmanship with old tools and materials.

There are undoubtedly fields — musical instrument making, for example — where most of the work is still done using good old-fashioned craftsmanship and extremely sharp hand tools. Yet even there, modern equipment, materials and tools have been incorporated as a compromise. The more specialized and exclusive an object and its production methods, the higher its price. The almost magical word "handmade" is added to product descriptions as a mark of quality.

We work with machines!

Beyond construction, machines have also revolutionized intellectual work. Take writing, for example. Not so long ago, producing a properly typed manuscript required considerable technical skill and patience. A mistyped letter had to be erased or typed over, while more extensive corrections meant retyping an entire page.

If an author decided to move a paragraph elsewhere, out came the scissors and glue. The text was literally cut into pieces and the words were pasted onto paper in a new order. The command "cut and paste" originally referred to precisely this kind of manual work. Producing multiple copies simultaneously meant struggling with carbon paper. Editorial offices and publishing houses employed people whose job was to retype, correct and prepare manuscripts for printing. And that's before even getting to typesetting.

Then came word processors — electronic machines. In the 1970s, specialized word-processing systems allowed specially trained operators to make corrections to written text.

With the spread of personal computers in the 1980s, these same capabilities became available to an increasingly broad range of users. The first version of Microsoft Word appeared in 1983 and by the middle of the decade, Macintosh computers, laser printers and desktop publishing software were beginning to bring professional print production capabilities to ordinary users' desks.

During the 1990s, Word became an increasingly common tool and with it capabilities that had previously required dedicated specialists began to be taken for granted. In essence, the circular saw of text production had arrived: skilled professionals still had the advantage, but amateurs could manage too.

Naturally, machines and software established new standards here as well. Today, a document with consistent formatting (12-point Times New Roman, 1.5 line spacing), proper page layout, automatic page numbering and a table of contents hardly seems like a remarkable achievement. Footnotes automatically appear in the right places, the table of contents updates when headings are changed and moving a paragraph from the beginning of a manuscript to the end takes just a moment.

Just a few decades ago, such a change might have meant retyping and renumbering numerous pages. Today, by contrast, it would be rather embarrassing to submit a document with page numbers manually typed in, text formatted using endless strings of spaces or a table of contents hopelessly scrambled after the latest revision.

Rage against the machine

"Drywall house" is probably the most common derogatory term for a modern building. At the same time, it is not universally applicable, referring instead to a particular process and its outcome — namely, hastily executed real estate development.

The negative judgment is not necessarily directed at the tools or materials themselves, but rather at a poor, "cheap" result. Standard-sized lumber, construction panels, metal brackets, screws and expanding foam are, after all, simply materials, not "construction slop," just as a cordless circular saw is merely a cutting tool, not a "stupid machine." The result produced with these materials and tools is still a building, not "garbage" or something that prompts the remark, "You can tell it was made with a cordless drill."

Poor artificial intelligence! It had barely arrived before it was subjected to a torrent of abuse: AI slop, vomit, empty verbiage, trash, drivel, garbage, gremlins, brain rot and brain worms. These are just a few of the expressions used to describe what the technology does and the results it produces.

In academic circles, the term "stochastic parrot" has become well known. On the internet, however, the much more colloquial "clanker," a rattling heap of metal, has gained currency, with roots tracing back to the battle droids of "Star Wars." Science fiction offers other derogatory terms as well. In the television series "Battlestar Galactica," artificial beings are called "toasters," reducing a sophisticated artificial entity to a primitive kitchen appliance. The world of "Blade Runner," meanwhile, gave us "skin-job," a derogatory term for human-looking artificial beings.

Disparaging AI and treating it with condescension is becoming something of a mark of good taste, even in academic and cultural circles. Using chatbots developed by major corporations for research is considered improper, while condemning their environmental footprint and criticizing their energy consumption is seen as the morally correct position.

At the Estonian Annual Conference of the Humanities this spring, a new term, "free-range presentation," was enthusiastically introduced to describe a presentation created without AI as something authentic and genuine (the happy, individualistic free-range chicken versus the miserable, enslaved masses of a factory farm). This despite the fact that even a "homemade" presentation all too often amounts to little more than a digital overhead transparency called PowerPoint.

"Insulting a machine is itself a peculiar way of attributing human qualities to it."

In September 2025, the British newspaper The Guardian pondered whether "clanker" had already become a discriminatory slur against robots. Such expressions are seen as potentially normalizing the kind of derogatory language used against groups of people. Insulting a machine is itself a peculiar way of attributing human qualities to it. There are no outright calls yet to pick up the Luddites' blacksmiths' hammers again, but that moment may not be far off. One thing is certain: AI is generating plenty of anxiety about the end of the world.

Assigning a bot

Recently, editors were urged to ask authors directly "whether they might have used the help of a digital gremlin (kratt in Estonian — ed.) when writing." What remained unclear, however, was what to do if the answer was yes — automatically reject the text, declare it a non-text, "slop"? More broadly, though, determining what constitutes AI assistance, or the work of a "gremlin," may prove rather complicated.

Indeed, there are legitimate reasons to be concerned about the encroachment of machines (or gremlins) in academia, too. Take reference management software (such as Zotero, EndNote and Mendeley), which has gradually taken over one of the essential skills of a humanities scholar: compiling bibliographies and formatting citations.

Just a few decades ago, any self-respecting historian, for example, had to meticulously record their sources and literature and format every last citation by hand. Completing a manuscript involved endless fiddling with authors' names, publication years, volume numbers, page numbers and punctuation marks.

Today, however, an increasing number of scholars shamelessly let a digital gremlin do this work for them. A few mouse clicks are all it takes for the software to compile a bibliography, format citations correctly and, if necessary, convert the entire referencing system from one style to another. What kind of humanities scholar cannot even manage their own references? How is a young researcher supposed to acquire the fundamental skills of academic work if a machine puts all the commas, periods and italics in the right places for them?

Most astonishing of all, universities not only turn a blind eye to this practice but even organize training sessions teaching students to entrust the compilation of their bibliographies to computer programs. Who still formats references by hand these days!? And so we are raising a generation of scholars who know how to click a button but may no longer know where a comma belongs in a citation or why an en dash should be used.

Shouldn't academic papers prepared with the help of reference management software also carry a warning: "Machine assistance was used in preparing the references for this article"? Better still, of course, would be to require genuine humanities scholars to continue writing their citations by hand.

At least then we could be certain that we were dealing with authentic human intellectual work rather than the output of some digital gremlin. This illustrates how society takes the automation of certain forms of intellectual work for granted while treating the automation of others as almost a moral transgression.

A machine as a tool

The recent anxiety over the use of AI in writing can easily be alleviated if we remember one fundamental point: we are not, after all, dealing with a supernatural being summoned through a pact with the devil. As Alexander Stubb recently remarked at the opening of the academic year at the College of Europe in Bruges: "Use AI as an instrument, but do not allow it to replace your capacity to think."

A tool does not determine the quality or cultural value of the work it produces. Technology has changed, and will continue to change, the ways we work, without relieving people of the need to make decisions, possess skills or take responsibility for the results.

AI is a machine, an extraordinarily powerful circular saw that helps us work more efficiently and quickly. That includes producing texts. A screw can be driven incorrectly and a saw blade can make a crooked cut. The result is shoddy work that nobody will pay for and that needs to be fixed. In inexperienced hands, AI also produces empty, meaningless text, but responsibility for it still lies with the amateur author — the human being.

As countless presentation slides demonstrate, humanities scholars tend to be, at best, technologically timid, if not downright out of touch with technology. It is unrealistic to expect a humanities scholar whose technical repertoire otherwise extends little beyond a lackluster PowerPoint presentation to suddenly master AI overnight. Every tool takes practice. The arrival of this new machine will undoubtedly bring new standards to creative work, including writing, but these need not necessarily be feared or demonized. A witch hunt targeting AI users and texts produced with its assistance would be equally absurd, even if understandable from a human perspective.

And there will always be the option of returning to the world of well-sharpened hand chisels — sending Sirp neatly handwritten, calligraphic fair copies in an envelope. How to get them to the post office or a parcel locker and, if accepted, into print can be left to the specialists.

World.title: Mart Võsu: State should not treat entrepreneurs as if they don't know how to count money
World.content:
The Ministry of Climate appears to believe Estonian entrepreneurs do not know how to count money. How else can one explain a draft proposal that would require businesses to renovate old commercial and industrial buildings, asks Mart Võsu.

By 2030, non-residential buildings with the poorest energy performance must reach at least energy class F, and by 2033, energy class E. The estimated cost is €290 million, yet government support is generally not considered necessary.

The state orders, entrepreneurs pay

Does the ministry really believe entrepreneurs voluntarily pay large heating bills and cannot decide for themselves when insulation upgrades or heating system improvements will pay for themselves? Entrepreneurs know how to count money. Now an official comes along who thinks they know better.

In one industrial building, equipment generates enough heat on its own. In another, constant ventilation is required. In a third, only a small portion of the space is heated. Some tractor repair shops or production buildings are used for only a few months each year. Insulating such a building may never pay for itself. Have these differences been taken into account, or is it simply easier to impose the same obligation on everyone?

"The bill will be paid by Estonian consumers through higher food, goods and service prices."

It creates the impression that government agencies must continually invent new requirements to justify their own existence. The entrepreneur's role is to pay the bill. Businesses have only recently been forced to make costly upgrades to comply with new fire safety requirements. Now another mandatory investment looms. Has anyone calculated how much all these successive requirements will cost entrepreneurs and ultimately the state itself?

Small and medium-sized rural businesses will be hit hardest because they lack the financial resources available to large corporations. For some, it could mean shutting down operations. In rural areas, every business closure means lost jobs, lower tax revenue and another blow to local communities.

If people do not move away from their hometowns, they will have to travel dozens of kilometers farther to work. More driving, more fuel consumption and more emissions. Where is the climate benefit in that? Has anyone calculated the environmental impact of lost local jobs and longer commutes?

€290 million is money entrepreneurs could invest in production, equipment, jobs and wages. Instead, the state dictates how the money must be spent, even when the investment will not pay for itself during the building's useful life.

Will an official be held responsible if an entrepreneur has to take out a loan, abandon expansion plans or close a business? Of course not. And does the ministry understand that those hundreds of millions will ultimately be reflected in the price of products and services? The bill will be paid by Estonian consumers through higher food, goods and service prices.

We must also consider the footprint of construction work

A separate issue is the climate footprint of the renovation process itself.

The production of insulation materials, transportation, construction work and waste all generate CO₂ emissions. If a building is used only a few months per year, the resulting energy savings may be minimal. Has anyone calculated how much CO₂ would actually be saved through renovation and how much additional CO₂ would be generated in the process? Do the savings even offset the environmental impact of the construction work?

No one disputes the need for energy savings, but they must make economic and environmental sense, not simply serve as another box checked in an official's report.

The goal of climate policy cannot be to move people from rural areas to cities, end livestock farming and agriculture, and close barns, industrial buildings and tractor repair shops because they are not insulated well enough.

Estonian entrepreneurs know very well how difficult it is to earn money. Yet the state seems to believe their wallets are bottomless. Perhaps it is time to stop telling entrepreneurs how to spend their money and start thinking about how to let them earn it.

World.title: Estonia's exports grew by 6% in third quarter
World.content:
In the third quarter, exports of goods grew by 6 percent and imports by 7 percent, data from Statistics Estonia shows.

Exports totalled €4.7 billion and imports €5.8 billion in July, August and September.

Jane Leppmets, foreign trade statistics analyst at Statistics Estonia, said trade in electrical equipment and agricultural products and food preparations held the biggest share in both exports and imports in the third quarter.

"Finland, Latvia and Lithuania were the top export partners, and the largest imports were registered from Lithuania, Finland and Germany," she added.

The agency also said that in September, exports increased by 12 percent and imports by 8 percent on year. Exports amounted to nearly €1.8 billion and imports to more than €2 billion at current prices.

Compared with September 2025, exports of mineral products increased the most, by €77 million. Exports of transport equipment decreased the most, by €18 million.

Exports of goods of Estonian origin grew by 16 percent year on year and represented 66 percent of total exports in September.

"This rise in exports has been widespread; there were only a few commodity groups where exports decreased," Leppmets said.

Electrical equipment, wood and articles of wood and agricultural products and food preparations were the most exported commodities of Estonian origin. Compared with September last year, there were more exports of mineral products, including shale oil, and electrical equipment and parts of Estonian origin.

Estonia's top export partner in September was Finland (15 percent of total exports), followed by Latvia (11 percent) and Sweden (9 percent).

World.title: Parties differ on how to secure more money for health care
World.content:
A recent audit by the National Audit Office found Estonia's health care funding model is unsustainable, prompting broad agreement among politicians that resources must be used more effectively, even as they disagree on whether additional funding is needed and how to secure it.

Before allocating more money to health care, the way existing resources are used must be changed, Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller (Reform Party) said. Drawing on her experience as a family physician, she sees how part of the budget is sometimes spent on the wrong processes, failing to direct patients to the care they actually need.

"Where the money goes definitely needs to be reviewed, and simply injecting more money into a system where the deficit keeps growing is certainly not a magic solution. Additional funding is needed, I agree with that, but we need to look very carefully at ensuring that money reaches the patient," Joller said.

Riina Sikkut. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Former Health Minister Riina Sikkut (Social Democratic Party) said additional funding is essential and will require a political decision.

"I don't see how we can squeeze more out of the current system by saying there will be no additional funding and people should simply work more, better and faster, especially in a situation where the share of people aged 75 and over is set to double in our society. We will definitely need more resources to ensure they receive modern treatment. Finding money is a much easier problem than finding and training health care professionals. So a political decision is needed on how to gradually increase tax revenue directed to health care. One proposal is to do this for children, just as the state contributes to the Health Insurance Fund on behalf of non-working pensioners," Sikkut said.

Another option that could help direct funding more effectively would be to partially link financing to patient experience. The idea is supported by the Reform Party, the Social Democrats and Isamaa.

Keskerakonna esimees Mihhail Kõlvart. Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Center Party chairman Mihhail Kõlvart, however, does not consider the idea feasible.

"I don't think this idea is workable because every evaluation is subjective. Subjective evaluations create the risk of disputes, which in turn creates more tension and problems than solutions. What really needs to be reviewed is which areas are priorities and where resources need to be directed. We need to further develop health care information systems," Kõlvart said.

The National Audit Office's latest audit also pointed to the large number of reforms and development plans that often fail to make it into practice. For example, options for integrating the health care and social care systems have been analyzed for nearly 10 years, and implementation of the reform is planned to begin next summer. The Social Democrats and the Center Party see potential savings from the change, while Isamaa argues that a lack of funding will prevent it from succeeding.

Riina Solman Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

"In principle, it is right that we want to prevent problems, but once again it turns out to be a nice idea without money to implement it," said Isamaa Vice Chair Riina Solman. "This has become almost endemic in Estonia. We produce attractive projects for desk drawers, strategies for desk drawers, even building designs for desk drawers. We spend enormous effort, energy, vision and noble ideas on them, but they never become reality because we cannot afford to carry them out. The Health Insurance Fund's deficit, which is already a leaking bucket, will only grow larger if we do not review other spending lines, find savings there and organize services in a way that avoids duplication."

World.title: Estonia's domestic pig numbers still below pre-African swine fever levels
World.content:
Eight of 11 pig farms hit by African swine fever (ASF) last summer have restocked, but despite no new outbreaks this year, Estonia's domestic pig numbers have yet to recover.

ASF was detected at the Ekseko breeding farm in Viljandi County late last August, prompting the emergency culling of 8,000 sows and 21,000 piglets.

Maag Agro board member Priit Dreimann told ERR that the farm has now been restocked with 2,700 sows, with the first piglets due in late November or early December. The downtime was also used to renovate and update the facility, including its animal housing and manure-handling systems.

"We started bringing in sows in June, and that process is now complete," Dreimann said. "Normal operations will hopefully be fully back up and running by early next year."

The outbreak also prompted major changes to the farm's everyday operations in terms of biosecurity measures, including redesigned entry procedures, additional disinfection points and facilities to reduce contact between people and vehicles.

The surrounding woodland was also cleared and converted into parkland to discourage wildlife from sheltering there.

Ekseko previously housed nearly 8,000 sows but will now keep just 2,700 to reduce the risk of another outbreak. The cutback also resulted in staff layoffs.

Helen Prommik, an expert at the Agriculture and Food Board (PTA), said ASF did not reach any pig farms this year, although the disease was detected in 122 wild boars, or 1.2 percent of those tested.

Rapla County had the most confirmed cases with 33, followed by Harju County with 19 and Lääne County with 14 cases. No domestic pigs tested positive for ASF this year.

'Hopefully the subsidies will help'

Of the 19 farms affected by previous ASF outbreaks, two have closed, while another farm that operated in rented premises has resumed operations under a new tenant.

Estonia's overall domestic pig population, however, remains well below pre-outbreak levels. As of this September, the country had around 215,000 domestic pigs in all, compared with approximately 280,000 pigs in early summer 2025, Prommik said.

Pig prices are also currently low across Europe, she noted.

"Hopefully, the investment subsidies aimed at pork producers will help," the PTA official said. "Perhaps the measure will even lead to the establishment of an entirely new pig farm in Estonia."

World.title: Expert: Ukrainian security and Russia's ambitions rule out U.S. deal
World.content:
What should we make of the grand deal promised by President Donald Trump, which would concern both Ukraine and Europe as a whole?

It certainly reflects Russia's thinking on European security, as we may recall from December 2021, before Russia invaded Ukraine. Moscow was making similar demands back then: a complete overhaul of Europe's security architecture, a return of NATO to its 1997 borders and so on.

However, it is also worth noting that all the mechanisms American negotiators are now proposing for Europe — such as various dialogue formats, confidence-building measures and arms control measures — have actually existed in Europe before, for example within the framework of the OSCE. Russia even had a dialogue format with NATO, which was used quite regularly at certain times. There were also various arms control and confidence-building agreements, inspections under the Vienna Document and the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe. Russia itself has either altered, rendered completely ineffective or withdrawn from almost all these agreements.

In that sense, it is difficult to see how anything could be established that would, on the one hand, meet the requirements the Americans themselves have put forward — namely, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries and their right to make their own political decisions — while, on the other hand, accommodating Russia's wishes and addressing its so-called security concerns. This is a particularly significant issue when it comes to Ukraine, because it is clear that Russia has not abandoned its previous objectives there.

And perhaps the third aspect is how an agreement between the United States and Russia on Europe's security architecture could even be possible without Europeans taking part. We have now seen the French foreign minister say that Europeans will be represented in some capacity at next week's talks in Abu Dhabi.

But in the current situation, with Russia conducting gray-zone attacks against Europe virtually every day, it is very difficult to see sufficient common ground for any progress on these issues at present. And if President Trump believes that expanding the scope of negotiations from Ukraine to the whole of Europe will make reaching an agreement easier or faster, I fear that is probably a mistaken assumption.

It is very difficult to imagine how such an agreement could come about if its terms are unacceptable to Ukraine and Europe.

Yes. There are several areas where it is difficult to imagine a compromise or common position. Take the issue of security guarantees, for example. Ukraine has made it clear that it wants certain European military units stationed on its territory, that it is not prepared to reduce the size of its armed forces below a certain level and that it is not prepared to give up capabilities such as long-range strikes. Russia, meanwhile, wants all of those things.

So it is difficult to see how a solution could be reached in which Ukraine feels its security is sufficiently guaranteed while Russia believes its ambitions in Ukraine have also been satisfied.

Let's talk a little about the results of the U.S. midterm elections and their potential impact on this war. Donald Trump suffered a painful defeat, but what does that mean? After all, the president still has a very significant role in foreign policy. And although the Financial Times, for example, has reported that Democrats are already rushing to prepare a $15 billion aid package and want to tighten sanctions, what opportunities do they actually have to do so under the American political system?

First, it is worth remembering that the current Congress will remain in office until the beginning of next year. Republicans still control Congress at present. That said, congressional Republicans are generally fairly supportive of Ukraine. Previously, they have tended to follow the president's and the administration's lead and have been reluctant to allocate much additional aid to Ukraine. But following an electoral defeat of this magnitude, it is possible that they may become somewhat more willing to challenge the White House.

Of course, it is true that the president has very extensive powers in foreign policy and it is extremely difficult for Congress to fundamentally change that direction. Lawmakers may be able to delay certain things or create some obstacles, but broadly speaking, the president can continue doing exactly what he wants.

As for sanctions specifically, there has been talk that the president might want to lift sanctions on the Russian Direct Investment Fund and release some of the frozen funds. Here again, it is not entirely clear whether he has the authority to do so. Congress has already placed certain restrictions on the president's ability to take such steps through legislation that establishes conditions that must be met, including that peace must have been achieved in Ukraine and that Congress must be notified 30 days in advance.

However, we have also seen this administration frequently attempt to bypass Congress, in some cases even disregarding the law. All of this can, of course, be challenged in court, but those legal proceedings take time. So Congress does not have many direct ways to block the administration or force it to take particular actions.

If Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will, of course, be able to pass legislation and allocate precisely the kind of financial assistance to Ukraine that they want. But all legislation in the United States still requires the president's signature. Yes, Congress can override a presidential veto, but that requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.

Looking at the numbers now, Democrats do not have enough votes to do that on their own. It would mean that a significant number of congressional Republicans would have to vote alongside Democrats. Whether they would be willing to oppose a president elected from their own party in that way is a major question.

How important is the Ukraine issue to Democrats and to those Republicans who support Ukraine? If they end up negotiating with the president over various issues, will Ukraine be near the top of their priorities or further down the list, where they might be more willing to compromise?

I think congressional Republicans have been quite frustrated by the way President Trump has tried to conduct the Ukraine peace process. They clearly have not liked the agreements that the administration has sought to reach with Russia or has already reached, for example on purchases of Russian diesel and on lifting or postponing certain sanctions that Congress had approved.

So I think this is important to them. And indeed, leading Democratic senators have already indicated that initiating legislation to provide aid to Ukraine will be one of their priorities if they take control of Congress.

But we should not forget that Democrats must now demonstrate to their voters, first and foremost, that they will hold Trump and those close to him accountable before Congress. Various investigations will be launched into a range of issues, from how immigration policy has been implemented to the Trump family's business ties and how certain profits have been made.

Domestic politics will probably remain the Democrats' primary focus, at least initially, but I think they will still have the energy to put Ukraine back on the agenda.

Those investigations could also target Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, who are serving as special envoys in the Ukraine negotiations. Could that have an impact on the peace talks?

Unfortunately, I think it could actually have a negative impact in some respects.

During Trump's first term, investigations were conducted into possible Russian interference in the presidential election, including the support and connections that Russian representatives had with Trump's campaign team. Even then, this generated considerable anger toward Ukraine and a sense of victimhood, with Trump feeling that he was being persecuted by such accusations.

I fear that could happen again. Certain people close to the president will undoubtedly come under congressional investigation and Jared Kushner is likely to be one of them. These investigations will not concern only Russia and Ukraine; Middle Eastern issues are also involved. So it will not be possible to separate this from the broader peace process and relations with Europe and Ukraine.

And perhaps Donald Trump will start taking out his frustrations through foreign policy?

During his second term, Trump has already been more focused on foreign policy. My interpretation is that he wants to emulate great American leaders and presidents such as Ronald Reagan, who achieved very significant arms control agreements with the Soviet Union. Trump wants to accomplish something similar.

I think he will remain very active internationally and will try to implement as much of his agenda as possible, particularly over the next few months, while Republicans still control Congress.

Peace talks are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi next week. What can we expect from them and what role might Europeans play? There was renewed discussion this week about how Europe should be represented at the talks.

Yes, indeed, those talks in Abu Dhabi are scheduled for next week. Let us recall that the previous trilateral meetings of this kind took place in January and February, before the United States launched its military campaign in Iran. So there has been quite a long break in this format.

Very ambitious proposals have now been put on the table. But if we look at what the Ukrainians themselves are saying and what their expectations are, they are much more modest than what the American negotiators are describing.

The Ukrainians' objective is more to try to reach a limited ceasefire, perhaps an agreement to refrain from attacking certain types of facilities on either side. Previous progress has also tended to come on technical and military issues, whether discussions of security guarantees or prisoner-of-war exchanges.

For that reason, I certainly would not expect any major headline-making breakthroughs next week. Rather, this is another attempt to get a major process underway. There are still very few indications that Russia is prepared to abandon certain demands in a way that would make any agreement possible.

As for European participation in these talks, there is still no clear understanding or agreement today about who should represent Europe at such a meeting.

Who should that be?

Fortunately, I am not the one who has to make that decision. But it is clear that for countries on NATO's eastern flank and the European Union's eastern flank, such as Estonia, it is extremely important that our voices are heard.

Everything being discussed there concerns us, particularly if we are talking about the broader European security architecture or restrictions on NATO activities in countries along its borders. Naturally, we would all want to be at that table, which is obviously not possible.

The countries will have to reach an agreement among themselves, but as we can see, that has simply not proved possible so far.

And, in fact, Europe more broadly still lacks confidence in Russia's sincerity in these talks, because we have not seen any signals of goodwill toward Europe suggesting that the Russians are genuinely open to de-escalation at all.

World.title: Estonian real estate developer to build new city district in Latvia's Riga
World.content:
Estonian real estate developer Invego plans to demolish Riga's Skonto, the home stadium of the Latvian national football team, and will build a new, modern urban district in its place.

Invego has agreed to acquire Skonto Stadium at the end of last month and plans to redevelop the site as an urban district connecting historic Riga with Skanste, north of the city center.

The company plans to invest around €100 million to transform the area currently home to Skonto Hall and Stadium into a residential area over 12 years, connecting the Old Town, the city center, and new developments.

"Our vision is to bring the urban environment of the future here. While 15 years ago people wanted to live in their own homes behind fences, today the world's top residential districts or environments are places where there are apartment buildings above, but life happens at ground-floor level – cafes, restaurants, shops, hairdressers and kindergartens," said Invego board member Kristjan-Thor Vähi.

The company has worked in Riga for several years and now considers Latvia its home market. Invego has received several awards for its Latvian projects.

Vähi said, compared with Estonia, large construction projects can be carried out much faster in Latvia.

"In Riga, it took two years from purchasing the property for our large-scale Vitolsi Parks project, with 400 homes, to the start of construction. In Tallinn, that would be unthinkable. What has happened here over the past five years in the cityscape and in all the authorities we deal with, or at every other level – both politically and in business – shows us that something has been done right in Latvia over the past five years. Right now, we certainly feel that Latvia is moving in a very good direction," he said.

A new national stadium will also be built in the same area, on the site of the parliament's vehicle depot opposite Arena Riga.

Edgars Bergholcs, head of the Riga City Council's Urban Development Committee, said the area is Riga's historic center and a protected area, which means strict construction rules apply.

"At the same time, Skonto Stadium no longer meets the requirements of the urban environment that residents would like to see there. Access and car parking are difficult, and its status as part of the historic center is also unsuitable. This creates problems with people getting there, safety and everything else," he said.

World.title: New packaging law draws both praise and criticism from manufacturers
World.content:
The Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce has said it supports the government's plan to abolish the excise duty on packaging but has criticized additional reporting rules.

Under the new draft Packaging Act, the state plans to abolish the excise duty, introduced in 1997, saying it has outlived its usefulness.

The duty has been paid by companies that put packaged goods on the market but have not collected and recycled sufficient packaging waste. It is planned to scrap the tax from July 1, 2027.

In recent years, the state has earned around €300,000 a year from the excise duty. However, Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis (Reform) said revenue from the duty has declined significantly over the years.

"As time has passed and the recycling targets are being met, and on the other hand, only smaller companies are left that have to pay or have paid the duty, there is no longer any point in collecting the packaging excise duty in this form," he said.

Abolishing the tax will not exempt companies from collecting and recycling packaging waste in the future. This obligation also stems from the new waste reform.

"The plan is to transpose the European Union's Packaging Regulation, and the broader goal there is to reduce all kinds of waste generation, particularly packaging waste, and to recycle more packaging," Leis said.

Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis (Reform). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

The Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce supports abolishing the tax as this will reduce producers' obligations.

The organization is also satisfied with a clause in the draft which means companies who place less than 100 tons of packaging on the Estonian market annually will no longer have to submit packaging reports

Until now, the threshold has been 20 tons, said Meeli Lindsaar, the chamber's head of food policy.

"This obligation will remain, but it will apply to those companies whose packaging recycling volumes are significantly larger and whose share of the overall recycling volume is certainly greater," she said.

However, the chamber is concerned about the new EU rules, under which companies will have to give more detailed breakdowns on exactly what type of packaging they use and what they contain, Lindsaar pointed out.

"Here, we are not just distinguishing whether the packaging is made of cardboard, plastic or metal, but within all these groups, it must be specified very precisely what material, what composition, for example, the plastic packaging is made of. But it is not possible to assess this with certainty and know at all times that it is exactly the same. At the same time, industry must declare very precisely all the packaging it receives and what kind of packaging the product is then sent out in," she explained.

Lindsaar added that the idea is understandable from the perspective of packaging recycling, but for industry and producers it represents a major additional burden.

Leis said cooperation with business organizations is ongoing and the current content of the draft may still be refined.

"The broader aim is still to continuously encourage us to waste as little packaging as possible and to recycle more," the minister said.

World.title: Aramco world’s 2nd-most valuable oil and gas brand at $47.3bn: Brand Finance
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi energy giant Aramco retained its position as the world’s second-most valuable oil and gas brand in 2026, with its brand value rising 14 percent to $47.3 billion, its strongest growth in four years, according to a new Brand Finance report.

The increase comes as the Saudi energy giant expands natural gas operations, strengthens its international presence and increases production amid shifting global energy markets.

Shell retained the top position for the 12th consecutive year, with its brand value climbing 14 percent to $51.8 billion. PetroChina ranked third at $35.7 billion, followed by Sinopec Group at $30.4 billion and ExxonMobil at $26 billion.

“Higher production volumes, expansion in gas and a growing international presence have strengthened the brand's revenue outlook,” Brand Finance said in its report.

The consultancy highlighted Aramco’s increased production as OPEC+ eased voluntary output cuts, alongside progress at the Jafurah gas development and Tanajib Gas Plant.

Aramco’s Brand Strength Index score also rose to 81.8 out of 100, reflecting stronger awareness, reputation and engagement, supported partly by its growing presence in international sports.

Global standing

Ali Al-Riyami, former director general of oil and gas marketing at Oman’s Ministry of Energy and Minerals, told Arab News that the ranking reflects Aramco’s evolution beyond crude production.

“Aramco’s brand strength is underpinned by something very tangible: exceptional scale, reliability of supply and a growing presence across the global energy value chain,” he said.

Al-Riyami added that the valuation also reflects the Kingdom’s strategic influence over global energy markets and its expanding capabilities in gas and downstream operations.

Ramzi Abou Abdallah, senior market research analyst at Phystone Financial Advisory, told Arab News that Aramco’s ranking highlights its financial resilience and international expansion.

“Aramco’s position as the world’s second-most valuable oil and gas brand reflects more than its production capacity,” he said.

Abou Abdallah noted that maintaining this position would increasingly depend on revenue diversification, natural gas expansion and adapting to the global energy transition.

Financial momentum

The ranking follows Aramco’s third-quarter results, which showed net profit rising 34.5 percent year on year to $36.3 billion, supported by higher revenue and a gain from selling its stake in Malaysian venture PRefChem.

The company also declared a $21.9 billion quarterly base dividend, up 3.5 percent year on year.

Amid geopolitical tensions and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Aramco has increasingly relied on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline while exploring alternative export routes and overseas storage capacity.

Regional growth

Elsewhere in the Gulf, the UAE’s ADNOC retained sixth place globally, with its brand value rising 11 percent to $21.1 billion.

Across the industry, the combined value of the world’s 50 leading oil and gas brands increased 6 percent to $468.9 billion, reflecting stronger revenue expectations, higher production and continued investment in diversified energy portfolios.

World.title: Erdogan says he conveyed Turkiye’s concerns on potential attacks on Iran to Trump
World.content:
ANKARA: Turkiye does not want to see a new wave of attacks against Iran, President Tayyip Erdogan said, adding that ‌he conveyed ‌his concerns ‌to US President Donald Trump in a recent phone call.

“We emphasize at every opportunity that it is possible ‌to resolve ‌these issues ‌through dialogue and ‌diplomacy. Unfortunately, we see a negative shift once again. ‌We are doing our utmost to prevent this,” Erdogan told reporters on a return flight from Azerbaijan, according to a transcript shared by his office on Monday.

World.title: Kremlin says Abu Dhabi Ukraine talks still ‘trilateral’
World.content:
Moscow: The Kremlin on Monday insisted that upcoming talks in Abu Dhabi to end the Ukraine war will still be held in the Ukraine-Russia-US format, after France announced that Europe will also send representatives.

“What is set to take place in Abu Dhabi are trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine under the mediation of the United States,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

“As for the Europeans, there are separate channels of communication between the Ukrainians and Europeans, as well as the Americans and Europeans,” he added.

World.title: UAE non-oil trade reaches $802bn as exports hit record
World.content:
RIYADH: Record exports helped push the UAE’s non-oil foreign trade up 10.1 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, reaching 2.94 trillion Emirati dirhams ($801.9 billion).

Non-oil exports increased 21.6 percent to 706 billion dirhams, while imports climbed 11.5 percent to 1.66 trillion dirhams. Re-exports totaled 578 billion dirhams, according to the Emirates News Agency.

Exports accounted for 24 percent of total non-oil trade, compared with 21.7 percent a year earlier. Monthly exports exceeded 100 billion dirhams for the first time in September.

The increase highlights the UAE’s efforts to diversify its trading partners and strengthen its position as a regional and global economic hub through a series of international trade deals.

Non-oil trade with the 23 countries covered by the 19 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements in force as of Oct. 20 reached around 510.8 billion dirhams.

UAE Minister of Foreign Trade Thani bin Ahmed Al-Zeyoudi described the CEPAs as playing a “pivotal role” in the exports rise, saying: “They open new markets for UAE exports, ease the movement of goods, lower trade barriers and give national companies wider access to consumers and partners around the world.”

Export markets

Switzerland, Hong Kong and India were the leading export destinations, with gold, jewelry and tobacco products topping shipments.

Saudi Arabia was the largest destination for re-exports, followed by Iraq and Oman.

Non-oil trade with the 23 countries covered by the 19 CEPAs in force as of Oct. 20 reached around 510.8 billion dirhams.

Expanding trade agreements

The figures come as the UAE expands its network of agreements designed to lower trade barriers and improve market access.

Its agreement with Vietnam entered into force on Feb. 3, immediately removing tariffs on more than 95 percent of qualifying goods, including products from free zones, according to the UAE Ministry of Economy and Tourism.

The deal also simplifies customs procedures and covers services and investment.

More recently, the UAE and Canada signed a CEPA during Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan’s October visit to Ottawa, following negotiations that concluded in July.

A joint statement published by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the countries aimed to improve access to each other’s markets, strengthen supply chains and increase investment flows.

Their priorities include logistics, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, agriculture and digital technologies.

World.title: Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
World.content:
DUBAI: Iran ‌defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran’s conditions “outrageous and ridiculous.”

“Is it unreasonable that Iran ‌demands that ‌US illegal sanctions and its ‌naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio’s remarks.

Iran has ‌made the ‌offer to shorten the time to ‌restart talks from an earlier seven-day ‌proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.

Baghaei ‌also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq’s foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran’s land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump’s Republicans’ losses in midterm elections.

World.title: Oman-India Joint Naval Exercise “Sea Breeze 2026” Begins
World.content:
The joint Omani-Indian naval exercise “Naseem Al Bahr 2026” began today, carried out by a number of ships from the Royal Navy of Oman and the Indian Navy, in the Al Batinah maritime area in the Sultanate of Oman.

The exercise, which continues until November 12, includes many theoretical and practical applications, the execution of a number of naval maneuvers and exercises, in addition to the exchange of experiences between the crews of the participating ships, according to the planned exercise schedule.

World.title: Palestinian cookbook releases new edition as author reflects on food as ‘a form of resistance’
World.content:
TORONTO: Written amid hopes for a Middle East peace process, “Classic Palestinian Cookery” was first released in 2001. “We really thought that peace was becoming a reality” and the book was “an expression of all this hope,” author Christiane Dabdoub Nasser told Arab News.

More than two decades later, as the book — now titled “Classic Palestinian Cuisine” — releases its 25th-anniversary edition this month, Dabdoub said that hope has faded, even as the book’s importance remains.

More than two decades later, as the book — now titled “Classic Palestinian Cuisine” — releases its 25th-anniversary edition this month. (Supplied)

For her, food is a form of cultural preservation, bound up with memory and identity amid years of war and displacement.

“We are dealing with an opponent that wants to erase (our) memory and our presence,” Dabdoub said. Israel takes “(our) land, our rights and sometimes our very humanity,” but also appropriates food such as falafel, “hijacking” it to rewrite history and build the country’s identity, she added.

Food culture is used to brand nations, she said, and Palestinians “really have to get on the bandwagon,” because food is the “national identity,” “political struggle” and “form of resistance” of the Palestinian people.

Among the new recipes, Dabdoub said, are three from Gaza — her small way of “putting a different label” on the war-torn territory — where people are “living their lives over the rubble.” It is an invitation for readers to view Gaza as a place “where people lived, loved and died,” because “the way Israel has portrayed Gaza over the years is scandalous,” she said.

Christiane Dabdoub Nasser. (Supplied)

The book also features family favorite recipes such as ruz hashweh, which Dabdoub’s grandchildren consider “comfort food,” and m’loukhiyeh, an elaborate Sunday dish, she said. It closes with suggested menus, such as for a Ramadan iftar or Christmas Eve dinner, made up of dishes from its recipe sections.

Ultimately, Dabdoub hopes the book will “create a buzz.” It is “not just about cooking,” she said, but about “a lifestyle that has all but disappeared,” and it matters because “people should look at Palestinians as human beings.”

World.title: Building fire kills 14 in China’s northern city of Taiyuan
World.content:
BEIJING: ‌A fire on Sunday at a high-rise building in Taiyuan, the capital of China’s ​northern province of Shanxi, killed at least 14 people, the official Xinhua news agency said on Monday.

State media said 25 people were still in hospital, nine with serious injuries, citing authorities after the fire broke ‌out on Sunday ‌evening in the ​building ‌on ⁠a ​busy downtown ⁠main road.

Smoke billowed over the 40-story structure as firefighters poised on cranes outside fought flames that spread upward from a lower annex, video images circulated online and verified by Reuters showed.

The ⁠fire appears to have ‌started around the ‌fourth floor of the annex ​before spreading ‌to the eighth and ninth floors, ‌which house a hotel, the state broadcaster said.

The entire building is a mixed-use commercial and residential property with several hotels, short-term ‌rental apartments, smaller venues as well as tutoring centers, the report ⁠said.

The ⁠fire was put out after about two hours and authorities said rescue operations wrapped up by 8:30 p.m. on Sunday night, with 38 people taken to hospital.

Authorities are investigating the cause of the fire in the northern manufacturing hub, state media added.

World.title: World Bank backs Iraq’s shift toward program and performance budgeting
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The World Bank reaffirmed its institutional support on Monday, November 9, 2026, for the Iraqi Ministry of Finance’s ongoing modernization agenda, focusing on technical requirements to transition Iraq’s fiscal planning toward a program- and performance-based budgeting framework.

According to a Ministry of Finance statement reported by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Senior Undersecretary Abdul-Hasan Jamal convened an extensive technical working session with a World Bank mission.

The deliberations were attended by the directors general of the Public Debt and Information Technology departments, alongside the ministry’s dedicated project implementation task force, to evaluate core prerequisites and execution roadmaps for the budgeting shift.

Jamal emphasized the necessity of finalizing statutory and regulatory frameworks, conducting rigorous cost-benefit assessments, and clearly designating spending units across line ministries.

He noted that moving away from conventional line-item budgeting to performance-driven fiscal management aligns directly with broader economic and administrative reform programs, ensuring cohesive institutional alignment among spending entities.

For its part, the World Bank delegation reiterated its commitment to supporting public financial management (PFM) reforms across Iraq, underlining that digitizing accounting frameworks and automating treasury workflows remain essential catalysts for curbing fiscal leakage, improving capital allocation, and enhancing aggregate expenditure efficiency.

World.title: Iraq weather: Freezing cold wave sweeps in as rainfall tapers off
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Meteorological and Seismology Organization announced that rain chances will taper off gradually starting Monday morning, November 9, 2026, as a brisk cold air mass moves across the country, driving overnight temperatures down toward the freezing mark across northern highlands and the Kurdistan Region.

According to an official weather advisory, satellite telemetry tracked the departing active front alongside dense cloud bands moving across central, northern, and eastern governorates.

Lingering precipitation will remain concentrated across Baghdad, Diyala, Wasit, Sulaymaniyah, Erbil, Kirkuk, Saladin, eastern Anbar, and Maysan before dissipating during early morning hours, with isolated showers persisting until midday Monday around eastern Sulaymaniyah and northern Erbil.

Meteorologists indicated that the incoming cold front will become pronounced by Monday morning, precipitating a steep temperature drop initially felt in northern governorates and the Kurdistan Region before extending across central and western provinces, with milder cooling across the south.

Low temperatures across northeastern basins are projected to hover near 0°C (32°F) by dawn on Tuesday, with sub-zero conditions across high-altitude mountain elevations. Authorities urged the public to dress warmly and take standard cold-weather precautions during late-night and early-morning commutes.

World.title: Iraq budget deficit widens to 32.8 trillion dinars through September 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Official budget execution figures released by Iraq’s Ministry of Finance for the first nine months of 2026 revealed a widening fiscal deficit of 32.858 trillion dinars, driven by a sharp drop in hydrocarbon returns and the continued dominance of mandatory operational expenditures.

According to treasury disclosures, aggregate state revenues through late September 2026 reached 52.822 trillion dinars, against total public expenditures of 85.680 trillion dinars.

Hydrocarbon revenues constituted 76% of total treasury receipts, generating 40.202 trillion dinars, while non-oil revenues contributed 12.620 trillion dinars, or roughly 24% of state income.

Operational spending categories consumed the vast majority of resources, with public-sector payroll obligations (employee compensation) totaling 46.135 trillion dinars—effectively absorbing 87.3% of all state revenues collected during the period.

Social welfare transfers ranked second at 20.572 trillion dinars, followed by subsidies, grants, debt interest, and incidental outlays at 7.601 trillion dinars. Commodity procurement totaled 3.007 trillion dinars, service requirements accounted for 203.9 billion dinars, and asset maintenance spending stood at 57.7 billion dinars.

On an annualized basis, federal revenues experienced a steep 42.1% contraction, dropping by 38.347 trillion dinars from the 91.168 trillion dinars recorded during the corresponding period in 2025. The decline was heavily precipitated by a 50.8% plunge in crude oil earnings, down from 81.749 trillion dinars in 2025.

Conversely, non-oil domestic revenues registered a 34% increase, rising from 9.420 trillion dinars to 12.620 trillion dinars—a fiscal expansion driven by enhanced customs and tax enforcement, though still insufficient to offset high public payroll allocations.

World.title: US dollar ticks up across Iraqi parallel markets near 169,500 dinars
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate of the U.S. dollar against the Iraqi dinar edged upward across parallel exchange markets on Monday morning, November 9, 2026, with buying rates consolidating at the 168,000 IQD threshold across major commercial hubs after roughly a week of stabilizing around 167,000 IQD per $100. Retail selling rates in the capital, Baghdad, approached the 169,500 IQD barrier.

According to morning monitoring data from major trading centers, physical cash rates stood as follows:

Baghdad: Currency exchange counters posted retail selling rates at 169,450 IQD against buying bids of 168,000 IQD per $100.

Erbil: Selling desks recorded 168,550 IQD, with purchasing offers settling at 168,000 IQD per $100.

Basra: Foreign exchange bureaus quoted retail sales at 168,750 IQD alongside buying prices of 168,250 IQD per $100.

This upward momentum further widens the spread between secondary physical cash markets and the Central Bank of Iraq’s (CBI) official benchmark rate, fixed at 152,000 IQD per $100 (1,520 IQD per dollar), underscoring persistent informal market demand for banknotes to finance regional trade flows outside official wire mechanisms.

World.title: Tech firms claw back some losses after midterms rout, eyes on Nvidia
World.content:
Hong Kong – Tech firms rose Monday to claw back some of last week’s painful losses fuelled by AI regulation worries, though traders were keeping a wary eye on a probe into Nvidia boss Jensen Huang amid claims of an affair with a Chinese spy.

Chipmakers and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence boom took a hammering in the days after Tuesday’s US midterms saw Democrats sweep both houses of Congress in a rebuke to Donald Trump and his Republican party.

The results suggested voters were angry at the president’s Iran war and tariffs, which have sent prices soaring, as well as a sharp kickback against the huge data centre buildout that has taken place across the country in recent years.

That has led to speculation the new Congress will seek to wind in tech firms’ construction drive, which could put thousands of jobs at risk.

The uncertainty comes with traders already nervous about when the hundreds of billions of dollars pumped into the sector would actually see a profit.

After taking a lashing on Thursday, Wall Street enjoyed a little stability at the end of last week, and Asia — which had suffered a hammering itself on Friday — largely followed suit to start this week.

Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei — which are heavily weighted with AI-linked tech giants — led the advances.

The Japanese Nikkei 225 piled on more than three percent thanks to rallies in Kioxia, Tokyo Electron and Advantest, while SK hynix and Samsung piled on around three percent to push the South Korean Kospi sharply higher.

Taiwan’s TSMC rocketed nearly six percent to drag the Taiex five percent higher.

There were also healthy gains in Hong Kong and Shanghai, though Sydney, Wellington and Manila edged down.

“Investors will be watching carefully this week to get a sense as to whether these gains are just short-covering, bargain hunting or the beginning of something more sustainable in nature,” said Sally Auld at National Australia Bank.

“Fears around AI regulation, the outlook for (capital expenditure) and free cash flow have been the driver of risk reduction in recent weeks and these issues are not likely to be resolved with any conviction in the near term.

“Nonetheless, the valuation of many tech stocks now looks less expensive.”

– Nvidia probe –

However, a little more uncertainty was injected into markets with news that Nvidia’s board was launching an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted in a foreign espionage plot following his admission that he was unfaithful to his wife.

The New York Times reported last month that US intelligence officials concluded a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed had been funnelling information to Beijing.

The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.

Nvidia is a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models and one of the world’s most valuable companies, and last year became the first to reach a market capitalisation of $5 trillion.

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the AI revolution and a close informal adviser to Trump, and the Times said the Nvidia boss’s extra-marital relationship could have revealed insights into Trump’s thinking around AI.

Technology analyst Dan Ives, at investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the crisis will at the very least spark multiple congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons”.

“This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” Ives added. “This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC.”

Investors will be keeping tabs this week on the release of fresh US inflation data, after figures Friday showed the economy created far more jobs than expected in October.

The figures will key for the Federal Reserve in determining whether or not to hike interest rates when it meets next in December, with markets saying there is an 80 percent chance of a lift.

World.title: Under fire over AI, effective altruism wants to tell its own story
World.content:
New York – The effective altruism movement, which has close ties to the AI community and the companies leading the artificial intelligence boom, has drawn mainstream attention and accusations of cult-like behavior and alarmism.

The hard-to-define movement is still growing, and wants to better explain its values amid bitter criticism from the Trump administration and some powerful voices in Silicon Valley.

Its founding principle is to give money or time to major causes as effectively as possible, an intentionally dispassionate approach has at times been called out of touch.

The New York Post called it a “wacky cult,” the conservative Daily Caller dubbed it “The AI Doomsday Cartel,” and a White House memo accused it of preferring the saving of “shrimp over families.”

Once little known outside the tech world and some academic and political circles, effective altruism (EA) has been in the spotlight in recent weeks after a series of warnings about AI risks.

Those warnings were linked to EA. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and adviser to President Donald Trump, argued that organizations tied to EA are part of a “Doomer Industrial Complex” pushing for tougher AI regulation.

– ‘Strange’ ideas –

EA is deeply rooted in Silicon Valley and counts controlling AI’s dangers among its priorities.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei is considered a key figure in EA’s early days, although he now distances himself from the movement.

Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, Dario’s sister, is married to Holden Karnofsky, an Anthropic employee and a leading EA proponent.

The movement has also influenced researchers and staff at other AI companies, including ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, particularly those working on AI safety.

The movement, which took shape about 15 years ago, is used to criticism.

Wealthy EA donors have often been accused of self-importance and of believing they alone know how best to give.

“Our ideas are just strange enough that people genuinely misinterpret them sometimes, and we can do a better job explaining how effective altruism approaches hard questions and tradeoffs,” said Zachary Robinson, head of the Centre for Effective Altruism.

Robinson, whose organization supports the movement without directing it, sees the scrutiny since the summer as an opportunity to open up rather than retreat, because “people are curious to learn about us now.”

After growing steadily until 2022, EA was badly damaged by the collapse of cryptocurrency platform FTX and its founder Sam Bankman-Fried, once the face of EA and later convicted of fraud.

After several difficult years, “We’re on an up right now,” Robinson said, pointing to attendance at the EA Global conference in New York in mid-October.

Like many at EA Global, Shanil Wijesinghe who works at a Canadian non-profit rejected the image of EA as monolithic. “It is a values-based movement and not an identity-based movement,” he said.

“We’re all trying to do the most good, with the resources we have,” he said. Those values “can be interpreted differently, and I think we have to embrace those differences.”

– No leader –

EA has no leader or spokesperson. Sjir Hoeijmakers, head of the charity platform Giving What We Can, said that is a good thing, even if it means “sometimes the story doesn’t get told.”

Still, “effective altruism is now a movement large enough that it’s actually really influencing the world, and that’s getting noticed,” he said.

“I think the work that they’re doing has been quite valuable,” said Nadav Brandes, a genetics researcher also at EA Global, referring to AI safety.

“Without those pioneers… nobody would still today take this issue very seriously,” he added.

Brandes said he was initially skeptical when AI became a major EA cause, joining climate change and animal welfare.

“It was even a little bit off-putting to me,” he recalled. “I was totally wrong about it.”

Robinson stressed, however, that EA is about more than AI.

“The cause that gets the most emphasis right now is AI safety, but I think it would be false to say EA is AI safety,” he said.

“If you look at the money side of things, actually, it’s been the case for many years that global health and development gets much more money than AI,” he said.

World.title: G7 ministers meet on efforts to end Ukraine conflict, halt new Iran war
World.content:
Paris – Foreign ministers of the G7 group meet in Paris from Monday for two days of talks expected to see European powers press the United States to seek a fair settlement for Ukraine in the war against Russia and deter Washington from further military action against Iran.

Ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will be gathering with preoccupations strikingly similar to those of the last such meeting in March.

Russia’s war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterms.

All eyes will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who is due to attend both days, unlike the March meeting where he only came for one.

This G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Donald Trump for the leaders’ summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille.

But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change.

The visit by Rubio — seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump — will be his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will also in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France.

– ‘Europeans will be represented’ –

The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that on this occasion “Europeans will be represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these talks”.

Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a “very big” deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but “all of Europe”.

Jared Kushner, the US president’s envoy and son-in-law, said the United States was working on “a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace”, a concept met with scepticism in the past by Europe.

On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.

“We’re dealing with them now,” Trump said of the Iranians Friday. “They want to make a deal very badly.”

The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine’s Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year.

Around 500 million euros is required but only just over half has been raised so far with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP.

Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said.

As he addressed reporters while preparing to leave for France, Rubio declined to comment directly on Trump’s and the Republicans’ crushing loss in the US midterm elections.

“It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country,” Rubio told reporters, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats.

Asked about widespread protests in France, Rubio added that he was not worried and trusted US counterparts on the ground who advised him it is safe to attend the G7 meeting.
