World.title: #CourageON: Why this climate activist still believes in COP31
World.content:
JOSHUA VILLALOBOS. Climate activist and secretary-general of Negrosanon Initiative for Climate and the Environment, Joshua Villalobos, visits Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, to work on the solar-powered facilities of the island in October 2026.

For Joshua Villalobos, COP31 would be a success if it means more money flowing into the communities he works with, particularly for projects that provide renewable energy

“Am I optimistic about this COP? Well, that’s a challenging question.”

Usually quick-witted, Joshua Villalobos took time to gather his thoughts about the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) happening this November. He is a climate activist and secretary-general of the Negrosanon Initiative for Climate and the Environment (NICE). In November 2025, we featured him in a story on young Filipinos championing renewable energy across the Philippines.

JOSHUA VILLALOBOS. Climate activist and secretary-general of the Negrosanon Initiative for Climate and the Environment, Joshua Villalobos, visits Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, to work on the solar-powered facilities of the island in October 2026. Photo courtesy of Joshua Villalobos

“Sometimes, the talks within the negotiations are taking so much time. The talks have been ongoing [for] the past three decades.”

The world has struggled to meet the commitments made in these negotiations. For one, countries agreed in 2015 to keep global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

“There’s a new report that we’ll overshoot the 1.5,” he said.

The work of climate activists like Joshua isn’t confined to the streets. Behind the placards and protests, they pore over lengthy documents and study climate policies. Joshua, in fact, finds the law “beautiful.” But what keeps him invested in the negotiations is the possibility of seeing solutions.

“Most of these solutions are being championed by communities, people’s organizations, environmental movements. These are things that I am optimistic about.”

WORK. Members of NICE conduct a meeting at their hub in Bacolod City. Photo by Aidan Bernales/Rappler

Based in Bacolod City, Joshua works closely with the people of Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental. Matabas, like many small islands in the Philippines, used to have no electricity.

Once, at night, Joshua witnessed island residents sleeping outside their homes. Without electricity, households didn’t have the luxury of electric fans or air-conditioning. “We are seeing how they are paying the price in their daily lives, sleeping outside because of the heat,” he said.

Through partnerships with foundations, Joshua’s organization, NICE, installed solar panels to light up communal areas, including the island’s walkways. NICE now hopes to power the island’s water desalination facility to give residents access to fresh water. It also plans to bring electricity to the island’s only school.

For Joshua, COP31 would be a success if it meant more money flowing into the communities he works with, particularly for projects that provide renewable energy.

During COP30 in 2025, parties agreed to develop a just transition mechanism. This year, discussions are expected to further define how the mechanism will work.

NICE is a member of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, a Philippine civil society network that prepares policy positions and proposals ahead of COP. The network also held a pre-COP31 conference on just transition in October.

For Joshua, the pre-COP31 conference was an important opportunity to bring the realities of communities in Negros and other parts of the Philippines into the discussions.

“We know that these communities are already paying the price for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Joshua explained.

“If we don’t make the transition just, then they will most likely pay the price of the transition… through job displacement, land displacement, or environmental degradation.”

MATABAS ISLAND. Joshua Villalobos (extreme left) visits Matabas Island in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, to work on the island’s solar-powered facilities in October 2026. Photo courtesy of Joshua Villalobos

Joshua will attend the second week of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, bringing with him stories from the communities he has worked with.

“It is exactly because of the work that we are doing year-round [that] we are going to the COP more informed about the realities of the communities and demand what the COP should deliver.”

Still, Joshua is not confident that the negotiations will deliver political breakthroughs. Climate negotiations tend to be exclusive, technical, and jargon-laden. Joshua understands why young people and communities affected by the climate crisis might lose faith in the process. Many of them also struggle to find the money to participate.

Asked why he continues to attend the annual climate conference despite its shortcomings, he answered: “For now, there’s no alternative for that kind of global space where communities can raise our voices and governments are there.”

“It is still a space that we must not give up on, and we should continue to fight for.” – Rappler.com

#CourageON is a bi-monthly newsletter providing updates from our communities. In time for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), the month of November features stories of courage and resilience from our partner communities and advocates.

World.title: [Rear View] A ‘pink wave’ in 2028? Not so fast.
World.content:
The pink movement needs to accept that the ground shifted in 2016, a shift affirmed in 2019 and 2022. It cannot wait for history to repeat itself, and should not plan for it.

The day after the historic midterm elections in the United States, the Liberal Party (LP) and Akbayan, the organized core formations of the pink movement, released statements hailing the Democratic “blue wave.” Pink online pundits and the faithful boldly prophesied a “pink wave” in 2028, declaring that if it can happen in Donald Trump’s America, it can happen here.

The liberal progressive bloc’s affinity with the Democrats, the democratic socialist wing in particular, runs deep. They share the vocabulary and cultural anchors. They are evangelistic in their campaigns to fire up the youth vote. But the “blue wave” rode a national grievance over prices and an unpopular war. The pinks would do well to proceed with caution.

The 2028 election is not a midterm; it’s an open race for the presidency. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., thankfully, cannot run again, but he is very much a player in 2028 despite his absence from the ballot. The abysmal state of the economy, the high cost of living, soaring prices, inefficient public services, and corruption are his legacy, and that legacy gives voters the permission structure to support anybody but a Marcos clone.

Who gets the grievance voters in 2028?

The question, and the challenge, for the pinks is who collects the grievance vote. The surveys all say it’s Vice President Sara Duterte.

She remains the front-runner despite unexplained wealth allegations now at the center of her impeachment trial and persistent questions about her grasp of policy. Pulse Asia’s September survey had her at 50% nationally, nearly double Leni Robredo’s 26. In Mindanao, where identity politics comes into play, she is at 92%. Other surveys show support for her thinning, but she remains, for now, the candidate of the aggrieved.

Unless the Senate impeachment court convicts her and declares her unfit for public office, the Vice President is the competition for the anti-incumbent vote, and the pinks will have to capture those voters from her.

Unlike the two-party system, our multi-party system extends to voters a wide range of choices. In a crowded field, a fractured opposition in 2028 is a gift to the Vice President. Brazil and Serbia offer better models of coalition building than the US: progressive presidential candidates won by working with people and parties outside their own base, a concept that the pink movement has always found hard to embrace.

The pinks did have their “pink wave” moment in the 2025 midterms, with real and hard earned victories. But the presidency is a winner-take-all contest, and the same movement that can elect senators and party-lists can lose the presidency. We saw it in 2022: the pink movement mustered the largest rallies and the most star-studded endorsements in recent memory, and Robredo still finished with roughly 15 million votes to Marcos’s nearly 32 million.

With presidential voter turnout at above 80%, the pinks cannot win by just mobilizing their own. They have to persuade voters who voted for Marcos and Duterte in 2022, the same voters they continue to regard with disdain and talk down to.

‘Disente’

The LP also carries a burden the US Democrats, for all their troubles, do not. For many voters, the LP has come to embody elitist politics. It is a damaged brand, and the damage is partly self-inflicted.

The Democrats did not win on decency. They won on affordability, and on high gas prices as a result of the Iran war, with strong candidates perfectly fitted for the states they ran in. The Liberals and their pink allies proudly declared itself “disente” in 2016 and 2019, and the DDS caricatured them as preachy, elitist, and out of touch.

Unfortunately, that caricature has taken hold, and it is an uncomfortable weakness they must confront. If they want to be relevant in 2028, talk less about character and more about gut issues, about bigas, kuryente, at trabaho.

2010 rewind

The party’s old guards still wish for another 2010. The late Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino was an accidental candidate. His mother’s death in August 2009 put him front and center, Mar Roxas stepped aside, and a grieving nation found its standard-bearer in a matter of weeks, one who was the opposite of outgoing president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo.

It happened at a time when mainstream media still had the power to make or unmake candidates. That country no longer exists.

Voters today live in partisan chambers that are both political and identity-based. Partisans are willing to overlook the character flaws of politicians they regard as their own, and to disbelieve anything that comes from the other side. A sympathy wave needs a shared audience, and there is no shared audience anymore. The pinks cannot wait for history to repeat itself, and they should not plan for it.

Self-reflection

Before the pink movement plunges into the murky, gritty battles of 2028, it needs to look inward, to accept that the ground shifted in 2016, a shift affirmed in 2019 and 2022. The liberal opposition failed, or refused, to recalibrate, bemoaning disinformation without confronting it head on, dismissing unfavorable surveys while extolling favorable ones, no matter how questionable the science. And it bears repeating: it must stop blaming the voters for their own shortcomings.

Finally, it must accept one inconvenient fact: Robredo, hailed as the movement’s face and hope, has said she will not run in 2028. Liberal stalwarts and ardent supporters, however, refuse to give up.

So go ahead and admire the Democrats, but use their victory as an opportunity for self-reflection. With neither a machinery nor, as of today, a candidate, the pinks are not yet primed to secure the votes of aggrieved Filipinos. The hard work began yesterday. – Rappler.com

Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

World.title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to ‘move faster’ on climate
World.content:
COP31. Vehicles drive under an overpass near the venue on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9, 2026.

The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference are an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders of the COP31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as rising temperatures and an increasing number of climate-driven disasters threaten lives and the global economy, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday, November 9.

The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention.

“The urgency of this moment must drive us forward,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in prepared remarks for the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was “nowhere near fast enough.”

A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already set to overshoot 1.5ºC of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.

This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Niño, a UN report showed on Monday. 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still ​missing.

Turkey’s COP31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

“We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs,” Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said in prepared remarks.

But climate advocates have criticized the pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

War and tech

The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.

The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.

US President Donald Trump’s administration — which is shunning climate talks for the second year running — has encouraged policies maximizing oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions.

South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.

Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.

“This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” he said.

“But the solutions are clear,” he added, saying renewable energy installations had saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.

The rapid rollout of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.

Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at COP31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of COP31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.

“Paris is working,” he said, referring to the landmark 2015 deal to limit global warming. “But we must move faster.” – Rappler.com

World.title: 4,000 multipurpose buildings cover just 10% of barangays – solons
World.content:
House of Representatives. Inquirer file photo

MANILA, Philippines — The roughly 4,000 multipurpose buildings proposed under the 2027 national budget represent only 10 percent of the country’s more than 42,000 barangays, House lawmakers said on Monday as they defended funding for community facilities.

Bataan 2nd District Rep. Albert Garcia, senior vice chair of the House Committee on Appropriations, said the number highlighted the continuing need for public facilities, particularly in remote communities outside Metro Manila.

“If I recall correctly, we have around 4,000 multi-purpose buildings. And how many barangays do we have? 42,000 barangays. So that is a mere 10 percent of the needs of our barangays across the nation,” Garcia said at a press conference.

Article continues after this 

READ: House backs purge of undocumented projects in 2027 national budget

Garcia said multipurpose buildings serve as evacuation centers, covered courts, barangay meeting places, and venues for community activities.

He said some facilities in agricultural areas are also used to dry palay [unhusked rice], providing additional support to farmers.

Negros Oriental 3rd District Rep. Janice Degamo of Lakas said many remote sitios have no public facilities apart from schools, forcing residents to use a single structure for different community activities.

“Sometimes, in one structure, you do everything you have to do there because there are no other venues,” Degamo said in Filipino.

Article continues after this 

Camarines Sur 4th District Rep. Arnie Fuentebella of the Nationalist People’s Coalition said the proposed 4,000 facilities would still be insufficient to meet the needs of barangays nationwide.

“If you think about those 4,000, they seem insufficient because they’re only 10 percent of the barangays in the entire Philippines,” Fuentebella said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Solon says House only amended P115B in 2027 budget bill

He stressed that requests for multipurpose buildings originated from local officials and communities that lacked the resources to construct their own facilities.

The lawmakers made the remarks amid questions over the reported ₱43-billion increase in funding for multipurpose buildings under the House-approved 2027 national budget.

World.title: Village councilor, pastor found dead in Cagayan
World.content:
TUGUEGARAO CITY – The bullet-riddled remains of a village councilor and a church pastor were found dumped at a mountainous section of Barangay Capissayan Norte in Gattaran, Cagayan last weekend.

Responders recovered the bodies of Johnny Agarpao, a 52-year-old San Miguel village councilor and 30-year-old pastor Jeferson De Leon of Baggao town.

A farmer, who was tending to his grazing carabao, saw one of the bodies.

Article continues after this 

When disaster responders and police arrived at the area, they also discovered the other body about 35-meter away from the first discovered remains

Further investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Court inspects Payatas jail after tackling Romualdez detention issues
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division on Monday inspected the New Quezon City Jail-Male Dormitory of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), where former House Speaker Martin Romualdez is detained.

Romualdez was jailed in connection with a plunder case stemming from an alleged P7.44 billion kickback in infrastructure projects.

WATCH: COURT INSPECTS PAYATAS JAIL AFTER ROMUALDEZ ISSUE Sandiganbayan Third Division chair Karl Miranda and Associate Justice Fritz Bryn Anthony Delos Santos, along with representatives from the prosecution and defense, inspect Payatas Jail on Monday afternoon. @inquirerdotnet https://t.co/uv3cf7prc7 — John Eric Mendoza (@JEMendozaINQ) November 9, 2026

Third Division chairperson Associate Justice Karl Miranda and Associate Justice Fritz Bryn Anthony Delos Santos led the inspection.

Article continues after this 

Also with them were Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal and Romualdez’s lawyer Judd Roy.

“The purpose of this inspection is to verify compliance with the Court’s commitment order and determine whether established procedures are being faithfully observed,” the Third Division said in a statement.

The ocular inspection, the court said, “should not be interpreted as a finding that any irregularity has occurred.”

“The Court has reached no conclusion concerning the allegations or the conduct of any person,” it added.

A post by columnist Ramon Tulfo that Romualdez allegedly could go in and out of jail prompted the court to conduct a hearing to check on the lawmaker’s condition in jail.

Article continues after this 

Tulfo, who has since retracted his post, reported that Romualdez was riding in an ambulance and that the brownouts were happening so he would not be seen leaving and returning to his cell.

The columnist said that “no such thing happened when the facts started coming in yesterday.”

Article continues after this 

During its hearings, however, the court learned that Romualdez has an aide who is on call 24 hours a day to attend to his medical needs.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has said that he will also conduct a “surprise” visit at the BJMP after learning that Romualdez has a staffer inside the facility. /gsg

World.title: Ex-Sultan Kudarat solon facing malversation raps yields in GenSan
World.content:
COTABATO CITY – Former Sultan Kudarat Rep. Arnulfo Go, who was charged for alleged malversation of public funds and corruption, voluntarily surrendered to police authorities in General Santos City on Sunday, Brig. Gen. Alan Manibog, Police Regional Office-12 director, confirmed Monday.

“He voluntarily and peacefully surrendered to us on Sunday and we have turned him over to the Sandiganbayan today (Nov.9),” told the Inquirer by phone.

Manibog said Go, a businessman from Lebak, Sultan Kudarat, surrendered to police units from Sultan Kudarat province and General Santos City along Mabuhay Road, Barangay San Isidro.

Article continues after this 

The surrender stemmed from four warrants of arrest issued by the Sandiganbayan in connection with cases involving alleged violations of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code on Malversation of Public Funds.

Manibog said Go was informed of the nature of the warrants and apprised of his constitutional rights.

“The voluntary surrender of a wanted person underscores the importance of sustained coordination and the enforcement of arrest warrants,” Manibog said.

“We will continue to intensify our operations to ensure that individuals facing criminal charges are brought before the proper legal process,” Manibog added.

On July 27, 2026, anti-graft court Sandiganbayan issued an arrest warrant against Go in a malversation case involving over P8.8 million in public funds.

Article continues after this 

The warrant also includes municipal accountant Allan Gayoso Bayani and municipal treasurer Mario Abasolo Labrador.

The anti-graft court Third Division said it found probable cause for the arrest of Go and the two others.

Article continues after this 

State prosecutors indicted Go as well as Bayani and Labrador on November 25 last year for violation of Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code (Malversation of Public Funds).

The Sandiganbayan also issued a hold departure order against the accused. /gsg

World.title: Son stabs dad to death in Lipa City
World.content:
LUCENA CITY – A 40-year-old man was stabbed to death by his 20-year-old son following a heated argument inside their home in Lipa City, Batangas on Sunday night (November 8), police said.

In a report on Monday, the Police Regional Office 4-A said the father and son, who were both reportedly under the influence of liquor, were having dinner at their residence in Barangay Banay-Banay at around 8:30 p.m. when an argument broke out.

The disagreement escalated into a physical altercation.

Article continues after this 

During the scuffle, the father was being restrained by his nephew when his son suddenly grabbed a kitchen knife and stabbed him in the chest.

The victim was rushed to a hospital, where he was declared dead on arrival.

Police later arrested the suspect, who is now detained and will face appropriate criminal charges.

The police report did not disclose what triggered the argument between the father and son.

World.title: Month-long drive vs. loose firearms nets 311 weapons in Soccsksargen
World.content:
COTABATO CITY – Three hundred eleven assorted weapons were recovered and 27 individuals were arrested in the campaign against unlicensed firearms in the Soccsksargen region (Region 12) in October, police said Monday.

“The intensified operations aim to prevent loose firearms from falling into the hands of criminal elements across the region,” Brig. Gen. Alan Manibog, Police Regional Office-12 (PRO-12), director, said.

He said the operations resulted in the recovery, confiscation, surrender, deposit, abandonment, or forfeiture of 311 firearms, one explosive device, and 803 rounds of ammunition.

Article continues after this 

The 311 firearms recovered consisted of 299 small arms and 12 light weapons. Manibog said.

He said all the 311 firearms were confiscated under the “Bilang Boga operations,” “101 Oplan Katok” activities, implementations of search warrants, police responses to crime, implementations of warrants of arrest, checkpoints operation, “Oplan Bakal Sita,” buy-bust, and internal security operations.

The North Cotabato Police Provincial Office (PPO) recorded the most number of firearms recovered, with 91 consisting of 88 small arms and three light weapons followed by South Cotabato PPO with 72 firearms.

Sultan Kudarat PPO recovered 64 firearms while the Sarangani PPO recovered 52 firearms and 10 rounds of ammunition.

The General Santos City Police Office (GSCPO) recovered 32 small firearms and 50 rounds of ammunition.

Article continues after this 

“We will continue to intensify our campaign against loose firearms and illegal weapons through sustained operations, community engagement, and strict enforcement of the law,” Manibog said in a statement.

“We also urge the public to cooperate with our police personnel to prevent the use of firearms and explosives in criminal activities and ensure the safety and security of our communities,” he added. /gsg

World.title: EcoWaste bats for crackdown on mercury-laced beauty products
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—EcoWaste Coalition has urged health product and digital trade regulators to remove online listings of mercury-laced skin lightening products and step up enforcement against their sellers ahead of the 11.11 and 12.12 shopping sales.

The group identified Goree Beauty Cream as a priority for enforcement, describing it as the most visible mercury-laden skin-lightening brand on the market and the one most frequently flagged by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

“We are outraged that illegal, high-mercury skin lighteners continue to be smuggled and sold openly all over the country, whether online, on social media, or in physical stores,” said Aileen Lucero, EcoWaste Coalition national coordinator.

Article continues after this 

“Despite the Minamata Convention’s ban on mercury-added cosmetics and nonstop FDA public health warnings, the illegal trade continues without being stopped or punished,” she said.

Lucero warned that mercury exposure could damage the skin, kidneys, brain and central nervous system, while also threatening reproductive health and unborn children.

“Mercury buildup in the body is a critical health hazard. It can seriously damage the skin, kidneys, brain, and central nervous system, while also threatening reproductive health and the safety of unborn children,” she said.

READ: EcoWaste Coalition warns consumers of cosmetics with high levels of mercury

The FDA first banned Goree Beauty Cream with Lycopene and Goree Day & Night Whitening Cream through Advisory No. 2017-289 in 2017.

Article continues after this 

Since then, it has issued warnings against other variants, including Goree Day and Night Beauty Cream, Goree 24K Gold Beauty Cream, Goree 24K Gold Beauty Kit and Goree Beauty Kit, according to the coalition.

“Targeting law enforcement operations against Goree is a top priority. The product often contains mercury levels exceeding 20,000 ppm. Despite multiple public health warnings, it remains available on e-commerce and social media platforms driven by local influencers who falsely promote its efficacy and safety,” Lucero said.

Article continues after this 

The group also cited online sellers’ use of promotional bundles, including “buy 5, get 1 free facial wash” and “buy 4, get 1 free soap,” as well as sales pitches such as “ito lang ang nakapagpaputi ng kadiliman ko,” “it’s time for a skincare upgrade” and “sikreto ng mga kutis artista.”

The coalition said government agencies in Brunei, India, Singapore, Hong Kong, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States have also banned Goree products.

In April 2026, Pakistan’s Standards and Quality Agency (PSQA) suspended the licenses of six beauty cream brands, including Goree, over violations of quality and safety standards, including mercury adulteration, it added.

The coalition reiterated its demand for authorities to remove listings of contaminated cosmetics and hold sellers accountable.

“We call upon the authorities to enforce the law to its furthest limit, remove listings for mercury-contaminated cosmetics, and ensure violators face legal consequences,” Lucero said.

On Oct. 29, the group staged a protest in Manila against the sale of Goree and other imported mercury-laced skin lightening products.

The demonstration also marked the ninth anniversary of FDA Advisory No. 2017-289 and called for enforcement of the Minamata Convention’s restrictions on mercury-laden cosmetics. /gsg

World.title: House backs purge of undocumented projects in 2027 national budget
World.content:
(INQUIRER file photo)

MANILA, Philippines – The House of Representatives is prepared to join the Senate in striking out from next year’s proposed P7.2-trillion national budget infrastructure line items lacking documentation, lawmakers said on Monday, amid criticism of projects without pertinent documents.

FPJ Panday Bayanihan party-list Rep. Brian Poe said the House will reject projects without detailed plans and paper trails as including them in the 2027 budget will be unfair for their constituencies and undermine careful district infrastructure planning.

“We will not accept projects that do not have proper papers or proper coordinates because that is unfair to the constituents,” Poe, an assistant majority leader and vice chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, said in a media briefing.

Article continues after this 

“That is also unfair to the representatives who have been working so hard to make sure that the people get the right kind of projects.”

Camarines Sur Rep. Arnie Fuentebella, also a vice chairman of the House’s budget committee, backed Poe’s statement, saying “that is the stand of the leadership of the House.”

Last week, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the Senate would remove about 295 infrastructure projects worth P8.8 billion from its version of the budget bill, citing the lack of supporting documents for proposed public works projects.

The Senate’s push to expunge undocumented projects comes on the heels of warning calls from budget watchdogs, which raised concerns over thousands of projects with the Department of Public Works and Highways that lack planning documents.

READ: Gatchalian: Senate will axe P8.8B infra projects from 2027 budget

Article continues after this 

“No papers, no geotag… when we meet in the bicam, those will be stricken off,” said Poe, referring to the joint congressional committee of congressmen and senators that will finalize the spending bill.

The House is also “flexible” in restoring slashed funding for foreign-assisted projects, including flagship railway projects under construction, when it meets the Senate in bicameral conference committee talks, according to Bataan Rep. Albert Garcia, the second-ranking lawmaker of the House appropriations committee.

Article continues after this 

“Whatever is appropriate, we’re willing to be flexible and adjust depending on reality or what is more accurate,” he said at the same briefing in mixed English and Filipino.

“At the end of the day, we all want the exact same thing: to craft a good budget that will genuinely improve people’s lives,” he added.

‘No pork’

Garcia was also firm that the House’s budget bill contained “no pork,” as he pushed back against claims that the chamber “politicized” the spending plan when lawmakers amended it.

“The House maintains its position that there is no pork,” he said

He said that amendments made by the House from the executive’s spending plan came from agencies and were validated by a “bottom-up budgeting” approach that took into consideration each locality’s needs.

READ: Solon says House only amended P115B in 2027 budget bill

“Those are legitimate amendments so that our budget can be more responsive to the challenges and needs of our country and our people,” Garcia said.

‘We welcome scrutiny’

Also on Monday, House Speaker Faustino Dy III said the lower chamber welcomes public scrutiny of the spending bill, but urged critics to respect the process as criticism for its own sake undermines the House’s budget reform efforts.

“Our efforts to demonstrate accessibility, transparency and continued reform are undermined by those who want to picture Congress as having amended the NEP without consultation or due regard for what is best for our people,” he said in his opening speech to lawmakers, referring to the National Expenditure Program.

Acknowledging that the public demands higher standards of transparency, Dy ordered congressional oversight committees to convene and inspect whether this year’s budget is being spent “in faithful compliance with their original purpose.”

READ: House majority parties back disclosure of every districts’ 2027 funding

The House will also publish a “transparency platform” where the public can check projects allotted to each lawmaker’s congressional district, the Dy added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.

“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Kazakhstan Maps Out New Opportunities for International Investors
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan presented the key provisions of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state-of-the-nation address on foreign policy, transport and logistics, industry and construction to heads of diplomatic missions and international organizations in Astana on Nov. 9.

Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said the address carried particular significance as it was delivered in the year marking the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s independence.

“The address not only reflects on our past achievements but also maps out a long-term development strategy for the decades ahead. We are living in a time of unprecedented global turbulence and geoeconomic fragmentation. In these challenging circumstances, Kazakhstan remains firmly committed to a consistent, balanced and pragmatic foreign policy,” he said.

Tileuberdi noted that Kazakhstan aimed to turn international partnerships into practical cooperation through joint ventures, greater localization of manufacturing, technology transfer and investment in human capital.

“Recognizing that partnership must be mutually beneficial, Kazakhstan offers predictable long-term planning and large-scale contracts under the People’s Construction program, institutional protection for investments, as well as a production and investment platform with access to the market of the Eurasian continent,” he said.

He identified energy, agriculture, digitalization and artificial intelligence as priority areas for investors. Opportunities include clean coal power generation, renewable and nuclear energy, agricultural processing and machinery production.

Tileuberdi also emphasized opportunities in water infrastructure and digital connectivity, including the construction of fiber-optic cables and the introduction of applied AI solutions.

“The construction of a fiber-optic cable across the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan has been completed, and new data center projects are under construction. We intend to actively deploy applied AI solutions in public administration, agriculture and the financial sector,” he said.

He invited international partners to take part in developing computing infrastructure, introducing AI across the economy, digitalizing transport and logistics, and advancing blockchain technologies.

Tileuberdi also highlighted the planned development of Alatau city as a new center for infrastructure and high technology. Drawing on the experience of the Astana International Financial Centre, the government plans to establish a legal framework to strengthen investor protection, including an investment court based on English common law principles. A new civil court is expected by the end of 2027.

Construction program to support domestic industry

Minister of Industry and Construction, Yersayin Nagaspayev, outlined the nationwide construction program for 2027, which aims to modernize infrastructure and expand the country’s industrial and production capacity. The program covers highways, railways, bridges, industrial and energy facilities, utility networks, water infrastructure, schools, hospitals and cultural facilities.

“The nationwide construction program is intended to provide additional momentum to domestic industry, attract investment, create new production facilities and expand international cooperation. Engaging leading international companies with advanced technologies, extensive expertise and access to global markets will play an important role in this process,” Nagaspayev said.

According to him, manufacturing now accounts for 13% of Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product. Since 2023, the country has implemented 647 projects, with another 200 scheduled for this year.

Kazakhstan also aims to strengthen its position in global critical minerals supply chains by developing the full production cycle, from exploration and extraction to processing and finished products.

The government plans to establish a national system for managing critical mineral reserves and develop a list of priority minerals based on resource potential, industrial capacity and global demand.

Nagaspayev said the country was seeking foreign investors and technology partners for projects involving battery and semiconductor materials, specialty alloys and other advanced products.

Kazakhstan strengthens its role as Eurasian logistics hub

Transport Vice Minister Damir Kozhakhmetov outlined plans to make Kazakhstan a leading logistics hub in Eurasia, saying the country aims not only to facilitate transit but also to organize international freight flows.

“On the railway, the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway line, expected to add 20 million metric tons of annual capacity toward China, and the 800-kilometer Aral-Caspian highway, which is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route by around 1,000 kilometers,” Kozhakhmetov said.
