Kazakhstan plans to modernize 37 road border crossings, with four scheduled for completion this year and 33 next year. Their capacity is expected to double. Other projects include a new airport in Astana, additional transit corridors, new berths at the Port of Aktau and terminals in Kuryk.

The country is also renewing its transport fleet with hybrid locomotives and new aircraft. Kazakhstan’s national aircraft fleet is expected to reach 160 by 2030.

“Road construction and repair work is underway across a record 11,000 kilometers this year, including 3,400 kilometers of new construction and reconstruction,” Kozhakhmetov said.

By 2030, Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports are expected to handle about 45 million metric tons of cargo annually, including 740,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) of containers. The country also plans to modernize 11,000 kilometers of railway track by 2029 and double the capacity of road border crossings.

On the Trans-Caspian route, Kazakhstan aims to transport 10 million metric tons of cargo and operate 3,000 container trains annually by 2030, compared with 358 trains last year. Air cargo volumes are also expected to double.

He emphasized that the route’s development depends on coordination among all countries along the corridor, particularly on investment, schedules, terminal capacity, border procedures and tariffs.

“The cooperation is already producing results. Freight transported through Kazakhstan along the route increased by nearly 30% in the first nine months of this year. In ten months, 522 container trains have been sent, compared with 292 in the same period last year, and our target for the year is 600. A container train now takes 15 to 18 days to reach Georgia’s Port of Poti from Xi’an in China and nine to 11 days to reach Azerbaijan,” he said.

He identified five areas for cooperation with international partners: investment in ports, airports, logistics centers and roads, including through public-private partnerships; coordination of corridor capacity; digital document exchange; new air routes and cargo services; and the sharing of expertise and standards.

World.title: Tokayev Honors Asian Games Medalists, Calls for Stronger Olympic Preparations
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev honored Kazakhstan’s medalists at the 20th Asian Games and the fifth Asian Para Games, highlighting their achievements and calling for intensified preparations for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

Speaking at the award ceremony, Tokayev praised the athletes for representing Kazakhstan at major international competitions and inspiring younger generations, reported Akorda.

“This is truly a tremendous achievement that fills us with deep pride for Kazakhstan! I congratulate you on your outstanding success!” he said.

President Tokayev highlighted several athletes, including Aisulu Suleimenova, who set an Asian record in the 100-meter race at the Para Games, and Tamirlan Tleules, who won Kazakhstan’s first Asian Games gold medal in taekwondo.

He also praised boxing champions Torekhan Sabyrkhan and Aibek Oralbay, two-time Asian Games karate champion Sofya Berultseva, six-time Asian Games cycling champion Alexey Lutsenko and Paralympic powerlifting champion David Degtyarev.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan has allocated more than 616 billion tenge (US$1.4 billion) to sports development over the past five years. He announced plans to build new sports facilities and inclusive centers nationwide as part of a large-scale national construction program.

“Every child in Kazakhstan must have the opportunity to participate in sports. This is not merely a social project, but a strategic political task,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s preparations to host world championships in boxing, judo, taekwondo, table tennis and esports in 2027, along with the World Junior Short Track Championships and the 51st UEFA Congress in Astana.

Looking ahead to the Los Angeles Olympics, Tokayev called on the relevant ministry and sports federations to ensure the highest level of preparation.

The ceremony concluded with the presentation of state awards to athletes for their achievements at the Asian Games and Asian Para Games.

The 20th Asian Games were held in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, Japan, from Sept. 19 to Oct. 4. The fifth Asian Para Games followed in the same host region from Oct. 18 to 24, bringing together athletes from across Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan Turns Its Dual AI Partnerships Into Regional Security Agenda
World.content:
Kazakhstan is trying to turn its reliance on foreign AI technology into leverage. It works with Washington and Beijing at the same time, which lets it seek a voice where the rules of the game are still open. On Nov. 6 it used the Aqaba Process to put its own AI security agenda in front of Central Asian leaders and King Abdullah II of Jordan. Tokayev and the King co-hosted the first Aqaba Process meeting ever held in Central Asia.

Structural power still leaves Astana room to choose

AI capabilities are concentrated around two poles, the United States and China. Middle powers join the emerging hierarchy on terms they did not write. In States and Markets, political economist Susan Strange defined structural power as the capacity to set the frameworks within which other states and corporations operate. In this division of labor, a country like Kazakhstan supplies territory, energy and raw materials, and the core technologies stay outside its borders. Strange also argued that structural power does not remove choice. States still make their own decisions, though from options others have defined.

Kazakhstan uses this space more and more. Its national language model AlemLLM was launched in partnership with China’s 01.AI. Teachers across the country gained mass access to generative AI through OpenAI licenses. Working with both poles gives Astana a base for initiatives of its own. Its goal, in my view, is to build a narrative of agency in AI and back it with action. The production and knowledge structures are set abroad. Norms, institutions and venues for dialogue are still forming, and there Kazakhstan has a chance to shape the agenda.

The domestic foundation took two years. The government adopted the AI Development Concept for 2024-2029. The country launched the Alem.cloud supercomputer, created a dedicated ministry and passed the Law on Artificial Intelligence, the first of its kind in Central Asia. Tokayev set out the external principle in Shanghai, saying no country should remain solely a consumer of AI.

Astana gives each pole a different role

Kazakhstan is the only country known to have joined both the U.S.-led Pax Silica and China’s WAICO. That position has a cost. In August, Reuters reported a draft State Department letter warning that Pax Silica membership may be incompatible with rival frameworks. The letter, addressed to 35 partner countries, has not been sent and its wording may still change. It still shows how narrow Astana’s room to maneuver has become. Astana has not commented publicly and continues to work with both sides. It responds by splitting roles. It offers Washington norms and a platform to promote them, and it offers Beijing an institutional presence. Both offers support the same story, that Kazakhstan is a place where rules get discussed and written.

Pax Silica brings together countries around semiconductor and critical minerals supply chains. Kazakhstan joined on June 25. Its normative side is the Washington Model, a set of voluntary rules for safe AI development. Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia signed it at the White House on Sept. 29. Kazakhstan has to negotiate with these same companies on labeling AI content and fighting deepfakes. Its AI law makes owners of AI systems responsible for labeling synthetic content, and the most widely used models for generating text, images and voices mostly belong to these firms. On Oct. 2, Tokayev proposed making the Washington Model the basis of a future UN treaty and ordered an initiative prepared for the G20 summit in Miami. The move also reassures Washington that membership in WAICO does not mean a tilt toward Beijing.

The Chinese track works differently. WAICO is an intergovernmental organization, so governments write its rules. Tokayev proposed holding its first meeting in Astana, opening its Central Asian office in Kazakhstan and launching a Kazakhstan-China Digital Bridge. The office offers something the American track lacks, a permanent institutional foothold that can channel Chinese investment and technical training. Alongside these proposals, Samruk-Kazyna announced on July 16 that it had signed 19 agreements with Chinese companies valued at $4.29 billion in total. The agreements covered digitalization, energy, transport, telecommunications and industry.

The Aqaba Process offers a venue no great power controls

King Abdullah II launched the Aqaba Process in 2015. It brings heads of state, intelligence chiefs, defense agencies and international organizations together to build a shared view of threats and agree on responses. Its agenda has moved from social media to drones and online gaming, and now to generative AI. In February 2026, participants met at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst to discuss drone threats. In Astana, representatives of international organizations, the gaming industry and civil society joined the discussions.

Jordan runs the process, and none of the powers competing in AI leads it. The United States and China were also absent from the participants the organizers named for the Astana meeting, which suits Kazakhstan’s balanced approach to AI diplomacy. Astana gets a rare chance to discuss AI security with Arab and Western partners without choosing a side. Tokayev said the meeting should let Central Asia present its own vision of AI security. He called the theme “particularly timely” when he met the King on Nov. 5. Astana and Amman also agreed to expand cooperation in technology and defense.

Regional approaches will need time to converge

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev offered to host a regional office of the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism, which would help Central Asian countries set up channels for reporting terrorist content and detect terrorist financing. He also proposed a program called “Enlightenment Against Ignorance in the Digital Age.” Tashkent is already setting up an SCO Universal Center for Countering Security Threats. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon proposed linking the Aqaba Process with the Dushanbe Process on countering terrorism and its financing. He also recalled a UN resolution that envisages the Dushanbe AI center as a regional platform for AI security. Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov attended after a personal invitation from Tokayev and spoke about preventive diplomacy and neutrality. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov did not attend. Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev represented Kyrgyzstan and spoke about sharing experience.

These proposals reflect different national starting points. Uzbekistan also signed up to WAICO and applied to Pax Silica in August 2026, so Tashkent and Astana follow similar balanced strategies. Each capital is still building its own AI institutions, laws and partnerships, and bringing these national tracks closer will take time. The initiatives from Astana, Tashkent and Dushanbe can complement each other once the region agrees on how to divide functions among them.

Trust remains an open question. In the published speeches, no country linked the fight against extremist content to human rights safeguards, such as a judicial basis for takedown requests and protection of user data. Platforms and Western companies treat these guarantees as a main condition for long-term work in the region.

A joint regional position would turn agency into influence

Kazakhstan builds its agency narrative consistently. It offers each pole what that pole values, and the Aqaba Process adds a third, neutral venue. In Strange’s terms, this is still a choice within frameworks the hegemons have set. The model holds as long as Washington tolerates dual membership. If the draft letter becomes a formal requirement, Astana will face the choice it has so far avoided. A common regional position could strengthen its hand, and the Nov. 6 meeting laid groundwork for one.

Real agency in AI security needs coordinated regional steps. Central Asian capitals should first agree on a division of roles in AI, deciding which capital leads on which function. They should then add AI threats to the catalogue of risks and preventive measures adopted for the Consultative Meetings of Central Asian Heads of State for 2026-2028. Australia and Malaysia announced plans to host the next round of the process in 2027, focused on online extremism and emerging technologies. Central Asia should arrive there with joint proposals, including on Afghanistan. A common solution would make the region one actor that helps shape the global agenda.

The author is Allen Alekeyev, the deputy head of research at Nightingale Int. analytical center.

The article is published as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and Nightingale Int. analytical center.

World.title: Build! Once Again – Build!: Kazakhstan Opens New Schools, Railway Stations and Housing Across Regions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan continued upgrading its regional infrastructure over the past week, with new education, transport, housing and public service facilities opening across the country, while construction began on a major congress center in the Burabay resort area.

The projects are being implemented to modernize regional infrastructure in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Nov. 9.

New construction in Burabay

Construction has begun on a 12,800-square-meter international-standard multifunctional congress center in the Burabay resort area under the Khalyktyq Qurylys, or the People’s Construction program.

The facility will include an auditorium, exhibition spaces and a multimedia hall. The project aims to strengthen business tourism, attract more visitors during the off-season and stimulate the regional economy by creating opportunities for local businesses, service providers and transport operators.

Education and public spaces

A new school with a capacity of 120 students has opened in Kokshetau, replacing a building in emergency condition. The facility features 11 classrooms, workshops, a library, a medical unit, an assembly hall and a sports hall.

In Makinsk, the Akmola Region, a 33,700-square-meter cultural and recreation park has opened. Its facilities include playgrounds, sports grounds, a running track, gazebos, swings and an amphitheater for public events.

Railway modernization

Reconstruction of the Zhaipak and Saryozek railway stations in the Zhetysu Region has been completed. The upgrades improved infrastructure, passenger facilities and safety standards.

The work is part of a nationwide program to modernize 124 railway stations. To date, 106 stations have been renovated.

Gasification and digital services

Four villages in the Zhetysu Region – Aulieagash, Akzhazyk, Akkuduk and Sholakay – have been connected to natural gas, providing access to approximately 9,000 residents who previously relied on solid-fuel heating.

Nationwide gasification has reached 64.2%, with 13.1 million people now having access to natural gas.

Karagandy has also opened a new-format digital AI office for public services. Unlike traditional public service centers, the facility combines document processing with free training in digital literacy and using online government services.

Housing for families

Housing distribution continued across the regions, with 136 apartments and houses handed over to socially vulnerable citizens, people on housing waiting lists and large families in Shymkent, as well as the Almaty, Akmola and Turkistan Regions.

In Almaty, families of emergency responders received keys to service apartments in the new Qutqarushylar Ui (Rescuers’ House) residential complex, located near a fire station. The apartments are fully furnished and equipped with household appliances, so they are ready for immediate occupancy.

World.title: Rybakina Withdraws From WTA Finals Due to Medical Reasons
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s world No. 1 Elena Rybakina has withdrawn from the 2026 WTA Finals in Indian Wells, the United States (U.S.), due to medical reasons, ending her season with four titles, including two Grand Slam victories.

“I am really sad to inform all my fans and supporters that I unfortunately have to withdraw from the WTA Finals this year. I’ve had an incredible season but my body is just not physically ready to compete,” Rybakina said in a statement published on the WTA website on Nov. 7.

“I’m going to spend some time resting and recovering at home and getting myself ready for the 2027 season. The WTA Finals is a very special tournament and I wish everyone the best of luck this week. Can’t wait to be back in Indian Wells in March!” she added.

Rybakina was due to defend the title she won at the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh, where she went undefeated.

Ukrainian tennis player Marta Kostyuk took her place in the draw as the first alternate. However, she lost her opening match to Czech player Linda Noskova 2-6, 4-6.

Rybakina finished the 2026 season with 54 wins and 14 losses, claiming four titles at the Australian Open, U.S. Open, Stuttgart and Ningbo. She also finished the year ranked world No. 1.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Sign 28 Cooperation Documents at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is preparing to sign around 28 cooperation documents, including 19 memorandums of understanding, at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), which opens Nov. 9 in Antalya, Türkiye.

The preliminary package covers meteorology, energy transition, climate investment, clean technologies, environmental protection and healthcare. The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources will determine the final list after consultations with international partners.

Kazakhstan’s national pavilion, organized by the state-owned waste management company Zhasyl Damu with the ministry’s support, will host more than 35 events bringing together government officials, international organizations, financial institutions, businesses and climate experts.

A key event will bring together environment ministers from five Central Asian countries to discuss regional cooperation and joint responses to environmental challenges.

The pavilion’s program will focus on turning climate commitments into investment opportunities and practical projects. The International Center for Green Technologies and Investment Projects (IGTIC) will present several initiatives, including the Kazakhstan Climate Investment Platform (QCIP), developed in cooperation with the Ministry of Ecology, the Ministry of Energy and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

Other priorities include developing international carbon market mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, with the participation of Verra, Evident and Zhasyl Damu, and strengthening climate transparency through enhanced reporting systems and a Capacity-building Initiative for Transparency (CBIT) project in cooperation with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Secretariat and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

Discussions will also cover circular economy initiatives, waste processing, industrial decarbonization, clean technologies and climate adaptation. Regional priorities include the restoration of the Northern Aral Sea, protection of Caspian ecosystems, sustainable water management, climate-resilient agriculture and the restoration of forests and steppes.

The technology agenda will address the use of artificial intelligence and space technologies in climate monitoring, methane emissions tracking and building energy efficiency. Other sessions will examine climate change impacts on public health, environmental education and youth engagement.

Türkiye hosts COP31 for the first time

Türkiye is hosting the UN climate conference for the first time. The event runs through Nov. 20 and is expected to bring together delegations from 196 countries and the European Union. According to Türkiye’s Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, leaders from 102 countries and more than 300 ministers have confirmed their participation.

The summit of heads of state and government is scheduled for Nov. 11-12 and will be chaired by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum will lead the conference on behalf of the host country.

The agenda will cover clean energy transition, food security, climate-resilient cities, green industrialization, waste reduction, marine protection and resilient healthcare systems.

Türkiye has promoted the concept of an “action-oriented” COP, emphasizing the implementation of climate commitments through concrete projects.

Organizers expect around 100,000 visitors at the official conference venue and up to 1.5 million in the public exhibition area. More than 45,000 climate volunteers from 154 countries have also registered.

Among Türkiye’s initiatives are its Zero Waste program and plans to build 455,000 climate-resilient homes across 11 provinces affected by the Feb. 6, 2023 earthquakes.

World.title: Progress Achieved, Promise Unfulfilled: Eradicating Poverty and Empowering People in Asia and Pacific
World.content:
Countries across Asia and the Pacific have made remarkable strides over the past three decades in tackling poverty through a combination of economic growth, government-led programmes and community-based initiatives.

At the same time, the nature of poverty and vulnerability is evolving as climate change, population ageing, digital transformation and recurring economic shocks reshape who is poor, how people experience deprivation and their exposure to future risks. But we have the tools and evidence to address these challenges.

We have myriad examples from across the region: Universal health coverage in Thailand cut out-of-pocket health spending and infant mortality, with the largest gains for the poorest households. Nepal nearly halved child stunting through coordinated nutrition policy, despite limited economic growth. China established targeted employment assistance mechanisms for people in vulnerable situations to broaden their employment channels.

Additionally, Malaysia is expanding access to childcare and eldercare through public investment, community-based services and financial incentives. Mongolia supports unpaid family caregivers through a government-funded care allowance. Cooperatives from Cambodia, India, Kiribati and Viet Nam are already showing how community-owned, participatory models can generate income and resilience, especially in rural areas.

These actions have helped the region to record one of the most significant success stories in modern human development. Driven primarily by economic growth, extreme poverty, the reality for roughly half of the region’s population only 30 years ago, has fallen to just 4 per cent in 2024, with hundreds of millions of people being lifted out of acute deprivation. Yet this headline figure masks a significant reality: 190 million people continue to live in extreme poverty; nearly 500 million people are multidimensionally poor while 660 million are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty.

Considering hybrid poverty lines that reflect what a dignified life actually costs in each country, the trends are even starker: more than 1.1 billion people live in poverty in 2026, an additional 1.2 billion people live above but very close to their respective poverty lines and 310 million people are classified as extremely poor. People are deprived not only of income, but of adequate housing, education, nutrition or social protection. More critically, millions remain one shock away from falling, or slipping deeper, into poverty.

Because so many drivers of poverty cross borders, regional cooperation is not optional but essential. Through regional public goods such as the Leaving No One Behind Platform, the Social Protection Online Toolbox, the Risk and Resilience Platform and the SDG Gateway, we help translate shared regional knowledge into nationally adapted, evidence-based policy, while platforms such as the ESCAP Action Plan to Strengthen Regional Cooperation on Social Protection allow governments to facilitate knowledge exchange and scale policy approaches. And because government action alone cannot close the gap, the private sector and civil society organizations have a critical role to play too, through inclusive business models that reach people in vulnerable situations.

Our study, the Social Outlook 2026, highlights three transitions unfolding simultaneously, climate change, digital transformation and rapid population ageing, that are reshaping who is vulnerable. Extreme climate events are destroying working hours equivalent to millions of jobs and reducing agricultural yields, adversely impacting food security. The region is ageing faster than any other in human history, moving from an ageing to an aged society. And while digital technologies have already lifted people out of poverty by expanding access to markets, finance and services, the digital divide continues to exclude the most vulnerable, who are also the most exposed to automation and face existing labour market disadvantages.

Moreover, the ongoing crisis in Western Asia has already disrupted energy and fertilizer markets, trade routes and remittance flows across our wider region, amplifying inflation especially for households who have the least room to absorb it. This follows the cost-of-living crisis, and before that, the pandemic, each shock striking a population still recovering from the last. These overlapping crises underscore a stark reality: progress against poverty is reversible, placing the region at risk of a lost decade for inclusive development.

The report not only measures poverty and analyses its drivers, it also reshapes our understanding of who is poor and why. Poverty in our region concentrates, again and again, among large rural households and in remote areas, among people with little or no education, among children, among informal workers and among women bearing a disproportionate share of unpaid care work. In the 25 countries studied with ESCAP’s Leaving No One Behind algorithm, disaggregation of monetary and multidimensional poverty using household surveys found that the intersection of multiple disadvantages, rather than one disadvantage alone, defined those furthest behind in unique ways. Understanding these overlapping country-specific disadvantages is essential to designing tailored policies that address the interconnected barriers that trap people in poverty.

Integrated investments in human capital, health coverage, decent work and social protection underpinned by gender-responsive, disability-inclusive and age-sensitive policies are key anchors of one agenda: empowering people and eradicating poverty across our region. We have the blueprint and the Asia-Pacific region has already proven it can reduce poverty at a scale and speed unmatched elsewhere in the world. What is required now is coordinated action to apply it at scale.

The evidence base for action is strong and sustained progress depends on coherent strategies that align economic, social and environmental objectives, strengthen institutions and expand people’s capabilities and resilience over the life course.

The question the Social Outlook 2026 puts before us is whether we will make one final big push to finish the job by 2030 or keep a business-as-usual mindset and allow the next shock to undo progress.

The author is Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, the Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations and Executive Secretary of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP).

World.title: Three Kazakh Traditions Move Closer to UNESCO Recognition
World.content:
ASTANA – UNESCO’s Evaluation Body has recommended adding Kazakhstan’s Salburyny hunting festival, traditional embroidery and feltmaking to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, according to a document published by the organization.

Salburyn

Rooted in nomadic traditions, Salburyny is an annual equestrian festival featuring Tazy hunting dogs and golden eagle falconry. Usually held between late autumn and early winter, the weeklong celebration brings together falconers, musicians, storytellers and young people.

Participants learn horseback riding, falconry, dog care and hunting, while the tradition promotes respect for animals, environmental awareness and cooperation across generations.

The UNESCO document said the inscription would raise awareness of an ancient tradition that combines falconry, dog breeding, horsemanship, oral traditions, music and close interaction with nature. It would also promote wildlife conservation, sustainable tourism and traditional crafts while strengthening cultural identity and intergenerational knowledge-sharing.

Salburyny was added to Kazakhstan’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013. The Kiran Federation, Zhalayr Shora and the Kansonar Association took part in preparing the nomination.

Art of embroidery

Kazakhstan submitted the nomination for the art of embroidery jointly with Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

Embroidery is a traditional craft involving decorative and symbolic patterns sewn with colorful threads onto cotton, wool, silk and, in some cases, leather. It is used to decorate wall hangings, pillows, clothing, accessories, headdresses and household textiles.

Techniques vary across regions, while patterns often draw on nature and mythology, featuring flowers, animals and celestial symbols with meanings specific to local communities. The craft is practiced mainly by women, who work individually or in groups. Beyond decorating clothing and household items, embroidery provides a source of income.

Traditional feltmaking

Kazakhstan joined Azerbaijan, Iran, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mongolia, Tajikistan, Türkiye and Uzbekistan in submitting a joint nomination for traditional feltmaking. The UNESCO document praised the countries’ “exemplary cooperation” in promoting a shared cultural tradition that transcends geographical boundaries.

Felt, traditionally made from wool, is used for carpets, prayer mats, yurt coverings, clothing and accessories. The labor-intensive process involves cleaning and dyeing wool, laying it on a mat, rolling and tightening it, and then stretching and drying the material.

Feltmaking is closely linked to the cultural identity of the communities that practice it. The collective process strengthens social ties and connects generations.

A total of 59 nominations were submitted for inclusion on the Representative List this year. The Evaluation Body recommended 56 for inscription, while returning three others to the submitting countries for revisions.

The final decision is expected to be made at the session of UNESCO’s Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, scheduled for Nov. 30-Dec. 5 in Xiamen, China.

World.title: Nakhchivan’s Baku office closed: What remains of autonomy?
World.content:
Nakhchivan’s representative office in Baku closed

On 5 November, Prime Minister of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic Jabbar Musayev abolished the autonomous republic’s Permanent Representative Office in Baku. It had been established in February 1992, when Heydar Aliyev headed Nakhchivan’s Supreme Assembly.

The office maintained regular communication between the Supreme Assembly and state authorities in Baku. In September, its head, Bakhtiyar Asgarov, was dismissed. The authorities have not explained the reasons for abolishing the office. A liquidation commission is to be established within five working days, although it remains unclear which body will take over the office’s functions.

However, this is not simply the closure of a single institution. Over the past four years, control over Nakhchivan’s administration has gradually shifted to Baku. We reported on the new governance model in February.

The president says Nakhchivan’s autonomous status will be preserved. But what remains of its autonomy in practice?

What has changed?

Vasif Talibov led Nakhchivan from 1995 until December 2022. Following his resignation, President Ilham Aliyevestablished the post of presidential plenipotentiary representative in the autonomous republic. The new body was given the authority to oversee the activities of local executive officials and issue instructions to them.

Subsequently, investigations were launched against several local officials on charges of embezzling public funds and other offences. The representative office was initially headed by Fuad Najafli. Since November 2025, the position has been held by former Nakhchivan Prime Minister Jeyhun Jalilov.

However, the most significant changes took place this year. On 2 February, the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijan’s parliament) adopted a constitutional law, and on 10 March, the president signed a decree on its implementation. The law changed Nakhchivan’s system of governance:

The provision establishing the autonomous republic’s highest-ranking official was abolished.

The presidential representative office was enshrined in Nakhchivan’s Constitution as an executive authority.

The Cabinet of Ministers is no longer subordinate to the Supreme Assembly and is now only required to report on its activities to it. The government’s operating procedures must be agreed with the president, while central executive bodies can only be established or abolished with his consent.

The president sets the dates for elections to the Supreme Assembly. He can also dissolve the parliament if it is unable to perform its functions.

Heads of local executive authorities are appointed by the president on the recommendation of the chairman of the Supreme Assembly.

The requirement for the chairman of the Supreme Assembly to be a permanent resident of Nakhchivan was abolished.

Future amendments to Nakhchivan’s Constitution will be made through ordinary legislation rather than constitutional law.

Under the same decree, the president gave the government three months to bring existing legislation into line with the new provisions.

The local branches of the State Security Service and the State Customs Committee in Nakhchivan already report directly to the central authorities in Baku.

Meanwhile, the position of chairman of the Supreme Assembly remains vacant. No new parliamentary leader has been elected since Talibov’s resignation. At the first session of the newly elected assembly, the proposed candidate failed to secure sufficient support.

Sessions during the autumn parliamentary term were also chaired by First Deputy Chairman Bakhtiyar Mammadov.

What remains of Nakhchivan’s autonomy?

Formally, Nakhchivan retains considerable powers. The autonomous republic still has its own Constitution, an elected Supreme Assembly, a Cabinet of Ministers and a Supreme Court. The Supreme Assembly passes laws and approves the autonomous republic’s separate budget. Under the revised Constitution, the chairman of the Supreme Assembly represents Nakhchivan in relations with foreign states and international organisations.

However, the key change concerns whom these authorities are accountable to. The activities of the executive branch, the appointment of local officials, the timing of elections and the fate of the parliament now depend, to varying degrees, on decisions made by the president of Azerbaijan. The parliament remains in place, but the government is no longer subordinate to it. The position of chairman of the Supreme Assembly also still exists, although it has remained vacant for almost four years.

Why were references to the Treaty of Kars removed?

The same law removed references to the 1921 Treaties of Moscow and Kars from Nakhchivan’s Constitution. They were replaced by documents relating to Azerbaijan’s independence in 1991 and the country’s 1995 Constitution as the legal basis for Nakhchivan’s status. The preamble also now states that Nakhchivan is an “integral part” of Azerbaijan.

Article V of the Treaty of Kars, to which Turkey was among the signatories, recognises Nakhchivan as an autonomous territory under Azerbaijan’s protection. In this context, Bakı-Xəbər newspaper editor-in-chief Aydin Guliyev described Turkey as “one of the guarantors of autonomy”.

Russian political analyst Sergei Markedonov, meanwhile, argues that it makes little sense to speak of the termination of guarantees by Russia and Turkey. In his view, the treaty’s main provision is that Azerbaijan cannot transfer its right of protection over Nakhchivan to a third state. Baku has taken no such steps.

Lawyer Yalchin Hajizade also points out that Nakhchivan’s status is determined by Azerbaijan’s Constitution:

“Amendments to the autonomous republic’s own Constitution cannot change this legal reality.”

Neither Ankara nor Moscow has officially commented on the changes. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan also made no mention of Nakhchivan in his speech in Shusha on 8 November.

What are officials in Baku saying?

In August, Ilham Aliyev commented on the debate surrounding Nakhchivan’s autonomous status in an interview with AzTV conducted in Nakhchivan:

“The status of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic must be preserved, but its system of governance needs to be improved.”

He said the governance model based on special presidential representative offices, already in place in Karabakh and East Zangezur, had also been introduced in Nakhchivan:

“In this way, we are effectively integrating these three regions from an administrative perspective as well.”

The issue was also discussed in parliament in June 2025. MP Hikmet Babaoglu said:

“The need for changes is dictated by current realities.”

MP Mazahir Efendiyev described the new governance model as a step towards strengthening coordination with the central authorities. MP Elman Nasirov stressed that the issue of Nakhchivan’s autonomous status was not covered by the draft law.

Deputy Speaker of Parliament Ziyafet Asgarov opposed abolishing the autonomy, while MP Gudrat Hasanguliyev called for a broader discussion of its status.

Figures close to the authorities have presented the changes as an end to the “dual power” system that existed under Talibov.

As early as 2022, historian Kamran Ismayilov had called for reforms to Nakhchivan’s governance system:

“An excessively bloated bureaucracy creates fertile ground for corruption.”

What do critics say?

Human rights defender Yalchin Imanov told OC Media that the changes effectively reduced Nakhchivan’s autonomy to zero and reflected the concentration of power in the hands of one person.

In July, political analyst Nasimi Mammadli told Radio Liberty:

“After the establishment of the presidential representative office, Nakhchivan’s autonomous status began to become largely symbolic.”

According to him, the Supreme Assembly has “largely lost its political influence”.

Where are these changes leading?

Mammadli does not rule out the possibility of a constitutional referendum in the future that could lead to a revision of Nakhchivan’s status.

Political analyst Zaur Mammadov also suggested in 2025 that the designation “autonomous republic” could be replaced with “region”. In his view, such a change would reduce the powers of the Supreme Assembly and the executive authorities.

Meanwhile, the implementation of the TRIPP project would establish a land connection between Nakhchivan and the rest of Azerbaijan. This raises the question of whether the autonomous republic would still need its special status.

For now, Article 134 of Azerbaijan’s Constitution defines Nakhchivan as an autonomous state within Azerbaijan.

World.title: Chinese vice-president’s first visit to Georgia: Key messages and assessments
World.content:
Chinese vice-president’s visit to Georgia

Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng paid an official visit to Georgia from 6 to 8 November. He met the country’s senior leadership, attended a meeting of the Georgian-Chinese business community and took part in an official dinner.

It was the first visit to Georgia by a Chinese official of such high rank.

In their statements, Georgian government representatives emphasised the particular political significance of a visit by such a senior Chinese official.

According to official statements, key topics discussed during talks between the Georgian and Chinese delegations included trade, investment, transport corridors, the Anaklia port project and political cooperation between the two countries.

The main message of the visit was that Tbilisi and Beijing were seeking to further deepen their relations. No new agreements were announced.

According to statements made during the visit, Tbilisi intends to expand economic cooperation with China, attract investment and strengthen Georgia’s role as a transit hub. For Beijing, Georgia is of interest as a key link in the Middle Corridor, a route connecting China and Europe.

Visit at a glance

Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng arrived in Georgia on 6 November. He was welcomed at Tbilisi International Airport by Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili.

During his visit, Han Zheng met Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. The meetings included both one-on-one talks and discussions between the wider delegations.

The Chinese vice-president also met representatives of the Georgian and Chinese business communities at an event organised by the Georgian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

The visit concluded on 8 November. Han Zheng was seen off at Tbilisi International Airport by Irakli Kobakhidze and Maka Bochorishvili.

“I proposed holding a global summit in Tbilisi in 2027” – Kavelashvili

Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili received Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng at the Presidential Palace.

According to the president’s official website, the main topic of the meeting was the development of the strategic partnership between Georgia and China. The two sides discussed trade and economic cooperation, Chinese investment, cooperation in education and science, as well as student exchange programmes.

They also discussed Georgia’s transit potential and the development of the Middle Corridor, with particular attention paid to expanding transport and logistics infrastructure. Plans to hold the sixth Belt and Road Forum in Tbilisi were also considered.

Mikheil Kavelashvili presented the Chinese delegation with Georgia’s initiative to hold a global summit in Tbilisi in 2027 dedicated to promoting peace and healthy lifestyles.

“I presented the Chinese side with my initiative to hold a global summit in Tbilisi in 2027 dedicated to promoting peace and healthy lifestyles. I expressed hope that China would participate in this important international event,” the president’s administration said in an official statement.

“Special relations based on shared values” – Kobakhidze

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze placed particular emphasis on economic cooperation.

He noted that trade between the two countries was growing year on year and that China had become Georgia’s largest investor this year.

The prime minister highlighted Georgia’s advantageous geographical location and its role in the transit corridor connecting Europe and Asia.

He said Georgia was interested in deepening its partnership with China under the Belt and Road Initiative:

“For us, relations with China are of particular importance. In today’s world, China is the only peaceful superpower, fully focused on progress, modernisation, moving forward and development.”

The prime minister noted that Georgia and China enjoyed “special relations based on shared values”:

“Of course, this foundation of shared values provides us with a unique incentive to further develop bilateral relations.”

“Sincere, friendly and productive” – Han Zheng on visit

Han Zheng described his meetings with the Georgian side as “sincere, friendly and productive”.

He said that upgrading relations between the two countries to a comprehensive strategic partnership had opened up new opportunities for cooperation.

The Chinese vice-president placed particular emphasis on trade relations. He noted that trade between the two countries had grown steadily in recent years, with increasing volumes of Georgian agricultural products entering the Chinese market, while Chinese-made goods — particularly electric vehicles and other new-energy vehicles — were proving popular in Georgia.

Han Zheng said China was ready to purchase more Georgian products and support the further development of trade between the two countries.

He also stressed that China would support competitive Chinese companies in investing in Georgia and expanding their operations in the local market.

Anaklia port among topics discussed

The Middle Corridor and the Anaklia deepwater port were among the key economic issues discussed during the visit.

The Middle Corridor is a transport route connecting China and Europe via Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Goods travel from China to Kazakhstan, then across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan and Georgia, before continuing towards the Black Sea. The route allows goods to be transported between Europe and Asia while bypassing Russia.

The importance of this corridor has grown since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the introduction of sanctions against Russia. For China, it offers an opportunity to diversify trade links with Europe, while for Georgia, it presents a chance to strengthen its role as a transit hub and increase economic revenues.

At a meeting with business representatives, Georgian Deputy Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili highlighted the key role of the Anaklia deepwater port in the development of the Middle Corridor:

“Particular importance is attached to the Anaklia deepwater port, which will serve as the Middle Corridor’s gateway to the Black Sea and play a crucial strategic role in trade between China, Central Asia and Europe.”

The Anaklia port project has faced delays for many years. In 2024, the Georgian government selected a Chinese-Singaporean consortium, which included Chinese state-owned enterprises, to build the port.

The decision raised questions about the role of Chinese companies and the potential risks associated with handing over strategic infrastructure to them. However, the negotiations eventually collapsed. Georgia is now developing the port independently, using the so-called “landlord model”.

Background: Georgia’s growing distance from the West and closer ties with China

Georgia’s deepening relations with China come at a time when ties between the Georgian government and its Western partners have deteriorated significantly.

In 2024, the United States suspended its strategic partnership with Georgia. The country’s EU accession process has also effectively been halted. Against this backdrop, strengthening ties with China has taken on particular significance for Georgia’s foreign policy.

In July 2023, China and Georgia announced the establishment of a strategic partnership. This year, a decision was made to upgrade relations to a “comprehensive strategic partnership”.

Cooperation with China is no longer limited to trade. It now encompasses investment, transport, tourism, education and political dialogue.

Statistics from recent years confirm China’s growing economic importance to Georgia.

During a Georgian-Chinese business meeting, Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili described China as one of Georgia’s largest trading partners. She cited figures showing that bilateral trade reached $2.3bn between January and September 2026, an increase of 41% compared with the same period last year. This makes China Georgia’s second-largest trading partner after Turkey.

Kvrivishvili also noted that total Chinese investment in Georgia had exceeded $1bn since 2002. In the first two quarters of 2026, China became Georgia’s largest foreign investor, with investments totalling $236m.

The Chinese market is also becoming increasingly important for Georgia’s tourism sector. Between January and September 2026, Georgia welcomed 119,081 visitors from China, up 23.6% compared with the same period last year. This was the highest figure recorded in the past 15 years.

What does the visit mean? Expert assessment

Paata Zakareishvili, an expert on conflicts and international relations, described Han Zheng’s visit to Georgia as primarily a geopolitical event in an interview with JAMnews.

In his view, Beijing is using the visit to highlight its growing presence and interests in the South Caucasus, including Georgia.

As for Georgia, the expert believes the visit holds primarily symbolic significance for the government:

“Against the backdrop of deteriorating relations with Western partners, the government can present the visit by a senior Chinese official as a sign of international support and recognition.”

The fact that Bidzina Ivanishvili himself did not meet the Chinese official further underscores the largely symbolic nature of the visit. According to Zakareishvili, this is noteworthy given that Ivanishvili has recently attended several publicly announced official meetings, including one with the Israeli ambassador just last week.

Zakareishvili does not rule out the possibility that the Chinese vice-president brought specific proposals to Tbilisi. He suggests that the Anaklia port could have been among the topics discussed, with Chinese companies potentially more interested in operating the port and managing its terminals than in constructing it.

However, the expert stressed that this was merely speculation and that he had no information to confirm it:

“If such proposals were indeed made, they will not remain secret. We will certainly find out about them in two or three months.”

Discussing political support from China, Zakareishvili stressed the need to distinguish between economic cooperation and political backing.

He explained that China’s approach to Georgia differs from that of the West or Russia. Beijing is not concerned with Georgia’s political orientation, prioritising pragmatic economic relations rather than which political or geopolitical bloc the country aligns itself with:

“China has made its position perfectly clear: ‘I do not interfere in your political affairs or your political orientation. Go wherever you want. I am only interested in pragmatic economic matters.'”

According to Zakareishvili, China lacks the historical, religious and cultural ties to the South Caucasus that Russia, Turkey and Iran have with the region. He therefore believes Beijing seeks to compete with these countries primarily in the economic sphere, without interfering in its partners’ political orientation.

However, he noted that this does not mean Georgia can expect the same level of Chinese support on international political issues as the development of economic cooperation might suggest.

As Zakareishvili explained, China’s interests are primarily pragmatic and economic.

World.title: ‘We didn’t even get chance to ask’ – Georgia’s new gambling law takes Patriarchate by surprise
World.content:
The head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations service, Archpriest Andria Jagmaidze, says the Patriarchate was caught by surprise when parliament fast-tracked amendments to the law on gambling. According to him, the process moved so quickly that Patriarchate representatives had no opportunity to examine the draft law in detail or ask questions.

“Events moved so quickly that we didn’t even get a chance to ask anything,” Jagmaidze said.

He said the Patriarchate plans to look into the matter more closely and discuss it with the authorities. The archpriest explained that the Patriarch was in western Georgia while parliament considered the bill, which meant the Patriarchate could not properly engage in the process.

Jagmaidze expressed particular concern about the state of gambling in the country. He believes the authorities and the Patriarchate should discuss ways to reduce the harm caused by the industry.

“The current situation with gambling is already alarming. It would be good to discuss with the authorities how to reduce the harm gambling causes to the population. We need to talk about setting up and funding rehabilitation centres. Gambling addiction is a condition that requires psychological support,” he said.

In the archpriest’s view, the authorities should also discuss the minimum age for players and how they enforce existing regulations. He added that previous efforts to introduce regulations aimed at reducing harm had taken around four years and involved a working group from the Patriarchate.

“It took us around four years to introduce regulations aimed at reducing harm. A working group from the Patriarchate took part in the process. But parliament passed this new law in just two days last week. So there are a great many questions,” Jagmaidze stressed.

What the amendments involve

Georgia’s parliament approved a package of amendments to the law on gambling on 28 October 2026. The changes allow international casinos to organise international gambling tournaments.

Under the draft law, an international gambling tournament is a competition in which at least 80% of participants hold foreign citizenship.

The amendments exempt casinos from paying gambling business tax on a club table if they use it exclusively for an international gambling tournament with a prize pool exceeding 3 million lari (around $1 million). Organisers can still earn revenue from hosting the tournament. They can hold these competitions either inside casino premises or elsewhere.

Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze responded to questions from Patriarchate representatives about the bill. He said the amendment was not significant and did not warrant a broad public debate.

According to Kobakhidze, the changes concern a specific type of international tournament, including poker competitions broadcast on international sports channels. He explained that the amendment simply introduces a specific tax framework for such tournaments and does not fundamentally change the existing rules.

“There was no need for a broad discussion on this issue at all. For example, I myself knew nothing about it. That shows how insignificant the amendment is in substance,” Kobakhidze said.

He claimed he only learned about the bill after parliament had already introduced it.

World.title: Russia signals new opportunities for closer ties with Georgia
World.content:
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow was ready to support initiatives aimed at deepening cooperation between Russia and Georgia.

She also briefly expressed her wish to see a fully fledged Russian embassy in Tbilisi. At present, because the two countries have no diplomatic relations, the Russian Interests Section at the Swiss Embassy performs this role.

At a press conference, journalists asked Zakharova about the activities and initiatives of the Foundation for Russian-Georgian Unity, established by businessman Mamuka Pipia. She replied that she viewed positively all initiatives aimed at developing bilateral cooperation in education, culture and humanitarian affairs, involving representatives of civil society, academic and cultural circles.

Maria Zakharova

“We believe that the new foundation’s activities will make a significant contribution to further strengthening ties between the peoples of the Russian Federation and Georgia. We are ready to examine the specific projects the foundation plans to undertake and consider providing any necessary assistance.

“We are open to this. You can contact us or our… We would, of course, like to say embassies, but unfortunately we have to say interests sections,” Zakharova said.

Who is Mamuka Pipia?

Mamuka Pipia is a businessman with dual Georgian and Russian citizenship and one of the leaders of Solidarity for Peace, a pro-Russian, Putinist political party. He is publicly known for supporting Kremlin policies and justifying Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Pipia’s name also came up in the case involving Otar Partskhaladze, Georgia’s former prosecutor general, who faces US sanctions. Pipia appeared as a defence witness in the case and publicly confirmed his links to Partskhaladze.

Pipia recently posted a video on social media showing him training on a Russian tank while wearing a Russian military uniform. In a statement accompanying the video, he said he stood ready to take part in Russia’s war if necessary.

Maria Zakharova and Georgia

Maria Zakharova is the official spokesperson for Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She regularly sets out Moscow’s foreign policy positions, including on relations with Georgia.

Her statements on Georgia mainly focus on the need to normalise relations, expand economic and humanitarian ties, and justify Russia’s position on the 2008 war.

Georgia severed diplomatic relations with Russia on 2 September 2008, following the August war. The decision came after Russia recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) and occupied Georgian territories. Since the break in diplomatic relations, Russia and Georgia have each maintained an interests section at the Swiss embassy in the other country.

Zakharova has repeatedly called for the restoration of diplomatic relations with Georgia. In June 2024, she said Moscow supported efforts to normalise Russian-Georgian relations and stood ready to respond to initiatives from Tbilisi in that direction. Around the same time, she welcomed a call by Georgia’s pro-Russian Solidarity for Peace party to restore diplomatic relations.

In October 2024, Zakharova described statements by Georgian officials about the possibility of apologising to the people of South Ossetia for the 2008 war as an encouraging signal for Moscow. However, she also demanded concrete steps from Georgia, including the signing of a legally binding agreement on the non-use of force.

In April 2025, Zakharova reiterated that Russia stood ready to restore relations with Georgia and faced ‘no restrictions’ in this process. At the same time, she linked closer ties to a change in Georgia’s approach to Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

In June 2026, Zakharova said Russia stood ready to expand relations with Georgia, but stressed that the process required steps from both sides. She also welcomed the ‘pragmatic policy’ pursued by the Georgian authorities and highlighted trade, transport, tourism and humanitarian ties.

However, Moscow’s position on Georgia’s territorial integrity remains unchanged in Zakharova’s statements. Russia recognises Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as independent states, while Tbilisi regards this as Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory.

On Russia’s rapprochement with Georgia

World.title: Armenia takes a step closer to EU with launch of biometric passport system
World.content:
Introduction of biometric passports in Armenia

Armenia launched a new system for issuing biometric passports on 1 November. The system fully complies with international standards. The Armenian authorities say its introduction marks the most significant reform under the country’s visa liberalisation process with the European Union.

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, wrote on Facebook that the new passports would make border crossings easier for travellers. She also stressed that Armenian citizens had moved one step closer to visa-free travel to EU countries.

“Armenia is choosing closer ties with Europe, and we are working to make this choice benefit its citizens,” Kos said.

The private company HayPass will provide the new services. The relevant government agencies assure citizens that this partnership will deliver high-quality services and secure, reliable documents.

The new system has moved the entire document application process from paper to digital format. Applicants can submit their applications and complete preliminary registration online. They then receive a QR code by email and must visit a service centre at their appointed time to verify their documents and personal details.

At the centre, staff take photographs and fingerprints and record signature samples. Applicants can collect their biometric passports from the same centre 14 days later.

The biometric passport will remain valid for 10 years and cost 28,650 drams ($80). The government plans to introduce discounts for certain social groups, although it has yet to specify how much of the cost it will cover.

The authorities do not require citizens to replace their existing passports with biometric ones. People can continue using their current passports until they expire.

Which other documents will become biometric?

The Interior Ministry has announced that several other types of documents will also become biometric, in addition to passports:

Identity cards (IDs);

Diplomatic passports;

Residence permits;

Identity cards and passports for stateless persons;

Identity cards and travel documents issued to refugees under international conventions.

The risk of document forgery will be minimal

The Interior Ministry says the introduction of the biometric passport system will help address several issues at once. These include:

Ensuring reliable identity verification;

Reducing the risk of document forgery or the use of another person’s personal data.

Nelly Davtyan, head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, says the new system will minimise the risk of forgery at every stage, from data processing at service centres to the production of the actual document:

“The previous system depended entirely on human factors. As a result, during the preparatory stage, we identified numerous inaccuracies in the State Population Register.”

Davtyan believes a biometric passport is more than just an identity document. It also provides an important safeguard for a person’s legal rights:

“The particular value of the new system lies in the fact that international standards guarantee the establishment, identification and mutual recognition of a person’s legal status worldwide. This is not simply our assessment. We built the entire system in strict compliance with these standards.”

Gold-number passports to go on sale at auction

Armenia also plans to introduce a scheme offering “special” passport numbers, known as “gold numbers”. Some of these will go on sale at auction.

“We will launch the programme next year using two approaches. Passports with repeating digits will cost more, while numbers with ‘special’ combinations will go on sale at auction,” Nelly Davtyan said.

Faster service at HayPass offices: 3–5 minutes instead of 25

HayPass received 7,700 applications within just a few days. Some 2,700 people have already visited the company’s offices and completed the first stage of the process by submitting their biometric data.

According to Nelly Davtyan, head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, the previous document application process took 25 minutes. The new system allows applicants to complete registration in just 3–5 minutes:

“For all 2,700 citizens who have already used the service, data processing took no more than five minutes.”

Staff from the Migration and Citizenship Service have also visited regional branches. They say these offices are operating normally and have no queues either.

“This does not mean that we are providing fewer services. It means that we can now handle a much higher volume of applications,” Davtyan stressed.

Company has already invested €20 million

Interior Minister Arpine Sargsyan said the private partner, HayPass, had already invested €20 million in the project and continued to invest in it. She also stressed that citizens pay the private company 28,650 drams for a biometric passport and 5,950 drams for the accompanying identity card. These payments cover the company’s services. The state, she said, makes no profit from them.

The minister also rejected claims that the company receives payments for its services from both the state budget and citizens.

“We do not pay HayPass any money. Nothing has been paid from the state budget,” she assured.

HayPass operates 14 offices across the country

On 1 November, the first day of biometric data collection, HayPass opened service centres in two Yerevan shopping malls: Yerevan Mall and Mega Mall. Twelve regional branches began operating the following day.

Interior Minister Arpine Sargsyan said the government plans to increase the number of service centres to 23 by March 2027.

“Overall, we will have two branches in each region,” the minister said.

Introduction of biometric passports in Armenia

World.title: Divorce rates are rising in Armenia: divorced women and experts explain why
World.content:
Divorce in Armenia: women share their stories

For some, divorce means a painful separation; for others, it is a happy “liberation” from each other. Either way, former spouses remain part of each other’s lives, albeit in a different capacity.

For some, divorce marks the beginning of a new life. For others, it leads to a prolonged struggle, with endless disputes over issues such as property division and access to their children. Mutual accusations often accompany the process.

In Armenia, divorce can also spark heated public debate. This can be a real ordeal, particularly for women.

Women who have divorced told JAMnews why they decided to end their relationships. Experts offered their explanations for the rise in divorce rates in recent years.

“When you realise nothing can be saved”

Juliette Babayan is 38. She separated from her husband after 15 years together and has been raising their two sons on her own for the past two years. She says divorce had always seemed like a last resort:

“When I got married, I could never have imagined that one day I would have to make such a decision. But when a relationship reaches a dead end, there is no other way out. My children were no longer very young at the time. When we divorced, one was 12 and the other 14. They had seen our arguments and the tension between us. Then one day I realised it was better for them to see us apart, living separately but happy, rather than together and miserable.”

She felt that people around her did not understand how difficult it was to decide to divorce:

“But that is not how it works. You do not decide to separate in a minute. You think about it for a long time and give each other another chance. But when you realise there is no other way out and nothing left to save, you eventually reach that decision. Everything good has a beginning and an end. Once you come to terms with that, separation becomes easier to bear.”

She explains that women face both practical and psychological challenges after divorce. She notes that many women in Armenia face hostility from their former husbands and their families, who accuse them of “breaking up the family”.

She is happy with her relationship with her ex-husband. He provides financial support, pays child maintenance and often spends time with their children.

“I believe both parents have equal rights, both during a relationship and after it ends. I respect my children’s father and stay in touch with him. It is very important to me that the children feel both parents are present in their lives and take part in them. I want to make sure they never feel they have no mother or no father, even if we no longer live together,” Juliette says.

“I got married for life”

Araksi Poghosyan is 40. She married at 23 and separated from her husband after 11 years of marriage. She says it is impossible to explain in a few words why they divorced. But after thinking for a moment, she adds: “We no longer loved each other.”

She insists that they tried to save their marriage and decided to divorce only when they realised there was no other way:

“People talk about divorce more than ever now, especially on social media. Many think it is easy to make such a decision. But it isn’t. I belong to a generation that married believing it was ‘for life, until death do us part’. It was very difficult for me to accept that reality had turned out differently and that I needed to get divorced. It took me around three years to reach that decision. I worked with a psychologist and tried to get back on my feet financially because I was leaving with my son, who was seven at the time. I had no idea what would happen next or how I would manage.”

It is very important to me that the children feel both parents are present in their lives and take part in them. I want to make sure they never feel they have no mother or no father, even if we no longer live together,” Juliette says.
