It was very difficult for me to accept that reality had turned out differently and that I needed to get divorced. It took me around three years to reach that decision. I worked with a psychologist and tried to get back on my feet financially because I was leaving with my son, who was seven at the time. I had no idea what would happen next or how I would manage.”

Statistics and reasons

According to official statistics, the number of marriages in Armenia has fallen in recent years, while the number of divorces has risen:

2022 – 16,795 marriages and 4,525 divorces (26.9%)

2023 – 16,330 marriages and 4,525 divorces (27.5%)

2024 – 15,324 marriages and 4,689 divorces (30.5%)

2025 – 13,821 marriages and 4,881 divorces (35.3%)

Domestic violence, infidelity, financial difficulties and everyday problems are commonly cited as reasons for divorce.

“In the past, couples who had been married for many years tended to divorce. Now, even those who have been married for just three or four years are splitting up. The main reasons for divorce are arguments, accounting for 50%; incompatibility, 14%; and going abroad for work, 8%,” says Tsovinar Harutyunyan, a development and demography expert who has held senior positions at the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

However, some psychologists say these factors have taken a back seat in recent years.

Family psychologist Naira Kharatyan says most of her female clients cite their husbands’ indifference as the reason for seeking a divorce. She believes women marry for love, but men become less attentive as the years go by:

“Women mostly say they feel neglected and that their partners have become indifferent towards them. Marriage is not just about everyday life and money; it is also about emotions and psychological connection. Women want to feel heard and understood.

“The second reason I would highlight is unmet expectations. Women have certain expectations of marriage, and when these are not fulfilled, they become disappointed. Another factor is unspoken competition within the couple. When a woman earns more or holds a higher position, a man may feel jealous. As a result, they stop acting as a couple and become unspoken rivals, each waiting to see who will win.”

Arus, 37 (not her real name, at her request), says that nowadays women “do not marry for money”.

In her words, “women marry for love and divorce because it is no longer there”. This is what happened to her. Arus left her husband after 13 years of marriage, taking their two children with her.

“My husband subjected me to psychological abuse. He put pressure on me and humiliated me. In the last few years, he did not earn any money. I was the only one working. But he told me I was worthless and that nobody wanted me. He told the children I was a bad mother. He said I could not even cook a decent meal. He did not feel like a proper man and wanted to crush me and humiliate me too. When I stood up to him, he threatened to beat me and take the children away,” she says.

While preparing this article, we spoke to many women who had experienced physical and psychological abuse. But all of them, like Arus, refused to speak on camera. They explained that they feared their former husbands might start harassing them.

“It took everything I had to get away from my husband. I am finally living in peace. Now, if he sees me on screen talking about him, he will turn up again and demand answers,” Arus says.

She adds that her former husband provides no support. She does not need financial help from him and wants no further contact with him.

“On my way home from work, I would pick up the children from nursery and school, get home and make dinner. He would come home in the evening, throw his lunch in the bin or spit into it. He would say it was inedible and that I had never learned how to run a household,” Arus says through tears.

The mother-in-law factor

Psychologist Naira Kharatyan argues that mothers can also contribute to the breakdown of their sons’ marriages:

“When sons remain overly attached to their mothers from childhood, they struggle to build strong families of their own. They have wives, but they listen to their mothers and follow their advice. Mothers encourage this dynamic without realising that they are creating a problem. As a result, the woman and the man never truly become a couple. A mother should tell her son: you are married now, and you must make decisions together with your wife. But in many cases, we see men whose wives were chosen for them, whose marriages their families arranged, and whose mothers then interfered in raising their children. The man never grew up.”

She says the “mother-son-daughter-in-law triangle can lead to tragic consequences”. Even when young couples do not live with their parents, the bond can remain so strong that the man still struggles to establish an independent family life.

Psychologist Mariam Manukyan also believes that marriage is more than a union between two people. She notes that the institution of marriage has acquired new dimensions and meanings over the centuries:

“It is a relationship in which two different people’s habits and ideas about life come together. When people enter a relationship, they begin to go through different stages. At the first stage, for example, a couple learns to share everyday responsibilities. At the second stage, after the birth of a child, they become parents and learn how to raise a child. This can also trigger a crisis and become a challenge for young couples. Relationships go through many such stages and crises. When couples fail to resolve them and the problems deepen, they separate because divorce becomes the only possible solution.”

At the same time, divorce brings new problems for many people. Couples struggle to agree on the terms of separation, while disputes arise over child custody, maintenance payments and the division of property.

“I divorced four years ago, and in all that time I have probably spent just four hours having proper conversations with my children. After the divorce, their father decided that they should stay with him. He wanted to punish me, and he succeeded. The court awarded him custody. We spent four years fighting in court. Eventually, the guardianship authority, which decides which parent the children should live with, concluded that staying with their father was in their best interests.

“My former husband’s close relatives work on that council, and its head is one of his friends. They knew what kind of mother I was and how attentive I had always been to my children, but… For four years, I collected documents to prove that I was a good mother so that my children could live with me. But no one cared about the children’s interests. They cared about my former husband’s interests,” says Susanna (not her real name, at her request).

All the women we interviewed on this subject agree on one thing: divorce does not always end on the day two people decide to stop living together. They also say that society often judges divorced women without considering what led them to make that decision.

“It is easier to talk about the importance of keeping a family together than to consider what it takes to achieve that. A family is not simply people living under one roof. It is also an environment where a child learns what love means, how people treat each other, what women and men deserve, and whether it is possible to live without fear,” one divorced woman says.

Divorce in Armenia: women share their stories

World.title: ‘The purge has only just begun’? South Ossetia’s new authorities arrest ‘chief baker’
World.content:
The authorities in South Ossetia have placed Vadim Tskhovrebov, the long-serving director of the local bread factory, under house arrest for two months, from 31 October to 29 December. They have opened a criminal case against him on charges of abuse of office.

This is no routine arrest. It forms part of a sweeping purge, one of the key campaign promises made by the new president, Marat Kambolov.

A hotel at the bread factory

According to investigators, Tskhovrebov appropriated a plot of land on the bread factory’s premises, leased it to his wife at a below-market rate and built a hotel, a billiards room and commercial premises there.

Some Telegram channels have also alleged that Tskhovrebov installed cryptocurrency mining equipment on the factory grounds, while the state budget covered the huge electricity bills.

In addition, unofficial reports suggest that the company owes millions in unpaid taxes, which may simply have been written off.

Alina Chochieva, deputy prosecutor of Tskhinval, explained that the General Prosecutor’s Office had requested Tskhovrebov’s house arrest. His defence team tried to persuade the court to impose a travel ban instead, citing a positive reference from his workplace and numerous awards recognising his contribution to the development of South Ossetia.

Tskhovrebov himself fully accepts both the charges against him and the restrictive measure.

“I admit my guilt and am ready to compensate the damage in full as soon as the investigation determines the final amount,” South Ossetia’s “chief baker” said.

An enterprising bun

For many years, Vadim Tskhovrebov, whom Tskhinval residents affectionately nicknamed “Bun”, was actively involved in politics and even served as a member of parliament. But he took the greatest pride in keeping production running during the August 2008 war. The factory never stopped operating, not even for a day, and continued supplying bread to residents of the South Ossetian capital.

Vadim Tskhovrebov

“Bun” took over as head of the bread factory around 20 years ago.

Over the years, he survived two assassination attempts and efforts to seize his business. He secured state funding and expanded production, while gradually raising the price of his products.

During Tskhovrebov’s time in his “bread kingdom”, South Ossetia went through five presidential administrations. “Bun” managed to get along with every one of them.

Many people now believe that previous presidents may have turned a blind eye to abuses of office in exchange for certain financial arrangements.

It seems, however, that he failed to strike a deal with Marat Kambolov.

Gaps in the logic

However, some JAMnews sources in Tskhinval question the logic behind the new authorities’ actions.

“How does this make sense? The director of the bread factory has been arrested, while his former boss, Atsamaz Kabisov, has actually been promoted to deputy prime minister in the new government, despite long-standing suspicions that he too abused his office,” one of our sources said.

Atsamaz Kabisov previously headed the Committee for Industry, Transport and Energy, which oversees the bread factory.

Local bloggers report that South Ossetia’s debt to Russia for gas and electricity had already exceeded 1 billion roubles [around $12 million] in 2024 and has not fallen since. One of the main reasons is losses in the power grid, which Russian specialists estimate at 40–50%. Unofficial sources link these losses to illegal cryptocurrency mining operations. Kabisov, who oversees electricity consumption records, may have provided protection for these mining farms.

Has the purge only just begun?

Nevertheless, Tskhovrebov’s arrest fits the purge of corrupt officials and those accused of misappropriating public funds that Marat Kambolov announced. “Bun” is not the first person to face scrutiny. Criminal cases have already been opened against several businessmen from the inner circle of former president Alan Gagloev and former prime minister Konstantin Dzhussoev.

One of them is Oleg Bosikov, a close relative of Dzhussoev and CEO of the construction company Megapolis-T. Investigators allege that the company served as a money-laundering operation through which hundreds of millions of roubles from Russia were siphoned off. The money came under an investment programme for South Ossetia’s socio-economic development.

The General Prosecutor’s Office has also turned its attention to former Interior Minister Erislav Mamiev and his first deputy, Atsamaz Sagkaev. Investigators say Sagkaev illegally registered two service firearms in his superior Mamiev’s name.

World.title: Erdogan to visit Baku after hijab dispute: what concessions has Ankara made, and what does Baku want?
World.content:
Turkey–Azerbaijan relations

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told journalists on 5 November that he planned to visit Azerbaijan on 8 November, Victory Day, provided no extraordinary circumstances arose. He also said he had spoken by phone with President Ilham Aliyev and sent Turkey’s intelligence chief and foreign minister to Baku.

“The unbreakable ties between our countries rest on a shared history, culture and destiny – and, God willing, a shared future.”

However, Erdoğan’s planned visit comes amid a two-month cooling of relations between the two countries. On 30 October, President Aliyev skipped the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States in Ankara, even though the meeting marked the transfer of the organisation’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Turkey.

We reported in October on Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s visit to Baku.

What steps has Ankara taken to resolve the disagreements, what does Baku want, and what does the current situation reveal about relations between the two countries?

How did the dispute erupt?

In September, new school uniform requirements came into force in Azerbaijan. Although the rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, schools began turning away pupils who wore one. Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan criticised bans on wearing the hijab in schools without naming any specific countries. In Baku, his remarks were seen as an indirect criticism of Azerbaijan.

The subsequent events unfolded as follows:

2 October. At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”.

The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit. 25 October. Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser.

Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser. 30 October. Aliyev did not attend the Ankara summit. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented the country at the meeting.

What concessions has Ankara made?

The most significant step was Erdoğan’s dismissal of Oktay Saral as his chief adviser. According to Middle East Eye, which cites its own sources, Baku made three demands of Ankara:

Dismiss Erdoğan’s adviser, prosecute commentators who insulted Aliyev, and block the social media accounts named on a list. The publication reports that Ankara has already blocked some of those accounts.

Saral himself, however, has not retracted his remarks. He said he left his post at the president’s request but stressed that he had said nothing that warranted an apology: “Azerbaijan is my homeland too.”

According to Middle East Eye, Turkish officials have described the disagreements as a “misunderstanding”. Speaking at the summit, Erdoğan made no direct reference to Azerbaijan but said:

“There is no room for division, hostility or discord in the family photograph of the Turkic world.”

On 3 November, while travelling to South Korea, Erdoğan also sent Aliyev Victory Day greetings as his plane passed through Azerbaijani airspace. He delivered the message over the radio through the aircraft’s pilot.

What does Baku want?

Baku has not officially explained why Aliyev skipped the summit. According to APA, the president was due to attend the closing ceremony of the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku that day.

Baku has also taken issue with other statements from Ankara. Middle East Eye reports that, at an event organised by a foundation in October, Erdoğan said Turkish children no longer had to go abroad to study because of restrictions linked to their clothing or political views. Azerbaijan also interpreted these remarks as another rebuke.

An Azerbaijani source cited by Middle East Eye summed up Baku’s position as follows: Turkey must recognise the principle of “one nation, two states”. In other words, Baku does not want Ankara to interfere in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.

Elman Fattah, head of the Khazar Centre for Research and Analysis, shares a similar view. In an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, he said: “This means rejecting Turkey’s right to veto.” Fattah believes Aliyev is “deliberately shifting the hidden tensions between the two countries into the religious sphere”.

Political analyst Asif Narimanli, meanwhile, argues that

“The tensions between Baku and Ankara have deeper roots.”

Speaking to TodayPress, he noted that Aliyev’s absence…на саммите дает основания для такого вывода.

What lies behind the disagreements?

One of the deeper sources of tension concerns Israel. In Turkey, Azerbaijan’s close ties with Israel have caused considerable discontent, particularly since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip. Middle East Eye reports that Erdoğan declined to attend the October summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to avoid meeting Israeli President Isaac Herzog. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also boycotted Herzog’s address. Baku saw this as an unfriendly gesture towards Aliyev.

Another source of disagreement concerns Armenia. According to an analysis by OC Media, Ankara wants to normalise relations with Yerevan, while Baku insists that this process must remain linked to a peace settlement between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

At the same time, the two countries share significant interests. According to OC Media, on 30 September they signed defence contracts worth around $500 million in total. In early 2026, they also reached a 15-year agreement on gas supplies from the Absheron field to Turkey. Azerbaijan accounted for around 22% of all the gas Turkey imported in 2024. According to figures from Turkey’s Ministry of Trade, bilateral trade reached $4.3 billion in 2025.

What could the visit change?

Political analyst Elkhan Shahinoglu described Erdoğan’s decision to visit Baku as “the right one”. He said:

“If tensions arise between two allies for any reason, they should not delay resolving them.”

Shahinoglu recalled that Erdoğan also visited Baku and addressed the Milli Majlis in 2009, when Turkey was moving closer to Armenia. Relations between the two countries returned to normal afterwards.

There is another sign that tensions may be easing. According to the newspaper Karar, when Turkey considered nominating former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu for the post of UN secretary-general, Azerbaijan backed a candidate from the United Arab Emirates instead. However, in late October, Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry spokesman Aykhan Hajizada welcomed Turkey’s nomination of Sinirlioğlu.

The next test for relations will be the UN climate conference COP31, which will take place in Antalya this month. Middle East Eye reports that Ankara hopes Aliyev will attend the conference. Baku has yet to confirm his visit.

Turkey–Azerbaijan relations

World.title: Turkmenistan, EU seek to expand ties as trade reaches €1.3 billion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. Turkmenistan and the European Union are exploring ways to advance bilateral cooperation, building on trade ties that reached 1.3 billion euros in 2025, the EU Delegation to Turkmenistan said.

The issue was discussed at a meeting between Chairman of the Central Bank of Turkmenistan Toyly Malykov and EU Ambassador to Turkmenistan Luke Devine.

The two officials exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and considered opportunities to further develop dialogue and cooperation.

The scale of existing economic ties is reflected in bilateral trade figures. According to data presented by Devine at the Turkmenistan Investment Forum (TIF 2026) on October 1, 2026, trade between Turkmenistan and the EU totaled 1.3 billion euros in 2025.

EU exports to Turkmenistan accounted for 900 million euros, while imports from Turkmenistan reached 400 million euros.

The European Union and Turkmenistan maintain structured dialogue through mechanisms such as the EU-Turkmenistan Joint Committee and regular high-level contacts. Cooperation covers trade, energy, transport connectivity, climate and sustainable development. The EU has repeatedly supported Turkmenistan’s efforts to diversify its economy and integrate into regional and international markets, including through technical assistance and investment promotion.

World.title: Turkmenistan concludes $226,523 cotton yarn and textile deal with UAE
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. A foreign trade transaction in the textile sector was concluded during the October 29 trading session at SCRMET.

According to the press release by the State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), entrepreneurs from the United Arab Emirates signed a deal with Turkmen businesses to purchase cotton yarn and textile products during exchange trading on October 29.

SCRMET noted that one transaction was concluded with a total value of $226,523.

The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities.

SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade.

World.title: Kazakhstan's electricity exports rise 25.6% in 2025, led by Russia - Kazenergy
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. Kazakhstan increased electricity exports by 25.6% in 2025, reaching 3.9 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh), mainly due to a 42.6% rise in supplies to Russia, according to the National Energy Report prepared by the Kazenergy Association in cooperation with S&P Global.

Data from Kazakhstan's electricity grid operator KEGOC show that exports to Russia increased by 805.1 million kWh compared with 2024, reaching 2.16 billion kWh. The entire increase was driven by electricity sales to settle imbalances, which rose by 45.5%, from 1.46 billion to 2.12 billion kWh. Meanwhile, commercial exports under contracts declined from 58.8 million to 41.5 million kWh.

Electricity exports to Central Asian countries also increased, rising by 9.9% to 1.78 billion kWh in 2025, compared with 1.62 billion kWh a year earlier. Commercial exports to the region grew by 16.8%, from 1.24 billion to 1.45 billion kWh.

Kyrgyzstan remained the main destination for Kazakhstan's electricity supplies in Central Asia. Exports to the country increased from approximately 1.2 billion to 1.4 billion kWh.

Despite the growth in exports, Kazakhstan remained a net importer of electricity. According to the country's trade statistics, electricity imports reached 5.2 billion kWh in 2025, up approximately 7% year-on-year.

The increase was driven by higher supplies from Central Asian countries, primarily Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, while imports from Russia declined slightly. KEGOC data show a similar trend, although the absolute import volumes differ.

Over the 2015-2025 period, Kazakhstan's electricity exports increased by an average of 7% annually, according to trade statistics. A particularly strong rise was recorded in 2025, when exports grew by 24% and exceeded 3 billion kWh, with most supplies going to Russia.

The average export price increased from $0.016 per kWh in 2020 to $0.023 in 2025. Electricity supplied to Kyrgyzstan fetched an average of approximately $0.031 per kWh, with deliveries concentrated mainly in winter, when the country faces electricity shortages.

At the same time, electricity imports have increased by an average of 13% annually over the past decade, with a particularly noticeable rise since 2021, mainly due to supplies from Russia. The average price of imported Russian electricity more than doubled from 2020, reaching $0.092 per kWh. Uzbekistan began exporting electricity to Kazakhstan in 2024, while imports from Kyrgyzstan remained relatively small.

World.title: Green Energy Corridor applies for EU Project of Mutual Interest status
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. Green Energy Corridor Power Company (GECO) has successfully submitted an application to the European Commission to have the “Green Energy Corridor” (GEC) project recognized as a Project of Mutual Interest under the EU’s Trans-European Energy Networks (TEN-E) regulation, the statement from GECO says.

Furthermore, the statement notes that the “Green Energy Corridor” will create a new route for supplying electricity from renewable sources in the Caspian region to European markets: “It will connect Azerbaijan, Georgia, Romania, and Hungary via a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) subsea cable laid across the Black Sea, as well as the corresponding onshore infrastructure.”

According to GECO, obtaining the status of a project of mutual interest will confirm the project’s strategic importance for the EU and its partners.

“In addition, this will expand opportunities for receiving support from the EU, simplify permitting procedures, and strengthen investor confidence as the project progresses through the development phase.

The submission of the application was the result of close cooperation among GECO’s shareholders: Azerenerji, Georgian State Electrosystem, Transelectrica, and MVM. We are grateful to them for their hard work, as well as for the ongoing support from the governments of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Romania, and Hungary, the European Commission, and our technical partners.

We look forward to the next stage of the application evaluation process and to continuing our work toward creating a secure, diversified, and decarbonized energy future for the region and Europe," GECO stated.

World.title: WA Aboriginal affairs minister visits Pilbara amid child welfare crisis
World.content:
Western Australia's Minister for Aboriginal Affairs Don Punch has slammed the politicisation of child protection failures in the state's north and rejected calls for his resignation during a visit to South Hedland.

The town has been subject to intense attention in recent months after evidence of systemic child protection failings emerged.

Facing questions about his role in the crisis, Mr Punch said he was "lobbying for better outcomes for Aboriginal people" and had travelled to South Hedland after receiving a letter from Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton.

"Aboriginal issues and Aboriginal people are beyond politics," Mr Punch said.

Media and politicians have swarmed South Hedland in recent months. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Last month the WA government announced it would hold a coronial inquest in the 2022 murders of three Aboriginal children in nearby Port Hedland, which had been the subject of a lengthy campaign by their grandmother, Dorothy Papertalk.

The case received fresh scrutiny as media reports revealed further allegations of neglect and triggered visits from senior politicians, including the premier, but not the Aboriginal affairs minister.

Coronial inquest set for death of Hedland children A coronial inquest is announced into the deaths of three children killed by their mother in Port Hedland in 2022.

Mr Punch has faced severe public backlash for ruling out a trip to the Pilbara unless he was specifically asked by elders.

Multiple local elders, including Ms Eaton, told the ABC that Mr Punch should not need an invitation.

In South Hedland today, Mr Punch walked back statements he made about the Aboriginal affairs portfolio only being about native title and heritage protection.

"My job is to go out and listen to Aboriginal people, Aboriginal elders, talk with communities and understand the issues that they're facing," he said.

Calls to step down

Mr Punch's visit came as the opposition launched a petition calling for his sacking from the portfolio.

It has been signed by Robert Isaacs, who has spent decades working to improve the lives of First Nations people.

Don Punch met with Kariyarra elder Pat Mason and other elders. (ABC Pilabara: Kimberley Putland)

He said he was motivated by watching decades of Aboriginal affairs ministers who "really haven't performed the work that Aboriginal people expected".

"I want parliament now — the state parliament in WA — to look at appointing an Aboriginal commissioner that reports directly to the parliament," Dr Isaacs said.

"So every member of parliament is getting the metrics across, they're understanding about where this funding is going, billions of dollars, about policies, about directions of programs."

That would replace what he described as a largely powerless portfolio and address concerns about too many people speaking on behalf of Aboriginal Australians, which he said he'd had a "gutful" of.

Don Punch says his political opponents are exploiting the situation. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Mr Punch said he suspected Mr Isaacs was prompted by WA Liberal Leader Basil Zempilas.

"He is making a football of Aboriginal people to simply score his own political goals and it's appalling behaviour," Mr Punch said.

Engaging with politicians 'draining'

Kariyarra elder Patricia Mason was one of the elders who met with Mr Punch during his visit.

"I think Punch just wants it to go away," she said.

"They're about a quick fix, and a quick fix leaves us in a crisis."

Ms Mason said constantly engaging with politicians and the media was taking a toll.

"I'm feeling mentally and physically drained," she said.

Labor won't consider petition

Premier Roger Cook said his party would not consider the parliamentary petition under any circumstance.

"Don's doing a great job. He's working well with the community and we're really proud of his work," he said.

Basil Zempilas rubbished the premier's comments about the monister's performance. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Zempilas hit back at the premier's defence of the minister.

"Has he not read or heard any of the comments from the Aboriginal elders form the Hedland region who are so exasperated by Don Punch's actions?" he said.

Mr Punch has pledged to return to South Hedland in six months.

World.title: Ukrainian drone attack sets Russia's Kirishi refinery ablaze
World.content:
Russia's second-largest oil refinery has been set on fire following a Ukrainian drone attack that killed a local woman, according to Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko.

The Kirishi refinery in the Leningrad region came under attack in the early hours of Monday, local time, and the woman was killed by falling drone debris.

The governor wrote on Telegram that the fire had been contained.

Earlier, he said that air defence forces had downed 113 Ukrainian drones, and that an apartment building in Kirishi had been damaged in the same overnight attack.

The wider region is a major export outlet for grain and oil from Russia's Baltic Sea ports.

Drone strikes have hit about 30 Russian oil refineries, including this facility in Moscow. (Reuters )

Ukraine has now disrupted operations at nearly 30 major Russian oil refineries through precise long-range drone strikes.

Attacks on key infrastructure from both sides of the Ukrainian war have intensified in recent days.

On Monday, Russia's armed forces said they struck three power substations across Ukraine.

They also claimed to have hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea that Moscow said was providing arms to Ukraine, state news agencies reported.

Loading...

Russia is seeking to undermine Ukraine's resolve as winter sets in with strikes on its power system.

Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that "every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by attacks" and urged Kyiv's allies to provide generators and other equipment to keep the electricity flowing.

He also pleaded with allies to tap their own air defence stockpiles to help Ukraine fend off Russia's attacks and replenish them later.

Abu Dhabi to host peace talks

The latest skirmishes come as Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators prepare for Tuesday talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.

The two-day session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous rounds of negotiations that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe's most devastating conflict since World War II.

It is their first peace talks since February.

A truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine gave onlookers hope of progress towards peace. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

The negotiations follow last month's localised truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of US first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.

But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the week-long ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometre front line.

Ukrainians escape Oleshky 'kill zone' In Oleshky, Ukrainians say they were forcibly starved before an evacuation allowed them to flee.

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed early in the war but never fully captured.

He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Mr Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that such a pause would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Mr Zelenskyy rejects Mr Putin's demands to voluntarily cede Ukrainian territory Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield and agreed to limits on the military and arrangements with Western partners, which it sees as essential security guarantees to stop Russia invading again in the future.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Mr Putin and Mr Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Police charged over alleged e-bike hit and run in Sydney
World.content:
Two police officers have been charged over an alleged hit and run of an e-bike rider in Sydney's inner west.

A 25-year-old woman was struck by a fully marked police vehicle while riding an e-bike near Glebe Point Road, about 5am on Tuesday, May 12.

According to a statement from NSW Police, the officers who were on duty allegedly failed to stop to render assistance and drove from the scene.

The woman called emergency services before reporting the incident to police.

On Monday, detectives charged a 27-year-old male constable with neglect, refuse or not carry out lawful order as a police officer, negligent driving and not give particulars to the other driver.

NSW Police will allege in court that he was driving the police car at the time of the crash.

A second male constable, aged 25, was charged with neglect, refuse, not carry out any lawful order as a police officer.

They were issued Court Attendance Notices and are due to appear at Downing Court on January 15.

NSW Police said the employment status of both officers is under review.

World.title: Fagan's understudy Bruce named Brisbane's new senior coach
World.content:
Brisbane has chosen Cameron Bruce to be its new head coach after the departure of three-time premiership winner Chris Fagan.

The 47-year-old, who served as an assistant under Fagan for the last five seasons, beat out a strong collection of candidates including Nathan Buckley and Adam Simpson.

Bruce wins the Brisbane role having acquired more than a decade of AFL assistant coaching experience at three different clubs.

His coaching career began with Hawthorn, where he was an assistant under Alastair Clarkson for five seasons between 2013 and 2017, a period which yielded the club three premierships.

Bruce served as an assistant under Fagan for all three of Brisbane's premierships over the last three seasons. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

Bruce then joined Carlton as an assistant under Brendon Bolton before departing at the end of 2021 following an extensive review into the underperforming club.

Bruce enjoyed a 13-year career as a player, making a combined 234 appearances for Melbourne and Hawthorn. He was a member of Melbourne's 2000 grand final side and was also a best and fairest winner for the Demons in 2008.

Fagan has joined Carlton as the club's new director of coaching after his exit from Brisbane following a decorated, decade-long stint.

Bruce is expected to be formally named Brisbane's senior coach on Tuesday.

World.title: Fuel retailer accused of selling unleaded 91 as premium petrol
World.content:
A chain of Perth petrol stations sold unleaded 91 fuel as higher octane 95 and 98 fuel, WA's consumer watchdog has alleged, prompting it to begin a civil claim against the company in the Supreme Court for alleged breaches of the Australian Consumer Law.

Burk Fuel operates 14 outlets across Perth and regional WA.

In a statement released on Monday, the Consumer Protection Agency said it had ordered independent testing on samples taken from several of its service stations between July 2025 and February this year.

"All of the samples came back as 91 fuel," Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Ms Blake said that would constitute a "massive breach of trust for the consumers" if the allegations were found to be true.

"Particularly for something like fuel, where you do not have the independent ability as a consumer to inspect the product and know if you're getting what you've paid for," she said.

"You have to be able to rely and trust on the trader."

Trish Blake says the agency will seek significant penalties if the allegations are upheld. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

When authorities announced the investigation in April this year, Burk Fuel strenuously denied the allegations, saying they used a reputable supplier and their fuel was regularly tested.

Unleaded 91 is regarded as the minimum standard for most petrol cars. Higher-octane 95 and 98 fuels are recommended or required for more high-performance vehicles.

Ms Blake said buying allegedly mislabelled fuel could have a significant impact on customers.

"It's a significant difference in value," she said.

"But also a lot of the high-performance cars only run well on the high-performance fuel.

"Some people will have been putting, in good faith, what they believe to be premium 98 unleaded fuel into their high-performance car."

Unleaded 91 is cheaper than higher-octane varieties of fuel. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Ms Blake said the agency would seek significant financial penalties if the allegations were proven true in court.

She said the agency had also sampled fuel from other traders in WA.

"I was very pleased to find that all the other traders, all of their fuel samples came back exactly as they were being promoted to the consumer," Ms Blake said.

The investigation was sparked after a consumer contacted 102.5 ABC Perth, raising questions about fuel quality at Burk Fuel.

Ms Blake praised the person for coming forward.

"They're an absolute deadset legend in my book, because the more that we can help consumers to have trust in the economy and keep traders honest, the better it is for everyone," she said.

In a statement, Burk Fuel said it intended to defend the proceedings.

"Burk's operations continue to operate as normal. Burk will not be commenting further while the matter is before the court."

World.title: This bouquet may look beautiful, but the weeds are killing our native plants
World.content:
A bouquet featuring some of the worst invasive weeds in Western Australia's South West has won a top award at the Margaret River Agricultural Show.

Nature Conservation Margaret River entered the unusual floral arrangement in a bid to raise awareness of the environmental damage caused by invasive weeds, including plants commonly found in home gardens.

The bouquet featured arum lilies, English ivy, watsonia, Flinders Range wattle, agapanthus, periwinkle and Victorian tea tree.

Margaret River Agricultural Show vice-president Julie Kirby said there had been a record-breaking 200 floral exhibits across several individual categories, including roses, wedding bouquets, mixed arrangements, floral art, and mixed weed arrangements.

Obelia Walker with winning bouquet of weeds. (Supplied)

Nature Conservation Margaret River's entry was awarded ribbons in the mixed weeds category and best overall exhibit.

"The best exhibit is one that really catches the judges' eyes," Ms Kirby said.

"We have trained and accredited judges from the Western Australian Horticultural Council and they thought that the overall design, the workmanship, and the colour harmony and the quality and the condition of this particular display was just so impressive.

"With the mixed weed arrangement you don't need to grow it yourself, you can go and collect it from bushland or the roadside, or wherever you've got weeds present and enter them."

She said the bouquet was disposed of safely to prevent the seeds from spreading.

"It was a beautiful and educational way to show how garden plants can escape to become bushland weeds," Ms Kirby said.

Nature Conservation Margaret River biodiversity officer Obelia Walker said the organisation saw the competition as an opportunity to draw attention to some of the region's most problematic invasive plants.

Obelia Walker didn't expect the top gong. (Supplied)

She said she was surprised to discover the arrangement had taken out the overall bouquet award.

"I didn't realise that I'd actually won the champion bouquet for the whole category," Ms Walker said.

She said the judges recognised the arrangement as a creative way to get the community thinking about the threat posed by invasive weeds.

"Weeds are sometimes a tricky one to get people to pay attention to," Ms Walker said.

"They really take over and smother all our lovely native plants.

"Arum lily, of course, can just become such a monoculture and a carpet, but the others can as well."

Invasive plants thrive in the South West

The arum lily, considered one of the most damaging weeds in the country, was banned from sale in WA more than 20 years ago, but the rogue garden plant's infestation of forests across WA's South West shows no sign of slowing.

Arum lilies are infesting Boranup Forest. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

More than 3,000 private landowners have requested help to eradicate the weed on their properties.

Ms Walker said invasive weeds often thrived because they had no natural predators encouraged gardeners to consider alternative plants rather than risk introducing invasive species into the environment.

The organisation hopes the unusual prize-winning bouquet will encourage people to look more closely at what they are planting in their backyards.

World.title: Warner says Khawaja's ball-tampering claim '100 per cent accurate'
World.content:
David Warner has backed Usman Khawaja's claims on the 2018 ball tampering scandal, saying the statements in his book, Sabr, are "100 per cent accurate".

Warner, who was Australia's vice-captain at the time, was suspended from domestic and international cricket as a result of the scandal and was also permanently barred from leadership positions.

Speaking for the first time in eight years on the saga, Warner emphatically backed Khawaja, his childhood friend.

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for everything you've done," he said in an Instagram statement.

Loading Instagram content

"It's 100 per cent accurate, what you've said.

"Now everyone knows the truth, it's out there. People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzie, thank you."

Warner slammed Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident in the wake of the 2018 tour of South Africa. Khawaja was not interviewed as a part of the probe.

David Warner was suspended from all international and domestic cricket for 12 months following Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident. (AAP Image/Ben Rushton)

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched," he said.

"Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft [in the dressing room]. Uzzie was not interviewed. How that is a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds.

"It's about accountability, transparency ensuring that the truth is properly examined, and perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability, and asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it.

"There [were] a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent."

Khawaja says he has thrown nobody 'under the bus' Usman Khawaja has revealed Steve Smith talked him out of going public with claims of widespread knowledge around ball-tampering during the 2018 saga.

Warner said his delayed response to Khawaja's claims being made public was down to explaining his involvement in the scandal to his daughters.

"The last couple of days, I've been talking to my daughters and that is why it's taken me a couple of days to get this out, because I've had to tell them exactly what had happened, especially my 12-year-old Ivy," he said.

"[She] wanted to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras and why we were all crying on TV.

"That was a hard thing to do, but one thing I did say is, 'Girls, tell the truth because lies will eventually get out.' It is a very tough time.

"This is for everyone in Australia. It has been the question that everyone is asking. Uzzie, you've said it how it is, it is 100 per cent accurate.

"It has been a tough time for my family, Steven [Smith] and Cameron [Bancroft] no doubt, but this is what needed to come out."

Warner is the first of the banned trio to speak publicly in the wake of Khawaja's comments being made public.

World.title: Premier says tougher laws 'will be considered' after war memorials damaged
World.content:
Two men have been charged with wilful damage after two separate acts of vandalism at war memorial monuments in Cleveland and Hervey Bay.

The pillar of a 106-year-old war memorial cenotaph in Anzac Park at Cleveland, east of Brisbane, was found broken on Sunday morning.

Police allege a 20-year-old Cleveland man climbed on the war memorial monument whilst intoxicated and broke it before leaving the scene.

Photos show the pillar which sat atop the memorial shattered on the ground below.

A war memorial in Anzac Park in Cleveland was damaged overnight between Saturday and Sunday. (Supplied: Redlands RSL Facebook)

At around midday on Monday a 20-year-old Cleveland man attended a Gold Coast police station and has since been charged.

Meanwhile, sub-branch president of the Hervey Bay RSL, Brad Gray, came to work on Monday morning to find the club's flagpole damaged.

CCTV footage shows a black Nissan Navara driving into the pole three times just before 7am.

Police attended the scene a short time later and apprehended a 38-year-old man in the vehicle nearby.

The man has been charged with a range of offences including wilful damage, possessing a knife in a public place and drug charges.

The vehicle had a mattress placed over its bonnet and windscreen.

Both incidents occurred just days before Remembrance Day.

Queensland Premier and Minister for Veterans David Crisafulli said the damage done to the Cleveland memorial was "disgraceful".

"We will watch the outcome very closely if it progresses through court, and it tougher laws are needed, they will be considered."

Hervey Bay RSL president Brad Gray said the vandalism won't stop Remembrance Day events. (Supplied)

Mr Gray said the damage to the RSL's flagpole was not good timing.

"I've got no hope I get anybody in to repair ir before Remembrance Day. It'll have to be like that."

"I don't get what these people get out of desecrating a war memorial," he said.

" I can't see the sense in it. It's just sheer vandalism. "

He said there are no changes planned for Wednesday's Remembrance Day events.

Australian Oscar Piastri has split from his management team, led by former Formula 1 driver Mark Webber and his wife Ann, after a challenging 2026 season on the track. Piastri and Webber released a joint statement on Monday evening, confirming the agreement to separate was a mutual decision. McLaren star Oscar Piastri has parted ways with Mark Webber. Getty Images “We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar’s career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on,” Mark Webber said in the statement. “Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.



“This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career.” Piastri also released a statement, thanking the Webbers – who have been working with him since 2019. “I’d like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years,” he said. “Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.” The Webbers guided Piastri through major milestones in his career, including his Formula 2 and Formula 3 championship victories in successive years.



It’s been a challenging season for McLaren star Piastri. The Australian driver hasn’t won a race in more than a year – in a 2026 F1 season marred by poor luck, errors and reduced pace. Piastri crashed out of his home grand prix in Melbourne in March falling victim to an unfortunate combination of cold tyres, torque spike and driver error. Then there were electrical issues in Shanghai, which saw his McLaren unceremoniously towed from the grid before the formation lap. There have been glimpses of a potential resurrection, with a podium finish in Miami and Japan and a close call in Austria. However, F1’s new regulations and changed cars have completely changed the landscape for his team McLaren and Piastri was unable to realistically fight for the championship – which was won last week by 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli, of Italy. Loading



Piastri’s McLaren teammate Lando Norris has clinched three victories this year, including a recent triumph at the Brazilian Grand Prix. In July Webber dismissed lingering reports suggesting Piastri might swap places with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Verstappen ended up signing another contract with Red Bull and Piastri remains contracted with the papaya team. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Punch hits back at petition, claims WA Liberals’ real target is his Bunbury seat

NationalWAWA Parliament Punch hits back at petition, claims WA Liberals’ real target is his Bunbury seat Cameron Myles November 9, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Embattled minister Don Punch has accused Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas of “exploiting vulnerable Aboriginal people” to score political goals in response to a petition demanding the Bunbury MP’s resignation from cabinet. The petition, launched on Monday, is backed by prominent Aboriginal elder Dr Robert Isaacs, a respected public health figure and member of the Stolen Generation who helped establish Clontarf Aboriginal College. WA Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch and Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas. Getty Images Punch’s performance in his Aboriginal affairs portfolio has come under intense scrutiny in recent months following the revelation of a series of child protection failures relating to families in the state’s north-west. Zempilas took aim at the Bunbury MLA over his response to a crisis that has “played out on the national stage, with Aboriginal elders and families crying out for help”.



It follows a series of reports in The Australian revealed more than a dozen children were living unsupervised and in squalor in South Hedland, prompting an investigation by WA’s top child protection worker. There were also growing calls for the WA government to order a coroner’s inquest into the deaths of three children at the hands of their mother in Port Hedland in 2022, which Attorney General Tony Buti insisted could not be done until new evidence came to light – which it eventually did, and an inquest was subsequently ordered. Zempilas said it had taken until Monday for Punch to visit Hedland in response to the reports and inquest calls, and also criticised Punch’s parliamentary attendance record. “I went to South Hedland, visited Frisby Court, spoke to the elders and witnessed first-hand a community desperate for leadership and answers,” Zempilas said. “Don Punch has missed two of the four parliamentary sitting weeks since this crisis erupted. He has also been absent from one-in-five Question Times in the past 12 months.



“Ministers have a responsibility to turn up to parliament, face scrutiny and answer questions. Related Article WA Parliament ‘Not a game show’: Saffioti hits out at petition to sack WA minister “Mr Punch’s attendance record and his handling of this crisis have raised serious questions about his priorities.” But speaking from Hedland on Monday, Punch accused the opposition leader of “making a football of Aboriginal people”, describing it as “appalling behaviour” and linking the push to oust him to the Liberals’ desire for his seat in the state’s South West. “Aboriginal issues and Aboriginal people are beyond politics,” Punch said.



“We should be working together to get the best outcomes possible. “That’s exactly what I’ve been doing in my job since I was appointed Aboriginal affairs minister, and I intend to continue doing that. And that’s why I’m meeting with elders today.” Punch said he believed Port Hedland was “suffering from the political ambition” of Zempilas, and that the real target was his seat of Bunbury. “He is clearly after me, and after me means he’s after my seat in Bunbury, and he knows he cannot become premier without winning Bunbury,” he said. “Bunbury is a bellwether seat, and the people up here have been exploited in that process.



“I’ve never seen it before in a leader of the opposition, and it highlights that he’s more interested in a headline than he is in genuine conversation.” Punch insisted his role as Aboriginal affairs minister was to listen and speak to Aboriginal people, elders, and communities, to inform the programs and policies set out by his cabinet colleagues and inform the portfolio’s Call To Action Plan. “I’m lobbying for better outcomes for Aboriginal people, whether it’s in housing, whether it’s in health, whether it’s in education, and whether it’s in child protection,” he said. “And the feedback that I take back from local communities, together with our commitment to closing the gap, informs the advice that I give to ministers.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

“George Zivkovic bemoans the omission of AC/DC, INXS, Cold Chisel, John Farnham, Kylie and even Joe Dolce from the first 10 songs inducted into Australia’s inaugural National Songbook (C8),” says Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “Surely, a greater omission is John Meillon’s rousing 1967 ode to Australian culinary prowess, Hot Pie and Tomato Sauce. Now that’s Australian!”

“I was discussing the demise of David Jones (C8) with my elderly mother,” says Jack Dikian of Mosman. “Apparently, she stopped shopping there when they removed the soda fountains and the haberdashery counter. I don’t know; this might be important information for the appointed administrators.”

“In a past era, among all the fashionable and elegant frocks, David Jones also ran a ‘used clothing’ section” writes Joan Gandy of Alstonville. “It was during World War II. I remember going with my mother to this shrine of elegance and purchasing two dresses to wear when I started business college. After years of school uniforms, they were so glamorous. These two frocks were admired by many friends and when asked where Mum had purchased them I could honestly reply ‘David Jones’ without elaborating any further that they were from DJs’ Clothing Pool (as that section was called) and were pre-loved. The original op shop.”

“As a country kid in Bega I can’t tell you the excitement I had with the arrival of the David Jones catalogue as I pored over the pictures of clothing,” recalls Anne Stearman of Downer (ACT). “I even have a memory of real bits of material being stuck on some pages, but maybe that is fabricated.”

“Apropos Ginger Nut biscuits (C8) being different in NSW and Queensland – yes the Queensland biscuits are thinner. But in Tamworth, where I live, we can get both types,” claims Gregory Nell. If you buy Ginger Nuts from Coles in Tamworth, they are the thinner Queensland variety. But if you buy them from a Woolworths here, they’re the fatter NSW variety, although both packets are identical. As the NSW variety is fatter, presumably you get less biscuits in a packet bought from Woolworths compared to a packet from Coles, although I have not checked, not yet anyway. Perhaps that is a task for this week.”

World.title: The special commissioner for lawn-mowing with one eye on a senate spot
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The special commissioner for lawn-mowing with one eye on a senate spot Matt Dennien and James Hall November 9, 2026 — 8:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Andrew Cripps eyes a regional public servant push – and the senate, voluntary assisted dying board wants scheme eligibility changes considered, and election watchdog’s warning on IR changes. Now seven months into a plum post as Crisafulli and Co’s hand-picked Special Commissioner for Regional and Rural Queensland, it seems Andrew Cripps has finally hit (some form of) a stride. The question now is what inroads the Newman-era minister will be able to make on delivering more public sector roles to the regions before another opportunity knocks: a jump to federal politics. Special Commissioner for Rural and Regional Queensland Andrew Cripps announcing his first day in the role, and one of three post-mowing toasts shared since. LinkedIn / Andrew Cripps Estimates hearings in July taught us Cripps’ exact work plan for the reportedly $392,000-a-year role was still being hashed out – as had a formal “landing page” for his non-Hotmail inbox.



Department of Premier and Cabinet director-general Damien Walker said at the time he had “no doubt” there would be a “level of communication around what the special commissioner will be focused on as a result of concluding the work program itself”. Since then, however, it’s been relative crickets from Cripps and the three full-time staff he was handed from two departments. We say relative crickets because Cripps has still managed to maintain his series of post-mowing beverage philosophising, with a recent admission he’d forgotten to keep his fridge stocked. “With my sensibilities impaired, I sourced a glass of water and perched myself on the back steps to survey my freshly maintained square footage,” Cripps recounted in early October on LinkedIn, while asking for follower feedback.



“What emerged from my disorientation was a question: ‘If you cut the grass in the Deep North, but can’t enjoy a cold beer afterwards, have you really mowed the lawn?’ I think not.” Related Article Public service Little fanfare as state-run water body lands well-connected new chief Thought-provoking stuff. Following up a few weeks later with a post at 4.30pm on a Tuesday, Cripps – previously appointed by government to co-ordinate the north’s 2025 flood recovery – said he was “suitably chastised and humbled” by the ribbing in the comments and “fully intend[s] to plan better, with the appropriate supplies at hand”. So what else has Cripps been up to? The Department of Premier and Cabinet has told us only that his work plan has been approved by the Public Sector Governance Council chaired by Walker, but skimped on any real detail. Luckily, Circus has also learned that despite Walker’s dancing around estimates questions of whether Cripps might have a role in a push to see more public servants set up in the regions, the man has been busy writing to each of the state’s directors-general and commissioners.



This forms part of what’s been described as an initial consultation phase from Cripps seeking feedback on barriers and opportunities around the idea, and how it might happen – if it does. Given the current squeeze on departmental budgets, however, we can only imagine any systemic (and costly) program to shift bureaucrats from Brisbane would be off-the-cards. Which brings us back to the more capital P politics of the moment. Circus has also heard from those elements of the tent that Cripps is expected to raise his hand for the party’s second federal senate ticket spot when Matt Canavan leaves to run for the lower house at an election due by early 2028. While holding strong internal party support, sources granted anonymity to discuss internal LNP rumblings said the former senate preselection candidate has become somewhat of a lightning rod in state politics after landing the special commissioner gig. Some sources said a senate tilt would ruffle feathers among state colleagues given the media scrutiny that followed. He’s also likely to come up against a “Melbourne Cup field” for the once-prized second Senate spot.



The other likely challenger is Toowoomba mayoral advisor Michael Duff – currently at fourth position on the ticket and with the support of Canavan as a factional heavyweight from the Christian far right. How prized the preselection remains will depend on the scale of support bleeding to One Nation in the Sunshine State. The one certainty is that Cripps, who we contacted for comment, would appear to have his work cut out for him. It’s enough to make you thirsty. Queensland MPs voting on the Palaszczuk government’s voluntary assisted dying bill in 2021. Matt Dennien Voluntary assisted dying board wants LNP to look at eligibility changes Its one of the topics the government would rather not have to talk about: the state’s now almost four-year-old voluntary assisted dying scheme.



Unlike with abortion or uranium mining, however, the Crisafulli LNP – while coming to power promising no changes to euthanasia laws – is required by those very laws to review the scheme. “As soon as practicable” after its three-year milestone, even. We’re now into month 11, and have no news except assurances by the government the review will happen, and that no change will come of it. We can only hope public cash isn’t being spent paying some external firm to do the doomed work. A Right to Information application by Circus for any to-and-fro between responsible minister Tim Nicholls and the scheme’s independent oversight body has turned up little cabinet-excluded detail except a letter from members of the Voluntary Assisted Dying Review board confirming they spoke to Nicholls about the looming review at a meeting one year ago (and got little insight themselves). Since then, the associate professor Helen Irving-chaired board has lobbed its 2025-26 annual report, which landed among the avalanche of other agency updates in late September and managed to slip media attention at the time.



Inside, however, is a handful of new recommendations from the board. One explicitly calls for the minister to ensure the review involves “broad consultation with the public and other stakeholders to determine the desirability and feasibility of amending existing eligibility criteria”. Currently, adults must be diagnosed with an advanced condition that would cause death within 12 months, be assessed by two doctors, and make three separate requests to access the scheme. Federal laws mean this all has to be done in-person, too. Advocates nationwide have long called for this pre-existing roadblock to be lifted – and for changes to improve the scheme and its accessibility. At least one anti-VAD group, Right to Life, has clocked the remarks and data from the report to urge that Nicholls instead call an “urgent inquiry” into the state’s scheme, citing the increased number of deaths (1082) and fact this placed Queensland at the higher end of Australian jurisdictions.



We reached out to Nicholls’ office for an update on the review last week. They pointed us to the government’s statement – unchanged from late July. Feel free to tweak your working definitions of “ASAP” accordingly. Electoral watchdog’s plea to government on ‘not insubstantial’ IR overhaul While the government’s controversial proposed industrial relations overhaul is given an air of public consultation via parliamentary committee, one official has made a particularly pointed plea. Electoral Commissioner Pat Vidgen, in a written submission, has made clear he had no prior heads-up about the broadened union election program his team would have to oversee with new, so-far vaguely described “electronically assisted voting”. With only a short time to prep feedback as a result, Vidgen warned the “not insubstantial” changes would have the effect of “rendering ECQ’s current staffing for industrial elections inadequate” and require the commission to set up something it doesn’t even currently do: online voting.



The commission currently oversees elections for fewer than 20 employer and employee organisations with a full-time equivalent team of two people. Under the draft changes, this could balloon to 74 groups – some with up to 50,000 members. On top of this, from next year the team enters a “critical preparation stage” for the four-yearly statewide council and state government elections in 2028, and carry out 11 council divisional boundary reviews before October. Electoral Commissioner Pat Vidgen appears before an estimates hearing in July. Queensland Parliament “Given those constraints, ECQ cannot presently administer the amendments as proposed, without additional time, funding and staff,” Vidgen wrote in his covering letter, urging the relevant changes be delayed until he had enough resources – or until at least October 2029 for any online system. “Upfront funding will be required to expand capacity and make the necessary preparations, which may be recouped once the amendments [for a user-pays model] are in force.



“However, significant funding will be required to implement and maintain the online voting system, which may not be recoverable as a user pays cost.” Vidgen, like the rest of us, will have to wait and see what – if any – tweaks might be made to the bill by Deputy Premier and Industrial Relations Minister Jarrod Bleijie before it sails into law. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com.

The Queensland government will investigate claims of fraud in a scheme designed to support victims of crime, as its cost blows out. Victim Assist Queensland (VAQ) provides financial assistance for victims of crime in the state, who may require services such as counselling or legal advice. Minister for youth justice and victim support, Laura Gerber, called for anyone with evidence of fraud or rorting to come forward. Jamila Filippone The Australian reported on Monday costs were on track to top half-a-billion dollars this financial year amid claims of rorting, including by prison inmates. It said applicants were predicted to hit 70,000 by 2032, up from fewer than 10,000 in 2022.



The office of Laura Gerber, minister for youth justice and victim support, urged anyone with information about rorting of the scheme to come forward. “Our priority is supporting victims, including domestic and family violence victims,” Gerber said in a statement. “Any financial assistance fraud is not only a crime but takes support away from victims in their time of need.” She did not comment on the dramatic increase in payouts. Associate professor doctor Heather Lovatt, director of the Queensland Centre for Domestic and Family Violence Research, said alleged fraud should be investigated, but the government needed to be careful it did not increase the barriers to entry for those genuinely in need.



“Sexual assault and domestic violence is traumatic enough, and you want victim survivors feeling they can come forward,” Lovatt told this masthead. “Any potential rorting should be investigated, but it needs to be very carefully considered with how you build in greater risk-mitigation and governance … that doesn’t involve making it more difficult for those applying.” She added she had seen the importance of VAQ firsthand. “We know that when you’re leaving or trying to leave a situation, you’re often leaving with nothing … you may well go into poverty,” Lovatt said. “To be able to access financial support, and also to be linked with the right people that can provide further support, is just so vital.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Our sacrifices are not seen’: Queen is one of a brave group of women who gave too much for Australia
World.content:
NationalNSWRemembrance Day ‘Our sacrifices are not seen’: Queen is one of a brave group of women who gave too much for Australia Daniel Lo Surdo November 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queen Dunbar never carried a gun or wore a uniform, but counts herself among the most steadfast servants of Australia’s armed forces. She’s been serving since 1996, when husband Adam enlisted in the army, starting a career that took him to Solomon Islands, Iraq and Afghanistan. He was discharged in 2015 after his post-traumatic stress disorder diagnosis. Queen Dunbar’s husband served in Solomon Islands, Iraq and Afghanistan, in a 19-year military career. KATE GERAGHTY Dunbar raised their children, Joshua and Sarah, in Sydney while Adam fought for Australia. She was 41 when Adam died by suicide in 2017, owing to injuries suffered in service. Their children were 15 and 11 at the time of their father’s death, while Dunbar worked three jobs to get by. It took Dunbar, by her estimation, one year to realise she was a war widow. She credits her fellow war widows for helping her to “start breathing” again.



Adam Dunbar in uniform. “Our sacrifices are not seen, and if they are seen, they are seen once or twice a year,” she said. “I was trying to make it through the pain and the grief, and knowing that I actually have a place where I belonged, changed my outlook on life.” Dunbar is among more than 28,000 war widows in Australia, according to the Families of Veterans Guild, many of whom are preparing to honour their loved ones in Remembrance Day events this week. Australian war widows often raised children, worked jobs and supported the home while their spouses fought in conflicts overseas. Most veteran families experience financial stress, according to a survey conducted by the Guild last year, and three-fifths report their children have faced problems at school in the past year.



Dunbar, who is NSW president of the Guild, considers herself underemployed, as she balances work as an English teacher and flight attendant with supporting her children. Her daughter, 20, faces mental health challenges stemming from her father’s service, which Dunbar expects will be a lifelong struggle. She has pushed the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to tailor support packages for specific families and improve aid for former soldiers as they transition into civilian life. Assistance often comes too late, Dunbar warned, resulting in devastating consequences for families struggling to stay afloat. “My children’s wellbeing has impacted my employment because I’ve had to sit there and try to find support for my daughter,” she said. “My career has been impacted because of their needs that the department wasn’t able to meet.” The Department of Veterans’ Affairs said it recognised there were persisting challenges in its delivery of tailored support, and that “work continues” to better understand families’ needs and priorities. It expects to have implemented two-thirds of recommendations from the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide by the end of 2026.



Shirley McLaren, a 94-year-old who lives in a rural cottage south of Canberra, was booted from her family’s Defence accommodation two days after the funeral of her husband, Roy, a Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) member who died unexpectedly on Christmas Eve 1972. Shirley McLaren, a 94-year-old W-RAAF veteran, sits next to a photo of her late husband. Alex Ellinghausen McLaren, who was one of the first to enlist in the Women’s RAAF as an 18-year-old in 1951, was 39 when Roy died. She had three small children and a dog in tow. McLaren had met her husband at a dance at Canberra’s Albert Hall in 1953, and Roy proposed shortly before he was posted to Korea. She recalls receiving “no help at all” from any widows network as she packed her young family into a car and drove to Canberra, where they slept in sleeping bags in friends’ dining rooms while she picked up the pieces of her life. McLaren dipped her toes into widows networks while juggling her responsibilities as a mother and breadwinner in subsequent years, but largely felt unwelcome by groups of elderly women whose husbands fought in earlier conflicts than Roy.



A portrait of Shirley and Roy McLaren on their wedding day, hanging on the wall at the home of Shirley McLaren. Alex Ellinghausen Now McLaren ensures that no new widow attending Guild meetings sits alone. Only a widow, she said, can understand the loss that comes from the death of a spouse in the service. “You’ve gone from a couple, doing everything together, and suddenly, you’re on your own,” she said. “Tears are the price we pay [for love].” McLaren pays tribute to Roy every week, laying six stems of rosemary at a photograph of her husband at her Royalla cottage. She continues the tradition with her two great-grandchildren, Will and Tom, who have learned of their great-grandfather through stories told by their family.



“I encourage the widows who are coming for the first time to the group to never be ashamed of your tears,” McLaren said. “Talk about your husband, and you’ll find that we are all very supportive to help you through this grieving process because we’ve all been there.” McLaren’s son, Noel, and granddaughter Brooke served in the Royal Australian Navy, while Will expects to join the Australian Defence Force once he finishes school next year. His enlistment would mark the fourth generation of service in the family. McLaren’s great-grandsons have planted hand-made poppies in her yard, in a range of colours to honour the Diggers, nurses, wounded soldiers and animals that served in conflict. War widows placed wattle at the Cenotaph in Martin Place last month. KATE GERAGHTY The Families of Veterans Guild was established as the Australian War Widows NSW in 1946 by Jessie Vasey, seven months after losing husband George in World War II.



She wrote to 2000 widows as she grieved: “Real help for widows could only come from among themselves,” she wrote. “Now, as one of them, I am sure of it.” More than 300 people joined the first widows meeting in Sydney in June 1946, sparking the creation of what is now the Families of Veterans Guild. War Widows Day has been commemorated on October 19, Jessie Vasey’s birthday, since 2022, through national services. McLaren will lead the Ode of Remembrance at the Families of Veterans Guild’s inaugural Remembrance Day Lunch at the Australian War Memorial on Tuesday, to about 70 war widows, including Dunbar, and veteran families honouring those who served. “[I] lost a wonderful, loving husband, the father of my children, the love of my life, so my remembrance goes out to all veterans, of course, who have served and are no longer with us,” McLaren said. “It doesn’t matter how long it is … the grief is very deep and long-lasting.” If you are a current or former ADF member, or a relative, and need counselling or support, you can contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. Crisis support is also available from Lifeline on 13 11 14. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.
