Mandy Noffs was many things. She was the mother of two boys, the chief operating officer of the Ted Noffs Foundation, a member of the Order of Australia for the youth health programs she established, and a right character. “Mum had the most wonderful collection of sayings,” her son Rupert says. Rupert Noffs sings to his mother, Mandy, who has advanced Alzheimer’s. Steven Siewert There was: “You’ve gotta roll with the ponchos” and “We may be bohemians, but this time you’ve gone too far”, and Rupert’s favourite: “Do what you can and can’t what you can’t.” But, before 2017, when Mandy was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease at 65, she was never a singer.



In the years that followed, she became less responsive and her memory deteriorated. Rupert, 43, a cabaret singer, began singing to distract and soothe her when she became anxious and started asking the same questions repetitively. To his surprise, Mandy lit up. Loading “She started singing things note for note, word for word, with harmonies, phrasing and an incredible musical memory,” he recalls. “It was quite astonishing. I realised there was this whole musical ability in Mum that we’d never really seen before.”



Music therapy is well known for providing comfort to people living with dementia, relieving common symptoms such as agitation, depression and anxiety. Dr Benjamin Slade used rare magnetoencephalography to map brain activity in people with dementia who underwent music therapy Eddie Jim But a new Australian study suggests it may have a more powerful impact in the brain than previously realised, altering neural wiring to compensate for dysfunction and even recruiting alternative pathways to help complete tasks. Using a rare type of imaging called magnetoencephalography (MEG) to map activity in the brain, researchers from Swinburne University in Melbourne tested their hypothesis that targeted music therapy can improve cognitive function in people with dementia by targeting compensatory neural networks. Lead author Dr Benjamin Slade reported participants improved their performance in tests after undergoing an eight-week music therapy program, which included singing tasks and playing individual tune bells as part of a group to the melody of Doggie in the Window as part of a performance.



“Broadly we saw there was a definite change in brain connectivity in each person after therapy,” he said. “We found that change was directly linked to compensatory neural networks, where there was increased activity after therapy. “We also found areas not associated with these networks were activated. We hypothesised these areas of the brain were recruited to help complete the task.” While the study was small – with just six participants and a control group – and limited by health, recruitment and neuroimaging requirements, it’s important because it provides new clues into the mechanisms underpinning music therapy’s impact on cognitive symptoms of dementia. The findings suggest music therapy could be used to awaken, and tap into, a person with dementia’s cognitive reserve, which is the brain’s accumulated ability to improvise, adapt and find alternative ways of solving problems when areas become damaged.



Musician Yoshi Masuda has seen first hand how patients with dementia respond when he plays them songs on his gramophone. It can elicit “pure joy”. Yoshi Masuda plays his gramophone to connect with people’s hearts. James Brickwood For years, the 75-year-old has visited elderly residents in care homes on Sydney’s north shore. He invites them to be physically involved with selecting a shellac record, winding the motor, replacing the needle and then watching the disc rotate.



Related Article Dementia ‘There’s plenty you can do’: The lifestyle changes you can make to curb the risk of dementia “Surface noise, mechanical sounds and pauses for preparation form part of the listening experience,” says Masuda, a PhD student researching music and psychology. Through this sensory ritual, he says residents often begin clapping or tapping along, laughing or responding to the lyrics such as You Are My Sunshine, Love Me Tender, and Que Sera, Sera. Music, Masuda believes, taps into our emotional memory and is like speaking to our heart. Active participation in music therapy is key to securing cognitive benefits for people living with dementia, according to the Swinburne study.



The research involved giving participants tasks, such as singing the lyrics of a known song but skipping words beginning with specific letters. Delivered via a helmet fitted with sensors sitting in pools of helium within the scanner in a room with a vault-like heavy door, MEG imaging gives researchers an unparallelled view of electromagnetic activity in a brain. Music therapist Dr Romy Engelbrecht, co-author of the study published in the journal biomedicines, expected positive results but said participants had also enjoyed the therapy. Benjamin Slade and his team used this magnetoencephalography (MEG) scanner to record brain activity in participants with dementia before and after music therapy Eddie Jim “These people had real changes of behaviour,” she said. “If you go past the room and look in, it looks like everyone is happy and having fun but when you look underneath, what’s happening is quite scientific.”



Pharmaceutical options are usually first line treatments for dementia. Given music therapy can provide relief, improve quality of life and may have cognitive benefits at low cost and with no immediate side effects, Slade believes it should be considered as a frontline co-therapy. “Music therapy is implemented a lot in aged care but it’s variable in how it’s delivered,” he said. “It needs to be targeted and active to be beneficial.” Related Article Wellbeing Is ‘cognitive endurance’ the antidote in the age of distraction? Engelbrecht, who is also a clinical psychologist, said a challenge in therapy is prescribing music because it’s so personal. The study culminated in a handbell performance at an aged care facility. “They learnt a handbell song – they had to remember the information, wait for their turn and then perform,” she said. “You could see their happiness and sense of accomplishment. On performance day, they kept performing over and over again, they were so happy.”



The study team is calling for further research to build on their findings and establish a stronger evidence base. “There’s very little neuroimaging research relating to music or reminiscence therapy,” Engelbrecht added. In Mandy Noffs’ bedroom, overlooking gum trees on the NSW Central Coast, the television plays music: George Michael, Tina Arena, the Beatles. Her son sits by her bedside singing, and playing the part of the Vaudeville Dame. It’s a nod to his mother’s sense of humour and the Broadway shows they loved attending together when he lived in New York. Even while he feels so much of his mother slipping away, music remains his way of connecting.



“Alzheimer’s changes so much about a person, but it doesn’t necessarily take away the essence of who they are,” he says. “And perhaps that’s what music has shown us more than anything. Even when so much else has disappeared, there’s still something there.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: The busiest part of a suburb isn’t always its true character. This place is proof
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After a seven-minute ride on Sydney’s 100 bus from the Queen Victoria Building in the CBD to Neutral Bay, a contrast emerges. Many Sydneysiders mistakenly assume that Neutral Bay is synonymous with Military Road. Loud, noisy, full of traffic lights, intersections, crowded footpaths and an incessant flow of vehicles heading somewhere else. Admittedly, that crazy road is the suburb’s most visible face. Yet it belies what lies beneath. Military Road is Neutral Bay’s most visible face. George Chan When you get off the main artery, Neutral Bay reveals a very different side: hidden pockets of activity, places for play, harbourside walks and tables perched at the water’s edge. The natural beauty, energy and unexpected pleasures of the suburb reveal its surprisingly relaxed, carefree character. An easy stroll down Barry Street and you find the 140-year-old Neutral Bay Club, where you can play tennis, pickleball or barefoot bowls, all under stunning palm trees. It prides itself on its casual vibe, delicious eats and drinks and of course yappy hour (dogs welcome, Tuesday-Sunday 5-6pm). Any afternoon here means the slowing of time, immersing yourself in nature. Neutral Bay beach. Paul Rovere Or visitors could consider a cold dip at Hayes Street Beach. George Chan The newly refurbished Cammeray Golf Club has social play every day, open to the public. The course – which we locals like to call “Royal Cammeray” – has nine par 3 holes and any skill level is genuinely welcome. The clubhouse now has live music on Friday nights, and thanks to the recently opened Lusso Kitchen, dinner or lunch is available from Wednesday through Sunday. Don’t be put off by the expanded expressway and any noise; the short course is challenging and also surprisingly quiet.



After all this activity, you could consider a cold water dip at Hayes Street Beach – yes, a harbour foreshore beach in Neutral Bay that is open to the public. I haven’t swum there myself but braver souls do. At the harbour foreshore is the brilliantly casual waterfront cafe Thelma and Louise, where they serve the best scrambled eggs in Sydney. If you are after a casual waterside meal with good friends, wine and a locals’ view of Sydney Harbour, you can’t go wrong. Thelma and Louise, George Chan Thelma and Louise, left, with the Hayes Street Beach, right. George Chan If gluten-free is your thing, the newly opened Wholegreen Bakery serves the lightest pastries. Founder Cherie Lyden now has several bakeries across Sydney where every item is 100 per cent gluten-free and coeliac accredited. Their coffees are also excellent. Further up the street is 5 Loaves 2 Fish cafe – here you will taste the best chilli crab scramble ever. The dining options in the heart of Neutral Bay are plentiful. Grosvenor Street is now a burgeoning foodie precinct, home to many cafes and restaurants that have the benefit of all day sun and gentle evening ambience, just one street away from Military Road. For lovers of Italian, a few relatively new establishments are worth a visit. Pocket Pizza has arrived from the northern beaches with its New York-style pizza. Then there is Enoteca 128, an upscale eatery and wine bar with an extensive wine list of more than 300 curated wines. The newest edition is Trattor, which opened its doors in June and the neighbourhood Farinas, which allows you to bring your own wine.



Enjoying a drink at the 140-year-old Neutral Bay Club. George Chan If you are looking for something other than Italian, Grosvenor Street has alternatives. We are fans of Bombay Bloomers and their delicious Indian dishes. There is also the recently opened Japanese – Fujitori Yakitori & Sake Bar – a smaller, timber lined restaurant with a curated sake list. And if your group is large, the Neutral Bay institution that is Kyushu is great for family and friend gatherings. If you feel like walking off all of this lovely cuisine, you can head downhill and follow Kurraba Road for more scenic harbour views. Here there are wonderful vantage points to see Sydney Harbour Bridge – particularly Spains Wharf Lookout and further along Kurraba Road, Hodgson Lookout Park, which sits at the tip of the peninsula. These walks make up the broader network of harbour-side walking tracks connecting many reserves and lookouts around the peninsula, taking you through to Cremorne Point, Mosman and onto the stunning areas around Balmoral Beach. As you walk through the residential streets of Neutral Bay, you come to appreciate its architectural heritage. So much of the suburb was built between about 1890 and 1915, during the Federation period. This architecture is infused with much of the Australian way of life – deep verandahs, curved timber fretwork, tall ceilings to cool the houses and Australian native flora featured in stained-glass windows. The homes are worth a wander through these streets. As you head home, you may want to try a different form of public transport and jump on a ferry at Neutral Bay Wharf, which is a 10-minute downhill walk from Grosvenor Street and a 10-minute ride from Circular Quay. Ferries run every hour. Neutral Bay Wharf. Jacky Ghossein Reading on the wharf. George Chan

World.title: ‘Guidance has been invaluable’: Oscar Piastri parts ways with Mark Webber after tough F1 season

Updated SportMotorsportFormula 1 ‘Guidance has been invaluable’: Oscar Piastri parts ways with Mark Webber after tough F1 season Hannah Kennelly Updated November 9, 2026 — 9:13pm ,first published 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian Oscar Piastri has split from his management team, led by former Formula 1 driver Mark Webber and his wife Ann, after a challenging 2026 season on the track. Piastri and Webber released a joint statement on Monday evening, confirming the agreement to separate was a mutual decision. McLaren star Oscar Piastri has parted ways with Mark Webber. Getty Images “We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar’s career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on,” Mark Webber said in the statement. “Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.



“This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career.” Piastri also released a statement, thanking the Webbers – who have been working with him since 2019. “I’d like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years,” he said. “Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.” The Webbers guided Piastri through major milestones in his career, including his Formula 2 and Formula 3 championship victories in successive years.



It’s been a challenging season for McLaren star Piastri. The Australian driver hasn’t won a race in more than a year – in a 2026 F1 season marred by poor luck, errors and reduced pace. Piastri crashed out of his home grand prix in Melbourne in March falling victim to an unfortunate combination of cold tyres, torque spike and driver error. Then there were electrical issues in Shanghai, which saw his McLaren unceremoniously towed from the grid before the formation lap. There have been glimpses of a potential resurrection, with a podium finish in Miami and Japan and a close call in Austria. However, F1’s new regulations and changed cars have completely changed the landscape for his team McLaren and Piastri was unable to realistically fight for the championship – which was won last week by 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli, of Italy. Loading



Piastri’s McLaren teammate Lando Norris has clinched three victories this year, including a recent triumph at the Brazilian Grand Prix. In July Webber dismissed lingering reports suggesting Piastri might swap places with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Verstappen ended up signing another contract with Red Bull and Piastri remains contracted with the papaya team. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Punch hits back at petition, claims WA Liberals’ real target is his Bunbury seat
World.content:
NationalWAWA Parliament Punch hits back at petition, claims WA Liberals’ real target is his Bunbury seat Cameron Myles November 9, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Embattled minister Don Punch has accused Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas of “exploiting vulnerable Aboriginal people” to score political goals in response to a petition demanding the Bunbury MP’s resignation from cabinet. The petition, launched on Monday, is backed by prominent Aboriginal elder Dr Robert Isaacs, a respected public health figure and member of the Stolen Generation who helped establish Clontarf Aboriginal College. WA Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch and Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas. Getty Images Punch’s performance in his Aboriginal affairs portfolio has come under intense scrutiny in recent months following the revelation of a series of child protection failures relating to families in the state’s north-west. Zempilas took aim at the Bunbury MLA over his response to a crisis that has “played out on the national stage, with Aboriginal elders and families crying out for help”.



It follows a series of reports in The Australian revealed more than a dozen children were living unsupervised and in squalor in South Hedland, prompting an investigation by WA’s top child protection worker. There were also growing calls for the WA government to order a coroner’s inquest into the deaths of three children at the hands of their mother in Port Hedland in 2022, which Attorney General Tony Buti insisted could not be done until new evidence came to light – which it eventually did, and an inquest was subsequently ordered. Zempilas said it had taken until Monday for Punch to visit Hedland in response to the reports and inquest calls, and also criticised Punch’s parliamentary attendance record. “I went to South Hedland, visited Frisby Court, spoke to the elders and witnessed first-hand a community desperate for leadership and answers,” Zempilas said. “Don Punch has missed two of the four parliamentary sitting weeks since this crisis erupted. He has also been absent from one-in-five Question Times in the past 12 months.



“Ministers have a responsibility to turn up to parliament, face scrutiny and answer questions. Related Article WA Parliament ‘Not a game show’: Saffioti hits out at petition to sack WA minister “Mr Punch’s attendance record and his handling of this crisis have raised serious questions about his priorities.” But speaking from Hedland on Monday, Punch accused the opposition leader of “making a football of Aboriginal people”, describing it as “appalling behaviour” and linking the push to oust him to the Liberals’ desire for his seat in the state’s South West. “Aboriginal issues and Aboriginal people are beyond politics,” Punch said.



“We should be working together to get the best outcomes possible. “That’s exactly what I’ve been doing in my job since I was appointed Aboriginal affairs minister, and I intend to continue doing that. And that’s why I’m meeting with elders today.” Punch said he believed Port Hedland was “suffering from the political ambition” of Zempilas, and that the real target was his seat of Bunbury. “He is clearly after me, and after me means he’s after my seat in Bunbury, and he knows he cannot become premier without winning Bunbury,” he said. “Bunbury is a bellwether seat, and the people up here have been exploited in that process.



“I’ve never seen it before in a leader of the opposition, and it highlights that he’s more interested in a headline than he is in genuine conversation.” Punch insisted his role as Aboriginal affairs minister was to listen and speak to Aboriginal people, elders, and communities, to inform the programs and policies set out by his cabinet colleagues and inform the portfolio’s Call To Action Plan. “I’m lobbying for better outcomes for Aboriginal people, whether it’s in housing, whether it’s in health, whether it’s in education, and whether it’s in child protection,” he said. “And the feedback that I take back from local communities, together with our commitment to closing the gap, informs the advice that I give to ministers.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

“George Zivkovic bemoans the omission of AC/DC, INXS, Cold Chisel, John Farnham, Kylie and even Joe Dolce from the first 10 songs inducted into Australia’s inaugural National Songbook (C8),” says Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “Surely, a greater omission is John Meillon’s rousing 1967 ode to Australian culinary prowess, Hot Pie and Tomato Sauce. Now that’s Australian!”

“I was discussing the demise of David Jones (C8) with my elderly mother,” says Jack Dikian of Mosman. “Apparently, she stopped shopping there when they removed the soda fountains and the haberdashery counter. I don’t know; this might be important information for the appointed administrators.”

“In a past era, among all the fashionable and elegant frocks, David Jones also ran a ‘used clothing’ section” writes Joan Gandy of Alstonville. “It was during World War II. I remember going with my mother to this shrine of elegance and purchasing two dresses to wear when I started business college. After years of school uniforms, they were so glamorous. These two frocks were admired by many friends and when asked where Mum had purchased them I could honestly reply ‘David Jones’ without elaborating any further that they were from DJs’ Clothing Pool (as that section was called) and were pre-loved. The original op shop.”

“As a country kid in Bega I can’t tell you the excitement I had with the arrival of the David Jones catalogue as I pored over the pictures of clothing,” recalls Anne Stearman of Downer (ACT). “I even have a memory of real bits of material being stuck on some pages, but maybe that is fabricated.”

“Apropos Ginger Nut biscuits (C8) being different in NSW and Queensland – yes the Queensland biscuits are thinner. But in Tamworth, where I live, we can get both types,” claims Gregory Nell. If you buy Ginger Nuts from Coles in Tamworth, they are the thinner Queensland variety. But if you buy them from a Woolworths here, they’re the fatter NSW variety, although both packets are identical. As the NSW variety is fatter, presumably you get less biscuits in a packet bought from Woolworths compared to a packet from Coles, although I have not checked, not yet anyway. Perhaps that is a task for this week.”

World.title: The special commissioner for lawn-mowing with one eye on a senate spot
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The special commissioner for lawn-mowing with one eye on a senate spot Matt Dennien and James Hall November 9, 2026 — 8:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Andrew Cripps eyes a regional public servant push – and the senate, voluntary assisted dying board wants scheme eligibility changes considered, and election watchdog’s warning on IR changes. Now seven months into a plum post as Crisafulli and Co’s hand-picked Special Commissioner for Regional and Rural Queensland, it seems Andrew Cripps has finally hit (some form of) a stride. The question now is what inroads the Newman-era minister will be able to make on delivering more public sector roles to the regions before another opportunity knocks: a jump to federal politics. Special Commissioner for Rural and Regional Queensland Andrew Cripps announcing his first day in the role, and one of three post-mowing toasts shared since. LinkedIn / Andrew Cripps Estimates hearings in July taught us Cripps’ exact work plan for the reportedly $392,000-a-year role was still being hashed out – as had a formal “landing page” for his non-Hotmail inbox.



Department of Premier and Cabinet director-general Damien Walker said at the time he had “no doubt” there would be a “level of communication around what the special commissioner will be focused on as a result of concluding the work program itself”. Since then, however, it’s been relative crickets from Cripps and the three full-time staff he was handed from two departments. We say relative crickets because Cripps has still managed to maintain his series of post-mowing beverage philosophising, with a recent admission he’d forgotten to keep his fridge stocked. “With my sensibilities impaired, I sourced a glass of water and perched myself on the back steps to survey my freshly maintained square footage,” Cripps recounted in early October on LinkedIn, while asking for follower feedback.



“What emerged from my disorientation was a question: ‘If you cut the grass in the Deep North, but can’t enjoy a cold beer afterwards, have you really mowed the lawn?’ I think not.” Related Article Public service Little fanfare as state-run water body lands well-connected new chief Thought-provoking stuff. Following up a few weeks later with a post at 4.30pm on a Tuesday, Cripps – previously appointed by government to co-ordinate the north’s 2025 flood recovery – said he was “suitably chastised and humbled” by the ribbing in the comments and “fully intend[s] to plan better, with the appropriate supplies at hand”. So what else has Cripps been up to? The Department of Premier and Cabinet has told us only that his work plan has been approved by the Public Sector Governance Council chaired by Walker, but skimped on any real detail. Luckily, Circus has also learned that despite Walker’s dancing around estimates questions of whether Cripps might have a role in a push to see more public servants set up in the regions, the man has been busy writing to each of the state’s directors-general and commissioners.



This forms part of what’s been described as an initial consultation phase from Cripps seeking feedback on barriers and opportunities around the idea, and how it might happen – if it does. Given the current squeeze on departmental budgets, however, we can only imagine any systemic (and costly) program to shift bureaucrats from Brisbane would be off-the-cards. Which brings us back to the more capital P politics of the moment. Circus has also heard from those elements of the tent that Cripps is expected to raise his hand for the party’s second federal senate ticket spot when Matt Canavan leaves to run for the lower house at an election due by early 2028. While holding strong internal party support, sources granted anonymity to discuss internal LNP rumblings said the former senate preselection candidate has become somewhat of a lightning rod in state politics after landing the special commissioner gig. Some sources said a senate tilt would ruffle feathers among state colleagues given the media scrutiny that followed. He’s also likely to come up against a “Melbourne Cup field” for the once-prized second Senate spot.



The other likely challenger is Toowoomba mayoral advisor Michael Duff – currently at fourth position on the ticket and with the support of Canavan as a factional heavyweight from the Christian far right. How prized the preselection remains will depend on the scale of support bleeding to One Nation in the Sunshine State. The one certainty is that Cripps, who we contacted for comment, would appear to have his work cut out for him. It’s enough to make you thirsty. Queensland MPs voting on the Palaszczuk government’s voluntary assisted dying bill in 2021. Matt Dennien Voluntary assisted dying board wants LNP to look at eligibility changes Its one of the topics the government would rather not have to talk about: the state’s now almost four-year-old voluntary assisted dying scheme.



Unlike with abortion or uranium mining, however, the Crisafulli LNP – while coming to power promising no changes to euthanasia laws – is required by those very laws to review the scheme. “As soon as practicable” after its three-year milestone, even. We’re now into month 11, and have no news except assurances by the government the review will happen, and that no change will come of it. We can only hope public cash isn’t being spent paying some external firm to do the doomed work. A Right to Information application by Circus for any to-and-fro between responsible minister Tim Nicholls and the scheme’s independent oversight body has turned up little cabinet-excluded detail except a letter from members of the Voluntary Assisted Dying Review board confirming they spoke to Nicholls about the looming review at a meeting one year ago (and got little insight themselves). Since then, the associate professor Helen Irving-chaired board has lobbed its 2025-26 annual report, which landed among the avalanche of other agency updates in late September and managed to slip media attention at the time.



Inside, however, is a handful of new recommendations from the board. One explicitly calls for the minister to ensure the review involves “broad consultation with the public and other stakeholders to determine the desirability and feasibility of amending existing eligibility criteria”. Currently, adults must be diagnosed with an advanced condition that would cause death within 12 months, be assessed by two doctors, and make three separate requests to access the scheme. Federal laws mean this all has to be done in-person, too. Advocates nationwide have long called for this pre-existing roadblock to be lifted – and for changes to improve the scheme and its accessibility. At least one anti-VAD group, Right to Life, has clocked the remarks and data from the report to urge that Nicholls instead call an “urgent inquiry” into the state’s scheme, citing the increased number of deaths (1082) and fact this placed Queensland at the higher end of Australian jurisdictions.



We reached out to Nicholls’ office for an update on the review last week. They pointed us to the government’s statement – unchanged from late July. Feel free to tweak your working definitions of “ASAP” accordingly. Electoral watchdog’s plea to government on ‘not insubstantial’ IR overhaul While the government’s controversial proposed industrial relations overhaul is given an air of public consultation via parliamentary committee, one official has made a particularly pointed plea. Electoral Commissioner Pat Vidgen, in a written submission, has made clear he had no prior heads-up about the broadened union election program his team would have to oversee with new, so-far vaguely described “electronically assisted voting”. With only a short time to prep feedback as a result, Vidgen warned the “not insubstantial” changes would have the effect of “rendering ECQ’s current staffing for industrial elections inadequate” and require the commission to set up something it doesn’t even currently do: online voting.



The commission currently oversees elections for fewer than 20 employer and employee organisations with a full-time equivalent team of two people. Under the draft changes, this could balloon to 74 groups – some with up to 50,000 members. On top of this, from next year the team enters a “critical preparation stage” for the four-yearly statewide council and state government elections in 2028, and carry out 11 council divisional boundary reviews before October. Electoral Commissioner Pat Vidgen appears before an estimates hearing in July. Queensland Parliament “Given those constraints, ECQ cannot presently administer the amendments as proposed, without additional time, funding and staff,” Vidgen wrote in his covering letter, urging the relevant changes be delayed until he had enough resources – or until at least October 2029 for any online system. “Upfront funding will be required to expand capacity and make the necessary preparations, which may be recouped once the amendments [for a user-pays model] are in force.



“However, significant funding will be required to implement and maintain the online voting system, which may not be recoverable as a user pays cost.” Vidgen, like the rest of us, will have to wait and see what – if any – tweaks might be made to the bill by Deputy Premier and Industrial Relations Minister Jarrod Bleijie before it sails into law. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com.

World.title: Government to investigate claims of fraud in victims of crime scheme
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government Government to investigate claims of fraud in victims of crime scheme William Davis November 9, 2026 — 8:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Queensland government will investigate claims of fraud in a scheme designed to support victims of crime, as its cost blows out. Victim Assist Queensland (VAQ) provides financial assistance for victims of crime in the state, who may require services such as counselling or legal advice. Minister for youth justice and victim support, Laura Gerber, called for anyone with evidence of fraud or rorting to come forward. Jamila Filippone The Australian reported on Monday costs were on track to top half-a-billion dollars this financial year amid claims of rorting, including by prison inmates. It said applicants were predicted to hit 70,000 by 2032, up from fewer than 10,000 in 2022.



The office of Laura Gerber, minister for youth justice and victim support, urged anyone with information about rorting of the scheme to come forward. “Our priority is supporting victims, including domestic and family violence victims,” Gerber said in a statement. “Any financial assistance fraud is not only a crime but takes support away from victims in their time of need.” She did not comment on the dramatic increase in payouts. Associate professor doctor Heather Lovatt, director of the Queensland Centre for Domestic and Family Violence Research, said alleged fraud should be investigated, but the government needed to be careful it did not increase the barriers to entry for those genuinely in need.



“Sexual assault and domestic violence is traumatic enough, and you want victim survivors feeling they can come forward,” Lovatt told this masthead. “Any potential rorting should be investigated, but it needs to be very carefully considered with how you build in greater risk-mitigation and governance … that doesn’t involve making it more difficult for those applying.” She added she had seen the importance of VAQ firsthand. “We know that when you’re leaving or trying to leave a situation, you’re often leaving with nothing … you may well go into poverty,” Lovatt said. “To be able to access financial support, and also to be linked with the right people that can provide further support, is just so vital.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Not in my backyard, or upwards and onwards?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Not in my backyard, or upwards and onwards? November 9, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. HIGH RISE Do we really want to destroy Melbourne’s suburban heritage with an inundation of high-rise buildings? (“The high-rise transformation that’s set to sweep Melbourne’s suburbs”, 9/11).

High rises in suburbs will radically alter the character of those suburbs. They are unsightly, steal sunshine from neighbours, create wind tunnels and impose inordinate pressure on local infrastructure and services. Melbourne does not need more people; we struggle already with traffic congestion and meeting basic services. However, the regions would greatly benefit from increased population and its associated economic benefits.

Greenfield housing development would provide a more healthy lifestyle for families and kids would benefit physiologically compared with being boxed up in high rises with limited access to open spaces.

Community interests must prevail over interests of governments, unions and developers if Melbourne’s livability is to prevail.

Martin Newington, Aspendale High rise will overlook houses, gardens

It is concerning to read suggestions from some Brighton residents that a proposed development of six to 12 storeys would have no impact on existing dwellings.

As a homeowner whose property extends to the Church Street retail right-of-way, I would be directly affected; a multi-storey structure would overlook our garden and residence. No thanks.

Lucrezia Mecca, Brighton



We only have four possibilities

With respect to development in Melbourne, there are only four possibilities – stop Melbourne’s population growing, expand outwards, expand upwards or expand outwards and upwards. We must decide what we want.

Malcolm Fraser, Oakleigh South Six storeys, how would you like 16?

It’s hard to feel too much sympathy for Brighton residents facing developments of six storeys when one of Frankston’s most iconic row of houses is forced to watch luxury buildings 16 storeys-high rise up in front of them, blocking light and destroying the natural beauty of this area.

These inappropriately high towers will also deprive everyone on the other side of them, including the new multimillion-dollar hospital, of the views of Frankston’s beautiful bayside beach. Six storeys would have been a gift.

Joan Kerr, Frankston Brighton’s singular status

Would it seem that the amenity of Brighton is more important than any other suburb?

Peter Baddeley, Portland Footscray reaches for the sky

I agree, six-story buildings in Brighton is just wrong. They should be much taller. In Footscray, there are residential towers of up to 30 storeys, so why should Brighton be an exception? Just think of the health benefits for the residents living so close to the bay and excellent amenities the neighbourhood has to offer.

While we’re at it, why not build some data centres there too (Centre Road is already appropriately named) as the well-heeled local residents will no doubt be first to benefit from the financial windfalls AI promises.

Mark Kennedy, Sebastopol Brighton, come down from your ivory tower

Why would Brighton want to be known as selfish, snobbish and uncaring? Like the rest of us, its citizens need to stand up and be counted. The six- to 12-storey towers mooted for this exclusive suburb could be turned into an experiment in living greenery – ‘The Hanging Gardens of Brighton’.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove



THE FORUM Cautionary tale

It is highly probable that Jess Wilson will be premier after November 28. What is a certainty is that in the first 100 days, a forensic audit will be undertaken of the state’s finances and the result will be ″⁣that the situation is diabolical; much worse than we were told or anticipated″⁣. It will then be solemnly announced that the planned spending promised in the run up to the election will have to be seriously curtailed.

Why so cynical? I was a resident of Williamstown when Jeff Kennett was elected. He inherited major issues with the state’s finances. His government’s response was severe expenditure cuts across the board with a particular focus on Joan Kirner’s ALP seat of Williamstown.

One primary school was slated for closure, the hospital was scheduled for heavy reduction in services, the branch railway line from Newport was to be discontinued, and Point Gellibrand, one of Melbourne’s true historical sites, was to be sold for housing. All were planned but fortuitously reversed when Steve Bracks became premier.

My conclusion is to take promises by all parties, particularly if they require large public investment, with a large grain of salt.

Richard Caven, Melbourne Pesutto dreams

Re ″⁣John Pesutto tipped for frontbench return″⁣, 9/11. The former state Liberal leader is reported as ″⁣hungry″⁣ to get back in power as the state’s deputy leader and treasurer if his party wins the state election.

He is a man who led himself down a deep litigation hole, despite being warned, and then having pursued litigation in the Moira Deeming saga, was on the brink of insolvency, almost having to sell his family home.

Saved by a million-dollar-plus loan from his own political party, which reluctantly lent him the money, only so they didn’t lose his parliamentary seat, and now he’s going to help ″⁣lead″⁣ and look after the state and its budgets and finances.

He, or we, must be dreaming.

Kim Kaye, Surrey Hills One Nation protest vote

Presumably your correspondent (Letters, 9/11), whose ″⁣long-held opinion about the crippling awfulness of One Nation″⁣ was completely confirmed by your article (″⁣Top One Nation official’s strip club links to bikie figure″⁣, 8/11) and had never considered voting for One Nation anyway.

Those who are considering voting for One Nation, often as a protest against Labor, are unlikely to have had their minds changed by such disclosures.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne Some law and order

Until recently, I assumed One Nation lived rent free in the heads of the media, however recent revelations of criminal activity both proven and alleged by candidates makes a mockery of their law and order policies. Victorian electors deserve better

Denis Evans, Coburg



Express to airport

As your Letters’ correspondent explains, (″⁣Take the Tulla″⁣ 9/11), the initial planning of the Tullamarine Freeway was a bold yet simple project that included an elevated, two-way train line down the middle of the roads.

The aim was to get to the airport from the CBD as quickly as possible. It had nothing to do with looping around suburbs to pick up some extra airport passengers and, in the process, adding to the time the trip took to make.

Since the ‘Tulla’ opened in 1970, great advances have been made in heavy engineering skills. It would take very little time to build off-site all of the cantilevered sections, install them and have the project finished as it was envisioned over half a century ago.

The mess we are in at the moment involving the Big Build projects is now a mish-mash of various visions, often competing with one another, and costing us taxpayers an insane amount of money .

Peter Dodds, Montmorency No express to airport

Suggesting the airport rail be built down the centre of the Tullamarine Freeway can only be described as naive (Letters, ″⁣Take the Tulla″⁣, 9/11). Apart from those catching the train, presumably at Southern Cross, there would be no opportunity for others to board. Outcome – low patronage and future announcements that the line is not viable.

Look to Sydney, where the rail line is part of a suburban line.

Denise Chadwick, Soldiers Hill We need green

Amid the clamour of election pitches and cost-of-living anxiety, it was good to read Henrietta Cook’s article, ″⁣Doctors keen to prescribe a decent dose of fresh air and nature″⁣, (9/11).

While the data is patchy, anecdotal evidence of improved wellbeing from experiencing nature is loud and clear. Many mental and physical benefits have been documented. Even hospital patients with a view of green space benefit.

In Japanese, there is an expression, ‘shakkei’, which refers to the ‘borrowed landscape’.

As the blocks in our suburb are being steadily transformed from garden villas to mansions with pocket patches of turf and a few plants, I am grateful for the beautiful, residual trees of our neighbours. To awake to birdcall and watch the seasons pass via garden detail is a great pleasure, as well as knowing that green space, and trees in particular, are assisting to combat the urban heat island effect.

I am grateful that Boroondara council recently introduced the Greenways Connecting Paths plan to enhance opportunities for walking, cycling and running. Our wellbeing linked to nature and our environment, a simple counter to the stress of economic pressures and political uncertainty.

Jennie Stuart, Balwyn Impressive reading

Incisive article from Maureen Dowd (9/11) eviscerating Trump and his acolytes. Crony capitalism at its core!

Greg Curtin, Nunawading ANZ’s move

The ANZ 2026 annual report reveals that as one of ‘big four’ banks standing that might have funded the Beetaloo Basin gas pipeline to the east coast, has undertaken to ″⁣not directly finance ... new midstream infrastructure dedicated solely to new upstream oil and gas projects (such as new transmission pipelines).″⁣ This has been the ask of a months-long nationwide campaign from many climate action groups. It is wonderful news.

Lesley Walker, Northcote



Labor’s health vision lost

Whilst the extreme co-payments of some non-GP specialists may need to be addressed by capping Medicare fees and other measures, the main problem for most patients is the lack of timely access to publicly funded outpatient clinics and public hospital inpatient stays.

Previously, although there were modest delays in getting access, Labor governments did provide adequate funding which ensured outpatient access in almost all specialties and shorter waiting times for access to inpatient services.

State governments are refusing to fund adequate outpatient services in public hospitals, and it would seem timely to consider federal government funding for such services to ensure that those who have no particular desire for private services can be seen in a timely manner.

Medicare was set up for just that purpose, but that vision appears to have been lost by the current Labor Party.

Dr Tim Woodruff, president, Doctors Reform Society Who will care for you?

Dr Janet Duke bravely uses her personal experience to highlight the important role overseas-born carers play in our health system (Letters, ″⁣Gentle patient care″⁣, 9/11). My mother recently had the benefit of such care as she finally reached the end of her 96 years. Her last bed-bound days required constant physical attention by a team of sensitive, aged care staff who also gave emotional support to our grieving family. All these aged care workers were born overseas and even the only native English speaker grew up in the UK.

As a member of the upcoming ageing ″⁣Boomer Tsunami″⁣ I may also require support in the future and hope there will be similar workers to care for me.

Hence, I deplore the short-sighted anti-immigration stance of some vocal politicians. Our society can’t provide enough workers to fulfill many vital jobs and this this knee-jerk response to a complex problem can only lead to future distress.

I hope voters in upcoming elections avoid using the ballot box as a means of unthought through protest.

Dr Jenny Dowd, Ivanhoe East Ball-tamper tradition

Thank goodness Geoff Lawson has spoken up (″⁣I don’t know a bowler who hasn’t licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball″⁣, 9/11).

It doesn’t matter whether you use sandpaper, bottle tops or apply chewed up Murray Mints to one side of the ball, the desired end result is to produce unnatural reverse swing. This has been the practice of fast bowlers for 50 years.

John Uren, Blackburn Life lessons

Monday’s Letters to the Editor (9/11) have reminded me of three life lessons: respect, kindness and care. Thank you, letter writers.

Cheryl Williams, Doncaster And lessons learnt

I consider myself lucky to have been born in the mid-1940s and to have been brought up by hard-working people who were sensible with money.

My mother made all of my clothes, at first on a toy sewing machine. And when the elastic on my underpants failed, I became used to dealing with my falling undies.

So, I can cope with spending little. Being vegetarian, and not addicted to coffee and tattoos, helps. So too, do my major concerns, the environment and social cohesion.

Virginia Heller, St Kilda East



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Cage fights

Is Donald Trump ghost-writing Jess Wilson’s policy announcements? Promoting UFC’s cage fighting events is straight out of his playbook. What’s next? Holding UFC events at the steps of Parliament House?

Bruce Prosser, Balwyn North So Wilson wants to get UFC to Melbourne. The Romans always wanted ’bread and circuses including the gladiatorial and other combats in the Colosseum. Haven’t we progressed to more civilised sports? Or is Trump’s style following Nero and Caligula to be brought to Victoria?

John Crossley, Clayton Would it help if Victorian voters pretended that Pauline Hanson is on the ballot?

Hans Paas, Castlemaine



Victorians! Vote like Gina is on top of the ballot paper!

Luise Mock, Tawonga South When voters think that politics is about daily life and politicians think that daily life is about politics, mind the gap!

Jim Pilmer, Burwood Jess Wilson in a fake boxing exercise sent the wrong message to potential voters. Promoting violence will not win thinking adults.

Helen Hayward, Wonthaggi Furthermore

Re: ″⁣Nature as medicine. Why GPs are writing medical scripts for fresh air″⁣, 9/11. Who would have thought that nature could be healing? Hang on – 80,000 years of continuous culture immersed in and in tune with nature. Maybe we should begin to listen.

Anna Hayman-Arif, Ringwood East Musk’s Cybertruck monstrosity is coming to an end – there is a motoring God.

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon



Finally

I am so relieved the Liberal Party has promised more fire trucks. We’ll need every one of them if the Liberals continue to ignore the existential threat of global warming. Let’s hope we’ll still have enough water to fill the trucks!

Susan Cranage, Malvern East The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Our sacrifices are not seen’: Queen is one of a brave group of women who gave too much for Australia
World.content:
NationalNSWRemembrance Day ‘Our sacrifices are not seen’: Queen is one of a brave group of women who gave too much for Australia Daniel Lo Surdo November 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Queen Dunbar never carried a gun or wore a uniform, but counts herself among the most steadfast servants of Australia’s armed forces. She’s been serving since 1996, when husband Adam enlisted in the army, starting a career that took him to Solomon Islands, Iraq and Afghanistan. He was discharged in 2015 after his post-traumatic stress disorder diagnosis. Queen Dunbar’s husband served in Solomon Islands, Iraq and Afghanistan, in a 19-year military career. KATE GERAGHTY Dunbar raised their children, Joshua and Sarah, in Sydney while Adam fought for Australia. She was 41 when Adam died by suicide in 2017, owing to injuries suffered in service. Their children were 15 and 11 at the time of their father’s death, while Dunbar worked three jobs to get by. It took Dunbar, by her estimation, one year to realise she was a war widow. She credits her fellow war widows for helping her to “start breathing” again.



Adam Dunbar in uniform. “Our sacrifices are not seen, and if they are seen, they are seen once or twice a year,” she said. “I was trying to make it through the pain and the grief, and knowing that I actually have a place where I belonged, changed my outlook on life.” Dunbar is among more than 28,000 war widows in Australia, according to the Families of Veterans Guild, many of whom are preparing to honour their loved ones in Remembrance Day events this week. Australian war widows often raised children, worked jobs and supported the home while their spouses fought in conflicts overseas. Most veteran families experience financial stress, according to a survey conducted by the Guild last year, and three-fifths report their children have faced problems at school in the past year.



Dunbar, who is NSW president of the Guild, considers herself underemployed, as she balances work as an English teacher and flight attendant with supporting her children. Her daughter, 20, faces mental health challenges stemming from her father’s service, which Dunbar expects will be a lifelong struggle. She has pushed the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to tailor support packages for specific families and improve aid for former soldiers as they transition into civilian life. Assistance often comes too late, Dunbar warned, resulting in devastating consequences for families struggling to stay afloat. “My children’s wellbeing has impacted my employment because I’ve had to sit there and try to find support for my daughter,” she said. “My career has been impacted because of their needs that the department wasn’t able to meet.” The Department of Veterans’ Affairs said it recognised there were persisting challenges in its delivery of tailored support, and that “work continues” to better understand families’ needs and priorities. It expects to have implemented two-thirds of recommendations from the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide by the end of 2026.



Shirley McLaren, a 94-year-old who lives in a rural cottage south of Canberra, was booted from her family’s Defence accommodation two days after the funeral of her husband, Roy, a Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) member who died unexpectedly on Christmas Eve 1972. Shirley McLaren, a 94-year-old W-RAAF veteran, sits next to a photo of her late husband. Alex Ellinghausen McLaren, who was one of the first to enlist in the Women’s RAAF as an 18-year-old in 1951, was 39 when Roy died. She had three small children and a dog in tow. McLaren had met her husband at a dance at Canberra’s Albert Hall in 1953, and Roy proposed shortly before he was posted to Korea. She recalls receiving “no help at all” from any widows network as she packed her young family into a car and drove to Canberra, where they slept in sleeping bags in friends’ dining rooms while she picked up the pieces of her life. McLaren dipped her toes into widows networks while juggling her responsibilities as a mother and breadwinner in subsequent years, but largely felt unwelcome by groups of elderly women whose husbands fought in earlier conflicts than Roy.



A portrait of Shirley and Roy McLaren on their wedding day, hanging on the wall at the home of Shirley McLaren. Alex Ellinghausen Now McLaren ensures that no new widow attending Guild meetings sits alone. Only a widow, she said, can understand the loss that comes from the death of a spouse in the service. “You’ve gone from a couple, doing everything together, and suddenly, you’re on your own,” she said. “Tears are the price we pay [for love].” McLaren pays tribute to Roy every week, laying six stems of rosemary at a photograph of her husband at her Royalla cottage. She continues the tradition with her two great-grandchildren, Will and Tom, who have learned of their great-grandfather through stories told by their family.



“I encourage the widows who are coming for the first time to the group to never be ashamed of your tears,” McLaren said. “Talk about your husband, and you’ll find that we are all very supportive to help you through this grieving process because we’ve all been there.” McLaren’s son, Noel, and granddaughter Brooke served in the Royal Australian Navy, while Will expects to join the Australian Defence Force once he finishes school next year. His enlistment would mark the fourth generation of service in the family. McLaren’s great-grandsons have planted hand-made poppies in her yard, in a range of colours to honour the Diggers, nurses, wounded soldiers and animals that served in conflict. War widows placed wattle at the Cenotaph in Martin Place last month. KATE GERAGHTY The Families of Veterans Guild was established as the Australian War Widows NSW in 1946 by Jessie Vasey, seven months after losing husband George in World War II.



She wrote to 2000 widows as she grieved: “Real help for widows could only come from among themselves,” she wrote. “Now, as one of them, I am sure of it.” More than 300 people joined the first widows meeting in Sydney in June 1946, sparking the creation of what is now the Families of Veterans Guild. War Widows Day has been commemorated on October 19, Jessie Vasey’s birthday, since 2022, through national services. McLaren will lead the Ode of Remembrance at the Families of Veterans Guild’s inaugural Remembrance Day Lunch at the Australian War Memorial on Tuesday, to about 70 war widows, including Dunbar, and veteran families honouring those who served. “[I] lost a wonderful, loving husband, the father of my children, the love of my life, so my remembrance goes out to all veterans, of course, who have served and are no longer with us,” McLaren said. “It doesn’t matter how long it is … the grief is very deep and long-lasting.” If you are a current or former ADF member, or a relative, and need counselling or support, you can contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. Crisis support is also available from Lifeline on 13 11 14. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Astonishing’: Music therapy ignites compensatory brain wiring in dementia
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleHealth & wellnessDementia ‘Astonishing’: Music therapy ignites compensatory brain wiring in dementia Sarah Berry and Clair Weaver November 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Mandy Noffs was many things. She was the mother of two boys, the chief operating officer of the Ted Noffs Foundation, a member of the Order of Australia for the youth health programs she established, and a right character. “Mum had the most wonderful collection of sayings,” her son Rupert says. Rupert Noffs sings to his mother, Mandy, who has advanced Alzheimer’s. Steven Siewert There was: “You’ve gotta roll with the ponchos” and “We may be bohemians, but this time you’ve gone too far”, and Rupert’s favourite: “Do what you can and can’t what you can’t.” But, before 2017, when Mandy was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease at 65, she was never a singer.



In the years that followed, she became less responsive and her memory deteriorated. Rupert, 43, a cabaret singer, began singing to distract and soothe her when she became anxious and started asking the same questions repetitively. To his surprise, Mandy lit up. Loading “She started singing things note for note, word for word, with harmonies, phrasing and an incredible musical memory,” he recalls. “It was quite astonishing. I realised there was this whole musical ability in Mum that we’d never really seen before.”



Music therapy is well known for providing comfort to people living with dementia, relieving common symptoms such as agitation, depression and anxiety. Dr Benjamin Slade used rare magnetoencephalography to map brain activity in people with dementia who underwent music therapy Eddie Jim But a new Australian study suggests it may have a more powerful impact in the brain than previously realised, altering neural wiring to compensate for dysfunction and even recruiting alternative pathways to help complete tasks. Using a rare type of imaging called magnetoencephalography (MEG) to map activity in the brain, researchers from Swinburne University in Melbourne tested their hypothesis that targeted music therapy can improve cognitive function in people with dementia by targeting compensatory neural networks. Lead author Dr Benjamin Slade reported participants improved their performance in tests after undergoing an eight-week music therapy program, which included singing tasks and playing individual tune bells as part of a group to the melody of Doggie in the Window as part of a performance.



“Broadly we saw there was a definite change in brain connectivity in each person after therapy,” he said. “We found that change was directly linked to compensatory neural networks, where there was increased activity after therapy. “We also found areas not associated with these networks were activated. We hypothesised these areas of the brain were recruited to help complete the task.” While the study was small – with just six participants and a control group – and limited by health, recruitment and neuroimaging requirements, it’s important because it provides new clues into the mechanisms underpinning music therapy’s impact on cognitive symptoms of dementia. The findings suggest music therapy could be used to awaken, and tap into, a person with dementia’s cognitive reserve, which is the brain’s accumulated ability to improvise, adapt and find alternative ways of solving problems when areas become damaged.



Musician Yoshi Masuda has seen first hand how patients with dementia respond when he plays them songs on his gramophone. It can elicit “pure joy”. Yoshi Masuda plays his gramophone to connect with people’s hearts. James Brickwood For years, the 75-year-old has visited elderly residents in care homes on Sydney’s north shore. He invites them to be physically involved with selecting a shellac record, winding the motor, replacing the needle and then watching the disc rotate.



Related Article Dementia ‘There’s plenty you can do’: The lifestyle changes you can make to curb the risk of dementia “Surface noise, mechanical sounds and pauses for preparation form part of the listening experience,” says Masuda, a PhD student researching music and psychology. Through this sensory ritual, he says residents often begin clapping or tapping along, laughing or responding to the lyrics such as You Are My Sunshine, Love Me Tender, and Que Sera, Sera. Music, Masuda believes, taps into our emotional memory and is like speaking to our heart. Active participation in music therapy is key to securing cognitive benefits for people living with dementia, according to the Swinburne study.



The research involved giving participants tasks, such as singing the lyrics of a known song but skipping words beginning with specific letters. Delivered via a helmet fitted with sensors sitting in pools of helium within the scanner in a room with a vault-like heavy door, MEG imaging gives researchers an unparallelled view of electromagnetic activity in a brain. Music therapist Dr Romy Engelbrecht, co-author of the study published in the journal biomedicines, expected positive results but said participants had also enjoyed the therapy. Benjamin Slade and his team used this magnetoencephalography (MEG) scanner to record brain activity in participants with dementia before and after music therapy Eddie Jim “These people had real changes of behaviour,” she said. “If you go past the room and look in, it looks like everyone is happy and having fun but when you look underneath, what’s happening is quite scientific.”



Pharmaceutical options are usually first line treatments for dementia. Given music therapy can provide relief, improve quality of life and may have cognitive benefits at low cost and with no immediate side effects, Slade believes it should be considered as a frontline co-therapy. “Music therapy is implemented a lot in aged care but it’s variable in how it’s delivered,” he said. “It needs to be targeted and active to be beneficial.” Related Article Wellbeing Is ‘cognitive endurance’ the antidote in the age of distraction? Engelbrecht, who is also a clinical psychologist, said a challenge in therapy is prescribing music because it’s so personal. The study culminated in a handbell performance at an aged care facility. “They learnt a handbell song – they had to remember the information, wait for their turn and then perform,” she said. “You could see their happiness and sense of accomplishment. On performance day, they kept performing over and over again, they were so happy.”



The study team is calling for further research to build on their findings and establish a stronger evidence base. “There’s very little neuroimaging research relating to music or reminiscence therapy,” Engelbrecht added. In Mandy Noffs’ bedroom, overlooking gum trees on the NSW Central Coast, the television plays music: George Michael, Tina Arena, the Beatles. Her son sits by her bedside singing, and playing the part of the Vaudeville Dame. It’s a nod to his mother’s sense of humour and the Broadway shows they loved attending together when he lived in New York. Even while he feels so much of his mother slipping away, music remains his way of connecting.



“Alzheimer’s changes so much about a person, but it doesn’t necessarily take away the essence of who they are,” he says. “And perhaps that’s what music has shown us more than anything. Even when so much else has disappeared, there’s still something there.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: 'I've never seen anything like this': RNZ plans job cuts after shock $12m loss
World.content:
Loss blows out to $11.8m, compared to $470,000 forecast

Nearly 60 full-time jobs to go by March, about one in six

Internal financial reporting gave wrong picture of finances to senior management

RNZ broke the law by setting up a $5m overdraft without approval

The revelations come after CFO Hilary Parker quit unexpectedly in October

Audio player for " RNZ plans job cuts after shock $12m loss " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2466817%2Fi-ve-never-seen-anything-like-this-rnz-plans-job-cuts-after-shock-12m-loss

RNZ plans job cuts after shock $12m loss Checkpoint Download MP3 14m

RNZ has revealed a near $12 million budget blowout after a litany of financial blunders, setting the stage for sweeping job cuts.

In its just-published annual report, the public broadcaster set out plans to axe the equivalent of 58 full-time jobs - about one in six staff - by the end of March and cut running costs by at least 5 percent.

The company had already signalled in August an intent to cut 25 to 30 roles, which are included in the new 58 number.

The $11.8m loss is more than 25 times the $470,000 RNZ had expected to lose over the year to June.

Among the errors, RNZ wrongly counted $2m from land sales as income in its budget. Staff costs also came in $3.2m over budget, including $1.4m in redundancy payments.

Other running costs went $6.4m over budget, with much of the extra spending tied to the recent Auckland office move and work to get properties ready to sell.

In a statement, Media Minister Paul Goldsmith said the matter was "disappointing" and he expected "clear steps to be taken to improve the situation".

RNZ chair: "I've never seen anything like this"

RNZ chair Brent Impey - who assumed the role in July - told Checkpoint the board would commission an independent review into what went wrong.

"It's incomprehensible to have got to this position," he said.

"This is unique in my whole experience over many many years. I've never seen anything like this, and it's almost inexplicable."

The review would look into RNZ's culture, why its own reports failed to pick up the errors, whether it had the right disciplines and accountabilities in place, and whether senior leaders had been intentionally misled, Impey said.

Impey said the board and senior managers only learnt the full scale of the loss in mid-October, after interim finance chief Richard Dellabarca began to "unpick some of the issues".

Dellabarca - who's a board member - stepped into the role after Hilary Parker quit and left immediately on 2 October. Impey would not comment on the circumstances of Parker's departure, citing "private employment matters".

Impey said RNZ had found "zero evidence of criminality and fraud". He confirmed non-disclosure agreements had been signed in connection with the matter.

Impey said he shared responsibility for what had happened having joined the board in 2024, but noted he had relied on reports from management and the board's audit and risk committee.

"This is an organisational failure," he said.

Impey also defended keeping chief executive Paul Thompson in the job until his planned departure on 31 December, saying he had accepted responsibility for the result and still had work to do.

Asked why those in charge still had their jobs, Impey replied: "Well, someone's got to run the place, don't they? What do you suggest?"

E tū, the union for media workers, said no final decisions on jobs should be made until the next government is formed.

It said the country did not yet know who the next broadcasting minister would be and "there was no need to rush".

CEO: 'I am gutted'

Chief executive Paul Thompson says he takes responsibility for the "poor and unsustainable" result. Nick Monro

Thompson declined a request for an interview. In the annual report's foreword, Thompson said he took responsibility for the "poor and unsustainable" result.

"Personally, I am gutted this has occurred after more than a decade of leadership of RNZ," he wrote.

"This was not the outcome RNZ anticipated or one that management regards as acceptable. We recognise this is a poor result, and it deserves a clear explanation."

The board and management had relied on "internal financial reporting" that gave them the wrong picture, meaning the company failed to cut spending enough after a 7 percent drop in regular funding, RNZ said.

Thompson said his focus now was on restoring RNZ to a "sustainable financial position".

"We must make difficult choices to live within our means, and I recognise those changes will be hard for our people," he wrote.

Proposed changes affecting staff would be subject to the required employment processes, RNZ said.

Former chair Jim Mather, who had oversight during the financial year, said the result was "extremely disappointing" and acknowledged the board was ultimately responsible for "prudent financial stewardship".

RNZ brought in $70.6m over the year, putting the loss at about $1 for every $6 of income. Government funding made up $67.3m of that total, most of it through NZ On Air.

The company expected to lose another $7.8m this financial year and said it had enough money in reserve to get through until its finances stabilised in 2027/28.

The broadcaster ended June with $8.5 million in cash, down from $18.8 million a year earlier.

Impey told Checkpoint he had not asked the minister for extra money, pointing to a one-off $51m RNZ expected to receive soon from the sale of its Henderson land.

RNZ would discuss with Treasury how much of those proceeds it could keep, he said.

"You've got to live within your means. And at this stage, RNZ is not living within its means," Impey said.

EY, which audited the accounts for the Auditor-General, also flagged a breach of the Crown Entities Act over a $5m overdraft RNZ set up without the required approval from ministers.

RNZ was authorised for an overdraft only up to $3.5m. The report said RNZ drew down no more than $2.3m through the financial year and had since closed the overdraft.

The broadcaster was also checking whether it needed approval for a separate $3.7m deal to sell equipment for its new Auckland office and rent it back.

Thompson is due to leave RNZ at the end of the year, having announced his resignation on 22 May. NZME's chief audio officer Jason Winstanley will take over in 2027.

World.title: More heavy rain expected for upper North Island
World.content:
MetService has issued severe thunderstorm watches across parts of Northland and Auckland, and heavy rain watches from Northland to the central plateau.

MetService meteorologist John Law said there had been been intense bursts of rainfall and flashes of lightning on Monday, with more to come.

Most of the lightning struck off the coast of western Auckland and Waikato, with rain from Northland to Waitomo, he said.

Warm, humid weather provided perfect conditions for the intense rain showers to form, he said.

A heavy rain watch was in place for Northland from 9pm Monday until 10pm Tuesday, and in Auckland/Great Barrier Island from 11pm Monday until 1am Wednesday.

"Periods of heavy rain. Thunderstorms and localised downpours possible with rainfall intensities of 25 to 40 mm/h."

Coromandel's watch also began at 9pm, and would last through to 4am Wednesday, at least.

As for the central North Island, a heavy rain watch is in place from 3am Tuesday until early Wednesday morning for Waikato, Waitomo, Taupō, Taranaki, Taumarunui and Tongariro National Park, with a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

The forecasts follow heavy rain and storms in Auckland, and Canterbury on Friday and Saturday.

MetService earlier issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North before 7am on Monday, which had since lapsed.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vzWx0Z3M8BM

"There is a moderate risk of severe thunderstorms with localised downpours (25 to 40 mm per hour) over Auckland and Great Barrier Island from late morning until this evening," MetService said on Monday morning.

"Rainfall of this intensity can cause surface and/or flash flooding, especially about low-lying areas such as streams, rivers or narrow valleys, and may also lead to slips.

World.title: Swarbrick accuses Luxon of 'voter suppression' and lying about enrolment change
World.content:
Audio player for " Chloe Swarbrick discusses Green’s election result " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2468540%2Fswarbrick-accuses-luxon-of-voter-suppression-and-lying-about-enrolment-change

Chloe Swarbrick discusses Green’s election result Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says the government 'indulged voter suppression' and has accused Christopher Luxon of lying about it.

"Lie is the truth, I am calling a spade a spade here," Swarbrick told Morning Report's John Campbell.

The government changed the law so people could not enrol to vote on election day, or during the advanced voting period, this election, instead putting a deadline at 25 October.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408113222112

The National leader has previously defended the changes, saying it had been "about a year" since they were announced and that people have had "plenty of time" to enrol.

Before the election, Luxon said he expected enrolment rates to be higher this year than in previous elections, despite changes to enrolment rules. He said it was no different to the approach taken in Australia, the UK, Ireland and France.

The provisional enrolment rate this year was 93.6 percent of the eligible population, down from 94.7 percent in 2023, but higher than in 2014 or 2017.

The turnout for the 2026 election is on track to be the second lowest in New Zealand history.

Swarbrick told Campbell this year's election "left a sour taste in a few people's mouths".

"It was a deeply cynical election ... we saw the government knowingly indulge in voter suppression," she said.

"Anybody, hopefully even those on the far right of politics, can understand just how slippery a slope it is if we start to justify taking away people's ability to easily and accessibly engage in our democracy."

Chlöe Swarbrick says there is no reason that same-day voting enrolment needed to be removed. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Luxon has previously said the rule change was partly aimed at preventing increases to the time taken for the Electoral Commission to formally count the vote.

He said it was "an overwhelming experience" for the Commission to simultaneously encourage enrolment and voting, run voting booths, and count the vote.

Swarbrick said there was no reason same day voting enrolment needed to be removed.

"Originally he lied and said the reason for doing so was to make it faster to count the votes," she said.

Audio player for " Christopher Luxon discusses election result with John Campbell " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2468540%2Fswarbrick-accuses-luxon-of-voter-suppression-and-lying-about-enrolment-change

Christopher Luxon discusses election result with John Campbell Morning Report Download MP3 7m

"There is no justifiable reason that those barriers were put up because it is taking the same period of time, and arguably it could even take longer or be more complicated by virtue of what constitutes a legitimate vote now, because of those changes."

It took three weeks to count special votes after the 2023 election and is currently expected to take three weeks again this year.

Luxon on Monday said he had nothing to add to his previous comments in response to a request for reply.

Audio player for " Qiulae Wong discusses Opportunity’s election success " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2468540%2Fswarbrick-accuses-luxon-of-voter-suppression-and-lying-about-enrolment-change

Qiulae Wong discusses Opportunity’s election success Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said her party did not agree with the enrolment changes, but said Swarbrick's choice of words was strong.

"We are not supportive of those changes. I don't think it's had the results that were intended in terms of making things quicker or clearer and so we would be doing everything we can to make it easier for people to engage with democracy."

"I think that [lied is] a strong word to use, but I absolutely believe we shouldn't be restricting people's ability to engage in democracy and we've seen one of the lowest turnouts in history which is really disappointing to see," Wong said.

"They put out some reasons, the Electoral Commission said that those reasons were not necessarily valid or going to come to fruition.

"I think that New Zealanders need to ask that question seriously of those parties that were responsible for that decision."

Speaking on Monday, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the previous government had "disenfranchised voters".

Labour promised to reverse the changes to enrolment during the election campaign.

World.title: Election weekend police operation catches bus driver four times over alcohol limit
World.content:
A bus driver four times the legal alcohol limit has been suspended after hitting a parked vehicle then continuing his route over the election weekend.

The accident happened in Wellington's northern suburbs on Sunday afternoon.

"The driver was subsequently located in central Wellington and underwent an evidential breath test," police said on Monday.

He failed, and was immediately suspended. He will appear in Porirua District Court on Tuesday, charged with transport service driver breath alcohol level over 400mcg per litre, careless driving and failing to stop or ascertain injury.
