The catch was part of an "upscaled" effort by police over election weekend, with more than 3000 passive breath tests and 90 oral fluid screening tests conducted.

"We work hard to ensure that our roads are safe and to prevent deaths and serious injuries from happening on our roads," Senior Sergeant Pete Dear said.

More than 900 breath tests were carried out on Friday evening, with six failing - one more than three times above the limit and another on a licence with zero tolerance. Others tested positive for meth, MDMA and cannabis - one had all three in their system.

A person allegedly driving a car with a child in it crashed into a parked car on Sunday while under the influence of GBL, police added. Five more people were found driving over the alcohol limit on Sunday in Paraparaumu, out of 1414 tested.

"The consequences of crashes caused by alcohol or drugs are devastating, and that's something we see as police too often," Dear said.

World.title: Ruapehu mayor says data centre power fears are 'scaremongering' as mill site plan unveiled
World.content:
Audio player for " Hopes data centre, factory development could Ruapehu jobs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2471929%2Fruapehu-mayor-says-data-centre-power-fears-are-scaremongering-as-mill-site-plan-unveiled

Hopes data centre, factory development could Ruapehu jobs Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The Ruapehu District has been hit hard by the loss of a pulp mill two years ago, but proposed new developments are bringing hope to locals.

Due to soaring wholesale electricity prices, Winstone Pulp International permanently closed its two central North Island mills at Karioi and Tangiwai in 2024 after 45 years of operation. The closure displaced about 230 jobs - in a community of around 13,000.

"It was actually devastating," said local Airbnb host Andre Bezuidenhout.

He said neighbours had to sell their homes and families had to move out of the region to find work.

Last week, plans for a $300 million development that would establish a wood pellet factory and a data centre at the old mill site were unveiled - potentially creating up to 100 new jobs. Bezuidenhout said it would be "excellent for the region". As to the nature of the developments, he didn't seem to mind.

"It's just another business opening [up in] this area."

He said he didn't know much about data centres, but that he thought the region - where forestry was a strong industry - was a good place for a wood pellet factory.

Mountain Rocks Cafe & Bar owner Carl Christensen said anything that would keep people employed and families in the area where they had grown up would be a positive. He said the mill's closure had been tough on the community, with younger generations moving abroad for work.

"But [the community]'s pretty resilient and I think that's the reason why we've carried on."

He said dairy, forestry and agriculture had kept the region going, but more jobs would bring stability. He said local contractors were already gearing up to refit and redevelop the site.

"So it's going to be a huge win, you know, in the next short-term and then in the long-term."

Ruapehu District Mayor Weston Kirton said the council and other agencies had worked hard with the site's owners to progress new developments.

"We're looking for opportunities in a responsible way, of course."

Weston Kirton. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

But he said the community had struggled with unemployment and moving away from seasonal work.

"We are deprived of some of the things that our counterparts in the urban area have.

"So we need to have - when we get the opportunity - businesses because of our isolation. And the way we are at the moment, we rely predominantly on ski seasons... and rely heavily on farming."

Te Ara Hiko put forward the plans for the wood fuel pellet manufacturing facility, where 180,000 tonnes of pellets a year would be made for domestic and export customers. It would repurpose existing wood-processing infrastructure, use regional forestry resources and support employment in the wood-processing sector.

"It's similar to what we had before," said Kirton. He said it would provide "appropriate and sustainable" energy and "avoid potentially the use of coal".

Data Igloo was planning a data centre on the same site providing secure, energy-efficient storage and processing. Globally, the construction of large-scale data centres - especially AI ones - has caused controversy due to their high water and energy use. But Kirton didn't think it would be the case with this proposal.

"I think it's scaremongering to suggest that this business is going to take away power in any shape or form to local homes. It's just nonsense."

Data Igloo said there were sufficient resources available for its planned operations.

A spokesperson said: "Creating local employment and training opportunities is an important part of our plans."

It said further details of the development would be made public after engaging with the community.

Helen Leahy. Whakaata Māori/Screenshot

Ngāti Rangi's pou ārahi Helen Leahy said the iwi supported quality employment opportunities. According to the iwi's research, half the people who had lost their jobs two years ago had left Ruapehu or worked outside the region, with a third still looking for work or only employed seasonally.

"Our concern is that this shouldn't be at the detriment of the environment, which we all rely on."

In particular, the iwi was concerned for the impact on the Whangaehu River, which flowed from the crater lake of Mount Ruapehu.

World.title: Parents shocked by school hostel suspension as students forced to learn online
World.content:
Audio player for " Manawatu secondary school's boarding hostel licence suspended " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/education/2470976%2Fparents-shocked-by-school-hostel-suspension-as-students-forced-to-learn-online

Manawatu secondary school's boarding hostel licence suspended Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Students at a Manawatū secondary school where the boarding hostel's licence to operate has been suspended may have to sit their end-of-year exams elsewhere.

The students are likely to spend the next few weeks learning online after the suspension at Hato Pāora College, near Feilding, took effect at 5pm on Friday.

The Education Review Office (ERO), which is responsible for school hostels, said the decision was made because "it is contrary to the boarders' interests for the hostel to remain open".

Parents spoken to by RNZ said they had been given little information about the reasons behind the suspension, but communication from the school to families said it had four weeks to deal with the problems identified by the ERO.

Hato Pāora is a state-integrated Catholic Māori boys' school, with a roll of about 110 students.

Officials and school tight-lipped

The ERO said on Friday the decision to suspend the licence was "based on information obtained through carrying out ERO's statutory functions in relation to school hostels", including information obtained during an inspection last week.

RNZ asked further questions about the reasons behind the suspension and criticism from some parents of boys at the school about the haste of the suspension.

ERO director of regulation Ray McMillan said: "As this is an active regulatory matter, we're unable to provide further details about the individuals or evidence underpinning the decision.

"The Hato Pāora College Hostel Trust is aware of the areas identified by ERO and the conditions it must meet."

ERO remained in contact with the hostel trust, the Ministry of Education and NZQA to look at how to support students and minimise disruption, he said.

Staff at the school on Monday directed RNZ to the school board's chairperson for comment. They have been approached.

The communication to parents, sent on Sunday, said that following the sudden notice from ERO about the suspension there had been a "series of meetings and planning around operations to determine the next steps and support for our tauira [students] and whānau".

The school's trust board had four weeks to complete work it required. A project manager was in place, supported by an independent overseer appointed by the diocese.

"The trust board has already addressed some of the concerns that have been identified as requiring work."

The school said it was overwhelmed with support, and it was still in operation. For its junior programme staff were working over the weekend to prepare for learning on Monday and in the coming weeks.

Ministry of Education regional director of education Melanie Tait echoed ERO in saying officials were working with the school and NZQA to minimise disruption, particularly with exams approaching.

"Our priority is to make sure students can continue their learning and are supported during this period."

NZQA deputy chief executive for assessment Jann Marshall said exams would be offered at Hato Pāora, while alternative arrangements could be made for students to sit then elsewhere if required.

"The derived grade process is also available for eligible students to have their achievement recognised, where circumstances beyond their control mean they cannot attempt an exam, or their performance is significantly affected."

Parents of students at Hato Pāora College say they've not been told the reasons for the suspension. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Sudden closure a shock for parents

Parents spoken to by RNZ have expressed concern about the disruption on their sons' education.

One mother, who had boys at the school, said she would now have to buy a laptop so they could do remote learning - a cost they had not planned for.

She had heard the school was open for boys living locally, while other boarders were trying to sort accommodation in the area nearby.

The mother said she had paid hostel fees for the year, but had not heard more about these, and she suddenly had to make a long journey to collect them from the school last week.

Overall, she was supportive of the school, but questioned if the consequences of the hostel licence suspension were thought through at this stage of the year.

"Like many parents I am extremely shocked by the sudden suspension of the hostel licence and the immediate requirement for all boys to return home," she said.

"What concerns me most is that parents and whānau do not appear to have been consulted or given any meaningful opportunity to prepare for such a significant disruption."

A limited statutory manager was also appointed to the Hato Pāora College board in June, and that manager took over board powers such as employment and curriculum management. The mother said parents understood work was under way to improve matters there, although it wasn't said what areas were of concern.

"I also find it heartbreaking that the school only recently celebrated the opening of its new boarding facilities in July, an investment intended to support future generations of Hato Pāora boys."

World.title: RNZ job cuts: 'Our staff and the public deserve better' - union
World.content:
No final decisions on job cuts at RNZ should be made until the next government is formed, says the union for media workers.

The public broadcaster is facing sweeping job cuts after shock revelations the company lost nearly $12 million dollars, with plans to axe the equivalent of nearly 60 full-time jobs.

Chief executive Paul Thompson said internal reports gave an inaccurate picture of the finances, and management only found out about the size of the loss in October.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408124192112

RNZ also broke the law by setting up a $5 million overdraft without approval from ministers and the board is commissioning an independent review to find out what went wrong.

E tū - the union for media workers - said RNZ staff had already been through voluntary rounds of redundancies and as a result many teams were running short as people who left were not replaced.

It said 18 people had chosen to leave.

"Our workforce is already feeling significant pressure from job losses and the loss of so many more jobs will make it even harder for us to meet the needs of New Zealanders and provide the stories that need to be told," Auckland-based RNZ journalist and E tū delegate Melanie Earley said.

"Our staff and the public deserve better," she said.

E tū director Amy Hansen said the country did not yet know who the next broadcasting minister would be, and RNZ had enough money in reserve to get through this year.

"There's no need to rush," she said.

"This government has cut RNZ's funding two years running and signalled more cuts to come. Decisions about RNZ's future shouldn't be made while the country waits for a government.

"Get the review done, find out what went wrong, and hold off on cutting jobs until there's a government in place to make decisions about public media.

"New Zealanders trust RNZ more than any other news outlet. That trust was built by the people who work there. Don't make them pay for someone else's mistakes."

Cuts will 'impact the quality of the product' - commentator

Media commentator and Newsroom website co-founder Mark Jennings told Checkpoint that the revelations from RNZ on Monday were a "complete shocker".

He said he expected new RNZ chair Brent Impey to be "absolutely furious" over the news, and that it was hard to fathom how the executive and senior management were caught out by the financial shortfall.

Newsroom co-founder Mark Jennings. RNZ / Dru Faulkner

Jennings said both staff morale and the product itself would suffer under the proposed cuts, with a "decent chunk" of the cuts inevitably coming from the news operations.

"Chopping that many people out of a newsroom will really impact the quality of the product.

"I think that at a time when the whole media is retracting and lots of people have looked to RNZ as sort of a safety net around that, that's going to have a major impact when they start whittling people out of the newsroom."

With Thompson already leaving at the end of this year and former chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigning unexpectedly in early October, Jennings said he expected other executives would be following them out the door.

Jennings said he was not sure why an independent review was even needed.

"Brent could go and find out exactly what's gone on within a few minutes, really. I just think that's another kind of expenditure that RNZ doesn't really need."

He said he was puzzled by the silence from the rest of the finance team.

"It's not just one CFO who has access to the finances, in an organisation of the size of RNZ, there would be four or five - or even more - finance people, what were they doing, were they just sitting quiet?

World.title: Pacific news in brief for 9 November
World.content:
Vanuatu

Health officials in Vanuatu have declared an influenza A outbreak on the island of Tanna.

The Vanuatu Daily Post is reporting the Ministry of Health saying 163 flu-like illness cases have recently been reported, with cases rising over the last month.

Two people have become severely ill, but no one has been admitted to hospital.

The illness is mostly affecting young adults.

Authorities are urging people to wash their hands, cover coughs, and stay home when sick.

Cook Islands

Cook Islands Police have launched a new online tool for visitor driver licences.

The new system allows tourists and other visitors to apply for a visitor licence online before arriving in Rarotonga.

Most overseas licences are valid in the Cook Islands, but rental companies may still require visitors, particularly those hiring motorbikes, to obtain a local visitor licence.

Police recommend applying online at least 48 hours before arriving.

Pacific

Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) members will push for a management procedure for bigeye tuna at an upcoming commission meeting.

The FFA said if it is adopted, the bigeye tuna measure would be the Commission's first management procedure covering both purse seine and longline fisheries.

The FFA said its members are seeking a balanced approach that protects bigeye tuna while recognising the economic interests of Pacific Island countries, and ensuring that conservation responsibilities are shared more fairly between the two fishing methods.

The 23rd Regular Session of the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC23) will be held in Port Vila, Vanuatu, starting 30 November.

West Papua

Indonesia's Minister of Human Rights has voiced concern over revelations that President Prabowo has allegedly had his phone wiretapped by high-ranking police officers.

Natalius Pigai, who is a Papuan, said the alleged activity is a serious problem that threatens human rights, defense, and state security.

Three police generals have been detained on suspicion of illegally tapping the phones of Indonesia's president and other state officials.

Police allege the wire-tapping took place between 2025 and 2026.

Detik News reported Pigai describing it as an act of treason, saying a thorough investigation is required

He said wiretapping of the President's communications has the potential to endanger national security and disrupt the administration of government.

Vanuatu

Deputy Prime Minister Johnny Koanapo says the government is investing millions of vatu in airport upgrades to boost air connectivity.

Pacnews reported the Council of Ministers (Cabinet) agreed to sign a new agreement with Fiji for flights to Santo and Tanna.

Six-hundred million vatu (approx. NZ$8.76m) will also go toward repairs at Whitegrass Airport on Tanna, and Norsup Airport in Malekula will be fully tar-sealed early next year.

World.title: Greene's ex-teammate says he abandoned Giants with Cats move
World.content:
One of former GWS captain Toby Greene's ex-teammates has likened his move to Geelong as an abandonment.

The Giants' greatest player in their 15-year history, Greene left for the Cats in search of more family support for his young clan in his home state Victoria.

It was a sucker punch for the Giants, who had already parted ways with veteran forwards Jesse Hogan (Collingwood) and Jake Stringer (St Kilda).

The Giants' list overhaul did not end there, with star defender Lachie Whitfield (Carlton) and Kieren Briggs (Richmond) also leaving.

Toby Greene wasn't the only Giant to depart this summer, with veteran duo Jesse Hogan (left) and Jake Stringer (right) also joining rival clubs. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Young GWS defender Joe Fonti didn't waste time sugarcoating when asked about Greene's trade to the Cats.

"It's obviously hard when your captain abandons your side," Fonti said on Monday.

"I know Toby's a great, great fella, and he would have had his reasons.

"I suppose that sort of justifies it for him, so I can respect that.

"But it's not easy when your captain abandons you.

"It does sting a little bit, but yeah, onto bigger and better things, I guess."

The Giants at least received a vote of confidence in their mission from midfielder Tom Green.

Due to come off contract at the end of next season, vice-captain Green knocked back big money from Tasmania and instead added two more years to his deal at GWS.

The 25-year-old, who missed all of last season with an ACL tear, has long been touted as Greene's replacement as captain.

Last year's vice-captain, Connor Idun, has been touted as a potential captain of the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Brendon Thorne)

Star defender Connor Idun is also a ready-made leader for the Giants after serving as a vice-captain last season with Green.

"It's definitely really special that that's something that he's done and committed to the club," Fonti said of Green.

"He's one of our best leaders, really well-spoken and a great role model.

"To have him potentially step into that captaincy role would be really special.

"We've got a bunch of good leaders, so it could be anyone, but he's definitely one of them."

Joe Fonti (left) says GWS's young brass of players are ready to step up in the absence of the departed veterans. (AAP/Darren England)

The Giants have lost 1,088 games of experience during the trade period, but Fonti says the young group is ready to rise to the challenge.

Fonti, who has played 44 games across three seasons, will be looking to take up Whitfield's spot in defence.

"That's really cool and exciting that we've sort of got a young core coming through," Fonti said.

"A lot of what's coming from the media at the moment is that we're young and we potentially might struggle this year.

"But I don't see it in that way whatsoever. We play our best when our backs are against the wall."

AAP

World.title: Leniu handed two-match ban after making money gesture to referees
World.content:
Parramatta's marquee off-season recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign — including the Eels' trip to Las Vegas — after being sin-binned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sin-binned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Against Samoa, Australia's old power conquered the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home-ground calls".

"It was a real home-ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home-ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

AAP

World.title: Luckless Test hopeful Morris continues horror injury run at party
World.content:
Test hopeful Lance Morris is again under an injury cloud after hurting his hand at a social event following Western Australia's one-day clash against England on Saturday.

It is understood Morris was at a party when he cut his non-bowling left hand.

Morris is set to consult a hand specialist today to determine the extent of the injury, and a timeline on his return to playing.

It comes just over a year after Morris had spinal fracture surgery he hoped would save his cricket career, after struggling to string games together in recent years.

Morris (centre) picked up three wickets in Western Australia's tour match against England at the weekend. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

There were encouraging signs in Saturday's outing as Morris finished with figures of 3–29 off 10 overs, claiming the wickets of England superstar Joe Root, as well as Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson.

Morris was called into Australia's Test squad in late 2022 after an impressive start to the Sheffield Shield season, with some considering it a matter of time until he made his Test debut.

However, since then he has managed just three one-day internationals, six Shield matches and 22 Big Bash games, due to a wretched injury run.

Ahead of last season Morris underwent stabilisation surgery, a process that involves bolts and wire being put into his lower back.

Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests Australia's chairman of selectors confirms the omission of Marnus Labuschagne after an extended lean run of form at the Test level.

Just last week he told ABC Sport's Tom Wildie he hoped to bowl faster than ever after the procedure, hopeful it would not affect his pace and strength.

"That [a loss of pace] was a huge question for me leading into the surgery because I knew that was the asset that made me potentially selectable for red-ball cricket," he said last week.

"I had to look around at other guys that have had the surgery, the likes of Jofra [Archer], Jasprit Bumrah, the guys that have returned to Test cricket at the same speed if not better.

"I've got one eye on the speed gun at all times to see where things are at, but I'm pretty happy with where it's at."

With regular fast bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Captain Pat Cummins all well into their 30s, Australia is expected to soon be looking for other pace bowling options in the Test arena, with Morris long considered a likely contender for a spot in the XI.

World.title: Alcaraz downs Shelton in final to claim maiden Paris Masters title
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz says he feels proud of taking "one step forward mentally" after following up his Vienna title last week with a 7-6 (5), 7-5 victory over Ben Shelton in the Paris Masters final.

The Spanish showman, who missed more than four months of the season because of an injured right wrist, continued his late-season surge in style.

He has won all three finals he has reached since the US Open two months ago.

Alcaraz took his total to five titles for the year and 29 overall, including the Japan Open last month.

The second-seeded Alcaraz threw his arms out wide in celebration after clinching victory on his second match point with a two-handed backhand winner down the line at the indoor Plenitude Arena.

The seven-time grand slam champion cracked a broad smile and briefly appeared to cry after earning a ninth Masters title and first in Paris.

"It is something I have been chasing for a long time. Some of the toughest defeats I ever had in my career I have had here," Alcaraz said.

"Finally, I got my level here. I found the right path and the right way to do things."

With the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin starting next Sunday he feels in a good position to win that trophy for the first time, too.

"I would say this week I made one step forward mentally," Alcaraz said.

"Trying to be positive, trying to stay strong mentally. I'm happy I controlled my emotions every single match."

Earlier finish this time

Alcaraz won for the fourth time in five meetings with Shelton, who had beaten Alcaraz in a quarterfinal marathon at the US Open ending at 3:33am.

Shelton went on to reach the final, where he lost to Alexander Zverev.

There was to be no late marathon finish between Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton this time around. (Getty Images: Ibrahim Ezzat/NurPhoto)

Alcaraz saved six break points in the first set of Monday morning's final and overcame a break of serve in the second set by breaking the third-seeded Shelton straight back, no mean feat considering Shelton had 12 aces compared to six for Alcaraz.

"He is always in a position to attack after that serve," Alcaraz said.

"It is really difficult to dominate that ball. It is not only coming fast, it is coming with a lot of power."

Alcaraz, 23, did not drop a set in Vienna. But it was harder work in Paris and he almost went out on Friday, saving two match points against Taylor Fritz in their quarterfinal.

Shelton, 24, was seeking his eighth title overall and third Masters, having twice won the Montreal title.

The American recently added Juan Carlos Ferrero to his coaching staff, following on from Alcaraz's split with long-time coach Ferrero last year.

There is clearly no animosity between the players over that. Both congratulated each other's shots, and Alcaraz made a point of walking around the net to hug Shelton and pat him on the chest after winning.

Net battle

Both blessed with speed and agility, Alcaraz and Shelton drew each other to the net throughout, trading low, angled volleys.

Ben Shelton says he learns a lot from playing in big matches against the best. (Getty Images: Sport News/Quality Sport Images)

Pushing the other to the extremities of the court, there were some improbable retrieves, including one by Shelton in the ninth game when the American almost did the splits.

Shelton had an early advantage when he had Alcaraz 0-40 down in the fourth game. The Spaniard went on to save four break points before finally holding.

In the second set, Alcaraz was 4-2 down but broke Shelton back when he hit a forehand long from the back of the court.

After that he definitively changed the momentum.

Closing the gap

Shelton was "frustrated" at the missed opportunities, especially against someone like Alcaraz.

"The window is small. If you miss your chance, it's likely that another isn't going to come," he said. "It also speaks to his level, his ability to be clutch."

That is the next step for Shelton, who believes this defeat and the US Open final loss to Zverev will serve him well.

"When you get to play against the best consistently in big matches, I think that you learn so much," he said.

"Now going to Turin against the eight best players in the world, that's the positions that I want to be in."

AP

World.title: Coach Aloisi oversees stunning capitulation in Chinese Super League title race
World.content:
John Aloisi's hopes of beginning his new coaching adventure with a title have spectacularly failed after the former Western United mentor's side capitulated on the final matchday.

The Socceroos legend was looking to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Aloisi's Chengdu Rongcheng were in the box seat to do so, leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining and needing to pick up just one point to secure a maiden title.

The Sichuan club had also been top of the standings since the opening day, but things began to unravel when they lost three consecutive games while their main chasers, Dalian Yingbo, recorded three successive victories.

Going into the final matchday on Sunday, Dalian began three points behind Chengdu and defeated Tianjin Jinmen Tigers 3-1 in front of 60,000 fans.

Aloisi's club still only needed a point, but by 63 minutes in, they were 3-1 down to their final opponents Shandong Taishan.

Brazilian forward Wellington Silva did pull one back for Chengdu but they couldn't find the all-important equaliser, and Dalian claimed the title.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams level on points and Dalian had won both meetings between them.

Footage showed furious fans yelling at Aloisi and his players at the team hotel following the match, with police stepping in to push the angry supporters back.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Aloisi came to the Chinese Super League in January hoping to replicate the success he found with Western United in the A-League.

He led his team to the competition's championship in the 2021/2022 season, but his coaching career was thrown into limbo when the Melbourne-based club was placed into "hibernation" following legal issues and financial collapse last year.

He brushed away questions about whether he would resign because of the failure to secure the title in China.

"Now is not the time to talk about this," Aloisi said.

"As a team, together with the club and everyone, we need to review where we fell short in our past five matches. We need to face our problems, and then work on those aspects."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Labuschagne axed from Aussie squad for New Zealand Tests
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne has been axed from Australia's Test squad.

Chairman of selectors George Bailey confirmed on Monday that Labuschagne would be omitted from Australia's yet-to-be-named squad for the first Test against New Zealand.

Australia's next Test begins on December 9 in Perth, but Bailey and his panel have made an early call to put Labuschagne out of his misery.

Khawaja says one state was best at ball tampering in Sheffield Shield Usman Khawaja says players went as far as using super glue to tamper with the ball in the Sheffield Shield.

Bailey told reporters the out-of-form star wouldn't be considered for the entire four-Test series against New Zealand.

However, the door remains open for a recall on ensuing tours to India and England.

"This gives him a little bit of space and clears up a bit of conjecture … and we'll pick the rest of that squad at the end of round four of Sheffield Shield," Bailey said.

"It's [a Test recall] still possible, absolutely.

"He's always been an incredible performer at first-class level. So I expect that'll be the case.

"There's no message to go back and do anything in particular, the currency is pretty obvious."

Labuschagne averaged just 21.83 in six innings during the South Africa series. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Labuschagne burst onto the scene with 10 centuries from his first 33 Tests, when he averaged 59.43 and at one stage was the world's top-ranked batter.

But a tortured tour of South Africa, where he logged scores of zero, four, 14, 39, 37 and 37, extended a miserable run of 49 innings without a Test century.

Labuschagne was briefly dropped for last year's tour of the West Indies, but batted his way straight back into the side for the home Ashes with two centuries for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield.

The 32-year-old, once touted as a future national captain by some pundits, will return to leading Queensland in the Shield as he bids to restore confidence and form.

"We all know how good and how effective Marnus can be at his best, but that performance hasn't been there," Bailey said.

"He's pragmatic, he knows that the fundamental nature of being a batter in the top six is to score runs and that just hasn't happened."

AAP

World.title: Boland rejects Khawaja's Victorian 'dark arts' ball-tampering claim
World.content:
Scott Boland has rejected Usman Khawaja's claim that Victoria was the best at tampering with the ball at the Sheffield Shield level.

Following his explosive claims that all Australian players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the South Africa tour of 2018, Khawaja has made a further claim about tampering in the domestic first-class competition.

"The Victorians were probably the best at it. The MCG used to be dead and flat. Reverse swing and a bit of spin was the only way you could win a game there," Khawaja wrote in his new book Sabr, which is to be released to the public tomorrow.

"I personally never tampered with a ball — in terms of scratching it or anything — but I knew everything that was going on and I wasn't against it, which made me complicit.

Scott Boland says he is unaware of the "dark arts" Usman Khawaja mentions in his book. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"The Victorians of that 2000s and 2010s era were genius at it. Throwing it into the wicket and doing other dark arts to rough it up and make the shiny side relatively shinier. It was all fair game."

However, when asked about Khawaja's comments, Boland said he knew nothing of the aforementioned "dark arts".

"I don't know what the 'dark arts' are. You probably have to ask Usman for that," Boland said on Monday in Melbourne.

"But in general, the last [eight] years since Cape Town, reverse swing has really gone out of the game.

"I don't know. If you went back to club cricket, without cameras, you would probably see a lot of things happen.

"From my point of view, I haven't really seen anything untoward."

Khawaja named former Australian ODI fast bowler Mick Lewis as someone who was caught out changing the state of the ball.

Mick Lewis was caught raking the ball across concrete in 2016. (Supplied)

"It was no surprise when, years later, Victoria's bowling coach, Micky Lewis, was caught on cameras scraping the ball in the gutter when it got hit for a boundary. This kind of stuff was very normal," Khawaja wrote.

"There were plenty of times we hoped a spinner got hit for a six so someone could fetch the ball and scrub it while no one was watching and we could reverse swing it.

"To be honest, everyone knew what was going on in those teams I played in growing up. So whether you did it personally or not we were all complicit. The world game was the same. Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won the matches, come day four and five.''

The former Australian Test batter also claimed an unnamed player had used super glue to tamper with the ball.

Loading...

"One of the players had super glue on his towel,'' Khawaja wrote about his first year in Sheffield Shield.

"He'd get the ball on the rough side and scrub it against the dried-up super glue. It worked a treat and the ball would always reverse."

Khawaja's claim about the prevalence of ball tampering matches comments made by former Australian coach Darren Lehmann on ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand on Saturday.

Lehmann, who has joined the ABC's Cricket Podcast as co-host this season, said ball tampering had been a "big part of the game" until the Australians were caught in South Africa.

"You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Darren Lehmann (left) stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja has been on the media trail promoting his book for the past two weeks, but the chapter about ball tampering had been redacted until Saturday morning.

The batter has been criticised for sitting on the information for eight years, however Khawaja defended the timing in a social media post while saying he felt he had not thrown anyone "under the bus" with his revelations.

Cricket Australia has continuously denied all players and staff knew about the South African ball tampering.

World.title: Wallabies' woes mount after terrible Twickenham outing
World.content:
When Max Jorgensen sprinted away to score the Wallabies' first try on the stroke of half time, supporters may have felt a faint stirring of half-remembered joy.

Just two years earlier, Jorgensen raced down that same touchline, albeit running in the other direction, to snatch a thrilling victory at the death.

That the try came at the end of a magnificent move of swift ball movement and rapid running imbibed a justified sense of hope in where the national team was heading.

The possibilities that victory seemed to promise were endless.

Two years ago, it felt like the Wallabies were building.

Back in the present and Jorgensen's solo score, via an intercept pass against the run of play, meant that the Wallabies only trailed England by 9 points at half time, sugar-coating a desperate first half in which that was the Wallabies' only line break.

Max Jorgensen scored a superb try at the end of the first half to keep the Wallabies in touch. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

And it would only get worse.

The Wallabies came away from Twickenham having lost a third-straight match by a big score, conceding a record total against an England team that has now won 12 of their past 14 matches against them.

Incredibly, coming into the game, England were the team under pressure.

Steve Borthwick's team won just a single game in the Six Nations, and that was only against the basket case Welsh, to finish fifth on the ladder.

In fact, England, the richest and best-equipped nation in world rugby, had only won three of their eight matches in 2026.

A report in The Times on match week suggested a deepening rift between the head coach and his players that put further pressure on Borthwick, although senior players angrily denied those claims in the lead-up to the game.

The Wallabies had hoped they could use that distraction to put England to the sword, build on the sensational victory against South Africa in Perth and prove that the All Black thrashings were merely aberrations built on the kryptonite qualities Eden Park holds over the side.

Rob Valetini should start against Scotland next week. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

Instead, it is the Wallabies who leave south west London in even deeper trouble than before, with time running out to effect reasonable change.

England hammer Wallabies The Wallabies's spring tour started in the worst possible way, as England ran rampant at Twickenham to pile the pressure on coach Les Kiss.

Despite the closeness of the half time score, in truth the Wallabies barely featured in the opening 40 minutes.

England, rampaging forward with impunity, had dominated.

In fact, it was only the hosts' errors that had kept the Wallabies in touch at all — Jorgensen's intercept score included.

England's speed at the breakdown had the Wallabies on the back foot.

Their bravery with the ball in hand contrasted dramatically with the Wallabies' insipid defence, forced too narrow by the pace of England's outside backs.

Les Kiss appeared to grow increasingly angry in the coaching box throughout the first half and well into the second.

Les Kiss appeared to be seething at times in the contest. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Bob Bradford)

But heading into the break within touching distance, despite the way they had played, could have given the Wallabies a boost.

Sadly, the Wallabies came out for the second half just as insipidly as they started the first.

Within 15 minutes of the restart, England were 38-10 up and the game was well and truly over, with all but one of the Wallabies' tries essentially a gift from England errors.

"I am disappointed, there is frustration," Kiss told the BBC after the match.

"A credit to England, they kept us in our third in the first half and made their way into our tryline area. They were very good and clinical.

"This wasn't a true reflection of us but that is what happened."

If Wallabies fans want to look for positives, they will have to spend a long time searching.

Ben Donaldson and Filipo Daugunu did OK off the bench: In the short time they were together on the field they had a combined total of four clean breaks, while the rest of the team had just three in total.

But those are thin straws to clutch at.

Henry Slade crashed into Max Jorgensen to deny him a second try in the second half. (Getty Images: PA Images/Ben Whitley)

The worry for the Wallabies now is how to arrest this slide.

Maro Itoje said pre-game that this match would be crucial ahead of any potential meeting at the World Cup, which could occur at the quarterfinal stage if projections bare out.

"Each game is new but there's no doubt that against teams you're going to play down the line, you want them to know that you've got their number," Itoje said.

"We want to win this weekend for this weekend's sake, but we also want to win because we don't want to give the opposition an inch.

"We want to show ourselves and show England fans that we've turned a corner.

"For that reason, this game is huge."

Henry Pollock scored two tries as a flanker playing on the wing. (Getty Images: Patrick Khachfe)

One match does not change an entire mindset, but if Itoje believes England may use it to turn a corner, what direction are the Wallabies now heading in?

"We need to be better," Kiss said simply.

"Losses like that make you sit back and make you take an internal look into a few things.

"It is important to not look too far and too wide, we need to narrow down a few things that we can work on together.

"It is a disappointment tonight but we have seven days to turn that around."

The problem is that seven days may not be anywhere near enough.

Tech.title: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
Tech.content:
To my colleagues at NVIDIA,

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

— Jensen

Tech.title: Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Soul Glo has a new record called NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it’s not enough to truly tide me over, so I’ve been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 — Diaspora Problems.

“Gold Chain Punk (whogonbeatmyass?)” is an opening salvo for the ages. Bong rip, into a catchy-as-hell hardcore riff, with frontman Pierce Jordan ranting. Then comes the half-time stomp as Jordan gets fully unhinged, screaming “Who gon beat my ass? Who the fuck gon beat my ass?” From here on out, as the music shifts through a few different sections, the energy never comes down. Jordan shreds his vocal cords, begging, “Can I live?” Before finally spelling it out for anyone still confused:

Say more, say less, it’s all the same

When it’s time to die we can meet outside

To see who gon feel my pain

The record barely lets up from here on out. “Coming Correct” opens with a cough and a steady 808, giving you literally three seconds to catch your breath before Jordan jumps on the mic shouting, “I try to listen the way, I wanna be listened to.” The song starts stacking elements quickly, reaching full firestorm by 25 seconds in, and then doesn’t let up for the rest of its three-minute runtime.

The front chunk of the record is just perfect unrelenting hardcore song after perfect unrelenting hardcore song. Jordan’s crazed charisma is undeniable as he ricochets between leftist rhetoric, goofy bits about smoking weed, and vulnerable explorations of his struggles with depression. You’d be forgiven for struggling to keep up with his rapid-fire delivery, which owes almost as much to modern rappers as it does to classic hardcore acts like Minor Threat or Bad Brains.

Track six, “Driponomics,” fully embraces those more modern influences with trap snares, wall-rattling 808 kicks, and a guest verse from Mother Maryrose. The sampled guitar calls to mind the sax squeals favored by the Bomb Squad… just heavier.

The album eventually culminates in “Spiritual Level Of Gang Shit,” which features guest verses from McKinley Dixon and Lojii over gently echoed guitar melodies and dub-inspired groove. Then, around the 2:20 mark, things take a turn as the guitars turn punishing and the drums shift to a standard hardcore beat. But the song hasn’t reached its final form yet. That comes almost a minute later when the horn section kicks in.

Next to other modern hardcore standard bearers like Turnstile, Soul Glo might almost seem like traditionalists heavily influenced by the DC scene. But Diaspora Problems shows their ambition and willingness to take risks. Soul Glo plays with genre, is confrontational in its politics, and is generally just uncompromising.

Oh, and they put on a hell of a live show (I’ve seen them at least four times now). Don’t miss their incredible Tiny Desk Concert either, which I’m pretty sure is the first mosh pit to even open up in the NPR offices.

Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Qobuz, Deezer, YouTube Music, Apple Music, and Spotify.

Tech.title: Epic Games Launcher is coming to SteamOS
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In October, Epic Games said that it was “investigating” making Fortnite compatible with Valve’s Linux-based SteamOS. At the time, Epic Games Launcher was in preview, but SteamOS was not specifically listed as a supported distro. Now, Communications Director Jake Jones has confirmed SteamOS compatibility, along with a handful of other distros, to GamingOnLinux. In response to a question about the AppImage being replaced with Debian / Ubuntu .deb downloads, Jones said:

“The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We’re testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we’ll restore AppImage this month.”

That doesn’t necessarily mean Fortnite will come to SteamOS. Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2 support still remains an open question. When it announced its work to bring Fortnite to Linux, the company said that the Steam Deck “does not support the required features for our EAC v2 solution, but we are actively talking with Valve and hope to support it in the future.”

Tech.title: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Tech.content:
The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.

The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.

The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.

Tech.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.

Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

Tech.title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.

In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of

cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.

Later in the complaint, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”

Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”

This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir Media, and more.

Tech.title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.

If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.

Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.

If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub. There’s a flag listed for a “Conversational Apps” category. Tech.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
Tech.content:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.

The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

Tech.title: Apps to distract you from the endless cycle of doomscrolling
Tech.content:
You open your phone to check the time or a quick message. The next thing you know, an hour has passed and you’ve scrolled through endless celebrity drama, cat videos, awful news stories, influencer rants, and whatever else the algorithm decided to throw at you.

Even though you probably don’t want to keep wasting your time and energy on this mind-numbing content, you do it again the next day.

Doomscrolling, the habit of spending excessive amounts of time consuming content on social media, has become incredibly widespread. A survey from last year found that 64% of Americans say they doomscroll.

Researchers have warned that doomscrolling can negatively affect several aspects of your well-being, including your mental health and attention span. Spending long periods scrolling can lead to brain fatigue, difficulty focusing, and disrupted sleep. And if a lot of the content you’re consuming is negative or stressful, it can leave you feeling disheartened, anxious, and emotionally drained.

It’s hard to break the cycle of doomscrolling, but there are plenty of apps that provide content that’s engaging and productive.

Of course, you could always read a book or go for a walk (we have a guide on how to stop doomscrolling), but this list is for when you have a few spare minutes and want something to do on your phone that isn’t endless scrolling.

Finch

Image Credits:Finch /

Finch is a self-care pet app that’s designed to help you build healthy habits. You care for a cute virtual pet by completing small daily goals, such as drinking enough water, going on a walk, and practicing mindfulness. You can write about your day, complete a breathing exercise, or send good vibes to a friend by adding them to the app.

The more self-care you do, the more your pet thrives. The app offers a fun way to trade mindless scrolling for small moments of self-care.

Finch is available for free on iOS and Android.

Libby

Image Credits:Libby /

Libby is a free reading app that connects you to your local public library’s digital collection of ebooks, audiobooks, and magazines. All you need is a library card to borrow thousands of titles, which makes it easy to turn screen time into something productive.

You can explore a new book during a commute or while waiting at a doctor’s office, turning moments when your fingers might otherwise itch to scroll into opportunities to read.

Libby is available for free on iOS and Android.

Dudel Draw

Image Credits:Dudel Draw

If you want to take a break from doomscrolling and try something creative, Dudel Draw might be a good app for you. Each day, the app gives you a random shape that you turn into a drawing. These daily shapes vary from basic geometrical forms to more complex and abstract designs.

You can also get your friends in on the creativity with some fun competition by comparing your different creations, which could provide a nice break from sending each other endless TikToks or Instagram Reels.

Dudel Draw is available for free on iOS.

Radio Garden

Image Credits:Radio Garden

If you still want to feel connected to the world without scrolling through social media, you can check out Radio Garden. The app lets you listen to over 25,000 live radio stations from across the globe.

Once you open the app, you’ll see green dots marking cities and towns. Tap any dot to listen to radio stations broadcasting from that location. You can add favorites or search for radio stations, countries, and places.

Radio Garden is free, but it also offers an ad-free premium plan for $2.99 per month. The app is available on both iOS and Android.

Elevate

Image Credits:Elevate

Elevate is an app designed to help improve focus, memory, reading, math skills, and other cognitive abilities. It includes over 40 games to train different abilities you use in everyday life, from reading faster to comparing prices more efficiently.

You can track training streaks and compare your mind’s performance over time.

The app offers a free version with access to three games per day, or a yearly subscription of $39.99 for unlimited access. It’s available on both iOS and Android.

Vocabulary

Image Credits:Vocabulary

Vocabulary is an app that helps you learn new words every day. You can pick your difficulty level and choose categories that interest you, like emotions, the human body, business, and more. Each word comes with a definition, example sentences, and a guide on how to pronounce it.

The app also includes mini-games to help you review the words you’ve learned. You can set a goal of how many words you want to learn each week and create a regular learning routine.

Vocabulary offers a free trial, and then costs $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year. It’s available on iOS and Android.

Seterra

Image Credits:Seterra

If you’re a geography nerd looking to test your knowledge or just want to improve your geography skills, Seterra is perfect for you. The app features over 300 different games to test your map skills. You can test your knowledge of world flags; discover oceans, seas, and rivers; and explore mountain ranges and volcanoes across the globe.

Seterra lets you track your progress across categories and see leaderboards for top scorers for each game.

The app is free and available on both iOS and Android.

NYT Games

Image Credits:NYT

The NYT Games app offers several word, logic, and number games that change every day to exercise your mind. You can play the crossword, try the word-guessing game Wordle, group words with a common theme in Connections, see how many words you can make from seven letters in Spelling Bee, and more.

The app costs $5.99 per month for unlimited access and archives, but some games like Wordle, Strands, and the Mini Crossword are available to play for free.

NYT Games is available on both iOS and Android.

Drops

Image Credits:Drops

If you want to learn a new language but want to try something other than Duolingo, Drops is a good option. The app uses visually engaging mini‑games to help you build vocabulary and common phrases in more than 45 languages, with bite‑sized lessons designed to be completed in about five minutes a day.

Drops is designed for both beginners and experts who want to grow their foreign language vocabulary.

The free version of the app offers five-minute lessons per day. You can get unlimited access and premium features for $11.99 per month or $79.99 per year. The app is available on both iOS and Android.

This story was originally published in March 2026 and is updated regularly with new information.

Tech.title: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
Tech.content:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation.

Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry.

In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.

Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.

Tech.title: If Snap’s Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they’re also a lot more comfortable than they used to be
Tech.content:
When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood.

Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway.

What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had.

Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable.

However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless.

I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were:

Watching TV or movies while you’re on a train or some other form of public transportation . There are places where you just have to hang out for awhile and, not infrequently, one way to pass the time is streaming. Specs provides a much more immersive form of mobile entertainment than simply watching a video on your cell phone. The device’s integrations with HBO Max and YouTube make it an appealing entertainment option for users who are in-transit.

. There are places where you just have to hang out for awhile and, not infrequently, one way to pass the time is streaming. Specs provides a much more immersive form of mobile entertainment than simply watching a video on your cell phone. The device’s integrations with HBO Max and YouTube make it an appealing entertainment option for users who are in-transit. Reading . Because of the immersive nature of Snap’s headset, I feel like they could be a good option for reading while traveling. When you’re reading with Specs, it feels like you’re locked into whatever text you happen to be looking at. It weirdly helped me focus. An integration for newspapers or Kindle could make the glasses a good way to read while you’re mobile (I’m envisioning the ideal setting being on a plane, train, or the back of a car).

. Because of the immersive nature of Snap’s headset, I feel like they could be a good option for reading while traveling. When you’re reading with Specs, it feels like you’re locked into whatever text you happen to be looking at. It weirdly helped me focus. An integration for newspapers or Kindle could make the glasses a good way to read while you’re mobile (I’m envisioning the ideal setting being on a plane, train, or the back of a car). Taking easily shareable weird videos. Like many of Meta’s smart glasses, Specs allows users to take photographs and videos, which is an odd but fun component of the user experience. The ability to generate GoPro-like videos and easily text them to your friends is something that I could see the casual user doing on a somewhat regular basis.

By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases:

Specs as a daily workspace and productivity tool . Snap is selling Specs as a way to work. The company claims its headset can “transform almost any location into an immersive, flexible workspace.” However, I have a really hard time imagining Specs being something that the average worker is going to want to incorporate into their workflows. It’s less convenient to strap the glasses to your head than it is to simply sit at your computer typing. What can Specs provide that a cell phone and laptop can’t? The social stigma of wearing weird, large glasses and gesticulating to operate them would also seem to be a deterrent.
